article.content:
Frailty is not 'giving up' — it is reduced reserve. Arthritis can accelerate that by making every transfer cost more. This article is about when pain and low mood shrink meals, written for people and carers in Northern Ireland, especially around a home.

Quick answer: Frailty is not 'giving up' — it is reduced reserve. Arthritis can accelerate that by making every transfer cost more. This article is about when pain and low mood shrink meals, written for people and carers in Northern Ireland, especially around a home.

Families often notice arthritis with frailty first as a slower walk across a home, then as a person who starts declining invitations. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with when pain and low mood shrink meals, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in Northern Ireland.

What 'frailty' means when you already have arthritis with frailty

Arthritis is about joints, tendons and the way pain changes movement. Frailty is about the whole system — muscle, stamina, appetite, mood, medicines and how quickly you bounce back after a setback. Arthritis with frailty sits in the middle because sore several joints quietly train you to sit more, shorten your stride and skip the movements that keep muscle.

NICE is clear that exercise is core care for osteoarthritis, not an optional extra after tablets. That still holds if you are becoming frailer, but the dose must respect today's several joints and today's energy. Rest has a place in a flare; rest as a lifestyle is how deconditioning joins the diagnosis.

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Pain in several joints can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual arthritis with frailty.

Eating to support frail several joints

Frailty loves skipped meals. Arthritis with frailty makes that easy: sore several joints turn a sandwich into a logistics problem. Ready-to-eat protein — yoghurt, cheese, eggs, tinned fish, beans, leftover chicken — is a strategy, not a failure.

A Mediterranean-style pattern (vegetables, fruit, pulses, olive oil, fish when you can) is a familiar UK nutrition message. Keep the spirit, shrink the labour. Frozen vegetables and tinned tomatoes count.

NHS advice is that adults should consider a daily 10 microgram vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter. That is not a cure for arthritis with frailty. Mention it to a pharmacist if you already take other tablets or have kidney problems.

Self-management that respects arthritis with frailty

  • Plan the scariest transfer of the day — often the bathroom — with lighting, a rail conversation and unhurried time. Rushing with stiff several joints is how near-misses happen.
  • Use heat for stiffness if your skin is healthy, but protect thin skin. Never fall asleep on a hot water bottle.
  • Write three daily anchors: a meal, a movement, a conversation. Frailty grows in unstructured days.
  • Ask a pharmacist to look at the whole list if dizziness, constipation or night sedation have arrived with the pain tablets. Do not add a new painkiller just in case.
  • Carers: help the last 20 percent of a task, not the first 80, unless pain or safety says otherwise. Practice is treatment for frailty.
  • If you live in a home, tell one other person the plan for a fall: who to call, where the spare key sits, whether you wear a pendant you can actually press.

A Northern Ireland day with arthritis with frailty and less reserve

  • A hospital or infection week that ends with clothes feeling looser and stairs feeling taller.
  • New fear after a near-miss, even if you did not hit the floor. Fear of falling is itself a reason people sit more.
  • Carers doing the last steps of a task to be kind, which removes the last practice the muscles were getting.
  • Shorter outdoor range, then shorter indoor range, then a home that has quietly rearranged itself around the chair.
  • A flare of arthritis with frailty that lasts, then a slower baseline even when the flare eases.

Help in Northern Ireland if arthritis and frailty overlap

Red flags — do not wait this out

  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.
  • Chest pain, trouble breathing, or signs of a stroke — 999, not a wait for the arthritis with frailty nurse.
  • Sudden confusion, new incontinence, or a crash in mobility over hours to days — think infection or delirium, not only arthritis.
  • If you cannot get to the surgery because of arthritis with frailty, ask about a home visit or a proper phone review. Silence is not a care plan.
  • A knock to the head, especially if you take blood thinners — do not sleep it off as a plan.

What should a carer do in the home without taking over?

Stand nearby for the risky bit, set the environment up (chair height, shoes, light), and leave the bits the person can still do. Taking over every transfer trains both of you into a hoist-by-default life. If moving and handling is already unsafe, stop DIY lifting and ask for a proper care and OT review.

Do I need a geriatrician as well as a rheumatologist?

Not always. Many people are supported by GP, community physio and, where it exists, a frailty team. If medicines are stacking, falls are repeating, or memory and continence are changing alongside arthritis with frailty, ask whether a comprehensive older-person assessment would help.

Are painkillers the main treatment for frail arthritis with frailty?

No. For osteoarthritis, NICE puts exercise, weight management where relevant, and topical options at the centre. Tablets may help some people some of the time, but in frail adults they need a hard look at stomach, kidneys, heart, constipation and falls. Never share someone else's medicines.

article.title: Apprenticeships and Arthritis: A Realistic Look
article.excerpt: Apprenticeships with arthritis are achievable, often requiring a combined approach of appropriate medical treatment and practical workplace strategies. Open…
article.content:
Quick answer: Apprenticeships with arthritis are achievable, often requiring a combined approach of appropriate medical treatment and practical workplace strategies. Open communication between you, your employer, and healthcare providers is vital. Workplace adjustments like ergonomic equipment, flexible working, and regular breaks can significantly improve job retention. Regular medical reviews and self-management strategies are also important to your success.

Overview

Manual trades, office routes and adjustments that work.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis editorial team using UK NICE guidance, NHS information and peer-reviewed sources. We aim to update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Current clinical guidelines in the UK consistently highlight the importance of early intervention and personalised management for individuals living with arthritis, especially when considering career paths like apprenticeships. Systematic reviews of occupational health interventions demonstrate that workplace adjustments, flexible working patterns, and ergonomic support can significantly improve job retention and satisfaction for people with chronic conditions.

Observational studies and patient surveys repeatedly show that open communication between the individual, their employer, and healthcare providers leads to better outcomes. This multi-faceted approach, combining medical treatment with practical workplace strategies, is more effective than focusing solely on one aspect of care.

Evidence also supports the benefit of vocational rehabilitation programmes. These programmes often include assessments of functional capacity, advice on job modification, and strategies for managing fatigue and pain in the workplace. They aim to empower individuals to maintain employment and thrive in their chosen field.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Ignoring early symptoms: Pushing through pain can lead to greater joint damage and fatigue. *Fix: Document new symptoms and discuss them with your care team promptly. Not disclosing your condition to your employer: Hiding your arthritis can make it harder to get necessary support if things get difficult. *Fix: Have an open conversation with your employer or HR about your condition and potential needs, ideally during the hiring process or as soon as you feel comfortable. Skipping regular medical reviews: Your treatment plan may need adjustments as your condition changes. *Fix: Attend all scheduled appointments with your rheumatologist or GP. Neglecting self-management strategies: Relying solely on medication without lifestyle changes can be less effective. *Fix: Incorporate gentle exercise, healthy eating, and stress management into your daily routine. Not exploring workplace adjustments: Many simple changes can make a big difference, but you might not know what's available. *Fix: Research common workplace adjustments for arthritis and discuss options with your employer.

When to Speak to a Clinician

While self-management is key, there are times when you need prompt medical advice. Catching potential issues early can prevent further complications and help keep your apprenticeship on track.

You should speak to your GP, physiotherapist, or rheumatologist if you experience:

  • New or sudden severe joint pain that doesn't improve with rest or over-the-counter pain relief.
  • Persistent swelling, redness, or warmth in a joint.
  • Rapid loss of movement or function in a joint.
  • Unexplained fever, significant fatigue, or general unwellness alongside joint symptoms.
  • Side effects from medication that are concerning or unmanageable.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I still do a physically demanding apprenticeship with arthritis?

It depends on your specific type of arthritis, its severity, and how well it's managed. Many people with arthritis successfully pursue apprenticeships that involve physical tasks, especially with appropriate adjustments and support. It's crucial to discuss the demands of the apprenticeship with your healthcare team and potential employer.

What workplace adjustments are common for apprentices with arthritis?

Common adjustments include ergonomic equipment (e.g., specialised seating, height-adjustable desks), regular breaks, flexible working hours (if feasible), assistance with heavy lifting, and changes to workstation layout. The key is to identify specific tasks that cause difficulty and find practical solutions.

How do I talk to my employer about my arthritis and potential needs?

Choose a time and place where you can speak privately and openly. Focus on how your arthritis affects your ability to do specific tasks and what reasonable adjustments might help. Emphasise your commitment to the apprenticeship and your willingness to work together to find solutions. Remember, you do not have to disclose every detail of your health.

Practical next steps for Apprenticeships and Arthritis: A Realistic Look

If you came here about Apprenticeships and Arthritis: A Realistic Look, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Benefits conversations

Personal Independence Payment (PIP) looks at how your condition affects daily living and mobility, not the diagnosis name alone. Keep a short diary of bad days, help you need with dressing or cooking, and walking limits. Welfare rights advisers at local councils or charities can check forms before you submit them.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

Peer support etiquette

Share what helps you without prescribing it for others. Conditions, medicines and life circumstances differ. If someone is in crisis, encourage them toward NHS 111, their GP, or emergency services rather than relying on a forum alone.

Quick questions about Apprenticeships Arthritis Realistic Look

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

article.title: Water-Based Exercise for Arthritis: A Complete UK Guide to Pool Exercise
article.excerpt: A practical UK guide to water-based exercise for arthritis: why water helps, hydrotherapy, aqua classes, swimming and water walking compared, a 30-minute pool routine you can do in the shallow end, an 8-week plan, tips for non-swimmers and changing rooms, safety and when to get help.
article.content:
Quick answer: Water-based exercise suits arthritis because the water supports your weight, warm water eases stiffness and moving against water gently builds strength. Options include water walking, aqua classes, swimming and physiotherapist-led hydrotherapy. Start with 15 to 20 minutes in the shallow end, two or three times a week, and build up gradually. You do not need to be able to swim.

Exercising in water is one of the most comfortable ways for many people with arthritis to get moving. The water takes some of your body weight off painful joints, warmth helps loosen stiff muscles, and pushing against the water gently builds strength. Water-based exercise is much more than swimming lengths: you can walk, march, stretch and do strengthening exercises in the shallow end, join an aqua class, or have physiotherapist-led hydrotherapy. This guide explains the options, gives you a 30-minute pool routine and an 8-week plan, and covers safety, practical tips and when to get help.

Why water helps arthritic joints

  • Buoyancy. Water supports part of your body weight. The deeper you stand, the less weight goes through your hips, knees and feet, so movements that hurt on land can feel easier.
  • Resistance. Water resists movement in every direction, so walking and arm movements gently work your muscles. Moving faster increases the resistance; moving slowly reduces it.
  • Warmth. Warm water can ease stiffness and muscle tension. Hydrotherapy pools are usually kept warmer than ordinary swimming pools.
  • Support and confidence. The water slows movement down and reduces the fear of falling while you practise balance.
  • Whole-body fitness. Water exercise can raise your heart rate and count towards the UK target of 150 minutes of moderate activity a week.

NICE guideline NG226 recommends therapeutic exercise, including muscle strengthening and general aerobic fitness, for everyone with osteoarthritis. Water-based exercise is one way to do both, particularly if land-based exercise is painful. Many people use it as a stepping stone to land exercise, or alongside it.

Your options compared

OptionWhat it involvesBest forHow to access
Water walking and pool exercises on your ownWalking, marching and simple exercises in the shallow endMost people, including non-swimmersPublic pools, often during quieter or adult-only sessions
Aqua aerobics or aqua fit classesInstructor-led group exercise to musicFitness, motivation and companyLeisure centres and gyms; look for gentle or low-impact classes
SwimmingSwimming lengths or widthsFitness, if you can swim comfortablyPublic pools and lane sessions
Arthritis or condition-specific water classesGentle sessions in warmer waterPeople with arthritis or other long-term conditionsSome leisure centres, charities and community groups
Hydrotherapy (aquatic physiotherapy)Exercises tailored and supervised by a physiotherapist, usually in a warm poolSevere pain, after surgery, or when land exercise is very difficultUsually by referral from an NHS physiotherapist or rheumatology team; availability varies

Our guide to hydrotherapy for arthritis explains NHS access and what to expect at sessions, and our guide to hydrotherapy pools covers how to find one.

Before you start

Most people with arthritis can start water exercise safely. Check with your GP or physiotherapist first if you have heart or lung problems, very high or low blood pressure, epilepsy that is not well controlled, have had recent surgery or have an open wound, or a skin infection. Do not go in the pool if you have an infection, diarrhoea or a high temperature.

  • Choose your session: quieter, adult-only or "lane and shallow" sessions are easier. Ask your pool about water temperature and the depth of the shallow end.
  • Waist to chest depth is a good level for most exercises. Deeper water takes more weight off joints; shallower water gives more stability.
  • Pool shoes give grip on the pool floor and on wet changing room floors.
  • Use the steps or a hoist rather than jumping or climbing in. Many pools have handrails, ramps or a hoist; ask staff.
  • Drink water before and after. You still sweat in a pool.

A 30-minute shallow-end routine

Stand in waist- to chest-deep water near the side so you can hold the rail if needed. Move slowly and smoothly. Start with 5 to 8 repetitions of each exercise and build to 10 to 15.

Warm-up (5 minutes)

  1. Water walking: walk forwards across the pool, swinging your arms, then walk backwards. Take normal-sized steps and land heel first when walking forwards.
  2. Side stepping: step sideways along the pool wall, then back the other way.
  3. Shoulder rolls and arm circles under the water.

Legs and hips (10 minutes)

  1. Marching: holding the rail, lift each knee towards hip height in turn. 10 to 15 each leg.
  2. Leg swings forward and back: side-on to the wall, swing one leg forward and back from the hip, keeping your body upright. 10 each leg.
  3. Leg swings out to the side: facing the wall, lift one leg out to the side and back. 10 each leg.
  4. Mini squats: holding the rail, bend your knees slightly and straighten. 10 times.
  5. Heel raises: rise up onto your toes and lower slowly. 10 to 15 times.
  6. Knee bends: holding the rail, bend one knee to bring your heel towards your bottom, then lower. 10 each leg.

Upper body and core (7 minutes)

  1. Arm sweeps: with arms just under the surface, sweep them forwards and back, palms facing the direction of movement. 10 to 15 times.
  2. Arm openings: bring your arms together in front of you, then open them wide to the sides, keeping them under the water. 10 to 15 times.
  3. Wall press-up: hands on the pool edge, bend your elbows to bring your chest towards the wall, then push back. 8 to 12 times.
  4. Standing twist: with feet steady and arms in front, gently turn your upper body side to side. 10 each way.

Balance and cool-down (8 minutes)

  1. Single-leg stand: holding the rail lightly, stand on one leg for up to 30 seconds, then swap. Let go for a few seconds if you feel steady.
  2. Heel-to-toe walking along the wall.
  3. Slow water walking for 2 to 3 minutes.
  4. Gentle stretches: calf stretch against the wall, thigh stretch holding your ankle (or a towel round it), and a chest stretch with hands on the rail behind you. Hold each for 15 to 20 seconds.

Making it easier or harder

To make it easierTo make it harder
Move more slowlyMove faster to increase resistance
Stand in deeper water to reduce weight on jointsStand in shallower water for more load
Keep arm movements small and close to the bodyUse cupped hands, gloves or a float to push against
Hold the rail with both handsHold on lightly, then not at all
Fewer repetitionsMore repetitions or a second round

An 8-week plan

WeeksSessionsLengthFocus
1–21–2 a week15–20 minutesGet used to the pool; warm-up, legs and cool-down
3–42 a week20–25 minutesAdd upper body exercises
5–62–3 a week25–30 minutesFull routine; try an aqua class or a few widths of swimming
7–82–3 a week30–40 minutesMove faster in parts; add balance challenges

Combine pool sessions with some land-based strength exercises and walking where you can, because these help bones and everyday function in ways water exercise alone may not.

Tips for your main joint

JointMost helpful in waterTake care with
KneeWater walking, marching, mini squats, knee bends, gentle kicking holding the railBreaststroke kick and pushing off hard from the wall
HipLeg swings forward, back and to the side, water walking, side steppingWide breaststroke kick; after hip replacement, positions your surgical team has advised against
BackWater walking, gentle twists, floating on your back with a floatHead-up breaststroke, which arches the neck and lower back
ShoulderArm sweeps and openings under the water, wall press-upsFront crawl and backstroke arm movements if overhead reaching is painful
Hands and wristsSlow opening and closing of the hands under water, wrist circlesGripping floats tightly for long periods
Feet and anklesHeel raises, ankle circles, water walking in pool shoesRough pool floors without shoes

Water exercise with inflammatory arthritis and during flares

Many people with rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis or ankylosing spondylitis find warm water especially comfortable, and NICE guideline NG100 says adults with rheumatoid arthritis should have access to specialist physiotherapy to improve fitness and learn exercises for flexibility and strength. During a mild flare, a short, gentle session of slow walking and stretching in warm water can help stiffness, but skip the pool if a joint is very hot and swollen, or if you feel unwell or feverish. If you take medicines that affect your immune system, such as methotrexate or biologics, keep cuts covered with waterproof dressings and avoid swimming if you have an infection.

Cost and concessions

Prices vary widely between pools. Many councils and leisure trusts offer reduced-price or concession memberships for older adults, people on certain benefits and disabled people, and some offer free or reduced sessions through exercise referral schemes from a GP or practice nurse. Carers may be able to go in free with the person they support. Ask your local pool what is available, and whether there are off-peak, adult-only or condition-specific sessions.

Swimming with arthritis

If you enjoy swimming, it is a good way to build fitness. Choose strokes that feel comfortable: backstroke and front crawl are often easier on the neck and back than head-up breaststroke, while breaststroke kick can bother some knees and hips. Mixing strokes, using a float, and swimming widths before lengths all help. See our guides to swimming for arthritis and swimming exercises for hip osteoarthritis.

Tips for non-swimmers and nervous beginners

  • You do not need to swim. All the exercises above are done standing in the shallow end.
  • Tell the lifeguard or staff that you are new and have arthritis.
  • Go with a friend for the first few sessions.
  • Use a float or noodle for extra support.
  • Ask about adult swimming lessons if you would like to learn.

Changing rooms and getting there

For many people, the hardest part is not the exercise but getting changed. Ask whether your pool has an accessible changing room, seats in cubicles, grab rails or a pool hoist. Wear clothes that are easy to take on and off, such as elasticated waists and slip-on shoes, and wear your costume under your clothes. A long-handled sponge or towel and a towelling robe make drying easier. Allow time to rest before you leave, as you may feel more tired than you expect after warm water.

After a session

It is normal to feel pleasantly tired. Some people find their joints ache a little later the same day. If pain is worse the next day, or lasts more than 24 hours, do less next time: a shorter session, slower movements or fewer repetitions.

When to get medical help

Get out of the water and rest if you feel dizzy, faint, sick, unusually breathless, or have chest discomfort or sharp joint pain. Tell the lifeguard.

  • Call 999 for chest pain, severe breathlessness, or if someone collapses.
  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with a high temperature or feeling unwell.
  • See your GP or physiotherapist if water exercise consistently makes your pain worse, you would like hydrotherapy, or you are not improving after 8 to 12 weeks. In many areas you can refer yourself to NHS physiotherapy, and the physiotherapist can advise whether hydrotherapy is available and suitable for you.

Is water exercise good for arthritis?

Yes, for many people. The water supports your weight, warmth eases stiffness and moving against water builds strength gently. It is especially useful if exercise on land is painful, or if you have arthritis in several joints.

Is hydrotherapy the same as aqua aerobics?

No. Hydrotherapy (aquatic physiotherapy) is treatment planned and supervised by a physiotherapist, usually in a specially heated pool. Aqua aerobics is a general fitness class. Both can help, but hydrotherapy is tailored to your condition.

Can I get hydrotherapy on the NHS?

Sometimes. NHS hydrotherapy is usually accessed by referral from an NHS physiotherapist or rheumatology team, and availability varies across the UK. Ask your physiotherapist, or your GP, whether it is offered locally and suitable for you.

How often should I do water exercise?

Two or three sessions a week of 20 to 40 minutes is a good aim, once you have built up. Start with shorter, less frequent sessions and increase gradually.

Is warm water better for arthritis?

Many people with arthritis find warmer water more comfortable because it eases stiffness. Ordinary pools are cooler, so keep moving to stay warm, and ask your local pool about warmer sessions.

Will water exercise strengthen my bones?

Water exercise is excellent for joints and fitness, but because the water supports your weight it does less for bone strength than weight-bearing exercise. Combine it with walking or land-based strength exercises if you can.

article.direct_answer: Water-based exercise suits arthritis because the water supports your weight, warm water eases stiffness and moving against water gently builds strength. Options include water walking, aqua classes, swimming and physiotherapist-led hydrotherapy. Start with 15 to 20 minutes in the shallow end, two or three times a week, and build up gradually. You do not need to be able to swim.

faqs.q: Is water exercise good for arthritis?
faqs.a: Yes, for many people. The water supports your weight, warmth eases stiffness and moving against water builds strength gently. It is especially useful if exercise on land is painful, or if you have arthritis in several joints.

faqs.q: Is hydrotherapy the same as aqua aerobics?
faqs.a: No. Hydrotherapy (aquatic physiotherapy) is treatment planned and supervised by a physiotherapist, usually in a specially heated pool. Aqua aerobics is a general fitness class. Both can help, but hydrotherapy is tailored to your condition.

faqs.q: Can I get hydrotherapy on the NHS?
faqs.a: Sometimes. NHS hydrotherapy is usually accessed by referral from an NHS physiotherapist or rheumatology team, and availability varies across the UK. Ask your physiotherapist, or your GP, whether it is offered locally and suitable for you.

faqs.q: How often should I do water exercise?
faqs.a: Two or three sessions a week of 20 to 40 minutes is a good aim, once you have built up. Start with shorter, less frequent sessions and increase gradually.

faqs.q: Is warm water better for arthritis?
faqs.a: Many people with arthritis find warmer water more comfortable because it eases stiffness. Ordinary pools are cooler, so keep moving to stay warm, and ask your local pool about warmer sessions.

faqs.q: Will water exercise strengthen my bones?
faqs.a: Water exercise is excellent for joints and fitness, but because the water supports your weight it does less for bone strength than weight-bearing exercise. Combine it with walking or land-based strength exercises if you can.

article.title: Arthritis and Alcohol – What You Need to Know
article.excerpt: Can you drink alcohol with arthritis? UK guide to safe limits, medication interactions with methotrexate and NSAIDs, and how alcohol affects inflammation.
article.content:
Alcohol and arthritis is a topic that causes confusion. Can you still enjoy a drink? Does alcohol make arthritis worse? And what about interactions with your medication? Here's what the evidence says.

Quick answer: Moderate alcohol consumption may slightly reduce rheumatoid arthritis risk but can also worsen inflammation, gout, and sleep. Alcohol interacts with many arthritis medications: combining it with methotrexate increases liver damage risk, and with NSAIDs or steroids, it raises stomach ulcer risk. The NHS recommends no more than 14 units per week. Discuss alcohol intake with your rheumatologist.

How Alcohol Affects Arthritis

Potential Benefits (in Moderation)

Some studies suggest that moderate alcohol consumption may slightly reduce the risk of developing rheumatoid arthritis, possibly through anti-inflammatory effects. However, this doesn't mean alcohol is recommended as a health measure.

Potential Harms

  • Inflammation — heavy drinking increases systemic inflammation
  • Weight gain — alcohol is calorie-dense, contributing to weight that stresses joints
  • Gout — alcohol (especially beer and spirits) is a major trigger for gout attacks
  • Sleep disruption — alcohol impairs sleep quality, worsening fatigue and pain
  • Bone health — heavy drinking reduces bone density, increasing fracture risk

Medication Interactions

Methotrexate

This is the most important interaction. Methotrexate and alcohol are both processed by the liver. Combining them increases the risk of liver damage. Current UK guidance from the BSR (British Society for Rheumatology) advises:

  • Stay within NHS guidelines (14 units per week maximum)
  • Some rheumatologists recommend lower limits or complete abstinence
  • Discuss your individual risk with your rheumatologist
  • Regular liver blood tests are essential while on methotrexate

NSAIDs (Ibuprofen, Naproxen)

Alcohol combined with NSAIDs increases the risk of stomach bleeding and ulcers. If you take regular NSAIDs, limit alcohol carefully.

Steroids (Prednisolone)

Both steroids and alcohol can irritate the stomach lining. Combining them increases ulcer risk.

UK Alcohol Guidelines

The NHS recommends no more than 14 units per week, spread across 3 or more days. For context:

  • 1 pint of beer/cider = 2-3 units
  • 1 glass of wine (175ml) = 2 units
  • 1 single spirit (25ml) = 1 unit

Practical Tips

  • Have several alcohol-free days per week
  • Choose lower-strength drinks when you do drink
  • Alternate alcoholic drinks with water
  • If you have gout, avoid beer entirely and limit all alcohol
  • Be honest with your rheumatologist about your alcohol consumption

Everyone's situation is different. Discuss alcohol with your rheumatologist, especially if you take methotrexate or other liver-processed medications.

Practical next steps for Arthritis and Alcohol – What You Need to Know

If you came here about Arthritis and Alcohol – What You Need to Know, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Reliable UK sources

Cross-check major decisions with NHS.uk, your clinical team, and NICE guidance summaries where relevant. Be wary of social posts that promise reversal of arthritis or attack standard medicines without evidence.

Peer support etiquette

Share what helps you without prescribing it for others. Conditions, medicines and life circumstances differ. If someone is in crisis, encourage them toward NHS 111, their GP, or emergency services rather than relying on a forum alone.

Quick questions about Arthritis Alcohol What Need

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

Keep expectations kind while you work on arthritis and alcohol – what you need to know. Arthritis symptoms fluctuate; a quieter week does not mean you imagined earlier pain, and a flare does not mean every helpful habit has failed. Adjust one variable at a time so you can see what truly helps.

article.title: Cycling for Arthritis: Benefits, Tips and Getting Started (UK)
article.excerpt: Complete UK guide to cycling with arthritis. Learn about benefits for knee and hip joints, choosing the right bike, e-bikes and safe riding tips for joint pain.
article.content:
Cycling is one of the most highly recommended forms of exercise for people with arthritis, particularly those with knee and hip osteoarthritis. As a low-impact activity that builds strength, improves cardiovascular fitness and enhances joint mobility without the jarring impact of running or high-impact sports, cycling offers a uniquely arthritis-friendly way to stay active. In the UK, the growth of cycle paths, e-bike availability and indoor cycling options means there has never been a better time to start pedalling for your joint health. This guide covers everything from the science behind cycling's benefits to practical advice on choosing the right bike and riding safely with arthritis.

Quick answer: Cycling is highly recommended for arthritis, especially for knee and hip osteoarthritis, as it is a low-impact exercise. It strengthens supporting muscles like quadriceps, glutes, and hamstrings, while improving joint range of motion through gentle, repetitive pedalling. Stationary bikes, e-bikes, and standard bikes are suitable options. Begin with 10–15 minutes of gentle cycling, three times a week, gradually increasing duration and resistance.

Why Cycling Is Excellent for Arthritis

Low Impact, High Benefit

Unlike running or walking, cycling is a non-weight-bearing exercise. Your body weight is supported by the saddle, eliminating the ground-reaction forces that can aggravate arthritic joints. This makes cycling accessible even for people who find walking painful. Research in Journal of Rheumatology shows that cycling produces significantly less joint loading than walking while providing comparable cardiovascular and muscular benefits.

Strengthens Supporting Muscles

Cycling powerfully strengthens the quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes and calf muscles — the key muscle groups that support and stabilise the knee and hip joints. Stronger muscles absorb more of the forces that would otherwise be transmitted to joint cartilage. A 12-week cycling programme for knee OA patients showed a 30% improvement in quadricep strength and a significant reduction in pain scores.

Improves Joint Range of Motion

The smooth, circular pedalling motion takes the knee through a controlled range of approximately 70–110 degrees of flexion with each revolution. This repetitive, gentle movement helps maintain and even improve joint mobility while stimulating the production and distribution of synovial fluid — the natural lubricant within joints.

Cardiovascular and Mental Health

Cycling is an effective cardiovascular exercise that helps manage weight, reduce blood pressure and improve heart health — all important for arthritis patients who may be at increased cardiovascular risk. The outdoor variety also provides mood-boosting benefits through fresh air, scenery and a sense of independence and achievement.

Choosing the Right Bike

Stationary Bikes (Indoor)

An excellent starting point, especially for those new to cycling or with significant joint limitations:

  • Upright exercise bikes — Mimic outdoor cycling position. Good for general fitness. Available at most UK gyms and leisure centres
  • Recumbent bikes — A reclined seating position with back support. Reduces strain on hands, wrists and lower back. Often recommended by physiotherapists for hip and knee arthritis
  • Home options — Basic exercise bikes start from around £100–£200 at retailers like Argos, Decathlon and Amazon UK. Higher-end models with interactive screens (Peloton, Wattbike) offer guided classes

E-Bikes (Electric-Assist)

E-bikes have transformed cycling for people with arthritis in the UK. The electric motor provides assistance when you need it — on hills, into headwinds or when fatigue sets in — while still requiring you to pedal and exercise. Key benefits include the ability to ride further with less fatigue, to tackle hills without excessive joint strain, and to adjust the assistance level to match how your joints feel on any given day. Prices in the UK range from around £800 for basic models to £3,000+ for premium brands. Many UK cycle shops offer test rides. The government's Cycle to Work scheme can provide tax savings on e-bike purchases.

Standard Bikes

For those with milder arthritis, a standard bicycle works well. Hybrid bikes (a cross between road and mountain bikes) offer a comfortable, upright riding position with wider tyres for stability. Key setup considerations include ensuring the saddle height is correct (your knee should have a slight bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke — about 25–35 degrees), using flat pedals rather than clipless until you're confident, and considering wider, cushioned saddles for comfort.

Getting Started: A 6-Week Beginner Plan

Weeks 1–2: Familiarisation

Start with 10–15 minutes of gentle cycling at very low resistance on a stationary bike. Pedal at a comfortable cadence (around 60–70 RPM). Focus on smooth, pain-free pedalling. Ride 3 times per week with rest days between sessions.

Weeks 3–4: Building Duration

Increase to 20 minutes per session. Add a small amount of resistance if comfortable. If cycling outdoors, start with flat, quiet routes. Continue 3 times per week.

Weeks 5–6: Progressing

Aim for 25–30 minutes per session. Introduce gentle variations — slight resistance changes, brief intervals of slightly faster pedalling. Consider adding a fourth session if recovery is good. By the end of week 6, most people notice meaningful improvements in joint stiffness, leg strength and overall energy.

Safety Tips for Cycling with Arthritis

  • Warm up — Pedal gently for 5 minutes with no resistance before increasing intensity
  • Low resistance is key — High gear/resistance increases force through the knee. Use lower gears and higher cadence (spinning faster with less resistance)
  • Don't push through sharp pain — Mild discomfort is normal; sharp or increasing pain means stop
  • Adjust your bike properly — A professional bike fit (available at most UK cycle shops for £50–£150) is highly recommended. Poor setup can worsen joint problems
  • Wear a helmet — Always, regardless of distance or speed
  • Visibility — Use lights and high-visibility clothing, especially during UK winter months
  • Listen to your joints — Some days will be better than others. Adjust your ride accordingly

Cycling Resources in the UK

  • Cycling UK (cyclinguk.org) — Britain's national cycling charity, offering route planning, group rides and cycling holiday information
  • British Cycling — Offers Breeze rides (women-only), guided rides for beginners and accessible cycling programmes
  • Sustrans — Manages the National Cycle Network with over 12,000 miles of routes across the UK, many traffic-free
  • Local cycling groups — Many areas have gentle or social cycling clubs suitable for all abilities
  • Wheels for All — Provides inclusive cycling sessions using adapted cycles for people with disabilities, including hand-cycles and trikes

Cycling offers a perfect combination of joint-friendly exercise, independence and enjoyment. Whether you choose a stationary bike in your living room, an e-bike for weekend adventures or a gentle spin around your local park, every pedal stroke brings benefits for your joints and overall health. Try our virtual assistant for personalised cycling advice for your specific joints.

This article is for general information only. Consult your GP or physiotherapist before starting a new exercise programme.

  • Tai Chi for Arthritis – A UK Beginner's Guide — This ancient Chinese practice is now one of the most evidence-backed exercises for arthritis.
  • Best Plantar Fasciitis Shoes for Women (UK, 2026) — A UK-focused guide to choosing supportive shoes for plantar fasciitis: the eight features that matter, indicative £ prices, insoles, daily.
  • Yoga for Arthritis Beginners – Safe Gentle Poses UK — Start yoga safely with arthritis.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have chest pain, sudden weakness or numbness, severe breathlessness, a suspected broken bone after a fall, or back pain with new loss of bladder or bowel control or numbness around your bottom or genitals.

Contact NHS 111 or your GP urgently if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel unwell or have a fever, or if your symptoms are getting rapidly worse.

article.title: Popular Arthritis Diet Myths: 16 Claims Checked Against the Evidence (UK)
article.excerpt: From cutting out tomatoes to drinking apple cider vinegar, arthritis diet advice is full of myths. This guide checks 16 popular claims against NHS, NICE, Arthritis UK and research evidence, explains what is true, and shows what actually helps.
article.content:
Quick answer: Many popular arthritis diet claims are not supported by evidence. Nightshade vegetables, citrus fruit and gluten have not been shown to worsen arthritis for most people; apple cider vinegar and manuka honey have no evidence of benefit; and no diet or supplement cures arthritis or replaces medicines. What does help is a balanced, Mediterranean-style diet, oily fish, and a healthy weight.

Evidence checked on 10 October 2026 against Arthritis UK's diet information, NICE NG100, NICE NG226 and NHS guidance.

When you live with arthritis, you will hear a lot of diet advice: from friends, social media, magazines and well-meaning relatives. Some of it is helpful. A lot of it is not, and some can lead people to cut out nutritious foods, spend money they do not need to, or feel that their pain is their own fault. This guide checks 16 popular claims against the evidence.

Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) sums it up: there are no diets or supplements that will cure arthritis, but some people find their condition is affected by what they eat, how much they weigh and how active they are.

Myth 1: "Tomatoes, potatoes and other nightshades make arthritis worse"

Verdict: not supported. Arthritis UK says research suggests no link between inflammation and nightshade (solanaceous) vegetables, which include tomatoes, potatoes, peppers and aubergines. They contain important vitamins and minerals. Food allergies linked to this family are possible, so if you notice a clear reaction, speak to a healthcare professional. Our guide to foods that may trigger symptoms explains how to test a suspected food safely rather than cutting out whole groups.

Myth 2: "Citrus fruit and acidic foods cause joint inflammation"

Verdict: not supported. Arthritis UK says there is no clear link between citrus fruit and inflammation, and some evidence that citrus may reduce the risk of inflammatory arthritis. Citrus fruits provide vitamin C, which helps absorb iron from plant foods. Allergy is possible but uncommon. Note that grapefruit can interact with some medicines, including ciclosporin, colchicine and warfarin, which is a medicine issue, not an inflammation one.

Myth 3: "Everyone with arthritis should go gluten-free"

Verdict: not supported for most people. Arthritis UK says there is no research directly linking gluten to any type of arthritis. However, coeliac disease is an autoimmune condition, and people with one autoimmune condition, including some types of inflammatory arthritis and Sjögren's, may be at slightly higher risk of another. If you have tummy pain, diarrhoea, bloating or unexplained weight loss, ask your GP to test for coeliac disease before you cut out gluten, because the test needs you to be eating gluten to be accurate.

Myth 4: "Dairy causes inflammation and should be avoided"

Verdict: mixed evidence; not a reason to cut it out. Arthritis UK says research on dairy-free diets is mixed. Dairy foods are a major source of calcium, and many people with arthritis are at higher risk of osteoporosis. If you feel unwell after dairy, you could be lactose intolerant. If you do avoid dairy, choose calcium-fortified alternatives and consider advice from a dietitian.

Myth 5: "Apple cider vinegar cures arthritis"

Verdict: no evidence. Arthritis UK says there is no evidence that apple cider vinegar improves arthritis symptoms, and it can be expensive. Drinking it undiluted can also irritate your throat and teeth.

Myth 6: "Manuka honey reduces joint inflammation"

Verdict: no evidence. Arthritis UK says the same about manuka honey. It is also a source of free sugars; the NHS says adults should have no more than 30g of free sugars a day.

Myth 7: "The right diet can replace arthritis medicines"

Verdict: false, and potentially harmful. NICE guidance on rheumatoid arthritis says there is no strong evidence that diet changes will benefit arthritis, and that complementary therapies should not replace conventional treatment. Arthritis UK says changing your diet probably will not have as great an impact as medical treatment and you should not stop any treatments. In inflammatory arthritis, untreated disease can cause permanent joint damage.

Myth 8: "There is one special arthritis diet that works for everyone"

Verdict: false. Arthritis UK points out that there are many types of arthritis and differences between people, so what works for one person may not work for another. The best-supported approach is a balanced, Mediterranean-style diet, which NICE suggests for people with rheumatoid arthritis who want to change their diet. See our anti-inflammatory diet guide.

Myth 9: "Cod liver oil is good for osteoarthritis"

Verdict: not supported. Arthritis UK says there is no evidence that cod liver oil makes a difference to osteoarthritis, and large doses of fish liver oil could lead to too much vitamin A, which is particularly risky in pregnancy. Pure fish oil (not liver oil) has some evidence in rheumatoid arthritis. See our omega-3 evidence review.

Myth 10: "Glucosamine and collagen rebuild cartilage"

Verdict: not supported. NICE guidance on osteoarthritis (NG226) says glucosamine should not be offered, because there is no strong evidence of benefit. Arthritis UK says there is currently no good evidence that collagen supplements can rebuild cartilage that has already been damaged, and that the NHS does not recommend collagen for arthritis. Some people report symptom benefits, but research is mixed.

Myth 11: "Food allergies cause rheumatoid arthritis"

Verdict: not supported. Arthritis UK says some people believe allergies or intolerances worsen conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, but there is no research to support this. People with arthritis can also have allergies or intolerances, which a doctor or dietitian can help identify. Elimination diets have sometimes helped people with rheumatoid arthritis, but the foods involved differ between people, and Arthritis UK says there is no evidence they help osteoarthritis.

Myth 12: "A detox, juice cleanse or alkaline diet will flush out inflammation"

Verdict: not supported. Your liver and kidneys remove waste products; there is no good evidence that detox products or "alkalising" foods change joint inflammation. Juices are high in free sugars, and the NHS suggests limiting fruit juice and smoothies to a combined total of 150ml a day. Very restrictive regimes can also cause unplanned weight loss.

Myth 13: "Probiotics and gut supplements fix arthritis"

Verdict: not proven. Arthritis UK says there is no evidence that changing the gut microbiome affects autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, and probiotics have not been shown to help. The NHS advises people with a weakened immune system, including those on some arthritis medicines, to talk to a doctor before taking probiotics. See our gut health guide.

Myth 14: "Weight does not matter if you have inflammatory arthritis"

Verdict: false. NICE says weight loss improves pain, function and quality of life for people with osteoarthritis who are living with overweight or obesity. Arthritis UK says excess weight can also increase inflammation and is linked to a higher risk of rheumatoid arthritis and gout. Being underweight is also a concern, as it is linked with fracture risk.

Myth 15: "You must cut out red meat completely if you have rheumatoid arthritis"

Verdict: not supported. Arthritis UK says there is no evidence that avoiding foods such as red meat helps rheumatoid arthritis. Eating less red and processed meat is good general health advice, and the NHS suggests cutting down to about 70g a day if you eat more than 90g. But you do not need to avoid it completely, and red meat is a good source of iron, which matters because anaemia is more common with inflammatory arthritis.

Myth 16: "You can never drink alcohol if you take methotrexate"

Verdict: outdated for many people, but check with your team. Arthritis UK says it used to be thought that people taking methotrexate needed to avoid alcohol, but recent research suggests it is safe for people taking this drug to drink within the UK low-risk guideline of 14 units a week. Both alcohol and methotrexate can affect the liver, so drinking in moderation matters, and your rheumatology team may give you individual advice based on your blood tests. Alcohol also increases the risk of stomach problems and bleeding with NSAIDs, and drowsiness with some painkillers.

What is true

  • A balanced, Mediterranean-style diet supports overall health and is suggested by NICE for rheumatoid arthritis.
  • Oily fish has the strongest food evidence, mainly for rheumatoid arthritis.
  • Reaching a healthy weight helps osteoarthritis and general health.
  • Calcium and vitamin D matter for bone health.
  • For gout, diet genuinely matters: some foods high in purines and alcohol can trigger attacks.
  • Some foods and supplements interact with arthritis medicines, such as grapefruit with some drugs and vitamin K-rich foods with warfarin.

Why do diet myths spread?

Arthritis symptoms naturally go up and down. If you cut out a food just before a good spell, it is easy to conclude that the food was the problem. Testimonials are powerful, and the people selling diet books, tests and supplements benefit from bold claims. Arthritis UK suggests reading beyond the headline, checking whether claims are backed by research, using a fact-checking service such as Full Fact, and asking your healthcare team.

Myths are not always harmless. Cutting out several food groups at once can lead to low calcium, iron, fibre or protein, unplanned weight loss and a lot of stress around eating. Money spent on unproven tests, supplements and "special" products is money not spent on foods with real benefits. Most importantly, anyone who delays or stops proven treatment because of a diet claim risks their arthritis getting worse.

If you still think a food affects you

Your experience matters. If you suspect a food, keep a food and symptom diary for a few weeks, then, with advice from a doctor or dietitian, cut out one food completely for a few weeks and reintroduce it to see whether symptoms return. Arthritis UK recommends speaking to a doctor or dietitian first so the change is made safely and you do not miss out on nutrients.

When to see a dietitian

Ask your GP or rheumatology team about a referral to a registered dietitian if you are considering cutting out a food group, think you have a food intolerance, follow a restrictive diet, or are confused by conflicting advice. "Dietitian" is a protected title in the UK; dietitians must be registered with the HCPC.

When to get medical help

Do not stop prescribed arthritis medicines because of diet advice. Check with a pharmacist before taking supplements, especially if you take warfarin or other anticoagulants, methotrexate or NSAIDs. See your GP if you have gut symptoms, unexplained weight loss or think you have a food allergy. Get same-day advice from your GP or NHS 111 if a joint suddenly becomes hot, swollen and very painful, especially with a fever.

Frequently asked questions

Should I stop eating tomatoes if I have arthritis?

No, not unless you have a specific allergy. Arthritis UK says research suggests no link between nightshade vegetables and inflammation.

Is dairy bad for arthritis?

The evidence is mixed, and dairy is an important source of calcium. If you avoid it, choose calcium-fortified alternatives.

Does apple cider vinegar help joint pain?

Arthritis UK says there is no evidence that it improves arthritis symptoms.

Should I go gluten-free for arthritis?

Not unless you have coeliac disease or a diagnosed sensitivity. Get tested for coeliac disease before cutting out gluten if you have symptoms.

Can any diet cure arthritis?

No. No diet or supplement cures arthritis, but a healthy diet and weight support your overall health and can help some symptoms.

Why do some people say diet changes helped them?

Some people genuinely feel better, perhaps because of weight loss, a food intolerance or a healthier overall diet. Arthritis also naturally varies, which can make changes look more effective than they are.

article.title: Gardening With Arthritis: Joint-Friendly Tips, Tools and Safety
article.excerpt: A practical UK guide to gardening with arthritis: warming up, pacing jobs, protecting hands, knees and backs, helpful tools, raised beds, and safety for people on methotrexate or immune-suppressing medicines.
article.content:
Quick answer: You can usually keep gardening with arthritis by pacing jobs into short sessions, changing position often, and using lightweight, padded or long-handled tools, raised beds and seating. If you take methotrexate, protect your skin from the sun. Wear gloves, keep tetanus jabs up to date and follow RHS precautions when handling compost.

Checked on 10 October 2026 against NHS physical activity guidelines, NHS medicines information on methotrexate and sun sensitivity, the NHS page on tetanus, and Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) advice on minimising health risks in the garden. We do not recommend or sell any tools or brands.

Gardening can be one of the most rewarding things you do with arthritis. It gets you moving, outdoors and absorbed in something other than pain. It can also be hard on hands, knees, hips and backs if you try to do too much at once. This guide covers how to plan your garden and your gardening sessions so you can keep enjoying it, with practical ways to protect your joints and stay safe.

Why gardening can be good for you

NHS guidance says adults should aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, plus strengthening activities on at least 2 days. The NHS lists pushing a lawn mower as an example of moderate activity, and many gardening tasks, such as digging, carrying and raking, also use your muscles. Exercise is a core treatment for osteoarthritis in NICE guidance, so activity you enjoy and do regularly is valuable.

Beyond the physical side, many people find gardening helps with mood, a sense of purpose and getting outside. Thrive, the gardening for health charity, uses gardening to support people living with disabilities or ill health and offers gardening guides and advice.

Before you start: warm up and plan

  • Warm up. A few minutes of gentle movement, such as marching on the spot, shoulder rolls, and opening and closing your hands, can ease stiffness before you start.
  • Choose your time of day. If you are stiffest in the morning, garden later. Avoid the hottest part of the day in summer.
  • Plan the session. Decide on one or two jobs rather than "doing the garden".
  • Gather tools first so you are not going back and forth.
  • Set a timer to remind yourself to change position or take a break, perhaps every 20 to 30 minutes.

Pacing: the key to gardening without a flare

Many people do too much on a good day and pay for it for days afterwards. Pacing means breaking jobs into smaller chunks and spreading them out:

  • Alternate heavy and light jobs, for example digging, then potting at a table, then deadheading.
  • Alternate positions, so you are not kneeling, bending or reaching for too long.
  • Spread big jobs, such as clearing a border, over several days or weeks.
  • Stop before you are sore. If a job is causing pain that lasts more than a couple of hours afterwards, do less next time.
  • Accept help for the heaviest seasonal jobs if you can.

Our guide to pacing techniques explains how to find your baseline and build up gradually.

Protecting your joints while you garden

Hands and wrists

  • Use tools with thicker, padded or angled handles, so you do not have to grip tightly. Foam tubing can be added to existing handles.
  • Ratchet secateurs and loppers can cut in stages, needing less force each time.
  • Keep your wrist straight where you can, and use your whole arm rather than twisting your wrist.
  • Wear well-fitting gloves to protect skin and give a better grip.
  • Use both hands to carry things, and spread the load.

Knees and hips

  • Use a kneeling pad, or a kneeler with handles to help you get up and down.
  • Sit on a low stool or garden seat for ground-level work instead of kneeling.
  • Work at a raised bed or potting bench to avoid bending and kneeling altogether.

Back and shoulders

  • Use long-handled tools to avoid stooping.
  • Bend your knees, not your back, when lifting, and keep loads close to your body.
  • Buy compost and soil in smaller bags, or ask for delivery close to where you need it.
  • Use a wheelbarrow, sack trolley or garden cart rather than carrying.
  • Avoid working with your arms above shoulder height for long. Use a step or long-reach tools carefully.

Our guide to joint protection explains the principles behind these tips.

Tools and equipment that can help

You do not need to replace everything. Start with the tasks you find hardest:

  • Lightweight tools, such as aluminium or plastic rather than heavy steel
  • Long-reach tools, such as grabbers, weeders and pruners on extension poles
  • Lightweight or expanding hoses, a hose reel on wheels, or watering cans with two handles that you only half fill
  • Battery-powered tools, which can be lighter than petrol and easier to start than pull-cord tools
  • A wheeled garden seat or kneeler to move along borders
  • Tool belts or aprons to keep small tools close

An occupational therapist can advise on tools and techniques if your hands are particularly affected. Ask your GP or specialist team about a referral.

Designing a lower-effort garden

Small changes to the layout can make a big difference over time:

  • Raised beds at a comfortable height for sitting or standing. Our guide to raised beds covers heights and widths.
  • Containers and pots on stands or wheeled bases, with lightweight compost.
  • Level, firm paths wide enough for a wheelbarrow or walking aid, with no trip hazards.
  • Handrails on steps and slopes.
  • Seating dotted around the garden, so you can rest wherever you are working.
  • Low-maintenance planting, such as shrubs and perennials rather than annual bedding, and mulching to reduce weeding.
  • A water butt or tap close to your beds to reduce carrying.
  • Vertical growing, such as climbing beans or wall planters, at a reachable height.

If you rent, ask your landlord before making permanent changes.

Gardening after a joint replacement

Gardening can be a goal to work towards after surgery, but give your new joint time to heal and follow your surgical team's advice. NHS recovery advice includes:

  • After a knee replacement: avoid twisting your knee, bending down and reaching up as much as possible in the early weeks, and do not kneel on your new knee until your doctor says you can.
  • After a hip replacement: in the early weeks, the NHS advises not bending your hip more than 90 degrees and not bending down to touch your feet or ankles.

Raised beds, a potting bench and long-handled tools are especially useful during recovery. Ask your physiotherapist when you can return to heavier jobs such as digging, and which positions to avoid. Our guide to preparing for joint replacement suggests getting the garden low-maintenance before your operation.

A sample 45-minute gardening session

This is just an example to adapt to your own needs and limits:

  1. 5 minutes: gentle warm-up, such as walking round the garden, shoulder rolls, and opening and closing your hands.
  2. 15 minutes: one heavier job, such as weeding a section of raised bed with a long-handled hoe.
  3. 5 minutes: sit down with a drink.
  4. 15 minutes: a lighter job at a different height, such as potting up seedlings at a bench.
  5. 5 minutes: tidy up using a cart, then a few gentle stretches for your back, hips and hands.

Notice how you feel that evening and the next day, and adjust next time. If you are fine, you can gradually add a little more.

Getting help with the garden

If the garden is becoming too much, it is not a failure to get help. Options include family or neighbours, local volunteer or befriending schemes, gardening services, or swapping jobs with a friend: you sow seeds and pot plants for them, they do your heavy digging. If you need support at home more generally, a needs assessment from your local council may help. For many people, keeping the parts of gardening they love while handing over the hardest jobs is the best of both worlds.

Staying safe in the garden

Sun and medicines

Some arthritis medicines can make your skin more sensitive to sunlight. The NHS says methotrexate can cause a sunburn-like reaction, and advises staying out of bright sun, using a high factor sunscreen of SPF 30 or above, and wearing clothes that protect you from the sun. Check the leaflet for your own medicines, or ask your pharmacist.

Cuts and tetanus

The NHS says there is a risk of tetanus if soil or manure gets into a wound, such as a scratch from a thorn. The RHS advises keeping tetanus vaccinations up to date. Check with your GP surgery if you are not sure you have been fully vaccinated. Clean any cuts straight away.

Infections and immune-suppressing medicines

If you take medicines that suppress your immune system, you may be more vulnerable to infections. The RHS notes that elderly gardeners and those with a suppressed immune system are most vulnerable to Legionella bacteria, which can be found in compost and potting media. RHS precautions include:

  • wearing gloves whenever handling soil and compost
  • not opening bags of compost with your face right over the opening
  • moistening dry potting media before use
  • considering a dust mask when turning compost or handling dusty materials
  • not storing potting media in greenhouses, where it heats up
  • emptying hoses after use and not leaving full hoses in the sun
  • washing your hands after gardening, before eating or touching your face

Get any cuts or scratches that become red, hot, swollen or painful checked promptly, especially if you take immune-suppressing medicines.

Heat, cold and falls

  • Drink water regularly and take breaks in the shade in hot weather.
  • Keep warm in cold weather, as many people find cold makes stiffness worse.
  • Keep paths clear and avoid wet, slippery surfaces. Take a phone with you if you garden alone.

During a flare

You do not have to give up entirely. Try lighter jobs, such as sowing seeds at a table, deadheading from a seat, planning next season, or simply sitting in the garden. Some people keep a few pots by the back door for days when going further is too much. Rest the affected joints, and return gradually as the flare settles.

If you do not have a garden

  • Grow herbs, salad or flowers in window boxes or pots on a balcony.
  • Look for community gardens or allotment groups, which may have raised beds or accessible plots.
  • Thrive and other gardening for health organisations run programmes in some areas.
  • Indoor plants can give some of the same pleasure with very little physical effort.

Allotments

An allotment can be a lot of work. If you have one, or are on a waiting list, ask your council or allotment society whether there are smaller plots, raised beds or plots closer to the entrance and water supply. Share a plot with a friend to halve the work.

Seasonal jobs and how to make them easier

  • Spring: sow seeds in trays at a table, and plant out in small batches over several days.
  • Summer: water in the cooler parts of the day; use mulch to keep moisture in and reduce watering.
  • Autumn: rake leaves little and often; use a leaf grabber to pick them up.
  • Winter: plan next year, clean and sharpen tools sitting down, and keep active indoors.

When to get medical help

See your GP or physiotherapist if pain after gardening lasts more than a few days, or if a joint keeps swelling after activity. Get urgent advice the same day from your GP or NHS 111 if a joint becomes hot, swollen and very painful, especially with a fever, or if a cut becomes red, hot, swollen or painful, or you are unsure about your tetanus protection. Call 999 for severe bleeding, chest pain or a fall with a suspected broken bone.

Frequently asked questions

Is gardening good exercise for arthritis?

It can be. Gardening keeps you moving and builds strength. The NHS lists pushing a lawn mower as moderate activity. Pace yourself so you do not trigger a flare.

What gardening tools are best for arthritic hands?

Lightweight tools with thick, padded or angled handles, ratchet secateurs and long-reach tools. An occupational therapist can give personalised advice.

How can I garden without kneeling?

Use raised beds, containers on stands, a garden stool or long-handled tools.

Is gardening safe if I take methotrexate?

Generally, yes, with sensible precautions. The NHS says methotrexate can make skin sensitive to sunlight, so use SPF 30 or above and cover up. Wear gloves, clean cuts and wash your hands.

Do I need a tetanus jab for gardening?

Check you are fully vaccinated. The RHS advises keeping tetanus jabs up to date. If you are unsure, ask your GP surgery.

How long should I garden for?

Start with short sessions, such as 20 to 30 minutes, with breaks and changes of position. Build up gradually.
