article.title: Arthritis Blood Tests Explained: CRP, ESR, Rheumatoid Factor, Anti-CCP and More
article.excerpt: A plain-English UK guide to the blood tests used in arthritis: inflammation markers, antibodies, HLA-B27, urate and monitoring tests, what results mean and why no single test diagnoses most arthritis.
article.content:
Quick answer: Blood tests support, but rarely prove, a diagnosis of inflammatory arthritis. CRP and ESR measure inflammation; rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies point towards rheumatoid arthritis; HLA-B27 helps assess axial spondyloarthritis; urate helps diagnose and treat gout. Osteoarthritis has no blood test. Medicines such as methotrexate need regular blood count, liver and kidney checks.

Checked on 10 October 2026 against the NHS guide to blood tests, NHS pages on diagnosing rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis and polymyalgia rheumatica, NHS methotrexate guidance, and NICE guidelines NG100, NG65 and NG219.

Blood tests are part of almost every arthritis journey: to help find out what is causing joint symptoms, to check how active a condition is, and to keep medicines safe. But results are easy to misread. A positive test does not always mean you have a condition, and a normal test does not always rule one out. This guide explains the common tests, what they can and cannot tell you, and what to do with your results.

The key point: no single blood test diagnoses most arthritis

The NHS says no blood test can definitively prove or rule out rheumatoid arthritis. The same is true for most types of inflammatory arthritis. Doctors combine your symptoms, the examination, blood tests and sometimes scans such as X-rays or MRI. Osteoarthritis has no blood test at all; NICE says it is diagnosed clinically.

NICE also says blood tests ordered in primary care should not delay referral to rheumatology for someone with suspected persistent synovitis (joint inflammation). If your joints are swollen, a normal blood test does not mean you should not be referred.

Tests for inflammation: CRP and ESR

C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) are general markers of inflammation. The NHS lists both as main blood tests used when rheumatoid arthritis is suspected.

  • They can be raised in inflammatory arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica and many other conditions, including infections.
  • They can be normal even when a joint is inflamed, particularly in psoriatic arthritis and axial spondyloarthritis.
  • For polymyalgia rheumatica, the NHS says that if both ESR and CRP are normal, PMR is unlikely. Sometimes ESR is normal and CRP is raised, which is why both are usually done.
  • Rheumatology teams use CRP to monitor how active a condition is. For adults with active rheumatoid arthritis, NICE recommends measuring CRP and a disease activity score monthly in specialist care until the treatment target is reached.

A raised result does not tell you where the inflammation is or what is causing it.

Antibody tests for rheumatoid arthritis

Rheumatoid factor (RF)

NICE recommends offering a rheumatoid factor test to adults with suspected rheumatoid arthritis who have synovitis on examination. The NHS explains that more than half of people with rheumatoid arthritis have high levels of rheumatoid factor when the disease starts, but about 1 in 20 people without rheumatoid arthritis also test positive. So a positive RF is a clue, not a diagnosis, and a negative RF does not rule it out.

Anti-CCP antibodies

NICE says to consider measuring anti-CCP antibodies if rheumatoid factor is negative, and to measure them at diagnosis if not done already. The NHS says people who test positive for anti-CCP are very likely to develop rheumatoid arthritis, but not everyone with rheumatoid arthritis has this antibody. People who test positive for both RF and anti-CCP may be more likely to have more severe disease, which can affect how intensively it is treated.

NICE is clear that urgent referral is still needed for suspected persistent synovitis even if RF or anti-CCP is negative.

HLA-B27 for axial spondyloarthritis

HLA-B27 is a genetic marker, tested with a blood sample. The NHS explains it is found in most people with ankylosing spondylitis, but not everyone with the condition has it, and some people have it without ever developing the condition. NICE's guideline uses HLA-B27 as part of deciding whether someone with long-standing back pain that started before age 45 should be referred for a spondyloarthritis assessment.

Urate for gout

NICE recommends measuring serum urate in people with symptoms and signs of gout. A level of 360 micromol/litre or more supports the diagnosis. Urate can fall during a flare, so if it is below this during a flare and gout is still strongly suspected, NICE says to repeat it at least 2 weeks after the flare has settled.

If you take urate-lowering treatment such as allopurinol, NICE recommends a treat-to-target approach: monthly urate checks to guide dose increases until you reach a target below 360 micromol/litre, or below 300 for some people with tophi or frequent flares.

Other tests you may have

  • Full blood count (FBC): checks red cells, white cells and platelets. The NHS notes anaemia is common in rheumatoid arthritis, although anaemia does not prove you have it. FBC is also key for monitoring medicines.
  • Kidney function (urea and electrolytes, eGFR): important before and during many arthritis medicines, and for gout.
  • Liver function tests (LFTs): used to monitor medicines such as methotrexate and leflunomide.
  • Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) and related tests: used when a connective tissue disease such as lupus is suspected. The NHS says lupus may be diagnosed if tests show high levels of a certain type of antibody together with typical symptoms. ANA is also positive in many healthy people, so it is interpreted with your symptoms.
  • Thyroid tests, vitamin D, calcium and glucose: may be used to look for other causes of aches, fatigue or bone problems.
  • Infection screening (for example hepatitis B and C, HIV and tuberculosis tests) before starting some immune-suppressing or biologic medicines.

Monitoring blood tests when you take arthritis medicines

Many disease-modifying medicines can affect your blood count, liver or kidneys, so regular blood tests are part of taking them safely. For methotrexate, for example, the NHS says that when you first start, you will have a check-up and blood tests to check your blood, liver and kidneys every 1 to 2 weeks. Once the dose is right and your treatment is working, this usually becomes every 2 to 3 months. You will usually be given a booklet to record your dose and results.

Once you are stable, the hospital may ask your GP to continue prescribing and monitoring under a shared care arrangement. Check who is responsible for booking your tests and acting on the results.

Tips for monitoring tests:

  • Put your test dates in your calendar and set reminders.
  • Keep your monitoring booklet or app up to date and bring it to appointments.
  • If you are going on holiday, plan your test around it rather than missing it.
  • Never carry on taking a medicine that needs monitoring if you have missed several tests. Contact your team.
  • Ask what results would mean a change in your dose, and who will contact you if one is abnormal.

See our guide to leflunomide blood tests and side effects for an example of a monitoring schedule, and starting a new arthritis medicine for questions to ask.

Having a blood test

The NHS explains that blood tests are usually done at a GP surgery or hospital and take about 10 minutes. Blood is usually taken from the inside of your elbow with a needle. Some surgeries and hospitals let you book online.

  • Check whether you need to fast. Most arthritis tests do not need fasting, but cholesterol or glucose tests sometimes do.
  • Drink water beforehand unless told not to; it can make veins easier to find.
  • Wear a top with sleeves that roll up easily.
  • If you are worried about needles, tell the person taking blood. You can bring someone with you.
  • If your hands or arms are painful or swollen, say which arm is better.

You may get some bruising, which should go away in a few days.

Getting and understanding your results

The NHS says you may get results after a few days, and usually within a few weeks. Some GP surgeries only contact you if they need to discuss them. You may be able to see results in the NHS App or your NHS account.

When you look at results yourself:

  • Reference ranges vary between laboratories. Results are shown alongside the normal range for that lab.
  • A result just outside the range is often not significant. Normal ranges are based on most healthy people, so some healthy people fall slightly outside them.
  • Trends matter more than single results. Your team will look at how results change over time.
  • Results need context. A positive antibody without symptoms may mean nothing; a normal CRP with swollen joints still needs assessment.

If you do not hear anything after a few weeks, or you do not understand a result, contact your GP surgery or specialist team. If you are waiting for a rheumatology appointment, take copies or a list of recent results with you; our guide to what happens at a rheumatology appointment explains what to bring.

Why tests are sometimes repeated

Being asked for another sample does not necessarily mean something is wrong. Common reasons include:

  • a borderline result that needs checking, because many results vary from day to day
  • a sample that clotted, was too small or was delayed getting to the laboratory
  • timing, such as repeating a urate level after a gout flare has settled, as NICE recommends
  • checking a trend, for example whether inflammation markers are falling after starting treatment
  • a new medicine that needs a baseline before you start

Questions to ask about your results

  • Which results were outside the normal range, and do they matter for me?
  • Do they change my diagnosis or treatment?
  • Do I need any further tests, and when?
  • Who will contact me if a monitoring result means I need to change or stop a medicine?
  • Can I have a copy, or see them in the NHS App?

Blood tests while you wait for rheumatology

Your GP may arrange tests such as CRP, ESR, full blood count, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP or urate before or after referring you. These can help the rheumatology team prioritise your referral, but NICE is clear they should not delay it. If your symptoms change while you wait, for example more joints become swollen, tell your GP: repeat tests and an updated referral letter may help. Our waiting list guide explains what else you can do.

Quick reference

TestMainly used forRemember
CRP, ESRInflammation, disease activity, PMRNot specific; can be normal in inflamed joints
Rheumatoid factorSuspected rheumatoid arthritisAbout 1 in 20 people without RA test positive
Anti-CCPSuspected rheumatoid arthritis, prognosisNot everyone with RA has it
HLA-B27Suspected axial spondyloarthritisMany people with HLA-B27 never develop it
Serum urateGout diagnosis and treatment targetCan fall during a flare
FBC, liver, kidney testsGeneral health and medicine monitoringRegular checks with many DMARDs

When to get medical help

  • Same day: if you take methotrexate, leflunomide, sulfasalazine, a biologic or another immune-suppressing medicine and develop a fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, unexplained bruising or bleeding, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or a new cough or breathlessness. Contact your rheumatology advice line, GP or NHS 111.
  • Urgently: a hot, swollen, very painful joint, especially with fever. Get an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111.
  • Soon: if you have been told a result is abnormal and nobody has explained the next step.
  • 999: severe breathlessness, chest pain or collapse.

Frequently asked questions

Can a blood test show if I have arthritis?

Blood tests can support a diagnosis of some types of inflammatory arthritis and gout, but no single test proves or rules out most types. Osteoarthritis does not show on blood tests.

My rheumatoid factor is positive. Do I have rheumatoid arthritis?

Not necessarily. The NHS says about 1 in 20 people without rheumatoid arthritis test positive. Diagnosis depends on symptoms and examination as well as tests.

My blood tests are normal but my joints are swollen. What now?

Normal tests do not rule out inflammatory arthritis. NICE says referral for suspected persistent synovitis should not be delayed by test results, and should be urgent even if inflammatory markers or antibodies are normal.

Do I need to fast before an arthritis blood test?

Usually not, but some tests, such as cholesterol or glucose, may need fasting. You will be told if you need to.

How often will I need blood tests on methotrexate?

The NHS says every 1 to 2 weeks when you start, and usually every 2 to 3 months once you are stable. Your team will confirm your schedule.

Can I see my results online?

You may be able to see them in the NHS App or your NHS account. Ask your GP surgery or team to explain anything you do not understand.

article.title: Clinically recommended Arthritis Exercises
article.excerpt: Discover NHS-recommended exercises for arthritis. UK physiotherapist-approved low-impact workouts to ease joint pain.
article.content:
Quick answer: To manage arthritis, the NHS recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise weekly, strengthening exercises targeting affected joints at least twice a week, and daily flexibility work. Examples include walking, swimming, cycling, Tai Chi, and light strength training. If joints are more painful 24 hours after exercise, reduce intensity, but do not stop exercising.

NHS-Recommended Exercises for Arthritis

The NHS and NICE guidelines strongly recommend exercise as a core treatment for arthritis. Regular physical activity is as effective as painkillers for many patients — with none of the side effects.

What NICE Recommends

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends:

  • Aerobic exercise — at least 150 minutes of moderate activity per week
  • Strengthening exercises — targeting muscles around affected joints, at least twice weekly
  • Flexibility work — daily stretching and range-of-motion exercises

Top NHS-Approved Exercises

Walking

The simplest and most accessible exercise. Start with 10 minutes and build up gradually. - Goal: 30 minutes, 5 days per week - Benefits: Improves cardiovascular health, supports weight management

Swimming & Aqua Aerobics

Water supports your body weight, making movement easier and less painful. - Pool temperature: Aim for 28–32°C for comfort - Benefits: Full-body workout with minimal joint impact

Cycling

Stationary or outdoor cycling strengthens leg muscles without high joint impact. - Start: 10 minutes at low resistance - Benefits: Builds quad and hamstring strength

Tai Chi

NICE specifically recommends tai chi for older adults with OA. - Frequency: 1–2 classes per week - Benefits: Improves balance, flexibility, and pain management

Strength Training

Light resistance work builds the muscles that protect joints. - Start: Bodyweight exercises (wall push-ups, chair squats) - Progress: Add resistance bands, then light weights

The 24-Hour Rule

If your joints are more painful or swollen 24 hours after exercising, you overdid it. Reduce intensity next time but do not stop entirely — rest is rarely the answer.

Where to Get Help

  • NHS Physiotherapy — ask your GP for a referral
  • NHS Fitness Studio — many leisure centres offer arthritis-specific classes
  • Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) — free exercise guides and videos
  • Living With Arthritis — our free virtual physiotherapy programme

Reviewed by Claire Watson, MCSP, NHS Senior Physiotherapist

Practical next steps for Clinically recommended Arthritis Exercises

If you came here about Clinically recommended Arthritis Exercises, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Building a joint-friendly routine

Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Making information usable

Treat articles like this as a starting map, not a personal care plan. Highlight one idea to try for two weeks, then review. If symptoms are new, rapidly worsening, or affecting several joints with fever or unexplained weight loss, contact your GP promptly rather than waiting on self-help alone.

Quick questions about Clinically recommended Arthritis Exercises

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

Keep expectations kind while you work on clinically recommended arthritis exercises. Arthritis symptoms fluctuate; a quieter week does not mean you imagined earlier pain, and a flare does not mean every helpful habit has failed. Adjust one variable at a time so you can see what truly helps.

article.title: Arthritis Fatigue Explained: Why It Happens and What Helps
article.excerpt: Arthritis fatigue is an overwhelming sense of physical and mental exhaustion that does not improve with sleep. It happens because your body uses vast amounts of energy fighting joint inflammation and…
article.content:
Arthritis fatigue is an overwhelming sense of physical and mental exhaustion that does not improve with sleep. It happens because your body uses vast amounts of energy fighting joint inflammation and managing chronic pain. Coping with this symptom involves balancing your daily activities, adjusting medications with your rheumatology team, and treating underlying factors like anaemia or poor sleep.

Quick answer: Arthritis fatigue is an overwhelming sense of physical and mental exhaustion that does not improve with sleep. It happens because your body uses vast amounts of energy fighting joint inflammation and managing chronic pain. Coping with this symptom involves balancing your daily activities, adjusting medications with your rheumatology team, and treating underlying factors like anaemia or poor sleep.

Living with a joint condition is often viewed by others purely as an issue of pain and stiffness. However, if you live with this condition, you know that the exhaustion can be just as debilitating as the physical discomfort. This profound lack of energy affects every aspect of your life, from your ability to concentrate at work to your desire to socialise with friends and family. It is an invisible symptom, which often makes it difficult to explain to those around you.

When you experience arthritis fatigue, the primary keyword driving your search for answers is usually validation. You want to know that this heavy, dragging sensation is a real, medically recognised part of your condition. It is. Whether you have an autoimmune condition or osteoarthritis, your body is working incredibly hard behind the scenes just to keep you moving. Understanding the root causes of this exhaustion is the first step toward regaining some control over your daily routine and improving your quality of life.

Because this exhaustion is so deeply tied to the way your body processes inflammation and pain, treating it requires a slightly different approach to simply getting an early night. It requires a comprehensive look at your daily habits, your medical management, and your emotional wellbeing. By breaking down exactly what is happening inside your body, you can begin to make targeted changes that conserve your energy and reduce the frequency of severe exhaustion crashes.

What arthritis fatigue actually is

To truly manage your energy levels, you first need to understand what you are dealing with. This is not the standard tiredness that follows a long day at work or a busy weekend. It is a systemic, whole-body experience that affects your physical strength, your cognitive abilities, and your emotional resilience. People often describe it as feeling as though their limbs are filled with lead, or as if they are trying to wade through thick mud just to complete basic household tasks.

There is a strong cognitive element to this exhaustion, commonly referred to as brain fog. You might find yourself forgetting common words mid-sentence, struggling to hold onto a train of thought, or finding it incredibly difficult to concentrate on a television programme or a book. This mental sluggishness is a direct result of your central nervous system being overwhelmed by chronic pain signals and inflammatory chemicals.

RA fatigue is a particularly intense variation experienced by those with rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune types of the condition. In these cases, the fatigue fluctuates alongside disease activity. During a flare-up, the exhaustion can hit suddenly and with little warning, forcing you to cancel plans and spend the day resting. However, even when the joints are relatively calm, a baseline level of exhaustion often remains, lingering in the background of your daily life.

The physical sensation of this exhaustion can also manifest as a general flu-like achiness. It is common to feel slightly feverish, completely drained, and physically weak, even if you have not exerted yourself. This unpredictability is one of the most challenging aspects of the symptom. You might wake up feeling capable of tackling the day, only to feel utterly depleted by lunchtime after doing nothing more than taking a shower and preparing breakfast.

Understanding these different facets of the symptom helps you to communicate your needs more effectively to your GP and your loved ones. It validates the fact that your struggle to get out of bed is not a lack of motivation or willpower, but a physiological symptom of a chronic illness that demands careful management and immense patience.

Why inflammation causes exhaustion

To understand why arthritis causes fatigue, we have to look closely at the immune system and the body's inflammatory response. In a healthy body, inflammation is a temporary, protective mechanism used to heal injuries or fight off infections. When you catch a severe viral infection, your immune system releases inflammatory proteins called cytokines. These cytokines tell your brain to induce a state of rest, making you feel lethargic so that your body can redirect all its energy into fighting the virus.

In autoimmune forms of arthritis, your immune system mistakenly attacks the healthy lining of your joints, keeping this inflammatory response switched on continuously. Your body is perpetually acting as though it is fighting off a massive infection. The continuous production and circulation of cytokines flood your bloodstream, sending constant signals to your brain that you need to shut down and rest. This internal battle consumes an enormous amount of calories and cellular energy.

Beyond the chemical messengers, there is the sheer physical effort required to move an inflamed body. When a joint is swollen, stiff, and painful, the muscles surrounding it have to work significantly harder to perform basic movements. Walking up a flight of stairs with an inflamed knee requires more muscular effort, more oxygen, and more energy than walking up the same stairs with healthy joints. Over the course of a day, this constant overcompensation acts as a heavy drain on your stamina.

Chronic pain itself is also incredibly taxing on the central nervous system. Your brain is constantly processing pain signals, and your body naturally tenses up to brace against the discomfort. Holding this tension in your neck, back, and shoulders burns through your energy reserves at an alarming rate. Even when you are sitting completely still, if you are in pain, your body is engaged in a highly active, energy-intensive process.

Furthermore, chronic joint pain and inflammation can lead to muscle wastage if it prevents you from staying active. As your muscles weaken, tasks require a higher percentage of your maximum effort, leading to faster exhaustion. It becomes a cyclical problem: inflammation causes pain, pain reduces movement, reduced movement weakens muscles, and weaker muscles make movement more exhausting. Breaking this cycle is a primary goal for your rheumatology team and local health service physiotherapists.

Fatigue versus ordinary tiredness

It is vital to distinguish between normal tiredness and the profound exhaustion associated with chronic joint conditions. When you try to push through arthritis-related exhaustion as if it were just standard tiredness, you risk triggering severe flare-ups and prolonged periods of recovery. Ordinary tiredness is a predictable response to exertion or a lack of sleep; it is proportional to what you have been doing and is resolved by rest.

In contrast, the exhaustion of a chronic condition is often completely disproportionate to your level of activity. You might experience a sudden, overwhelming need to lie down after simply writing a shopping list or chatting on the telephone. Furthermore, no amount of sleep completely clears it away. You can sleep for ten hours and still wake up feeling as though you have not rested at all.

Feature Ordinary Tiredness Arthritis Fatigue
Cause Direct result of physical or mental exertion, or lack of sleep. Inflammation, chronic pain, and immune system activity.
Recovery Resolved by a good night's sleep or a quiet weekend. Lingers despite long periods of sleep and rest.
Predictability Highly predictable (e.g., tired after a long run). Highly unpredictable; can strike suddenly without cause.
Impact Usually feels like sleepiness or heavy eyelids. Feels like full-body heaviness, flu-like aches, and brain fog.

Because the two states are so different, treating them the same way leads to a destructive pattern known as the boom-and-bust cycle. On days when your energy levels are slightly higher, it is incredibly tempting to catch up on all the chores, work, and socialising you have missed. You clean the house, do the grocery shopping, and visit family, acting as though you have a normal energy reservoir.

This is the "boom". However, because your energy reserves are artificially depleted by inflammation and pain, this overexertion completely drains your system. The following day, you experience the "bust"—a severe crash that leaves you bedbound or unable to function for several days while your body attempts to recover. Learning to recognise the difference between normal tiredness and your condition's specific exhaustion is essential for stopping this cycle and smoothing out your energy levels.

How medication and anaemia contribute

While the disease process itself is the main culprit, other factors significantly contribute to your daily energy levels. The medications you take to manage your condition can be a double-edged sword. Disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) and biologics are crucial for slowing joint damage and lowering inflammation, which ultimately helps improve energy. However, some of these medications can cause drowsiness, nausea, or a general feeling of lethargy as side effects, particularly in the days immediately following a dose.

Pain relief medications also play a complex role. Strong analgesics, including those containing codeine or other opioids, are central nervous system depressants. They alter your perception of pain by dampening nerve signals, but they also slow down your brain function, leading to daytime drowsiness and a lack of alertness. Even over-the-counter medications can sometimes leave you feeling sluggish if taken frequently. It is always worth reviewing your medication timetable with your GP or pharmacist to see if adjusting when you take your tablets could improve your daytime energy.

Another major, yet often overlooked, contributor to extreme exhaustion is anaemia. There is a specific type of anaemia known as "anaemia of chronic disease." When you have chronic inflammation, your body produces proteins that restrict how much iron is absorbed from your diet and how iron is released from your body's storage cells. Even if you are eating plenty of iron-rich foods, the inflammation prevents your body from using that iron to make healthy red blood cells.

Without enough healthy red blood cells to carry oxygen around your body, your muscles and organs are essentially starved of the oxygen they need to function efficiently, resulting in profound weakness and breathlessness. Typical iron supplements from the pharmacy often do not resolve this specific type of anaemia because the issue is absorption, not intake. Your GP or rheumatology nurse can perform a simple blood test to check your full blood count and iron pathways.

Additionally, chronic inflammation can deplete your body of other essential nutrients, such as Vitamin D and Vitamin B12, both of which are critical for maintaining energy levels. If you are experiencing a sudden worsening of your exhaustion, it is highly recommended to arrange a review with your local health service to check for these deficiencies, as correcting them can provide a noticeable lift in your daily vitality.

Tracking and measuring your fatigue

Because energy levels fluctuate wildly, it can be difficult to explain precisely how you are feeling during a short appointment with your rheumatology team. Memory is unreliable, especially when you are dealing with brain fog. Keeping a structured diary for a few weeks is one of the most powerful tools you have for taking control of the situation. It helps you identify personal triggers and provides your medical team with clear evidence of how the symptom impacts your life.

Tracking does not need to be complicated. You can use a simple notebook or a note-taking application on your mobile phone. The goal is to record your energy levels at different points in the day, alongside what you were doing, what you ate, and when you took your medication. By scoring your exhaustion on a scale of 0 to 10—where 0 is completely energised and 10 is unable to get out of bed—you create a clear visual map of your week.

  • Time of day: Note whether your exhaustion is worse first thing in the morning with joint stiffness, or if you experience a severe dip in the mid-afternoon.
  • Activity levels: Record what tasks you completed before feeling drained. Was it physical exertion, or emotional stress from a difficult conversation?
  • Pain scores: Track your joint pain alongside your energy. Often, you will see that on days your pain is a 7 or 8, your energy crashes accordingly.
  • Sleep quality: Write down roughly how many hours you slept and whether the sleep felt restorative or broken.
  • Medication timing: Note exactly when you took your painkillers or DMARDs to see if there is a correlation with feeling sluggish a few hours later.

After two to three weeks of tracking, patterns will usually emerge. You might notice that taking a hot shower in the morning drains a quarter of your daily energy, or that scheduling appointments in the late afternoon always results in a crash the following day. This detailed record is invaluable when discussing adjustments to your treatment plan with your GP or occupational therapist, as it moves the conversation from vague complaints to specific, manageable data.

Evidence-based solutions overview

While there is no single quick fix for the profound exhaustion caused by joint inflammation, a combination of lifestyle adjustments and medical management can make a significant difference. The most effective approach requires patience and a willingness to adapt how you tackle your daily routine. The foundation of this adaptation is pacing.

Pacing is the art of breaking your daily tasks into manageable chunks and resting before you feel completely exhausted. Exploring pacing techniques for working around arthritis pain can help you structure your day so that you spread your energy evenly. It involves planning your week to avoid scheduling too many demanding activities on the same day, prioritising what truly needs to be done, and delegating or dropping less important tasks. By working within your limits, you prevent the severe crashes of the boom-and-bust cycle.

Movement might seem counterintuitive when you feel completely drained, but gentle, consistent exercise is one of the most proven ways to boost energy levels over time. Inactivity leads to muscle weakness, which makes every physical movement harder and more exhausting. Working with a physiotherapist to find a gentle exercise routine—such as swimming, tai chi, or seated stretching—can help strengthen the muscles around your joints, ultimately requiring less energy for daily tasks.

Sleep quality is another critical pillar. Pain often fragments sleep, meaning you spend less time in the deep, restorative phases of sleep that your body desperately needs to heal. Understanding how sleep quality affects arthritis pain is an important step in taking your night-time routine seriously. Establishing good sleep hygiene and reading about how to sleep better with arthritis provides practical bedroom adjustments, like using supportive pillows for painful joints and maintaining a cool, dark environment.

Dietary choices also play a role in managing your body's inflammatory load. Eating a balanced diet rich in vegetables, lean proteins, and whole grains provides steady energy release rather than the sharp spikes and crashes associated with sugary snacks. Keeping hydrated is equally important, as even mild dehydration can significantly worsen feelings of lethargy and brain fog.

Finally, do not underestimate the emotional weight of living with a chronic condition. The frustration of dealing with unpredictable energy levels can lead to low mood and anxiety, which are exhausting in their own right. Seeking psychological support through counselling or local support groups can provide strategies for coping with the mental toll. For a more comprehensive look at all these strategies combined, reading our detailed guide on managing arthritis fatigue offers further practical steps to help you reclaim your daily life.

Key Takeaways

  • Arthritis-related exhaustion is a systemic issue caused by the body fighting chronic inflammation, not just standard tiredness.
  • The continuous release of inflammatory chemicals instructs your brain to rest, draining your energy reserves dramatically.
  • Treating this exhaustion like normal tiredness leads to the boom-and-bust cycle; pacing your activities is essential to prevent severe crashes.
  • Underlying issues such as anaemia, medication side effects, and poor sleep quality significantly worsen your daily energy levels and should be checked by your GP.
  • Keeping a detailed daily diary of your pain, activities, and energy levels helps you and your rheumatology team spot patterns and adjust your care plan.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does resting completely cure the exhaustion?

No, resting completely will not cure it. While rest is vital for recovery during a flare-up, too much inactivity can lead to muscle weakness and stiff joints, which makes movement even more tiring later. The most effective approach is balancing short periods of rest with gentle, low-impact activity.

Can changing my diet improve my daily energy levels?

Yes, maintaining a balanced diet can help. Avoiding highly processed foods and refined sugars prevents energy crashes. Consuming a nutrient-dense diet supports overall health, and ensuring you get enough vitamins and minerals can help combat the sluggishness associated with chronic inflammation. Speak to your GP or a dietitian for tailored nutritional advice.

Why do I feel so exhausted even when my joints do not hurt much?

Your immune system may still be highly active even if your joint pain is relatively low. The internal inflammatory process consumes a massive amount of energy behind the scenes. Furthermore, poor sleep quality and the mental strain of living with a chronic condition can leave you drained regardless of immediate pain levels.

Is there a specific medication to treat this symptom?

There is no single tablet designed solely to cure arthritis-related exhaustion. Treatment focuses on controlling the underlying disease with disease-modifying drugs, managing pain effectively to improve sleep, and treating any secondary issues like anaemia or vitamin deficiencies. Your rheumatology team will look at the whole picture.

Should I push through the tiredness to get things done?

Pushing through the heavy exhaustion usually backfires, leading to a severe crash that could put you out of action for days. It is much safer and more effective to practice pacing. Stop and rest before you reach your absolute limit, and spread demanding tasks across the week.

How do I explain this exhaustion to my employer?

Be clear that it is a recognised medical symptom of your condition, involving both physical weakness and cognitive fog. You might find it helpful to involve an occupational health professional who can recommend reasonable adjustments, such as flexible working hours, regular short breaks, or modifying physically demanding tasks.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have chest pain, sudden weakness or numbness, severe breathlessness, a suspected broken bone after a fall, or back pain with new loss of bladder or bowel control or numbness around your bottom or genitals.

Contact NHS 111 or your GP urgently if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel unwell or have a fever, or if your symptoms are getting rapidly worse.

article.title: Managing Arthritis Fatigue – A UK Guide
article.excerpt: UK guide to arthritis fatigue: why it happens, pacing and sleep strategies, gentle movement, work adjustments, and when to ask your GP for further checks.
article.content:
Quick answer: Arthritis fatigue is extreme tiredness that is not fully fixed by a night's sleep. Inflammation, pain, poor sleep, low mood, medicines, anaemia and deconditioning can all contribute. Start with pacing (plan rest before you crash), protect sleep, keep gentle movement, and see your GP if fatigue is new, severe or comes with red-flag symptoms.

Many people with inflammatory arthritis say fatigue is as disabling as pain — yet friends and employers often miss it because it is invisible. This UK guide explains what it is, what helps, and when to get checked. For day-to-day scheduling detail, use our gold-pass pacing and energy management article alongside this overview.

What arthritis fatigue feels like

  • Whole-body exhaustion that rest does not fully clear
  • Brain fog, slow thinking or short fuse
  • Sudden energy crashes mid-task
  • Motivation collapsing even for things you care about
  • Pain and stiffness feeling louder when energy is low

It is not laziness. Treating it as a real symptom — the same way you would treat a swollen knee — is the first step.

Common drivers

  • Inflammation and disease activity — cytokines and active joints drain energy
  • Pain and poor sleep — broken nights multiply daytime fatigue (see NHS sleep guidance)
  • Boom-and-bust activity — overdoing “good” days then crashing
  • Deconditioning — less movement lowers fitness, which worsens tiredness
  • Mood and stress — living with unpredictable pain is emotionally expensive
  • Medicines, anaemia or thyroid problems — worth a GP conversation if fatigue is new or escalating

During a symptom spike, follow the flare-up guide and shorten your activity targets until inflammation settles.

What helps most people

  1. Pacing with the 5 P's — Prioritise, Plan, Pace, Position (sit when you can), Permission to rest without guilt. Break tasks into chunks; rest while you still have fuel left.
  2. Protect sleep — regular bedtime, cool dark room, pillows for painful joints, caffeine cut-off mid-afternoon.
  3. Gentle regular movement — short walks, pool work or mobility drills often improve energy over weeks even when the first sessions feel costly. Start via the exercise hub.
  4. Joint protection and gadgets — save energy on dressing, cooking and transfers with joint protection tips.
  5. Work adjustments — shorter bursts, flexible hours or equipment via Access to Work if fatigue affects your job.

If daily living is heavily limited, explore the Benefits & PIP hub for working-age support, or Attendance Allowance routes if you are over State Pension age.

When to see your GP

  • Fatigue is new, rapidly worsening, or not explained by a known flare pattern
  • Unexplained weight loss, fever, night sweats or breathlessness
  • You suspect anaemia, thyroid disease, sleep apnoea or depression
  • Medicines may be contributing — never stop prescription drugs without advice
  • You cannot stay safe at work or with personal care

Ask about blood tests, medication review, OT referral, and talking therapies if mood is part of the picture. Pair clinical care with pain relief and newly diagnosed foundations if you are still finding your feet.

Talking about invisible fatigue

Try concrete language: “I have about four good activity hours today; after that my pain and thinking both drop.” Share your pacing plan with family and, where safe, with your manager. Invisible symptoms need explicit scripts.

Frequently asked questions

Will more sleep fix it?

Better sleep helps, but arthritis fatigue often needs pacing, disease control and graded movement as well.

Should I exercise when exhausted?

On crushing crash days, prioritise rest and essential care. On ordinary low-energy days, short gentle movement usually beats total inactivity — stop if a joint becomes hot and sharply worse.

Is coffee a good fix?

A morning cup is fine for many people; late caffeine often steals tonight's sleep and tomorrow's energy.

Sources and further reading

  • Arthritis UK: Managing fatigue
  • NHS: Sleep and tiredness
  • NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s
  • NHS: Occupational therapy
  • NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis

article.title: Arthritis Fatigue Recovery Guide: A 4-Week Plan to Rebuild Energy (UK)
article.excerpt: A step-by-step, four-week plan for recovering from a spell of arthritis fatigue: checking for treatable causes, finding your energy baseline, planned rest, pacing, building activity gently, sleep, food, mood and how to handle setbacks.
article.content:
Quick answer: Recovering from arthritis fatigue usually takes a gradual plan, not a single fix. Rule out treatable causes with your GP, find a daily activity level you can manage even on a bad day, add planned rests, protect your sleep, then build activity by small steps each week. Expect ups and downs, and adjust rather than push through.

Arthritis fatigue is not ordinary tiredness. It can feel like a heavy, drained exhaustion that a good night's sleep does not fix, and it can affect your concentration, mood and ability to do everyday things. Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) describes fatigue as a common and often difficult symptom of many types of arthritis. If you are coming out of a flare, a period of illness or a long spell of exhaustion, this guide gives you a structured, four-week plan to rebuild your energy gradually. For background on why fatigue happens, read arthritis fatigue explained; for causes and when to see your GP, see managing arthritis fatigue.

Before you start: check for treatable causes

Fatigue in arthritis often has more than one driver, and some of them can be treated. Before or alongside this plan, it is worth talking to your GP or rheumatology team, especially if fatigue is new, getting worse or very severe. They may consider:

  • Active inflammation. In rheumatoid and other inflammatory arthritis, fatigue is often worse when the disease is active. The NHS lists tiredness and lack of energy among the symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis, and NICE's guideline (NG100) supports adjusting treatment to bring disease activity under control.
  • Anaemia. Low iron or other types of anaemia are common in inflammatory arthritis and can cause tiredness and breathlessness. The NHS lists tiredness and lack of energy as common symptoms of iron deficiency anaemia.
  • Thyroid problems, low vitamin D, diabetes or other conditions, which a blood test can check.
  • Medicines. Some medicines, including some painkillers and those that affect sleep, can cause drowsiness.
  • Sleep problems, such as pain waking you at night, insomnia or sleep apnoea.
  • Low mood, depression or anxiety, which are common with long-term pain and closely linked to fatigue.

The plan below works alongside medical treatment, not instead of it.

How the four-week plan works

The plan is built on approaches widely used by NHS occupational therapists and physiotherapists: understanding your energy, pacing, planned rest, good sleep and gradually building activity. It avoids two common traps:

  • Boom and bust: doing a lot on a good day, then crashing for several days afterwards.
  • Too much rest: resting so much that fitness drops, which makes everyday tasks more tiring and fatigue worse.
WeekFocusMain goal
1Observe and stabiliseFind your baseline and stop the crashes
2Rest and sleepAdd planned rests and a steady sleep routine
3Gentle buildIncrease activity by small, planned steps
4ConsolidateAdd what matters to you and plan for setbacks

Four weeks is a starting framework, not a deadline. Many people take longer, and that is fine. Move to the next week only when the current one feels manageable.

Week 1: observe and stabilise

Keep a simple energy diary

For seven days, note what you do in blocks across the day and rate your energy from 0 (exhausted) to 10 (full of energy) morning, afternoon and evening. Note your sleep, pain and anything that drained or boosted you. Our pain tracking journal can be adapted for this.

Find your baseline

Your baseline is the amount of activity you can manage on a bad day as well as a good one, without crashing afterwards. Look at your diary. If you walked for 20 minutes on a good day and crashed, but 8 minutes was fine even on a poor day, your walking baseline is around 8 minutes. Do the same for other key activities, such as housework, computer time or standing to cook. It is better to start too low than too high.

Stop the crashes

  • Stick to your baseline every day this week, even if you feel able to do more.
  • Spread essential tasks across the day and week rather than doing them all at once.
  • Cancel or postpone anything that is not essential.
  • Ask for help with heavy tasks such as shopping, cleaning and gardening.

Week 2: planned rest and better sleep

Plan rests before you need them

Planned rests are short breaks taken at set times, before you are exhausted, not collapses after you have done too much. Aim for:

  • Two or three short rests through the day, of around 10 to 20 minutes each
  • A rest that is genuinely restful: sitting or lying quietly, breathing slowly, listening to calm music, rather than scrolling on your phone
  • Avoiding long daytime naps, which can disrupt night-time sleep; if you need to nap, keep it short and before mid-afternoon

Build a steady sleep routine

  • Get up at around the same time each day, including weekends.
  • Wind down for an hour before bed, with screens off and lights low.
  • Keep your bedroom dark, quiet and comfortable.
  • Cut down on caffeine in the afternoon and evening, and on alcohol.
  • Manage night pain with pillows, warmth and pain relief timed as your GP or pharmacist advises. See our guides to sleeping with arthritis and sleep positions for every joint.

Keep your baseline steady

Do not increase activity yet. Keep to your week 1 baseline while rests and sleep settle.

Week 3: build activity gently

Increase by small steps

Choose one or two activities and increase them by a small amount, often suggested as around 10 to 20 per cent, for example from 8 minutes of walking to 9 or 10. Keep the increase for several days. If you cope without a crash, increase again. If you crash, go back to the previous level for a while.

Add gentle exercise

Regular physical activity is one of the most helpful things for arthritis and often helps fatigue over time, even though it can feel like the last thing you want to do. Start gently:

  • Short walks, building up slowly
  • Seated or standing exercises at home; our exercise hub has routines
  • Gentle strengthening, as stronger muscles make everyday tasks less tiring
  • Warm-water exercise, tai chi or gentle yoga, if available locally

The NHS physical activity guidelines suggest building towards 150 minutes of moderate activity a week plus strengthening on two days, but that is a long-term goal, not a week-3 target. Start where you are.

Use pacing tools

  • Break tasks into smaller chunks with short rests between.
  • Sit to do tasks such as ironing, preparing vegetables or getting dressed.
  • Alternate heavy and light tasks, and physical and mental ones.
  • Use labour-saving gadgets and an online shopping delivery.

Our guide to how to pace activities properly explains these tools step by step.

Week 4: consolidate and add what matters

Add something you enjoy

Fatigue often squeezes out the activities that make life enjoyable, such as seeing friends, hobbies or going out. Once essentials are manageable, plan in one enjoyable activity each week, kept within your energy budget. Enjoyment and connection matter for mood, which in turn affects fatigue.

Plan your week

At the start of each week, look at what is coming up. Spread demanding activities out, plan rest around them, and leave some space for the unexpected. Many people find it helpful to think of energy as a budget: spend it on what matters most, and save some in reserve.

Plan for setbacks

Setbacks are normal. Flares, infections, poor nights or stressful events can knock energy back. Write a short setback plan:

  • Go back to your week 1 or 2 level for a few days
  • Keep planned rests and your sleep routine
  • Keep up a little gentle movement rather than stopping completely
  • Build back up gradually when things settle
  • Contact your GP or rheumatology team if a setback lasts or comes with a flare. See our flare-up guide.

Food, drink and fatigue

  • Eat regular meals; skipping meals can make energy dip.
  • Aim for a balanced diet with plenty of vegetables, fruit, wholegrains and protein. Batch cook on better days.
  • Drink enough fluids through the day.
  • Limit alcohol, which affects sleep and mood.
  • There is no good evidence that any supplement cures arthritis fatigue. If you are concerned about iron or vitamin levels, ask your GP for a blood test rather than taking supplements blindly.

Mood, stress and fatigue

Fatigue, pain and low mood are closely linked, and each can make the others worse. Helpful steps include talking to people you trust, relaxation and breathing techniques, and gentle activity outdoors. If you feel low or anxious most days, speak to your GP. In England, you can also refer yourself to NHS Talking Therapies. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, contact your GP, call NHS 111, or call Samaritans free on 116 123.

Fatigue at work

If fatigue affects your work, talk to your employer about reasonable adjustments, such as flexible hours, a phased return after sickness, more breaks or working from home on some days. Arthritis can count as a disability under the Equality Act 2010. Access to Work may be able to help with support or equipment. Our guide to the Access to Work scheme explains how to apply.

Getting extra support

  • Occupational therapy: occupational therapists help people manage everyday tasks with less effort. The NHS explains how to get a referral, which may be through your GP, rheumatology team or local council.
  • Physiotherapy: for help building up activity safely. Many areas allow self-referral.
  • Rheumatology nurse or advice line: if fatigue may be linked to active disease or medicines.
  • Self-management courses: some local NHS services and charities run courses for people living with long-term conditions.

When to get medical help

  • See your GP if fatigue is new, getting worse, not improving after a few weeks of pacing and rest, or stopping you doing everyday activities.
  • See your GP soon if fatigue comes with unexplained weight loss, fevers, night sweats, breathlessness, or feeling faint.
  • Contact your rheumatology team if fatigue comes with more joint swelling or stiffness, which may mean your arthritis is active.
  • Contact your GP or rheumatology team the same day if you feel unwell with signs of infection while on immune-suppressing medicines.
  • Call 999 for chest pain, severe breathlessness or signs of a stroke.

How long does it take to recover from arthritis fatigue?

It varies widely. Some people notice improvement within a few weeks of pacing, planned rest and better sleep; others take months, especially if inflammation, anaemia or low mood also need treating. Progress is often gradual with ups and downs, so judge it over weeks rather than days.

Should I rest or exercise with arthritis fatigue?

Both, in balance. Planned, short rests help, but too much rest reduces fitness and can make fatigue worse. Start gentle activity at a level you can manage even on a bad day, and build up by small steps.

What is boom and bust?

Boom and bust is doing a lot on a good day, then crashing for days afterwards. It is very common with fatigue and pain. Pacing, which means doing a steady, planned amount each day and building up gradually, helps break the cycle.

Can blood tests explain my tiredness?

Sometimes. Your GP may check for anaemia, thyroid problems, vitamin D levels, diabetes and markers of inflammation. Finding and treating a cause can help, but fatigue in arthritis often has several contributors, so self-management usually matters too.

Is arthritis fatigue a sign my arthritis is getting worse?

Not always, but in inflammatory arthritis fatigue is often worse when the disease is active. If fatigue comes with more swollen, stiff or painful joints, contact your rheumatology team, as your treatment may need reviewing.

Will supplements help my energy?

There is no good evidence that any supplement cures arthritis fatigue. If you are concerned about low iron, vitamin B12 or vitamin D, ask your GP about a blood test. In the UK, the NHS advises everyone to consider vitamin D in autumn and winter.

article.title: Spot a Flare Coming: Early Warning Signs, Triggers and a Printable Tracker
article.excerpt: A practical UK guide to spotting arthritis flares early: common warning signs, possible triggers and the evidence behind them, a printable weekly early-warning tracker and personal plan, and when to contact your team.
article.content:
Quick answer: No tool can predict a flare, but many people notice early signs such as heavier fatigue, longer morning stiffness, warmth in a joint or poorer sleep. Common triggers include overdoing it, stress, illness, missed medicines and, for gout, alcohol, large meals and dehydration. Track symptoms for at least four weeks to find your own pattern and start your flare plan early.

Checked on 11 October 2026 against the NHS pages on rheumatoid arthritis treatment and gout, NICE guideline NG100, and flare guidance from the National Rheumatoid Arthritis Society and the National Axial Spondyloarthritis Society. Nothing on this page can predict a flare. It helps you learn your own pattern.

A flare is a period when arthritis symptoms become worse and harder to control. It might be more pain and stiffness all over, or one or two joints becoming swollen and tender, often with tiredness that rest does not fix. Flares can range from short and manageable to severe enough to keep you in bed.

No app, test or website can reliably tell you when a flare is coming. But many people find that, over time, they notice early clues and things that seem to set flares off. Spotting those clues means you can start your flare plan sooner, adjust your day, and contact your team earlier if you need to. This guide explains common early warning signs, possible triggers and what the evidence says about them, and gives you a printable tracker to find your own pattern.

What a flare can look like

Flares are different for each person, and even for the same person no two flares are always the same. Common features include:

  • more joint pain, stiffness or swelling than usual
  • morning stiffness that lasts longer
  • fatigue that feels overwhelming and is not relieved by sleep
  • difficulty with usual tasks such as dressing, work or caring for others
  • poor sleep because of pain
  • feeling generally unwell, low or irritable
  • "brain fog" or difficulty concentrating

In osteoarthritis, a flare often means a period of more pain and stiffness in a joint, sometimes with some swelling, often after more use than usual. In inflammatory arthritis, such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis or axial spondyloarthritis, a flare usually reflects more inflammation. In gout, a flare is a sudden attack of severe pain, heat and swelling in a joint.

Early warning signs people notice

The National Rheumatoid Arthritis Society (NRAS) says you may get better at identifying early signs of a flare, and that fatigue sometimes feels worse just before a flare starts. It also notes that in some cases there may be no warning at all. Early signs people commonly describe include:

  • Tiredness that is heavier than usual or comes on earlier in the day
  • Stiffness that lasts longer in the morning or returns after sitting
  • A "niggle" or warmth in a joint that has flared before
  • Puffy fingers, rings feeling tight, or shoes feeling snug
  • Sleep becoming lighter or broken by pain
  • Mood changes such as feeling flat, tearful or short-tempered
  • Needing more painkillers than usual to get through the day
  • Feeling "fluey" or run down
  • In gout, a tingling, burning or aching in a joint that has had attacks before

Your signs may be quite different. The point of tracking is to find yours.

Possible triggers and what the evidence says

Flares can happen without any obvious cause. When there is a trigger, these are the ones most often described by NHS and patient organisations.

Overdoing it

NRAS and NASS both list "overdoing" things as a common trigger, such as a big clean, a long day out, or catching up on everything on a good day. Pacing activity across the week can help. See our guide to pacing and energy management.

Stress

Many people report that stress can trigger flares or make them harder to cope with. NRAS and NASS both mention it. Stress and flares can feed each other, so stress management is part of flare prevention.

Infections and illness

NRAS says flares sometimes follow periods of illness. Infections can also be more serious if you take immune-suppressing medicines. Follow your team's advice on vaccines and what to do with your medicines when you are unwell.

Missing or changing medicines

Missing doses, running out of a prescription, or reducing or switching a medicine can be followed by a flare. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine without advice. Set reminders and order repeat prescriptions early.

Poor sleep

Poor sleep can be both a cause and a result of flares. Keeping a steady routine helps.

Gout triggers

The NHS says a gout attack can be triggered by an illness that causes a high temperature, drinking too much alcohol or eating a very large meal, getting dehydrated, injuring a joint, or taking certain medicines. It advises getting treatment immediately if you feel an attack starting. See our guide to gout flares and diet.

Weather

Many people feel their arthritis responds to the weather. A large UK smartphone study of 2,658 people with chronic pain, published in 2019, found significant but modest links between pain and humidity, air pressure and wind speed. The effect is small, varies between people, and you cannot change the weather, so it is most useful as a reason to plan gentler days.

Food

Apart from gout, there is little reliable evidence that a particular food triggers flares for most people. If you suspect a food, track it, but do not cut out whole food groups without advice from a GP or dietitian.

Hormones

Some people notice changes around periods, pregnancy, after giving birth or around the menopause. Talk to your team if you notice a pattern.

How to find your own pattern

NASS suggests tracking symptoms over time to monitor your condition and identify anything that might trigger a flare, using a paper diary or an app. A simple approach:

  1. Track for at least four weeks, ideally through at least one flare.
  2. Score the same few things each day, such as pain, stiffness, fatigue, sleep and mood, from 0 to 10.
  3. Note possible triggers, such as a busy day, stress, illness, missed medicine, alcohol, poor sleep or weather.
  4. Look back after a flare. What changed in the 1 to 3 days before?
  5. Write down your personal warning signs and what you will do when you notice them.
  6. Share it with your team. Patterns are useful at appointments and help decisions about treatment.

Be careful not to read too much into one or two days. Flares sometimes happen for no reason, and coincidences are common. Look for things that happen again and again.

Printable personal early-warning tracker

Print this page or copy the table into a notebook. Score each item from 0 (none) to 10 (worst). Tick any possible triggers.

Week starting: ____________
ItemMonTueWedThuFriSatSun
Pain (0–10)
Morning stiffness (minutes)
Fatigue (0–10)
Sleep quality (0–10, 10 = best)
Mood (0–10, 10 = best)
Swollen or warm joints (which?)
Extra painkillers needed? (Y/N)
Trigger: very busy day
Trigger: stress or upset
Trigger: illness or infection
Trigger: missed or changed medicine
Trigger: alcohol or large meal
Trigger: cold, damp or windy weather
Other (write in)

My early warning signs

Fill this in after you have tracked a few weeks or a flare:

  1. The first thing I usually notice is: ______________________
  2. Other signs that a flare may be starting: ______________________
  3. Things that seem to come before my flares: ______________________

When I notice my warning signs, I will

  1. Cancel or move: ______________________
  2. Use these comfort measures: ______________________
  3. Take medicines as agreed in my plan: ______________________
  4. Tell: ______________________
  5. Contact my team if: ______________________
  6. My rheumatology advice line or GP number: ______________________

Keep this with your flare action plan, which sets out what to do once a flare has started.

How to read your tracker

After a few weeks, look back over your sheets and ask yourself:

  • Did fatigue, stiffness or sleep change in the 1 to 3 days before pain went up?
  • Do flares tend to follow particular kinds of day, such as a long shift, a busy weekend or travel?
  • Did a flare follow a missed dose, a cold or an upsetting event?
  • Is there a time of the month or season when scores are usually higher?
  • How long do flares usually last, and what helped them settle?

Circle anything that appears more than once. One coincidence is not a pattern, but the same sign before three flares is worth acting on. Bring the sheets to your next appointment: a few weeks of scores often explains more than trying to remember how things have been.

Lowering the chance of a flare day to day

You cannot prevent every flare, but these steps help many people:

  • Take medicines as prescribed and order repeat prescriptions in good time.
  • Pace activity: spread big jobs across days and build rest into busy days.
  • Keep moving with regular, gentle exercise that suits you.
  • Protect your sleep with a regular routine.
  • Manage stress with things that work for you, such as relaxation, time outdoors, or talking to someone.
  • Look after your general health, including vaccines your team recommends, as infections can trigger flares.
  • For gout, follow NHS advice: have alcohol-free days, drink plenty of fluids, and take any preventive medicine as prescribed.
  • Plan ahead for known busy times such as holidays or house moves.

When it might not be a flare

Not every worsening is a flare. A single hot, swollen joint with a fever could be an infection. New pain after a fall could be an injury. Pain in a new place, or symptoms unlike your usual flares, should be checked. If in doubt, ask your GP, pharmacist or specialist team.

What to do when you notice the signs

NRAS suggests these self-management steps at the first signs of a flare:

  • rest and relaxation, while keeping gently moving to stop stiffness building
  • taking pain medicines regularly and at the right dose, as advised by your pharmacist or doctor
  • hot baths or showers for morning stiffness, and cool packs for hot, swollen joints
  • using aids, such as a stick if a knee is affected, or splints
  • wearing comfortable, supportive shoes
  • letting those closest to you know so they can help

NASS suggests avoiding high-impact activity during a flare but keeping moving with gentle stretches, short walks or swimming, and asking your rheumatologist or GP how to adjust your usual medicines during a flare. Our guide to managing flare-ups at home has more ideas.

Getting help from your team

NICE guideline NG100 says adults with rheumatoid arthritis should have rapid access to specialist care for flares, and that short-term steroids can be considered to manage flares. Many rheumatology services have a telephone or email advice line. Contact your team if:

  • a flare does not settle with your usual measures within the time your team suggested
  • flares are happening more often or lasting longer
  • you have needed steroids for flares several times
  • you are unsure whether to take, pause or change a medicine

Frequent flares can be a sign that your treatment needs reviewing. Your tracker is useful evidence for that conversation.

If you are older or frail

In older people, a sudden worsening in mobility or confusion is not always a flare. It can be an infection, a fall or a medicine side effect. Our guide to flare or frailty explains the difference.

When to get medical help

  • Same-day help from your GP or NHS 111 if a joint is hot and swollen and you feel unwell, have a high temperature, or feel hot, cold or shivery. This can be an infection, especially if you take immune-suppressing medicines.
  • Urgent help for gout that is getting worse with a fever or feeling sick.
  • Urgent help for new headache, jaw pain when eating, or vision changes if you have polymyalgia rheumatica or are over 50.
  • Call 999 for back pain with numbness in both legs, or bladder or bowel changes.
  • Contact your team if flares are frequent, severe or not settling.

Frequently asked questions

Can an app predict my arthritis flares?

No app can reliably predict flares. Tracking apps or paper diaries can help you notice your own patterns, which is useful in itself.

What is the most common early sign of a flare?

It varies. NRAS notes that fatigue may feel worse just before a flare, but some flares come with no warning.

Does the weather really cause flares?

A large UK study found modest links between pain and humidity, air pressure and wind. The effect is small and varies between people.

Can stress cause a flare?

Many people with inflammatory arthritis report that stress triggers or worsens flares, and patient organisations list it as a common trigger.

How long should I track symptoms?

At least four weeks, ideally including a flare, so you can look back at what happened beforehand.

Should I take extra medicine when I notice warning signs?

Only as agreed with your doctor or pharmacist. Ask your team how to adjust medicines during a flare and write it in your plan.

When should I tell my rheumatology team about flares?

If a flare does not settle, flares are becoming more frequent, or you have repeatedly needed steroids. Bring your tracker to appointments.

article.title: Arthritis Flare-Ups — How to Recognise, Manage, and Recover
article.excerpt: Learn how to spot the early signs of an arthritis flare, what to do when one hits, the role of medication, and how to prevent future flare-ups.
article.content:
Clinically reviewed by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483. Last updated: June 2026.

Quick answer: An arthritis flare-up is a temporary worsening of arthritis symptoms, which can vary depending on the type of arthritis. It may involve increased pain, stiffness, swelling, and fatigue, lasting from days to several weeks. Early signs include unusual tiredness or increased stiffness. Managing a flare involves resting the affected joint(s), using heat or ice, and taking prescribed medications.

One day you feel steady. The next, your joints are swollen, stiff, and screaming — as if all your progress has been undone overnight. If this sounds familiar, you have experienced an arthritis flare-up. Flare-ups are frightening and frustrating. But they are also part of living with arthritis — and they can be managed. This guide will help you recognise a flare early, take the right steps when it happens, and reduce the chance of future flares.

What Is an Arthritis Flare-Up?

A flare-up (or "flare") is a sudden, temporary worsening of your arthritis symptoms. Instead of your usual background pain, you experience a spike that may last anywhere from a few days to several weeks. Flare-ups happen in all types of arthritis, but they feel different depending on your diagnosis:

  • Osteoarthritis (OA) flares: Often triggered by overuse or injury. Pain increases and the joint may swell. Typically settles within days to a week with rest.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) flares: Involve increased inflammation — joints become hot, red, swollen, and stiff (especially in the morning). Can last longer and may need medication changes.
  • Gout flares: A specific type of flare caused by urate crystals in the joint. Extremely painful and sudden, often affecting the big toe.

Early Warning Signs of a Flare

Your body often gives you clues before a full flare hits. Learning to spot these warning signs can help you act early:

  • Increased stiffness — especially in the morning, lasting longer than usual
  • Fatigue — unusual tiredness, feeling "drained"
  • Mild swelling or warmth — a joint that feels warmer or puffier than yesterday
  • "Foggy" feeling — trouble concentrating (common in RA flares)
  • Mood changes — feeling low or irritable for no clear reason
  • Reduced range of motion — a joint that does not bend or straighten as far as usual

If you notice these signs, it is time to ease up on activity and focus on self-care — before the flare worsens.

Immediate Steps to Take During a Flare

When a flare hits, the goal shifts from "push through" to "protect and settle." Your action plan:

  1. Pause high-impact activities. Cancel the gym session, the long walk, or heavy housework. Your joints need a break.
  2. But keep moving gently. Complete rest can make joints stiffer. Gentle range-of-motion movements help prevent this.
  3. Use your flare toolkit. Heat packs, ice packs, pain relief, and any flare-management plan you have discussed with your doctor.
  4. Prioritise sleep. Your body heals during rest. Make sleep non-negotiable.
  5. Be kind to yourself. Flares are not a personal failure. They are part of the condition.

Medications That Help During a Flare

What you take depends on your type of arthritis and what your GP or rheumatologist has prescribed. For OA flares: paracetamol or NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen), topical NSAID gel, or a short course of stronger pain relief if prescribed. For RA flares: NSAIDs or COX-2 inhibitors, a temporary increase in corticosteroids as directed, a steroid injection into the affected joint, or a review of your DMARDs if flares become frequent. Do not stop or change your DMARDs or biologics without medical advice.

Rest, Ice, Heat — What Works?

Heat is best for stiff, achy joints (especially OA) — warm bath, heated wheat bag, or heat pad for 15–20 minutes. Ice is best for hot, swollen, inflamed joints (common in RA or gout) — ice pack wrapped in a tea towel for 10–15 minutes, never directly on skin. Rest is appropriate for all types during the acute phase, but avoid total bed rest. Elevate the joint if swollen. Some people find alternating heat and ice helpful — experiment gently.

Preventing Future Flares

You cannot prevent every flare — but you can reduce how often they happen and how severe they become. Pace yourself — break tasks into smaller chunks, alternate activity with rest. Stay active regularly — strong muscles protect joints. Maintain a healthy weight — less load equals less joint stress. Take medication as prescribed — skipping doses invites trouble. Manage stress — stress and inflammation are linked. Eat an anti-inflammatory diet — a Mediterranean-style diet may help reduce background inflammation. Track your flares — keep a simple diary to spot patterns.

When to Contact Your GP or Rheumatologist

Contact your doctor if: the flare lasts more than two weeks without improvement, pain is severe and not responding to usual pain relief, you develop a fever alongside joint pain (could indicate infection), a single joint becomes suddenly very hot, red, and swollen (could be septic arthritis — needs urgent treatment), or you are having flares more than once per month disrupting your life.

Continue reading

  • Arthritis & Alcohol UK – Safe Limits & Interactions — Can you drink alcohol with arthritis?

Practical next steps for Arthritis Flare-Ups — How to Recognise, Manage, and Recover

If you came here about Arthritis Flare-Ups — How to Recognise, Manage, and Recover, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your local integrated care board about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Making information usable

Treat articles like this as a starting map, not a personal care plan. Highlight one idea to try for two weeks, then review. If symptoms are new, rapidly worsening, or affecting several joints with fever or unexplained weight loss, contact your GP promptly rather than waiting on self-help alone.

Reliable UK sources

Cross-check major decisions with NHS.uk, your clinical team, and NICE guidance summaries where relevant. Be wary of social posts that promise reversal of arthritis or attack standard medicines without evidence.

Using evidence carefully

Marketing claims for joint supplements often outrun the research. Look for products that state dose clearly, avoid miracle language, and fit alongside — never instead of — prescribed treatment. Stop and seek advice if you notice bruising, stomach pain, yellowing of the skin or new rashes.

Quick questions about Arthritis Flare Recognise Manage

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

article.direct_answer: An arthritis flare-up is a temporary worsening of arthritis symptoms, which can vary depending on the type of arthritis. It may involve increased pain, stiffness, swelling, and fatigue, lasting from days to several weeks. Early signs include unusual tiredness or increased stiffness. Managing a flare involves resting the affected joint(s), using heat or ice, and taking prescribed medications.

faqs.q: What Is an Arthritis Flare-Up?
faqs.a: A flare-up (or "flare") is a sudden, temporary worsening of your arthritis symptoms. Instead of your usual background pain, you experience a spike that may last anywhere from a few days to several weeks. Flare-ups happen in all types of arthritis, but they feel different depending on your diagnosis: Osteoarthritis (OA) flares: Often triggered by overuse or injury. Pain increases and the joint may swell. Typically settles within days to a week with rest. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) flares: Involve

faqs.q: Rest, Ice, Heat — What Works?
faqs.a: Heat is best for stiff, achy joints (especially OA) — warm bath, heated wheat bag, or heat pad for 15–20 minutes. Ice is best for hot, swollen, inflamed joints (common in RA or gout) — ice pack wrapped in a tea towel for 10–15 minutes, never directly on skin. Rest is appropriate for all types during the acute phase, but avoid total bed rest. Elevate the joint if swollen. Some people find alternating heat and ice helpful — experiment gently.
