article.title: Arthritis Flare-Up: What to Do When Symptoms Get Worse
article.excerpt: Practical UK steps for an arthritis flare-up: first 72 hours, heat versus cold, pacing, medication plans, and when to contact your GP, rheumatology team or NHS 111.
article.content:
Quick answer: An arthritis flare-up is a temporary spike in pain, stiffness, swelling or fatigue. In the first 24–72 hours: protect hot joints, keep gentle movement, use cold for swelling or heat for stiffness, follow any flare plan from your rheumatology team, and rest before you crash. Contact your GP, rheumatology advice line or NHS 111 if you have fever, a single very hot red joint, or symptoms that keep worsening.

Flares can hit even when you have been managing well. They are common in inflammatory arthritis and can also happen with osteoarthritis after overuse, illness or poor sleep. This page is a practical UK first-aid plan — educational, not a diagnosis.

How to recognise a flare

  • Joint pain clearly worse than your baseline
  • Morning stiffness lasting much longer than usual
  • Swelling, warmth or redness in one or more joints
  • Crushing fatigue or “flu-like” unwellness with inflammatory disease
  • Tasks you normally manage suddenly feel out of reach

Write down what changed and when. That note helps your GP or rheumatology nurse decide whether this is a short flare or a signal to review treatment. Download our printable flare action plan so the next spike is less chaotic.

First 24–48 hours

  1. Modify, do not freeze. Protect angry joints, but keep gentle range-of-motion so stiffness does not lock you in. Full bed rest often makes the next day worse.
  2. Cold for hot swelling; heat for stiff, non-swollen joints. Ice pack wrapped in a cloth for about 15 minutes; warm bath or wheat bag for stiffness. Never put ice or heat directly on skin.
  3. Follow your flare plan if your rheumatology team gave you one (for example a short steroid course or temporary pain-relief change). Do not exceed labelled or prescribed doses — ask a pharmacist if unsure.
  4. Prioritise sleep and pacing. Use pillows to support painful joints. Drop non-essential tasks. See pacing and energy management to avoid boom-and-bust recovery.

Days 3–7: active recovery

  • Short gentle stretches or walks on flat ground — often around half your usual load
  • Joint protection for kitchen, dressing and transfers
  • Steady meals and fluids; ease alcohol and ultra-processed snacks if they worsen sleep or pain
  • Tell work early if you need temporary adjustments — see arthritis at work UK and sick pay and fit notes

When the flare eases, rebuild activity slowly via the exercise hub and walking with arthritis rather than jumping straight back to a “catch-up” day.

When to contact a clinician

  • Flare lasts longer than your usual pattern (many teams say seek review if it is still escalating after about a week)
  • Fever, feeling systemically unwell, or a single joint that is extremely hot, red and swollen (infection must be ruled out)
  • You cannot manage basic personal care or take medicines safely
  • Flares are becoming more frequent — treatment may need review
  • Chest pain, sudden breathlessness, new rash with feeling very unwell, or eye pain — seek urgent care

Use NHS 111 for urgent advice, or 999 / A&E if you feel severely unwell. Pair self-management with our longer flare-up guide and pain relief guide.

Reducing the next flare

  • Keep taking disease-modifying or biologic medicines as prescribed unless your team says otherwise — stopping them is a common flare trigger
  • Track stress, sleep debt, infections and overexertion
  • Build rest before you crash; protect sleep
  • Ask about OT, physio or a written flare plan at your next review

Frequently asked questions

Is every bad day a flare?

Not always. Weather, sleep and overdoing chores can worsen pain without a true inflammatory flare. Still treat the day kindly and escalate if red-flag signs appear.

Should I stop all exercise?

Usually no. Swap intensity for gentle movement unless a clinician has told you to rest a specific joint.

Can diet stop flares?

No diet cures arthritis. A balanced pattern may support energy and recovery, but medication and pacing remain central. See our diet guides for food-first ideas, not miracle claims.

article.title: Arthritis-Friendly Gym Guide: How to Use a Gym Safely With Arthritis (UK)
article.excerpt: A practical UK guide to using a gym with arthritis: choosing an arthritis-friendly gym, exercise referral schemes, the most joint-friendly machines and how to set them up, a beginner full-body session, a first-month plan, gym etiquette and confidence tips, adapting for flares and when to stop.
article.content:
Quick answer: A gym can be a great place to exercise with arthritis. Choose one with accessible equipment and helpful staff, tell them about your condition, and start with joint-friendly machines such as a recumbent bike, cross-trainer and leg press. Begin with light loads, 2 or 3 sessions a week, and build up gradually, stopping for sharp pain or swelling.

Walking into a gym for the first time can feel daunting, especially if you have painful joints and are not sure what you can safely do. But a gym can be one of the best places to exercise with arthritis: the machines let you control the load precisely, there are low-impact options for fitness, staff can help, and it is warm and dry all year round. This guide explains how to choose an arthritis-friendly gym, which equipment suits sore joints, how to set it up, and gives you a first-month plan.

Why the gym can help

  • Controlled strength training. Machines guide the movement and let you add weight in small steps. NICE guideline NG226 recommends muscle strengthening and aerobic fitness as core treatments for osteoarthritis.
  • Low-impact cardio. Bikes, cross-trainers and rowing machines build fitness with less load on joints than running.
  • All-weather. Cold, wet or icy weather does not stop your routine.
  • Support and structure. Inductions, classes and staff help you learn and stay motivated.
  • Meeting the guidelines. UK guidelines recommend at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week plus strengthening on 2 days; a gym makes both easier to plan.

Choosing an arthritis-friendly gym

Before joining, visit at a quiet time and ask for a tour. Look for:

FeatureWhy it matters
A free induction and programme reviewStaff show you how to use machines safely and set up a plan
Instructors with experience of long-term conditionsThey can adapt exercises for your joints; some have qualifications in exercise referral or for older adults
Recumbent bikes, cross-trainers and selectorised (pin-loaded) weight machinesEasy-to-adjust, joint-friendly equipment
Machines with small weight incrementsLets you progress gradually
Accessible parking, lifts, changing rooms and toiletsMakes getting there and changing easier
A pool, ideally with warmer-water sessionsA comfortable alternative on bad days
Quiet times, over-50s or beginner sessionsLess crowded, less intimidating
Flexible or pay-as-you-go membershipYou can try before committing

Many council leisure centres offer concessions for older people, people on certain benefits and disabled people. Ask about prices, joining fees and whether you can pause membership during a flare.

Exercise referral schemes

Many areas in the UK run exercise referral schemes. A GP, practice nurse or physiotherapist refers you to a local leisure centre for a set number of supervised sessions, often at a reduced price, with an instructor who has extra training in working with people with health conditions. Ask your GP practice whether there is a scheme near you. It is an excellent way to start using a gym with support. If a gym is not for you, there may be free or low-cost exercise classes in your area instead.

Before your first session

  • Check with your GP or physiotherapist first if you have heart or lung problems, uncontrolled blood pressure, recent surgery or joint replacement, or you have been told to avoid certain movements.
  • Book an induction and tell the instructor about your arthritis, which joints are affected, any joint replacements, and your medicines if relevant.
  • Wear comfortable clothes and supportive trainers.
  • Bring water and a small towel.
  • Plan to go at a quieter time, such as mid-morning or early afternoon on weekdays.

The most joint-friendly equipment

Cardio machines

MachineJoint loadGood forSetup tips
Recumbent bike (with a backrest)Very lowKnee, hip and back arthritis; balance concernsAdjust the seat so your knee is slightly bent at the furthest pedal point; start with low resistance
Upright bikeLowKnee and hip arthritisSeat at hip height when standing beside it; slightly bent knee at the bottom
Cross-trainer (elliptical)LowFitness without impactHold the fixed handles at first for balance; short strides if hips are stiff
Rowing machineLow to moderateWhole-body fitnessPush with the legs first, then lean back slightly and pull; avoid if back or hands are painful
Treadmill (walking)ModerateWalking practice in any weatherStart slowly on the flat, use the safety clip and hold the rails if needed
Arm bike (arm ergometer)Very low for legsWhen leg joints are too painfulKeep shoulders relaxed and below shoulder height

Strength machines

MachineWorksTips for arthritis
Leg pressThighs and buttocksLimit the depth so knees bend no more than is comfortable; do not lock the knees
Leg extensionFront of thighUse a light weight and a smaller range if the kneecap area is painful
Seated leg curlBack of thighMove slowly and control the return
Hip abductor and adductorOuter and inner thighsStart light; useful for hip arthritis
Seated rowUpper backKeep shoulders down; use neutral handles if wrists are sore
Chest pressChest, shoulders, armsSet handles at chest height; avoid deep stretching at the start position
Lat pulldownUpper backPull to the front, never behind the neck
Cable machineMany musclesAsk staff to show you options; good for gentle shoulder work

Machines are often easier than free weights at first because they guide the movement. If gripping is painful, choose machines with padded or neutral handles, or use straps and cuffs. Our strength training guide explains sets, repetitions and how heavy to go.

A beginner full-body session (40–45 minutes)

  1. Warm-up, 8–10 minutes: recumbent bike or cross-trainer at an easy pace, then a few gentle mobility movements for shoulders, hips and ankles.
  2. Strength circuit, 20 minutes: leg press, seated row, leg curl, chest press, hip abductor, and a core exercise such as a supported plank on the wall or a dead bug on a mat. 1 to 2 sets of 10 to 12 with a light weight; rest 60 seconds between exercises.
  3. Cardio, 8–10 minutes: bike or cross-trainer at a moderate pace, where you can talk but not sing.
  4. Cool-down, 5 minutes: slow pedalling or walking, then stretches for calves, thighs, hips and chest.

Your first month

WeekSessionsFocus
12Induction; 10–15 minutes cardio; learn 3–4 machines with very light weights
22Full beginner session with 1 set of each exercise
32–3Add a second set to exercises that feel comfortable; extend cardio by a few minutes
42–3Small weight increases where 12 repetitions feel easy; review with an instructor

Leave at least one day between strength sessions. On other days, walk, swim or rest.

Signs your gym plan is about right

Some extra aching in muscles and joints after a session is normal, especially in the first few weeks. A common guide used by physiotherapists is that pain during exercise should stay at a level you find acceptable, often around 4 out of 10 or below, and should settle back to your usual level within 24 hours. If pain is higher than this, or your joints feel worse the next morning, reduce the weight, the number of sets or the range of movement next time rather than stopping altogether. If sessions feel very easy and your joints feel fine, that is a sign you are ready to progress a little.

Using the pool and classes

If your gym has a pool, water walking and gentle pool exercises are a good option on stiff or sore days; see our guide to water-based exercise for arthritis. Many gyms also run classes. Low-impact options often suit arthritis better: indoor cycling at your own pace, gentle yoga or Pilates, tai chi, aqua classes, and strength classes for beginners or older adults. Tell the instructor about your arthritis before the class and work at your own level. It is fine to skip or adapt any exercise.

Gym confidence tips

  • Remember that everyone started somewhere; most people are focused on their own workout.
  • Write your plan on your phone or a card so you know what to do next.
  • Ask staff to show you a machine again; that is what they are there for.
  • Wipe down equipment after use and share machines during busy times.
  • Go with a friend for the first few visits.

Adapting for flares and bad days

  • Lower the weights, do fewer sets, or swap leg machines for upper-body work if your legs are flaring (and vice versa).
  • Use the recumbent bike or pool for gentle movement.
  • Shorten the session to 15–20 minutes.
  • Skip the gym if a joint is hot and very swollen or you feel unwell, and do gentle movement at home instead.

Gym tips by joint

Main joint affectedOften comfortableGo carefully with
KneeBike, cross-trainer, leg press with limited depth, leg curl, hip machinesDeep squats, lunges, running, high step-ups
HipBike (raise the seat if bending is stiff), hip abductor, leg press, poolVery low seats, deep hip bending, wide-legged squats
BackRecumbent bike, cross-trainer, seated row, supported core workHeavy lifting from the floor, twisting under load
ShoulderSeated row, cable outward rotation with a light weight, arm bike below shoulder heightOverhead presses, behind-the-neck movements, dips
Hands and wristsLeg machines, recumbent bike, machines with padded or neutral handlesTight gripping of bars and dumbbells, bent-wrist press-ups
Feet and anklesBike, rowing machine, pool, seated strength machinesLong treadmill walks at first, jumping, high-impact classes

Everyone is different. If you are not sure where to start, our guide to choosing the right exercise for arthritis has decision tables by joint and ability.

After a joint replacement

Most people can return to the gym after a hip or knee replacement once their surgical team or physiotherapist agrees. Follow any specific precautions you have been given, such as limits on how far you bend a new hip. Low-impact machines like the bike and cross-trainer are usually good choices, and strength machines can help you rebuild muscle. Ask your physiotherapist which exercises to include and which to avoid, and tell the gym instructor about your operation.

Making it a habit

  • Book your gym sessions in your diary like appointments.
  • Keep a simple log of the machines, weights and how your joints felt the next day.
  • Set a small goal, such as 2 sessions a week for a month, then review.
  • Ask for a programme review every 6 to 8 weeks so your plan keeps progressing.
  • If you miss a week, restart at a slightly lower level rather than giving up.

Exercises to approach with caution

  • High-impact moves such as jumping, box jumps and running on hard surfaces, until you know how your joints respond.
  • Deep squats and lunges with heavy weights if your knees or hips are painful.
  • Behind-the-neck presses and pulldowns, and heavy overhead lifting with shoulder arthritis.
  • Exercises that put full weight through bent wrists, such as standard press-ups, if your hands are painful; try knuckle or wall versions.
  • Heavy lifting with a rounded back.

When to stop and get medical help

Stop exercising if you get sharp joint pain, a joint locking or giving way, sudden swelling, dizziness, or unusual breathlessness.

  • Call 999 or ask staff to call for you if you have chest pain or tightness, severe breathlessness, feel faint, or someone collapses.
  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with a high temperature.
  • See your GP or a physiotherapist if gym sessions keep causing joint pain that lasts more than a day despite reducing the load, if you are unsure which exercises suit you after joint replacement, or if you are not improving after 8 to 12 weeks.

Can I go to the gym with arthritis?

Yes. Most people with arthritis can use a gym safely, and it can be a very good way to build strength and fitness. Start gently, tell staff about your condition, and build up gradually.

What is the best gym machine for knee arthritis?

A recumbent or upright bike is often the most comfortable cardio machine for knee arthritis. For strength, the leg press (with a limited depth), seated leg curl and leg extension with a light weight can help strengthen the muscles that support the knee.

Should I use free weights or machines?

Machines are often easier to start with because they guide the movement and let you adjust the load in small steps. Free weights can be added later for variety. Either can work well with good technique.

How often should I go to the gym with arthritis?

Two or three sessions a week is a good aim, with at least one rest day between strength sessions. Walking, swimming or rest on other days helps you recover.

What should I tell the gym staff?

Tell them which joints are affected, whether you have had any joint replacements or surgery, any movements you have been told to avoid, and any other health conditions. This helps them adapt your programme.

Is the cross-trainer good for arthritis?

For many people, yes. The cross-trainer is low-impact and works the whole body. Start at a low resistance for short periods, hold the fixed handles for balance, and stop if it aggravates your hips or knees.

Examples include salmon, turmeric, ginger, beetroot, berries, lentils, mackerel, and oats, which provide compounds like omega-3 fatty acids, curcumin, betalains, and fibre.

Anti-Inflammatory Recipes for Joint Health

What you eat has a direct impact on inflammation levels in your body. The Mediterranean diet — rich in omega-3 fats, antioxidants, and fibre — has the strongest evidence for reducing arthritis symptoms.

Here are five simple, affordable recipes using ingredients available in any UK supermarket.

1. Turmeric & Ginger Salmon Tray Bake (Serves 2)

Prep: 10 mins | Cook: 20 mins

Ingredients:

  • 2 salmon fillets
  • 1 sweet potato, cubed
  • 1 red pepper, sliced
  • 1 courgette, sliced
  • 2 tbsp olive oil
  • 1 tsp ground turmeric
  • 1 tsp fresh ginger, grated
  • 1 clove garlic, crushed
  • Juice of half a lemon
  • Salt and pepper

Method:

  1. Preheat oven to 200°C/180°C fan
  2. Toss vegetables in 1 tbsp olive oil, turmeric, ginger, and garlic. Spread on a baking tray
  3. Place salmon fillets on top, drizzle with remaining olive oil and lemon juice
  4. Bake for 18–20 minutes until salmon flakes easily

Why it helps: Salmon provides omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA), turmeric contains curcumin, and ginger provides gingerols — all potent anti-inflammatory compounds.

2. Berry & Beet Recovery Smoothie (Serves 1)

Prep: 5 mins

Ingredients:

  • 1 small cooked beetroot (vacuum-packed is fine)
  • 100g frozen mixed berries
  • 1 banana
  • 1-inch piece fresh ginger
  • 200ml oat milk
  • 1 tbsp ground flaxseed

Method: Blend everything until smooth. Add more milk if needed.

Why it helps: Beetroot contains betalains that reduce inflammation markers. Berries are rich in anthocyanins. Flaxseed adds plant-based omega-3 (ALA).

3. Warming Lentil & Spinach Dhal (Serves 4)

Prep: 10 mins | Cook: 30 mins

Ingredients:

  • 200g red lentils, rinsed
  • 1 onion, diced
  • 2 cloves garlic, crushed
  • 1 tsp turmeric
  • 1 tsp cumin
  • 1 tsp garam masala
  • 400ml coconut milk
  • 400ml vegetable stock
  • 200g fresh spinach
  • 1 tbsp olive oil

Method:

  1. Sauté onion and garlic in olive oil for 3–4 minutes
  2. Add spices and cook for 1 minute
  3. Add lentils, coconut milk, and stock. Simmer for 25 minutes
  4. Stir in spinach until wilted. Season to taste

Why it helps: Lentils provide plant protein and fibre. Turmeric and cumin are anti-inflammatory. Spinach is rich in vitamin K, which supports bone health.

4. Mackerel & Avocado Toast (Serves 1)

Prep: 5 mins

Ingredients:

  • 1 tin smoked mackerel fillets
  • 1 slice sourdough or wholegrain bread, toasted
  • Half an avocado
  • Cherry tomatoes, halved
  • Lemon juice
  • Black pepper

Method: Mash avocado onto toast. Flake mackerel on top. Add tomatoes, a squeeze of lemon, and black pepper.

Why it helps: Mackerel is one of the richest sources of omega-3 in the UK. Avocado provides vitamin E and healthy monounsaturated fats.

5. Golden Turmeric Porridge (Serves 1)

Prep: 2 mins | Cook: 5 mins

Ingredients:

  • 50g porridge oats
  • 250ml oat or semi-skimmed milk
  • 1 tsp turmeric
  • Half tsp cinnamon
  • 1 tsp honey
  • Handful of walnuts and blueberries

Method: Cook oats with milk, turmeric, and cinnamon. Top with honey, walnuts, and blueberries.

Why it helps: Oats provide beta-glucan fibre that reduces inflammatory markers. Walnuts are the only nut rich in ALA omega-3. Cinnamon has antioxidant properties.

Key Takeaway

You don't need exotic superfoods — everyday UK ingredients like salmon, lentils, berries, and oats are powerful anti-inflammatory allies when eaten consistently.

Practical next steps for Anti-Inflammatory Recipes: Easy UK Meals for Joint Health

If you came here about Anti-Inflammatory Recipes: Easy UK Meals for Joint Health, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your local integrated care board about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Everyday eating patterns

No single food cures arthritis. Patterns rich in vegetables, fruit, pulses, wholegrains and oily fish are the ones most often discussed in UK dietetic advice for inflammatory conditions. Keep changes realistic: swap one ultra-processed snack for fruit and nuts, or cook with olive oil more often than seed oils marketed as miracle cures.

Supplements versus meals

Food-first is usually safer than stacking capsules. If you do try a supplement, choose a reputable UK brand, check for interactions with your medicines (especially blood thinners), and give any trial a clear stop date so you can judge whether symptoms truly changed.

Using evidence carefully

Marketing claims for joint supplements often outrun the research. Look for products that state dose clearly, avoid miracle language, and fit alongside — never instead of — prescribed treatment. Stop and seek advice if you notice bruising, stomach pain, yellowing of the skin or new rashes.

Quick questions about Anti Inflammatory Recipes Easy

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

Keep expectations kind while you work on anti-inflammatory recipes: easy uk meals for joint health. Arthritis symptoms fluctuate; a quieter week does not mean you imagined earlier pain, and a flare does not mean every helpful habit has failed. Adjust one variable at a time so you can see what truly helps.

article.title: Arthritis - How's Life Living With Arthritis?
article.excerpt: A practical UK guide to what living with arthritis can involve, including symptoms, daily activities, movement, work, flares and when to seek help.
article.content:
Quick answer: Living with arthritis can affect pain, stiffness, fatigue, sleep, movement, mood, work and everyday activities. Arthritis is not one single condition, so experiences vary. Helpful support may include suitable movement, pacing, sleep support, treatment discussions and practical adjustments.

There is no single way that arthritis feels or affects daily life. Some people have symptoms in one joint, while others have inflammation, fatigue or symptoms affecting several parts of life. This guide explains common experiences and practical questions to discuss with a GP, pharmacist, physiotherapist or rheumatology team.

What can living with arthritis feel like?

  • pain or tenderness in one or more joints
  • stiffness after waking or sitting still
  • swelling, warmth or reduced movement
  • fatigue that makes ordinary tasks harder
  • sleep disrupted by pain or stiffness
  • less confidence with walking, stairs, work or social activities
  • low mood or frustration when symptoms change from day to day

These symptoms can have different causes. Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, gout and other conditions need different assessment and treatment. A symptom pattern alone cannot confirm a diagnosis.

How arthritis can affect an ordinary day

Morning and getting moving

Some people notice stiffness or pain when getting out of bed. Gentle movement, time to get ready and an agreed exercise plan may help. If morning stiffness is new, prolonged or worsening, discuss it with a healthcare professional.

Work, caring and household tasks

Arthritis may make lifting, typing, standing, driving, dressing or concentrating more difficult. Breaking tasks into smaller parts, changing position regularly and asking about reasonable workplace adjustments can help. Benefits and work-support decisions depend on individual circumstances.

Evenings, sleep and fatigue

Pain and worry can disturb sleep, while poor sleep can make pain and fatigue harder to manage. Keep a simple record of sleep, symptoms and activity, and ask for help if fatigue is severe, new or interfering with safety and daily care.

Movement, pacing and flare planning

Many people benefit from regular, suitable activity, but the right amount depends on the condition, symptoms and general health. Start gradually, avoid sudden increases and ask a qualified professional how to adapt movement if a joint becomes hot, sharply more painful or swollen.

  • plan important activities for the time of day when you have most energy
  • alternate activity with planned rests instead of waiting until exhausted
  • use gentle range-of-motion or low-impact activity where appropriate
  • keep a flare plan with agreed medicines and contact details
  • avoid changing or stopping prescribed medicines without advice

Explore our arthritis exercise hub, flare-up guidance and arthritis pain-relief guide for related information.

Living with different types of arthritis

Osteoarthritis often involves pain and stiffness related to use and joint change. Inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis may involve swelling, prolonged stiffness, fatigue and symptoms beyond the joints. Gout can cause sudden, severe attacks in a joint. The right diagnosis matters because treatment and monitoring differ.

Read more about osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis and arthritis generally.

When to seek medical advice

Arrange medical advice if joint pain, stiffness, swelling or fatigue is new, worsening, limiting daily activities or not settling. A GP, pharmacist, physiotherapist or specialist team can help decide what assessment and treatment are appropriate.

Seek urgent advice from NHS 111 or an urgent GP service if a joint is hot and swollen and you feel feverish, shivery or generally unwell. Call 999 for a life-threatening emergency, severe breathing difficulty, collapse, or sudden neurological symptoms.

Questions to take to an appointment

  • What could be causing my symptoms?
  • What movement or exercise is suitable for me?
  • How should I manage a flare?
  • Could medicines, sleep, mood or another condition be contributing?
  • Would physiotherapy, occupational therapy or other support help?
  • What symptoms should prompt urgent help?

Frequently asked questions

Can people live well with arthritis?

Many people find ways to manage arthritis and continue activities that matter to them. It may take time to find the right combination of treatment, movement, pacing and practical support.

Should I exercise if I have arthritis?

Suitable activity often forms part of arthritis self-management, but the type and amount should match your health and symptoms. Stop and seek advice if exercise causes marked or persistent worsening.

Can arthritis affect mood?

Long-term pain, fatigue, sleep disruption and uncertainty can affect mood. Speak to a GP or another healthcare professional if low mood, anxiety or hopelessness is persistent or affecting daily life.

Where can I find UK arthritis support?

Start with your GP, NHS 111 when urgent advice is needed, your pharmacist, physiotherapy services or rheumatology team. You can also explore our Benefits and PIP hub and self-help resources.

Sources and further reading

  • NHS: Arthritis
  • NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s
  • NHS: Rheumatoid arthritis
  • NHS: Exercise

Educational information only; this is not a diagnosis or personal medical advice. Please follow advice from your own healthcare professionals.

article.title: Arthritis in Older Adults: What Changes and What Helps (UK Guide)
article.excerpt: Arthritis becomes more common with age, but it is not inevitable and it is not untreatable. Here is what genuinely changes in later life — from medication.
article.content:
Quick answer: Arthritis risk rises with age due to cartilage changes, muscle loss and conditions like polymyalgia rheumatica and gout becoming more common — but it is not inevitable. Treatment often needs extra care around kidney/liver function and drug interactions, and joint pain is closely linked to falls risk, making strength and balance exercise a genuinely protective measure.

Arthritis and Ageing: What Actually Changes

Arthritis becomes more common as we get older, but it isn't an inevitable part of ageing that everyone must simply accept. Understanding what genuinely changes with age — and what doesn't — makes it easier to manage joint health well into later life rather than assuming pain is just "part of getting old."

Cartilage naturally becomes slightly less resilient with age, joints lose some of their range of motion, and muscle mass tends to decline unless it's actively maintained — all of which raise the risk of osteoarthritis and make joint pain more noticeable. Conditions such as polymyalgia rheumatica, which almost exclusively affects people over 50, and gout, which becomes more common with age, are also more relevant in later life. But plenty of older adults have strong, comfortable joints well into their 80s and 90s — age alone doesn't guarantee arthritis, and lifestyle factors continue to matter throughout life.

Conditions More Common in Older Adults

  • Osteoarthritis — the most common form overall, and its prevalence rises steadily with age as cartilage wear accumulates.
  • Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) — causes stiffness and aching in the shoulders, neck and hips, almost always in people over 50, and responds well to low-dose steroid treatment.
  • Gout — becomes more common with age, partly due to increasing use of medications (like some blood pressure treatments) that raise uric acid levels.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis — can develop at any age but a second peak in new diagnoses occurs in later life.

Why Diagnosis Can Be Trickier in Older Adults

Joint pain in later life is sometimes dismissed — by patients and, occasionally, by services — as an unavoidable consequence of ageing, which can delay proper diagnosis and treatment. Older adults are also more likely to have several health conditions at once, which can mask or mimic arthritis symptoms, and some blood markers used to help diagnose inflammatory arthritis can behave differently with age. It's worth being persistent: new or worsening joint pain, especially with stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes each morning, is always worth raising with a GP rather than assuming nothing can be done.

Medication Considerations Specific to Older Adults

Treating arthritis in older adults often requires extra care around medication choices:

  • NSAIDs (like ibuprofen) carry higher risks of stomach, kidney and cardiovascular side effects in older adults, particularly alongside other common medications such as blood pressure tablets or blood thinners. GPs often recommend topical NSAID gels over oral tablets where possible, or the lowest effective dose for the shortest necessary time.
  • Kidney and liver function naturally decline somewhat with age, which affects how the body processes many arthritis medications — doses may need adjusting, and blood tests to monitor organ function are more frequently used.
  • Polypharmacy — taking several medications for different conditions — increases the risk of drug interactions, so it's worth a pharmacist or GP periodically reviewing your full medication list together.
  • Steroid treatment for conditions like PMR is very effective but requires monitoring for bone density (osteoporosis risk) and blood sugar, both of particular relevance in later life.

None of this means older adults can't be treated effectively — it means treatment plans are usually more individualised, with closer monitoring built in.

Mobility, Falls and Independence

One of the most important, and most under-discussed, aspects of arthritis in older adults is its link to falls risk and long-term independence. Painful or stiff joints change the way people walk, often unconsciously, which affects balance. Weak muscles around an arthritic joint — particularly the knee or hip — reduce the body's ability to catch a stumble before it becomes a fall. This matters because falls are a leading cause of injury and loss of independence in older adults.

The encouraging part: this is one of the most modifiable risk factors in arthritis care. Regular strength and balance work — even simple, seated or supported exercises — measurably improves stability and confidence in walking, and physiotherapists can tailor a programme to whatever level of mobility someone currently has.

Staying Active Safely

  • Low-impact exercise — walking, swimming, water aerobics and cycling — puts less strain on joints than high-impact activity while still building the strength and cardiovascular fitness that protect against falls and frailty.
  • Strength training, even with light resistance bands or bodyweight, helps counter the natural muscle loss (sarcopenia) that compounds joint problems with age.
  • Balance exercises, such as tai chi, have good evidence behind them specifically for reducing falls risk in older adults with joint conditions.
  • Pacing and rest remain important — the goal is consistent, manageable activity, not pushing through pain, especially during a flare of an inflammatory condition like PMR.

Always check with a GP or physiotherapist before starting a new exercise routine if you have other health conditions alongside arthritis, so the plan can be tailored safely.

Nutrition and Bone Health

Diet plays a supporting role in joint health at any age, but a few things become particularly relevant in later life. Adequate calcium and vitamin D intake matter more as bone density naturally declines with age, and this becomes especially important for anyone on long-term steroid treatment (such as for PMR), which can further reduce bone density over time — bone density scans (DEXA scans) are often recommended periodically in this situation. Maintaining sufficient protein intake helps counter age-related muscle loss, working alongside strength exercise rather than replacing it. And for gout specifically, dietary triggers such as excess alcohol, red meat and sugary drinks become worth managing more actively, since gout risk increases with age.

None of this requires a dramatically different diet from general healthy-eating advice — it's more a case of paying closer attention to a few specific nutrients that matter more as the body changes with age.

Getting the Right Support

Later life often comes with access to services specifically geared toward joint health and independence that are worth knowing about: falls-prevention clinics, community physiotherapy services, occupational therapy assessments for home adaptations, and social prescribing schemes that can connect people to local exercise groups or peer support. A GP or local Age UK service can point toward what's available in your area — many people aren't aware how much support exists until they ask.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is joint pain just a normal part of getting older? Some increase in joint stiffness is common with age, but persistent pain, swelling, or stiffness lasting over 30 minutes each morning is not something to simply accept — it's worth discussing with a GP, since effective treatments exist regardless of age.

Are older adults less able to have joint replacement surgery? Age alone is rarely a barrier — overall health and fitness for surgery matter far more than age itself, and many people have successful joint replacements well into their 80s.

Why does polymyalgia rheumatica mainly affect older people? It's not fully understood why PMR is so strongly age-related, but it's rare under 50 and most commonly diagnosed in people over 70, likely reflecting age-related changes in immune function.

Can exercise make arthritis worse in older adults? Appropriately paced, low-impact exercise generally improves arthritis symptoms rather than worsening them. The main risk is doing too much too quickly rather than exercise itself — building up gradually is key.

Key Takeaways

  • Arthritis risk increases with age, but it isn't an unavoidable consequence of ageing, and effective treatment is available at any age.
  • Conditions like polymyalgia rheumatica and gout become more relevant in later life alongside the more familiar osteoarthritis.
  • Medication choices often need extra care in older adults due to kidney/liver changes and interactions with other medicines.
  • Joint pain is closely linked to falls risk in older adults, making strength and balance work a genuinely protective, not just comfort-focused, intervention.
  • Persistent joint symptoms are always worth raising with a GP, regardless of age.

This article provides general information and is not a substitute for personalised medical advice. Speak to your GP about any new or worsening joint symptoms.

  • Arthritis & Pregnancy UK – Medication Safety & Planning — Planning a pregnancy with arthritis?
  • Gout Medication UK: Complete Guide to Drugs for Gout — From managing a gout attack to long-term uric acid control — everything you need to know about gout treatment in the UK.
  • Winter gout, dehydration and frailty (UK) — Painful feet plus slower recovery is a common UK picture in later life.
  • Painkillers in older adults with arthritis: caution, not dosing (UK) — UK readers managing pain in several joints often need smaller doses of movement more than a heroic gym restart.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have chest pain, sudden weakness or numbness, severe breathlessness, a suspected broken bone after a fall, or back pain with new loss of bladder or bowel control or numbness around your bottom or genitals.

Contact NHS 111 or your GP urgently if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel unwell or have a fever, or if your symptoms are getting rapidly worse.

article.title: Arthritis in Young Adults: Recognising It Early (UK Guide)
article.excerpt: Arthritis in your 20s and 30s: reactive arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis and psoriatic arthritis explained, why diagnosis is often delayed, and how to manage.
article.content:
Quick answer: Several forms of arthritis, including reactive arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis, characteristically begin in a person’s 20s or 30s. Diagnosis is often delayed because joint pain in younger adults is frequently attributed to injury or posture rather than investigated for inflammatory disease — persistence in seeking assessment matters, since untreated inflammation causes more damage the longer it continues.

Arthritis Isn't Just an "Older Person's" Condition

Arthritis carries a stubborn stereotype as something that only affects older people, which means younger adults with real joint symptoms are sometimes dismissed — by friends, family, and occasionally by health services — before they're taken seriously. In reality, several forms of arthritis specifically affect younger people, and getting an early, accurate diagnosis matters just as much at 25 as it does at 65, arguably more, since untreated inflammatory arthritis has more years ahead of it to cause joint damage.

Types of Arthritis More Common in Younger Adults

  • Reactive arthritis typically develops in people in their 20s and 30s, triggered by an infection elsewhere in the body (commonly a gut or genital infection) days to weeks earlier. It often resolves within months but can become longer-lasting in some people.
  • Ankylosing spondylitis usually first causes symptoms — typically lower back pain and stiffness — in the late teens to early 30s, and is frequently misattributed to posture, gym injuries, or general back strain for years before diagnosis.
  • Juvenile idiopathic arthritis, diagnosed in childhood, can persist into adulthood, meaning many "young adults" with arthritis have actually been managing it since childhood.
  • Psoriatic arthritis can develop at any age but often appears in people already living with psoriasis in their 20s to 40s.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis, while more common later in life, does affect younger adults too, and early-onset cases are sometimes more aggressive if not caught quickly.

Why Diagnosis Is Often Delayed

Younger adults with joint pain face a specific set of obstacles to getting diagnosed quickly:

  • Assumption bias — both patients and clinicians can unconsciously assume joint pain in a young person is more likely to be an injury, overuse, or unrelated to arthritis, delaying the right tests.
  • Symptoms attributed to lifestyle — back pain in a 25-year-old is more likely to be blamed on posture, gym training, or a mattress than investigated for inflammatory disease, even when the pattern (worse at night, improves with movement, morning stiffness over 30 minutes) points toward something like ankylosing spondylitis.
  • Normal or borderline blood tests — some younger patients with genuine inflammatory arthritis have blood markers within a "normal" range, which can be misread as ruling out arthritis entirely rather than prompting further specialist assessment.
  • Reluctance to push for referral — many younger adults, especially early in their working lives, are hesitant to repeatedly go back to their GP about ongoing symptoms, which can add months of delay.

The practical takeaway: if joint pain or stiffness — particularly back stiffness that's worse first thing in the morning and eases with movement, or joint swelling that doesn't resolve — persists for more than a few weeks, it's worth asking directly about a rheumatology referral rather than waiting to see if it resolves on its own.

The Cost of Delayed Diagnosis

For inflammatory types of arthritis in particular, the gap between symptom onset and diagnosis matters. Ankylosing spondylitis, for example, has historically taken years to diagnose from first symptoms in many cases, partly because it was under-recognised in younger patients. During that delay, ongoing inflammation can cause changes to the spine that are harder to reverse than if treatment had started early. This is one of the strongest arguments for younger adults being persistent about unexplained, persistent joint symptoms rather than accepting reassurance that "you're too young for arthritis."

Managing Arthritis Alongside Work, Study and Family Life

A diagnosis in your 20s or 30s comes with a different set of practical challenges than one later in life — often balancing a chronic condition against building a career, studying, starting a family, or simply the busy pace of that life stage.

  • Workplace adjustments — in the UK, arthritis can qualify as a disability under the Equality Act 2010, meaning employers have a legal duty to consider reasonable adjustments (flexible hours, ergonomic equipment, modified duties during flares).
  • Fertility and pregnancy planning — some arthritis medications need to be reviewed or changed before trying to conceive; this is worth raising proactively with a rheumatologist rather than waiting until pregnancy is already underway.
  • Energy management — fatigue from inflammatory arthritis can be as limiting as joint pain itself; pacing activity across the week, rather than pushing hard on good days and crashing afterward, tends to work better long-term.
  • Mental health — receiving a lifelong diagnosis at a younger age can bring a real sense of loss or anxiety about the future; connecting with others managing the same condition, whether through a support group or online community, consistently helps people process this.

Staying Active With a Younger-Onset Diagnosis

Contrary to a common fear, most people with inflammatory or joint conditions are encouraged to stay active rather than avoid exercise. The right type of activity depends on the specific condition and which joints are affected, but in general:

  • Low-impact cardio (swimming, cycling) protects joints while maintaining fitness
  • Core and back-strengthening exercise is specifically recommended for ankylosing spondylitis to help maintain posture and spinal mobility
  • Sport and exercise can usually continue with modifications during a flare rather than being abandoned altogether
  • A physiotherapist experienced in inflammatory arthritis can build a plan around your specific goals, whether that's returning to a sport or simply staying comfortable day to day

Building a Long-Term Relationship With a Rheumatology Team

Being diagnosed young often means decades of an ongoing relationship with rheumatology services, which is worth approaching differently than a short-term treatment plan. It's worth being an active participant in appointments — keeping notes on symptom patterns between visits, being honest about medication side effects rather than quietly stopping treatment, and asking directly about the long-term goals of your treatment plan (many services now aim for full remission as a realistic target, not just symptom control). Transition from paediatric to adult rheumatology services, for those diagnosed with juvenile arthritis, is a particular point worth planning for actively, since continuity of care can otherwise be lost during the handover.

Sport, Relationships and Social Life

A younger-onset diagnosis doesn't have to mean giving up an active social or sporting life, though it may mean adapting how you approach it. Being open with teammates, training partners or close friends about flare-ups — rather than pushing through silently — tends to lead to more sustainable participation over time than either overexerting or withdrawing entirely. Dating and relationships can raise their own questions about when and how to talk about a chronic condition; there's no single right answer, but many people find that treating it as a normal part of who they are, rather than something to hide, leads to more supportive relationships in the long run.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can you get arthritis in your 20s? Yes. Reactive arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis and even rheumatoid arthritis can all begin in your 20s, and juvenile arthritis diagnosed in childhood often continues into adulthood.

Why did it take so long to get diagnosed? Delayed diagnosis in younger adults is a well-recognised pattern, often due to symptoms being attributed to injury, posture or overuse rather than investigated for inflammatory arthritis. If you're facing ongoing delay, asking directly for a rheumatology referral can help.

Will arthritis affect my ability to have children? Most people with arthritis can have healthy pregnancies, though some medications need reviewing beforehand. This is best planned proactively with your rheumatology team rather than left until later.

Is reactive arthritis permanent? Often not — many cases resolve within several months of the triggering infection clearing. Some people do go on to have longer-lasting symptoms, which is why follow-up with a rheumatologist is worthwhile even after the initial flare settles.

Key Takeaways

  • Several forms of arthritis, including reactive arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis, characteristically begin in younger adulthood.
  • Diagnosis is often delayed in younger patients due to assumptions that joint pain "can't be arthritis" at a young age.
  • Delayed treatment of inflammatory arthritis allows more time for joint or spinal damage to occur — persistence in seeking a diagnosis matters.
  • UK employment law provides real protections and adjustment rights for younger adults managing a chronic joint condition at work.
  • Staying active, with the right guidance, remains encouraged rather than restricted for most younger adults with arthritis.

This article provides general information and is not a substitute for personalised medical advice. If you have persistent joint pain or stiffness, speak to your GP about further assessment regardless of your age.

  • Inflammatory Arthritis: Types, Causes and Treatment — Inflammatory arthritis covers conditions like rheumatoid, psoriatic and reactive arthritis, where the immune system — not wear and tear —.
  • Early Signs of Gout in the Big Toe UK — Recognising the early signs of gout in the big toe — what it feels like, how to confirm diagnosis and what to do at first attack.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have chest pain, sudden weakness or numbness, severe breathlessness, a suspected broken bone after a fall, or back pain with new loss of bladder or bowel control or numbness around your bottom or genitals.

Contact NHS 111 or your GP urgently if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel unwell or have a fever, or if your symptoms are getting rapidly worse.

article.title: Meal Plans for Arthritis: A Practical 7-Day UK Plan, Shopping List and Batch-Cooking Guide
article.excerpt: A practical seven-day meal plan for people with arthritis, built on the NHS Eatwell Guide and Mediterranean-style eating, using everyday UK supermarket food. Includes a shopping list, batch-cooking plan, low-effort swaps for painful days and advice on when to see a dietitian.
article.content:
Quick answer: A good meal plan for arthritis follows the NHS Eatwell Guide with a Mediterranean-style lean: vegetables and fruit at most meals, wholegrains, beans and lentils, oily fish at least once a week, olive or rapeseed oil, and less processed meat and sugar. Plan meals that are easy to prepare on bad days, batch cook on good days, and see a dietitian for advice on your own portions and needs.

Evidence checked on 10 October 2026 against the NHS Eatwell Guide, NHS healthy eating tips, NICE NG100 and NICE NG226.

Knowing what to eat is one thing. Actually getting healthy meals on the table when your joints hurt and you are tired is another. A simple meal plan takes away daily decisions, makes shopping easier and means you can cook on good days and rest on bad ones. This guide gives you a seven-day plan using everyday UK food, a shopping list, and practical ways to make it work with arthritis.

The principles behind the plan

No diet has been proven to cure arthritis. NICE guidance on rheumatoid arthritis (NG100) says there is no strong evidence that diet changes help arthritis itself, but people can be encouraged to follow Mediterranean diet principles: more bread, fruit, vegetables and fish, less meat, and plant-oil-based products in place of butter and cheese. For osteoarthritis, NICE guidance (NG226) highlights weight management for people living with overweight or obesity.

This plan is built on the NHS Eatwell Guide with a Mediterranean-style lean:

  • Fruit and vegetables: at least 5 portions a day, about a third of what you eat. Fresh, frozen, tinned and dried all count.
  • Starchy foods: just over a third of what you eat, ideally wholegrain or higher-fibre.
  • Protein: beans, pulses, fish, eggs and some meat. At least 2 portions of fish a week, 1 of them oily.
  • Dairy or alternatives: for protein and calcium, choosing lower-fat and lower-sugar options where possible.
  • Fats: small amounts of unsaturated oils such as olive and rapeseed oil.
  • Fluids: 6 to 8 cups or glasses a day.
  • Less often: foods high in fat, salt and sugar, and processed meats.

A note on portions and calories

This plan does not set calorie targets. The NHS gives a general guide that women need around 2,000 calories a day and men around 2,500, but needs vary with age, size and activity, and many people with arthritis are less active than average. If you want to lose or gain weight, or have other conditions such as diabetes or kidney disease, ask your GP for a referral to a registered dietitian, who can tailor portions to you. A simple visual guide is to fill about half your plate with vegetables or salad, a quarter with a starchy food and a quarter with protein.

The 7-day meal plan

DayBreakfastLunchEvening meal
MondayPorridge with milk, frozen berries and ground flaxseedLentil and vegetable soup (batch) with wholemeal breadBaked salmon, new potatoes with skins, peas and broccoli
TuesdayWholemeal toast with peanut butter and bananaLeftover salmon mixed with salad leaves, tomatoes and a wholemeal wrapChickpea and spinach curry (batch) with brown rice
WednesdayPlain yoghurt with oats, apple and walnutsJacket potato with baked beans and a side saladChicken and vegetable traybake (peppers, red onion, courgette) with olive oil and herbs, with couscous
ThursdayScrambled eggs on wholemeal toast with tomatoesLeftover chickpea curry with a wholemeal pittaWholewheat pasta with a tomato, lentil and vegetable sauce (batch), and a side salad
FridayOvernight oats with grated apple and cinnamonSardines on toast with cherry tomatoes and cucumberFish pie topped with mashed potato (shop-bought fish pie mix makes it easier), with green beans
SaturdayVegetable omelette with wholemeal toastHummus, falafel and salad in a wholemeal wrapBean and vegetable chilli (batch) with brown rice and plain yoghurt
SundayWholegrain cereal with milk and sliced fruitLeftover chilli in a jacket potatoRoast chicken with roast potatoes (in a little rapeseed oil), carrots, cabbage and gravy

Snacks if you need them: a piece of fruit, a small handful of unsalted nuts, plain yoghurt, carrot sticks and hummus, or wholegrain crackers with cheese.

Drinks: water, tea, coffee and milk all count towards your fluids. The NHS suggests limiting fruit juice and smoothies to a combined 150ml a day.

Why this plan works for arthritis

  • Oily fish twice a week (salmon on Monday, sardines on Friday) provides long-chain omega-3 fats, which have some evidence of benefit in rheumatoid arthritis and support heart health.
  • Beans and lentils appear most days, adding protein and fibre at low cost.
  • Wholegrains such as oats, brown rice and wholemeal bread provide fibre and steady energy.
  • Calcium from milk, yoghurt, cheese and sardines supports bone health.
  • Little processed meat and few sugary foods, in line with NHS advice.
  • Leftovers are built in, so you cook less often.

Batch-cooking plan for good days

On a day when your joints are less painful, spend an hour or two making three big batches. Then you only need to reheat on most days.

  1. Lentil and vegetable soup: onion, carrots, celery, red lentils, tinned tomatoes and stock. Freeze in single portions.
  2. Chickpea and spinach curry: onion, garlic, ginger paste, curry paste, tinned chickpeas, tinned tomatoes and frozen spinach.
  3. Bean and vegetable chilli or lentil pasta sauce: tinned kidney beans or lentils, tinned tomatoes, frozen mixed peppers and onions, and spices.

Tips to save your joints:

  • Use frozen chopped onions, peppers and vegetables, and jars of garlic and ginger paste, so there is little chopping.
  • Use a lightweight saucepan or slow cooker, and sit on a perching stool while you stir.
  • Ladle food into containers rather than lifting heavy pans to pour.
  • Label portions with the name and date, and use them within the time recommended for frozen food.
  • Pace yourself: split the cooking across two short sessions if you need to.

Shopping list for the week

SectionItems
Fruit and vegBananas, apples, cherry tomatoes, cucumber, salad leaves, onions, carrots, celery, broccoli, cabbage, new potatoes, baking potatoes, courgette, peppers, lemons
FrozenMixed berries, peas, green beans, spinach, chopped onions and peppers, fish pie mix
Tins and jarsChopped tomatoes, chickpeas, kidney beans, green or brown lentils, baked beans (reduced sugar and salt), sardines, curry paste, garlic and ginger paste, stock cubes (low salt)
Dry goodsPorridge oats, red lentils, brown rice, wholewheat pasta, couscous, wholegrain cereal, wholemeal bread, wholemeal wraps and pitta, ground flaxseed, walnuts, peanut butter
FridgeMilk or fortified soya drink, plain yoghurt, eggs, hummus, falafel, cheddar, salmon fillets, chicken thighs or a whole chicken
Oils and flavourRapeseed oil, olive oil, dried herbs, cumin, chilli, cinnamon, black pepper

For a printable version of the basics, see our anti-inflammatory shopping list.

Swaps for painful or exhausting days

Planned mealLow-effort swap
Baked salmon with vegetablesMicrowave salmon fillet pouch, microwave rice and frozen veg steamed in the bag
Chicken traybakeReady-roasted chicken with a bag of salad and a wholemeal roll
Fish pieTinned mackerel on wholemeal toast with tomatoes
Any home-cooked evening mealA portion of frozen batch-cooked soup, curry or chilli
Roast dinnerSupermarket ready meal with extra frozen vegetables. Check the label for salt

It is fine to rely on convenience foods sometimes. A ready meal with added vegetables is a better choice than skipping a meal.

Adapting the plan

  • Vegetarian: swap fish and chicken for eggs, tofu, beans, lentils or Quorn. Include walnuts and ground flaxseed for plant omega-3.
  • Vegan: use fortified soya alternatives and plan for vitamin B12, iodine, calcium and vitamin D.
  • Gout: some foods, including red meat, offal and some seafood, are higher in purines. Ask your GP or a dietitian how to adapt the plan.
  • Weight loss: keep the same pattern but adjust portions of starchy foods and fats, and limit snacks. NICE says any amount of weight loss is likely to help osteoarthritis.
  • Small appetite: eat little and often, and include protein at each meal. See a dietitian if you are losing weight without trying.
  • Jaw arthritis or swallowing difficulty: choose soft options such as soups, fish pie, scrambled eggs and porridge, and ask for a speech and language therapy assessment if swallowing is difficult.
  • Warfarin: keep your intake of green leafy vegetables fairly steady from week to week, and tell your anticoagulant clinic if you make big diet changes.

Some people notice certain foods seem to affect their symptoms. Our guide to foods that may trigger symptoms explains how to test this without cutting out whole food groups.

Make your own plan: a weekly planner

Once you have tried the plan above, you may want to build your own around foods you enjoy. Copy this planner onto paper or into your phone. Fill in your good days first (for batch cooking) and plan the easiest meals for days when you have appointments, work or usually feel worse.

DayEnergy or pain expected (good / OK / hard)BreakfastLunchEvening mealOily fish? Beans or lentils? 5 A Day?
Monday
Tuesday
Wednesday
Thursday
Friday
Saturday
Sunday

A quick weekly check: have you included oily fish at least once, beans or lentils on several days, wholegrains most days, and fruit or vegetables at most meals? If so, your plan follows the same principles as the one above.

Storing and reheating leftovers safely

Batch cooking only works if leftovers are stored safely. Cool cooked food quickly, put it in the fridge or freezer once cool, and reheat until steaming hot all the way through. Only reheat food once. Defrost frozen portions in the fridge or microwave rather than on the worktop. The Food Standards Agency has more detailed food safety advice.

Getting help with food

If shopping and cooking are becoming too difficult, there are options. Supermarket online deliveries, frozen meal delivery services and community meal services can help, and a social care needs assessment from your local council may include help with meals. An occupational therapist can suggest equipment to make cooking easier. See our guide to meal delivery and help with food.

Want a longer plan?

Once you are comfortable with this week, try our 14-day Mediterranean plan for more variety, or our breakfast guide for easy morning ideas.

When to see a dietitian

A meal plan like this is a general starting point. Ask your GP or rheumatology team about a referral to a registered dietitian if you want help to lose or gain weight, have diabetes, kidney disease, coeliac disease, gout or food allergies, follow a vegan diet, or have lost weight without trying. Dietitians can tailor portions and food choices to your needs.

When to get medical help

Do not change your prescribed arthritis medicines because of diet changes. See your GP if you lose weight without trying, have ongoing digestive symptoms, or are struggling to eat enough. Speak to a pharmacist before starting supplements, especially if you take warfarin or another anticoagulant, methotrexate or NSAIDs. Get same-day advice from your GP or NHS 111 if a joint suddenly becomes hot, swollen and very painful, especially with a fever.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a special meal plan for arthritis?

No meal plan has been proven to treat arthritis. A plan based on the NHS Eatwell Guide with a Mediterranean-style lean is the best-supported approach and is good for your heart and weight.

How many calories should I eat?

The NHS gives a general guide of around 2,000 calories a day for women and 2,500 for men, but needs vary. A registered dietitian can advise on what is right for you.

Can I follow this plan if I have gout?

Much of it is suitable, but some foods are higher in purines. Ask your GP or a dietitian to help you adapt it.

Is it OK to use ready meals and frozen food?

Yes. Frozen vegetables, tinned fish and beans are nutritious, and a ready meal with extra vegetables is better than skipping a meal. Check labels for salt.

How do I eat healthily when cooking is painful?

Batch cook on good days, use frozen and pre-prepared ingredients, sit while you cook, and keep easy standbys such as tinned fish, eggs and microwave grains.

Will this meal plan help me lose weight?

It is based on healthy, filling foods, which can help. For weight loss, portion sizes matter; a dietitian or NHS weight management service can help you set realistic goals.

Sources and further reading

  • NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s – weight management

Food and supplements can interact with medicines, so check with your GP, pharmacist or rheumatology team before changing your diet significantly or starting a supplement, and ask for a referral to a registered dietitian for individual advice. article.title: Arthritis Medication — What Works, What to Expect
article.excerpt: A clear, plain-English guide to arthritis medications: painkillers, NSAIDs, DMARDs, biologics, corticosteroids, and how to get them on the NHS.
article.content:
Clinically reviewed by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483. Last updated: June 2026.

Quick answer: Arthritis medications include painkillers like paracetamol and stronger opioids for severe pain. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen reduce both pain and inflammation. DMARDs and biologics treat underlying disease processes in inflammatory arthritis. Corticosteroids offer potent anti-inflammatory effects. Topical gels and creams can provide localised relief. Most are available on NHS prescription.

Taking medication for arthritis can feel like navigating a maze. There are so many names, so many warnings — and you just want something that helps.

This guide explains every major type of arthritis medication in plain English. We cover what each one does, how it works, potential side effects, and how to get it on the NHS. Always speak to your GP or rheumatologist before starting or stopping any medication.

Painkillers (Paracetamol, Codeine) for Arthritis

Paracetamol

Paracetamol is often the first painkiller your GP will suggest. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you. Widely available, few side effects, inexpensive — but it does not reduce inflammation and may not be strong enough for severe pain.

Codeine and Other Opioids

Codeine, tramadol, and morphine-based drugs are stronger painkillers sometimes prescribed for short periods when pain is severe. Important warning: These medicines can cause dependence. The NHS recommends using the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible time. Common side effects include constipation, drowsiness, and nausea.

NSAIDs — Ibuprofen, Naproxen, and Cox-2 Inhibitors

NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) relieve both pain and inflammation. They are widely used for osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and other types.

  • Traditional NSAIDs: Ibuprofen, Naproxen, Diclofenac — available over the counter or on prescription.
  • Cox-2 inhibitors: Celecoxib, Etoricoxib — prescription-only; may be gentler on the stomach.

Potential side effects: NSAIDs can irritate the stomach lining. Your GP may prescribe a stomach-protecting drug (proton pump inhibitor, or PPI) alongside them. Long-term use at high doses may affect kidney function or blood pressure. People with asthma, stomach ulcers, kidney problems, or heart conditions should speak to their GP before taking NSAIDs.

DMARDs for Inflammatory Arthritis

DMARDs (disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs) treat the underlying disease process in rheumatoid arthritis — they aim to slow or stop the immune system from attacking the joints. Common DMARDs include:

  • Methotrexate — Usually the first DMARD prescribed for RA. Taken once a week (not daily). Regular blood tests needed.
  • Sulfasalazine — Often used when methotrexate is not suitable or in combination with it.
  • Leflunomide — Another alternative or add-on DMARD.
  • Hydroxychloroquine — Milder DMARD, sometimes used for milder RA or lupus.

Key facts: They take 6–12 weeks to work. Regular blood monitoring is essential. They can affect the immune system, increasing infection risk. Stopping suddenly can cause a flare-up.

Biologics — Newer Treatments for RA

Biologics are a newer class of DMARD, made from living cells. They target very specific parts of the immune system involved in inflammation. Examples include Adalimumab (Humira), Etanercept (Enbrel), Infliximab (Remicade), and Tocilizumab (RoActemra). On the NHS, they are usually offered to people whose RA has not responded well to at least two standard DMARDs and whose disease activity remains high. They are given by injection or infusion and require careful monitoring.

Corticosteroid Injections and Tablets

Corticosteroids (often simply called "steroids") are powerful anti-inflammatories — not the same as anabolic steroids misused in sport. Steroid injections delivered directly into a painful joint can provide rapid relief lasting weeks to months (limit of 3–4 per year in the same joint). Steroid tablets (prednisolone) are used for short courses during severe flares or low-dose long-term control, though long-term use carries risks including weight gain, osteoporosis, and high blood pressure.

Topical Treatments (Gels and Creams)

Topical NSAIDs — ibuprofen gel or diclofenac gel — are applied directly to the skin over a painful joint. They cause fewer stomach side effects than tablets, deliver medication exactly where needed, and are available over the counter. Topical capsaicin cream (from chilli peppers) works by reducing substance P, a chemical that sends pain signals — it can take a few weeks of regular use to show benefit.

Getting Arthritis Medication on the NHS

Most arthritis medications are available on NHS prescription. Over-the-counter drugs (paracetamol, ibuprofen gel, low-dose ibuprofen tablets) can be bought yourself — buying paracetamol in bulk is often cheaper than a prescription. Prescription NSAIDs, DMARDs, biologics, and steroids are prescribed by your GP or rheumatologist at the standard NHS prescription charge (£9.90 per item as of 2024/25), unless you qualify for free prescriptions. If you need regular medication, a Prescription Prepayment Certificate (PPC) costs around £32 for three months of unlimited prescriptions.

Talking to Your GP About Medication

  1. Be specific about your pain. "I struggle to open jars and my hands hurt every morning for an hour" is more helpful than "I'm in pain."
  2. Mention what you have already tried. Include exercise, over-the-counter medication, and lifestyle changes.
  3. Ask questions. Write them down beforehand.
  4. Discuss side effects openly. If a medicine makes you feel unwell, say so. There are usually alternatives.
  5. Do not stop medication suddenly. Some drugs (especially steroids) need to be reduced gradually under medical supervision.

  • How Arthritis Medications Affect Sexual — Arthritis treatments manage pain and inflammation but can sometimes impact your intimate life.

  • Travelling Abroad With Arthritis Medication: A UK Checklist — Prescription rules, controlled medication paperwork and time-zone dosing for biologics and DMARDs.
  • Arthritis Treatment — Complete Guide to Managing Pain — Explore every treatment option for arthritis, from NHS pathways and exercise to medication, physiotherapy, surgery, and complementary.

Practical next steps for Arthritis Medication — What Works, What to Expect

If you came here about Arthritis Medication — What Works, What to Expect, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Benefits conversations

Personal Independence Payment (PIP) looks at how your condition affects daily living and mobility, not the diagnosis name alone. Keep a short diary of bad days, help you need with dressing or cooking, and walking limits. Welfare rights advisers at local councils or charities can check forms before you submit them.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Quick questions about Arthritis Medication What Works

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.
