article.title: How Arthritis Medications Affect Sexual Function: DMARDs, Biologics and NSAIDs
article.excerpt: Arthritis treatments manage pain and inflammation but can sometimes impact your intimate life. While physical dysfunction is rare, indirect methotrexate sexual side effects can include lowered libido…
article.content:
Arthritis treatments manage pain and inflammation but can sometimes impact your intimate life. While physical dysfunction is rare, indirect methotrexate sexual side effects can include lowered libido due to severe fatigue or nausea. Other drugs, like steroids or opioids, might reduce desire or alter hormone levels. Always discuss rheumatoid arthritis sexual dysfunction with your rheumatology team.

Quick answer: Arthritis treatments manage pain and inflammation but can sometimes impact your intimate life. While physical dysfunction is rare, indirect methotrexate sexual side effects can include lowered libido due to severe fatigue or nausea. Other drugs, like steroids or opioids, might reduce desire or alter hormone levels. Always discuss rheumatoid arthritis sexual dysfunction with your rheumatology team.

Living with arthritis brings a multitude of physical changes, and taking long-term medication is a routine part of managing your condition. You already know that disease-modifying drugs and daily painkillers help to control joint damage, reduce severe swelling, and ease your morning stiffness. However, the impact these powerful treatments can have on your sexual health is a topic that is often left in the shadows during busy clinic appointments.

Intimacy and physical closeness are important parts of your overall wellbeing and relationship health. When you start a new treatment plan, it is entirely natural to wonder how it might affect your body beyond your joints. Many people quietly worry about maintaining a healthy sex life while relying on heavy medications, yet feel too embarrassed to raise the issue.

Understanding exactly how your prescriptions work helps you take control of your sexual health. You deserve to feel comfortable, informed, and confident in your intimate relationships. If you suspect your daily medication is causing difficulties in the bedroom, remember that you are not alone. There are many practical steps you can take, and your medical team is there to help you balance joint protection with a fulfilling quality of life.

How medication can affect sexual health

Medications designed to treat inflammatory arthritis work by fundamentally altering how your immune system functions, aggressively reducing systemic inflammation, or blocking pain signals in your brain. Because these drugs act on various complex systems throughout your body, they can sometimes cause unintended changes to your sexual function and desire.

These medication-induced changes can manifest in several different ways. You might notice a sudden or gradual drop in your sex drive. You could experience new physical difficulties with arousal, such as difficulty maintaining an erection or experiencing unexpected vaginal dryness. Often, the issue is not a direct chemical effect of the drug on your reproductive organs, but rather a secondary side effect. Symptoms such as severe fatigue, chronic nausea, or dizziness naturally leave you feeling physically depleted and much less interested in sex.

It is also incredibly important to untangle the effects of the medication from the effects of the arthritis itself. Joint pain, restricted mobility, muscle stiffness, and the heavy emotional weight of living with a chronic, unpredictable condition can all contribute heavily to your symptoms. Your medication is actually designed to reduce these primary physical barriers. In many cases, an effective treatment plan actively improves your sex life by reducing your overall pain levels and increasing your physical mobility.

However, when a specific drug does interfere with intimacy, it usually happens through hormonal shifts or neurological dampening. Certain strong pain medications can blunt the transmission of nerve signals, which directly affects physical sensation and pleasure. Other drugs might temporarily alter your delicate hormone balance, which is closely linked to your baseline libido.

Your mental health is equally relevant to this conversation. Some arthritis medications can subtly affect your mood, leaving you feeling emotionally flat, irritable, or mildly depressed. When your mood drops, your desire for physical intimacy almost always follows suit. Recognising this connection is the first critical step towards addressing the problem.

Before altering any of your dosages, you must speak to your rheumatology team. They can help you identify whether a specific drug is responsible for your symptoms. Exploring a comprehensive arthritis medication guide can help you understand the vast array of available options. Finding the right balance ensures you manage your joint pain without sacrificing your intimate life.

DMARDs and sexual function

Disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) form the absolute cornerstone of treatment for many types of inflammatory arthritis. They work quietly in the background to suppress your overactive immune system, preventing long-term, irreversible damage to your joints. Because these are powerful, systemic medications, they require careful monitoring and carry a unique set of potential side effects.

Methotrexate is the most commonly prescribed DMARD in the UK. Generally speaking, methotrexate does not directly cause physical erectile dysfunction or vaginal dryness. However, the secondary impacts of the drug can be significant. If you experience persistent nausea, painful mouth ulcers, or profound fatigue in the days following your weekly dose, your desire for intimacy will naturally plummet. Feeling physically unwell and exhausted is one of the most common, yet unrecognised, barriers to a healthy sex life.

If you are struggling with these general systemic symptoms, managing methotrexate side effects with practical tips from your specialist nurse can make a world of difference. Taking your medication on a specific day of the week when you do not plan to be intimate, or adjusting your daily folic acid routine under your doctor's strict guidance, can help alleviate the crushing exhaustion that suppresses your libido.

Sulfasalazine is another frequently used conventional DMARD. This medication is generally very well-tolerated by most people, but it has a specific, well-documented effect on male fertility. It can significantly reduce a man's sperm count and negatively affect sperm motility. While this does not usually cause sexual dysfunction or a drop in physical desire, it is a critical factor if you and your partner are actively planning to start a family. Another quirk of sulfasalazine is that it can temporarily turn your bodily fluids, including your urine and semen, a yellowish-orange colour. Knowing this in advance prevents unnecessary alarm during intimate moments.

Leflunomide operates in a similar way to calm your immune system. Like other drugs in this class, its primary impact on your sexual health is usually secondary. Frequent gastrointestinal upset, unexpected weight loss, or general lethargy can severely diminish your energy levels. When you lack physical energy, sexual interest naturally wanes.

By understanding how DMARDs like methotrexate slow rheumatoid arthritis, you can better rationalise why these side effects occur. Routine blood tests are an essential part of taking these drugs, ensuring your liver and blood counts remain safe. If you feel that your current DMARD is negatively impacting your relationships, always mention it during these routine monitoring appointments. Your specialist nurse can often adjust your dose to find a more comfortable fit.

Biologics and sexual function

Biologic medications are advanced, highly targeted treatments that block specific proteins in your immune system to halt the inflammatory process. If conventional DMARDs have not adequately controlled your symptoms, your rheumatologist might prescribe a biologic therapy. These drugs are highly effective for many people, but they also bring entirely new considerations for your daily life and overall wellbeing.

In the vast majority of cases, biologic medications have a profoundly positive effect on sexual function. Because they are so incredibly targeted, they often bring rapid, dramatic relief from severe joint pain, chronic swelling, and the debilitating, heavy fatigue associated with active inflammatory arthritis. When your disease is finally well-controlled and you are no longer living in constant pain, your energy levels and libido frequently return to their natural state. Many people find their sex life significantly improves once they settle into a biologic therapy routine.

However, no medication is entirely without risks or potential side effects. The primary medical concern with these advanced treatments is an increased susceptibility to illness. You must be vigilant regarding biologic side effects, including infections and injection monitoring. Getting frequent chest colds, persistent urinary tract infections (UTIs), or recurrent thrush can make sexual intercourse highly uncomfortable or temporarily impossible. Recurrent thrush, in particular, can cause severe itching, soreness, and stinging pain during sex for both men and women.

If you notice an increase in these types of irritating infections, you must speak to your GP or local pharmacist promptly. They can provide targeted, fast-acting treatments for the infections themselves without necessarily needing to stop or pause your arthritis therapy.

Another crucial factor to consider is the psychological and logistical impact of taking biologics. These drugs are usually administered via a self-injection pen at home or through a lengthy intravenous infusion at a hospital clinic. Some people feel highly anxious about injecting themselves or develop mild, unsightly injection-site reactions, such as bruising, redness, or swelling on their stomach or thighs. This physical anxiety, or feeling deeply self-conscious about visible bruising on your skin, can subtly affect your body confidence and your desire to be physically vulnerable with a partner.

Logistics also play a role in romance. Many biologics must be kept strictly refrigerated. If you are planning a romantic weekend away or a holiday with your partner, having to travel with cooler bags and strict temperature-controlled medication can feel deeply unromantic and highly medicalised. Communication with your partner is vital here. Explaining exactly how your treatment works helps remove any stigma, normalises the routine, and prevents misunderstandings in your relationship.

NSAIDs, steroids and painkillers

Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), corticosteroids, and various analgesic painkillers are frequently used alongside your main DMARDs or biologics to manage acute, day-to-day symptoms. While they are incredibly useful for easing sharp, immediate pain, their long-term impact on your sexual function is heavily overlooked in routine medical consultations.

NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen, naproxen, or celecoxib, are standard, front-line treatments for reducing joint swelling and morning stiffness. Generally speaking, NSAIDs do not directly interfere with your sex drive, hormone levels, or physical arousal. However, if they are taken on an empty stomach or used long-term without gastric protection, they can cause severe indigestion, stomach ulcers, or painful heartburn. Experiencing persistent stomach pain is a surefire way to lose interest in physical intimacy. If this occurs, your GP might prescribe a secondary medication, like omeprazole, to protect your stomach lining, or suggest switching to a topical NSAID gel that you rub directly onto the affected joint to avoid stomach upset.

Corticosteroids, commonly referred to as steroids, are powerful, fast-acting anti-inflammatory drugs. They can be given as daily tablets, joint injections, or intravenous infusions to quickly bring severe arthritis flare-ups under control. Short-term use of steroids rarely causes sexual problems. In fact, a steroid injection often rapidly improves your libido by instantly reducing agonising pain and restoring your physical mobility.

Long-term, high-dose steroid use, however, presents a very different scenario. Taking oral steroids for extended periods can lead to noticeable weight gain, changes in the distribution of your body fat (often causing a rounded face), and severe thinning of the skin, making you highly prone to dark bruising. These visible physical changes can significantly impact your body image, self-esteem, and sexual confidence. Furthermore, long-term steroids can deeply interfere with your natural hormone production, potentially lowering essential testosterone levels in both men and women. This hormonal shift can result in a stark, noticeable drop in your sex drive.

Strong painkillers, particularly opioids or compound medications containing codeine, have a well-documented, powerful suppressive effect on the central nervous system. These drugs are highly effective at dampening pain signals, but they also indiscriminately dull other physical sensations across your entire body. This makes physical arousal much more difficult to achieve and maintain.

Opioids are also notoriously known to cause chronic constipation, nausea, and heavy drowsiness. Over time, the regular, daily use of strong painkillers can interfere with the brain's production of sex hormones. This directly leads to a profound loss of libido and, for many men, physical erectile dysfunction. If you rely heavily on strong opioid painkillers just to get through the day, it is well worth discussing alternative, long-term pain management strategies with your local health service to protect your sexual wellbeing.

Fertility, pregnancy and contraception cautions

When discussing sexual health, intimacy, and heavy arthritis medications, the delicate topic of fertility and pregnancy requires special, urgent attention. Many of the most highly effective drugs used to treat inflammatory arthritis are completely unsafe for a developing baby. If you are sexually active and of childbearing age, using strict, highly reliable contraception is an absolute medical necessity while on certain treatments.

Methotrexate is known to be highly teratogenic, meaning it can cause severe, life-threatening birth defects or lead to an early miscarriage. Crucially, this severe medical risk applies whether the drug is being taken by the man or the woman. If you are taking methotrexate, you must use reliable contraception at all times. If you decide that you want to try for a baby, you must speak to your rheumatologist well in advance of stopping your contraception. NICE guidance dictates a specific, mandatory "washout" period—usually lasting several months—during which you must completely stop taking the drug and allow it to clear from your system entirely before it is safe to conceive.

Leflunomide presents an even more complex challenge. This particular DMARD remains active in your bodily tissues for a very long time—sometimes up to two years—and carries highly similar severe risks for pregnancy. A specific, intensive washout procedure involving another binding medication is usually required to clear leflunomide from your body quickly and safely if you suddenly wish to conceive.

For men, as highlighted earlier, sulfasalazine can significantly, though temporarily, reduce your active sperm count. If you are a man taking this specific drug and you are having difficulty conceiving with your partner, your doctor can usually swap it for a safer alternative medication. Once the drug is stopped, your sperm count should return to normal, healthy levels within a few short months.

Biologic medications have widely varying guidelines regarding pregnancy and breastfeeding. Some older biologics are now considered safe to continue during the first and second trimesters of pregnancy, while others must be stopped months before conception. The safety data for newer, advanced biologics is constantly evolving as more research is conducted.

Because unplanned pregnancies do happen, you should have a frank, open conversation with your rheumatology team about your future family plans as early as possible. If you do become pregnant accidentally while taking a dangerous medication, contact your rheumatology team immediately for urgent advice. They will ensure your long-term treatment plan keeps your arthritis safely under control while fiercely protecting your future fertility and the health of any potential children.

What to do if you notice changes

If you strongly suspect your current medication is negatively affecting your sex life, the most important thing you can do is refuse to suffer in silence. It is completely normal to feel embarrassed, awkward, or shy when discussing physical intimacy, but your healthcare team handles these exact queries on a regular basis. Your sexual health is a fundamental, valid part of your overall medical care.

Start by discreetly tracking your symptoms. Note down exactly when you experience a drop in libido, extreme fatigue, or physical difficulties, and see if these patterns align with the specific days you take your injections or tablets. This clear, written information will be incredibly helpful for your GP or rheumatologist to review during your appointment.

You must never stop taking your prescribed medication abruptly just because you are experiencing sexual side effects. Stopping heavy drugs like oral steroids or biologics without strict medical supervision can cause a severe, painful arthritis flare-up, or trigger highly dangerous physical withdrawal symptoms.

Instead, request a routine appointment specifically to discuss your medication concerns. Your doctor might suggest slightly adjusting your dose, changing the time of day you take your pills to minimise fatigue, or switching to an alternative drug entirely. Sometimes, simply treating the secondary side effects—like prescribing an effective anti-sickness tablet for nausea—is all it takes to revive your energy and your sex drive.

Consider the timing of your intimacy in relation to your dosing schedule. If your weekly biologic injection leaves you feeling entirely wiped out for 24 hours, plan your romantic evenings for the days just before your next scheduled dose, when your physical energy levels are at their absolute highest.

Do not underestimate the immense value of speaking plainly to your partner. Chronic illness and complex medication side effects can easily create unspoken tension in any relationship. Explaining that your lack of desire is a documented chemical side effect of your tablets, rather than a lack of deep affection, can completely prevent feelings of rejection and help to build emotional intimacy.

Finally, remember that your local pharmacist is an excellent, highly accessible resource. They have extensive, specialised knowledge of complex drug interactions and common physical side effects, and they can offer you completely confidential, practical advice in a private consultation room, without the need for a GP appointment.

Key Takeaways

  • Medications effectively manage arthritis symptoms but can sometimes cause indirect side effects like extreme fatigue or nausea that significantly lower your sex drive.
  • Methotrexate does not typically cause direct physical sexual dysfunction, but the resulting exhaustion and malaise can heavily reduce your desire for intimacy.
  • Biologics often improve sexual function by eliminating joint pain, but they can increase your risk of irritating infections like thrush, which make sex uncomfortable.
  • Long-term use of oral steroids or strong opioid painkillers can directly alter your natural hormone levels and significantly dampen your physical libido.
  • Strict, reliable contraception is essential when taking certain DMARDs, as powerful drugs like methotrexate can cause severe harm to a developing baby.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I take erectile dysfunction medication with arthritis drugs?

Yes, in many cases, you can safely take common erectile dysfunction tablets alongside your arthritis treatment. However, you must speak to your GP or pharmacist first. They will carefully check for any potential chemical interactions, particularly if you also take medications for your heart, high blood pressure, or other chronic conditions alongside your standard arthritis prescriptions.

Will stopping my medication bring my sex drive back immediately?

It is dangerous to stop your arthritis medication suddenly, and it may not fix the issue immediately. Some powerful drugs take weeks or months to fully clear from your system. Furthermore, stopping treatment could cause a severe joint pain flare-up, which will likely worsen your sex drive. Always consult your rheumatology team before making any changes.

Do arthritis medications cause vaginal dryness?

While arthritis medications are not typically the direct, physical cause of vaginal dryness, certain strong drugs can disrupt your hormonal balance or dry out your mucous membranes. Sometimes, the dryness is actually linked to conditions like Sjogren's syndrome, which frequently occurs alongside rheumatoid arthritis. Speak to your GP, as simple lubricants or local hormone creams offer great relief.

Is it safe to try for a baby while on biologics?

Safety depends entirely on the specific biologic medication you are taking. Some modern biologics are considered perfectly safe to use during certain stages of pregnancy, while older ones must be stopped several months before conception. You must discuss your family planning with your rheumatology team well in advance to arrange a safe, closely monitored treatment transition.

Can over-the-counter painkillers affect my libido?

Standard over-the-counter painkillers like paracetamol or standard ibuprofen rarely affect your libido directly. However, if you rely heavily on pharmacy products that contain codeine, frequent daily use can heavily dampen your central nervous system, leading to chronic fatigue and a noticeably lower sex drive. If you need painkillers daily, seek professional advice from your local health service.

Why does my sex drive fluctuate during the week?

If you take strong medications on a strict weekly schedule, such as specific DMARD tablets or biologic injections, you may experience a predictable cycle of side effects. Many people feel exhausted, foggy, or nauseous for a day or two directly after their dose, which temporarily suppresses their physical desire. Planning intimacy for days when you feel your best can certainly help.

article.title: Arthritis Pain Management — A Kind, Practical Guide
article.excerpt: Manage arthritis pain with a whole-person UK approach: movement, heat and cold, medication, mindfulness, sleep, complementary therapies and emotional support.
article.content:
Clinically reviewed by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483. Last updated: June 2026.

Quick answer: Arthritis pain is influenced by physical factors, muscle tension, nervous system sensitisation, emotions, and sleep. Effective management takes a whole-person approach: exercise, sensible medication use, heat and cold therapy, and mindfulness. Prioritising sleep, setting realistic daily goals, and having a plan for flare-ups reduces pain and improves well-being. If pain affects your mood, speak to your GP.

Pain is the thing people most fear about arthritis. It can steal your sleep, sap your energy, and shrink your world. But pain is not simply something you must endure. It can be understood, managed, and — for many people — significantly reduced. This guide takes a whole-person approach. Pain is not just about joints. It is affected by how you move, eat, sleep, think, and feel. The more tools you have, the more control you gain.

Understanding Arthritis Pain

Arthritis pain is not a simple signal from a damaged joint to your brain. It is shaped by many factors: physical damage (cartilage loss, inflammation, joint changes), muscle tension (when joints hurt, surrounding muscles tighten protectively — causing more pain), sensitisation (over time the nervous system can become "tuned up" making pain feel worse than the physical damage alone would suggest), emotions and stress (anxiety, low mood, and stress lower pain tolerance and amplify pain), and fatigue and poor sleep (pain and sleep are locked in a miserable dance — pain disrupts sleep, and poor sleep makes pain worse). Managing pain effectively requires addressing more than just the joint.

Movement and Exercise for Pain Relief

It is the oldest paradox in arthritis: movement hurts, but not moving hurts more. Every NICE guideline on arthritis places exercise at the centre of pain management. Why it works: strengthening muscles reduces load on joints; movement stimulates synovial fluid release lubricating joints; exercise triggers endorphins — your body's natural painkillers; regular movement "calms down" a sensitised nervous system over time. What kind? Walking (start with 5–10 minutes), swimming or pool-based exercise, cycling, yoga or tai chi, physio-prescribed strength exercises. The key is pacing. A little every day beats a lot once a week.

Heat and Cold Therapy

Simple, cheap, and genuinely effective. Heat therapy is best for stiff, achy chronic pain (especially OA-related) — it relaxes muscles, improves blood flow, and eases stiffness. Try a warm bath or shower, a microwavable wheat bag, an electric heat pad (low setting, never sleep with it on), or warm water exercises. Cold therapy is best for hot, swollen, inflamed joints (common in RA, gout, or acute OA flares) — it numbs the area and reduces swelling. Try a bag of frozen peas wrapped in a tea towel (15 minutes max), a gel ice pack (never directly on skin), or a bowl of cool water for hands or feet. Some people find alternating heat and cold helpful.

Pain Medications — What Works

Medication is one tool among many. Paracetamol for mild-to-moderate pain (over the counter). NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) for pain plus inflammation (over the counter or prescription). Topical gels for localised joint pain (over the counter). Opioids (codeine, tramadol) for severe short-term pain (prescription only). DMARDs/biologics for underlying inflammation in RA (prescription, specialist). Steroid injections for flare-ups in a single joint (GP or rheumatologist). Always take medication at the dose prescribed and speak to your GP before making changes.

Mindfulness and Relaxation Techniques

It might sound "soft" compared to medication or surgery — but mindfulness and relaxation have solid evidence for reducing chronic pain. A 2019 review in the British Journal of Pain found mindfulness-based interventions reduced pain intensity and improved quality of life. Why it helps: reduces muscle tension, lowers stress hormones that amplify pain, changes your relationship with pain — making it feel less overwhelming. Simple techniques: box breathing (in for 4, hold for 4, out for 4, hold for 4 — repeat 5 times), body scan (lie down and mentally scan from toes to head noticing and releasing tension), guided relaxation apps (NHS-recommended like Headspace and Calm offer free sessions), progressive muscle relaxation (tense each muscle group for 5 seconds then release — work from feet to face).

Sleep and Pain — Breaking the Cycle

Pain makes sleep hard. Poor sleep makes pain worse. Breaking this cycle is one of the most impactful things you can do. Stick to a schedule — same bedtime and wake time every day. Create a wind-down ritual: a warm bath, a book (not a screen), gentle stretches, a heat pack. Manage your sleep environment: a supportive mattress, a pillow between your knees for hip or knee pain, cool room temperature. Avoid caffeine after 2pm and alcohol close to bedtime. If you wake in pain, have a plan — a wheat bag by the bed, medication within reach, a guided breathing exercise queued on your phone. If sleep problems persist, speak to your GP.

Complementary Approaches

Some approaches with reasonable evidence: acupuncture (NICE does not recommend it for OA on the NHS, but some people report meaningful relief — private sessions cost £40–£80), massage therapy (may ease muscle tension around painful joints), TENS (a small device delivering mild electrical pulses — NICE does not recommend for OA but some find it helpful, units cost £20–£50), capsaicin cream (from chilli peppers, applied to skin over a joint — takes 1–2 weeks of regular use to work).

Creating Your Pain Management Toolkit

Daily tools: gentle movement, heat pack during your morning coffee, anti-inflammatory food choices, mindfulness practice. Bad-day tools: pain medication as prescribed, ice or heat as needed, pacing — do one important thing then rest, distraction — a film, a friend, a book. Emergency tools (severe flare): GP or rheumatologist contact details, flare plan (medications, rest strategy), support network — someone to help with shopping, children, or pets.

When Pain Affects Your Mood — Getting Support

Living with persistent pain changes how you feel. It is not a sign of weakness to struggle. Anxiety and depression are more common in people with arthritis than in the general population. The NHS takes this seriously. Talk to your GP — they can refer you to NHS talking therapies (IAPT). These are free and effective. Join a support group — Arthritis Action and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) run groups across the UK, in person and online. Be honest with loved ones — hiding how you feel makes it harder for people to support you. Pain is not your fault. And you do not have to manage it alone.

  • How to Manage Fibromyalgia Flare Ups Without Medication — Practical, evidence-based strategies for managing fibromyalgia flare ups without increasing medication — pacing, sleep, heat, movement and.
  • Expert Q&A: How to Talk to Your GP About Medication Worries — Concerns are valid. A practical script for an honest conversation.
  • Managing Methotrexate Side Effects: Practical Tips — Nausea, fatigue and mouth ulcers are common — and largely manageable with simple tweaks.
  • Arthritis Flare-Ups — How to Recognise, Manage, and Recover — Learn how to spot the early signs of an arthritis flare, what to do when one hits, the role of medication, and how to prevent future.

Practical next steps for Arthritis Pain Management — A Kind, Practical Guide

If you came here about Arthritis Pain Management — A Kind, Practical Guide, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your local integrated care board about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Making information usable

Treat articles like this as a starting map, not a personal care plan. Highlight one idea to try for two weeks, then review. If symptoms are new, rapidly worsening, or affecting several joints with fever or unexplained weight loss, contact your GP promptly rather than waiting on self-help alone.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

Quick questions about Arthritis Pain Management Kind

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

article.title: Arthritis Pain Map by Joint: Where It Hurts and What It May Mean
article.excerpt: A plain-English, joint-by-joint guide to where arthritis tends to cause pain, from hands and knees to hips, spine, shoulders and feet, which patterns point to which types of arthritis, what else can mimic them, and when to get checked.
article.content:
Quick answer: Different types of arthritis tend to affect different joints. Osteoarthritis commonly affects knees, hips, the base of the thumb, finger end joints and the spine. Rheumatoid arthritis often starts in the small joints of the hands and feet on both sides. Gout often affects the big toe. A pain map is a guide only; your GP can confirm the cause.

Where your pain is can say a lot. Different types of arthritis have favourite joints and typical patterns, and other common problems such as tendon pain, bursitis or trapped nerves can mimic them. This pain map walks through the body joint by joint, explaining what is common, what else it could be, and when to get checked. It is for understanding, not self-diagnosis: only a clinician who examines you, sometimes with tests, can tell you what is causing your pain.

How to use this pain map

  1. Find the joint or area that hurts in the sections below.
  2. Note the pattern: which side, whether it is one joint or many, whether both sides are affected equally, how long morning stiffness lasts, and whether there is swelling.
  3. Read the "could also be" notes. Many joint-area pains come from tendons, muscles or nerves rather than the joint itself.
  4. Write it down and take it to your GP or physiotherapist. A simple record helps them a lot. Our pain tracking journal includes a joint map you can tick.

The big picture: patterns that point to different types

PatternOften seen in
Weight-bearing joints (knees, hips), base of thumb, end finger joints, spine; pain worse with use, short morning stiffnessOsteoarthritis
Small joints of hands (knuckles, middle finger joints) and feet, wrists, often both sides; swelling; morning stiffness over 30 minutesRheumatoid arthritis
Sudden, very painful, hot, swollen single joint, often the big toeGout (but infection must be ruled out)
Finger or toe end joints, a whole swollen "sausage" finger or toe, heel pain, often with psoriasisPsoriatic arthritis
Lower back and buttock pain and stiffness, worse with rest and at night, better with exercise, usually starting before 45Axial spondyloarthritis, including ankylosing spondylitis
Aching and stiffness in both shoulders and hips, usually over 50, coming on over days to weeksPolymyalgia rheumatica
Widespread pain, tiredness, poor sleep, tender areas rather than swollen jointsFibromyalgia (can occur alongside arthritis)

Hands and wrists

Base of the thumb

Aching at the base of the thumb, where it meets the wrist, especially when gripping, turning keys or opening jars, is a very common site for osteoarthritis. The base of the thumb may look slightly squared off over time.

Could also be: de Quervain's tenosynovitis, a tendon problem causing pain on the thumb side of the wrist, often with pain when moving the thumb.

Finger end joints and middle joints

Hard, bony lumps on the end joints of the fingers (Heberden's nodes) or the middle joints (Bouchard's nodes) are typical of hand osteoarthritis. They can be red and sore when they first form, then often settle. Psoriatic arthritis can also affect the end joints, sometimes with nail changes.

Knuckles and middle finger joints with swelling

Soft, puffy swelling of the knuckles or middle finger joints, often on both hands, with stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes in the morning, is a typical pattern in rheumatoid arthritis. The NHS lists the hands, feet and wrists as commonly affected first.

Wrist

Rheumatoid arthritis often affects the wrists. Osteoarthritis of the wrist is less common and often follows an old injury.

Could also be: carpal tunnel syndrome, which causes tingling, numbness or pain in the thumb, index and middle fingers, often worse at night. The NHS notes it can be linked to arthritis.

See our hand arthritis guide and hand exercises.

Elbows

Elbow arthritis is less common. It can occur in rheumatoid arthritis, after an old injury, or in people who have done heavy manual work. Signs include stiffness, difficulty fully straightening the arm, and sometimes locking.

Could also be: tennis elbow or golfer's elbow (tendon pain on the outer or inner elbow), or olecranon bursitis, a soft swelling over the point of the elbow. A hot, red bursa with fever needs urgent assessment for infection.

Shoulders

Deep ache and stiffness in the shoulder joint

Osteoarthritis of the main shoulder joint can cause a deep ache, stiffness and grinding, and difficulty lifting the arm or reaching behind you. It is less common than knee or hip osteoarthritis.

Top of the shoulder

Pain on the top of the shoulder, at the bony point where the collarbone meets the shoulder blade, can come from osteoarthritis of that smaller joint, often worse when reaching across the body.

Both shoulders, with hip stiffness, over 50

Aching and stiffness in both shoulders and often both hips, worse in the morning, coming on over a short time, can be polymyalgia rheumatica. See a GP promptly. If you also have headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain when chewing or vision changes, get same-day help.

Could also be: rotator cuff problems (pain on the outer upper arm when lifting), or frozen shoulder (severe stiffness in all directions). See our shoulder arthritis guide.

Neck and back

Neck

Age-related changes in the neck joints and discs, sometimes called cervical spondylosis, are very common and often cause stiffness and aching. Pain can spread to the shoulders or between the shoulder blades. In long-standing rheumatoid arthritis, the top of the neck can be affected, so new neck pain with tingling in the hands or feet should be checked promptly.

Lower back

Osteoarthritis of the small spinal joints is a common cause of stiffness and aching, often worse after sitting or first thing, and better after moving around. Inflammatory back pain from axial spondyloarthritis is different: it usually starts before age 45, comes on gradually, is worse with rest and in the second half of the night, and improves with exercise. The NHS notes that ankylosing spondylitis symptoms often improve with exercise and worsen with rest.

Could also be: muscle strain, a disc problem, or sciatica, which causes pain shooting down the leg.

Hips and groin

Groin and front of the hip

Hip osteoarthritis most often causes pain in the groin or front of the thigh, sometimes spreading to the knee. People often notice difficulty putting on socks and shoes, getting in and out of cars and walking longer distances.

Outer side of the hip

Pain on the outside of the hip, often worse lying on that side or climbing stairs, is commonly due to tendon or bursa irritation (greater trochanteric pain syndrome) rather than the hip joint itself.

Buttock

Buttock pain can come from the lower back or the sacroiliac joints, which are commonly affected in axial spondyloarthritis.

See our hip arthritis guide.

Knees

Inner side of the knee

The inner part of the knee is the most common site of knee osteoarthritis, causing pain on walking, stairs and getting up from chairs, with stiffness after rest that usually eases within 30 minutes.

Front of the knee and behind the kneecap

Pain around or behind the kneecap, worse on stairs, kneeling or squatting, can come from osteoarthritis behind the kneecap or from irritation of the tissues around it.

Swollen knee

Knee swelling can happen in osteoarthritis, especially after a busy day. A large, warm, swollen knee can also occur in inflammatory arthritis, gout or pseudogout. A sudden hot, swollen, very painful knee with fever needs urgent help.

Could also be: a meniscus (cartilage) tear, especially after a twist, or a Baker's cyst, a swelling behind the knee. See our knee arthritis guide.

Ankles and feet

Big toe

Two common causes: gout, which the NHS describes as sudden severe pain, often in the big toe, with a hot, swollen, red joint; and osteoarthritis of the big toe joint (hallux rigidus), which causes stiffness and pain when pushing off to walk, sometimes with a bony lump on top.

Ball of the foot and toes

Pain and swelling across the balls of the feet, sometimes feeling like walking on pebbles, is a common early sign of rheumatoid arthritis. Psoriatic arthritis can cause a whole toe to swell.

Midfoot and ankle

Osteoarthritis of the midfoot causes aching across the top of the foot, often with a bony bump. Ankle osteoarthritis usually follows an old injury or fracture.

Heel

Heel pain is usually plantar fasciitis, but in psoriatic arthritis and axial spondyloarthritis, inflammation where the tendons attach to the heel is common.

See our foot and ankle arthritis guide.

Jaw

The jaw joint can be affected by osteoarthritis and inflammatory arthritis, causing pain when chewing, clicking or difficulty opening the mouth. Jaw pain when chewing in someone over 50, especially with headache or scalp tenderness, needs same-day medical advice because it can be a sign of giant cell arteritis.

What to do with your pain map

  • Book a GP appointment if you have joint pain that has lasted more than a few weeks, or has no diagnosis yet. In many areas you can also self-refer to NHS physiotherapy for joint and muscle problems.
  • Bring your notes: which joints, when the pain started, morning stiffness time, swelling, and what makes it better or worse.
  • Do not wait for tests to start helping yourself. NICE's osteoarthritis guideline (NG226) says osteoarthritis can usually be diagnosed clinically, without X-rays or blood tests, in people over 45 with typical symptoms. Exercise, weight management where relevant, and the right information are core treatments.
  • Do not self-diagnose from a chart. Patterns overlap, and some people have more than one condition.

When to get medical help

  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E for a suddenly hot, red, swollen, very painful joint, especially with fever or feeling unwell, or if you cannot weight-bear after a fall.
  • Go to A&E or call 999 for back pain with new numbness around the bottom or genitals, problems controlling your bladder or bowel, or weakness in both legs.
  • Get same-day help if you are over 50 with a new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain on chewing or vision changes. Call 999 or go to A&E for any loss of vision.
  • See your GP soon for swollen joints, morning stiffness over 30 minutes most days, new stiffness in both shoulders or hips if you are over 50, or joint pain with unexplained weight loss, fevers or night sweats.
  • Call 999 for chest pain, severe breathlessness or signs of a stroke.

Which joints does osteoarthritis usually affect?

Osteoarthritis most commonly affects the knees, hips, the base of the thumb, the end and middle finger joints, the big toe and the spine. Pain is usually worse with use and stiffness after rest tends to ease within about 30 minutes.

Which joints does rheumatoid arthritis affect first?

Rheumatoid arthritis often starts in the small joints of the hands and feet and the wrists, usually on both sides of the body. Joints may be swollen, warm and tender, with morning stiffness lasting longer than 30 minutes.

Is pain on the outside of my hip arthritis?

Often not. Pain on the outer hip, worse lying on that side or on stairs, is commonly from tendons or a bursa around the hip. Hip joint arthritis more often causes pain in the groin or front of the thigh. A GP or physiotherapist can tell the difference.

Can arthritis in the hip cause knee pain?

Yes. Hip arthritis can cause pain felt in the thigh or knee, which is called referred pain. If you have knee pain but your knee looks and feels normal when examined, your clinician may check your hip.

What does gout in the big toe feel like?

The NHS describes sudden, severe pain in a joint, often the big toe, with the joint becoming hot, swollen and red, and the skin shiny. Attacks often start at night. Because joint infection can look similar, get urgent advice if you have a fever or feel unwell.

Do I need an X-ray to find out which type of arthritis I have?

Not always. NICE says osteoarthritis can usually be diagnosed from your symptoms and an examination in people over 45. Blood tests, X-rays or scans may be used if inflammatory arthritis, gout or another cause is suspected.

article.title: Natural Pain Relief for Arthritis: Evidence-Based Home Remedies
article.excerpt: Evidence-based natural pain relief methods for arthritis. From heat therapy and turmeric to TENS machines and essential oils — what the research says about.
article.content:
While medication plays an important role in arthritis management, many people seek natural, drug-free approaches to complement their treatment. The good news is that several natural remedies have genuine scientific evidence supporting their use. This comprehensive guide examines the most effective evidence-based natural pain relief methods for arthritis, separating proven approaches from popular myths.

Quick answer: Heat relaxes muscles and reduces stiffness, useful for chronic pain. Cold numbs pain and reduces swelling, effective for flare-ups. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you. TENS machines use electrical currents for pain relief. Topical capsaicin cream and arnica gel can also alleviate joint pain.

Heat and Cold Therapy

The simplest and most time-tested natural pain relief for arthritis. Both heat and cold have distinct benefits and can be used at different times.

Heat Therapy

Heat relaxes muscles, increases blood flow, reduces stiffness and improves joint flexibility. It's most effective for chronic, aching pain and morning stiffness. Methods include hot water bottles wrapped in a towel (15–20 minutes), warm baths or showers, heated wheat bags (microwaveable), paraffin wax baths (particularly for hand arthritis), warm packs from pharmacies, and heated blankets or pads for overnight use. Best for: Morning stiffness, before exercise, chronic aching pain.

Cold Therapy

Cold reduces inflammation, numbs pain receptors and decreases swelling. It's most effective during flare-ups and after activity. Methods include ice packs wrapped in a towel (never directly on skin), frozen pea bags (conformable and reusable), cold gel packs from pharmacies, and cold-water immersion. Apply for 10–15 minutes at a time, with at least 1 hour between applications. Best for: Acute flare-ups, after exercise, hot swollen joints.

Turmeric and Curcumin

Turmeric is the most evidence-based herbal remedy for arthritis. Its active compound curcumin has powerful anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. A systematic review of 8 randomised controlled trials (involving over 800 participants) found that curcumin supplementation produced significant improvements in pain, physical function and stiffness in osteoarthritis patients. Some studies suggest effects comparable to NSAIDs like ibuprofen, with fewer side effects. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you. Look for formulations containing piperine (black pepper extract) or using liposomal/nano-curcumin technology, which increase absorption by up to 2,000%. Available from UK pharmacies and health food shops.

Ginger

Ginger contains gingerols and shogaols that inhibit inflammatory pathways (COX-2 and cytokine production). A meta-analysis published in Osteoarthritis and Cartilage found that ginger supplementation produced modest but significant pain reduction in OA. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you. Fresh ginger can be used in cooking — 1–2 cm fresh root grated into meals, smoothies or hot water for tea. Generally well tolerated but may cause mild digestive effects. Start low and increase gradually.

TENS (Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation)

TENS uses low-voltage electrical currents to reduce pain signals. Evidence is moderate but many patients find significant benefit. A Cochrane review found that TENS provided short-term pain relief for knee OA. TENS machines are available from UK pharmacies for £20–£60 without prescription. They're safe, drug-free and can be used alongside other treatments. Place electrode pads around the painful joint as directed. Use for 20–30 minutes per session. Adjust intensity to feel a comfortable tingling without pain.

Omega-3 Fatty Acids

Strong evidence supports omega-3s from oily fish and fish oil supplements for reducing inflammation. Particularly effective for inflammatory types of arthritis (RA, PsA). Target 2–3g combined EPA+DHA daily for anti-inflammatory effect. Include oily fish at least twice weekly: salmon, mackerel, sardines, herring. See our detailed omega-3 guide for comprehensive information.

Topical Remedies

Capsaicin Cream

Derived from chilli peppers, capsaicin works by depleting substance P (a pain neurotransmitter) from nerve endings. Apply to the affected joint 3–4 times daily. Expect an initial burning sensation that diminishes with regular use over 1–2 weeks. Available over the counter in UK pharmacies (e.g., Zacin cream). Evidence supports its use for both OA and RA pain.

Arnica

Topical arnica gel has some evidence for musculoskeletal pain relief. A randomised trial found arnica gel comparable to ibuprofen gel for hand OA. Available from pharmacies and health food shops. Apply 3–4 times daily to affected joints. Do not use on broken skin.

Essential Oils

Limited but emerging evidence for several oils when used in massage. Eucalyptus oil has anti-inflammatory properties. Lavender may help with pain and relaxation. Peppermint provides a cooling sensation that can distract from pain. Rosemary has shown anti-inflammatory effects in laboratory studies. Always dilute in a carrier oil (e.g., sweet almond, coconut). Massage itself provides additional benefit through improved circulation and relaxation.

Acupuncture

Acupuncture involves inserting thin needles at specific points. NICE currently recommends considering acupuncture as part of a multi-component approach for chronic pain. A meta-analysis in the Journal of Pain found that acupuncture provided clinically meaningful improvement in OA pain versus sham acupuncture. Available through some NHS pain clinics (GP referral) or privately. Look for practitioners registered with the British Acupuncture Council. Typical course involves 6–12 sessions.

Mind-Body Approaches

Mindfulness Meditation

It is generally thought that mindfulness can change pain perception, reduce distress and improve coping. An 8-week Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) programme produced significant improvements in pain, physical function and psychological well-being in arthritis patients.

Tai Chi

Endorsed by NICE and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis). A major systematic review found tai chi significantly improved pain, stiffness and physical function in OA. Free tai chi classes are available in many UK community centres and parks. Online programmes make it accessible from home.

Yoga

Gentle, modified yoga improves flexibility, strength and mental well-being. See our dedicated yoga for arthritis guide.

What Doesn't Work (or Lacks Evidence)

  • Copper bracelets — No credible evidence despite widespread use
  • Magnetic therapy — Systematic reviews find no significant benefit over placebo
  • Collagen drinks — Oral collagen may have modest benefit, but trendy "collagen water" products rarely contain therapeutic doses
  • Alkaline diets — The body tightly regulates blood pH regardless of diet. No evidence for arthritis benefit
  • Cider vinegar — Popular folklore remedy with no scientific evidence for arthritis

Building Your Natural Pain Relief Toolkit

The most effective approach combines multiple evidence-based methods. A practical natural pain management routine might include morning heat therapy and gentle stretching (15 minutes), turmeric and omega-3 supplements with breakfast, regular low-impact exercise, TENS machine during flare-ups, cold therapy after activity, mindfulness or relaxation practice in the evening, and weekly tai chi or yoga class. These approaches work best alongside — not instead of — any prescribed medical treatment. Always inform your GP about supplements you take, as some may interact with medications.

Our virtual assistant can help you build a personalised natural pain relief plan based on your arthritis type and preferences.

This article is for general information only. Consult your GP before starting new supplements or therapies, particularly if you take prescription medication.

  • TENS Machines for Arthritis – Do They Work? UK Guide — Complete UK guide to using TENS machines for arthritis pain.
  • Topical NSAIDs: Often Overlooked, Often Effective — Gels and creams deliver pain relief with fewer systemic side effects — especially for knees and hands.
  • Painkillers in older adults with arthritis: caution, not dosing (UK) — UK readers managing pain in several joints often need smaller doses of movement more than a heroic gym restart.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have chest pain, sudden weakness or numbness, severe breathlessness, a suspected broken bone after a fall, or back pain with new loss of bladder or bowel control or numbness around your bottom or genitals.

Contact NHS 111 or your GP urgently if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel unwell or have a fever, or if your symptoms are getting rapidly worse.

Turmeric (500–1,000 mg curcumin daily) and ginger (500–1,000 mg extract daily) have anti-inflammatory benefits. TENS machines use electrical currents for pain relief. Topical capsaicin cream and arnica gel can also alleviate joint pain.

article.title: Pain Scale Explained: How to Rate Your Arthritis Pain (UK)
article.excerpt: A plain-English guide to pain scales: what 0 to 10 really means, a description for each number, how to score arthritis pain consistently, other scales NHS clinicians use, and how to describe your pain so your GP or physio understands it.
article.content:
Quick answer: A pain scale is a way to describe how much something hurts, usually from 0 (no pain) to 10 (the worst pain you can imagine). Rate your pain the same way each time, for example your average over the day, and add how it affects sleep, work and daily tasks. There is no right or wrong number.

"On a scale of 0 to 10, how bad is your pain?" It is one of the most common questions in healthcare, and one of the hardest to answer. Is a 6 a lot? Will saying 8 sound like an exaggeration? Should you score the worst moment, or today in general? This guide explains what pain scales are for, how to use them consistently with arthritis, and how to go beyond the number so your GP, physiotherapist or rheumatology team really understands what you are living with.

Why clinicians use pain scales

Pain cannot be seen on an X-ray or measured in a blood test. Only you know how much it hurts. A pain scale turns that personal experience into something that can be compared over time. It helps:

  • Track change. Is your pain better, worse or the same as last month?
  • Judge whether treatment is working. If a new exercise programme, medicine or injection is helping, your scores should come down.
  • Spot flares. A jump above your usual level can signal a flare.
  • Start a conversation. The number opens the discussion; it does not close it.

A pain score is not a test you can pass or fail. There is no correct number for a particular condition, and your score does not decide whether you deserve treatment. NICE's chronic pain guideline (NG193) emphasises a person-centred assessment that looks at how pain affects your life, not just its intensity.

The 0 to 10 scale explained

The most common scale in the NHS is the numeric rating scale, from 0 to 10. Descriptions vary between services. The table below is a common, practical guide, not an official definition.

ScoreWhat it often meansTypical effect on daily life
0No painNone
1–3Mild pain: noticeable but you can ignore it much of the timeYou can do most things; pain is in the background
4–6Moderate pain: hard to ignore, interrupts concentrationYou can do daily tasks but with difficulty or changes; may affect sleep
7–9Severe pain: dominates your attentionHard to do normal activities, sleep or concentrate; may need to stop and rest
10The worst pain you can imagineUnable to do anything else

Many people with long-term arthritis live with pain in the 2 to 5 range on ordinary days, with higher scores during flares, but everyone is different. Your scores are about you, not about anyone else.

How to score your pain consistently

The number is most useful when you use it the same way every time. Decide on your approach and stick to it:

  1. Choose what you are scoring. Common choices are your average pain over the last 24 hours, your pain right now, or your worst pain today. Average pain is often the most useful for tracking.
  2. Score at a similar time each day. For example, each evening for the day just gone.
  3. Score the main painful area, or score key joints separately if they behave differently, such as knee 5, hands 3.
  4. Anchor your top end. Think of 10 as the worst pain imaginable, not the worst pain you have had. This leaves room above, and stops you running out of scale during a bad flare.
  5. Do not compare with others. Your 6 does not have to match someone else's 6.
  6. Be honest, not strategic. Scoring higher to be taken seriously, or lower to seem brave, makes the number less useful. Describe the impact instead (see below).

Why your score can change from day to day

It is normal for pain scores to vary, even when nothing obvious has changed. Pain is shaped not only by what is happening in your joints but also by sleep, stress, mood, tiredness, activity levels and what else is going on in your life. A poor night or a worrying week can push scores up; a good night's sleep or an enjoyable day can bring them down. This is not "all in your head". It reflects how the nervous system processes pain, which our guide to understanding pain explains. It is also why looking at the pattern over a week or a month is more useful than any single day's number.

Other scales you may come across

Verbal rating scale

Instead of numbers, you choose a word: none, mild, moderate or severe. It is simple and useful if numbers feel unnatural.

Visual analogue scale

A 10 cm line with "no pain" at one end and "worst pain imaginable" at the other. You mark where your pain sits, and the distance is measured. It is often used in research.

Faces scales

A row of faces from happy to very distressed. Originally designed for children, they can help adults who find numbers difficult.

Observational tools

For people who cannot easily communicate their pain, for example some people with advanced dementia, staff may use tools such as the Abbey Pain Scale or PAINAD, which look at facial expression, breathing, body language and behaviour. Carers' observations are very valuable here.

Arthritis-specific questionnaires

Your clinicians may use questionnaires that combine pain with function. Examples include the Oxford Knee Score and Oxford Hip Score, often used before and after joint replacement, and questionnaires that ask about daily activities, such as the Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ) in rheumatoid arthritis. In rheumatoid arthritis, clinicians also use a measure of disease activity called DAS28, which combines a count of swollen and tender joints, a blood test and your overall rating of how you are.

Going beyond the number

A number alone misses a lot. Two people who both score 6 may have very different experiences. To give the full picture, describe:

Where

Which joints or areas, one side or both, and whether pain spreads. Our pain map by joint can help you describe this.

What it feels like

Words help clinicians understand the type of pain:

  • Aching, stiff, grinding are common in osteoarthritis
  • Throbbing, hot, swollen can suggest inflammation
  • Burning, shooting, tingling, electric can suggest nerve involvement
  • Sharp, catching may come with particular movements

When

Morning stiffness and how long it lasts, pain with activity or rest, night pain, and whether it is constant or comes and goes.

What makes it better or worse

Activity, rest, warmth, cold, medicines, weather, stress or sleep.

How it affects your life

This is often the most important part. Examples: "I can only walk for 10 minutes", "I wake three times a night", "I can no longer open jars", "I have had to cut my hours at work", "I have stopped seeing friends". NICE's chronic pain guideline highlights the impact of pain on daily life, sleep, mood and relationships as central to assessment.

Example: two ways to describe the same pain

Number only: "My knee is a 7."

Full picture: "My right knee averages about 5 out of 10 on a normal day, but it has been 7 most days this month. It aches and feels stiff for about 20 minutes in the morning, and it is worst on stairs and after walking more than 10 minutes. It wakes me most nights. I have stopped walking the dog, and I am struggling with my job, which involves standing."

The second gives your clinician much more to work with, and makes it far more likely that the conversation leads to useful next steps.

Using pain scores at appointments

  • Track your scores for two to four weeks beforehand. Our pain tracking journal makes this easy.
  • Bring your usual score, your worst recent score, and how often you have flares.
  • Add two or three examples of how pain affects your daily life.
  • Say what matters most to you, such as sleeping through the night or getting back to work.
  • Our clinic appointment pack helps you prepare.

What a "good" result looks like

For many long-term conditions, being completely pain-free is not a realistic goal. A meaningful improvement might be a drop of a couple of points, fewer flares, better sleep or being able to do something important again. When you start a new treatment, agree with your clinician what improvement you are hoping for and how you will judge it. The NHS page on ways to manage chronic pain also emphasises self-help approaches such as staying active, pacing and relaxation alongside treatment.

Pain scores and carers

If you care for someone who finds it hard to rate their pain, ask them simple questions ("Is it a little or a lot?"), use a faces or verbal scale, or note what you observe, such as wincing, guarding a joint, being restless, sleeping poorly or eating less. Write down who recorded each score. These observations are useful for GPs, nurses and care home staff.

When to get medical help

A pain score is for tracking, not for deciding whether to seek urgent help. The type and pattern of symptoms matter more than the number:

  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E for a suddenly hot, red, swollen, very painful joint, especially with fever or feeling unwell, even if you score it lower than you expect.
  • Call 999 for chest pain, severe breathlessness, signs of a stroke, or sudden severe pain with collapse.
  • Go to A&E or call 999 for back pain with numbness around the bottom or genitals, bladder or bowel problems, or weakness in both legs.
  • See your GP if your usual scores are rising, pain is waking you most nights, or it is stopping you doing things that matter to you.
  • See your GP if pain is affecting your mood. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, call NHS 111 or Samaritans free on 116 123.

What does a 7 out of 10 pain score mean?

A 7 usually means severe pain that dominates your attention and makes normal activities, sleep or concentration hard. Descriptions vary, and the number is personal. Explaining how the pain affects your day gives your clinician the most useful information.

Should I score my worst pain or my average pain?

Choose one and stay consistent. Average pain over the last 24 hours is often the most useful for tracking change over weeks. If you have occasional severe spikes, note your worst score as well.

What if I find it hard to give my pain a number?

That is common. Try a word scale (none, mild, moderate, severe), a faces scale, or describe what you can and cannot do. Clinicians are used to working with different ways of describing pain.

Will my GP think I am exaggerating if I say a high number?

Your pain score is your own report, and there is no right or wrong number. Describing the impact on your daily life, sleep and work alongside the number helps your clinician understand your score and plan next steps.

What pain scale do NHS physiotherapists use?

Many use the 0 to 10 numeric rating scale, often alongside questionnaires about function, such as the Oxford Knee or Hip Score. They will also ask what makes pain better or worse and what activities you find difficult.

How much should my pain score drop for a treatment to be working?

There is no single figure for everyone. A drop of a couple of points, fewer flares, better sleep or being able to do an important activity again can all be meaningful. Agree with your clinician what you are aiming for.

article.title: Arthritis Pain Tracking Journal: Free Printable Template (UK)
article.excerpt: A free, printable arthritis pain tracking journal with daily and weekly tables, a flare log and an appointment summary, plus simple guidance on what to record, how to spot patterns and how to share it with your GP or rheumatology team.
article.content:
Quick answer: An arthritis pain journal is a simple daily record of pain, stiffness, swelling, sleep, activity and medicines. Filling it in for a few minutes each day helps you spot patterns and triggers, see whether changes are helping, and give your GP or rheumatology team clear information. Print the free template on this page and start today.

When a GP or rheumatology nurse asks "How has it been?", it is surprisingly hard to answer. Good days blur into bad ones, and it is easy to remember only the last week. A simple pain journal solves that. It takes a few minutes a day, and over a few weeks it shows you, and your clinicians, what is really going on. This page gives you a ready-to-print template and explains how to use it well, without turning your life into a spreadsheet.

Why keep an arthritis pain journal

  • Spot patterns and possible triggers. You may notice pain is worse after certain activities, poor sleep, stress, missed medicines or busy weekends.
  • See whether changes help. When you start a new exercise, splint, medicine or pacing plan, the journal shows whether things are improving over weeks, not just on the day.
  • Make appointments count. Clear, dated information helps clinicians judge how active your arthritis is. NICE's rheumatoid arthritis guideline (NG100) is built around regular monitoring and adjusting treatment, and good records from you support that.
  • Recognise flares early. Comparing today with your usual pattern makes it easier to tell a real flare from an ordinary bad day.
  • Support benefit or work conversations. A record of how symptoms affect daily life can help when discussing adjustments at work or applying for benefits. For PIP, use our dedicated PIP evidence diary, which focuses on daily living tasks.

What to record (and what you can skip)

The best journal is one you actually keep. Start with the essentials and add more only if it is useful.

Essentials (every day, about 2 minutes)

  • Pain score from 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst pain imaginable), ideally at the same time each day. Our pain scale guide explains how to score consistently.
  • Morning stiffness in minutes, from waking to feeling "loosened up".
  • Sleep as good, fair or poor.
  • Main activity that day, for example a long walk, gardening, a work day or a rest day.

Useful extras

  • Which joints hurt, and whether any are swollen, warm or red
  • Tiredness from 0 to 10
  • Mood from 0 to 10, or a word such as calm, low or worried
  • Medicines taken, including any extra pain relief
  • What helped, such as warmth, a walk, a rest or a gadget
  • Possible triggers, such as an infection, stress, travel or a change in routine

What you can skip

You do not need to record every meal, every step or every twinge. Over-tracking can make you more focused on pain and can be tiring. If a detail is not helping you or your clinicians make decisions, leave it out.

Your printable pain tracking journal

Use your browser's print option to print this page, or save it as a PDF from the print window. Print the weekly table several times so you have one sheet per week.

Template 1: my baseline (fill in once)

QuestionMy answer
My type of arthritis (as diagnosed) 
Joints usually affected 
My usual pain score on an ordinary day (0–10) 
My usual morning stiffness (minutes) 
Things that usually make it worse 
Things that usually help 
Regular medicines and doses 
What I want to be able to do (my goals) 

Template 2: weekly pain journal

Week starting: ____________________

DayPain 0–10 (am / pm)Stiffness (mins)Swollen or warm jointsSleep (good / fair / poor)Tiredness 0–10Main activityExtra pain reliefNotes / what helped
Mon /        
Tue /        
Wed /        
Thu /        
Fri /        
Sat /        
Sun /        

Weekly review: best day ______ worst day ______ anything I noticed: ______________________________

Template 3: joint map for the week

Tick the joints that were painful (P), swollen (S) or stiff (St) this week.

JointLeftRight
Jaw  
Neck / back (write which) 
Shoulder  
Elbow  
Wrist  
Hand / fingers (write which)  
Hip  
Knee  
Ankle  
Foot / toes (write which)  

Template 4: flare log

Start dateEnd dateJointsWorst pain (0–10)Possible triggerWhat I didDid I contact anyone?
       
       
       

Template 5: appointment summary (fill in the day before)

QuestionMy notes
Since my last appointment, my pain has been: better / same / worse 
Average pain score over the last 4 weeks 
Number of flares and how long they lasted 
Usual morning stiffness now (minutes) 
Any side effects from medicines 
Things I can no longer do, or struggle with 
My top 3 questions 

Our clinic appointment pack has more help preparing for appointments.

What to focus on for your type of arthritis

Osteoarthritis

Osteoarthritis pain is often linked to activity and load. It is most useful to note what you did and how your joints felt later that day and the next morning. This helps you find the right amount of activity: enough to keep joints and muscles strong, which NICE recommends, without regular big spikes. Note whether stiffness after rest eases quickly once you get moving, which is typical.

Rheumatoid, psoriatic and other inflammatory arthritis

Here, swollen and tender joints, the length of morning stiffness and tiredness are especially useful, because they help show how active the inflammation is. Note any missed or delayed doses of your medicines, infections, and any side effects. If you have psoriatic arthritis, it can also help to note skin flares and any swollen "sausage-like" fingers or toes, or heel pain.

Gout

For gout, the flare log is the most important part. Record the date, which joint, how long it lasted and anything that came before it, such as alcohol, a large meal, dehydration, illness or a change in medicines. This helps you and your GP decide whether long-term treatment to lower urate is needed.

Fibromyalgia alongside arthritis

Many people have fibromyalgia as well as arthritis. Widespread pain, sleep quality, tiredness and "brain fog" are worth tracking, as is how much activity you did, so that pacing can be adjusted.

If you are a carer filling in the journal

If you help someone who finds writing difficult, or who has memory problems, you can fill in the journal with them. Ask them to give their own pain score where possible rather than guessing. If they cannot tell you, note what you observe instead, such as facial expressions, guarding a joint, changes in walking, being restless at night, eating less, or being more withdrawn. These signs are useful for GPs and nurses, and are the kind of thing observational pain tools used in care settings look for. Note who filled in each entry.

How to keep your journal going

  1. Pick one time each day. Many people fill it in in the evening, or first thing for stiffness and last thing for pain.
  2. Keep it visible. Leave the sheet and a pen by the kettle or your bed.
  3. Do not aim for perfect. Missing a day is fine. Just pick it up again.
  4. Be consistent with scores. Use the same scale and think about the same thing each time, for example your average pain today rather than the worst moment.
  5. Use a phone if you prefer. A notes app, a simple spreadsheet or a symptom-tracking app can work. If you use an app, check what it does with your health data before you sign up.
  6. Review weekly, not hourly. Looking for patterns every day can make you anxious. Ten minutes once a week is plenty.

How to read your journal

After two to four weeks, look back and ask:

  • What is my usual range? Knowing your normal makes it easier to recognise a flare.
  • What tends to come before a bad day? Look one or two days back. A big shopping trip, a poor night or a stressful event may show up.
  • Is morning stiffness changing? Stiffness lasting longer than usual can be a sign of more active inflammation in inflammatory arthritis.
  • Do my best days have anything in common? Often these show what to do more of, such as regular walks, pacing or earlier bedtimes.
  • Is something I tried helping? Compare average scores for a couple of weeks before and after a change.

Be careful not to over-read single days. Pain naturally varies, and one bad day after eating a particular food or doing a particular activity does not prove a link. Patterns that repeat several times are more meaningful. Talk to your clinician before cutting out foods, stopping medicines or making big changes based on your journal.

Sharing your journal with your GP or rheumatology team

  • Bring the appointment summary rather than every sheet, but have the sheets with you in case they want detail.
  • Highlight anything new, such as a joint that has started swelling or a side effect.
  • Be honest about what you find hard. Clinicians make better decisions when they know how arthritis affects your daily life.
  • For telephone or video appointments, have your summary in front of you before the call.
  • Ask how they would like you to report flares between appointments, for example through an advice line.

When to get medical help

A journal is for tracking, not for waiting out symptoms that need attention. Do not wait to record a pattern if you have:

  • A suddenly hot, red, swollen, very painful joint, especially with fever or feeling unwell: call NHS 111 or go to A&E
  • Signs of infection while taking immune-suppressing medicines: contact your GP or rheumatology team the same day, or NHS 111
  • Chest pain, severe breathlessness, signs of a stroke or collapse: call 999
  • New joint swelling, morning stiffness lasting over 30 minutes most days, or pain without a diagnosis: book a GP appointment
  • Low mood, hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm: speak to your GP, call NHS 111, or call Samaritans free on 116 123

How long should I keep a pain journal?

Two to four weeks is usually enough to see your normal pattern and bring useful information to an appointment. Many people then keep a lighter version, such as a weekly score, and go back to daily tracking when they start a new treatment or have a flare.

What is the best pain scale to use in a journal?

A 0 to 10 scale is simple and widely used by NHS clinicians, with 0 meaning no pain and 10 the worst pain you can imagine. The most important thing is to use the same scale in the same way each day, for example scoring your average pain rather than the worst moment.

Is there a free printable arthritis pain diary?

Yes. The templates on this page are free to print. Use your browser's print option or save as a PDF from the print window. Print the weekly table once for each week you plan to track, and the appointment summary before each appointment.

Will my GP actually look at my pain diary?

Appointments are short, so a one-page summary is more likely to be read than weeks of sheets. Bring the summary with your top questions, and offer the detailed sheets if they want to see them. Clear, dated information can help your clinician judge how your treatment is working.

Should I use an app instead of paper?

Either works. Use whatever you will keep up. Apps can make charts and reminders easy, but check what happens to your health data and whether you can export your records. Paper is private, simple and easy to bring to appointments.

Can a pain journal help with PIP or work adjustments?

It can help you describe how symptoms vary and affect daily life. For PIP, focus on how you manage specific daily living and mobility activities, which our PIP evidence diary is designed for. For work, a record can support conversations about reasonable adjustments.
