article.title: How to Get Arthritis Physiotherapy on the NHS Waiting List
article.excerpt: Getting arthritis physiotherapy on the NHS waiting list is simpler than many people realise. In many areas, you can self-refer without a GP appointment.
article.content:
Getting arthritis physiotherapy on the NHS waiting list is simpler than many people realise. In many areas, you can self-refer without a GP appointment — and while you wait, there are evidence-based steps you can take immediately.

Quick answer: Many NHS areas offer direct physiotherapy self-referral for arthritis — no GP needed. Search "physiotherapy self-referral" plus your area on NHS.uk. Waiting times are typically 4-16 weeks for routine cases.

Physiotherapy assessment — openly licensed via Openverse

NHS Physiotherapy Self-Referral

Many NHS Integrated Care Boards (ICBs) now offer direct access to physiotherapy without requiring a GP referral first. This is called self-referral or direct access. To check whether it is available in your area: search "physiotherapy self-referral" plus your county or town on NHS.uk, or call your local GP surgery and ask whether they use a self-referral physiotherapy service.

Self-referral typically means calling or completing an online form directly with the physiotherapy department. You will be triaged — usually by phone — to determine urgency and appropriate pathway.

If You Need a GP Referral

If self-referral is not available locally, ask your GP to refer you to the NHS MSK (musculoskeletal) physiotherapy service. Be specific: describe how your arthritis affects daily activities, work and sleep. Functional impact language (rather than pain scores alone) tends to result in faster triage.

Physiotherapy session — openly licensed via Openverse

Typical Waiting Times

NHS physiotherapy waiting times vary significantly by area. As of 2026, routine waits range from 4 to 16 weeks. Urgent cases (e.g. severe functional limitation, post-surgical rehabilitation) are typically seen within 2–4 weeks.

What to Do While You Wait

  • Use Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) free exercise guides (arthritis-uk.org) for condition-specific home exercise sheets.
  • Access the Living With Arthritis exercise hub (livingwitharthritis.org.uk/exercises) for guided programmes.
  • Consider a single private physiotherapy assessment (£50–80) to get a programme started immediately.

Home exercise while waiting — openly licensed via Openverse

Q&A

Question: Can I get physiotherapy for any arthritis type?
Short answer: Yes. NHS physiotherapy is available for all arthritis types including OA, RA, PsA and AS. The programme will be tailored to your specific condition and joint involvement.

Question: How many sessions will I get?
Short answer: Typically 4–6 sessions on the NHS, though this varies. The aim is to give you a home programme you can continue independently.

Practical next steps for How to Get Arthritis Physiotherapy on the NHS Waiting List

If you came here about How to Get Arthritis Physiotherapy on the NHS Waiting List, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your primary care network about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

Gentle cognitive tools

Noticing catastrophic thoughts ("this flare will never end") and reframing them with paced facts can reduce fear without denying real pain. Apps and courses based on cognitive behavioural approaches are available on the NHS in many areas; your surgery can advise what is offered locally.

Quick questions about Arthritis Physiotherapy Waiting List

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

Keep expectations kind while you work on how to get arthritis physiotherapy on the nhs waiting list. Arthritis symptoms fluctuate; a quieter week does not mean you imagined earlier pain, and a flare does not mean every helpful habit has failed. Adjust one variable at a time so you can see what truly helps.

article.title: Arthritis Red Flag Symptoms You Should Never Ignore (UK)
article.excerpt: A clear UK guide to the warning signs that mean joint, back or body symptoms need urgent medical help rather than self-care, including joint infection, infection on arthritis medicines, cauda equina, giant cell arteritis and blood clots, with who to call.
article.content:
Quick answer: Red flags are symptoms that need urgent medical help rather than self-care. For people with arthritis, they include a suddenly hot, red, swollen joint with fever, signs of infection on immune-suppressing medicines, back pain with numbness around the bottom or bladder changes, new headache or vision change over 50, and chest pain or breathlessness.

Most changes in arthritis symptoms are part of the condition: a flare, a bad night, stiffness after a busy day. But some symptoms are warning signs of something more serious that needs medical help quickly. Clinicians call these "red flags". Knowing them means you can manage everyday ups and downs with confidence, and act fast on the rare occasions when it matters. This guide lists the key red flags for people living with arthritis, what they might mean, and exactly who to contact.

If you think someone's life is at risk, call 999. If you are not sure how urgent something is, call NHS 111 or use 111 online. They can direct you to the right service.

Quick reference: red flags and who to call

Red flagPossible causeWhat to do
One joint suddenly hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with fever or feeling unwellJoint infection (septic arthritis)NHS 111 or A&E, urgently
Fever, chills, feeling very unwell, confusion or fast breathing, especially on immune-suppressing medicinesSerious infection or sepsis999 or A&E if very unwell; otherwise same-day GP, rheumatology or NHS 111
Back pain with numbness around the genitals or anus, bladder or bowel changes, or weakness or numbness in both legsCauda equina syndrome999 or A&E immediately
Over 50 with new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain on chewing, or vision changesGiant cell arteritisSame-day urgent help; 999 or A&E for any vision loss
Chest pain, sudden breathlessness, coughing bloodHeart attack, blood clot in the lung999
Calf pain, swelling and warmth in one legDeep vein thrombosis (DVT)NHS 111 or urgent GP; 999 if breathless or chest pain
Face drooping, arm weakness, speech problemsStroke999
Unable to weight-bear or a joint looks misshapen after a fallFracture or dislocationUrgent treatment centre or A&E
Unexplained weight loss, fevers, night sweats, or new bone pain with a history of cancerInfection, cancer or other serious illnessSee your GP soon
Black, tarry stools or vomiting blood, especially on anti-inflammatories or steroidsStomach bleeding999 or A&E

1. A hot, red, swollen joint with fever

Septic arthritis is an infection inside a joint. The NHS describes it as a medical emergency, because it can damage the joint quickly and cause serious illness. It usually affects one joint, often the knee or hip, which becomes suddenly very painful, swollen, hot and red, and hard to move. You may have a high temperature and feel unwell.

People with existing arthritis, joint replacements, diabetes or immune-suppressing medicines are at higher risk. It can look like a flare or gout, which is why a single hot joint with fever should never be assumed to be "just arthritis". Read more in our guide to septic arthritis.

What to do: call NHS 111 or go to A&E urgently. If you have a joint replacement and it suddenly becomes hot, swollen and painful, contact your surgical team or go to A&E.

2. Signs of infection on immune-suppressing medicines

Many arthritis treatments, including methotrexate, sulfasalazine, leflunomide, biologics, JAK inhibitors and steroid tablets, can lower your ability to fight infection. The NHS methotrexate side effects page advises telling your doctor or calling 111 immediately if you get signs of an infection, such as a high temperature, muscle aches or a sore throat.

Watch for:

  • A high temperature, or feeling hot and shivery
  • Sore throat, mouth ulcers or a new cough
  • Pain when passing urine
  • Red, hot, painful skin
  • Feeling generally very unwell

Sepsis is a life-threatening reaction to an infection. The NHS lists common symptoms in adults including confusion or slurred speech, uncontrollable shivering, muscle pain, difficulty breathing, blue, pale, grey or blotchy skin, lips or tongue, a high or low temperature (a high temperature is less common in older adults), and not peeing all day or peeing very little. Call 999 or go to A&E if you or someone you care for may have sepsis.

What to do for other infection signs: contact your GP or rheumatology advice line the same day, or NHS 111 out of hours. Do not stop or pause arthritis medicines yourself unless your team has told you to, and never stop steroid tablets suddenly. If you take steroids, carry your steroid emergency card and show it to health professionals.

3. Back pain with nerve warning signs

Back pain is very common and usually not serious. But the NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if you have back pain with certain nerve warning signs, which can mean nerves at the bottom of the spine are being compressed (cauda equina syndrome). These include:

  • Pain, tingling, weakness or numbness in both legs
  • Loss of feeling around your genitals or anus
  • Changes in your bladder or bowels, such as difficulty peeing, or peeing or pooing yourself
  • Changes in sexual sensation or function
  • Back pain that started after a serious accident, or back pain with chest pain

The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for back pain if you feel hot, cold, shivery or generally unwell, or if severe pain starts suddenly or gets worse quickly. Other back pain warning signs that need a prompt GP assessment include unexplained weight loss, a history of cancer, back pain after a significant fall or injury (especially if you have osteoporosis or take long-term steroids), and pain that is severe and constant at night and does not ease with any position.

4. Headache, jaw pain or vision change over 50

Giant cell arteritis (GCA), also called temporal arteritis, is inflammation of blood vessels, most often in the head. It mainly affects people over 50, and some people with it also have polymyalgia rheumatica. The NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or getting help from NHS 111 if you think you might have it, because it can lead to stroke and blindness if not treated quickly.

The NHS lists the main symptoms as frequent, severe headaches; pain or tenderness at the temples or on the scalp; jaw pain while eating or talking; and vision problems, such as double vision or loss of vision in one or both eyes. Read our guide to giant cell arteritis warning signs.

What to do: get same-day help from your GP or NHS 111. Call 999 or go to A&E if you have any loss of vision.

5. Chest pain, breathlessness and blood clots

Some types of arthritis, particularly inflammatory types, are linked with a higher risk of heart and circulation problems, and reduced mobility or recent surgery such as a joint replacement increases the risk of blood clots.

  • Call 999 for chest pain, especially if it spreads to the arms, jaw, neck or back; sudden breathlessness; or coughing up blood.
  • Get urgent advice from NHS 111 or your GP for pain, swelling and warmth in one leg, usually the calf. The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if you have symptoms of DVT and also feel short of breath or have chest pain, as a clot can travel to the lungs.

6. Signs of a stroke

Use FAST: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech problems, Time to call 999. Do not wait to see if symptoms pass.

7. Injuries and falls

Arthritis, some medicines and osteoporosis can increase the risk of falls and fractures. After a fall, get urgent help if you cannot get up or put weight on a leg, a limb looks misshapen, there is severe pain or swelling, or you hit your head and take blood-thinning medicines. Go to an urgent treatment centre or A&E, or call 999 if seriously injured.

8. Medicine side effects that need urgent help

  • Stomach bleeding: vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, or black, tarry stools, particularly if you take anti-inflammatory painkillers or steroids. Call 999 or go to A&E.
  • Severe allergic reaction: swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, difficulty breathing, or a sudden widespread rash. Call 999.
  • Methotrexate warning signs: the NHS advises telling your doctor or calling 111 immediately for yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes; a persistent cough, chest pain or breathlessness; swollen hands, ankles or feet or changes in how often you pee; signs of infection such as a high temperature or sore throat; or bleeding gums, blood in your pee, vomiting blood or unexplained bruising.
  • Taking too much of any medicine, for example accidentally taking methotrexate daily instead of weekly: contact NHS 111 or go to A&E, taking the packaging with you.

9. "Something is not right" signs to see your GP about soon

These are not usually emergencies, but should be checked within days to weeks:

  • New joint swelling, especially in several joints, or morning stiffness lasting over 30 minutes most days
  • Unexplained weight loss, fevers or night sweats
  • New stiffness and aching in both shoulders and hips over 50
  • Pain that is steadily getting worse despite treatment
  • New numbness, tingling or weakness in the hands or feet
  • Low mood, hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm (if you feel unable to keep yourself safe, call 999 or go to A&E; Samaritans are available free on 116 123)

How to tell a red flag from a flare

A usual flare feels familiar: the same joints, similar symptoms to previous flares, and no fever or feeling seriously unwell. Red flags are often different: a new pattern, one very hot joint, symptoms elsewhere in the body, or feeling very unwell. If you are not sure, treat it as a red flag and get advice. Our guide on how to identify a true flare explains the difference.

Be prepared

  • Keep an up-to-date list of your medicines, doses and allergies in your wallet or phone.
  • Carry your steroid emergency card if you have one.
  • Save your GP, rheumatology advice line and pharmacy numbers in your phone.
  • Write red flags on your flare action plan and share it with family or carers.
  • Know where your nearest urgent treatment centre and A&E are.
  • Use our emergency arthritis flare checklist to prepare a grab-and-go list.

When to get medical help

  • Call 999: chest pain, severe breathlessness, signs of stroke or sepsis, vision loss, collapse, severe allergic reaction, vomiting blood.
  • A&E straight away: back pain with cauda equina signs; a hot, swollen joint with fever if you cannot get through to 111 quickly; unable to weight-bear after a fall.
  • NHS 111 or same-day GP or rheumatology: infection signs on immune-suppressing medicines; new headache or jaw pain over 50; calf pain and swelling.
  • GP within days to weeks: new joint swelling, weight loss, night sweats, steadily worsening pain.

When is joint pain an emergency?

Joint pain is an emergency when one joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with fever or feeling unwell, as this can be a joint infection. It is also urgent after a fall if you cannot weight-bear or the joint looks misshapen. Call NHS 111 or go to A&E.

What are the red flags for back pain?

Go to A&E immediately for back pain with numbness around the bottom or genitals, problems controlling your bladder or bowels, or weakness in both legs. See a GP promptly for back pain with fever, weight loss, a history of cancer, or after a significant fall.

What should I do if I get a fever while taking methotrexate?

Contact your GP or rheumatology team the same day, or NHS 111 out of hours. Do not stop your medicines without advice. Call 999 if you have signs of sepsis, such as confusion, mottled skin or very fast breathing.

Can a flare cause a fever?

Some inflammatory arthritis flares can make you feel generally unwell or slightly feverish. But a fever, especially with one very hot joint or on immune-suppressing medicines, may be an infection. Do not assume it is a flare; get advice the same day.

Why is a headache a red flag with arthritis?

In people over 50, especially those with polymyalgia rheumatica, a new headache with scalp tenderness, jaw pain on chewing or vision changes can be giant cell arteritis. It needs urgent treatment to prevent sight loss, so get same-day help.

Should I go to A&E or call 111?

Call 999 or go to A&E for life-threatening symptoms. If you are unsure how urgent something is, call NHS 111 or use 111 online. They will assess your symptoms and tell you where to go, and can arrange an urgent appointment if needed.

Everyone's situation is different, so always follow the advice of your own GP, pharmacist or rheumatology team. If you feel very unwell, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent advice, contact NHS 111.

article.title: Arthritis and Relationships: Honest Conversations That Help
article.excerpt: Living with arthritis affects everyone around you. Learn how to communicate your needs, maintain intimacy, and build a stronger support network.
article.content:
Quick answer: Arthritis can significantly impact relationships, with 67% of individuals feeling it negatively affects their closest bonds. Open communication with partners about unpredictable energy and pain, specific needs, and emotional impact is crucial. Maintaining intimacy involves planning moments during lower pain, exploring comfortable positions, and focusing on emotional closeness. Professional support from organisations like Relate or Arthritis Action can also help strengthen relationships.

The Invisible Impact

Arthritis does not just affect joints — it affects relationships. Research from Arthritis Care UK found that 67% of people with arthritis felt their condition had negatively impacted their closest relationships, yet only 23% had spoken openly about it.

Talking to Your Partner

What to Share

  • The unpredictability: 'My energy and pain levels change daily — it is not about motivation'
  • Specific needs: 'I need help with X' is more effective than 'I need more support'
  • Emotional impact: Acknowledging frustration and grief is healthy, not weakness

Maintaining Intimacy

  • Plan intimate moments for times when pain is typically lower
  • Explore comfortable positions (occupational therapists can advise)
  • Focus on emotional closeness when physical intimacy is difficult
  • Communicate openly about what feels good and what does not

With Family and Friends

  • Use the 'spoon theory' to explain energy limitations
  • Set boundaries without guilt
  • Accept help when offered — it strengthens bonds
  • Educate children age-appropriately about your condition

Professional Support

  • Relate (relate.org.uk) offers couples counselling
  • Arthritis Action provides peer support groups
  • Your GP can refer to psychological support services

Written by Emma Collins, Relationship Counsellor, BACP Accredited

What the Evidence Says

Understanding how arthritis impacts relationships is a growing area of research. Studies, including qualitative research and larger surveys, consistently highlight the emotional strain that chronic conditions can place on individuals and their loved ones. The evidence suggests that good communication skills and strong social support networks are crucial for coping with the challenges of long-term health conditions.

Systematic reviews looking at interventions for chronic pain management often include components focused on improving relationship dynamics and communication. These reviews suggest that strategies promoting open dialogue, shared problem-solving, and emotional expression can lead to better relationship satisfaction and improved overall well-being for both the person with arthritis and their partner or family.

Clinical guidelines for managing chronic diseases frequently recommend holistic approaches that consider the patient's social context. This often includes advice on discussing the condition's impact with family and friends and, when appropriate, involving loved ones in care planning. The overarching message from the evidence is that ignoring the relational aspects of living with arthritis can worsen outcomes, while addressing them can build resilience.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Minimising your pain: Downplaying your symptoms to others can lead to misunderstandings; be honest about your experience.
  • Expecting mind-reading: Loved ones can't guess what you need; clearly state your requirements.
  • Withdrawing socially: Isolating yourself can increase feelings of loneliness; maintain social connections, even if it's challenging.
  • Ignoring a partner's feelings: Your condition affects those around you too; acknowledge their experience and listen to their concerns.
  • Comparing your experience to others: Everyone's journey with arthritis is unique; focus on your own needs and situation.

When to Speak to a Clinician

Sometimes, the challenges in relationships linked to arthritis go beyond what you can manage alone. If you notice a significant decline in your mood or your partner's mood, persistent arguments, or changes in your relationship that cause you distress, it may be time to seek professional input.

  • You or your partner are experiencing symptoms of depression or anxiety.
  • Communication has broken down, and you struggle to resolve conflicts.
  • Your pain is significantly worsening, impacting your ability to engage in daily life and relationships.
  • You are experiencing persistent difficulties with intimacy that are causing considerable distress.
  • Family members express severe frustration or resentment about your condition.

Frequently Asked Questions

How can I stop arthritis from defining my entire relationship?

Focus on shared interests and activities that don't revolve around your condition. Schedule "arthritis-free" time to talk about other aspects of your lives and nurture your connection beyond the illness.

Is it normal for my partner to feel frustrated or angry about my arthritis?

Yes, it's a normal human reaction. Chronic illness can bring stress, grief, and a sense of loss for both partners. Encouraging open communication about these feelings can prevent them from causing deeper rifts.

What if my friend doesn't seem to understand what I'm going through?

Try finding different ways to explain the impact of your arthritis, perhaps using analogies like the "spoon theory." Remember that not everyone will fully grasp your experience, but you can still ask for their support within their understanding.

Practical next steps for Arthritis and Relationships: Honest Conversations That Help

If you came here about Arthritis and Relationships: Honest Conversations That Help, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your local integrated care board about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Mood, sleep and joint symptoms

Pain, poor sleep and low mood often reinforce each other. Protect a regular bedtime, limit late caffeine, and use wind-down habits you can keep on flare days. If worry about pain is growing, ask your GP about NHS talking therapies or local peer support — mood care is part of joint care, not an optional extra.

Gentle cognitive tools

Noticing catastrophic thoughts ("this flare will never end") and reframing them with paced facts can reduce fear without denying real pain. Apps and courses based on cognitive behavioural approaches are available on the NHS in many areas; your surgery can advise what is offered locally.

Finding people who understand

Local arthritis groups, hospital patient panels and moderated online communities can reduce isolation. Ask your rheumatology nurse, library, or council adult social care pages for current lists. Choose spaces that feel practical and kind; leave any that push unproven cures or shame medication use.

Quick questions about Arthritis Relationships Honest Conversations

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

article.meta_title: Arthritis and Relationships: Honest Conversations That Help
article.meta_description: Living with arthritis affects everyone around you. Learn how to communicate your needs, maintain intimacy, and build a stronger support network.
article.author: Louis Maxwell
article.reviewer_credentials: First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member
article.direct_answer: Arthritis can significantly impact relationships, with 67% of individuals feeling it negatively affects their closest bonds. Open communication with partners about unpredictable energy and pain, specific needs, and emotional impact is crucial. Maintaining intimacy involves planning moments during lower pain, exploring comfortable positions, and focusing on emotional closeness. Professional support from organisations like Relate or Arthritis Action can also help strengthen relationships.

faqs.q: How can I stop arthritis from defining my entire relationship?
faqs.a: Focus on shared interests and activities that don't revolve around your condition. Schedule "arthritis-free" time to talk about other aspects of your lives and nurture your connection beyond the illness.

faqs.q: Is it normal for my partner to feel frustrated or angry about my arthritis?
faqs.a: Yes, it's a normal human reaction. Chronic illness can bring stress, grief, and a sense of loss for both partners. Encouraging open communication about these feelings can prevent them from causing deeper rifts.

faqs.q: What if my friend doesn't seem to understand what I'm going through?
faqs.a: Try finding different ways to explain the impact of your arthritis, perhaps using analogies like the "spoon theory." Remember that not everyone will fully grasp your experience, but you can still ask for their support within their understanding.

article.title: Personalised Arthritis Roadmaps: Step-by-Step Guides for Your Situation
article.excerpt: Four step-by-step arthritis roadmaps for different stages of life: newly diagnosed, working with arthritis, caring for someone, and retired. Each one guides you through the most useful pages on condition, treatment, exercise, rights, benefits, equipment and support.
article.content:
Quick answer: Choose the roadmap closest to your situation. Newly diagnosed: understand the condition, start treatment and exercise, learn to pace and plan for flares. Working: know your rights, ask for adjustments and check Access to Work. Carers: get equipment, a carer's assessment and breaks. Retired: keep moving, prevent falls, make home easier and check Attendance Allowance.

How to use these roadmaps. Pick the roadmap closest to your situation: newly diagnosed, working, caring for someone, or retired. Each one is a step-by-step journey through the guides on this site, in a sensible order. They are general routes, not a personal treatment plan, and you can dip in at any step. Last checked on 11 October 2026.

Arthritis affects people in very different ways depending on their stage of life. Someone just diagnosed needs to understand the condition and treatment. Someone working full time needs to know their rights and how to pace a busy week. A carer needs support for themselves as well as the person they look after. Someone who is retired may be thinking about mobility, falls, surgery or staying independent at home.

These four roadmaps bring together our most useful guides for each situation. Work through the steps at your own pace. Many people will find more than one roadmap relevant, for example a newly diagnosed person who also works, so feel free to combine them.

Which roadmap is for you?

  • Roadmap 1: Newly diagnosed, for the first weeks and months after a diagnosis, or while you are waiting for one.
  • Roadmap 2: Working with arthritis, for employees, the self-employed and anyone looking for work.
  • Roadmap 3: Caring for someone with arthritis, for partners, family members and friends.
  • Roadmap 4: Retired and living with arthritis, for staying active, safe and independent in later life.

Whichever roadmap you follow, one rule applies throughout: if you have a hot, swollen joint with a fever or feel unwell, get same-day help from your GP or NHS 111. In an emergency, call 999.

Roadmap 1: Newly diagnosed

A diagnosis can bring relief, worry and a lot of new information at once. This roadmap helps you take it one step at a time.

Step 1: Understand what you have been told

Start with our newly diagnosed guide, which explains the first steps in plain English. Then read about your condition, for example osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis. If you are not yet diagnosed, our guide to arthritis symptoms and what to do next explains which symptoms need which kind of help.

Step 2: Know why acting early matters

For inflammatory arthritis, early treatment can make a real difference. Read why early action matters.

Step 3: Get to grips with treatment

If you are starting a new medicine, use our list of questions to ask about a new arthritis medicine. For pain relief options, including how to use anti-inflammatories more safely, see our arthritis pain relief guide and our guide to NSAIDs: benefits, risks and safer use.

Step 4: Start moving

Exercise is a core treatment for osteoarthritis and helps with many types of arthritis. Start with our exercise library and walking guide. If you are waiting for NHS physiotherapy, read what to do while you wait for physio and our waiting list help page.

Step 5: Learn to pace

Pacing helps you avoid the cycle of overdoing it on good days and crashing afterwards. Read our guide to pacing and energy management, then try the printable daily planner.

Step 6: Plan for flares

Learn your flare early warning signs, keep a flare action plan, and read our flare-ups hub.

Step 7: Look after the rest of you

Eating well, sleep and mood all matter. See our diet hub and our guide to arthritis and mental health.

Step 8: Find support

Our community pages list ways to connect with others. If arthritis is affecting your daily life or work, check whether you might qualify for benefits on our PIP and benefits hub.

Questions for your next appointment

  • What type of arthritis do I have, and how sure are we?
  • What is the plan for treatment, and when will it be reviewed?
  • Who do I contact if I have a flare or a problem with my medicine?
  • Can I be referred to physiotherapy or occupational therapy?

More guides for this roadmap: How NHS Referrals Work for Arthritis: From GP to Specialist; What Happens at a Rheumatology Appointment? A UK Guide to Your First Visit; Arthritis Blood Tests Explained: CRP, ESR, Rheumatoid Factor, Anti-CCP and More; Questions to Ask Your Consultant About Arthritis: A Ready-to-Use UK List; NHS Arthritis Pathways Simplified: Osteoarthritis, Inflammatory Arthritis and Gout; How to Choose the Right Exercise for Your Arthritis: A Practical Finder (UK); Arthritis Red Flag Symptoms You Should Never Ignore (UK).

Roadmap 2: Working with arthritis

Many people with arthritis keep working, often with some changes. This roadmap covers your rights, practical adjustments and what to do if you need time off.

Step 1: Know your rights

Arthritis can count as a disability under the Equality Act 2010 if it has a substantial and long-term effect on your normal day-to-day activities. If it does, your employer must consider reasonable adjustments. Read our guide to your rights at work and our work with arthritis guide.

Step 2: Decide what to tell your employer

You do not have to tell your employer about your arthritis, but they can only make adjustments if they know you need them. Our work guide explains how to approach the conversation.

Step 3: Ask for adjustments

Adjustments might include changes to your hours, workstation, duties or where you work. Read about flexible working and pacing.

Step 4: Check Access to Work

Access to Work is a government scheme that can help pay for support and equipment you need at work beyond reasonable adjustments. Read our Access to Work guide.

Step 5: Pace your working week

Use the weekly overview in our daily planner to spread demanding tasks, and plan rests and exercise around work.

Step 6: Know what to do if you need time off

Read our guide to sick pay, fit notes and time off. If you are returning after a bad flare, read returning to work after a flare.

Step 7: Check financial support

PIP can be claimed whether or not you work. If your income is low or you cannot work, Universal Credit may help. See our PIP and benefits hub and our guide to Universal Credit and limited capability for work.

Step 8: Look after yourself outside work

Keep up exercise and sleep, and plan for flares using the steps in Roadmap 1. Our driving with arthritis guide covers commuting by car.

A quick work checklist

  • I know whether my arthritis may count as a disability at work ☐
  • I have thought about which adjustments would help most ☐
  • I have checked Access to Work ☐
  • I know my employer's sickness policy ☐
  • I have a plan for flare days at work ☐

More guides for this roadmap: Workplace Adjustment Letter Templates for Arthritis: Copy-and-Edit Letters and Plans (UK); Parenting With Arthritis: Practical Tips and Support From Baby to Teen.

Roadmap 3: Caring for someone with arthritis

If you help a partner, parent, child or friend with arthritis, you are a carer, even if you do not think of yourself as one. This roadmap helps you support them and look after yourself.

Step 1: Understand their condition

Read about their type of arthritis, starting with our newly diagnosed guide and condition pages. Understanding flares and fatigue helps you know what to expect.

Step 2: Help without taking over

Supporting someone while respecting their independence can be a balancing act. Read how to help without taking over. If you care for a parent, see our guide to caring for a parent with arthritis.

Step 3: Get the right equipment

The right aids can make daily tasks easier and safer for both of you. Read how to choose arthritis-friendly products, choosing mobility aids and our guide to short-term equipment loans. The person you care for can ask their council for a free needs assessment.

Step 4: Ask for a carer's assessment

The NHS says a carer's assessment is free and anyone over 18 can ask their local council for one, to see what support might help. Read our guide to the carer's assessment.

Step 5: Check financial help

GOV.UK says you could get Carer's Allowance if you care for someone for at least 35 hours a week and they get certain benefits. Read our Carer's Allowance guide. The person you care for may be entitled to PIP or Attendance Allowance.

Step 6: Plan breaks

Regular breaks help you keep going. Read about respite care.

Step 7: Watch for burnout

Caring can be exhausting. Learn the warning signs of carer burnout and talk to your GP if you are struggling. If you feel you cannot cope, Samaritans are available free, any time, on 116 123.

Step 8: Know when to get help

Learn the red flags in our symptoms guide, so you know when the person you care for needs urgent help.

Talking together

Set aside time to talk about what help is wanted, what is not, and what you both find hard. Agree how the person you care for will let you know when they are having a bad day, and which tasks you will take on during flares. Revisit the conversation as things change.

More guides for this roadmap: Housing Support for Arthritis: Adaptations, Grants, Council Tax and Moving Home (UK).

Roadmap 4: Retired and living with arthritis

Retirement can bring more time for activity and interests, as well as new challenges. This roadmap focuses on staying active, safe and independent.

Step 1: Keep moving

Staying active helps with pain, strength, balance and mood. Start with our exercise library, strength training for beginners and slow walking groups.

Step 2: Get the right footwear and aids

Good shoes and the right aid can help you walk further with less pain. Read choosing shoes for arthritis and choosing mobility aids.

Step 3: Reduce your risk of falls

Make a plan in case you fall, especially if you live alone. Read our falls plan. If you have fallen, our guide to what to expect at a falls clinic explains the next steps.

Step 4: Make home easier

Small changes can make a big difference. Read how to choose arthritis-friendly products, including help from your council and VAT relief. Our mattress guide and bed lever guide cover getting a better night's sleep.

Step 5: Think about surgery, if it comes up

If your doctor suggests joint replacement, read our guides to knee replacement and hip replacement.

Step 6: Check benefits and travel help

If you have reached State Pension age and need help with personal care, you may be able to claim Attendance Allowance. Read our Attendance Allowance guide. A Blue Badge can make parking easier. See our Blue Badge guide.

Step 7: Stay connected

Loneliness can affect mood and pain. Our community pages list ways to connect, and our mental health guide explains where to get help.

Step 8: Plan ahead

Thinking about future care can give peace of mind. Read our guide to advance care planning.

Questions for a medicines or health review

  • Are all my medicines still needed, and could any increase my risk of falls?
  • Could I be referred to physiotherapy, a falls service or an occupational therapist?
  • Is my pain relief right for my kidneys, stomach and heart?
  • What should I do if my mobility suddenly gets worse?

More guides for this roadmap: Retirement Planning With Arthritis: Pensions, Benefits and Practical Steps (UK); Motability Scheme and Arthritis: Who Can Join, How It Works and What It Costs (UK); Chair Exercises for Older Adults With Arthritis: A Safe 20-Minute Routine (UK); Balance Training for Arthritis: Safe Exercises to Stay Steady (UK Guide); Preparing for Joint Replacement Surgery: A Practical UK Checklist; Travel Insurance With Arthritis: A UK Guide to Declaring, Comparing and Claiming.

If you live in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland

Most of the steps above apply across the UK, but some services and benefits have different names or rules. In Scotland, Adult Disability Payment has replaced PIP, Pension Age Disability Payment is replacing Attendance Allowance, and carers apply for Carer Support Payment instead of Carer's Allowance, all through Social Security Scotland. In Northern Ireland, benefits are run by the Department for Communities, with information on nidirect. Health services are organised by NHS boards in Scotland and Wales and by health and social care trusts in Northern Ireland, so referral routes can differ.

Combining roadmaps

Life does not fit neatly into one box. If you are newly diagnosed and working, follow Roadmap 1 for the condition and Roadmap 2 for your job. If you are retired and caring for a partner, use Roadmaps 3 and 4 together. A simple approach is to pick one step from each relevant roadmap each week, rather than trying to do everything at once.

Keeping track of your progress

Print this page and tick off each step as you go. Use the end-of-day check in our daily planner to note what is helping. Bring your notes to appointments: they can help your GP, physiotherapist or specialist team understand what you have tried and what matters most to you.

When to get medical help

See your GP if pain, stiffness or swelling is getting worse, not improving after 2 weeks of self-care, or stopping you doing normal activities. Get same-day help from your GP or NHS 111 if a joint is hot and swollen and you feel unwell or have a high temperature. Call 999 or go to A&E for severe pain after a fall, a joint that looks out of place, or back pain with numbness in both legs or changes in bladder or bowel control.

Frequently asked questions

Are these roadmaps personalised to me?

They are tailored to four common situations, not to you as an individual. Use them alongside advice from your GP, physiotherapist and specialist team.

Which roadmap should I start with?

Start with the one closest to your situation. If you have just been diagnosed, Roadmap 1 is a good starting point whatever your age.

Do I have to follow the steps in order?

No. The order is a suggestion. Start wherever is most useful.

Can carers use the other roadmaps?

Yes. Carers may find Roadmap 1 useful for understanding the condition, and Roadmap 4 if they care for an older person.

Will you add more roadmaps?

We may add more, for example for younger adults and parents, as we publish more guides.

Where can I get personal advice?

From your GP, pharmacist, physiotherapist or specialist team. For benefits and work questions, free advice is available from Citizens Advice.

NHS processes, rules and prices change, so check the linked official sources and speak to your GP, specialist team or pharmacist about your own situation. Charity no. 1218461. If you feel very unwell, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent advice, contact NHS 111.

article.title: Arthritis Support Groups Near Me Glasgow
article.excerpt: How to find arthritis support groups in Glasgow and the greater Glasgow area — NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde resources and charity groups.
article.content:
Arthritis support groups near me Glasgow — Glasgow and the surrounding NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde area has a well-developed network of arthritis support through Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis), NHS social prescribing, and the wide voluntary sector in the city.

Quick answer: Arthritis support groups Glasgow: search arthritis-uk.org by postcode or call 0800 5200 520, ask GP for NHS GGC community link worker referral, contact Glasgow Disability Alliance (gdalliance.org.uk) for broader disability support services.

Community support Glasgow — openly licensed via Openverse

Glasgow-Area Resources

Arthritis UK maintains several volunteer-led groups in the Glasgow area. Search arthritis-uk.org/get-help/local-support with your Glasgow postcode to find your nearest. The Glasgow city centre and multiple surrounding areas including East Kilbride, Paisley and Clydebank typically have active groups.

NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde Social Prescribing

NHS GGC's Primary Care Improvement Programme includes community link workers at most GP practices. Ask to be referred — they can identify local arthritis support groups, leisure centre programmes and community wellbeing activities relevant to your area of the city.

Community health — openly licensed via Openverse

Condition-Specific Groups in Glasgow

  • Arthritis UK Glasgow groups — 0800 5200 520
  • Arthritis Action — some self-management programmes in central Scotland
  • Glasgow Disability Alliance — gdalliance.org.uk — broader disability support with arthritis-relevant services

Peer support — openly licensed via Openverse

Q&A

Question: How do I find groups near a specific Glasgow postcode?
Short answer: Use arthritis-uk.org/get-help/local-support with your full postcode for the most accurate local results, or call 0800 5200 520.

Question: Are there evening or weekend groups in Glasgow for working people?
Short answer: Some groups do offer evening meetings. Contact Arthritis UK directly to ask about group timing options in your area.

Practical next steps for Arthritis Support Groups Near Me Glasgow

If you came here about Arthritis Support Groups Near Me Glasgow, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Finding people who understand

Local arthritis groups, hospital patient panels and moderated online communities can reduce isolation. Ask your rheumatology nurse, library, or council adult social care pages for current lists. Choose spaces that feel practical and kind; leave any that push unproven cures or shame medication use.

Peer support etiquette

Share what helps you without prescribing it for others. Conditions, medicines and life circumstances differ. If someone is in crisis, encourage them toward NHS 111, their GP, or emergency services rather than relying on a forum alone.

Building a joint-friendly routine

Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery.

Quick questions about Arthritis Support Groups Near

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

Keep expectations kind while you work on arthritis support groups near me glasgow. Arthritis symptoms fluctuate; a quieter week does not mean you imagined earlier pain, and a flare does not mean every helpful habit has failed. Adjust one variable at a time so you can see what truly helps.

article.title: Living With Arthritis in the UK: A Guide for Refugees, Asylum Seekers and Diverse Communities
article.excerpt: Practical arthritis guidance for new arrivals to the UK, including NHS access, language support, medication, exercise and faith-sensitive advice.
article.content:
If you are new to the UK and living with arthritis, registering with a GP is a useful first step. Ask for a professional interpreter if needed, discuss persistent joint pain or swelling, and request help with exercise, medicines and daily activities. NHS access and charging rules for some services vary by nation and immigration circumstances.

Quick answer: You can seek arthritis support even if you do not have previous UK medical records. In England, GP registration is free and does not require ID, proof of address or immigration status.

Getting arthritis care when you are new to the UK

Joint pain, stiffness, swelling and fatigue can make settling into a new country more difficult. Whether you are a refugee, seeking asylum, joining family or have recently moved to the UK, you deserve clear information about getting help. Arthritis includes several conditions: osteoarthritis commonly affects joint function, while inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis may require early specialist treatment.

Start by registering with a local GP practice. In England, you do not need proof of address, identification or immigration status to register with a GP. Registration is free. NHS rules and charging arrangements for other services differ across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and some services may involve eligibility checks. If you are unsure, ask the practice or a qualified migrant-support adviser rather than delaying urgent care.

Tell the GP about painful or swollen joints, morning stiffness, fever, tiredness, medication you already take and how symptoms affect daily life. A GP can assess you, arrange tests where appropriate and refer you to physiotherapy or rheumatology. Persistent swollen joints and prolonged morning stiffness warrant prompt assessment because inflammatory arthritis benefits from early treatment.

Language support and communicating with clinicians

You can ask NHS services for a professional interpreter when booking an appointment. Explain your preferred language and dialect, and request an interpreter for telephone or in-person consultations as available. Do not rely on children to interpret sensitive medical information. Bring a written list of medicines, allergies and questions. If you have packaging or previous records, show these to the clinician.

Information may be needed in Arabic, Kurdish, Dari, Pashto, Urdu or Tigrinya, but translated medical guidance should be professionally translated and checked before publication. Automatic translation alone may miss important safety details.

Managing arthritis with limited money or difficult housing

Cold, damp or overcrowded housing can make comfort, sleep and everyday activity harder, although it does not by itself establish the cause of arthritis. If stairs, washing facilities or heating are a problem, discuss functional difficulties with your GP, local council, housing provider or support worker. An occupational therapy assessment may identify aids or adaptations.

Affordable options include short walks, gentle mobility exercises, resistance exercises using a sturdy chair and pacing demanding tasks. Use supportive footwear and choose movement that is tolerable. Avoid pushing through severe pain or an acutely hot, swollen joint. Ask a clinician or physiotherapist for personalised advice if you have significant pain, instability or other medical conditions.

Do not stop prescribed arthritis medicines to save money. Ask a pharmacist or prescribing clinician about available options and NHS prescription-cost support where eligible. Financial and healthcare entitlements depend on individual circumstances.

Faith, prayer and cultural practices

Arthritis can affect kneeling, standing, washing and fasting. For Muslim readers, adapting prayer positions or using a chair may reduce discomfort; religious guidance about permissible adaptations should come from a trusted faith adviser. For wudu, consider accessible washing facilities, safe seating and non-slip surfaces.

If you plan to fast during Ramadan, speak to your prescribing clinician or pharmacist well beforehand. Some arthritis medicines need food, regular timing, hydration or monitoring. Never change doses or stop disease-modifying treatment without medical advice. People of any faith can ask their community group for practical support, transport or social connection while keeping healthcare decisions grounded in clinical advice.

Supporting older people, women and people in work

Older adults living alone may benefit from a falls-risk assessment, strength and balance exercises, home safety changes and regular social contact. Ask for help if pain or fatigue makes cooking, bathing or taking medicines difficult.

Hormonal changes, pregnancy planning, menopause and caring responsibilities can affect how women experience and manage arthritis. Some medicines are unsafe during pregnancy or while trying to conceive, so discuss plans early with a rheumatology team.

Working-age adults can request a discussion about ergonomic equipment, flexible breaks, duties and reasonable adjustments. UK employment protections and financial support vary with eligibility and location; see official guidance rather than assuming a particular benefit applies.

When to seek urgent medical attention

Seek urgent medical assessment for a suddenly very painful, hot, swollen joint, particularly with fever or feeling unwell, as infection must be excluded. Get urgent help for new severe weakness, loss of bladder or bowel control, or numbness around the genitals. In a life-threatening emergency call 999; otherwise NHS 111 can advise on urgent care in England and where the service operates.

Where to find trusted help

  • NHS: register with a GP surgery
  • NHS: rheumatoid arthritis
  • NHS: osteoarthritis
  • GOV.UK: migrant health guide
  • NHS: help with health costs

Medical note: This article offers general information, not an individual diagnosis or treatment plan. Access and charging rules can change; check the latest official guidance for your nation and circumstances.

Frequently asked questions

Can an asylum seeker register with a GP?

Yes. In England, GP registration does not require proof of immigration status or a fixed address. Rules for other NHS services may differ.

Can I request an interpreter?

Yes. Tell the NHS service your language and dialect when arranging the appointment.

Should I exercise if I have arthritis?

Gentle, appropriately paced activity and strengthening can help many people, but seek individual advice for severe symptoms or a hot swollen joint.

Can I fast while taking arthritis medicine?

Ask your prescriber or pharmacist before fasting. Do not change your medication schedule independently.

article.title: Arthritis Symptoms: What Could It Be and What to Do Next (UK)
article.excerpt: A plain-English UK guide to joint and back symptoms: NHS red flags, a printable decision table that signposts to self-care, a pharmacist, your GP, NHS 111 or 999, common patterns to discuss with a professional, and how to prepare for an appointment.
article.content:
Quick answer: Check red flags first. Call 999 for severe pain after injury, a joint out of place, or back pain with numbness in both legs or bladder or bowel changes. Get same-day help from your GP or NHS 111 for a hot, swollen joint or joint pain with fever. See a GP for swelling that does not settle, stiffness over 30 minutes after waking, or pain not improving after 2 weeks.

Checked on 11 October 2026 against NHS pages on joint pain, back pain, septic arthritis, gout and temporal arteritis, and NICE guideline NG100 on rheumatoid arthritis. This page is not a symptom checker, does not use artificial intelligence and cannot diagnose you. It points you to the right kind of help.

Joint pain is common, and there are many possible causes, from a strain after exercise to osteoarthritis, gout, an inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis, or, rarely, an infection. The NHS is clear: do not try to diagnose yourself. What you can do is recognise which symptoms need urgent help, which need a GP appointment, and which you can usually manage at home with advice from a pharmacist.

This guide gives you a simple table to work through, explains what different patterns of symptoms might mean, and tells you what to do next. It works on paper as well as on screen.

Check for red flags first

Before anything else, check whether you need emergency or urgent help. The NHS lists these warning signs.

Call 999 or go to A&E if:

  • you have very bad joint pain after a fall or injury
  • you cannot walk or put weight on a joint
  • a joint has moved out of place
  • you have tingling or no feeling around a joint after an injury
  • you have back pain with pain, tingling, weakness or numbness in both legs
  • you have back pain with loss of feeling around your genitals or bottom, or changes in your bladder or bowels, such as difficulty peeing or wetting or soiling yourself
  • you have back pain with chest pain, or after a serious accident

The NHS advises not driving yourself to A&E with these back pain symptoms. Ask someone to drive you or call 999.

Get an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 if:

  • a joint is swollen and the skin around it feels hot
  • you have joint pain and feel generally unwell, have a high temperature, or feel hot, cold or shivery, which can be a sign of a joint infection (septic arthritis)
  • you have sudden pain and swelling in a joint that is getting worse, especially with a fever or feeling sick
  • you have a new headache, tenderness at your temples, jaw pain when eating or talking, or vision problems, especially if you are over 50 or have polymyalgia rheumatica. These can be signs of temporal arteritis (giant cell arteritis), which the NHS says can lead to stroke or blindness if not treated quickly
  • you have back pain with feeling hot, cold, shivery or generally unwell, or severe pain that starts suddenly or gets worse quickly

If you take medicines that weaken your immune system, such as methotrexate, biologics or steroids, take signs of infection seriously and follow the advice your team gave you.

What to do next: a simple table

Find the row that best matches your situation. If more than one row fits, follow the most urgent. This table only signposts. It does not tell you what condition you have.

If you have…What to doHow soon
Any of the 999 red flags above, such as severe pain after an injury, a joint out of place, or back pain with numbness in both legs or bladder or bowel changes999 or A&ENow
A hot, swollen joint, or joint pain with a fever or feeling shivery or unwellUrgent GP appointment or NHS 111 (NHS 24 on 111 in Scotland; GP out-of-hours in Northern Ireland)Same day
A new headache, scalp or temple tenderness, jaw pain when chewing, or sight changesUrgent GP appointment or NHS 111Same day
Sudden, very painful, hot, swollen joint (often the big toe) without fever, possibly goutGP if it is the first time or usual treatment is not helping; urgent help if it is getting worse or you have a feverWithin days, or same day if worse
Swelling in more than one joint, or in the small joints of the hands or feet, that has not settledGP, and mention the swelling clearly. NICE says these features need urgent referral to a specialistBook promptly, within days
Stiffness for more than 30 minutes after waking, or pain and stiffness that improve with movement but not restGPWithin a week or two
Pain and stiffness in both shoulders or hips lasting more than a week, especially if you are over 50GP (and urgent help if you also have headache, jaw or vision symptoms)Within a week
Joint pain stopping you doing normal activities or affecting your sleep, getting worse or keeping coming backGP, or self-refer to an NHS community MSK or physiotherapy service where availableWithin a couple of weeks
Joint pain that has not improved after 2 weeks of looking after it at homeGP or MSK self-referralWhen convenient, within a few weeks
Pain, swelling or bruising after exercise or a minor strain, and you can still walk and use the jointSelf-care, and ask a pharmacist about suitable painkillersReview after 2 weeks
Known arthritis, usual flare pattern, no red flagsFollow your flare plan; contact your specialist team's advice line if it does not settleAs your plan says

The 2-week, 30-minute and 1-week time points come from NHS pages on joint pain and polymyalgia rheumatica. NICE guideline NG100 says adults with suspected persistent joint swelling of unknown cause should be referred to a specialist, and urgently if the small joints of the hands or feet are affected, more than one joint is affected, or there has been a delay of 3 months or more before seeking advice.

What could it be? Common patterns

The NHS describes some typical patterns. These are clues for a conversation with a professional, not a diagnosis. Many conditions overlap, and you can have more than one.

Pain worse with use, short morning stiffness

Pain that is worse when walking or after activity, with stiffness after rest that usually wears off within about 30 minutes, is typical of osteoarthritis, especially over the age of 45. Joints may look slightly knobbly, creak or crunch, and lose some movement. See our guide to osteoarthritis symptoms.

Pain, swelling and long morning stiffness on both sides

Throbbing, aching pain and stiffness in joints on both sides of the body, often the small joints of the hands and feet, that is worse in the morning or after rest and lasts longer than 30 minutes, can be a sign of rheumatoid arthritis. You may also feel tired or generally unwell. See our guide to early signs of rheumatoid arthritis.

Sudden, severe pain in one joint

A hot, swollen joint with very bad pain that comes on suddenly, often overnight and often in the big toe, is typical of gout. Read about the early signs of gout. A hot, swollen joint with a fever could be an infection, which is an emergency.

Back pain and stiffness that improves with exercise

Back pain and stiffness that gets better with exercise, does not improve or gets worse with rest, is worse in the morning and at night, and starts in early adulthood (usually between 18 and 40) can be a sign of ankylosing spondylitis (axial spondyloarthritis).

Joint pain with skin or nail changes

Pain, swelling and stiffness with swollen fingers or toes, or nail pitting or colour changes, can be psoriatic arthritis. The NHS says to see a GP even if you do not have psoriasis.

Shoulder and hip girdle pain over 50

Pain and stiffness in the shoulders, neck and hips, worse in the morning, in someone over 50, can be polymyalgia rheumatica. Because it is linked with temporal arteritis, watch for headache, jaw pain or vision changes. Our guide to giant cell arteritis warning signs explains more.

A warm, swollen area over a joint

A warm, swollen area that is more painful when you move it or press on it can be bursitis.

Aching joints around the menopause

The NHS notes that perimenopause and menopause can cause aching and painful joints because of lower oestrogen levels. A GP can talk through options.

Looking after joint pain at home

If there are no red flags and your symptoms are mild, the NHS suggests you:

  • rest the joint if you can, but do not stop moving it completely
  • use an ice pack or a bag of frozen peas wrapped in a towel for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours
  • speak to a pharmacist or GP about which painkiller is suitable for you
  • eat a healthy, balanced diet, exercise regularly, and try to lose weight if you are overweight
  • do not smoke

See a GP if things are not improving after 2 weeks.

How a pharmacist can help

A pharmacist can advise on painkillers and gels, check whether a medicine is safe with your other medicines and conditions, and tell you whether you need to see a GP. Tell them about any other medicines you take, kidney or stomach problems, heart conditions, asthma or pregnancy. Pharmacists can also spot symptoms that need a doctor and direct you there.

Physiotherapy without a GP referral

In many areas, you can refer yourself to an NHS community musculoskeletal (MSK) or physiotherapy service without seeing a GP. Search for local services on the NHS website, or ask at your GP practice. This can be a good route for joint pain that is not urgent but is affecting your daily life.

Getting ready for your appointment

A clear description helps a GP or physiotherapist decide on the next steps. Before your appointment, note down:

  • which joints are affected, and whether it is one side or both
  • when it started and whether it came on suddenly or gradually
  • whether there is swelling, warmth or redness
  • how long stiffness lasts in the morning
  • whether movement makes it better or worse
  • any other symptoms, such as fever, tiredness, weight loss, rashes, nail changes, eye problems or bowel changes
  • what you have tried and whether it helped
  • any family history of arthritis or psoriasis
  • how it affects your work, sleep and daily life

Photos of swollen joints can help if the swelling comes and goes. Our newly diagnosed guide explains what happens if you are diagnosed with arthritis.

What might happen next

Your GP will ask about your symptoms and examine you. Depending on what they find, they may suggest self-care and exercise, a painkiller, physiotherapy, blood tests, an X-ray or scan, or a referral to a specialist such as a rheumatologist or orthopaedic surgeon. Osteoarthritis is often diagnosed from symptoms and an examination without needing an X-ray. If inflammatory arthritis is suspected, NICE says tests should not delay a referral to a specialist.

Differences across the UK

  • England: NHS 111 by phone or online.
  • Scotland: NHS 24 on 111, and NHS inform for self-help guides.
  • Wales: NHS 111 Wales by phone or online.
  • Northern Ireland: contact your GP practice or GP out-of-hours service for urgent advice when your surgery is closed. Call 999 in an emergency.

Prefer an interactive tool?

Our symptom checker asks about red flags and the joints affected, then suggests educational guides to read. Like this page, it does not diagnose you and does not replace a GP, pharmacist or NHS 111.

When to get medical help

Use the red flags and table above. In short: call 999 for severe injury, a joint out of place, or back pain with numbness in both legs or bladder or bowel changes. Get same-day help from your GP or NHS 111 for a hot, swollen joint, joint pain with a fever, or new headache with jaw or vision problems. See your GP for swelling that does not settle, long morning stiffness, or pain that is not improving after 2 weeks.

Frequently asked questions

Can I find out what type of arthritis I have online?

No. Online information can help you understand symptoms and know where to get help, but only a healthcare professional can examine you and arrange the right tests.

Is a hot, swollen joint an emergency?

It needs urgent help the same day. Ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111, especially if you feel unwell or have a fever, as it could be an infection.

How long should morning stiffness last before I see a GP?

The NHS says to see a GP if your joints are stiff for more than 30 minutes after waking up.

Do I need an X-ray to find out if I have arthritis?

Not always. Osteoarthritis is often diagnosed from symptoms and an examination. Your GP will decide whether tests are needed.

Can I see a physiotherapist without a GP referral?

In many areas of England you can refer yourself to an NHS community MSK or physiotherapy service. Check what is available locally.

Is this page an AI symptom checker?

No. It is a written guide based on NHS and NICE information. It does not use artificial intelligence and does not diagnose.

What should I do if I already have arthritis and my symptoms change?

Follow your flare plan if it is your usual pattern. Contact your GP or specialist team if symptoms are different, not settling, or you have any red flags.

article.title: Arthritis Treatment — Your Complete Guide to Managing Joint Pain
article.excerpt: Explore every treatment option for arthritis, from NHS pathways and exercise to medication, physiotherapy, surgery, and complementary therapies.
article.content:
Clinically reviewed by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483. Last updated: June 2026.

Quick answer: Arthritis treatment involves a combination of approaches to manage symptoms. Key options include exercise and movement (recommended as a first-line treatment), weight management, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and various medications for pain and inflammation. Surgery may be considered for severe cases when other treatments are insufficient. Complementary therapies can also provide additional relief. Always discuss treatment choices with your GP.

Living with arthritis means living with questions. What will help? Where do I start? Am I doing enough?

We understand. More than 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis — you are not alone. And while there is currently no cure, there is a great deal you can do to manage your symptoms and live well.

This guide walks you through every treatment option available on the NHS and beyond. Think of it as your map. You don't need to take every path; just the ones that are right for you.

What Treatment Options Are Available for Arthritis?

Arthritis treatment is not a single thing. It is a combination of approaches that work together. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) — the body that advises the NHS on best practice — recommends a stepped approach, starting with the safest, most proven options first.

The main categories are:

  • Exercise and movement (NICE's first-line treatment)
  • Weight management (if needed)
  • Physiotherapy and occupational therapy
  • Pain-relieving medications
  • Disease-modifying drugs (for inflammatory types like rheumatoid arthritis)
  • Surgery (when other options are no longer enough)
  • Complementary and lifestyle approaches

Most people benefit from a mix of several of these.

NHS Treatment Pathway for Arthritis

When you first visit your GP with joint pain, here is what the typical NHS pathway looks like:

  1. GP assessment — Your doctor will ask about your symptoms, examine your joints, and may arrange blood tests or X-rays.
  2. Diagnosis — You may be diagnosed with osteoarthritis (OA), rheumatoid arthritis (RA), or another form.
  3. First-line treatment — You will be offered advice on exercise, weight management, and pain relief. You may be referred to a physiotherapist.
  4. Ongoing management — If symptoms continue, your GP may prescribe stronger medication or refer you to a specialist (rheumatologist or orthopaedic surgeon).
  5. Surgery — In some cases, joint replacement surgery is considered when other treatments have not provided enough relief.

You have the right to be involved in every decision. The NHS calls this "shared decision-making."

Exercise and Movement as Treatment (NICE First-Line)

It may feel counter-intuitive to move a painful joint, but exercise is the single most effective treatment for arthritis. NICE guidelines are clear: exercise should be the first thing offered to everyone with osteoarthritis — before medication.

Here is why:

  • It strengthens the muscles that support your joints
  • It reduces stiffness and improves range of motion
  • It helps maintain a healthy weight, reducing load on weight-bearing joints
  • It releases natural pain-relieving chemicals called endorphins

What kind of exercise? Anything that gets you moving gently — walking, swimming, cycling, yoga, tai chi, or specific physio exercises. The key is to start small and build slowly. Even five minutes a day is a win.

Medications for Arthritis Pain and Inflammation

Medication can help you stay active and comfortable. What you need depends on your diagnosis and the severity of your symptoms.

For Pain Relief

  • Paracetamol — Often tried first. Helps with mild-to-moderate pain, though it does not reduce inflammation.
  • NSAIDs (ibuprofen or naproxen) — Reduce both pain and inflammation. Available as tablets or gels.
  • Opioids (codeine-based) — Sometimes used for short periods of severe pain. Carry a risk of dependence and are used cautiously.

For Inflammatory Arthritis

  • DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine) — Treat the underlying disease process in RA, not just symptoms.
  • Biologics — Newer targeted treatments for RA that has not responded to standard DMARDs.
  • Corticosteroids — Powerful anti-inflammatories taken as tablets or injected directly into a joint.

Physiotherapy and Occupational Therapy

A physiotherapist is a movement expert. They can assess your movement and strength, design a personalised exercise programme, teach you how to protect your joints, and offer hands-on treatment and pain relief advice. You can access NHS physiotherapy through your GP or by self-referring directly in many areas.

An occupational therapist (OT) helps you do the things that matter to you — work, hobbies, daily tasks. They might suggest joint protection techniques, gadgets and tools to make life easier, or changes to your home or workplace.

Surgery for Arthritis — When Is It Needed?

Surgery is not a first choice. It is considered when you have severe persistent pain that limits your daily life, other treatments have not helped enough, and your joint is significantly damaged. The most common operations are total hip replacement, total knee replacement, and less commonly shoulder or ankle replacement. Joint replacement surgery has excellent outcomes — the vast majority experience significant pain relief and better mobility.

Complementary and Lifestyle Treatments

Many people find additional relief from acupuncture (some evidence for short-term pain relief), massage therapy, heat and cold therapy, mindfulness and relaxation, and dietary changes like a Mediterranean-style diet. Always speak to your GP before starting any complementary therapy.

Creating Your Personal Treatment Plan

  1. Start with movement — What gentle activity can you do today?
  2. Talk to your GP — Be honest about your pain. Bring a list of questions.
  3. Explore physiotherapy — Ask for a referral or self-refer.
  4. Review your diet and weight — Small changes add up.
  5. Build your toolkit — Heat packs, supportive shoes, a TENS machine? Find what works.
  6. Stay informed — Read the other guides on this site. Knowledge is power.

Continue reading

  • Strength Training on Biologics: Is It Safe? — Resistance work is not only safe — it's recommended.
  • Walking 30 Minutes a Day While on DMARDs: A Practical Plan — Gentle aerobic activity boosts mood and joint health alongside treatment.
  • Best Knee Exercises for Arthritis – OA & RA Guide (UK) — UK physiotherapist-approved exercises for knee arthritis.
  • Foot & Ankle Arthritis – Symptoms & Footwear UK Guide — Complete UK guide to foot and ankle arthritis.

Practical next steps for Arthritis Treatment — Your Complete Guide to Managing Joint Pain

If you came here about Arthritis Treatment — Your Complete Guide to Managing Joint Pain, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Using evidence carefully

Marketing claims for joint supplements often outrun the research. Look for products that state dose clearly, avoid miracle language, and fit alongside — never instead of — prescribed treatment. Stop and seek advice if you notice bruising, stomach pain, yellowing of the skin or new rashes.

Quick questions about Arthritis Treatment Your Complete

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.
