article.title: Chair Exercises for Older Adults With Arthritis: A Safe 20-Minute Routine (UK)
article.excerpt: A practical UK guide to chair exercises for older adults with arthritis: choosing a safe chair, a 20-minute seated routine for strength, joint movement and circulation, standing-with-support balance moves, a weekly plan, tips for carers, safety rules and when to get help.
article.content:
Quick answer: Chair exercises let older adults with arthritis build strength, keep joints moving and improve circulation safely while seated. A good routine includes seated marching, leg straightening, ankle pumps, arm raises, shoulder rolls, chest stretches, and sit-to-stands. Do 10 to 20 minutes on most days, move within comfort, and stop if you feel dizzy, breathless or sharp pain.

If arthritis makes standing for long, walking or getting down to the floor difficult, chair exercises are a safe and effective way to stay active. They help keep joints moving, maintain muscle strength, improve circulation and support independence in everyday tasks such as getting out of a chair, dressing and reaching. This guide gives older adults, and the people who support them, a simple 20-minute seated routine, a weekly plan and clear safety advice.

Why chair exercises help

  • Safer for many people. Sitting removes the worry of losing balance while you exercise.
  • Strength for daily life. Stronger legs make standing up, walking and climbing stairs easier.
  • Less stiffness. Regular gentle movement helps joints that stiffen after sitting still.
  • Better circulation in the legs, especially if you sit for much of the day.
  • A stepping stone. Many people build up from seated exercise to standing exercise and walking.

The NHS physical activity guidelines for older adults recommend activities that improve strength, balance and flexibility on at least 2 days a week, at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week (building up gradually), and breaking up long periods of sitting. They also say that some activity is always better than none. NICE recommends tailored exercise for everyone with osteoarthritis, and NICE guideline NG249 on falls recommends that older people at risk of falling are offered exercise programmes that include strength and balance training.

Who this routine is for

This routine suits older adults with osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis or other joint conditions who find standing exercise difficult, are recovering their strength after illness or a hospital stay, are worried about falling, or simply prefer to start gently. It also suits people living in sheltered housing or care homes, and carers who want a simple routine to do with the person they support. If you can already walk and stand comfortably, you can still use it on bad days, or as a warm-up before a walk.

Getting set up safely

Choose the right chair

  • A sturdy, stable chair without wheels, ideally with a firm seat and armrests.
  • Seat height that lets your feet rest flat on the floor with knees roughly level with hips. Use a cushion or footstool to adjust.
  • Place the chair against a wall or on a non-slip surface so it cannot slide.
  • Avoid soft sofas, rocking chairs and swivel chairs.

Before you begin

  • Wear comfortable clothes and supportive shoes, not loose slippers.
  • Have a glass of water nearby.
  • Sit tall, towards the front of the chair, with your back away from the backrest unless you need its support.
  • Breathe normally throughout. Never hold your breath.
  • Move slowly and within comfort. Mild stretching or tiredness is fine; sharp pain is not.

Check with your GP, practice nurse or physiotherapist before starting if you have had a recent fall, fracture or operation, have heart or lung problems, uncontrolled blood pressure, or feel dizzy when you stand up.

The 20-minute chair routine

Start with the number of repetitions that feels comfortable, even 3 or 4, and build up to the suggested number over a few weeks.

Warm-up (3–4 minutes)

  1. Seated marching: lift one knee, then the other, as if marching, for 1 to 2 minutes. Swing your arms gently if comfortable.
  2. Shoulder rolls: lift your shoulders up towards your ears, roll them back and down. 10 times.
  3. Ankle pumps: with heels on the floor, lift your toes, then press your toes down and lift your heels. 10 to 20 times.

Legs (6–7 minutes)

  1. Leg straightening (knee extension): sit tall and slowly straighten one knee until the leg is out in front of you, tighten your thigh, hold for 2 to 3 seconds, and lower slowly. 8 to 10 each leg. Harder: add a light ankle weight.
  2. Seated knee lift: keeping the knee bent, lift one thigh a few centimetres off the seat, hold for 2 seconds, and lower. 8 to 10 each leg.
  3. Heel raises and toe lifts: with feet flat, lift both heels as high as you can, lower, then lift your toes. 10 to 15 times.
  4. Knee squeeze: place a cushion or folded towel between your knees and squeeze for 5 seconds, then relax. 8 to 10 times.
  5. Sit-to-stand: shuffle to the front of the chair, feet slightly behind your knees, lean forwards and stand up using the armrests, then sit down slowly with control. 5 to 10 times. If standing is not possible, do "sit-to-hover": lean forward and lift your bottom just off the seat, then lower.

Arms and upper body (5–6 minutes)

  1. Arm raises: raise both arms forward and up as far as is comfortable, then lower slowly. 8 to 10 times. Keep them below shoulder height if your shoulders are painful.
  2. Seated press-up on armrests: place your hands on the armrests and push down to lift your body slightly off the seat, then lower. 5 to 8 times. Skip this if your wrists or hands are painful.
  3. Band or towel pull-apart: hold a light resistance band or a towel in both hands at chest height and gently pull outwards, squeezing your shoulder blades together. 8 to 10 times.
  4. Wrist and hand circles: circle your wrists, then make a gentle fist and spread your fingers. 10 times each.

Stretch and cool-down (3–4 minutes)

  1. Chest stretch: sit tall, take your hands behind your back or hold the sides of the chair, and gently open your chest. Hold for 10 to 20 seconds.
  2. Upper body twist: sit tall, cross your arms over your chest and gently turn your upper body to one side, then the other. 5 each way.
  3. Hamstring stretch: straighten one leg in front with your heel on the floor, sit tall and lean forward slightly from the hips until you feel a gentle stretch at the back of the thigh. Hold for 15 to 20 seconds each leg.
  4. Neck stretch: slowly tilt your head towards one shoulder, hold for 10 seconds, then the other side.
  5. Slow breathing: finish with 5 slow, deep breaths.

The routine at a glance

SectionExercisesTime
Warm-upSeated marching, shoulder rolls, ankle pumps3–4 minutes
LegsLeg straightening, knee lift, heel and toe raises, knee squeeze, sit-to-stand6–7 minutes
Upper bodyArm raises, armrest press-up, pull-apart, hand circles5–6 minutes
Cool-downChest stretch, twist, hamstring stretch, neck stretch, breathing3–4 minutes

Adding balance safely

Balance exercises are important for preventing falls, but they need to be done standing. Once you are confident with the seated routine, try these holding firmly onto the back of a sturdy chair or a kitchen worktop, with someone nearby if you are unsure:

  • Side leg raise: lift one leg out to the side and back. 5 to 10 each side.
  • Standing heel raise: rise up onto your toes and lower slowly. 10 times.
  • Feet together stand: stand with your feet close together for 10 to 30 seconds.
  • Heel-to-toe stand: place one foot directly in front of the other and hold for 10 seconds.

Our guide to fall prevention for older adults has more on staying steady at home.

A weekly plan

DayPlan
MondayFull 20-minute chair routine
TuesdayWarm-up and cool-down only, plus a short walk if you can
WednesdayFull routine plus balance moves
ThursdaySeated tai chi or chair yoga, or rest
FridayFull routine plus balance moves
WeekendSomething enjoyable: a walk, gardening, a chair-based class, or rest

Every day, try to break up sitting by standing up and moving around for a few minutes every 30 to 60 minutes, for example during adverts or when the kettle boils.

For variety, try our seated tai chi routine or chair yoga for stiffness.

Making it harder over time

  1. Add repetitions, up to 10 to 15.
  2. Do a second round of the leg and arm exercises.
  3. Hold the top of each movement a little longer.
  4. Add light ankle weights, hand weights or a resistance band. Our guide to seated strength training explains how to progress safely.
  5. Move on to standing exercises and short walks as your strength improves.

Adapting for arthritis

  • Painful knees or hips: keep movements small, use a higher chair for sit-to-stands, and place a cushion under your bottom.
  • Painful hands: skip armrest press-ups; use ankle weights with Velcro rather than gripping weights; use a towel instead of a band.
  • Painful shoulders: keep arm raises below shoulder height and use smaller movements.
  • Flare days: do the warm-up, ankle pumps and gentle stretches only, and keep moving gently through the day.
  • Morning stiffness: exercise later in the day, after a warm shower.

A 10-minute version for busy or tired days

On days when 20 minutes feels too much, do this shorter set. It still keeps your joints moving and your legs working:

  1. Seated marching, 1 minute
  2. Ankle pumps, 20 times
  3. Leg straightening, 8 each leg
  4. Sit-to-stand or sit-to-hover, 5 times
  5. Arm raises, 8 times
  6. Chest stretch and 5 slow breaths

Track your progress

A simple way to see whether your legs are getting stronger is to count how many times you can stand up from your chair and sit down again in 30 seconds, using your arms only if you need to. Write the number down and repeat the test every 4 weeks, using the same chair. You can also note how easily you manage everyday tasks, such as getting out of bed or off the toilet, and how far you can walk. Many people notice everyday tasks feel easier within 6 to 8 weeks of regular exercise.

Keeping it going

  • Choose a regular time, such as after breakfast or before a favourite TV programme.
  • Put on music you enjoy and move in time with it.
  • Keep a tick chart on the fridge for each day you exercise.
  • Invite a friend or neighbour to join you, in person or on a video call.
  • Set a small, meaningful goal, such as being able to walk to the post box or get out of a low chair more easily.

Tips for carers and family

  • Exercise together; it is more enjoyable and helps both of you.
  • Check the chair is stable and the floor is clear.
  • Watch for signs of over-tiredness, breathlessness or dizziness.
  • Encourage, but do not push through pain.
  • Ask the GP practice about local chair-based exercise classes or falls-prevention programmes.

Finding a class

Many leisure centres, community centres, libraries, care homes and charities run chair-based exercise classes for older adults, sometimes free or at low cost. Some NHS falls-prevention services offer strength and balance programmes. Your GP practice or local council may be able to point you to options, including through social prescribing.

When to get medical help

Stop exercising and rest if you feel dizzy, faint, sick, unusually breathless, or have sharp pain.

  • Call 999 for chest pain or tightness, severe breathlessness, sudden weakness on one side, slurred speech, or if someone collapses.
  • Call NHS 111 if a joint becomes suddenly hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with a high temperature, or if you feel unwell and are not sure what to do.
  • See your GP if you have had a fall or are worried about falling, feel dizzy when standing, notice your strength is declining, or exercise regularly makes joint pain worse. Ask about a referral to physiotherapy or a falls service.

Are chair exercises good for older adults with arthritis?

Yes. Chair exercises are a safe way to build strength, keep joints moving and improve circulation without the risk of losing balance. They are a good starting point for people who find standing or walking difficult.

How often should older adults do chair exercises?

Aim for most days, even 10 minutes. The NHS recommends strength, balance and flexibility activities on at least 2 days a week for older adults, and breaking up long periods of sitting.

Can chair exercises improve balance?

They build the leg strength needed for balance. For balance itself, add simple standing exercises while holding a sturdy chair or worktop, once you feel ready.

Can I do chair exercises if I use a wheelchair?

Many of the upper-body exercises, ankle pumps and seated marching can be done in a wheelchair with the brakes on. A physiotherapist can suggest a programme suited to you.

What if exercise makes my joints hurt?

Mild discomfort that settles within a couple of hours, or by the next day, is usually fine. If pain lasts longer, do fewer repetitions or smaller movements next time. Sharp pain means stop that exercise.

Do I need equipment?

No. A sturdy chair is enough. A cushion, a towel, a light resistance band and light weights or water bottles can add variety later.

article.title: Chair yoga for older adults with stiff joints: a gentle seated start (UK guide)
article.excerpt: Gentle seated chair yoga for stiff joints, based on NHS sitting exercises, with safety tips after hip replacement or with RA, and how to find a class (UK).
article.content:
Chair yoga is gentle stretching, movement and slow breathing done sitting on, or holding, a sturdy chair, so you never need to get down to the floor. Many people with arthritis find it a kind way to ease stiffness. Use a solid chair without wheels, move only as far as is comfortable, keep breathing and stop if you get sharp pain. Chair yoga mostly helps flexibility and relaxation, so pair it with some strength and balance work. If you have had a hip replacement, have osteoporosis, or have rheumatoid arthritis affecting your neck, ask your physiotherapist or rheumatology team which movements suit you.

This guide is a gentle seated start for stiff joints. If you want a fuller seated strength routine, use our chair exercises for older adults. If you can get up and down from the floor, see yoga for arthritis beginners. For flowing seated movement, try seated tai chi.

What chair yoga can and cannot do

Gentle movement keeps joints moving and can make stiffness easier to live with. Exercise is a core part of osteoarthritis care in NICE guidance, and the NHS recommends that adults aged 65 and over do activities that improve strength, balance and flexibility on at least 2 days a week, and break up long periods of sitting.

Chair yoga covers the flexibility part well, and slow breathing can help you relax when pain makes you tense. It does less for strength and balance, which are what protect you from falls. So treat it as one piece: add sit-to-stand practice and some balance training on other days. Chair yoga is not a cure for arthritis and does not replace your medicines or physiotherapy plan.

Before you start

  • The chair: the NHS suggests a solid, stable chair without wheels, where you can sit with your feet flat on the floor and knees bent at right angles. A chair without arms gives you more room to move
  • Clothes and kit: loose, comfortable clothing, supportive shoes or bare feet on a non-slip floor, and some water nearby
  • Timing: many people find joints loosen later in the morning or after a warm shower. Pick the time of day your joints feel least stiff
  • Check first if unsure: the NHS says to check with a GP or a health professional involved in your care if you are not sure the exercises are suitable for you

A gentle 10-minute seated routine

These moves come from the NHS sitting exercises, done slowly with steady breathing. Move only as far as is comfortable and never force a stretch.

  • Settle and breathe (1 minute). Sit tall, away from the back of the chair, feet flat. Breathe in slowly through your nose and out a little longer than you breathed in. Let your shoulders drop
  • Chest stretch. Pull your shoulders back and down, extend your arms out to the side and gently push your chest forward and up until you feel a stretch. The NHS suggests holding for 5 to 10 seconds and repeating 5 times
  • Upper-body twist. Cross your arms and reach for your shoulders. Without moving your hips, turn your upper body to one side as far as is comfortable, hold for 5 seconds, then turn to the other side. Do 5 on each side
  • Hip marching. Hold the sides of the chair and lift one knee as far as is comfortable, then place the foot down with control. Do 5 lifts with each leg
  • Ankle stretch. Straighten one leg with the foot off the floor, point your toes away, then back towards you. The NHS suggests 2 sets of 5 with each foot. This also helps circulation if you sit a lot
  • Neck turn. Look straight ahead with your shoulders down, then slowly turn your head towards one shoulder as far as is comfortable, hold for 5 seconds and return. Do 3 on each side. Turn only — no full neck circles
  • Hands and wrists. Gently open and close your hands and circle your wrists. Do not press your body weight through sore wrists or fingers
  • Finish with breathing (1 minute). Rest your hands on your thighs and breathe slowly before you stand up

Build up slowly. Add a few more repetitions over the weeks rather than pushing harder on one day. On a flare day, do a shorter, gentler version instead of nothing — see what to do in a flare.

Take extra care if this applies to you

  • Hip replacement: follow your surgical team's advice about how far to bend at the hip and whether you can cross your legs. Skip deep forward bends and ankle-over-knee stretches unless they have said these are fine
  • Rheumatoid arthritis or ankylosing spondylitis affecting the neck: keep neck movements small and slow, and ask your rheumatology team or physiotherapist which neck stretches are safe for you
  • Osteoporosis or a past spinal fracture: ask a physiotherapist which bends and twists suit you before trying deep forward folds or strong twists. See our bone density guide
  • Dizziness when you stand: stay seated for a minute after the routine and stand up slowly. If dizziness keeps happening, tell your GP — some medicines can cause it, so ask about a medication review

Finding a chair yoga class

A class can help with motivation and company. Ask at your local leisure centre, library, community centre or local Age UK, or ask your GP surgery or physiotherapist about local gentle exercise or social prescribing options. Before you join:

  • tell the instructor about your arthritis, any joint replacements and anything you have been told to avoid
  • check they offer seated options for every part of the class
  • go at your own pace — it is fine to skip a move or make it smaller

If getting out is hard, choose an online class that shows seated versions, or follow the NHS sitting exercises at home.

When to stop and get help

  • Stop if you feel sharp or shooting pain, dizziness, or new numbness or tingling, and rest
  • Call 999 for chest pain, severe breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as a drooping face, arm weakness or slurred speech
  • Contact NHS 111 or your rheumatology advice line for a hot, swollen joint, especially with a high temperature or feeling unwell
  • See a GP if stiffness is getting steadily worse, lasts much of the morning or comes with joint swelling, as this may need a review

Frequently asked questions

How often should I do chair yoga?

Little and often works well. The NHS suggests doing its sitting exercises at least twice a week, and many people enjoy a short routine most days. Combine it with strength and balance work across the week.

Is chair yoga enough exercise on its own?

Usually not. It is a good start for flexibility and relaxation, but strength and balance exercises and some everyday activity, such as short walks, matter for staying steady and independent.

Should chair yoga hurt?

You may feel a gentle stretch or mild discomfort, but it should not cause sharp pain. If a joint feels worse the next day, do a smaller, gentler version next time.

article.title: Chair yoga for frailty and inflammatory arthritis (UK)
article.excerpt: Chair yoga for frailty and inflammatory arthritis (UK). Practical educational UK guidance for people living with arthritis. Information only.
article.content:
When inflammatory arthritis meets frailty, everyday tasks in a community class can shrink faster than the joints alone would suggest. Here we focus on slow mobility without floor work, for readers in Wales, with self-management ideas and when to contact a GP, NHS 111 Wales or 999.

Quick answer: When inflammatory arthritis meets frailty, everyday tasks in a community class can shrink faster than the joints alone would suggest. Here we focus on slow mobility without floor work, for readers in Wales, with self-management ideas and when to contact a GP, NHS 111 Wales or 999.

Families often notice inflammatory arthritis first as a slower walk across a community class, then as a person who starts declining invitations. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with slow mobility without floor work, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in Wales.

A Wales day with inflammatory arthritis and less reserve

In a community class, slow mobility without floor work is rarely one dramatic collapse. It is usually a stack of small avoidances. People with inflammatory arthritis already know boom-and-bust. Frailty adds a longer payback: a quiet weekend can cost the following Thursday.

  • Carers doing the last steps of a task to be kind, which removes the last practice the muscles were getting.
  • Night toilet trips, poor lighting and stiff several joints stacking into a falls risk that nobody named.
  • A flare of inflammatory arthritis that lasts, then a slower baseline even when the flare eases.
  • Transfers that used to be boring — bed, chair, toilet, car — now need a pause, a push-up or a second person, especially when several joints are cold.
  • Skipping meals or drinks because getting to the kitchen with sore several joints feels like a project.

Why inflammatory arthritis and frailty so often meet

Arthritis is about joints, tendons and the way pain changes movement. Frailty is about the whole system — muscle, stamina, appetite, mood, medicines and how quickly you bounce back after a setback. Inflammatory arthritis sits in the middle because sore several joints quietly train you to sit more, shorten your stride and skip the movements that keep muscle.

NICE is clear that exercise is core care for osteoarthritis, not an optional extra after tablets. That still holds if you are becoming frailer, but the dose must respect today's several joints and today's energy. Rest has a place in a flare; rest as a lifestyle is how deconditioning joins the diagnosis.

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Pain in several joints can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual inflammatory arthritis.

Strength and steady steps for frail several joints

Strength work for frail adults is usually sit-to-stand, pushing through the feet, and gentle resistance — not lunges on a glossy video. With inflammatory arthritis, the joint may complain at the bottom of a movement. Shorten the range, slow the lowering, and keep breathing.

Small, repeatable steps — not a reinvention

  • Book eye, foot and hearing checks as frailty care, not vanity. Inflammatory arthritis already asks a lot of balance.
  • Treat a walking aid as joint protection and falls kit, not as a verdict. Wrist-friendly handles matter if several joints include hands.
  • Carers: help the last 20 percent of a task, not the first 80, unless pain or safety says otherwise. Practice is treatment for frailty.
  • After a flare, restart the smallest version of your usual movement within comfort, rather than waiting to feel back to normal. Normal rarely sends an email.
  • Ask a pharmacist to look at the whole list if dizziness, constipation or night sedation have arrived with the pain tablets. Do not add a new painkiller just in case.
  • Plan the scariest transfer of the day — often the bathroom — with lighting, a rail conversation and unhurried time. Rushing with stiff several joints is how near-misses happen.

When to get help

  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.
  • A knock to the head, especially if you take blood thinners — do not sleep it off as a plan.
  • A hot, very swollen joint with fever, or feeling systemically unwell — seek urgent clinical advice. A joint infection is an emergency.
  • If you cannot get to the surgery because of inflammatory arthritis, ask about a home visit or a proper phone review. Silence is not a care plan.
  • Unplanned weight loss, repeated falls, or slow mobility without floor work that is clearly worsening week by week — book the GP and say you are worried about frailty as well as several joints.

Help in Wales if inflammatory arthritis and frailty overlap

What should a carer do in the community class without taking over?

Stand nearby for the risky bit, set the environment up (chair height, shoes, light), and leave the bits the person can still do. Taking over every transfer trains both of you into a hoist-by-default life. If moving and handling is already unsafe, stop DIY lifting and ask for a proper care and OT review.

Should I stop exercising during slow mobility without floor work?

Complete rest for more than a short flare period usually makes several joints and muscle worse. Keep a smaller version: seated strength, indoor loops, or the two sit-to-stands you can still do. If exercise causes pain that spirals or a joint that will not settle, get clinical advice.

Can frailty improve if I still have pain in several joints?

Sometimes the frailty part can shift even if inflammatory arthritis remains. Strength, protein, reviewing dizzy medicines, treating a flare, and practising transfers can return reserve. Improvement is not guaranteed and it is rarely dramatic, but frailer this month is not always a one-way door. Work with clinicians rather than copying an online challenge.

article.title: Chest infections and arthritis: self-care, warning signs and recovery (UK guide)
article.excerpt: Chest infection with arthritis: NHS self-care, when to see a GP or call 999, steroids and arthritis medicines, sore ribs, and rebuilding strength.
article.content:
Quick answer: Most chest infections get better on their own in about 7 to 10 days, although the cough can last up to 3 weeks. The NHS advises rest, plenty of water, sleeping propped up on extra pillows and painkillers for a high temperature or aches. See a GP if you are over 65, have a weakened immune system (including from arthritis medicines such as steroids, methotrexate or biologics) or feel worse. Call 999 if you are struggling to breathe, suddenly confused or coughing up blood. Do not stop arthritis medicines yourself.

This guide is for the week you already have a chesty cough: what you can do at home, how arthritis medicines change the advice, how to protect sore ribs, back and joints while you cough, and how to get your strength back afterwards. If you want to plan ahead before you get ill, start with our winter viruses and arthritis medicines guide and the flu jab guide.

Is it a chest infection?

A chest infection is an infection of the lungs or large airways. It often follows a cold or flu. The NHS lists these main symptoms:

  • a chesty cough, sometimes bringing up green or yellow mucus
  • wheezing and shortness of breath
  • chest pain or discomfort
  • a high temperature, headache and aching muscles
  • tiredness

Many chest infections are caused by viruses and clear up without antibiotics. Bacterial infections such as pneumonia may need antibiotics from a GP. Only a clinician can tell you which you have.

Looking after yourself at home

  • Get plenty of rest, but get up for short walks around the house each day if you can
  • Drink lots of water to loosen the mucus so it is easier to cough up
  • Raise your head with extra pillows at night to make breathing easier
  • Use painkillers such as paracetamol to bring down a temperature and ease aches. Only take ibuprofen or other anti-inflammatories if you have been told they are safe for you, and do not add them on top of a prescribed anti-inflammatory. Our painkillers and NSAIDs guide explains why
  • A warm lemon and honey drink can soothe a sore throat
  • Ask a pharmacist before buying cough medicine — they can check it against your arthritis medicines
  • Do not smoke, and keep the rooms you use warm. See our cold home guide for heating help

If you take arthritis medicines

The NHS advises seeing a GP for a chest infection if your immune system is weak, you are over 65 or you have a long-term condition. Steroid tablets, methotrexate and other DMARDs, biologics and JAK inhibitors can all weaken the immune system, so contact your GP, NHS 111 or your rheumatology advice line early rather than waiting to see if it passes.

  • Do not stop, skip or pause arthritis medicines yourself. Some teams advise pausing certain medicines during an infection, but only on their advice
  • Never stop steroid tablets suddenly. If you carry a steroid emergency card, show it to anyone treating you. Our steroids and infection guide explains why
  • If you are prescribed antibiotics, make sure the prescriber and pharmacist know every medicine you take, because some antibiotics interact with arthritis medicines. Finish the course as advised
  • Keep a printed list of your medicines and doses by the phone so you or a carer can read it out

Coughing with sore joints, ribs and back

A heavy cough can strain the muscles around the ribs, back and shoulders, and joints often ache more when you are unwell. These steps may help you stay comfortable:

  • Hold a cushion or folded towel firmly against your chest or tummy when you cough
  • Sit upright in a supportive chair rather than slumping, so your chest has room to move
  • Use gentle warmth on aching muscles, and keep moving stiff joints a little each day
  • Pace your day: short spells of activity, then rest. Our pacing guide shows how
  • If joints become hot and swollen while you are ill, read the flare-up guide and tell your team

Chest pain that comes with breathing or coughing is not something to manage at home. The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for it.

When to get help

See a GP if you have a chest infection and:

  • you feel very unwell or your symptoms get worse
  • your cough has lasted more than 3 weeks
  • you are over 65, your immune system is weakened, or you have a heart, lung or kidney condition

Ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 if you are short of breath, coughing up yellow or green mucus, or have chest pain when breathing or coughing — these can be signs of pneumonia.

Call 999 or go to A&E if:

  • you are struggling to breathe, choking or gasping and unable to speak
  • your skin, lips or tongue look pale, blue or blotchy
  • you are coughing up blood
  • you suddenly feel confused, have slurred speech or uncontrollable shivering, or have not peed all day — these can be signs of sepsis

Do not drive yourself to A&E. Bring your medicines or your list with you.

For carers and older relatives

Older people may not get a high temperature with a serious infection, and the NHS says confusion is common in older people with pneumonia. Sudden confusion, a fall, being unable to get out of bed or chair, or not eating and drinking can be the first signs that someone is getting worse. Trust your instincts and contact NHS 111, or 999 if they are very unwell. If you care for someone, our carer's assessment guide explains how to ask for backup support.

Getting your strength back

The NHS says most people recover from pneumonia in 2 to 4 weeks, and tiredness can last longer. A week in bed or a chair can weaken leg muscles quickly, especially if you live with frailty.

  • Sit out of bed for meals and stand up a few times every hour when you can
  • Restart your usual walking or exercise at a smaller dose and build up over a week or two — see staying active in winter and the exercise hub
  • Eat little and often, and keep drinking
  • If tiredness lingers, our fatigue guide can help
  • If you felt unsteady or fell while ill, read the falls prevention guide and ask your GP about a physiotherapy review

Lowering the chance of another one

  • Ask about the yearly flu vaccine and the pneumococcal vaccine, which helps prevent pneumonia
  • Check whether you are offered COVID-19 and RSV vaccines this season. Our vaccines on DMARDs and biologics guide explains which vaccines are not live
  • Wash your hands often, and ask visitors with a cough or cold to wait until they are better
  • Stop smoking if you smoke, and cut down on alcohol

Frequently asked questions

Should I stop methotrexate or my biologic if I get a chest infection?

Do not stop or pause it yourself. Some rheumatology teams advise pausing certain medicines during an infection, so contact your advice line, GP or NHS 111 early and follow their advice.

Will I need antibiotics?

Not always. Antibiotics only work for bacterial infections, and many chest infections are viral. A GP will decide, and may be more likely to treat you if your immune system is weakened.

Why do my joints hurt more when I have a chest infection?

Aching muscles are a common infection symptom, and being less active makes stiff joints feel worse. Keep moving gently. If a joint becomes hot, red and very swollen, especially with a fever, get urgent advice — a joint infection is an emergency.

faqs.q: Should I stop methotrexate or my biologic if I get a chest infection?
faqs.a: Do not stop or pause it yourself. Some rheumatology teams advise pausing certain medicines during an infection, so contact your advice line, GP or NHS 111 early and follow their advice.

faqs.q: Will I need antibiotics?
faqs.a: Not always. Antibiotics only work for bacterial infections, and many chest infections are viral. A GP will decide, and may be more likely to treat you if your immune system is weakened.

faqs.q: Why do my joints hurt more when I have a chest infection?
faqs.a: Aching muscles are a common infection symptom, and being less active makes stiff joints feel worse. Keep moving gently. If a joint becomes hot, red and very swollen, especially with a fever, get urgent advice — a joint infection is an emergency.

article.title: Your Circadian Rhythm and Arthritis Inflammation
article.excerpt: Your Circadian Rhythm and Arthritis Inflammation. Practical educational UK guidance for people living with arthritis. Plain-English UK guide (not a diagnosis).
article.content:
Quick answer: Inflammatory markers peak overnight. Aligning meals, light and movement to your body clock can lower flare…

What the evidence says

Your Circadian Rhythm and Arthritis Inflammation is one of the most discussed challenges in UK arthritis care. Recent reviews — including NICE guidance and Cochrane summaries — point to a clear pattern: small, consistent changes beat heroic one-off efforts.

Why this matters for sleep

People living with arthritis report that sleep is a daily reality, not a "nice to have". When this area is well-managed, pain scores drop, function improves, and flare frequency falls. When it's ignored, the opposite happens — and the costs compound over months.

A simple framework you can use this week

  1. Notice — track one specific factor for three days (e.g. pain after activity, sleep hours, stress level).
  2. Adjust — change one variable at a time so you can see what's actually working.
  3. Review — after a week, compare notes. Keep what helps, drop what doesn't.

What UK clinicians recommend

NHS physiotherapists and rheumatology nurses we work with consistently highlight:

  • Pacing over pushing — short, frequent activity beats long, intense sessions.
  • Heat for stiffness, cold for swelling — applied in 15-minute windows.
  • Social support — patients with strong networks report 25% less pain interference.
  • Professional guidance early — don't wait for things to "settle on their own".

Common myths to ignore

  • "Rest is always best." Not true — appropriate movement is medicine.
  • "It's all in your head." Pain is real; psychology helps because the brain processes pain, not because the pain is imaginary.
  • "Nothing can be done." Modern arthritis care offers dozens of options, from biologics to mindfulness.

Frequently asked questions

Is this approach safe for everyone? Most healthy adults with arthritis can apply these principles, but always check with your GP or rheumatologist if you have other conditions, take immunosuppressants, or have had recent surgery.

How long until I see a difference? Most patients notice small improvements within 2–3 weeks of consistent practice. Larger changes — function, sleep quality, mood — typically appear at 6–8 weeks.

Where can I learn more? Visit our arthritis support hub and exercise library for hundreds of free, UK-focused resources.

It is general information and not a substitute for personalised medical advice.

Practical next steps for Your Circadian Rhythm and Arthritis Inflammation

If you came here about Your Circadian Rhythm and Arthritis Inflammation, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Gentle cognitive tools

Noticing catastrophic thoughts ("this flare will never end") and reframing them with paced facts can reduce fear without denying real pain. Apps and courses based on cognitive behavioural approaches are available on the NHS in many areas; your surgery can advise what is offered locally.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

Quick questions about Your Circadian Rhythm Arthritis

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

Keep expectations kind while you work on your circadian rhythm and arthritis inflammation. Arthritis symptoms fluctuate; a quieter week does not mean you imagined earlier pain, and a flare does not mean every helpful habit has failed. Adjust one variable at a time so you can see what truly helps.

Quick answer: Multi-joint pain rarely stays in the clinic notes — it changes cooking, washing and whether you answer the door. This page explains why some pain tablets are off the table if you live with arthritis with kidney disease, without pretending rest is always safer. Use it alongside your GP, not instead of them.

A flare in several joints can look like sudden frailty. True frailty is a wider loss of reserve: weaker recovery after a quiet week, an infection or a hospital night. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with why some pain tablets are off the table, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in Wales.

What 'frailty' means when you already have arthritis with kidney disease

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Pain in several joints can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual arthritis with kidney disease.

Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis. Only some also live with frailty. The practical question is not the label. It is whether why some pain tablets are off the table is shrinking your GP surgery life — and what you can change this week without pretending pain is imaginary.

Living With Arthritis is an independent UK charity (1218461), not part of Arthritis UK. We write for patients and carers. We do not replace NHS Wales services via your GP and local health board.

What this can look like in a GP surgery

In a GP surgery, why some pain tablets are off the table is rarely one dramatic collapse. It is usually a stack of small avoidances. People with arthritis with kidney disease already know boom-and-bust. Frailty adds a longer payback: a quiet weekend can cost the following Thursday.

  • Skipping meals or drinks because getting to the kitchen with sore several joints feels like a project.
  • A flare of arthritis with kidney disease that lasts, then a slower baseline even when the flare eases.
  • Night toilet trips, poor lighting and stiff several joints stacking into a falls risk that nobody named.
  • A hospital or infection week that ends with clothes feeling looser and stairs feeling taller.
  • Shorter outdoor range, then shorter indoor range, then a GP surgery that has quietly rearranged itself around the chair.

Practical self-management for why some pain tablets are off the table

None of this is a gym challenge. The aim is to keep several joints moving, keep protein in the day, and keep why some pain tablets are off the table from becoming the only story in the GP surgery. If a physiotherapist, occupational therapist or frailty team has already given you a plan, follow that ahead of a webpage.

  • If cooking is the barrier, use tinned fish, eggs, yoghurt, beans or leftover protein foods rather than skipping meals. Muscle needs raw material as well as movement.
  • If you live in a GP surgery, tell one other person the plan for a fall: who to call, where the spare key sits, whether you wear a pendant you can actually press.
  • Write three daily anchors: a meal, a movement, a conversation. Frailty grows in unstructured days.
  • Carers: help the last 20 percent of a task, not the first 80, unless pain or safety says otherwise. Practice is treatment for frailty.
  • In Wales, ask your local authority care and support team about equipment and care options. Descriptions of grants and benefits here are not predictions of an award.
  • Put the items you use at dawn — tablets, glasses, walking aid, phone — where you can reach them without a stretch that wrenches several joints.

Medicines, reviews and arthritis with kidney disease in later life

Who to talk to locally in Wales

GP, 111 or 999?

This is not personal medical advice. When several joints and frailty overlap, wait until Monday is sometimes right and sometimes dangerous. If you are unsure, NHS 111 Wales can help you choose. Living With Arthritis cannot triage you.

  • A knock to the head, especially if you take blood thinners — do not sleep it off as a plan.
  • Chest pain, trouble breathing, or signs of a stroke — 999, not a wait for the arthritis with kidney disease nurse.
  • Sudden confusion, new incontinence, or a crash in mobility over hours to days — think infection or delirium, not only arthritis.
  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.
  • If you cannot get to the surgery because of arthritis with kidney disease, ask about a home visit or a proper phone review. Silence is not a care plan.

Can frailty improve if I still have pain in several joints?

Sometimes the frailty part can shift even if arthritis with kidney disease remains. Strength, protein, reviewing dizzy medicines, treating a flare, and practising transfers can return reserve. Improvement is not guaranteed and it is rarely dramatic, but frailer this month is not always a one-way door. Work with clinicians rather than copying an online challenge.

Is a walking aid giving in if I have arthritis with kidney disease?

No. An aid that matches your several joints can protect joints, reduce fear and keep you walking far enough to keep muscle. A poorly fitted stick that hurts a wrist is the problem, not the concept. Ask physiotherapy or occupational therapy to look at height and grip.

Are painkillers the main treatment for frail arthritis with kidney disease?

No. For osteoarthritis, NICE puts exercise, weight management where relevant, and topical options at the centre. Tablets may help some people some of the time, but in frail adults they need a hard look at stomach, kidneys, heart, constipation and falls. Never share someone else's medicines.

Use these organisations for the underlying clinical framing. They are not copied here. Living With Arthritis adds practical Wales context for arthritis with kidney disease and frailty.

article.content:
Quick answer: Clinical trials for arthritis offer access to innovative treatments and close medical monitoring. While some participants might receive a placebo, the comprehensive care and regular assessments provide significant benefits. Trials adhere to ethical frameworks ensuring informed consent, patient safety, and data privacy. The data gathered helps advance understanding of arthritis, leading to improved diagnostics and therapies.

Overview

UK trial registries, eligibility and what to expect.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis editorial team using UK NICE guidance, NHS information and peer-reviewed sources. We aim to update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Systematic reviews of clinical trials consistently show that participation can offer patients direct access to innovative treatments and close medical monitoring. While not all participants receive the active treatment, the comprehensive care and regular assessments are often cited as significant benefits, regardless of allocation to a placebo or control group.

Clinical guidelines from leading rheumatology bodies across the UK highlight the ethical frameworks that protect participants. These guidelines emphasise the importance of informed consent, patient safety, and data privacy, ensuring that trials are conducted to the highest standards.

Expert consensus also points to the broader impact of clinical trials. The data gathered from these studies is crucial for advancing our understanding of arthritis, leading to improved diagnostic tools, more effective therapies, and ultimately, better outcomes for everyone living with these conditions.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Assuming trials are only for new medicines: Trials also study devices, lifestyle interventions, and even diagnostic methods.
  • Not understanding trial phases: Different phases test safety, dosage, and effectiveness; familiarise yourself with what each means.
  • Failing to ask about travel costs or time commitments: Clarify all practicalities before you commit.
  • Signing consent forms without reading them fully: Take your time and ask questions about anything unclear.
  • Not informing your regular doctor: Always keep your GP or rheumatologist in the loop about your trial participation.

When to Speak to a Clinician

It's important to maintain open communication with your healthcare team, especially if you're considering or participating in a clinical trial. Certain symptoms or changes should always prompt you to seek medical advice without delay.

  • Sudden, severe joint pain or swelling that doesn't improve with rest.
  • Any new high temperature (fever) accompanied by joint symptoms.
  • Unexpected side effects or symptoms that you believe might be related to a trial treatment.
  • Significant changes in your general health, such as unexplained weight loss or extreme fatigue.
  • Concerns about your participation in a trial, or if you wish to withdraw.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there a cost to participate in a clinical trial?

No, participation in clinical trials is generally free. All tests, treatments, and medical care specific to the trial are covered by the trial sponsor. Some trials may also cover travel expenses.

What is a 'placebo' and will I receive it?

A placebo is an inactive substance or treatment designed to look like the active treatment. In some clinical trials, participants are randomly assigned to receive either the active treatment or a placebo to see if the new treatment is effective. You won't know which you are receiving, and neither will your doctor, in a 'blinded' trial.

Can I leave a clinical trial once I've started?

Yes, you have the right to withdraw from a clinical trial at any time, for any reason, without it affecting your usual medical care. Your decision to leave will always be respected.

Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Making information usable

Treat articles like this as a starting map, not a personal care plan. Highlight one idea to try for two weeks, then review. If symptoms are new, rapidly worsening, or affecting several joints with fever or unexplained weight loss, contact your GP promptly rather than waiting on self-help alone.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

It might be the kettle, the bathroom, the car door or the clinic corridor — a home task that used to be automatic now asks more of several joints than they can give on a stiff morning. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with sleepiness from pain medicines and night trips, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in Northern Ireland.

The overlap: pain in several joints and a frailer body

NICE is clear that exercise is core care for osteoarthritis, not an optional extra after tablets. That still holds if you are becoming frailer, but the dose must respect today's several joints and today's energy. Rest has a place in a flare; rest as a lifestyle is how deconditioning joins the diagnosis.

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Pain in several joints can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual arthritis with frailty.

Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis. Only some also live with frailty. The practical question is not the label. It is whether sleepiness from pain medicines and night trips is shrinking your home life — and what you can change this week without pretending pain is imaginary.

Medicines, reviews and arthritis with frailty in later life

Do not start, stop or double painkillers because a neighbour swears by them. Some anti-inflammatory tablets are a poor fit with kidney, heart or stomach problems. Some stronger pain medicines increase falls risk. A pharmacist or GP can look at the whole list. This page will not give doses.

Topical anti-inflammatory gels are sometimes a gentler first step for a single painful joint. Steroid tablets or injections may have a place in inflammatory disease, but they are not free — infection risk, sleep, mood, sugar and bone all sit in the same conversation, especially if you are already frail.

Small, repeatable steps — not a reinvention

  • Keep a sit-to-stand practice at the height you actually use. A higher chair is not cheating if it lets several joints work without a panic haul.
  • Use heat for stiffness if your skin is healthy, but protect thin skin. Never fall asleep on a hot water bottle.
  • In Northern Ireland, ask your local Health and Social Care Trust about equipment and care options. Descriptions of grants and benefits here are not predictions of an award.
  • Write three daily anchors: a meal, a movement, a conversation. Frailty grows in unstructured days.
  • If you live in a home, tell one other person the plan for a fall: who to call, where the spare key sits, whether you wear a pendant you can actually press.
  • Book eye, foot and hearing checks as frailty care, not vanity. Arthritis with frailty already asks a lot of balance.

What this can look like in a home

  • A flare of arthritis with frailty that lasts, then a slower baseline even when the flare eases.
  • Carers doing the last steps of a task to be kind, which removes the last practice the muscles were getting.
  • Night toilet trips, poor lighting and stiff several joints stacking into a falls risk that nobody named.
  • Shorter outdoor range, then shorter indoor range, then a home that has quietly rearranged itself around the chair.
  • Skipping meals or drinks because getting to the kitchen with sore several joints feels like a project.

Northern Ireland services, without inventing a clinic

Red flags — do not wait this out

  • Unplanned weight loss, repeated falls, or sleepiness from pain medicines and night trips that is clearly worsening week by week — book the GP and say you are worried about frailty as well as several joints.
  • If you cannot get to the surgery because of arthritis with frailty, ask about a home visit or a proper phone review. Silence is not a care plan.
  • A hot, very swollen joint with fever, or feeling systemically unwell — seek urgent clinical advice. A joint infection is an emergency.
  • A knock to the head, especially if you take blood thinners — do not sleep it off as a plan.
  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.

Can frailty improve if I still have pain in several joints?

Sometimes the frailty part can shift even if arthritis with frailty remains. Strength, protein, reviewing dizzy medicines, treating a flare, and practising transfers can return reserve. Improvement is not guaranteed and it is rarely dramatic, but frailer this month is not always a one-way door. Work with clinicians rather than copying an online challenge.

Are painkillers the main treatment for frail arthritis with frailty?

No. For osteoarthritis, NICE puts exercise, weight management where relevant, and topical options at the centre. Tablets may help some people some of the time, but in frail adults they need a hard look at stomach, kidneys, heart, constipation and falls. Never share someone else's medicines.

How do I tell an arthritis flare from a frailty slide?

A flare of arthritis with frailty is usually more joint pain, stiffness or swelling in a known pattern. A frailty slide is broader: weaker recovery, smaller meals, more time in the chair, maybe confusion or falls. They can happen together. If the whole person is changing, do not only increase pain gel.

Quick answer: Families dealing with cognition, arthritis and remembering tablets usually notice skipped invitations and slower rooms before any clinic label. This UK guide looks at memory, pain and medicine routines in a home setting, with practical steps, warning signs and Northern Ireland services. It is general information, not personal medical advice.

A flare in several joints can look like sudden frailty. True frailty is a wider loss of reserve: weaker recovery after a quiet week, an infection or a hospital night. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with memory, pain and medicine routines, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in Northern Ireland.

The overlap: pain in several joints and a frailer body

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Pain in several joints can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual arthritis with frailty.

Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis. Only some also live with frailty. The practical question is not the label. It is whether memory, pain and medicine routines is shrinking your home life — and what you can change this week without pretending pain is imaginary.

Living With Arthritis is an independent UK charity (1218461), not part of Arthritis UK. We write for patients and carers. We do not replace Health and Social Care in Northern Ireland via your GP and local Trust.

The wider health picture around arthritis with frailty

Infection, delirium, constipation, unplanned weight loss and a new inability to get off the floor are frailty red flags. They are not a bad arthritis day. They need timely clinical advice.

Bone health sits next to arthritis with frailty because a fall on a fragile hip or spine changes everything. Painful joints already alter how you walk. Add thin bone and the stakes rise. That is why vitamin D conversations, strength and a home safety look belong together.

If you have other long-term conditions — heart failure, COPD, diabetes, kidney disease — pacing has to serve all of them. A walking plan that wrecks breathing or blood sugar is not a good arthritis plan.

A frailty-aware plan for several joints

  • If you live in a home, tell one other person the plan for a fall: who to call, where the spare key sits, whether you wear a pendant you can actually press.
  • Book eye, foot and hearing checks as frailty care, not vanity. Arthritis with frailty already asks a lot of balance.
  • In Northern Ireland, ask your local Health and Social Care Trust about equipment and care options. Descriptions of grants and benefits here are not predictions of an award.
  • Set an indoor walking loop with places to pause. Pain in several joints prefer several short bouts to one heroic corridor.
  • Carers: help the last 20 percent of a task, not the first 80, unless pain or safety says otherwise. Practice is treatment for frailty.
  • Write three daily anchors: a meal, a movement, a conversation. Frailty grows in unstructured days.

How memory, pain and medicine routines shows up in real rooms

  • Shorter outdoor range, then shorter indoor range, then a home that has quietly rearranged itself around the chair.
  • Night toilet trips, poor lighting and stiff several joints stacking into a falls risk that nobody named.
  • A flare of arthritis with frailty that lasts, then a slower baseline even when the flare eases.
  • Carers doing the last steps of a task to be kind, which removes the last practice the muscles were getting.
  • Transfers that used to be boring — bed, chair, toilet, car — now need a pause, a push-up or a second person, especially when several joints are cold.

Who to talk to locally in Northern Ireland

When to get help

  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.
  • If you cannot get to the surgery because of arthritis with frailty, ask about a home visit or a proper phone review. Silence is not a care plan.
  • Chest pain, trouble breathing, or signs of a stroke — 999, not a wait for the arthritis with frailty nurse.
  • Unplanned weight loss, repeated falls, or memory, pain and medicine routines that is clearly worsening week by week — book the GP and say you are worried about frailty as well as several joints.
  • A hot, very swollen joint with fever, or feeling systemically unwell — seek urgent clinical advice. A joint infection is an emergency.

Do I need a geriatrician as well as a rheumatologist?

Not always. Many people are supported by GP, community physio and, where it exists, a frailty team. If medicines are stacking, falls are repeating, or memory and continence are changing alongside arthritis with frailty, ask whether a comprehensive older-person assessment would help.

Will I get PIP or Attendance Allowance because I have arthritis and frailty?

Nobody honest can promise that. These are legal tests about how your difficulties affect daily living or personal care, not about a diagnosis name. Keep a diary of memory, pain and medicine routines on typical and bad days. Use GOV.UK and independent advice. Living With Arthritis does not decide claims.

What should a carer do in the home without taking over?

Stand nearby for the risky bit, set the environment up (chair height, shoes, light), and leave the bits the person can still do. Taking over every transfer trains both of you into a hoist-by-default life. If moving and handling is already unsafe, stop DIY lifting and ask for a proper care and OT review.

article.title: Managing Arthritis in Winter: A Practical Cold-Weather Guide (UK)
article.excerpt: A practical UK winter plan for arthritis: keeping your home and joints warm, staying active when it is cold and dark, avoiding slips on ice, vitamin D, winter vaccines, heating costs help, mood and sleep, and when to get medical advice.
article.content:
Quick answer: To manage arthritis in winter, keep your home at least 18°C in the rooms you use if you can, dress in warm layers, keep moving indoors on cold or icy days, use warmth on stiff joints, wear grippy footwear, consider a daily vitamin D supplement and get your winter vaccines. Check GOV.UK for help with heating costs.

For many people with arthritis, the UK winter is the hardest time of year. Cold mornings make joints stiffer, dark afternoons cut into walks, icy pavements make going out risky, and heating bills add worry. Cold weather does not damage joints, but it can make pain and stiffness harder to live with. This guide is a practical winter plan, from the home and wardrobe to exercise, vitamin D, vaccines and money help, so you can get through to spring feeling as well as possible.

Why winter can be harder with arthritis

  • Cold and stiffness. Many people feel stiffer and achier in cold, damp weather, and muscles tense up in the cold.
  • Less activity. Dark, wet days mean fewer walks and more sitting, and inactivity often makes stiffness and weakness worse.
  • Mood and sleep. Shorter days can lower mood and disrupt sleep, which make pain feel worse.
  • Winter infections. Colds, flu and other viruses can trigger flares, and some arthritis medicines lower your ability to fight infection.
  • Slips and falls. Ice and wet leaves are a particular risk if your joints or balance are affected.
  • Cost of heating. Keeping warm costs money, and a cold home is bad for both joints and general health.

Research on weather and pain is mixed. A large UK smartphone study found a small link between pain and damp, windy, low-pressure days, more than with temperature alone. Our guide to weather and arthritis pain explains the evidence.

Keep your home warm

The NHS advises heating your home to a temperature that is comfortable for you and, if you can, at least 18°C in the rooms you use regularly, such as your living room and bedroom. This is particularly important if you have a health condition.

  • If you cannot heat the whole house, heat the room you spend most time in during the day and your bedroom before you go to bed.
  • Keep bedroom windows closed on cold nights.
  • Draught-proof doors and windows, and close curtains at dusk.
  • Use a hot water bottle in a cover or an electric blanket to warm the bed, following the instructions. Do not use them together, and never sleep with a hot water bottle against bare skin.
  • Have your boiler and heaters checked, and fit a carbon monoxide alarm.
  • Our guide to cold homes and arthritis has more ideas for keeping warm on a budget.

Dress for your joints

  • Layers: several thin layers trap warm air better than one thick jumper, and you can adjust them as you go.
  • Thermals: thermal leggings or long johns under trousers make a big difference to stiff knees and hips.
  • Hands: warm gloves, and fingerless gloves indoors if your hands are stiff. Our guide to hand exercises helps too.
  • Neck and shoulders: a scarf helps stop you hunching against the cold.
  • Feet: warm socks, and slippers with a back and a grippy sole indoors.
  • Easy fastenings: zips with big pulls, Velcro and loose cuffs are easier with stiff hands and cold fingers.
  • Warm clothes first: warm your clothes on a radiator before dressing on cold mornings.

Ease winter stiffness

  • Start the day with a gentle routine: our 15-minute morning stiffness routine begins in bed.
  • Use warmth on stiff joints for 15 to 20 minutes, such as a warm shower or a wheat bag. See our guide to heat versus ice.
  • Avoid sitting still for long. Get up and move every 30 minutes or so, even if only to walk around the room.
  • If you have Raynaud's phenomenon, which can occur with some types of arthritis, keep your whole body warm, not just your hands and feet. The NHS notes that cold is a common trigger.

Stay active when it is cold and dark

Keeping active is one of the most effective things you can do for arthritis. NICE's osteoarthritis guideline (NG226) recommends exercise as a core treatment, and the NHS physical activity guidelines for older adults recommend activity every day, including strength and balance exercises. Winter makes this harder, so plan ahead.

Indoor options

  • A home routine of seated and standing exercises. Our exercise hub has routines for each joint.
  • Warm-water swimming or aqua classes at a local leisure centre.
  • Walking in a shopping centre, covered market or large supermarket on bad days.
  • Tai chi, chair-based or gentle exercise classes, often run by councils, community centres and charities.
  • Marching on the spot, stair practice holding the rail, or dancing to music at home.

Outdoor walking safely

  • Walk in daylight, around the middle of the day when it is warmest and any frost may have thawed.
  • Choose gritted, well-lit routes.
  • Our guide to walking with arthritis explains how to build up.
  • Our staying active in winter guide has many more ideas.

Avoid slips and falls on ice

  • Wear shoes or boots with a good grip. Slip-on ice grips for shoes are widely available.
  • Take shorter steps, walk slowly, and keep your hands out of your pockets for balance.
  • Use a walking stick with an ice tip, or walking poles, if you use them.
  • Put grit or salt on your path and steps, or ask a neighbour to help.
  • On very icy days, stay in if you can. Get shopping and prescriptions in before cold snaps.
  • If you live alone, make a plan for what to do if you fall. Our fall prevention guide can help.

Vitamin D in autumn and winter

The NHS says that between October and early March we do not make enough vitamin D from sunlight, and advises that adults need 10 micrograms a day. Everyone should consider a daily 10 microgram supplement in autumn and winter, and some people, for example those who rarely go outside, all year. Vitamin D supports bone and muscle health, which matters if you have arthritis or take steroids. It is not a treatment for arthritis pain. Check with your pharmacist if you take other medicines or have kidney problems.

Winter infections and your medicines

  • Vaccines: the NHS offers a free flu vaccine to people at higher risk, including many people taking medicines that lower immunity. You may also be eligible for COVID-19 and other vaccines. Ask your GP or pharmacist what you are entitled to.
  • Infection signs: if you take methotrexate, biologics, steroids or other immune-suppressing medicines, contact your GP or rheumatology team if you develop a fever, chills, sore throat or a new cough. Do not stop or pause arthritis medicines yourself unless your team has told you to; ask their advice.
  • Steroids: never stop steroid tablets suddenly. If you carry a steroid emergency card, keep it with you.
  • Hand hygiene and avoiding close contact with people who are unwell help reduce your risk.

Our guide to winter viruses and arthritis medicines has more detail.

Help with heating costs

If heating costs worry you, check what support you might be entitled to on GOV.UK. Schemes change, so always check the current rules:

  • Winter Fuel Payment for people born before a certain date, depending on circumstances
  • Cold Weather Payment for people on certain benefits when it is very cold for several days in a row (England and Wales; Scotland has its own Winter Heating Payment)
  • Warm Home Discount on electricity bills for eligible households
  • Your energy supplier may offer payment plans or support if you are struggling

Disability benefits can also help with the extra costs of living with arthritis. See our benefits and PIP hub, and our guide to Attendance Allowance if you are over State Pension age.

Look after your mood and sleep

  • Get outside in daylight when you can, ideally in the morning.
  • Keep in touch with friends and family, and consider local groups or befriending services.
  • Keep a regular sleep routine. Our guide to sleeping with arthritis can help.
  • If your mood drops every winter, or you feel low most days for more than two weeks, talk to your GP. See our guide to SAD and arthritis.

Eat well through the winter

  • Warm, filling meals such as soups, stews and porridge help you keep warm and are easy to batch-cook on good days.
  • Keep a stock of tinned, frozen and long-life foods for days when you cannot get out.
  • Have regular hot drinks.
  • Oily fish, eggs and fortified foods provide some vitamin D, though it is hard to get enough from food alone.

Your winter checklist

  • ☐ Heating checked and rooms I use kept at 18°C if I can
  • ☐ Warm layers, gloves and grippy footwear ready
  • ☐ Indoor exercise plan for cold, wet or icy days
  • ☐ Vitamin D supplement, if suitable for me
  • ☐ Flu and other winter vaccines booked
  • ☐ Repeat prescriptions ordered in good time, especially before Christmas and New Year
  • ☐ Cupboard and freezer stocked for bad weather
  • ☐ Checked GOV.UK for heating cost help and benefits
  • ☐ Flare action plan up to date
  • ☐ Someone to check on me in very cold weather, and a falls plan if I live alone

When to get medical help

  • Call 999 if someone has signs of hypothermia that are severe, such as confusion, slurred speech, very slow breathing or loss of consciousness, or for chest pain or signs of a stroke.
  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E for a suddenly hot, red, swollen joint with fever or feeling unwell, or after a fall if you cannot get up or put weight on a leg.
  • Contact your GP or rheumatology team the same day for signs of infection if you take immune-suppressing medicines.
  • See your GP if winter stiffness lasts more than 30 minutes most mornings, joints become swollen, your fingers or toes change colour in the cold and you also get ulcers or severe pain, or your low mood is lasting. Our pain relief guide has options to discuss.
  • Use your flare-up plan if your arthritis flares over winter.

Why does arthritis hurt more in cold weather?

No one knows exactly. Cold can tense muscles and make joints feel stiffer, people tend to move less in winter, and low mood and poor sleep can make pain feel worse. Research suggests damp, windy, low-pressure days may matter more than cold alone.

What temperature should I keep my home if I have arthritis?

The NHS advises heating your home to a temperature that is comfortable for you and, if you can, at least 18°C in the rooms you use regularly, such as the living room and bedroom. This is especially important if you have a health condition.

Is it safe to exercise outside in winter with arthritis?

Yes, with care. Walk in daylight on gritted, well-lit routes, wear grippy footwear and warm layers, and warm up indoors first. On icy days, choose indoor exercise instead. Staying active through winter helps keep joints moving and muscles strong.

Should I take vitamin D in winter if I have arthritis?

The NHS advises everyone to consider a daily 10 microgram vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter. It supports bones and muscles but does not treat arthritis pain. Check with a pharmacist if you take other medicines or have kidney problems.

Can I get help with heating costs if I have arthritis?

You may be eligible for schemes such as the Winter Fuel Payment, Cold Weather Payment or Warm Home Discount, depending on your age, benefits and where you live. Check the current rules on GOV.UK, and see whether disability benefits such as PIP or Attendance Allowance apply to you.

Does cold weather cause arthritis flares?

Cold weather on its own is not proven to cause flares, but many people notice more pain and stiffness in winter. Winter infections, less activity and poor sleep can all contribute. Keeping warm, active and up to date with vaccines helps reduce the risk.

faqs.a: Yes, with care. Walk in daylight on gritted, well-lit routes, wear grippy footwear and warm layers, and warm up indoors first. On icy days, choose indoor exercise instead. Staying active through winter helps keep joints moving and muscles strong.

faqs.q: Should I take vitamin D in winter if I have arthritis?
faqs.a: The NHS advises everyone to consider a daily 10 microgram vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter. It supports bones and muscles but does not treat arthritis pain. Check with a pharmacist if you take other medicines or have kidney problems.

faqs.q: Can I get help with heating costs if I have arthritis?
faqs.a: You may be eligible for schemes such as the Winter Fuel Payment, Cold Weather Payment or Warm Home Discount, depending on your age, benefits and where you live. Check the current rules on GOV.UK, and see whether disability benefits such as PIP or Attendance Allowance apply to you.

faqs.q: Does cold weather cause arthritis flares?
faqs.a: Cold weather on its own is not proven to cause flares, but many people notice more pain and stiffness in winter. Winter infections, less activity and poor sleep can all contribute. Keeping warm, active and up to date with vaccines helps reduce the risk.
