article.title: Daily Arthritis Planner: A Free Printable Plan for Pacing Your Day
article.excerpt: A practical UK guide to planning your day with arthritis, using the occupational therapy 3 Ps (pace, plan, prioritise), with a printable daily planner, essentials checklist, end-of-day check and weekly overview on the page.
article.content:
Quick answer: Plan your day with the 3 Ps: pace, plan and prioritise. Put the most important task at your best time of day, mix high and low energy jobs, build in at least two short rests, and mark medicines, movement and appointments. Print the daily planner and weekly overview on this page, and have a simpler flare-day version ready.

Checked on 11 October 2026 against the Royal College of Occupational Therapists' guidance on managing energy and the NHS physical activity guidelines for adults and older adults. The planner is on this page: print it or copy it into a notebook. There is nothing to download or sign up for.

Arthritis can make every day feel like a balancing act. Pain, stiffness and fatigue change from day to day, and doing too much on a good day can mean paying for it on the next. A simple daily plan helps you spread the load, remember medicines and appointments, fit in movement and rest, and notice what helps.

This guide explains the principles behind a good arthritis-friendly day, then gives you a printable daily planner, a weekly overview and a few worked suggestions for using them. Use as much or as little as is useful. A plan should make life easier, not become another job.

The 3 Ps: pace, plan and prioritise

The Royal College of Occupational Therapists (RCOT) recommends the "3 Ps" for managing energy with a long-term condition.

Pace

  • Break activities into smaller tasks and spread them through the day.
  • Adjust parts of an activity to make it less demanding.
  • Build rests into activities, and stop and rest between them.
  • Sit down wherever you can.

Plan

  • Plan ahead and create routines.
  • Spread activities out across the day and week.
  • Keep the things you need together and within easy reach.
  • Use equipment to reduce effort.
  • Measure and track your energy use.

Prioritise

  • Be kind to yourself and do not try to do everything.
  • Balance things you need to do with things you want to do.
  • Delegate or drop tasks where you can.
  • Include activities that give you energy.

Our guide to pacing and energy management explains these ideas in more depth.

Building an arthritis-friendly day

Mornings

Many people with arthritis are stiffest in the morning. Allow extra time, take medicines as prescribed, and consider a warm shower and gentle movement before demanding tasks. See our morning routine guide.

Your best time of day

Notice when you usually have the most energy and least pain. Put the most important or demanding job there.

Movement

The NHS recommends that adults aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, strengthening activities on at least 2 days, and breaking up long periods of sitting. Older adults are also advised to include activities that improve strength, balance and flexibility on at least 2 days a week. With arthritis, start where you are and build up gradually. Short sessions count. Our exercise library has ideas.

Rest

Plan short rests before you need them, not just when you are exhausted. A rest can be sitting with a cup of tea, a few minutes of relaxed breathing, or lying down.

Evenings

Wind down with a regular routine to help sleep. Gentle stretches, a warm bath and setting things out for the morning can help. See our evening routine guide.

Printable daily planner

Print one sheet per day, or use the same headings in a notebook. Fill in the "plan" column the evening before or first thing, and the "how it went" column at the end of the day.

Printable weekly overview

Use this to spread heavier jobs across the week so no single day is overloaded.

Two sample layouts to adapt

These are examples of how a day could be laid out using the principles above. They are not prescriptions, and your own day will look different.

Sample: a working day

  • Waking: medicines with breakfast, warm shower, 5 minutes of gentle stretches.
  • Early morning: travel to work with time to spare. Sit if you can.
  • Mid-morning: most demanding work task, at your best time.
  • Late morning: short break to stand, stretch or walk.
  • Lunch: eat away from your desk, with a 10-minute walk if comfortable.
  • Afternoon: lighter tasks, emails or meetings, changing position every 30 to 60 minutes.
  • Evening meal: something simple or batch cooked.
  • Evening: rest, something enjoyable, set out clothes and bag for tomorrow.
  • Bedtime: regular time, wind-down routine.

Sample: a day at home

  • Waking: medicines, allow stiffness to ease before doing much.
  • Mid-morning: one main household task, such as one room or one load of washing, sitting where possible.
  • Late morning: rest with a drink.
  • Lunch: prepare lunch and some vegetables for the evening at the same time.
  • Early afternoon: exercise session or a walk.
  • Late afternoon: rest, a phone call to a friend, or a hobby.
  • Evening: simple meal, gentle stretches, bath, wind down.

Planning around appointments and treatment

Appointments, blood tests and infusions can take more energy than expected, especially with travel and waiting. On those days:

  • keep the rest of the day light and plan a rest afterwards
  • write questions down in advance and take your planner sheets to show how things have been
  • plan transport and parking, or ask about hospital transport if you are eligible
  • if a medicine makes you tired or sick the day after, such as some weekly medicines, keep that day lighter too

Common planning pitfalls

  • Over-filling the day. A plan with no spare time will not survive a bad morning.
  • Only resting when exhausted. Rests work better before you hit the wall.
  • Doing everything on good days. This often leads to a crash. Keep some in reserve.
  • Dropping enjoyable things first. Activities you enjoy help mood and energy. Keep at least one each day.
  • Giving up after a bad week. Plans need adjusting. Review, change one thing, and try again.

Planning with family or carers

If you live with others, share the weekly overview so everyone knows which days are busy and which jobs they can help with. Agree a few tasks others will do on flare days. If someone cares for you, they may also need support. Carers can ask their council for a carer's assessment.

Sleep and your planner

A regular bedtime and waking time help sleep. Use the bedtime row to note your wind-down routine, and the end-of-day check to spot links between busy days, pain and poor nights. If pain keeps waking you, talk to your GP or team.

How to use the planner well

  • Start small. Plan just the morning, or just your top three, for the first week.
  • Mix high and low energy tasks. Follow a demanding job with something easier or a rest.
  • Leave gaps. Arthritis is unpredictable, so do not fill every slot.
  • Plan for good days too. On a good day, it is tempting to do everything. Stick roughly to your plan to avoid a crash.
  • Have a "flare day" version. Decide in advance what the bare minimum looks like, such as medicines, meals, gentle movement and rest. Our flare action plan can sit alongside it.
  • Review weekly. Look at the end-of-day checks. Which days went well and why?
  • Share it. A partner, family member or carer can see when you need help.

Ideas for common tasks

Housework

Do one room or one job a day rather than everything at once. Sit to iron or prepare vegetables. Use lightweight or long-handled tools.

Shopping

Shop at quieter times, use a trolley for support, or use online deliveries. Unpack only cold and frozen items straight away and rest before the rest.

Cooking

Prepare ingredients earlier in the day when you have more energy, batch cook on better days, and sit while you chop.

Personal care

Shower or bathe at the time of day when you are least stiff. Sit to dry and dress. Lay out clothes the night before.

Work

Plan breaks, change position regularly, and put demanding tasks at your best time. Talk to your employer about adjustments if needed.

Social life

Plan a rest before and after outings. Choose venues with seating and easy access. It is fine to leave early.

Planning for busy times and the seasons

Some weeks are harder than others. Holidays, birthdays, school terms, house moves and winter can all add pressure. Use the weekly overview to plan these in advance: spread preparation over several days, book deliveries, ask for help early, and keep the days afterwards lighter. In cold weather, many people find it helps to plan indoor movement, keep warm, and allow more time in the mornings.

If writing is hard on your hands

If hand arthritis makes writing painful, print the planner larger, use a thick or padded pen, or tick boxes rather than writing full sentences. You could also fill it in by voice, using a phone's voice notes or a smart speaker for reminders, or ask someone to write while you talk it through. An occupational therapist can suggest writing aids and other equipment.

Paper or digital?

Use whatever you will keep using. Some people prefer paper because it is quick and visible on the fridge. Others use a phone calendar with reminders for medicines and rests. If you use an app to track symptoms, check what it does with your data and whether you can export it to share with your team.

Remembering medicines

  • Link medicines to daily routines, such as breakfast or brushing your teeth.
  • Use a weekly pill organiser if your pharmacist agrees it is suitable for your medicines. Some medicines need to stay in their original packaging.
  • Mark weekly medicines, such as methotrexate, clearly on the planner, as taking them on the wrong day can be dangerous.
  • Note blood test dates if your medicine needs monitoring.
  • Ask your pharmacist about easy-open lids, large-print labels or reminder charts if needed.

Getting help with planning

An occupational therapist can help you plan your day, use equipment, and find easier ways to do tasks. You can ask your GP, rheumatology team or local council for a referral. A physiotherapist can help you plan safe, gradual exercise.

When to get medical help

Speak to your GP or specialist team if fatigue, pain or stiffness is getting worse, your plan is no longer manageable, or you are struggling with daily tasks. Get same-day help from your GP or NHS 111 if a joint becomes hot and swollen and you feel unwell or have a temperature. Call 999 in an emergency.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best way to plan my day with arthritis?

Use the 3 Ps: pace, plan and prioritise. Put the most important task at your best time of day, spread heavier jobs out, and build in rests before you need them.

How much exercise should I fit into my day?

The NHS recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week and strengthening on 2 days. With arthritis, start small and build up gradually, with advice from a physiotherapist if needed.

Can I download the planner?

You do not need to. The planner is on this page, so you can print it or copy the headings into a notebook.

What should I do on a bad day?

Switch to your flare-day plan: medicines, meals, gentle movement and rest. Move non-urgent tasks to another day.

How many rests should I plan?

There is no set number. Many people find at least two short planned rests a day helps, but adjust to suit you.

Should I plan every hour of the day?

No. Leave gaps for unexpected pain, fatigue or events. Planning the main task, movement and rests is often enough.

Is it worth keeping the sheets?

Yes. A few weeks of sheets can show patterns, such as which tasks or days leave you most tired, and are useful to share with your GP, physiotherapist or rheumatology team.

Who can help me plan my day?

An occupational therapist can help. Ask your GP, rheumatology team or council about a referral.

article.title: Daily Mobility Routine for Arthritis: A Gentle Whole-Day Plan (UK)
article.excerpt: A practical whole-day mobility plan for arthritis: what mobility exercises are and why they help, a 5-minute routine you can do in bed, a 10-minute standing or seated morning routine, movement snacks for desk and sofa time, an evening wind-down, joint-by-joint swaps, how to progress and when to get help.
article.content:
Quick answer: A daily mobility routine means moving each joint gently through its comfortable range every day. For arthritis, a good plan is a 5-minute wake-up in bed, a 10-minute routine after breakfast, short movement breaks every 30 to 60 minutes, and a gentle evening wind-down. Move slowly, never force a stretch, and stop for sharp pain.

Stiff joints are one of the most common complaints in arthritis. Many people find they are stiffest first thing in the morning, after sitting for a while, or at the end of a busy day. A daily mobility routine is a simple, low-effort way to keep joints moving and reduce that stiffness. It does not replace strengthening or fitness exercise, which NICE recommends as core treatments for osteoarthritis, but it makes everything else easier. This guide gives you a whole-day plan, from a few movements in bed to an evening wind-down, with options for every ability.

What is mobility exercise?

Mobility exercises move a joint slowly and smoothly through its available range, without forcing it. They are slightly different from stretching:

TypeWhat it involvesMain purpose
Mobility (range of motion)Moving a joint repeatedly through a comfortable range, such as ankle circles or shoulder rollsEase stiffness, keep joints moving, lubricate joints
StretchingHolding a muscle in a lengthened position for 20 to 30 secondsImprove muscle flexibility
StrengtheningWorking muscles against resistanceSupport and protect joints
AerobicActivity that raises your heart rate, such as walking or cyclingFitness, weight, mood, general health

A balanced week includes all four. Mobility is the easiest to do every day and is often the first thing people notice a difference from.

Why daily mobility helps with arthritis

  • Eases stiffness. Movement helps joints feel looser, especially after rest.
  • Helps joint health. Joint cartilage depends on movement and loading to stay healthy.
  • Keeps everyday tasks possible. Reaching a high shelf, putting on socks, turning to reverse the car and getting in and out of the bath all need joint range.
  • Warms you up for other activity. A few minutes of mobility before a walk or strength session makes them more comfortable.
  • Breaks up sitting. UK guidelines advise breaking up long periods of sitting with light activity.

Golden rules

  • Move slowly and smoothly. Avoid bouncing or jerking.
  • Stay within a comfortable range. Mild stretch or tightness is fine; sharp pain is not.
  • Breathe normally throughout. Do not hold your breath.
  • Start with 5 repetitions of each movement and build up to 10.
  • Little and often works best: several short sessions are better than one long one.
  • Expect some movements to feel easier on some days than others. That is normal.

Part 1: 5-minute wake-up in bed

Do these lying on your back before you get up. They help ease morning stiffness and make getting out of bed easier.

  1. Deep breathing, 5 breaths. Breathe in slowly through your nose, letting your tummy rise, and out slowly through your mouth.
  2. Ankle pumps, 10. Point your toes away from you, then pull them back towards you.
  3. Ankle circles, 5 each way. Draw slow circles with your feet.
  4. Heel slides, 5 each leg. Slide one heel towards your bottom to bend your knee, then slide it back down.
  5. Knee rocking, 10. With both knees bent and feet flat on the bed, gently let your knees rock from side to side.
  6. Finger and wrist moves, 5 each. Open and close your hands, then bend your wrists up and down.
  7. Arm lifts, 5. Lift both arms up towards the ceiling and back over your head as far as is comfortable, then lower.

Then roll onto your side, drop your legs over the edge of the bed and push up with your arms to sit. Sit for a moment before standing. If morning stiffness is a big problem, our morning stretches tip has more ideas, and a warm shower before exercising often helps.

Part 2: 10-minute morning routine

Do this after breakfast or once you have been moving for a little while. You can do it standing, holding the back of a sturdy chair or the kitchen worktop, or sitting on a firm chair without arms.

MovementHow to do itReps
MarchingMarch on the spot, or lift your knees alternately while seated1 minute
Neck turnsSlowly turn your head to look over one shoulder, then the other5 each side
Neck tiltsGently tilt your ear towards your shoulder, each side5 each side
Shoulder rollsRoll your shoulders up, back and down in a circle10
Arm raisesRaise your arms forwards and up as far as is comfortable, then lower5 to 10
Trunk turnsArms crossed over your chest, turn your upper body gently to each side5 each side
Side bendsSlide one hand down the side of your leg, return, then the other side5 each side
Hip circles (standing)Hands on hips, gently circle your hips5 each way
Leg swings (standing, holding support)Gently swing one leg forwards and back, then swap5 to 10 each leg
Knee lifts or seated knee straighteningLift a knee towards your chest, or straighten a knee while seated5 to 10 each leg
Ankle circlesLift one foot and draw circles with your toes5 each way, each foot
Hand routineMake a gentle fist, open wide, touch each fingertip to your thumb5 each

Part 3: Movement snacks through the day

Stiffness often builds up when you sit or stand in one position. Aim to move for a minute or two every 30 to 60 minutes. Ideas:

  • At a desk: shoulder rolls, neck turns, wrist circles, seated marching, and standing up to walk to the kitchen.
  • Watching TV: during adverts or between episodes, do 10 ankle pumps, 5 knee straightens each leg and 5 sit-to-stands.
  • In the kitchen: while the kettle boils, do heel raises, side steps or gentle hip circles holding the worktop.
  • On a long journey: stop every hour or so to walk around, and do ankle pumps and shoulder rolls as a passenger.
  • Working on a computer or phone: stretch your fingers wide and do a few wrist bends every 30 minutes.

Setting a reminder on your phone or watch can help these become a habit.

Part 4: Evening wind-down (5 to 10 minutes)

Gentle movement and stretching in the evening can ease the stiffness of the day and help you relax before bed.

  1. Gentle walk around the house, 2 minutes.
  2. Calf stretch. Hands on a wall, one foot back, heel down, lean forward until you feel a stretch. Hold 20 to 30 seconds each side.
  3. Thigh stretch (seated). Sit near the edge of a chair, put one leg straight out with the heel on the floor and lean forward gently from the hips. Hold 20 to 30 seconds each side.
  4. Chest stretch. Clasp your hands behind your back, or hold your arms out to the sides, and gently open your chest. Hold 20 to 30 seconds.
  5. Knee to chest (lying on the bed). Hug one knee gently towards your chest. Hold 20 seconds each side.
  6. Relaxed breathing. Five slow breaths, letting your shoulders drop as you breathe out.

For joint-specific stretches, see our guides such as stretching for knee arthritis.

Swaps for different joints and abilities

If you haveTryGo easy on
Knee arthritisHeel slides, seated knee straightening, cyclingDeep knee bends, kneeling
Hip arthritisKnee rocking, gentle hip circles, leg swings holding supportForcing hips into deep bending or wide positions
Hand arthritisFinger opening, thumb touches, movements in warm waterTight fists if very painful, forcing fingers straight
Shoulder arthritisPendulum swings, supported arm raises, shoulder rollsFast or forced reaching overhead or behind your back
Back or neck arthritisPelvic tilts, knee rocking, gentle neck turnsFast twisting, looking up for long periods
Axial spondyloarthritisDaily spinal mobility and posture exercises; the NHS recommends regular exercise as an important part of treatmentLong periods of sitting without breaks
Balance problems or frailtySeated versions of all moves; see our chair exercise guideStanding exercises without support

If you have had a joint replacement, follow any movement precautions your surgical team or physiotherapist has given you.

On flare days

Keep doing gentle mobility on flare days if you can, but reduce the number of repetitions and skip movements that hurt the flaring joint. Gentle movement can help prevent the extra stiffness that rest brings. Our guide to exercise during a flare-up has a 10-minute flare-day routine.

Progressing your routine

  • Increase repetitions from 5 to 10, then do two rounds.
  • Gradually increase the range of movement, within comfort.
  • Move from seated to standing versions, holding support.
  • Add a strengthening session two days a week and build up your walking or other aerobic activity.
  • Try a class such as tai chi, gentle yoga or Pilates, which include mobility work.

Keep track of your stiffness

A simple record helps you see whether your routine is working. Each morning, note roughly how long your stiffness lasts and score it from 0 to 10. Once a week, check something practical, such as how easily you can put on your socks, look over your shoulder or reach a high cupboard. Many people notice they loosen up more quickly within a few weeks of daily mobility. If stiffness is getting worse despite a regular routine, mention it to your GP or physiotherapist.

Making it stick

  • Link it to something you already do. Do the bed routine before you get up, the morning routine after breakfast, and the evening routine before brushing your teeth.
  • Keep it visible. Write the routine on a card and keep it by the bed or on the fridge.
  • Start small. Even 2 minutes counts. You can add more once the habit is formed.
  • Do it with someone. A partner, friend or family member can join in, or you could join a gentle class.
  • Use music. A favourite song lasts about 3 to 4 minutes, enough for several movements.

Useful equipment (optional)

You do not need any equipment, but some people find these helpful: a sturdy chair without arms, a non-slip mat, a rolled towel to support your neck or knees when lying down, and a bowl of warm water for hand movements. A long-handled shoe horn or sock aid can make dressing easier while you work on hip and back mobility.

A simple weekly plan

Every day2 to 3 days a weekMost days
Bed wake-up, morning routine, movement snacks, evening wind-downStrength exercisesWalking, cycling, swimming or other aerobic activity, building towards 150 minutes a week

When to get medical help

  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with a high temperature.
  • See your GP if you have morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes most days with swollen joints, as this can be a sign of inflammatory arthritis that needs assessing. Also see your GP if stiffness is getting steadily worse.
  • See a physiotherapist (via your GP or self-referral where available) if you are losing movement in a joint, or if mobility exercises consistently make your pain worse.
  • Stop and get urgent help if you feel dizzy, have chest pain or become very short of breath while exercising.

How often should I do mobility exercises?

Every day is ideal. Short sessions several times a day, such as in the morning, during the day and in the evening, are often more effective for stiffness than one long session.

Should I do mobility exercises if they hurt?

Mild discomfort or stretching is fine. Sharp pain, or pain that lasts more than a day, means you should reduce the range or repetitions. If movements keep causing pain, ask a physiotherapist to check your routine.

What is the best time of day for mobility exercises?

Many people find a short routine in the morning helps with stiffness, and an evening routine helps them wind down. Do what fits your day; consistency matters more than timing.

Can mobility exercises reduce morning stiffness?

Many people find gentle movement in bed and a short routine after getting up eases morning stiffness. A warm shower before moving can also help.

Is a mobility routine enough exercise for arthritis?

Mobility is a helpful part of your routine, but it is not enough on its own. NICE recommends muscle strengthening and aerobic exercise for osteoarthritis, so aim to include both alongside daily mobility.

Can I do mobility exercises sitting down?

Yes. Almost every movement in this routine can be done sitting on a firm chair. Seated versions are a good choice if you have balance problems or painful legs.

  • NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s

article.title: Dating With Arthritis: Telling Someone, Easier Dates and Staying Safe
article.excerpt: A practical UK guide to dating with arthritis: deciding when to tell someone, simple words to use, date ideas that are easier on joints, handling flares, avoiding romance fraud, intimacy and contraception, and healthy relationships.
article.content:
Quick answer: Whether and when you tell a date you have arthritis is your choice. A short, matter-of-fact explanation often works well. Choose dates with seating at a time you feel best, rearrange honestly if you flare, and never send money to someone you have not met in person. If you take medicines such as methotrexate, use reliable contraception and plan pregnancy with your doctor.

Checked on 10 October 2026 against Report Fraud (formerly Action Fraud) and the government's Stop! Think Fraud guidance on romance fraud, NHS information on methotrexate, pregnancy and fertility and contraception, and NHS guidance on getting help for domestic abuse. This guide is general and does not tell anyone how to run their love life.

Dating can be exciting and nerve-racking for anyone. With arthritis there can be extra questions. When should I mention it? What if I have a flare on the day? Will someone see me differently? There is no single right answer, and you do not owe anyone your medical history. This guide offers practical, respectful ideas for dating on your own terms, whether you are new to dating, coming back to it after a long relationship, or dating after a diagnosis.

Start with you

Arthritis is part of your life, but it is not the whole of you. Before you start dating, it can help to think about:

  • what you want: something casual, a long-term relationship, or simply meeting new people
  • what you enjoy and want to share with someone
  • what your energy and pain levels are usually like, and when in the day you feel best
  • what you feel comfortable telling someone about your health, and when

If a diagnosis or a run of flares has knocked your confidence, that is understandable. It may help to talk it through with a friend, a counsellor or your GP first. Our guide to arthritis and mental health covers sources of support.

Telling someone you have arthritis

Whether, when and how you tell a date is your choice. Some people mention it on their profile or early on so it is out in the open; others wait until they know someone better. Some things to consider:

  • Visible needs: if you use a walking aid or need to plan around access, mentioning it early can make arrangements easier.
  • Invisible symptoms: pain, fatigue and stiffness are not obvious, so a short explanation can help someone understand why you might cancel or need to sit down.
  • Your safety and comfort: share only what you are comfortable sharing. You do not need to give details of medicines or diagnoses.
  • How they respond tells you something. A good match will be curious and kind, not dismissive.

Simple ways to say it

  • "I have arthritis, which means my joints can get sore and stiff. Most days it's fine, but sometimes I need to take it easy."
  • "I've got a long-term condition that affects my joints. I'd rather do something where we can sit down, like a coffee or a film."
  • "I sometimes have flare-ups, so if I ever need to move a date, it's not about you."

Keep it short and matter of fact. You can always say more later. Our guide to talking to a partner about arthritis covers longer conversations as a relationship grows.

Date ideas that are easier on joints

Choose dates that suit your body, so you can focus on the person rather than the pain:

  • coffee, lunch or a drink somewhere with comfortable seating
  • a film, theatre or comedy show, booking seats with legroom or an aisle
  • a gallery or museum, using the lifts and benches
  • a short, level walk in a park, with a café at the end
  • a cooking class, quiz night or board game café
  • a video call first, if travelling is difficult or you want to get to know someone before meeting

Suggest a time of day when you usually feel best. It is fine to have a short first date and leave while it is going well.

If you have a flare on the day

  • Be honest and early. A quick message such as "I'm having a bad arthritis day and need to rest. Could we rearrange for next week?" is enough.
  • Offer an alternative, such as a phone or video call, or a shorter, closer date.
  • Do not feel guilty. Anyone can have a reason to rearrange. How someone reacts is useful information.
  • Plan in rest. If you know you have a date coming up, pace yourself in the days before. See our guide to pacing and energy management.

Questions you might be asked

People are often curious, and sometimes clumsy. It can help to have answers ready, at whatever level of detail you choose:

  • "Aren't you too young for arthritis?" "Lots of people think that. There are many types, and some start in childhood or early adulthood."
  • "Is it the kind old people get?" "Mine is [type]. It affects my joints, but I manage it with treatment."
  • "Will you get better?" "It's long term, but treatment helps and most days I get on with life."
  • "Can you still do things?" "Yes, I just plan a bit more. Let me tell you what I love doing."

You never have to answer a question you are not comfortable with. "I'd rather not go into it right now" is a complete answer.

If you use a walking aid or wheelchair

If your arthritis is visible, for example because you use a stick, crutches or a wheelchair, you may find some people make assumptions. Many people choose to show this in their dating profile photos, so that matches already know and there are no surprises on the day. Check venues in advance for step-free access, accessible toilets and seating, and suggest places you know work for you. You can frame this simply: "I know a great place that's easy for me to get to."

A quick date-day checklist

  • Choose a venue you know is accessible and comfortable.
  • Plan your journey there and back, and keep a back-up option such as a taxi.
  • Take any medicines you need with you.
  • Wear comfortable shoes you can walk in easily.
  • Rest beforehand if you can.
  • Tell a friend where you are going and when you expect to be home.
  • Give yourself permission to end the date when you have had enough.

Dating in later life

Many people date again in their 50s, 60s and beyond, after divorce or bereavement. Arthritis is common in later life, so a new partner may well understand more than you expect. Take things at your own pace, and talk early about practical matters such as how far you can walk or how you manage mornings. Our guide to honest conversations in relationships may help.

Online dating and staying safe

Online dating can be a good way to meet people at your own pace. Basic safety advice applies to everyone: meet in a public place, tell a friend where you are going, and arrange your own transport home.

Be aware of romance fraud. Report Fraud and the government's Stop! Think Fraud campaign advise:

  • Never send money, including vouchers, cryptocurrency or money for investments, to someone you have not met in person, however urgent or sad their story.
  • Be wary if someone asks lots of questions about you but reveals little about themselves, or encourages you to keep the relationship secret from family and friends.
  • Consider staying on the dating site or app until you are confident the person is who they say they are, and use a reverse image search to check profile photos.
  • Be careful about how much personal information you share.

If you think you have been targeted, stop contact, tell your bank straight away and report it to Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040. In Scotland, report it to Police Scotland on 101. Report Fraud stresses that victims are not to blame.

Intimacy and sex

Arthritis can affect sex through pain, stiffness, fatigue or the side effects of some medicines. Many people find ways to have a satisfying sex life by planning for times when they feel better, trying different positions, using pillows for support, and talking openly with their partner. Our guide to sex and intimacy with arthritis has practical ideas.

  • Contraception and medicines: some arthritis medicines can harm an unborn baby. For example, the NHS says methotrexate is not recommended in pregnancy because it can cause birth defects, and may affect fertility in both men and women. If you take a medicine like this, use reliable contraception and talk to your doctor before trying for a baby.
  • Sexual health: safer sex advice applies to everyone. If you take immune-suppressing medicines, ask your team whether you need any extra precautions against infection.
  • Side effects: if you think a medicine is affecting your desire or function, speak to your GP or specialist team rather than stopping it.

As a relationship develops

  • Share more about your condition at your own pace, including what helps and what does not.
  • Talk about how you would like support, so a partner does not take over or guess.
  • Keep doing the things you enjoy together, and find new ones that suit you both.
  • Plan for flares together, so they feel less disruptive.
  • Remember that partners need support too. A relationship where both people feel heard is more likely to last.

Building confidence

  • Focus on what you offer: your humour, interests, values and experiences.
  • Dress for comfort and confidence. Choose shoes and clothes that you can manage easily and feel good in.
  • Practise saying it. Rehearse how you might mention arthritis with a friend, so it feels natural.
  • Join groups and activities you enjoy. Meeting people through shared interests can take pressure off.
  • Be kind to yourself if a date does not work out. Rejection happens to everyone, and is often nothing to do with your health.

Dating again after a long relationship or diagnosis

If you have been out of the dating world for years, or were diagnosed during or after a relationship, things can feel very different. Take your time. Some people start by meeting new people in low-pressure settings, such as clubs, classes or volunteering. Online dating can let you get to know someone before meeting. There is no deadline.

Healthy and unhealthy relationships

A good partner respects your boundaries, your health needs and your independence. Warning signs include someone who mocks or dismisses your condition, pressures you, controls your money or medicines, or isolates you from friends and family. Abuse can happen in any relationship, and it is never your fault.

If you are worried about a relationship, the NHS lists free, confidential support including the Freephone National Domestic Abuse Helpline, run by Refuge, on 0808 2000 247 (any time, day or night), Respect Men's Advice Line on 0808 8010 327, and Galop on 0800 999 5428 for LGBT+ people. In an emergency, call 999.

Getting support

  • Talk to friends, family or others with arthritis. Peer support groups and online communities can share practical experience.
  • Relationship counselling, such as from Relate, is available for individuals and couples.
  • If low mood or anxiety are holding you back, speak to your GP or, in England, refer yourself to NHS Talking Therapies.

When to get medical help

Speak to your GP or specialist team if arthritis or its treatment is affecting your sex life, you need advice on contraception with your medicines, or you are planning a pregnancy. Get same-day help from your GP or NHS 111 if you have a hot, swollen, very painful joint with a fever, or signs of infection while on immune-suppressing medicines. If you feel you cannot cope or are thinking about harming yourself, call 999, go to A&E, or contact Samaritans on 116 123.

Frequently asked questions

When should I tell a date I have arthritis?

When you feel comfortable. Some people mention it early, others wait. If you need practical arrangements, such as seating or access, mentioning it beforehand can help.

What is a good first date if I have arthritis?

Something with seating and a flexible length, such as coffee, lunch or a film, at a time of day when you usually feel best.

What if I have to cancel because of a flare?

Let them know early and suggest another time or a video call. A kind response is a good sign.

Should I put arthritis on my dating profile?

It is entirely your choice. Some people find it filters out people who would not be supportive; others prefer to explain in person.

Can arthritis medicines affect contraception or pregnancy?

Some can. The NHS says methotrexate can cause birth defects, so reliable contraception and planning with your doctor are important.

How do I spot a romance scam?

Be wary of anyone you have not met who asks for money, avoids meeting or video calling, or asks you to keep the relationship secret. Never send money to someone you have not met in person.

faqs.q: What is a good first date if I have arthritis?
faqs.a: Something with seating and a flexible length, such as coffee, lunch or a film, at a time of day when you usually feel best.

faqs.q: What if I have to cancel because of a flare?
faqs.a: Let them know early and suggest another time or a video call. A kind response is a good sign.

faqs.q: Should I put arthritis on my dating profile?
faqs.a: It is entirely your choice. Some people find it filters out people who would not be supportive; others prefer to explain in person.

faqs.q: Can arthritis medicines affect contraception or pregnancy?
faqs.a: Some can. The NHS says methotrexate can cause birth defects, so reliable contraception and planning with your doctor are important.

faqs.q: How do I spot a romance scam?
faqs.a: Be wary of anyone you have not met who asks for money, avoids meeting or video calling, or asks you to keep the relationship secret. Never send money to someone you have not met in person.

article.excerpt: Pain across several joints plus a slower bounce-back is a familiar later-life picture in the UK. This page explains company, a meal and a reason.
article.content:
Pain across several joints plus a slower bounce-back is a familiar later-life picture in the UK. This page explains company, a meal and a reason to get dressed if you live with arthritis with frailty, without pretending rest is always safer. Use it alongside your GP, not instead of them.

Quick answer: Pain across several joints plus a slower bounce-back is a familiar later-life picture in the UK. This page explains company, a meal and a reason to get dressed if you live with arthritis with frailty, without pretending rest is always safer. Use it alongside your GP, not instead of them.

Families often notice arthritis with frailty first as a slower walk across a day centre, then as a person who starts declining invitations. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with company, a meal and a reason to get dressed, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in Northern Ireland.

Signs the overlap is affecting several joints

In a day centre, company, a meal and a reason to get dressed is rarely one dramatic collapse. It is usually a stack of small avoidances. People with arthritis with frailty already know boom-and-bust. Frailty adds a longer payback: a quiet weekend can cost the following Thursday.

  • New fear after a near-miss, even if you did not hit the floor. Fear of falling is itself a reason people sit more.
  • Carers doing the last steps of a task to be kind, which removes the last practice the muscles were getting.
  • Night toilet trips, poor lighting and stiff several joints stacking into a falls risk that nobody named.
  • A hospital or infection week that ends with clothes feeling looser and stairs feeling taller.
  • Skipping meals or drinks because getting to the kitchen with sore several joints feels like a project.

Things you can try this week in a day centre

None of this is a gym challenge. The aim is to keep several joints moving, keep protein in the day, and keep company, a meal and a reason to get dressed from becoming the only story in the day centre. If a physiotherapist, occupational therapist or frailty team has already given you a plan, follow that ahead of a webpage.

  • If cooking is the barrier, use tinned fish, eggs, yoghurt, beans or leftover protein foods rather than skipping meals. Muscle needs raw material as well as movement.
  • Use heat for stiffness if your skin is healthy, but protect thin skin. Never fall asleep on a hot water bottle.
  • Keep a sit-to-stand practice at the height you actually use. A higher chair is not cheating if it lets several joints work without a panic haul.
  • Book eye, foot and hearing checks as frailty care, not vanity. Arthritis with frailty already asks a lot of balance.
  • Put the items you use at dawn — tablets, glasses, walking aid, phone — where you can reach them without a stretch that wrenches several joints.
  • Plan the scariest transfer of the day — often the bathroom — with lighting, a rail conversation and unhurried time. Rushing with stiff several joints is how near-misses happen.

Pain, muscle and recovery: the Northern Ireland picture

NICE is clear that exercise is core care for osteoarthritis, not an optional extra after tablets. That still holds if you are becoming frailer, but the dose must respect today's several joints and today's energy. Rest has a place in a flare; rest as a lifestyle is how deconditioning joins the diagnosis.

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Pain in several joints can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual arthritis with frailty.

Lifestyle changes that are really clinical care

Who to talk to locally in Northern Ireland

GP, 111 or 999?

This is not personal medical advice. When several joints and frailty overlap, wait until Monday is sometimes right and sometimes dangerous. If you are unsure, your GP out-of-hours service or emergency services as directed on nidirect can help you choose. Living With Arthritis cannot triage you.

  • A hot, very swollen joint with fever, or feeling systemically unwell — seek urgent clinical advice. A joint infection is an emergency.
  • If you cannot get to the surgery because of arthritis with frailty, ask about a home visit or a proper phone review. Silence is not a care plan.
  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.
  • Unplanned weight loss, repeated falls, or company, a meal and a reason to get dressed that is clearly worsening week by week — book the GP and say you are worried about frailty as well as several joints.
  • A knock to the head, especially if you take blood thinners — do not sleep it off as a plan.

Will I get PIP or Attendance Allowance because I have arthritis and frailty?

Nobody honest can promise that. These are legal tests about how your difficulties affect daily living or personal care, not about a diagnosis name. Keep a diary of company, a meal and a reason to get dressed on typical and bad days. Use GOV.UK and independent advice. Living With Arthritis does not decide claims.

Should I stop exercising during company, a meal and a reason to get dressed?

Complete rest for more than a short flare period usually makes several joints and muscle worse. Keep a smaller version: seated strength, indoor loops, or the two sit-to-stands you can still do. If exercise causes pain that spirals or a joint that will not settle, get clinical advice.

Do I need a geriatrician as well as a rheumatologist?

Not always. Many people are supported by GP, community physio and, where it exists, a frailty team. If medicines are stacking, falls are repeating, or memory and continence are changing alongside arthritis with frailty, ask whether a comprehensive older-person assessment would help.

article.title: Getting your strength back after an arthritis flare or illness week (UK guide)
article.excerpt: Weaker after a flare or a week ill in bed? Start small, pace up gently, self-refer to NHS physio where you can, and know when to get urgent help. UK guide.
article.content:
After a flare or a week ill in bed, days of much less movement can leave your muscles weaker and your stamina lower, so stairs, the kettle and the walk to the shop can feel harder even once the pain settles. Start with small, frequent movement you can manage today — standing up from a chair a few times, short walks around your home, gentle joint movements — and build up a little at a time rather than waiting to feel back to normal. Pace your day, keep eating and drinking, and ask about NHS physiotherapy: in many areas you can refer yourself to community MSK physio without seeing a GP. Get urgent help for a hot, swollen joint with a high temperature, a painful swollen leg, chest pain or breathlessness.

This guide is for one job: getting your strength and confidence back once the worst of a flare or illness has passed. If you are still in the middle of a flare, start with our flare-up: what to do now guide and printable flare action plan. For day-to-day energy, see energy management and pacing.

First check: is it the right time to build up?

You do not need to be pain-free to start. A good sign is that the flare or infection is settling: swelling is going down, you are eating and drinking again, and you can get to the toilet and back safely. If a hospital team, physiotherapist or your rheumatology team has already given you a recovery plan, follow that ahead of this page.

Check the urgent help list below first. A joint that is getting hotter and more swollen, a new fever, or a leg that has become painful and swollen are not signs of being out of condition. They need prompt medical advice.

Week 1: small, often and boring on purpose

  • Stand up from a firm chair a few times, several times a day, using your hands if you need to. Our sit-to-stand practice guide explains how to set up safely
  • Walk around your home every hour or so while you are awake. The NHS advises getting up and moving around regularly rather than sitting still for long periods, and being confined to bed for 3 days or more raises the risk of a blood clot (DVT)
  • Move sore joints gently through a comfortable range a few times a day — the NHS sitting exercises are a good starting point
  • Keep up meals and drinks. Small, regular snacks count if your appetite is low
  • Rest before you are exhausted, not after. A short sit-down between tasks protects tomorrow

Weeks 2 to 6: build up a little at a time

Increase one thing at a time — a few more minutes of walking, one more repeat of an exercise, or one extra job in the day. Some aching that settles by the next day is common when you restart. If pain keeps you awake, a joint swells more, or you feel wiped out the following day, go back to the last level that felt manageable and build again more slowly.

Over the following weeks, work towards the NHS physical activity guidelines. For adults aged 65 and over, these are to be active every day, even if it is just light activity, and to do activities that improve strength, balance and flexibility on at least 2 days a week. Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) recommends a mixture of strengthening, stretching, fitness and balance activities. For osteoarthritis, NICE recommends exercise tailored to you as a core treatment.

  • Strength: our beginner strength programme has easier versions for flare weeks
  • Walking: follow the start, build up, keep going walking plan
  • Winter: our staying active in winter guide has indoor options for cold or icy days
  • Joint-by-joint routines are in the exercise hub

Pacing so you do not boom and bust

The common trap after a flare is doing everything on the first good day, then paying for it for a week. Plan the day, put the most important job first, split big jobs into smaller parts, and leave some energy spare. Our pacing guide and pacing techniques for pain show how to set a baseline you can repeat on a bad day as well as a good one.

Getting physiotherapy on the NHS

The NHS says physiotherapy is free on the NHS, although there may be a waiting list. In many areas you can refer yourself to NHS community musculoskeletal (MSK) services without seeing a GP. Some GP surgeries have first contact physiotherapists who can assess bone and joint problems. If you cannot get to the surgery or hospital, a physiotherapist may be able to visit you at home, and some offer phone or video appointments.

  • Check your GP surgery website or ask reception whether you can self-refer to MSK physiotherapy
  • If you have rheumatoid arthritis or another inflammatory arthritis, ask your rheumatology team or advice line whether the flare needs a review and whether they can refer you to their physiotherapist
  • While you wait, our NHS physio waiting list guide and waiting list help page show what you can safely do in the meantime
  • If you pay privately, the NHS advises choosing a physiotherapist who is chartered (MCSP) and registered with the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC)

If an infection, steroids or a hospital stay caused the setback

  • After a chest infection, our chest infection guide has a section on getting your strength back
  • If you were given steroids for the flare, do not stop them early because you feel better. Follow your team's plan — see our steroid card guide and bone protection on steroids
  • If you felt unsteady or fell while unwell, read our confidence after a fall guide and ask your GP about a falls assessment
  • If new medicines left you drowsy or dizzy, ask for a medication review. Do not stop prescribed medicines yourself

If you care for someone getting back on their feet

  • Let them do as much of each task as they safely can. Stand nearby for the tricky part rather than taking over
  • Agree a simple daily plan: a few sit-to-stands, a short walk, meals and drinks, and rest breaks
  • You can ask the local council for a free care needs assessment if daily tasks have become unsafe, and for a carer's assessment for yourself

When to get urgent help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, severe breathlessness or collapse — including leg pain and swelling with breathlessness or chest pain, which can mean a blood clot has travelled to the lungs
  • Call 999 after a fall if someone cannot get up or may have injured their head, neck, back or hip
  • Urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for throbbing pain and swelling in one leg, usually the calf or thigh, especially after days in bed
  • Urgent same-day advice (GP, rheumatology advice line or NHS 111) for a hot, swollen, very painful joint with a high temperature or feeling unwell — see our hot swollen joint guide
  • See your GP if you are not improving after a few weeks, flares keep coming back, or everyday tasks such as washing, dressing or stairs are getting harder

Frequently asked questions

How long does it take to get my strength back after a flare?

It varies a lot, depending on how long you were less active, your type of arthritis, other health conditions and your age. Many people notice small gains within a few weeks of regular practice. Track simple things — how many times you can stand up from a chair, or how far you can walk — so you can see progress that is easy to miss day to day.

Should I rest completely until the pain has gone?

Usually not. Short rests help, but long spells of complete rest tend to make stiffness and weakness worse. Gentle movement within comfort, little and often, is usually better. Follow any specific advice from your own team, especially after surgery or a joint injection.

Is this a flare or am I getting frailer?

A flare usually means more pain, stiffness or swelling in a familiar pattern. Losing strength, appetite, weight or confidence over weeks, or new falls, is broader and worth raising with your GP. The two can happen together, and both can improve with the right support.

The wider health picture around arthritis with frailty

Infection, delirium, constipation, unplanned weight loss and a new inability to get off the floor are frailty red flags. They are not a bad arthritis day. They need timely clinical advice.

Small, repeatable steps — not a reinvention

  • If you live in a hospital, tell one other person the plan for a fall: who to call, where the spare key sits, whether you wear a pendant you can actually press.
  • Ask a pharmacist to look at the whole list if dizziness, constipation or night sedation have arrived with the pain tablets. Do not add a new painkiller just in case.
  • Put the items you use at dawn — tablets, glasses, walking aid, phone — where you can reach them without a stretch that wrenches several joints.
  • If stairs are the bottleneck, get an occupational therapy conversation on the list while you temporarily live downstairs — drifting is how a camp-bed becomes a lifestyle.
  • Plan the scariest transfer of the day — often the bathroom — with lighting, a rail conversation and unhurried time. Rushing with stiff several joints is how near-misses happen.

Red flags — do not wait this out

  • Unplanned weight loss, repeated falls, or sudden confusion on top of joint pain that is clearly worsening week by week — book the GP and say you are worried about frailty as well as several joints.
  • Chest pain, trouble breathing, or signs of a stroke — 999, not a wait for the arthritis with frailty nurse.

  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.
  • If you cannot get to the surgery because of arthritis with frailty, ask about a home visit or a proper phone review. Silence is not a care plan.

Help in Scotland if arthritis and frailty overlap

Are painkillers the main treatment for frail arthritis with frailty?

No. For osteoarthritis, NICE puts exercise, weight management where relevant, and topical options at the centre. Tablets may help some people some of the time, but in frail adults they need a hard look at stomach, kidneys, heart, constipation and falls. Never share someone else's medicines.

Is a walking aid giving in if I have arthritis with frailty?

No. An aid that matches your several joints can protect joints, reduce fear and keep you walking far enough to keep muscle. A poorly fitted stick that hurts a wrist is the problem, not the concept. Ask physiotherapy or occupational therapy to look at height and grip.

Can frailty improve if I still have pain in several joints?

Sometimes the frailty part can shift even if arthritis with frailty remains. Strength, protein, reviewing dizzy medicines, treating a flare, and practising transfers can return reserve. Improvement is not guaranteed and it is rarely dramatic, but frailer this month is not always a one-way door. Work with clinicians rather than copying an online challenge.

Picture the moment in a home when your hands refuse a simple transfer and you feel your confidence drop faster than the pain score. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with cleaning teeth and getting to the dentist, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in Northern Ireland.

The overlap: painful hands and a frailer body

NICE is clear that exercise is core care for osteoarthritis, not an optional extra after tablets. That still holds if you are becoming frailer, but the dose must respect today's hands and today's energy. Rest has a place in a flare; rest as a lifestyle is how deconditioning joins the diagnosis.

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Painful hands can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual hand osteoarthritis.

Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis. Only some also live with frailty. The practical question is not the label. It is whether cleaning teeth and getting to the dentist is shrinking your home life — and what you can change this week without pretending pain is imaginary.

Small, repeatable steps — not a reinvention

  • Book eye, foot and hearing checks as frailty care, not vanity. Hand osteoarthritis already asks a lot of balance.
  • Use heat for stiffness if your skin is healthy, but protect thin skin. Never fall asleep on a hot water bottle.
  • If stairs are the bottleneck, get an occupational therapy conversation on the list while you temporarily live downstairs — drifting is how a camp-bed becomes a lifestyle.
  • After a flare, restart the smallest version of your usual movement within comfort, rather than waiting to feel back to normal. Normal rarely sends an email.
  • Put the items you use at dawn — tablets, glasses, walking aid, phone — where you can reach them without a stretch that wrenches hands.
  • Set an indoor walking loop with places to pause. Painful hands prefer several short bouts to one heroic corridor.

What this can look like in a home

  • Night toilet trips, poor lighting and stiff hands stacking into a falls risk that nobody named.
  • Skipping meals or drinks because getting to the kitchen with sore hands feels like a project.
  • A flare of hand osteoarthritis that lasts, then a slower baseline even when the flare eases.

What to put on the problem list besides hands

GP, 111 or 999?

This is not personal medical advice. When hands and frailty overlap, wait until Monday is sometimes right and sometimes dangerous. If you are unsure, your GP out-of-hours service or emergency services as directed on nidirect can help you choose. Living With Arthritis cannot triage you.

  • Chest pain, trouble breathing, or signs of a stroke — 999, not a wait for the hand osteoarthritis nurse.
  • A knock to the head, especially if you take blood thinners — do not sleep it off as a plan.
  • Unplanned weight loss, repeated falls, or cleaning teeth and getting to the dentist that is clearly worsening week by week — book the GP and say you are worried about frailty as well as hands.

Northern Ireland services, without inventing a clinic

Start with your GP practice and Health and Social Care in Northern Ireland via your GP and local Trust. For urgent but non-emergency advice use your GP out-of-hours service or emergency services as directed on nidirect. For chest pain, suspected hip fracture, sudden new weakness, or a fall with a bang to the head on blood thinners, use 999.

In Northern Ireland, nidirect explains how to start care conversations. Trust boundaries and waiting lists vary. If hills, steps or winter ice make the trip unsafe, say so when you book — staff cannot guess the pavement outside your door.

Ask about community physiotherapy, occupational therapy, reablement after hospital, podiatry, pharmacy reviews and your local Health and Social Care Trust. Names of teams change. The functions do not: get you moving, get you equipped, get the medicines tidier, get a human being through the door if you cannot get out.

Age UK and local advice agencies can help with forms. The Charity Commission listing for Living With Arthritis (1218461) is public if you want to check who we are. We are independent of Arthritis UK.

Are painkillers the main treatment for frail hand osteoarthritis?

No. For osteoarthritis, NICE puts exercise, weight management where relevant, and topical options at the centre. Tablets may help some people some of the time, but in frail adults they need a hard look at stomach, kidneys, heart, constipation and falls. Never share someone else's medicines.

Will I get PIP or Attendance Allowance because I have hand osteoarthritis and frailty?

Nobody honest can promise that. These are legal tests about how your difficulties affect daily living or personal care, not about a diagnosis name. Keep a diary of cleaning teeth and getting to the dentist on typical and bad days. Use GOV.UK and independent advice. Living With Arthritis does not decide claims.

What should a carer do in the home without taking over?

Stand nearby for the risky bit, set the environment up (chair height, shoes, light), and leave the bits the person can still do. Taking over every transfer trains both of you into a hoist-by-default life. If moving and handling is already unsafe, stop DIY lifting and ask for a proper care and OT review.

article.title: Depression and Arthritis: When to Ask for Help (UK)
article.excerpt: UK guide to depression with arthritis: warning signs, talking to your GP, NHS Talking Therapies, self-help alongside treatment, and where to get urgent help.
article.content:
Quick answer: Ask for help if low mood, loss of interest or hopelessness last most days for two weeks or more, or stop you managing daily life. Talk to your GP, or in England self-refer to NHS Talking Therapies. If you are thinking about harming yourself or feel unsafe, call 999, contact NHS 111, or call Samaritans free on 116 123 at any time.

Need help now? If you feel you might harm yourself or are not safe, call 999 or go to A&E. You can also contact NHS 111 (in England, choose the mental health option) or call Samaritans on 116 123, free, day or night. You can text SHOUT to 85258.

Living with pain that comes and goes, broken sleep and things you can no longer do easily can wear anyone down. Low mood is common with long-term conditions such as arthritis, and it is not a sign of weakness. Depression is treatable, and getting help for mood often makes pain easier to manage too. This guide helps you spot when to ask for support and where to go in the UK.

Signs it may be more than a bad week

Everyone has low days, especially in a flare. The NHS suggests speaking to your GP if you have felt down or hopeless most days for more than two weeks, or if any of these are building:

  • Losing interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy
  • Feeling hopeless, guilty or worthless
  • Sleeping much more or much less, or waking very early
  • Changes in appetite, or feeling tired all the time
  • Pulling away from friends and family
  • Finding it hard to concentrate or make decisions
  • Thoughts that life is not worth living

Some of these overlap with arthritis itself, such as fatigue and poor sleep. That is a reason to mention them, not to dismiss them.

Talking to your GP

You can book a normal appointment just about mood. It helps to write down how long you have felt this way, how it affects your days and nights, and how pain and mood seem linked. NICE guidance on depression with long-term physical health problems asks clinicians to consider mood and physical symptoms together, so tell your GP, physiotherapist or rheumatology team about both.

NHS Talking Therapies

In England you can refer yourself to NHS Talking Therapies without seeing your GP first. Options often include guided self-help and cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), and some services have support for people with long-term conditions. In Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, ask your GP about local psychological therapies. Medicines can also help some people; your GP can explain whether they suit you and check how they fit with your arthritis medicines.

What helps alongside treatment

  • Gentle, regular movement. Short sessions from the exercise hub can help mood as well as joints
  • Pacing. Planning activity across the week avoids the boom-and-bust that can drag mood down; see our pacing guide and fatigue guide
  • Sleep. Settling pain before bed and keeping regular times can help; see how to sleep with arthritis
  • A flare plan. Knowing what you will do when pain spikes reduces fear; use our printable flare action plan
  • Staying connected. A regular call or visit, a local group or a befriending service can make a real difference

Our mental health hub and arthritis and mental health guide go into more depth.

Money, work and caring worries

Worries about money or work often feed low mood. If arthritis affects daily living, the Benefits & PIP hub explains what you may be able to claim. If someone cares for you, they may be entitled to a carer's assessment, which can support you both.

If you are supporting someone

Listen without trying to fix everything, encourage them to speak to their GP, and offer practical help such as booking the appointment. If they talk about ending their life or you think they are in danger, call 999.

Frequently asked questions

Is depression common with arthritis?

Low mood and depression are common in people with long-term pain. Your GP can help, and treatment works for many people.

Can treating depression help my arthritis pain?

Pain and mood affect each other, so many people find pain easier to cope with when mood improves. It does not mean your pain is imagined.

Can I refer myself for therapy?

In England, yes, through NHS Talking Therapies. Elsewhere in the UK, start with your GP.

If you are newly diagnosed and feeling overwhelmed, our newly diagnosed guide sets out first steps.

Osteoarthritis and frailty often travel together because pain changes how you walk, rise and recover. This UK guide looks at low mood that shrinks activity and muscle in a home setting, with practical steps, warning signs and Wales services. It is general information, not personal medical advice.

Quick answer: Osteoarthritis and frailty often travel together because pain changes how you walk, rise and recover. This UK guide looks at low mood that shrinks activity and muscle in a home setting, with practical steps, warning signs and Wales services. It is general information, not personal medical advice.

In Wales, clinicians may talk about frailty as a syndrome. You may simply feel that osteoarthritis has stolen bounce from ordinary home tasks. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with low mood that shrinks activity and muscle, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in Wales.

What this can look like in a home

In a home, low mood that shrinks activity and muscle is rarely one dramatic collapse. It is usually a stack of small avoidances. People with osteoarthritis already know boom-and-bust. Frailty adds a longer payback: a quiet weekend can cost the following Thursday.

  • Transfers that used to be boring — bed, chair, toilet, car — now need a pause, a push-up or a second person, especially when several joints are cold.
  • Shorter outdoor range, then shorter indoor range, then a home that has quietly rearranged itself around the chair.
  • A hospital or infection week that ends with clothes feeling looser and stairs feeling taller.
  • New fear after a near-miss, even if you did not hit the floor. Fear of falling is itself a reason people sit more.
  • Skipping meals or drinks because getting to the kitchen with sore several joints feels like a project.

Why osteoarthritis and frailty so often meet

Arthritis is about joints, tendons and the way pain changes movement. Frailty is about the whole system — muscle, stamina, appetite, mood, medicines and how quickly you bounce back after a setback. Osteoarthritis sits in the middle because sore several joints quietly train you to sit more, shorten your stride and skip the movements that keep muscle.

NICE is clear that exercise is core care for osteoarthritis, not an optional extra after tablets. That still holds if you are becoming frailer, but the dose must respect today's several joints and today's energy. Rest has a place in a flare; rest as a lifestyle is how deconditioning joins the diagnosis.

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Pain in several joints can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual osteoarthritis.

Mood, fear and identity when several joints slow the week

After a fall or a flare of osteoarthritis, people often need a deliberate confidence plan: one accompanied walk, one visitor, one practised transfer, not a lecture about positive thinking.

NHS talking therapies and social prescribing exist in many parts of Wales. They are allowed to be for older people with long-term conditions. If low mood, poor sleep or loss of interest last more than a couple of weeks, tell the GP. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, that is urgent — use NHS 111 Wales or 999.

Small, repeatable steps — not a reinvention

  • If stairs are the bottleneck, get an occupational therapy conversation on the list while you temporarily live downstairs — drifting is how a camp-bed becomes a lifestyle.
  • In Wales, ask your local authority care and support team about equipment and care options. Descriptions of grants and benefits here are not predictions of an award.
  • Treat a walking aid as joint protection and falls kit, not as a verdict. Wrist-friendly handles matter if several joints include hands.
  • If cooking is the barrier, use tinned fish, eggs, yoghurt, beans or leftover protein foods rather than skipping meals. Muscle needs raw material as well as movement.
  • Keep a sit-to-stand practice at the height you actually use. A higher chair is not cheating if it lets several joints work without a panic haul.
  • Write three daily anchors: a meal, a movement, a conversation. Frailty grows in unstructured days.

Red flags — do not wait this out

  • Sudden confusion, new incontinence, or a crash in mobility over hours to days — think infection or delirium, not only arthritis.
  • Chest pain, trouble breathing, or signs of a stroke — 999, not a wait for the osteoarthritis nurse.
  • If you cannot get to the surgery because of osteoarthritis, ask about a home visit or a proper phone review. Silence is not a care plan.
  • A hot, very swollen joint with fever, or feeling systemically unwell — seek urgent clinical advice. A joint infection is an emergency.
  • Unplanned weight loss, repeated falls, or low mood that shrinks activity and muscle that is clearly worsening week by week — book the GP and say you are worried about frailty as well as several joints.

Who to talk to locally in Wales

Will I get PIP or Attendance Allowance because I have osteoarthritis and frailty?

Nobody honest can promise that. These are legal tests about how your difficulties affect daily living or personal care, not about a diagnosis name. Keep a diary of low mood that shrinks activity and muscle on typical and bad days. Use GOV.UK and independent advice. Living With Arthritis does not decide claims.

Do I need a geriatrician as well as a rheumatologist?

Not always. Many people are supported by GP, community physio and, where it exists, a frailty team. If medicines are stacking, falls are repeating, or memory and continence are changing alongside osteoarthritis, ask whether a comprehensive older-person assessment would help.

How do I tell an arthritis flare from a frailty slide?

A flare of osteoarthritis is usually more joint pain, stiffness or swelling in a known pattern. A frailty slide is broader: weaker recovery, smaller meals, more time in the chair, maybe confusion or falls. They can happen together. If the whole person is changing, do not only increase pain gel.

What the evidence says

The Perfect Desk Setup for UK Workers with Arthritis is one of the most discussed challenges in UK arthritis care. Recent reviews — including NICE guidance and Cochrane summaries — point to a clear pattern: small, consistent changes beat heroic one-off efforts.

Why this matters for work & career

People living with arthritis report that work & career is a daily reality, not a "nice to have". When this area is well-managed, pain scores drop, function improves, and flare frequency falls. When it's ignored, the opposite happens — and the costs compound over months.

A simple framework you can use this week

  1. Notice — track one specific factor for three days (e.g. pain after activity, sleep hours, stress level).
  2. Adjust — change one variable at a time so you can see what's actually working.
  3. Review — after a week, compare notes. Keep what helps, drop what doesn't.

What UK clinicians recommend

NHS physiotherapists and rheumatology nurses we work with consistently highlight:

  • Pacing over pushing — short, frequent activity beats long, intense sessions.
  • Heat for stiffness, cold for swelling — applied in 15-minute windows.
  • Social support — patients with strong networks report 25% less pain interference.
  • Professional guidance early — don't wait for things to "settle on their own".

Common myths to ignore

  • "Rest is always best." Not true — appropriate movement is medicine.
  • "It's all in your head." Pain is real; psychology helps because the brain processes pain, not because the pain is imaginary.
  • "Nothing can be done." Modern arthritis care offers dozens of options, from biologics to mindfulness.

Frequently asked questions

Is this approach safe for everyone? Most healthy adults with arthritis can apply these principles, but always check with your GP or rheumatologist if you have other conditions, take immunosuppressants, or have had recent surgery.

How long until I see a difference? Most patients notice small improvements within 2–3 weeks of consistent practice. Larger changes — function, sleep quality, mood — typically appear at 6–8 weeks.

Where can I learn more? Visit our arthritis support hub and exercise library for hundreds of free, UK-focused resources.

It is general information and not a substitute for personalised medical advice.

If you came here about The Perfect Desk Setup for UK Workers with Arthritis, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your local integrated care board about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

Quick questions about Perfect Desk Setup Workers

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.
