article.title: Exercise Progression for Arthritis: When and How to Do More (Decision Guide)
article.excerpt: A practical decision guide to progressing exercise with arthritis: why gradual progression matters, the 24-hour pain rule, a step-up, hold or step-back decision table, how to progress strength, walking, cycling, swimming, balance and mobility, worked examples, a weekly check-in template, and when to see a GP or physiotherapist.
article.content:
Quick answer: Progress exercise with arthritis by changing one thing at a time, by a small amount, every 1 to 2 weeks. Step up when an exercise feels easy and pain stays acceptable and settles within 24 hours. Hold if you are still adjusting. Step back if pain is worse the next day or a joint swells.

Starting an exercise programme is one challenge; knowing when to do more is another. Do too little and you stop improving. Do too much too soon and you risk a flare that sets you back weeks. The key with arthritis is gradual, planned progression, guided by how your joints respond. This page is a decision guide rather than a calculator: it gives you simple rules and tables to decide each week whether to step up, hold or step back, and shows how to progress each type of exercise.

Why gradual progression matters

Muscles, tendons, bones and joint tissues all adapt to the load you put on them, but they adapt at different speeds. Muscles respond within weeks; tendons and cartilage more slowly. Increasing load gradually gives every tissue time to adjust. NICE guideline NG226 recommends that exercise programmes for osteoarthritis are tailored to the person and reviewed over time, and that people are supported to keep exercising long term. Progressing sensibly is how you keep getting the benefits without setbacks.

The 24-hour pain rule

Many physiotherapists use a simple guide to judge whether exercise is at the right level:

  • During exercise: pain stays at a level you find acceptable, often around 4 out of 10 or lower on a scale where 0 is no pain and 10 is the worst imaginable.
  • After exercise: any increase in pain settles back to your usual level within 24 hours.
  • Next morning: stiffness and swelling are no worse than usual.

If all three are true, the level is about right, and you may be ready to progress. If any are not, hold or step back. Some extra muscle aching after new exercise is normal and is not a reason to stop.

The decision table: step up, hold or step back

Use this at the end of each week, or after each session for strength exercises.

What you noticeDecisionWhat to do
Exercise feels easy (effort around 3–4 out of 10), pain acceptable and settles within 24 hours, for 2 sessions or a full weekStep upIncrease one thing by a small amount (see below)
Exercise feels moderately hard (effort 5–7), pain acceptable and settles within 24 hoursHoldStay at this level for another week
Pain higher during exercise, but settles within 24 hoursHold or ease slightlyReduce repetitions, range or speed a little next time
Pain or stiffness worse the next day, or lasting more than 24 hoursStep backReturn to the previous level for a week
Joint swelling, warmth, or a flareStep back moreSwitch to gentle movement until it settles, then restart at about half your previous level
Sharp pain, locking, giving way, or new symptomsStop that exerciseGet advice from a physiotherapist or GP

Rules for any progression

  • Change one thing at a time. For example, add repetitions or add weight, not both at once.
  • Make small changes. A common guide is no more than about 10% more time or distance a week for walking or cycling, and small steps in weight or band strength.
  • Allow time. Stay at each level for at least 1 to 2 weeks before increasing again.
  • Expect ups and downs. Progress is rarely a straight line. A step back is not failure.
  • Plan easier weeks. Every 4 to 6 weeks, an easier week can help you recover and consolidate.

How to progress strength exercises

Work through these steps in order. When you can do the top of one step comfortably for 2 sessions, move to the next.

StepChangeExample: sit-to-stand
1Increase repetitions from 8 towards 128, then 10, then 12 sit-to-stands using hands
2Add a second, then third set2 sets of 12
3Reduce support or increase rangeUse one hand, then no hands; or use a slightly lower chair
4Add resistance, then drop back to 8 repetitionsHold a light weight or a full water bottle, 2 sets of 8
5Slow the movementTake 3 seconds to lower
6Make it more challenging or functionalStep-ups, or sit-to-stand on one leg with support

For band exercises, move up to the next band strength when 12 repetitions feel easy; see our resistance band workouts. For more on choosing weights, see our strength training guide.

How to progress walking

StepChangeExample
1FrequencyWalk 10 minutes, 3 days a week, then 5 days
2DurationAdd 2 to 5 minutes to each walk every week or two
3PaceAdd short brisk spells, such as 1 minute brisk, 2 minutes easy
4TerrainAdd gentle slopes or grass and paths
5StepsAdd 500 to 1,000 steps a day over a week or two

Our guide to walking with arthritis has a full 8-week plan.

How to progress cycling and swimming

  • Cycling: first increase time, then resistance. Keep resistance low enough that you can pedal smoothly without strain on your knees.
  • Swimming and pool exercise: increase session length, then the number of lengths or exercises, then try deeper water or more effort. Change strokes if one aggravates your joints.

How to progress balance and mobility

TypeProgression steps
BalanceTwo hands on support → one hand → fingertips → hands hovering → longer holds → add head turns or a soft surface (with a physio's advice)
MobilityMore repetitions (5 to 10) → larger comfortable range → more sessions a day → seated to standing
StretchingLonger holds (up to 30 seconds) → repeat 2 to 3 times; never force

Worked examples

Example 1: knee osteoarthritis, sit-to-stand

Week 1: 2 sets of 8 using hands, pain 3 out of 10, settles within an hour. Week 2: same, feels easy. Decision: step up to 2 sets of 10. Week 3: pain 4 out of 10, settles overnight. Decision: hold. Week 4: feels easy. Decision: step up to 2 sets of 12.

Example 2: hip osteoarthritis, walking

Walking 20 minutes on 5 days. Increases to 25 minutes. The next morning the hip is stiffer than usual and pain lasts all day. Decision: step back to 20 minutes for a week, then try 22 minutes.

Example 3: rheumatoid arthritis, hand exercises

Doing finger exercises daily, adding putty twice a week. A flare starts, with swollen knuckles. Decision: stop putty, continue gentle range-of-motion only. When the flare settles, restart putty at half the previous amount.

Which thing should you progress first?

If you are unsure what to change, use this order of priority. It suits most people with arthritis:

  1. Consistency first. Before making anything harder, aim to exercise regularly, such as 2 strength sessions and several walks each week, for at least 2 to 3 weeks.
  2. Then amount. Add repetitions, sets or minutes.
  3. Then difficulty. Add resistance, reduce support, increase speed or try a harder variation.
  4. Then variety. Add new exercises or activities that work towards your goals, such as stairs, gardening or a class.

Link your progression to what matters to you. If your goal is to walk to the shops, progress walking time and sit-to-stands. If it is to lift your grandchild, progress squats and carrying.

A 12-week strength progression example

WeeksSets and repetitionsLoad
1–21 set of 8–10Body weight or lightest band
3–42 sets of 10Same
5–62 sets of 12Same
7–82 sets of 8–10Next band or a light weight
9–102–3 sets of 10–12Same
11–12Easier week, then reviewChoose the next step with the decision table

This is a typical pattern only. Use the decision table each week; some people move faster, others need to repeat weeks.

Adjusting for different types of arthritis

ConditionProgression tips
OsteoarthritisSteady progression works well; expect some ache that settles. Load is generally good for joints when increased gradually
Rheumatoid and other inflammatory arthritisProgress during settled periods; scale back quickly during flares. Fatigue may limit you more than pain, so watch energy levels too
Axial spondyloarthritisDaily mobility plus progressive strength and fitness; regular exercise is an important part of treatment
GoutProgress between attacks; avoid exercising an acutely inflamed joint
Fibromyalgia alongside arthritisVery small steps and pacing are important; increase more slowly than the general guide

For what to do when a flare interrupts your plan, see our guide to exercise during a flare-up.

Common progression mistakes

  • Doing too much on a good day. Stick to the plan even when you feel great; boom-and-bust patterns often lead to flares.
  • Changing several things at once. If you add weight, sets and a new exercise together and your knee flares, you will not know why.
  • Never progressing. Doing the same easy routine for months maintains, but rarely improves, strength and fitness.
  • Ignoring the next day. How you feel the morning after is often the most useful signal.
  • Restarting at full level after a break. Step back first, then build up.

A weekly check-in template

Copy this into a notebook or your phone and fill it in at the end of each week.

QuestionYour answer
What did I do this week (sessions, minutes, sets, repetitions, weights)?
How hard did it feel (0 to 10)?
Highest pain during exercise (0 to 10)?
Did pain settle within 24 hours?Yes / No
Any swelling, warmth or flare?Yes / No
Decision for next weekStep up / Hold / Step back
The one thing I will change

If detailed logging feels like a chore, our guide to tracking progress without constant measuring suggests simpler ways.

After a flare or a break

If you have had to stop for a flare, illness or holiday, do not restart where you left off. A useful guide is to restart at about half your previous level after a break of 1 to 2 weeks, and lower after longer breaks, then build back up over 2 to 4 weeks using the decision table. You will usually regain fitness faster than it took to build initially.

Signs you are progressing well

  • Everyday tasks such as stairs, getting out of a chair or carrying shopping feel easier.
  • You can walk further or for longer.
  • Your usual pain is the same or lower.
  • You feel more confident and have more energy.

Strength improvements are often noticeable within 6 to 8 weeks, with further gains over months.

When to see a GP or physiotherapist

  • You keep having to step back and cannot get past a certain level.
  • Pain is steadily worsening over weeks despite reducing exercise.
  • A joint locks, gives way, or swells repeatedly.
  • You are not sure how to progress after joint surgery.
  • You notice new symptoms such as numbness, tingling or weakness.
  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with a fever. Call 999 for chest pain or severe breathlessness during exercise.

How quickly should I increase exercise with arthritis?

Increase one thing at a time, by a small amount, every 1 to 2 weeks, as long as pain stays acceptable and settles within 24 hours. For walking or cycling, a common guide is no more than about 10% more a week.

Is it normal for joints to ache after exercise?

Some extra ache that settles within 24 hours is normal, especially when starting or progressing. Pain that lasts longer or comes with swelling suggests you should step back.

When should I increase the weight?

When you can do 2 or 3 sets of 12 repetitions with good form and the exercise feels easy, increase the weight slightly and drop back to 8 repetitions.

Should I progress if I have pain?

You can progress with mild pain if it stays at an acceptable level and settles within 24 hours. If pain is higher the next day, hold or step back.

Is there an exercise progression calculator?

We have not built a calculator because the right progression depends on how your joints respond, not a formula. The decision table on this page lets you make that judgement each week. A physiotherapist can personalise it further.

How long until I see progress?

Many people notice easier everyday tasks within a few weeks, with clearer strength gains after 6 to 12 weeks of regular exercise.

article.title: Best Exercises for Rheumatoid Arthritis in Hands and Wrists
article.excerpt: A clinically reviewed programme of the best exercises for RA affecting hands and wrists — improving grip, reducing stiffness and maintaining function.
article.content:
Best exercises for rheumatoid arthritis in hands and wrists — RA most commonly begins in the small joints of the hands and wrists. Regular hand and wrist exercises are one of the most important self-management strategies for maintaining grip strength, reducing stiffness and preserving function.

Quick answer: Best exercises for RA hands and wrists: tendon gliding, wrist flexion/extension, radial/ulnar deviation, soft foam grip squeezes, finger spreading. Do after morning stiffness eases, soak hands in warm water first. During flares: range-of-motion only, no resistance. Expect reduced stiffness in 2-3 weeks.

Arthritic hands — openly licensed via Openverse

Why Hand Exercises Are Essential in RA

RA causes synovitis (inflammation of the joint lining) in the hand and wrist joints, leading to pain, swelling and — if untreated — joint damage and deformity. Exercise does not cure or stop the inflammatory process, but it maintains the strength and range of motion that functional deformity threatens to reduce. NICE guidance recommends hand exercises as part of standard RA management.

The Core Hand and Wrist Programme

Tendon Gliding Exercises

Start with hand flat (extension), make a hook (straight fingers bent at middle joints), then full fist, then straight fist (fingers bent, thumb alongside). Hold each position 3 seconds. 10 repetitions each hand. These maintain full tendon movement through the hand.

Wrist Flexion and Extension

Rest forearm on a table, hand extending over the edge. Slowly bend wrist downward (flexion) and upward (extension) through full range. 10 repetitions each direction, both wrists.

Radial and Ulnar Deviation

Forearm flat, palm down. Move hand toward thumb side (radial deviation), then little finger side (ulnar deviation). 10 repetitions. Important for maintaining wrist side-to-side movement often lost early in RA wrist disease.

Rheumatoid arthritis hand changes — openly licensed via Openverse

Pinch and Grip Strengthening

Squeeze a soft foam ball or rolled-up towel 10 times each hand. Pinch a clothes peg open using thumb and each finger in turn. Do not use hard grip strengtheners during active inflammation — the resistance is too high.

Finger Spreading

Place hand flat on table. Spread fingers as wide as possible, hold 3 seconds, bring together. 10 repetitions. Maintains MCP joint mobility.

Timing and Flare Management

Perform exercises after morning stiffness has eased — typically 1–2 hours after waking or after medication has taken effect. Warm water soaking (5 minutes in warm water) before exercises significantly reduces stiffness. During a flare: gentle range-of-motion only, no resistance work. Resume strengthening 2–3 days after swelling reduces.

Hand physiotherapy — openly licensed via Openverse

Q&A

Question: Should I wear splints alongside exercises?
Short answer: Resting splints worn at night reduce joint loading and morning stiffness in RA. Working splints (softer, worn during activity) can support wrists during tasks. An occupational therapist can advise on the right type for your specific pattern of involvement.

Question: When will I notice improvement?
Short answer: Reduced morning stiffness is typically noticed within 2–3 weeks of consistent daily practice. Grip strength improvements take 6–8 weeks.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Building a joint-friendly routine

Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery.

Share what helps you without prescribing it for others. Conditions, medicines and life circumstances differ. If someone is in crisis, encourage them toward NHS 111, their GP, or emergency services rather than relying on a forum alone.

article.title: Expert Brief: The 12-Week Hip Exercise Protocol
article.excerpt: A structured 12-week protocol of progressive strengthening cuts hip OA pain by roughly a third in clinical trials. Phase-by-phase breakdown.
article.content:
Quick answer: The 12-week hip exercise protocol is a structured approach combining movement, healthy eating, and weight management to improve hip pain. It begins with small, manageable steps like five minutes of daily movement and aims for 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly. Most people notice meaningful improvement within 6–12 weeks, with earlier benefits often appearing in 2–3 weeks.

What this guide covers

This piece summarises what the current evidence says about expert brief: the 12-week hip exercise protocol, the practical steps that help most, and the red flags that mean you should speak to your GP or physiotherapist.

The underlying mechanism

Arthritis pain rarely has a single cause. Joint cartilage, synovial fluid, ligaments, surrounding muscle and the nervous system all contribute. Understanding which of these is driving your specific symptom is the first step toward targeted relief. For an in-depth condition overview, see our related guide.

Inflammatory and degenerative forms behave differently. Inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid, psoriatic, ankylosing spondylitis) typically worsens with rest and improves with gentle movement. Degenerative arthritis (osteoarthritis) typically worsens with prolonged use. Knowing which pattern matches your day-to-day experience helps you choose the right management approach.

What helps — by strength of evidence

  1. Movement and graded exercise. NICE NG226 (2022) and Cochrane reviews place structured exercise as a first-line treatment. Aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, split into 20–30 minute sessions.
  2. Anti-inflammatory eating. A Mediterranean-style pattern — oily fish twice a week, plenty of vegetables, olive oil, whole grains — is linked to reduced pain scores in OA and RA trials.
  3. Weight management. A 5 percent reduction in body weight reduces knee-OA symptoms measurably; a 10 percent reduction can match the effect of some medications.
  4. Heat and cold. Heat eases stiffness; cold eases acute swelling. Twenty-minute applications, with a towel barrier.
  5. Sleep hygiene. Pain perception rises sharply on fewer than six hours of sleep. Prioritise a consistent bedtime.

A practical seven-day starting plan

Begin with the smallest dose that feels manageable — five minutes of movement, one anti-inflammatory meal a day, a 10 pm screen-off rule. Track only three things weekly: pain on waking (0–10), longest pain-free interval, and one functional win (e.g., climbed stairs without grabbing the rail). Small, consistent inputs outperform big sporadic efforts.

When to seek clinical advice

Book an appointment with your GP or a first-contact physiotherapist if you notice: sudden hot, red, swollen joints; unexplained weight loss alongside joint pain; morning stiffness lasting longer than an hour for more than two weeks; or new numbness or weakness. These can signal inflammatory disease that benefits from early treatment.

Frequently asked questions

Will this approach work alongside my medication? Yes. Exercise, diet and pacing complement prescribed treatments and often improve their effectiveness. Always check with your prescriber before stopping any medication.

How long until I notice a difference? Most people report meaningful improvement at 6–12 weeks of consistent practice. Earlier wins (less morning stiffness, better sleep) often appear within 2–3 weeks.

Is this safe if I have other conditions? The principles above are broadly safe for adults with stable cardiovascular, metabolic and respiratory conditions. If you are unsure, ask your GP for a referral to a first-contact physiotherapist for a tailored plan.

article.title: Expert Brief: Exercise Order for Maximum Pain Relief
article.excerpt: The best exercise order for pain relief depends on the type of arthritis. Inflammatory arthritis improves with gentle movement, while degenerative arthritis.
article.content:
Quick answer: The best exercise order for pain relief depends on the type of arthritis. Inflammatory arthritis improves with gentle movement, while degenerative arthritis may worsen with prolonged use. Structured exercise, specifically 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, is recommended. Start slowly, aiming for 20-30 minute sessions.

What this guide covers

This piece summarises what the current evidence says about expert brief: exercise order for maximum pain relief, the practical steps that help most, and the red flags that mean you should speak to your GP or physiotherapist.

The underlying mechanism

Arthritis pain rarely has a single cause. Joint cartilage, synovial fluid, ligaments, surrounding muscle and the nervous system all contribute. Understanding which of these is driving your specific symptom is the first step toward targeted relief. For an in-depth condition overview, see our related guide.

Inflammatory and degenerative forms behave differently. Inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid, psoriatic, ankylosing spondylitis) typically worsens with rest and improves with gentle movement. Degenerative arthritis (osteoarthritis) typically worsens with prolonged use. Knowing which pattern matches your day-to-day experience helps you choose the right management approach.

What helps — by strength of evidence

  1. Movement and graded exercise. NICE NG226 (2022) and Cochrane reviews place structured exercise as a first-line treatment. Aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, split into 20–30 minute sessions.
  2. Anti-inflammatory eating. A Mediterranean-style pattern — oily fish twice a week, plenty of vegetables, olive oil, whole grains — is linked to reduced pain scores in OA and RA trials.
  3. Weight management. A 5 percent reduction in body weight reduces knee-OA symptoms measurably; a 10 percent reduction can match the effect of some medications.
  4. Heat and cold. Heat eases stiffness; cold eases acute swelling. Twenty-minute applications, with a towel barrier.
  5. Sleep hygiene. Pain perception rises sharply on fewer than six hours of sleep. Prioritise a consistent bedtime.

A practical seven-day starting plan

Begin with the smallest dose that feels manageable — five minutes of movement, one anti-inflammatory meal a day, a 10 pm screen-off rule. Track only three things weekly: pain on waking (0–10), longest pain-free interval, and one functional win (e.g., climbed stairs without grabbing the rail). Small, consistent inputs outperform big sporadic efforts.

When to seek clinical advice

Book an appointment with your GP or a first-contact physiotherapist if you notice: sudden hot, red, swollen joints; unexplained weight loss alongside joint pain; morning stiffness lasting longer than an hour for more than two weeks; or new numbness or weakness. These can signal inflammatory disease that benefits from early treatment.

Frequently asked questions

Will this approach work alongside my medication? Yes. Exercise, diet and pacing complement prescribed treatments and often improve their effectiveness. Always check with your prescriber before stopping any medication.

How long until I notice a difference? Most people report meaningful improvement at 6–12 weeks of consistent practice. Earlier wins (less morning stiffness, better sleep) often appear within 2–3 weeks.

Is this safe if I have other conditions? The principles above are broadly safe for adults with stable cardiovascular, metabolic and respiratory conditions. If you are unsure, ask your GP for a referral to a first-contact physiotherapist for a tailored plan.

This article is general health information, not medical advice. Always consult a qualified healthcare professional for decisions about your individual care.

Building a joint-friendly routine

Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Using evidence carefully

Marketing claims for joint supplements often outrun the research. Look for products that state dose clearly, avoid miracle language, and fit alongside — never instead of — prescribed treatment. Stop and seek advice if you notice bruising, stomach pain, yellowing of the skin or new rashes.

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

article.title: Expert Q&A: Are Steroid Tapers Always Necessary?
article.excerpt: Stopping steroids abruptly, especially after long-term use, can cause withdrawal symptoms or a flare-up. Your body may not produce enough natural steroids.
article.content:
Quick answer: Stopping steroids abruptly, especially after long-term use, can cause withdrawal symptoms or a flare-up. Your body may not produce enough natural steroids, causing extreme tiredness, muscle pain, nausea, or low blood pressure. Guidelines recommend a gradual reduction, tailored by a healthcare professional to your condition and previous dose, to help your body adjust.

Overview

Stopping steroids abruptly can backfire. Our clinical board explains safe tapering.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis editorial team using UK NICE guidance, NHS information and peer-reviewed sources. We aim to update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Current evidence from systematic reviews consistently highlights the risks associated with suddenly stopping long-term steroid treatment. These reviews, which pull together findings from many individual studies, show that people can experience a flare-up of their underlying condition or withdrawal symptoms if they reduce their dose too quickly. Clinical guidelines across the UK strongly recommend a gradual reduction, tailored to the individual's condition and previous dose.

Randomised trials, considered a strong form of evidence, have explored different tapering schedules for various conditions. While there's no single "best" way to taper for everyone, these studies generally support a slow, step-by-step reduction rather than abrupt cessation. This approach helps the body adjust and reduces the chances of negative side effects.

The consensus from expert opinion and published research is clear: managing steroid reduction safely requires careful planning and oversight from a healthcare professional. Self-managing a steroid taper without medical guidance significantly increases the risk of complications, including adrenal suppression, where your body temporarily stops producing enough of its own natural steroids.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Stopping steroids purely because you feel better: Even if symptoms improve, your body still needs to adjust to a lower dose.
  • Cutting your dose in half all at once: This can be too big a step and trigger withdrawal or a flare.
  • Listening to advice from friends or online forums over your doctor: Everyone's situation is unique; what worked for someone else might not be right for you.
  • Forgetting to pick up your next prescription for a lower dose: This can lead to an unplanned abrupt stop.
  • Ignoring withdrawal symptoms like fatigue or joint pain, hoping they’ll pass: These are signals your body might be reducing too quickly.

When to Speak to a Clinician

It's always best to discuss any concerns about your medication with a healthcare professional. If you're on steroids and experience new or worsening symptoms, or if you're struggling with side effects, don't wait. Contact your doctor, rheumatology nurse, or pharmacist for advice.

  • Sudden increase in pain or stiffness
  • Extreme fatigue or weakness
  • Feeling generally unwell or feverish
  • Significant mood changes, like anxiety or feeling low
  • Developing new, unexplained symptoms

Frequently Asked Questions

What happens if I stop steroids suddenly?

Stopping steroids abruptly, especially after taking them for a long time, can lead to withdrawal symptoms or a flare-up of your arthritis. Your body might not be able to produce enough of its own natural steroids, leading to issues like extreme tiredness, muscle pain, nausea, and even low blood pressure.

How long does a steroid taper usually take?

The length of a steroid taper varies a lot depending on how long you've been taking them, the dose, and your particular condition. It could range from a few weeks to several months, or even longer for some people. Your doctor will create a personalised plan for you.

Can I drink alcohol while tapering steroids?

Moderate alcohol consumption is generally acceptable for most people while tapering steroids, but it's wise to discuss this with your doctor. Some people find alcohol can worsen certain side effects, like stomach upset, or interfere with their sleep, which is important for recovery.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis editorial team using UK NICE guidance, NHS information and peer-reviewed sources. We aim to update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Current systematic reviews and clinical guidelines highlight the importance of work-life balance for those living with arthritis. Research consistently shows that understanding your condition and making informed career choices can significantly impact long-term well-being and disease management. Studies using patient reported outcomes indicate that job satisfaction and a supportive work environment are strongly linked to better mental health and reduced pain.

While there's no single ‘best’ job for everyone with arthritis, randomised trials focusing on workplace interventions demonstrate the positive effect of workplace accommodations. These can range from ergonomic adjustments to flexible working hours, all contributing to sustained employment and reduced disease flare-ups. The evidence points to a proactive approach, where individuals are empowered with information to make choices that support their health.

Furthermore, long-term observational studies have investigated the impact of various occupational demands on arthritis progression. They show that careers involving repetitive high-impact movements or prolonged static postures without regular breaks tend to be more challenging. Conversely, roles allowing for movement, variety, and breaks are often associated with better joint health outcomes and fewer disability claims.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Ignoring early symptoms: Don't push through pain; listen to your body and adjust tasks or seek advice.
  • Not communicating with employers: Keep your employer informed about your needs to access support and adjustments.
  • Overlooking ergonomic solutions: Simple changes to your workspace can make a big difference; explore options.
  • Neglecting regular breaks: Short, frequent breaks to move and stretch are vital, even in a busy work schedule.
  • Underestimating energy levels: Pacing yourself and managing fatigue is crucial; don't overcommit.
  • Delaying career adaptations: Waiting until symptoms are severe can limit options; plan ahead.

When to Speak to a Clinician

It's always a good idea to discuss any concerns you have about your arthritis and your work life with a healthcare professional. They can offer personalised advice and help you navigate challenges. You should specifically consider making an appointment if you experience any of the following:

  • New or worsening joint pain that interferes with your ability to perform work tasks.
  • Increased swelling, stiffness, or warmth in your joints affecting your daily function.
  • Persistent fatigue that significantly impacts your energy levels at work.
  • Difficulty with fine motor skills or grip strength that makes your job challenging.
  • Mental health changes, such as increased anxiety or low mood, related to your arthritis and employment.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I still work full-time with arthritis?

Many people with arthritis work full-time. The ability to do so depends on your specific condition, the type of work, and available workplace adjustments. Open communication with your employer and healthcare team is key to finding a sustainable balance.

What if my job involves a lot of standing or sitting?

Prolonged standing or sitting can be challenging. Look for opportunities to alternate between these positions, incorporate short walking breaks, or use ergonomic aids like sit-stand desks or anti-fatigue mats to reduce strain.

How do I talk to my employer about my arthritis?

Be honest and informative without oversharing. Focus on how your arthritis affects your ability to do your job and what reasonable adjustments could help. You don't have to disclose every detail of your condition.

Practical next steps for Expert Q&A: Choosing a Career-Friendly to Arthritis

If you came here about Expert Q&A: Choosing a Career-Friendly to Arthritis, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Benefits conversations

Personal Independence Payment (PIP) looks at how your condition affects daily living and mobility, not the diagnosis name alone. Keep a short diary of bad days, help you need with dressing or cooking, and walking limits. Welfare rights advisers at local councils or charities can check forms before you submit them.

Peer support etiquette

Share what helps you without prescribing it for others. Conditions, medicines and life circumstances differ. If someone is in crisis, encourage them toward NHS 111, their GP, or emergency services rather than relying on a forum alone.

Quick questions about Expert Choosing Career Friendly

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

article.title: Exercise During a Flare-Up: What to Do, What to Avoid and How to Restart
article.excerpt: A practical UK guide to exercise during an arthritis flare-up: how to tell a flare from normal exercise soreness, the traffic-light approach, gentle range-of-motion moves, a 10-minute flare-day routine, adjusting by arthritis type and joint, a step-by-step return to your usual exercise, and when to get medical help.
article.content:
Quick answer: During a flare-up you usually do not need to stop moving. Cut back to gentle range-of-motion exercises and short walks, and rest the most inflamed joint. Keep pain at a level you find acceptable that settles within 24 hours. Restart your usual exercise gradually once the flare eases, and get help if a joint is hot, red and very swollen.

When your arthritis flares, it is natural to want to stop moving and wait for it to pass. Rest does have a place, especially for a hot, swollen joint. But stopping completely for days or weeks can leave you stiffer, weaker and more tired, which makes the next flare harder to deal with. The aim during a flare is not to keep up your usual routine; it is to keep gently moving in a way that does not make things worse. This guide explains how to judge what is right on the day, gives you a short flare-day routine, and shows how to build back up once the flare settles.

Is it a flare, or normal exercise soreness?

It helps to know the difference, because they need different responses.

Normal soreness after exerciseArthritis flare
When it startsUsually within a day of new or harder exerciseCan happen any time, sometimes with no clear trigger
What it feels likeMuscle aching or mild joint acheIncreased joint pain, stiffness, warmth or swelling
How long it lastsUsually eases within 24 to 48 hoursCan last days or weeks
Other symptomsUsually noneWith inflammatory arthritis, often fatigue, longer morning stiffness, and feeling generally unwell
What to doKeep going, perhaps slightly lighter next timeScale back to gentle movement, use your flare plan, and get advice if needed

Osteoarthritis flares versus inflammatory arthritis flares

Osteoarthritis (OA) flares are often linked to doing more than usual, such as a long walk, gardening or decorating, though sometimes there is no obvious cause. The joint may ache more, feel stiff and sometimes swell a little. These flares usually settle within days to a few weeks. Gentle movement is generally helpful and NICE guideline NG226 recommends exercise as a core treatment for OA; during a flare you simply reduce the amount and intensity.

Inflammatory arthritis flares, such as in rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis or axial spondyloarthritis, are caused by increased inflammation. Joints may be hot, swollen and very painful, often with fatigue and long morning stiffness. Resting the most inflamed joints is sensible, but gentle range-of-motion movements help prevent stiffness. Contact your rheumatology team or advice line if a flare is severe or not settling, as your treatment may need reviewing.

Gout flares are different again: the joint is usually extremely painful, and rest, raising the joint and treatment are needed. Wait until the attack has settled before exercising that joint, but you can usually move other parts of your body gently.

The traffic-light approach

LevelHow you feelWhat to do
GreenNormal or mild extra ache, joints not hot or very swollenCarry on with your usual exercise, perhaps a little lighter
AmberMore pain and stiffness than usual, mild swelling, more tiredHalve the amount and intensity; swap to gentle range-of-motion, short walks, cycling or pool exercise
RedJoint hot, red, very swollen or very painful; feeling unwellRest the affected joint; gentle movement of other joints only; follow your flare plan and get advice

Many physiotherapists use a simple pain guide: pain during exercise that stays at a level you find acceptable (often around 4 out of 10 or lower) and settles back to your usual level within 24 hours is generally fine. If pain is higher, or you are worse the next morning, cut back further.

What helps during a flare

  • Gentle range-of-motion exercises. Moving each joint slowly through a comfortable range a few times a day helps reduce stiffness.
  • Short, frequent bouts of movement. Five minutes several times a day is often better than one long session.
  • Low-impact activity. Short walks on the flat, a stationary bike at low resistance, or gentle movement in a warm pool.
  • Isometric (static) exercises. Tightening muscles without moving the joint, such as pressing the back of your knee into the bed, helps maintain strength with very little joint movement.
  • Breathing and relaxation. Slow breathing and gentle stretching can ease muscle tension and help you cope with pain.
  • Heat or cold. Warmth before moving can ease stiffness; a cold pack wrapped in a towel can help a hot, swollen joint. Limit to about 15 to 20 minutes and check your skin.

What to avoid during a flare

  • High-impact exercise such as running or jumping.
  • Heavy strength training on the flaring joint.
  • Forcing stretches into pain or pushing through sharp pain.
  • Long sessions to "make up" for missed exercise.
  • Complete bed rest for long periods, unless your doctor has advised it.

A 10-minute flare-day routine

Do this once or twice a day, sitting or lying down if needed. Move slowly, breathe normally and stay within a comfortable range. Skip any move that hurts the flaring joint.

  1. Breathing, 1 minute. Breathe in slowly through your nose, and out slowly through your mouth.
  2. Neck turns, 5 each side. Turn your head slowly to look over each shoulder.
  3. Shoulder rolls, 10. Roll your shoulders up, back and down.
  4. Elbow bends, 10. With arms by your side, bend and straighten your elbows.
  5. Wrist circles and finger stretches, 5 each. Make gentle circles, then open and close your hands slowly.
  6. Seated marching, 1 minute. Lift your knees alternately in a comfortable range.
  7. Knee straightening, 5 each leg. Sitting, slowly straighten one knee, hold for 3 seconds, lower.
  8. Thigh squeezes, 10 each leg. Sitting or lying with your leg straight, tighten the thigh muscle to press the back of your knee down, hold 5 seconds.
  9. Ankle pumps and circles, 10 each. Point and flex your feet, then circle them.
  10. Buttock squeezes, 10. Squeeze your buttocks together, hold 5 seconds, relax.

For more gentle moves for better days, see our daily mobility routine. If standing is difficult, the moves in our chair exercise guide can be done from a seat.

Adapting by joint

Flaring jointGentle optionsEase off
KneeThigh squeezes, heel slides, seated knee straightening, pool walkingStairs, squats, long walks, kneeling
HipButtock squeezes, gentle hip rolls lying on your back, short flat walksLong walks, low chairs, crossing legs
Hand and wristGentle finger and wrist movements in warm waterStrong gripping, putty and grip-strength work, heavy carrying
ShoulderPendulum swings, gentle supported arm liftsOverhead reaching, resistance band work, lifting
BackKnee rocking lying on your back, short walks, pelvic tiltsProlonged sitting, heavy lifting, bending and twisting
Foot and ankleAnkle pumps and circles while seated, toe movementsLong periods on your feet, walking on uneven ground

Pacing and planning

Pacing means spreading activity through the day and alternating activity with rest, rather than doing a lot on a good day and paying for it later. During a flare:

  • Break tasks into smaller chunks with rests between.
  • Set a timer to remind you to change position every 30 to 45 minutes.
  • Prioritise what really needs doing and postpone the rest.
  • Get a good night's sleep where possible; fatigue tends to make pain feel worse.

It is worth writing a flare plan when you are well, so you know what to do when a flare starts. Our flare action plan includes space for your exercise steps, medicines and contact numbers, and our guide to managing flare-ups at home covers pain relief and self-care.

Restarting your usual exercise after a flare

Once the flare starts to settle, build up step by step. Going straight back to your full routine is a common reason for another flare.

StageWhenWhat to do
1Flare settling, still soreFlare-day routine plus short walks; about a third to a half of your usual amount
2Pain and swelling much betterAdd your usual strength exercises with fewer sets or lighter weight; walks a little longer
3Close to your normalReturn to about three-quarters of your usual routine
4Back to normal for a weekYour full routine, then resume gradual progression

Spend at least a few days at each stage, and move on only if your joints feel no worse the next day. If a longer flare has left you weaker, our guide to rebuilding after a flare has more detail.

An example flare week

This shows how one person with knee osteoarthritis might adjust a normal week of walking and strength exercise during a moderate flare. It is an illustration, not a prescription.

DayUsual planDuring the flare
130-minute walkFlare-day routine twice; two 5-minute walks around the house or garden
2Strength sessionThigh squeezes and seated knee straightening only; flare-day routine
330-minute walkFlare-day routine; two 10-minute flat walks if comfortable
4Rest or swimGentle pool walking for 15 minutes, or rest
5Strength sessionHalf the usual sets with no added weight
6Long walk15-minute flat walk
7RestRest and gentle mobility

Medicines and exercise during a flare

Pain relief can make gentle movement easier. Some people find it helps to time exercise for when their pain relief is working best. Follow the dose instructions and check with a pharmacist or GP if you are unsure which pain relief is suitable for you; NICE advises that topical anti-inflammatory gels are considered first for knee osteoarthritis. If you have inflammatory arthritis, keep taking your disease-modifying or biologic medicine unless your team tells you otherwise, and tell them about frequent flares. Steroid injections or other treatment changes are decisions for your clinical team. Never increase painkillers just so you can push through high-intensity exercise during a flare.

Working with your physiotherapist or rheumatology team

If flares keep interrupting your exercise, ask your physiotherapist to help you write a flare plan with specific exercises for your joints and clear rules for when to scale back and when to build up. If you have inflammatory arthritis, your rheumatology nurse or advice line can help you judge whether a flare needs a review of your treatment. Bring your flare diary to appointments; it helps them see patterns.

Reducing the chance of the next flare

  • Build up exercise gradually; avoid sudden big increases in activity.
  • Keep moving regularly, even on good days, rather than doing a lot at once.
  • Take medicines as prescribed and do not stop disease-modifying treatment without speaking to your team.
  • Keep a simple diary of flares, activity, sleep and stress to spot patterns.
  • Look after your general health, including sleep, weight and stress.

When to get medical help

  • Call 999 if you have chest pain, severe breathlessness or signs of a stroke.
  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E if a single joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with a high temperature or feeling unwell; this can be a sign of a joint infection. This is particularly important if you take medicines that affect your immune system.
  • Contact your rheumatology advice line or GP if a flare of inflammatory arthritis is severe, lasts more than a few days without improving, or flares are becoming more frequent.
  • See your GP or a physiotherapist if an OA flare does not start to settle within 2 to 3 weeks, if you cannot put weight on a joint, or if a joint locks or gives way.

Should I exercise during an arthritis flare?

Usually yes, but less. Rest the most inflamed joint and keep the rest of your body gently moving with range-of-motion exercises, short walks or pool movement. Stop or cut back if pain increases significantly or does not settle within 24 hours.

Can exercise cause a flare-up?

A sudden increase in activity can trigger a flare in some people, particularly with osteoarthritis. Building up gradually and pacing activity reduce this risk. Regular, moderate exercise is generally helpful for arthritis in the long term.

Is it OK to exercise with a swollen joint?

Gentle, pain-free movement of a mildly swollen joint is usually fine. If a joint is hot, red and very swollen, rest it and get advice, as this needs checking, especially if you feel unwell or have a high temperature.

How long should I rest during a flare?

Rest the most painful joint for short periods, but avoid long periods of complete rest. Keep up gentle movement every day if you can, and gradually return to your usual exercise as the flare settles.

Is walking good during a flare-up?

Short, gentle walks on flat ground are often helpful during a mild flare. Make them shorter than usual, use a walking aid if needed, and avoid hills and long distances until the flare settles.

Is swimming good during a flare-up?

Gentle movement in a warm pool can be comfortable during a flare because the water supports your weight. Keep sessions short and avoid strokes that strain painful joints.

How do I know if I have done too much?

If your pain is much worse during exercise, does not settle within 24 hours, or your joint is more swollen the next day, you have probably done too much. Reduce the amount next time rather than stopping completely.

article.title: Expert Q&A: How Do I Know If Surgery Is Right for Me?
article.excerpt: Non-surgical treatments are the first line of defence for most people with arthritis, aiming to reduce pain and improve joint function. These often include…
article.content:
Quick answer: Non-surgical treatments are the first line of defence for most people with arthritis, aiming to reduce pain and improve joint function. These often include specific exercises, pain management strategies, and medication, which can significantly improve quality of life. Doctors usually recommend trying various non-surgical options for several months before discussing surgery. Surgery often manages symptoms rather than providing a complete cure.

Overview

A patient-friendly decision framework.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis editorial team using UK NICE guidance, NHS information and peer-reviewed sources. We aim to update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Large-scale studies, including randomised trials and systematic reviews, consistently show that non-surgical treatments are the first line of defence for most people living with arthritis. These treatments, which include specific exercises, pain management strategies, and medication, aim to reduce pain, improve joint function, and slow disease progression. For many, these approaches are highly effective and can significantly improve quality of life, often delaying or even avoiding the need for surgery.

Clinical guidelines from professional bodies across the UK reinforce this staged approach. They recommend a comprehensive assessment of all non-surgical options before considering surgical interventions. This is because surgery, while sometimes necessary and highly effective, carries risks and requires a significant recovery period, which may not be suitable or beneficial for everyone.

The evidence also highlights the importance of individualised care. What works for one person may not work for another, even with similar conditions. Shared decision-making, where patients and clinicians discuss all available options, their potential benefits, and risks, is a cornerstone of effective arthritis management according to current evidence.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Ignoring early symptoms: Hoping pain will disappear often leads to more advanced problems. *Fix: Discuss new or worsening symptoms with your GP promptly. Overdoing it on good days: Pushing through significant pain can cause flare-ups and damage. *Fix: Adjust activity levels based on your energy and pain, even if you feel well. Stopping medication too soon: Discontinuing prescribed drugs without advice can worsen your condition. *Fix: Always consult your doctor before changing your medication regimen. Relying solely on surgery for a 'cure': Surgery often manages symptoms rather than curing the underlying condition. *Fix: Understand that post-surgical rehabilitation and ongoing self-management are crucial. Not asking enough questions: Feeling rushed or unsure about your treatment plan. *Fix: Prepare questions in advance and don't hesitate to ask for clarity.

When to Speak to a Clinician

While routine check-ups are important, certain changes or symptoms warrant a more urgent discussion with your GP, physiotherapist, or rheumatologist. Early intervention can often prevent more serious issues and help manage your condition more effectively.

  • Sudden, severe pain in a joint.
  • New, unexpected swelling or redness around a joint.
  • Fever alongside joint pain or swelling.
  • Rapid or unexplained loss of joint function or an inability to bear weight.
  • Symptoms that are significantly worsening despite your current treatment plan.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long should I try non-surgical treatments before considering surgery?

There isn't a one-size-fits-all answer, as it depends on your specific condition, symptoms, and how you respond to treatment. Your doctor will typically recommend trying a range of non-surgical options for several months, often longer, before discussing surgery.

Will surgery cure my arthritis completely?

In most cases, surgery for arthritis aims to relieve pain, improve function, and correct deformities, rather than providing a complete cure. Arthritis is a chronic condition, and even after surgery, ongoing management and lifestyle adjustments are usually necessary.

What should I expect during the recovery period after arthritis surgery?

Recovery varies greatly depending on the type of surgery and your overall health. You can expect a period of rehabilitation involving physiotherapy and pain management, often lasting several weeks to months. Your healthcare team will provide a detailed recovery plan tailored to your needs.

Practical next steps for Expert Q&A: How Do I Know If Surgery Is Right for Me?

If you came here about Expert Q&A: How Do I Know If Surgery Is Right for Me?, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Everyday eating patterns

No single food cures arthritis. Patterns rich in vegetables, fruit, pulses, wholegrains and oily fish are the ones most often discussed in UK dietetic advice for inflammatory conditions. Keep changes realistic: swap one ultra-processed snack for fruit and nuts, or cook with olive oil more often than seed oils marketed as miracle cures.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

article.direct_answer: Non-surgical treatments are the first line of defence for most people with arthritis, aiming to reduce pain and improve joint function. These often include specific exercises, pain management strategies, and medication, which can significantly improve quality of life. Doctors usually recommend trying various non-surgical options for several months before discussing surgery. Surgery often manages symptoms rather than providing a complete cure.

faqs.q: How long should I try non-surgical treatments before considering surgery?

faqs.q: Will surgery cure my arthritis completely?
faqs.a: In most cases, surgery for arthritis aims to relieve pain, improve function, and correct deformities, rather than providing a complete cure. Arthritis is a chronic condition, and even after surgery, ongoing management and lifestyle adjustments are usually necessary.

faqs.q: What should I expect during the recovery period after arthritis surgery?
faqs.a: Recovery varies greatly depending on the type of surgery and your overall health. You can expect a period of rehabilitation involving physiotherapy and pain management, often lasting several weeks to months. Your healthcare team will provide a detailed recovery plan tailored to your needs.

article.content:
Quick answer: Asking for help with arthritis is framed as a strength and part of self-management, not a personal failing. The post advises personalised clinical input, symptom tracking, gentle regular movement, accepting practical support and making specific requests. It warns against minimising symptoms or waiting for crisis, and recommends prompt review for swelling, fever, rapid functional loss, side effects or emotional distress.

Overview

Reframing assistance as a strength, not a weakness.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis editorial team using UK NICE guidance, NHS information and peer-reviewed sources. We aim to update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Current summaries of research consistently highlight the benefits of a proactive approach to managing long-term conditions like arthritis. Systematic reviews examining patient outcomes point to improved quality of life and better disease management when individuals feel empowered and actively participate in their care. This includes seeking support when needed and engaging with healthcare professionals.

Clinical guidelines from leading rheumatology bodies across the UK reinforce these findings. They recommend that individuals with arthritis are encouraged to voice their concerns, ask questions, and accept practical help. This collaborative model is shown to lead to more effective treatment plans tailored to individual needs and circumstances.

The evidence suggests that viewing assistance as a valuable tool for self-management, rather than a sign of personal failing, is key. Psychological studies indicate that those who can ask for help often experience lower levels of stress and a greater sense of control over their condition, fostering resilience.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Minimising symptoms: Downplaying your pain or discomfort can lead to under-treatment. *Be honest and specific about what you're experiencing. Expecting mind-reading: Your healthcare provider can only address what you tell them. *Prepare a few key points before your appointment. Comparing yourself to others: Every arthritis journey is unique. *Focus on your own progress and needs, not someone else's. Waiting for a crisis: Addressing issues early often prevents them from worsening. *Seek support proactively, not just when things become unmanageable. Ignoring practical help: Sometimes, simple assistance with daily tasks makes a big difference. *Consider accepting offers of help with chores or errands.

When to Speak to a Clinician

While tracking your symptoms and managing your condition day-to-day is important, there are times when you should definitely reach out to a healthcare professional. Don't hesitate to contact your doctor, physiotherapist, or rheumatology team if you notice any significant changes or new concerns.

  • Sudden, severe joint pain or swelling that doesn't subside.
  • New, persistent fever alongside joint symptoms.
  • Rapid loss of function or inability to use a joint that was previously manageable.
  • Side effects from medication that are concerning or severely impacting your life.
  • Significant changes in your mood or an inability to cope with your condition emotionally.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it normal to feel guilty about needing help with my arthritis?

Yes, it's very common to feel guilty or like a burden, especially if you're used to being independent. Remember that asking for help is a sign of strength and self-awareness, allowing you to manage your condition more effectively.

How can I explain what I need without overwhelming people?

Start by being specific about one or two things that would make a real difference. For example, "Could you help me carry the shopping this week?" is clearer and easier to respond to than a general plea for help.

What if I'm worried about being rejected when I ask for help?

It's natural to have this fear. Frame your request positively, focusing on how their help would allow you to do more, rather than dwelling on your limitations. Most people are happy to help when they understand the impact it can have.

In many areas you can ask your local integrated care board about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Making information usable

Treat articles like this as a starting map, not a personal care plan. Highlight one idea to try for two weeks, then review. If symptoms are new, rapidly worsening, or affecting several joints with fever or unexplained weight loss, contact your GP promptly rather than waiting on self-help alone.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

article.content:
Quick answer: Before joining a clinical trial, ask about its purpose, the treatments involved, and its duration. Inquire about expectations, potential risks and benefits, and what happens once the trial concludes. Ensure you understand how participation might affect your regular medical care and clarify who to contact with questions. You can withdraw from a trial at any time.

Overview

Questions to ask before signing the consent form.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis editorial team using UK NICE guidance, NHS information and peer-reviewed sources. We aim to update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Current evidence from systematic reviews consistently highlights the importance of shared decision-making in healthcare, particularly when considering clinical trials. This means that patients and clinicians work together to make choices about care, taking into account the best available research evidence and the patient's individual values and preferences. Clinical guidelines from professional bodies also stress the ethical imperative of informed consent, ensuring participants fully understand the implications of joining a trial.

Randomised controlled trials, the gold standard for testing new interventions, rely on volunteers who are fully aware of what their participation entails. Reviews of trial participation emphasise that clarity of information, presented in an easy-to-understand way, is crucial for people to make a genuine choice. This includes understanding potential benefits, risks, and the commitment involved.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Assuming 'experimental' means 'better': A new treatment is still unproven, even if it sounds promising. *Always ask about the current standard of care and how the experimental treatment compares. Not asking about costs: While trial participation itself shouldn't cost you money, travel or time off work might. *Clarify any potential indirect costs before you commit. Feeling pressured to say yes: You have the right to decline an invitation to a trial without affecting your ongoing care. *Take your time, discuss it with someone you trust, and only agree if you feel comfortable. Not understanding the time commitment involved: Some trials require frequent visits or lengthy appointments. *Ask for a clear schedule of appointments and procedures. Forgetting you can withdraw: You can leave a clinical trial at any time, for any reason, even if you've already started. *Remember this right and don't feel trapped. Not clarifying who to contact with questions or problems: You should have a clear point of contact during the trial. *Ensure you have the name and phone number of the research team member who can help you.

When to Speak to a Clinician

If you've been invited to a clinical trial and have concerns, or if new symptoms develop during your participation, it's always wise to discuss them with your general practitioner, physiotherapist, or rheumatologist. They can offer an objective perspective and help you weigh your options or address any issues that arise.

  • You're experiencing new or worsening pain after starting a trial.
  • You're unsure about the information you've been given about the trial.
  • You feel uncomfortable or pressured to continue participating.
  • You're developing side effects that weren't clearly explained.
  • Your general health changes in a way that might affect your trial participation.

Frequently Asked Questions

What kind of questions should I ask before joining a clinical trial?

You should ask about the purpose of the trial, what treatments are being studied, how long it will last, what's expected of you, and any potential risks or benefits. It's also helpful to ask about what happens after the trial ends.

Will participating in a clinical trial affect my regular medical care?

Generally, being in a clinical trial should complement your existing care, not replace it. However, some trials might require you to pause or change certain medications or treatments you're currently receiving. Always clarify how the trial might interact with your usual medical routine.

What happens if a clinical trial drug doesn't work for me, or I experience side effects?

The research team will closely monitor you for any changes or side effects. If a treatment isn't working or causes significant problems, they will discuss your options with you, which may include stopping the trial treatment. You always have the right to withdraw from a trial if you wish.

Supplements versus meals

Food-first is usually safer than stacking capsules. If you do try a supplement, choose a reputable UK brand, check for interactions with your medicines (especially blood thinners), and give any trial a clear stop date so you can judge whether symptoms truly changed.

article.content:
Quick answer: Open communication with your GP about medication is vital for long-term conditions like arthritis. Patients who feel heard about their concerns are more likely to follow their treatment plans, leading to better health outcomes. Decision-making about medication should be collaborative, considering your individual circumstances. Always discuss changes to your medication with your doctor – never stop treatment abruptly.

Overview

Concerns are valid. A practical script for an honest conversation.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis editorial team using UK NICE guidance, NHS information and peer-reviewed sources. We aim to update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Large-scale systematic reviews consistently highlight the importance of open communication between patients and their healthcare providers regarding medication for long-term conditions like arthritis. These reviews, which synthesise findings from many individual studies, show that patients who feel heard and understood about their concerns are more likely to stick with their treatment plans. This adherence, in turn, often leads to better health outcomes and a higher quality of life.

Clinical guidelines from professional bodies frequently recommend a shared decision-making approach. This means that decisions about medication should be made collaboratively, with the patient's individual circumstances, preferences, and concerns given equal weight alongside the clinical evidence. This contrasts with a model where treatment is simply prescribed without full patient involvement.

Randomised controlled trials, often considered a strong form of evidence, also support interventions that empower patients to discuss their medication worries. These trials have demonstrated that structured conversations and patient-centred resources can improve patient confidence in managing their condition and reduce feelings of anxiety or uncertainty about their prescribed treatments.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Stopping medication abruptly without discussion: This can lead to flare-ups or worsening of symptoms. Fix: Always talk to your GP or rheumatologist before changing your medication routine.
  • Assuming concerns are too minor to mention: Minor worries can grow into major barriers to treatment. Fix: No concern is too small to discuss with your healthcare team.
  • Searching online for self-diagnosis or alternatives without professional input: Internet information can be overwhelming and misleading. Fix: Use online resources to inform your questions, but bring them to your doctor for qualified advice.
  • Waiting until a crisis point to raise issues: Addressing concerns early can prevent bigger problems down the line. Fix: Bring up medication worries as soon as they arise, even if they seem minor.
  • Not keeping a simple record of side effects or questions: It's easy to forget details during an appointment. Fix: Jot down any concerns or side effects in a notebook or on your phone before your appointment.

When to Speak to a Clinician

It's always best to discuss any new or concerning symptoms related to your arthritis or medication with your healthcare provider. While some changes might be minor, others could indicate a need to adjust your treatment or investigate further. Don't hesitate to seek advice if you experience any of the following:

  • New or significantly worsening pain that doesn't respond to usual pain relief.
  • Sudden swelling, warmth, or redness in a joint.
  • Unexplained fever, chills, or night sweats.
  • Significant unexpected weight loss or fatigue.
  • Any new skin rashes or persistent stomach upset after starting a new medication.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I stop taking my arthritis medication when I feel better?

No, it's very important not to stop your medication without speaking to your doctor first. Arthritis is often a long-term condition, and feeling better usually means the medication is working to control it. Stopping suddenly can lead to a return of symptoms or even a flare-up.

What if I'm worried about the long-term side effects?

It's natural to have concerns about long-term side effects. Your doctor can explain the potential risks and benefits specific to your medication, often comparing them to the risks of uncontrolled arthritis. They can also discuss monitoring plans to keep an eye on any side effects.

How do I know if my medication is actually working?

The best way to tell if your medication is working is to track your symptoms, like pain levels, stiffness, and how well you can do daily activities. Share these observations with your doctor. They will also look at physical signs and sometimes blood tests to assess its effectiveness.

article.direct_answer: Open communication with your GP about medication is vital for long-term conditions like arthritis. Patients who feel heard about their concerns are more likely to follow their treatment plans, leading to better health outcomes. Decision-making about medication should be collaborative, considering your individual circumstances. Always discuss changes to your medication with your doctor – never stop treatment abruptly.

faqs.q: Can I stop taking my arthritis medication when I feel better?
faqs.a: No, it's very important not to stop your medication without speaking to your doctor first. Arthritis is often a long-term condition, and feeling better usually means the medication is working to control it. Stopping suddenly can lead to a return of symptoms or even a flare-up.

faqs.q: What if I'm worried about the long-term side effects?
faqs.a: It's natural to have concerns about long-term side effects. Your doctor can explain the potential risks and benefits specific to your medication, often comparing them to the risks of uncontrolled arthritis. They can also discuss monitoring plans to keep an eye on any side effects.

faqs.q: How do I know if my medication is actually working?
faqs.a: The best way to tell if your medication is working is to track your symptoms, like pain levels, stiffness, and how well you can do daily activities. Share these observations with your doctor. They will also look at physical signs and sometimes blood tests to assess its effectiveness.
