article.title: Giant Cell Arteritis: The Headache You Must Not Ignore
article.excerpt: Giant cell arteritis is an inflammation of arteries in the head that can threaten your sight. Learn the warning signs, why same-day help matters, and what treatment involves.
article.content:
Get help now

  • Go to A&E or call 999 if you have any sudden change in your vision, such as blurring, double vision, a curtain over part of your sight or loss of vision in one eye, alongside a headache, scalp tenderness or jaw pain.
  • Contact your GP for a same-day appointment, or call NHS 111, if you are over 50 and have a new headache that feels different from usual, tenderness over your temples or scalp, or pain in your jaw when you chew.
  • If you already have polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR), tell whoever you speak to that you have PMR.
  • Do not wait to see if it settles by itself. Early treatment protects your sight.

Quick answer: Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is inflammation of medium and large arteries, especially those in the head. It mainly affects people over 50 and can cause permanent sight loss if it is not treated quickly. A new headache, a tender scalp, jaw pain when chewing or any change in vision needs same-day medical help. Treatment with steroids usually starts straight away.

What is giant cell arteritis?

Giant cell arteritis, sometimes called temporal arteritis, is a type of vasculitis. That means the immune system causes inflammation in the walls of blood vessels. In GCA the arteries most often affected run up the sides of the head, by the temples, and supply the scalp, jaw and eyes. When they become inflamed they can narrow, which reduces blood flow. If the arteries that supply the eye are affected, sight can be damaged, sometimes suddenly and permanently.

GCA almost never occurs before the age of 50 and becomes more common with each decade after that. It is more common in women than in men. It is closely linked with polymyalgia rheumatica, a condition that causes pain and stiffness in the shoulders and hips. Some people have both at the same time, and some people with PMR go on to develop GCA later.

Symptoms to look out for

Symptoms can come on over a few days or weeks. Not everyone has all of them, and they can be easy to put down to something else. The ones that matter most are:

  • A new headache, often around the temples, that is different from any headache you have had before. It may be on one side or both.
  • Scalp tenderness, for example it hurts to brush or comb your hair or rest your head on a pillow.
  • Jaw pain when chewing that eases when you stop. Doctors call this jaw claudication, and it is an important clue.
  • Changes in vision, such as blurring, double vision, flashing lights or a shadow over part of your vision, even if they come and go.
  • Feeling generally unwell, with tiredness, a low-grade temperature, night sweats, poor appetite or weight loss.
  • Shoulder and hip stiffness in the mornings, if you also have PMR.

Less commonly, GCA can cause pain in the tongue, a sore throat, arm pain when using your arms, or a tender, thickened artery at the temple that you can feel.

Why speed matters

The biggest risk with GCA is sight loss. Once sight has been lost because of GCA, it usually does not come back. That is why the NHS treats suspected GCA as urgent and why doctors often start treatment before all the test results are back. It is always better to be checked and reassured than to wait.

If you are worried, say the words "I am worried this could be giant cell arteritis" when you call your GP practice or NHS 111. That helps the person triaging your call understand the urgency.

How GCA is diagnosed

Your GP or an emergency doctor will ask about your symptoms, examine your head and scalp, and check your eyes and blood pressure. You are likely to have:

  • Blood tests to look for inflammation, usually CRP and ESR. Raised levels support the diagnosis but are not proof on their own. Read more in our guide to getting to blood tests if travel is difficult.
  • An urgent referral to a specialist service. Many hospitals run a fast-track GCA pathway so you can be seen within days, often by a rheumatologist.
  • An ultrasound scan of the arteries in the temples and sometimes the armpits, which can show inflammation in the artery walls.
  • A temporal artery biopsy in some hospitals, where a tiny piece of artery is removed under local anaesthetic and looked at under a microscope.
  • An eye examination by an eye specialist if you have any visual symptoms.

Other scans, such as a PET-CT, are sometimes used if the doctors think larger arteries, such as the aorta, may be involved.

Treatment

The main treatment for GCA is a steroid medicine, usually prednisolone, started at a high dose to switch off the inflammation quickly. If you have visual symptoms, you may be given steroids through a drip in hospital at first. Most people notice their headache and general symptoms improve within a few days.

Once the inflammation is under control, the steroid dose is reduced slowly over many months. Your team will set the pace based on your symptoms and blood tests. Treatment often lasts one to two years, and sometimes longer. Never stop steroids suddenly or change the dose yourself, because your body needs time to adjust and stopping abruptly can make you seriously unwell. Always follow your own rheumatology team's plan.

Because long courses of steroids can affect bones, blood sugar, blood pressure, mood and sleep, your team may also offer:

  • Bone protection, such as calcium and vitamin D and sometimes a bisphosphonate. Our guide to bone protection on steroids explains why.
  • Stomach protection, if you are at risk of indigestion or ulcers.
  • Regular checks of blood sugar, blood pressure and weight.
  • A steroid emergency card, which you should carry at all times. See our guide to the steroid emergency card.

Some people need an extra medicine to help control GCA and allow the steroid dose to come down. Options include methotrexate or a biologic called tocilizumab, which NICE has approved for some people with GCA that keeps coming back or does not settle. Your specialist will explain whether these are suitable for you.

Living with GCA

Most people with GCA respond well to treatment, and many eventually come off steroids completely. The months of treatment can still be hard. Steroid side effects, worry about sight and fatigue are all common. These steps can help:

  • Learn the signs of a flare, such as your headache or jaw pain returning, and agree with your team how to contact them quickly.
  • Keep a simple diary of symptoms and your steroid dose, so appointments are easier.
  • Stay as active as you can. Gentle walking and strength exercises help protect bones and muscles while on steroids. See our steroids guide for more.
  • Ask about vaccinations, such as flu, COVID-19 and pneumonia, because steroids can make infections more likely.
  • Have regular eye tests with an optometrist, and tell them you have had GCA.

GCA and polymyalgia rheumatica

If you live with PMR, it is worth knowing the GCA warning signs well, because the two conditions overlap. A new headache, scalp soreness, jaw pain on chewing or any visual disturbance while you have PMR needs same-day advice, even if your PMR is well controlled. Your PMR steroid dose is usually lower than the dose used for GCA, so it may not be enough to prevent GCA. Our guides to PMR symptoms and PMR steroid tapers have more detail.

Frequently asked questions

Is giant cell arteritis an emergency?

It is treated as urgent because it can cause permanent sight loss. Any change in vision needs A&E or 999. A new headache, scalp tenderness or jaw pain on chewing if you are over 50 needs a same-day GP appointment or a call to NHS 111.

Can you get GCA under the age of 50?

It is very rare under 50. Headaches in younger people usually have other causes, but any severe, sudden or unusual headache should still be checked.

How long will I be on steroids for GCA?

Most people take steroids for one to two years, reducing the dose slowly over time. Some need them for longer. Your rheumatology team will guide the pace, and you should never stop or change the dose yourself.

Can GCA come back?

Yes, flares can happen, particularly as the steroid dose is reduced. Tell your team promptly if your symptoms return. Extra medicines can help if flares keep happening.

Will my sight come back if GCA affected it?

Sight lost because of GCA usually does not return, which is why fast treatment matters. Treatment aims to protect the other eye and any remaining sight.

Is GCA the same as a migraine?

No. Migraine usually starts earlier in life and follows a familiar pattern. GCA causes a new type of headache in people over 50, often with scalp tenderness, jaw pain or visual symptoms.

article.title: Ginger for Arthritis: An Honest Evidence Guide (UK)
article.excerpt: Ginger is a popular kitchen remedy for joint pain. Trials in osteoarthritis suggest a small benefit at best, and the evidence is of moderate to poor quality. This guide explains what the research shows, real safety points including blood thinners, ginger for medicine-related nausea, and simple ways to enjoy ginger as food.
article.content:
Quick answer: Ginger supplements may give a small reduction in osteoarthritis pain, but trials are few and of moderate or poor quality, and ibuprofen worked better in a head-to-head study. Ginger in food is safe for most people. If you take blood thinners such as warfarin, speak to a doctor or pharmacist before taking ginger supplements, as ginger might increase bleeding risk.

Evidence checked on 10 October 2026 against Arthritis UK's ginger information, the US National Institutes of Health's ginger fact sheet and a 2015 meta-analysis of trials.

Ginger has been used in cooking and traditional medicine for centuries, and it is often described as a natural anti-inflammatory. If you live with arthritis, you may have been told to try ginger tea, fresh ginger or ginger capsules. This guide sets out what the research actually shows, how strong that evidence is, and how to use ginger safely.

What is ginger?

Ginger is the underground stem (rhizome) of the Zingiber officinale plant, part of the same family as turmeric. It is sold fresh, dried and ground, as tea, in crystallised form and as extract capsules or oil. Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) notes that ginger extracts are available over the counter in pharmacies and high-street shops.

How might it work?

Arthritis UK explains that laboratory and animal studies have found ginger extracts can reduce the production of several chemical substances, including leukotrienes, that promote joint inflammation. Ginger also contains salicylates, which the body converts to salicylic acid, a substance related to aspirin that can reduce pain signals. These are plausible mechanisms, but they do not by themselves prove that ginger helps people with arthritis.

What the evidence shows

Trials in osteoarthritis

Arthritis UK describes three randomised trials in people with osteoarthritis:

  • Ginger vs ibuprofen vs placebo. 67 people with hip or knee osteoarthritis took ginger extract, ibuprofen or placebo three times a day for three weeks. Both ginger and ibuprofen reduced pain compared with placebo, but ibuprofen was more effective than ginger.
  • A crossover trial. 29 people with knee osteoarthritis took ginger or placebo for three months, then swapped. Ginger helped more than placebo in the first phase, but there was no significant difference in the second phase.
  • A six-month trial. 247 people with knee osteoarthritis took ginger extract or placebo twice a day. More people in the ginger group had a meaningful reduction in knee pain, but quality of life was similar in both groups, and the ginger group had more mild stomach side effects such as heartburn.

The meta-analysis

A 2015 meta-analysis (Bartels and colleagues) pooled placebo-controlled trials of ginger in osteoarthritis. It found a statistically significant but small reduction in pain and disability with ginger. People taking ginger were more than twice as likely to stop treatment as those on placebo. The authors concluded that ginger was "modestly efficacious and reasonably safe", and rated the evidence as moderate quality because of the small number of participants.

The US National Institutes of Health view

NCCIH says ginger supplements might help symptoms of knee osteoarthritis, but that much of the research has been of poor quality. It also says ginger applied to the skin has not been shown to help knee osteoarthritis.

Rheumatoid and other inflammatory arthritis

There is very little good-quality human research on ginger for rheumatoid arthritis. NICE guidance (NG100) says complementary therapies may give short-term relief for some people but have little or no evidence for long-term benefit, and should not replace conventional treatment.

Evidence at a glance

QuestionHonest answer
Does ginger reduce osteoarthritis pain?Possibly, a little. Trials show a small effect; quality is moderate to poor
Is it as good as ibuprofen?No. In the head-to-head trial, ibuprofen worked better
Does ginger cream or oil on the skin help?Not shown for knee osteoarthritis
Does it treat rheumatoid arthritis?No good evidence
Is it safe?Generally well tolerated; stomach upset is common; take care with blood thinners

For a side-by-side look at the two most popular spices, see our ginger vs turmeric comparison and our turmeric evidence guide.

Common claims, checked

  • "Ginger is a natural painkiller as strong as ibuprofen." Not supported. In the direct comparison described by Arthritis UK, ibuprofen worked better.
  • "Natural means safe." Ginger is generally well tolerated, but concentrated supplements can cause heartburn and might increase bleeding risk with blood thinners. Herbal products are not tested in the same way as medicines.
  • "More is better." No safe and effective dose has been established, and higher doses are more likely to upset your stomach. Taking several ginger products at once makes it harder to know how much you are having.
  • "Ginger shots reduce inflammation in your joints." There is no good evidence for this. Shots often contain added fruit juice and sugar, and the NHS suggests limiting fruit juice and smoothies to a combined total of 150ml a day.
  • "Ginger can replace my arthritis medicine." No. Do not stop or reduce prescribed treatment without speaking to your doctor.

Safety

Side effects

Arthritis UK describes ginger as relatively well tolerated, with minor side effects. The most common are stomach upset, heartburn and mouth irritation. In the meta-analysis, more people stopped taking ginger than placebo, which suggests side effects or taste put some people off.

Blood thinners

Arthritis UK advises taking ginger with care if you use anticoagulants, because ginger might increase the risk of bleeding. If you take warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran, clopidogrel or aspirin, speak to your doctor, anticoagulant clinic or pharmacist before taking ginger supplements. The NHS warfarin guidance says to tell your doctor about any herbal remedies or supplements and to check before starting new ones.

NSAIDs

Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen, naproxen and diclofenac can cause stomach irritation and bleeding. Ginger can also cause heartburn and might affect bleeding, so ask your pharmacist before combining a ginger supplement with regular NSAIDs.

Other medicines

NCCIH advises talking with a healthcare provider before using ginger if you take any medicine, because some herbs and medicines interact. For methotrexate, the NHS says there is not enough information to know whether herbal supplements are safe to take alongside it, so check with your rheumatology team or pharmacist.

Doses

Arthritis UK says no recommended safe and effective dose has been established for musculoskeletal conditions. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you. Supplement strengths vary, so do not assume one product is the same as another.

Pregnancy and breastfeeding

NCCIH says ginger supplements may be safe in pregnancy and are sometimes used for pregnancy sickness, but advises consulting a healthcare provider first. Little is known about safety while breastfeeding.

Ginger for medicine-related nausea

One area where ginger may be genuinely useful for people with arthritis is nausea. Arthritis UK suggests that if medication is making you feel sick, ginger or peppermint tea, foods containing ginger and even ginger biscuits can help some people, along with small regular meals and dry foods such as crackers or toast. If methotrexate or another medicine regularly makes you feel sick, tell your rheumatology team, because there are often ways to reduce this, such as adjusting folic acid, changing the timing or switching to injections.

Using ginger in food

Ginger in food is safe for most people and adds lots of flavour, which can make healthy meals more appealing. Ideas that need little effort:

  • Ginger tea: a few slices of fresh ginger in hot water, or a ginger tea bag.
  • Stir-fries: ready-prepared ginger paste with frozen stir-fry vegetables, tofu or chicken and noodles.
  • Soups: carrot and ginger, or butternut squash and ginger.
  • Curries and dals: ginger with garlic, turmeric and tinned tomatoes.
  • Porridge: a pinch of ground ginger with grated apple or pear.
  • Fish: salmon baked with ginger, soy sauce and spring onion.

If peeling and grating fresh ginger is hard on your hands, use jars of ginger paste, frozen chopped ginger or ground ginger. Freezing fresh ginger also makes it easier to grate. For more ideas, see our guide to anti-inflammatory herbs and spices.

Crystallised ginger, ginger biscuits and ginger beer are often high in sugar, so keep these as occasional treats.

Fresh, dried, tea or capsules?

FormWhat to know
Fresh rootBest flavour for cooking. Keeps in the fridge for a couple of weeks or the freezer for months
Ground (dried) gingerCheap and convenient for baking, porridge and curries. Easy on painful hands
Ginger paste or frozen chopped gingerNo peeling or grating. Useful if hand arthritis makes preparation hard
Ginger teaA comforting drink and may help nausea. Amounts are small compared with trial doses
Extract capsulesThe form used in arthritis trials. Strengths vary; check with a pharmacist before using, especially with blood thinners

If you want to try a ginger supplement

  1. Check with your pharmacist or GP first, especially if you take any blood thinner, NSAIDs or methotrexate.
  2. Choose a single-ingredient product with a clear dose on the label.
  3. Note your pain and stiffness before you start.
  4. Try it for a set period, for example two to three months, as in the longer trials.
  5. Stop if it upsets your stomach or you notice no clear benefit.
  6. Do not stop or reduce your prescribed treatment.

How to tell if it is helping

Arthritis pain naturally goes up and down, so it is easy to credit a supplement for a good week that would have happened anyway. A simple diary makes your decision more reliable. Fill this in once a week for two weeks before you start and then throughout your trial period:

WeekAverage pain (0–10)Morning stiffness (minutes)Painkiller doses this weekActivities I could doSide effects
Before 1
Before 2
Week 4
Week 8
Week 12

If your scores have not clearly improved by the end, the honest conclusion is that it probably is not worth continuing. Take the diary to your next GP or physiotherapy appointment; it is useful information whatever the result.

Put it in perspective

NICE guidance for osteoarthritis (NG226) puts therapeutic exercise and, where appropriate, weight management at the centre of treatment, with information and support. These have far stronger evidence than any supplement. If you are thinking about ginger because your pain is not well controlled, it is worth also asking your GP or a physiotherapist about an exercise programme and reviewing your pain relief.

For rheumatoid and other inflammatory types of arthritis, disease-modifying medicines are what protect your joints. No food or supplement can do that job.

When a dietitian can help

If you are trying lots of supplements, or have cut down what you eat because of nausea or reflux, a registered dietitian can help you build a balanced diet that suits you. Ask your GP or rheumatology team about a referral.

When to get medical help

Stop ginger supplements and get urgent medical advice if you notice signs of bleeding, such as black or bloody stools, vomiting blood or unusual bruising, especially if you take a blood thinner. See your GP if you have persistent heartburn, indigestion or difficulty swallowing, or if nausea from your medicines is stopping you eating. Get same-day advice from your GP or NHS 111 if a joint suddenly becomes hot, swollen and very painful, especially with a fever.

Frequently asked questions

Does ginger help arthritis pain?

Trials in osteoarthritis suggest ginger supplements may give a small reduction in pain, but the evidence is of moderate to poor quality. It has not been shown to help rheumatoid arthritis.

Is ginger better than ibuprofen?

No. In the trial that compared them directly, ibuprofen was more effective than ginger. Both have side effects, so ask a pharmacist which is suitable for you.

Can I take ginger with warfarin?

Ginger might increase bleeding risk. Ginger in normal food amounts is unlikely to be a problem for most people, but speak to your doctor or anticoagulant clinic before taking ginger supplements.

Does ginger tea help arthritis?

There is no good evidence that ginger tea eases arthritis, but it is a pleasant, caffeine-free drink that counts towards your fluids and may help with nausea.

Do ginger creams or oils help joint pain?

NCCIH says ginger applied to the skin has not been shown to help knee osteoarthritis. NICE recommends offering a topical NSAID gel for knee osteoarthritis and considering one for other joints; ask your pharmacist.

How much ginger should I take?

No safe and effective dose has been established for arthritis. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you. Check with a pharmacist before starting.

article.title: Ginger vs Turmeric for Arthritis: Which Actually Works?
article.excerpt: Ginger vs turmeric for arthritis: a UK clinician compares the evidence, doses, safety, and which one actually helps joint pain. UK educational guide.
article.content:
Quick answer: Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you. Check with your GP before starting.

Patients ask me this almost every week: *"If I only pick one — should it be ginger or turmeric?"* Both are cheap, widely available in UK supermarkets, and both have real anti-inflammatory evidence behind them. But they aren't interchangeable, and neither is a substitute for the treatments your GP or rheumatologist recommends.

Here is the honest, evidence-based comparison — written for people living with osteoarthritis or inflammatory arthritis in the UK.

What ginger actually does for joint pain

Ginger (Zingiber officinale) contains gingerols and shogaols, compounds that dampen the same inflammatory pathways NSAIDs act on — COX-2 and pro-inflammatory cytokines like TNF-α and IL-1β. That's the mechanism. What about real people?

Meta-analyses of randomised trials in knee osteoarthritis show ginger extract produces a modest but real reduction in pain and stiffness compared with placebo, typically over 4–12 weeks. The effect is smaller and less consistent than turmeric, and study quality varies, but ginger clears the "better than nothing" bar that most food-based interventions fail.

How much ginger, and in what form?

  • Standardised extract: Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.
  • Fresh root: Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.
  • Give it at least 4–8 weeks before deciding whether it helps.

Ginger is genuinely food. If you'd rather skip capsules, drinking two cups of strong ginger tea a day is a reasonable starting point.

What turmeric (curcumin) actually does

Turmeric's active molecule is curcumin, and this is where the evidence gets more interesting. Curcumin blocks NF-κB, COX-2, and multiple inflammatory cytokines — mechanistically similar to ginger, but usually with a bigger effect size in trials.

A well-cited 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis concluded that curcumin taken daily in study doses improves arthritis symptoms with an effect size comparable to some non-steroidal anti-inflammatories (like ibuprofen or diclofenac) over 8–12 weeks — but with fewer gastrointestinal side effects. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you. More recent knee OA trials broadly agree.

The catch: curcumin on its own is poorly absorbed. You need one of these:

  • Curcumin + piperine (black pepper extract) — the classic pairing, increases absorption dramatically.
  • Phytosome / liposomal / Meriva / Longvida formulations — engineered for better uptake.

A teaspoon of turmeric powder in your dhal is lovely, but it won't reach the doses used in trials. That is a supplement conversation.

Head-to-head: ginger vs turmeric

Factor Ginger Turmeric (curcumin)
Strength of evidence for arthritis Moderate Moderate to strong
Typical study dose Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.
Compared to ibuprofen Weaker Similar in several trials
Absorption issues Minimal Significant — needs piperine or a phytosome
Cost of a food dose Very low Very low (but food doses are sub-therapeutic)
Also helps Nausea, morning stiffness Systemic inflammation, gut lining

Is turmeric better than ginger for arthritis?

For pain and function in knee osteoarthritis specifically, turmeric (as a properly absorbed curcumin supplement) has the stronger evidence base. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.

Can I take ginger and turmeric together?

Yes — and it's what most trials of "arthritis blends" actually test. They work on overlapping pathways rather than the same receptor, so combining them is reasonable, not redundant. Just don't stack multiple high-dose supplements without telling your GP or pharmacist, especially if you're on other medication.

How long before ginger or turmeric works?

Give either at least 4 weeks, ideally 8–12, at a consistent daily dose. Skipping days makes it very hard to tell whether it's helping. Track your pain honestly — a simple 0–10 score in the morning and evening for a fortnight before you start is worth its weight in gold.

Safety flags — read this before you buy anything

Both are safe for most adults, but there are real interactions:

  • Blood thinners (warfarin, DOACs like apixaban, or high-dose aspirin) — both ginger and curcumin have mild antiplatelet effects. Check with your GP before starting.
  • Diabetes medication — both can nudge blood glucose down; monitor if you're on insulin or sulphonylureas.
  • Gallstones or bile-duct disease — turmeric stimulates bile flow and can trigger pain. Avoid high-dose curcumin.
  • Pregnancy — culinary amounts are fine; supplement doses of curcumin are not recommended.
  • Rare liver injury — a small number of case reports link high-dose curcumin (usually with piperine or phytosome formulations) to reversible hepatitis. Stop and see your GP if you develop jaundice, dark urine, or right-sided abdominal pain.

If you're on methotrexate, biologics, or long-term NSAIDs, treat these as add-ons, not replacements, and tell your rheumatology team.

How to actually eat more of both

You don't have to choose between capsules and cooking — most patients I see do both.

  • Golden milk: 1 tsp turmeric + a pinch of black pepper + grated fresh ginger, simmered in warm milk (dairy or plant-based) with a little honey.
  • Anti-inflammatory smoothie: frozen berries, banana, a thumb of fresh ginger, ½ tsp turmeric, black pepper, oat milk. See our anti-inflammatory smoothie recipes for more.
  • Weeknight dhal or curry: onion, garlic, fresh ginger, turmeric, black pepper — the Indian home kitchen has been doing this bioavailability trick for centuries.
  • Sheet-pan dinners: grated ginger + turmeric + olive oil + lemon over salmon and vegetables.

If you want the bigger picture, our Mediterranean diet 14-day plan for arthritis is where I'd start most patients before adding supplements.

The bottom line

  • Turmeric (curcumin, properly absorbed) has the stronger evidence Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.
  • Ginger is a genuine, well-tolerated adjunct Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.
  • Both are safe for most adults, but check with your GP if you're on blood thinners, diabetes medication, or have gallstones.
  • Neither is a cure. They sit alongside — never instead of — weight management, exercise, and the medication your rheumatology team recommends.

For a deeper dive into each on its own, see turmeric and curcumin for arthritis: the evidence and ginger root as a natural anti-inflammatory.

This article is for general information and does not replace personal medical advice. If your joint pain is new, worsening, or waking you at night, please speak to your GP.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have chest pain, sudden weakness or numbness, severe breathlessness, a suspected broken bone after a fall, or back pain with new loss of bladder or bowel control or numbness around your bottom or genitals.

Contact NHS 111 or your GP urgently if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel unwell or have a fever, or if your symptoms are getting rapidly worse.

article.direct_answer: For most people with arthritis, turmeric (as a properly absorbed curcumin supplement at around 1,000 mg/day for 8–12 weeks) has the stronger evidence for reducing pain and stiffness. Ginger at 500–1,000 mg/day is a well-tolerated adjunct, especially if you also have morning stiffness or nausea. Check with your GP before starting.

faqs.q: How much ginger, and in what form?
faqs.a: Standardised extract: Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you. Fresh root: Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you. Give it at least 4–8 weeks before deciding whether it helps. Ginger is genuinely food. If you'd rather skip capsules, drinking two cups of strong ginger tea a day is a reasonable starting point.

faqs.q: Is turmeric better than ginger for arthritis?
faqs.a: For pain and function in knee osteoarthritis specifically, turmeric (as a properly absorbed curcumin supplement) has the stronger evidence base . Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.

faqs.q: Can I take ginger and turmeric together?
faqs.a: Yes — and it's what most trials of "arthritis blends" actually test. They work on overlapping pathways rather than the same receptor, so combining them is reasonable, not redundant. Just don't stack multiple high-dose supplements without telling your GP or pharmacist, especially if you're on other medication.

faqs.q: How long before ginger or turmeric works?
faqs.a: Give either at least 4 weeks, ideally 8–12 , at a consistent daily dose. Skipping days makes it very hard to tell whether it's helping. Track your pain honestly — a simple 0–10 score in the morning and evening for a fortnight before you start is worth its weight in gold.

article.title: Glucosamine vs Collagen: Which Is Better for Joints?
article.excerpt: Compare glucosamine and collagen supplements for joint health. Evidence-based analysis of benefits, dosage and effectiveness.
article.content:
Quick answer: Glucosamine and collagen are both popular joint supplements. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you. There is no definitive winner, as benefits and onset times vary, with glucosamine effects typically seen in 4–8 weeks and collagen in 3–6 months.

Glucosamine vs Collagen: The Evidence

Both glucosamine and collagen are among the most popular joint health supplements in the UK, but how do they compare? This guide breaks down the science behind each.

Glucosamine: What the Research Says

Glucosamine sulfate is one of the most studied supplements for osteoarthritis. It occurs naturally in cartilage and is thought to support cartilage repair and reduce inflammation.

Key findings:

  • A 2018 Cochrane review found glucosamine sulfate provided modest pain relief in knee OA
  • The GAIT trial (3,800+ participants) showed limited benefit over placebo for most patients
  • Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.
  • Benefits typically take 4–8 weeks to appear

Collagen: Emerging Evidence

Hydrolysed collagen (collagen peptides) provides the amino acids glycine, proline, and hydroxyproline — building blocks of cartilage and connective tissue.

Key findings:

  • A 2023 meta-analysis of 15 RCTs found collagen supplements reduced joint pain and improved function
  • Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.
  • Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.
  • Generally well-tolerated with few side effects

Head-to-Head Comparison

Factor Glucosamine Collagen
Evidence quality Moderate (mixed) Growing (promising)
Typical dose Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.
Time to effect 4–8 weeks 3–6 months
Cost (monthly) £8–15 £15–30
Mechanism Cartilage support Tissue building blocks

Which Should You Choose?

There is no definitive winner. Consider:

  • Try glucosamine first if you have knee OA — it has the longest track record
  • Consider collagen if glucosamine hasn't helped after 3 months
  • Combining both is safe and may offer complementary benefits
  • Always choose pharmaceutical-grade products from reputable UK suppliers

Important Considerations

  • Glucosamine derived from shellfish — check allergies
  • Collagen typically from bovine or marine sources
  • Neither is a substitute for exercise and weight management
  • Discuss with your GP, especially if taking blood thinners

Reviewed by Dr. Sarah Bennett, Consultant Rheumatologist, Royal Free Hospital

Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your local integrated care board about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Using evidence carefully

Marketing claims for joint supplements often outrun the research. Look for products that state dose clearly, avoid miracle language, and fit alongside — never instead of — prescribed treatment. Stop and seek advice if you notice bruising, stomach pain, yellowing of the skin or new rashes.

Talking with your clinician

Bring the bottle or a photo to pharmacy or clinic appointments. Pharmacists can flag interactions with methotrexate, anticoagulants and other common arthritis medicines. Document start dates so you and your team can judge benefit honestly after several weeks.

Everyday eating patterns

No single food cures arthritis. Patterns rich in vegetables, fruit, pulses, wholegrains and oily fish are the ones most often discussed in UK dietetic advice for inflammatory conditions. Keep changes realistic: swap one ultra-processed snack for fruit and nuts, or cook with olive oil more often than seed oils marketed as miracle cures.

Quick questions about Glucosamine Collagen Which Better

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

article.title: Glute Bridges for Hip Osteoarthritis: Complete Guide
article.excerpt: Glute bridges activate the gluteus maximus without compressing the hip joint — ideal for hip OA. Three progressions from beginner to advanced.
article.content:
Quick answer: This guide explains that hip osteoarthritis pain can involve cartilage, fluid, ligaments, muscles and the nervous system, so patterns matter. It presents structured, graded exercise as first-line, alongside Mediterranean-style eating, weight management, heat or cold, sleep hygiene and small weekly tracking. It advises seeing a GP or physiotherapist for swollen joints, weight loss, prolonged stiffness, numbness or weakness.

What this guide covers

This piece summarises what the current evidence says about glute bridges for hip osteoarthritis: complete guide, the practical steps that help most, and the red flags that mean you should speak to your GP or physiotherapist.

The underlying mechanism

Arthritis pain rarely has a single cause. Joint cartilage, synovial fluid, ligaments, surrounding muscle and the nervous system all contribute. Understanding which of these is driving your specific symptom is the first step toward targeted relief. For an in-depth condition overview, see our related guide.

Inflammatory and degenerative forms behave differently. Inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid, psoriatic, ankylosing spondylitis) typically worsens with rest and improves with gentle movement. Degenerative arthritis (osteoarthritis) typically worsens with prolonged use. Knowing which pattern matches your day-to-day experience helps you choose the right management approach.

What helps — by strength of evidence

  1. Movement and graded exercise. NICE NG226 (2022) and Cochrane reviews place structured exercise as a first-line treatment. Aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, split into 20–30 minute sessions.
  2. Anti-inflammatory eating. A Mediterranean-style pattern — oily fish twice a week, plenty of vegetables, olive oil, whole grains — is linked to reduced pain scores in OA and RA trials.
  3. Weight management. A 5 percent reduction in body weight reduces knee-OA symptoms measurably; a 10 percent reduction can match the effect of some medications.
  4. Heat and cold. Heat eases stiffness; cold eases acute swelling. Twenty-minute applications, with a towel barrier.
  5. Sleep hygiene. Pain perception rises sharply on fewer than six hours of sleep. Prioritise a consistent bedtime.

A practical seven-day starting plan

Begin with the smallest dose that feels manageable — five minutes of movement, one anti-inflammatory meal a day, a 10 pm screen-off rule. Track only three things weekly: pain on waking (0–10), longest pain-free interval, and one functional win (e.g., climbed stairs without grabbing the rail). Small, consistent inputs outperform big sporadic efforts.

When to seek clinical advice

Book an appointment with your GP or a first-contact physiotherapist if you notice: sudden hot, red, swollen joints; unexplained weight loss alongside joint pain; morning stiffness lasting longer than an hour for more than two weeks; or new numbness or weakness. These can signal inflammatory disease that benefits from early treatment.

Frequently asked questions

Will this approach work alongside my medication? Yes. Exercise, diet and pacing complement prescribed treatments and often improve their effectiveness. Always check with your prescriber before stopping any medication.

How long until I notice a difference? Most people report meaningful improvement at 6–12 weeks of consistent practice. Earlier wins (less morning stiffness, better sleep) often appear within 2–3 weeks.

Is this safe if I have other conditions? The principles above are broadly safe for adults with stable cardiovascular, metabolic and respiratory conditions. If you are unsure, ask your GP for a referral to a first-contact physiotherapist for a tailored plan.

This article is general health information, not medical advice. Always consult a qualified healthcare professional for decisions about your individual care.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Building a joint-friendly routine

Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery.

Peer support etiquette

Share what helps you without prescribing it for others. Conditions, medicines and life circumstances differ. If someone is in crisis, encourage them toward NHS 111, their GP, or emergency services rather than relying on a forum alone.

This page looks at tiny goals for frail adults with arthritis with a frailty-aware lens for UK readers at home. Quick answer: This page looks at tiny goals for frail adults with arthritis with a frailty-aware lens for UK readers at home. This page explains one meaningful task a day, not a transformation if you live with arthritis with frailty, without pretending rest is always safer. Use it alongside your GP, not instead of them.

A flare in several joints can look like sudden frailty. True frailty is a wider loss of reserve: weaker recovery after a quiet week, an infection or a hospital night. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with one meaningful task a day, not a transformation, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in England.

Self-management that respects arthritis with frailty

None of this is a gym challenge. The aim is to keep several joints moving, keep protein in the day, and keep one meaningful task a day, not a transformation from becoming the only story in the home. If a physiotherapist, occupational therapist or frailty team has already given you a plan, follow that ahead of a webpage.

  • Write three daily anchors: a meal, a movement, a conversation. Frailty grows in unstructured days.
  • If cooking is the barrier, use tinned fish, eggs, yoghurt, beans or leftover protein foods rather than skipping meals. Muscle needs raw material as well as movement.
  • Set an indoor walking loop with places to pause. Pain in several joints prefer several short bouts to one heroic corridor.
  • Treat a walking aid as joint protection and falls kit, not as a verdict. Wrist-friendly handles matter if several joints include hands.
  • Use heat for stiffness if your skin is healthy, but protect thin skin. Never fall asleep on a hot water bottle.
  • Book eye, foot and hearing checks as frailty care, not vanity. Arthritis with frailty already asks a lot of balance.

Pain, muscle and recovery: the England picture

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Pain in several joints can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual arthritis with frailty.

Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis. Only some also live with frailty. The practical question is not the label. It is whether one meaningful task a day, not a transformation is shrinking your home life — and what you can change this week without pretending pain is imaginary.

Living With Arthritis is an independent UK charity (1218461), not part of Arthritis UK. We write for patients and carers. We do not replace NHS England services via your GP.

Flare, fear and slowing down

In a home, one meaningful task a day, not a transformation is rarely one dramatic collapse. It is usually a stack of small avoidances. People with arthritis with frailty already know boom-and-bust. Frailty adds a longer payback: a quiet weekend can cost the following Thursday.

  • Night toilet trips, poor lighting and stiff several joints stacking into a falls risk that nobody named.
  • Skipping meals or drinks because getting to the kitchen with sore several joints feels like a project.
  • New fear after a near-miss, even if you did not hit the floor. Fear of falling is itself a reason people sit more.
  • A hospital or infection week that ends with clothes feeling looser and stairs feeling taller.
  • Carers doing the last steps of a task to be kind, which removes the last practice the muscles were getting.

Help in England if arthritis and frailty overlap

Start with your GP practice and NHS England services via your GP. For urgent but non-emergency advice use NHS 111. For chest pain, suspected hip fracture, sudden new weakness, or a fall with a bang to the head on blood thinners, use 999.

The mental load of one meaningful task a day, not a transformation

When to get help

  • Chest pain, trouble breathing, or signs of a stroke — 999, not a wait for the arthritis with frailty nurse.
  • A knock to the head, especially if you take blood thinners — do not sleep it off as a plan.
  • A hot, very swollen joint with fever, or feeling systemically unwell — seek urgent clinical advice. A joint infection is an emergency.
  • Sudden confusion, new incontinence, or a crash in mobility over hours to days — think infection or delirium, not only arthritis.
  • Unplanned weight loss, repeated falls, or one meaningful task a day, not a transformation that is clearly worsening week by week — book the GP and say you are worried about frailty as well as several joints.

Are painkillers the main treatment for frail arthritis with frailty?

No. For osteoarthritis, NICE puts exercise, weight management where relevant, and topical options at the centre. Tablets may help some people some of the time, but in frail adults they need a hard look at stomach, kidneys, heart, constipation and falls. Never share someone else's medicines.

Can frailty improve if I still have pain in several joints?

Sometimes the frailty part can shift even if arthritis with frailty remains. Strength, protein, reviewing dizzy medicines, treating a flare, and practising transfers can return reserve. Improvement is not guaranteed and it is rarely dramatic, but frailer this month is not always a one-way door. Work with clinicians rather than copying an online challenge.

How do I tell an arthritis flare from a frailty slide?

A flare of arthritis with frailty is usually more joint pain, stiffness or swelling in a known pattern. A frailty slide is broader: weaker recovery, smaller meals, more time in the chair, maybe confusion or falls. They can happen together. If the whole person is changing, do not only increase pain gel.

article.title: Gout Flare Up Diet: What Foods to Avoid
article.excerpt: A practical guide to the gout diet — which foods trigger flares, what to eat instead, and how diet and medication work together to prevent attacks.
article.content:
Gout flare up diet and what foods to avoid is one of the most-searched topics for people diagnosed with gout — and with good reason. Diet is one of the most powerful modifiable factors in gout management, alongside urate-lowering medication.

Quick answer: Avoid for gout: organ meats, red meat (limit), sardines/anchovies, beer and spirits, and high-fructose drinks. Eat: cherries (some people include them; not a treatment), drink 2-3 litres water daily, include low-fat dairy. Diet alone rarely controls established gout — discuss allopurinol with your GP.

Healthy diet for gout — openly licensed via Openverse

Why Diet Matters in Gout

Gout is caused by elevated uric acid in the blood (hyperuricaemia). Uric acid is the breakdown product of purines — compounds found naturally in many foods and produced by the body. When uric acid levels rise too high, crystals form in joints, causing the agonising pain of a gout attack. Diet reduces uric acid by limiting purine intake and increasing excretion.

Foods to Avoid or Strictly Limit

High-Purine Animal Products

  • Organ meats: liver, kidney, sweetbreads (very high purines — avoid entirely)
  • Red meat: beef, lamb, pork — limit to 1–2 portions per week
  • Certain fish: sardines, anchovies, herring, mackerel, scallops, mussels
  • Game meats: venison, goose

Alcohol

Beer and spirits are particularly problematic — beer contains purines directly, and all alcohol raises uric acid by slowing its excretion. Even moderate alcohol consumption significantly raises attack risk. Wine in small amounts appears less harmful but should still be limited.

High-Fructose Foods and Drinks

Fructose raises uric acid independently of purines. Avoid: sweetened fizzy drinks, fruit juices, squash, high-fructose corn syrup products.

Gout-friendly foods — openly licensed via Openverse

Foods That Help Lower Uric Acid

  • Cherries: a food some people include. This page does not treat cherries as a proven treatment or quote an attack-reduction figure.
  • Water: 2–3 litres daily helps flush uric acid via the kidneys.
  • Low-fat dairy: milk, yoghurt and low-fat cheese are associated with lower uric acid levels.
  • Coffee: 4+ cups/day is associated with lower gout risk in studies (mechanism unclear — not recommended to start drinking coffee for gout, but existing coffee drinkers should not stop).
  • Vegetables: despite purines in some veg (asparagus, spinach), vegetable purines do not raise uric acid in the same way as animal purines.

Healthy eating for gout — openly licensed via Openverse

Movement when gout flares

There is no best exercise for gout. During a flare, rest the painful joint. When the flare has settled, return to gentle movement you can do without forcing it. This is not an exercise programme. If a joint is hot and swollen, or you feel unwell, get medical advice rather than pushing through it.

Q&A

Question: Is diet enough to control gout without medication?
Short answer: For mild hyperuricaemia, diet alone can sometimes normalise uric acid. For established gout with recurrent attacks, urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol, febuxostat) is usually needed alongside dietary changes. Discuss with your GP.

Question: Does cherry juice really work?
Short answer: Multiple studies suggest cherries and cherry juice reduce gout attack frequency. The mechanism involves anthocyanins reducing inflammation and directly lowering uric acid. Use concentrated cherry juice (30ml daily) or eat 10–12 fresh/frozen cherries.

Practical next steps for Gout Flare Up Diet: What Foods to Avoid

If you came here about Gout Flare Up Diet: What Foods to Avoid, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Everyday eating patterns

No single food cures arthritis. Patterns rich in vegetables, fruit, pulses, wholegrains and oily fish are the ones most often discussed in UK dietetic advice for inflammatory conditions. Keep changes realistic: swap one ultra-processed snack for fruit and nuts, or cook with olive oil more often than seed oils marketed as miracle cures.

Building a joint-friendly routine

Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery.

Quick questions about Gout Flare Diet What

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

Keep expectations kind while you work on gout flare up diet: what foods to avoid. Arthritis symptoms fluctuate; a quieter week does not mean you imagined earlier pain, and a flare does not mean every helpful habit has failed. Adjust one variable at a time so you can see what truly helps.

article.title: Gout Medication UK: A Complete Guide to Drugs for Gout
article.excerpt: From managing a gout attack to long-term uric acid control — everything you need to know about gout treatment in the UK.
article.content:
Quick answer: Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.

Gout is the most common form of inflammatory arthritis in the UK, affecting an estimated 2.5 million people — and rates have been rising for decades. A gout attack is one of the most painful medical events a person can experience: the intense burning, swelling, and redness, typically in the big toe but potentially in any joint, can be completely debilitating.

The good news is that gout is one of the most treatable forms of arthritis. With the right gout medication in the UK, attacks can be stopped quickly, and with consistent long-term treatment, many people become entirely gout-free. This guide covers everything from how gout develops, to the drugs used to treat acute attacks, to the urate-lowering therapies available to UK patients.

Understanding Gout: Why Medication Is Needed

Gout is caused by hyperuricaemia — elevated levels of uric acid in the blood. When uric acid exceeds its solubility threshold (approximately 360 micromol/L), it crystallises as monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in joint spaces and surrounding tissue. These sharp, needle-like crystals trigger an intense immune response, producing the extreme pain and inflammation of a gout attack.

Without treatment, gout attacks become more frequent and eventually chronic. Crystals can also accumulate in soft tissue (tophi), damage kidneys, and cause cardiovascular complications. This is why long-term medication to control uric acid levels — not just treating individual attacks — is essential for most people with recurrent gout.

Medications for Acute Gout Attacks

The priority during an acute gout attack is to reduce pain and inflammation as quickly as possible. Three types of medication are used.

NSAIDs (Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs)

NSAIDs are usually the first-line treatment for acute gout in the UK. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you. They work by inhibiting COX enzymes and reducing prostaglandin production, thereby rapidly reducing inflammation and pain. Most people notice significant improvement within 24 hours.

NSAIDs must be used with caution or avoided in people with kidney disease, stomach ulcers, heart failure, or who are taking anticoagulants. Always take NSAIDs with food. Naproxen is available over the counter in the UK at lower doses; higher prescription doses provide greater anti-inflammatory effect.

Colchicine

Colchicine is a plant-derived drug — originally extracted from the autumn crocus — that has been used for gout for over a century. It works by disrupting microtubule function in neutrophils, preventing them from migrating to the inflamed joint and releasing inflammatory mediators.

Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you. This low-dose regimen is as effective as the older high-dose approach but with significantly fewer gastrointestinal side effects (nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal cramping). Colchicine is particularly useful for people who cannot tolerate NSAIDs.

Important drug interactions for colchicine

  • Statins (increased risk of muscle damage — myopathy).
  • Ciclosporin (significantly increased colchicine levels — avoid combination).
  • Clarithromycin and other macrolide antibiotics.
  • Always inform your GP and pharmacist of all medications you take.

Corticosteroids

Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you. Intra-articular steroid injections directly into the affected joint provide rapid, targeted relief and are particularly useful for large joints such as the knee or ankle.

Corticosteroids should not be used long-term for gout due to well-known side effects including blood sugar elevation, bone thinning, weight gain, and adrenal suppression.

Long-Term Urate-Lowering Therapy (ULT)

After a confirmed gout diagnosis — particularly with two or more attacks per year, tophi, kidney stones, or chronic kidney disease — UK guidelines recommend starting urate-lowering therapy to permanently reduce uric acid levels. The target is to keep serum urate below 360 micromol/L (and below 300 micromol/L in those with tophi).

Allopurinol — The Gold Standard

Allopurinol is the first-line ULT in the UK and worldwide. It is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, meaning it blocks the enzyme responsible for the final step in uric acid production. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.

A key principle: allopurinol must always be started after an acute attack has fully resolved (usually two to four weeks after), never during one, as starting it during an attack can paradoxically prolong or worsen the flare. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.

Allopurinol is generally well tolerated. Rare but serious reactions include allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS) — a potentially life-threatening skin reaction. Risk is higher in people of Han Chinese, Thai, and Korean descent, who should be tested for the HLA-B*5801 allele before starting treatment.

Febuxostat — An Alternative for Allopurinol Intolerance

Febuxostat (brand name Adenuric in the UK) is a non-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor, available in the UK for people who cannot tolerate or do not respond adequately to allopurinol. It is often more potent than standard allopurinol doses and does not require dose adjustment for mild-to-moderate kidney impairment.

A 2019 clinical trial (CARES trial) raised concerns about cardiovascular mortality with febuxostat versus allopurinol, though subsequent European analyses have not replicated this finding. In the UK, febuxostat should be used with caution in people with established cardiovascular disease.

Benzbromarone and Other Uricosurics

Uricosuric drugs work differently — instead of reducing uric acid production, they increase its excretion via the kidneys. Benzbromarone is available on a named-patient basis in the UK for patients who overproduce uric acid or have failed other treatments. Probenecid is another option. These drugs are contraindicated in kidney stone formers as they increase urinary urate and the risk of stone formation.

Quick Answer

For acute gout attacks, UK doctors prescribe NSAIDs (naproxen, indomethacin), low-dose colchicine, or corticosteroids. For long-term prevention, urate-lowering therapy with allopurinol (first-line) or febuxostat is recommended. The target is to keep serum urate below 360 micromol/L. Medication should always be managed by a GP or rheumatologist.

Lifestyle Measures Alongside Medication

Medication is most effective when supported by lifestyle changes: staying well hydrated (aim for 2–3 litres of fluid daily), reducing beer and spirits, limiting red meat and seafood high in purines, avoiding fructose-rich drinks, achieving a healthy weight, and taking any prescribed diuretics (water tablets) only as directed by your doctor, as these can raise uric acid levels.

Conclusion

Gout is eminently treatable and, with the right medication and lifestyle management, entirely preventable. If you are experiencing recurrent attacks, speak to your GP about starting urate-lowering therapy. Do not wait — untreated gout causes cumulative joint damage that can be difficult to reverse.

  • Arthritis in Older Adults: What Changes and What Helps — Arthritis becomes more common with age, but it is not inevitable and it is not untreatable.
  • Topical NSAIDs for frail adults with hand or knee osteoarthritis (UK) — Frailty is a clinical syndrome — not a personality trait — and osteoarthritis can make it more visible.
  • Methotrexate in older frail adults with rheumatoid arthritis (UK) — Arthritis is common across the UK; frailty is less so — but when they overlap, days can shrink faster than joint pain alone would suggest.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have chest pain, sudden weakness or numbness, severe breathlessness, a suspected broken bone after a fall, or back pain with new loss of bladder or bowel control or numbness around your bottom or genitals.

Contact NHS 111 or your GP urgently if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel unwell or have a fever, or if your symptoms are getting rapidly worse.

article.title: Gout in winter: dehydration, uric acid and flares (UK guide)
article.excerpt: How winter dehydration can trigger gout flares, NHS fluid and flare advice, alcohol and sugary drinks, and when to seek help. UK educational guide.
article.content:
Quick answer: The NHS lists dehydration as something that can trigger a gout attack. In winter many people drink less because they feel less thirsty, while alcohol and sugary drinks can raise uric acid and dry you out further. Drink plenty of fluids unless your GP has set a fluid limit, keep alcohol-free days, and during a flare rest the joint, use ice wrapped in a towel, and take prescribed medicines as directed — do not stop urate-lowering tablets during a flare unless your clinician says so.

Gout is an inflammatory arthritis caused by urate crystals in a joint. Attacks are often sudden, very painful and hot — commonly in the big toe or midfoot. This guide is about the winter job many people ask about: how dehydration, colder-weather drinking habits and festive alcohol can link to flares. It is educational information for people in the UK, not a diagnosis or a personal treatment plan. For the full condition overview see our gout hub and gout treatment overview.

What the NHS says about gout and dehydration

  • Gout happens when there is too much uric acid (urate) in the blood, which can form crystals around joints
  • Things that can trigger an attack include illness with a high temperature, drinking too much alcohol, a very large meal, getting dehydrated, injuring a joint, and some medicines
  • During an attack, the NHS advises drinking lots of water unless a GP tells you not to, resting and raising the limb, and keeping the joint cool with an ice pack or bag of frozen peas wrapped in a towel for up to 20 minutes at a time
  • Longer term, the NHS advises drinking plenty of fluids to avoid dehydration, having some alcohol-free days each week, and not drinking more than 14 units of alcohol a week

If you have kidney disease, heart failure or another condition with a fluid limit, follow the limit your team gave you — do not force extra drinks.

Why winter can make fluid habits harder

Cold weather does not cause gout by itself. What often changes in autumn and winter is how you drink and socialise:

  • Less thirst outdoors: you may simply forget water when you are not hot
  • Heating and dry air: indoor heating can leave your mouth dry while you still skip drinks
  • Illness: a winter bug with fever is on the NHS trigger list for gout attacks
  • Festive alcohol and sugary drinks: beer, spirits and sugar-sweetened soft drinks can raise uric acid and also dehydrate you
  • Diuretics ("water tablets"): some blood-pressure or heart medicines increase uric acid; never stop them yourself — ask your GP or pharmacist if flares are frequent

If you are older, living with frailty, or need help getting to the kitchen, a drinks bottle within reach and a simple daily drinks plan matter more than willpower alone. Our gout, older people and hydration guide covers that overlap.

A practical winter drinks plan

  • Keep a reusable bottle or jug where you sit, and aim for regular sips through the day rather than one huge evening catch-up
  • Prefer water, sugar-free squash or tea and coffee in moderation; cut back on sugar-sweetened fizzy drinks and fruit drinks with added sugar
  • If alcohol features at Christmas or New Year, plan alcohol-free days and avoid binge drinking — alcohol itself is a common gout trigger
  • During a flare, prioritise water unless your GP has set a fluid limit; keep bedclothes off a very painful toe or foot if that helps
  • If swallowing or getting drinks is hard because of other health problems, ask your GP, pharmacist or carer support about practical help

For food patterns around gout (not a miracle diet), see gout flare diet and foods to be careful with and the diet hub.

During a flare: what helps, what does not

  • Take any medicine you have been prescribed for the attack as soon as possible — the NHS says it should start to work within about 2 days
  • Rest and raise the limb; ice with a cloth barrier for up to 20 minutes at a time
  • Drink lots of water unless told not to
  • If you take long-term urate-lowering medicine such as allopurinol or febuxostat, keep taking it during a flare unless your clinician tells you to stop — stopping suddenly can make attacks more likely later. See our febuxostat guide and gout medication UK overview
  • Do not start high-dose painkillers, steroids or colchicine yourself from someone else's leftover pack — ask a pharmacist or GP what is safe for you, especially if you have kidney, heart or stomach problems

When to get help

  • See your GP if gout attacks keep returning, if you have never had your uric acid or medicines reviewed, or if winter flares are becoming more frequent
  • A hot, very swollen joint with fever, or feeling systemically unwell, needs urgent clinical advice — a joint infection is an emergency and can look similar to a gout flare
  • Call 999 if you cannot get up after a fall, cannot weight-bear, or have severe unexplained illness
  • For urgent advice that is not an ambulance emergency, contact NHS 111 (NHS 24 on 111 in Scotland)

Frequently asked questions

Does cold weather cause gout?

Cold weather alone is not listed by the NHS as a cause. Dehydration, alcohol, large meals, illness with fever, joint injury and some medicines are the triggers to watch. Winter habits often change those factors.

How much should I drink if I have gout?

The NHS advises drinking plenty of fluids to avoid dehydration, and lots of water during an attack unless a GP says otherwise. Local NHS leaflets often suggest around 2 litres a day for people without a fluid restriction — follow your own team's advice if you have kidney or heart disease.

Should I stop allopurinol when I flare in winter?

Usually no. Urate-lowering medicine is meant to be taken regularly, including during flares, unless your clinician advises a change. Ask your GP, rheumatology team or pharmacist before stopping or skipping doses.

Sources and further reading

  • NHS: Gout

Everyone's situation is different, so always follow the advice of your own GP, pharmacist or rheumatology team. If you feel very unwell, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent advice, contact NHS 111.

article.title: GP frailty registers if you also live with arthritis (UK)
article.excerpt: When more than one joint hurts, the cost shows up as shorter walks, longer rests and a home that rearranges itself around the chair. This page explains.
article.content:
When more than one joint hurts, the cost shows up as shorter walks, longer rests and a home that rearranges itself around the chair. This page explains what being on a frailty register can mean in practice if you live with arthritis with frailty, without pretending rest is always safer. Use it alongside your GP, not instead of them.

Quick answer: When more than one joint hurts, the cost shows up as shorter walks, longer rests and a home that rearranges itself around the chair. This page explains what being on a frailty register can mean in practice if you live with arthritis with frailty, without pretending rest is always safer. Use it alongside your GP, not instead of them.

It might be the kettle, the bathroom, the car door or the clinic corridor — a GP surgery task that used to be automatic now asks more of several joints than they can give on a stiff morning. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with what being on a frailty register can mean in practice, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in England.

A frailty-aware plan for several joints

None of this is a gym challenge. The aim is to keep several joints moving, keep protein in the day, and keep what being on a frailty register can mean in practice from becoming the only story in the GP surgery. If a physiotherapist, occupational therapist or frailty team has already given you a plan, follow that ahead of a webpage.

  • If you live in a GP surgery, tell one other person the plan for a fall: who to call, where the spare key sits, whether you wear a pendant you can actually press.
  • Keep a sit-to-stand practice at the height you actually use. A higher chair is not cheating if it lets several joints work without a panic haul.
  • Carers: help the last 20 percent of a task, not the first 80, unless pain or safety says otherwise. Practice is treatment for frailty.
  • Write three daily anchors: a meal, a movement, a conversation. Frailty grows in unstructured days.
  • Set an indoor walking loop with places to pause. Pain in several joints prefer several short bouts to one heroic corridor.
  • Book eye, foot and hearing checks as frailty care, not vanity. Arthritis with frailty already asks a lot of balance.

Not 'just getting old': what being on a frailty register can mean in practice

NICE is clear that exercise is core care for osteoarthritis, not an optional extra after tablets. That still holds if you are becoming frailer, but the dose must respect today's several joints and today's energy. Rest has a place in a flare; rest as a lifestyle is how deconditioning joins the diagnosis.

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Pain in several joints can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual arthritis with frailty.

Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis. Only some also live with frailty. The practical question is not the label. It is whether what being on a frailty register can mean in practice is shrinking your GP surgery life — and what you can change this week without pretending pain is imaginary.

How what being on a frailty register can mean in practice shows up in real rooms

  • Night toilet trips, poor lighting and stiff several joints stacking into a falls risk that nobody named.
  • A flare of arthritis with frailty that lasts, then a slower baseline even when the flare eases.
  • A hospital or infection week that ends with clothes feeling looser and stairs feeling taller.
  • Shorter outdoor range, then shorter indoor range, then a GP surgery that has quietly rearranged itself around the chair.

England services, without inventing a clinic

What to put on the problem list besides several joints

GP, 111 or 999?

This is not personal medical advice. When several joints and frailty overlap, wait until Monday is sometimes right and sometimes dangerous. If you are unsure, NHS 111 can help you choose. Living With Arthritis cannot triage you.

Is a walking aid giving in if I have arthritis with frailty?

No. An aid that matches your several joints can protect joints, reduce fear and keep you walking far enough to keep muscle. A poorly fitted stick that hurts a wrist is the problem, not the concept. Ask physiotherapy or occupational therapy to look at height and grip.

Can frailty improve if I still have pain in several joints?

Sometimes the frailty part can shift even if arthritis with frailty remains. Strength, protein, reviewing dizzy medicines, treating a flare, and practising transfers can return reserve. Improvement is not guaranteed and it is rarely dramatic, but frailer this month is not always a one-way door. Work with clinicians rather than copying an online challenge.

Should I stop exercising during floor play, school gates and energy limits?

Complete rest for more than a short flare period usually makes several joints and muscle worse. Keep a smaller version: seated strength, indoor loops, or the two sit-to-stands you can still do. If exercise causes pain that spirals or a joint that will not settle, get clinical advice.

Sources and further reading

Use these organisations for the underlying clinical framing. They are not copied here. Living With Arthritis adds practical Wales context for arthritis and frailty.

  • NICE NG226 – Osteoarthritis in over 16s (NICE)

  • Age UK – Frailty (Age UK)
