article.title: Housing Support for Arthritis: Adaptations, Grants, Council Tax and Moving Home (UK)
article.excerpt: A practical directory of UK housing support if arthritis makes your home harder to live in: occupational therapy and care needs assessments, Disabled Facilities Grants (and Scotland's different system), VAT relief, the Council Tax Disabled Band Reduction Scheme, help with rent, the bedroom rules, council and housing association homes, sheltered and extra care housing.
article.content:
Quick answer: If arthritis is making your home hard to manage, start by asking your council (or health and social care trust in Northern Ireland) for a needs assessment, usually by an occupational therapist. They can recommend equipment and adaptations. Bigger changes may be funded by a Disabled Facilities Grant in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, or a mandatory grant under your council's Scheme of Assistance in Scotland.

Checked on 10 October 2026 against GOV.UK: Disabled Facilities Grants, GOV.UK: Council Tax discounts for disabled people and gov.scot: Funding adaptations to the home. Local rules vary, so always check with your council.

Stairs, a high bath, stiff taps, a step at the front door or a long walk to the bins: when you have arthritis, small features of your home can make a big difference to pain, safety and independence. The good news is that there is more help available than many people realise, from free assessments and equipment to grants for major adaptations and help with housing costs. This guide brings it together in one place, with the differences between England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

Step 1: Get a needs assessment

The best starting point is usually an assessment by an occupational therapist (OT) or trained assessor. They look at what you find hard at home and recommend equipment, adaptations or other support.

NationWho to contact
England and WalesYour local council's adult social services. GOV.UK says a needs assessment can lead to help such as home care, disability equipment and adaptations to your home.
ScotlandYour local council's social work team. mygov.scot says they will arrange a care needs assessment.
Northern IrelandYour local health and social care trust. Your GP can also refer you.

The assessment is free. Your GP, physiotherapist or rheumatology team can also refer you to an OT. Before the visit, write down the tasks you struggle with, and when: for example getting in and out of the bath, climbing stairs at the end of the day, or opening the front door during a flare.

Step 2: Small aids and simple changes

Many problems can be solved with equipment or small changes. After an assessment, councils can provide some equipment and minor adaptations; ask what your council offers and whether it charges. Common examples for arthritis include:

  • grab rails by the toilet, bath, shower and front door
  • a second stair rail
  • raised toilet seats, toilet frames and bath boards or seats
  • lever taps, which are easier than twist taps for painful hands
  • a perching stool for the kitchen
  • a key safe or a door entry system, so you do not have to rush to the door
  • chair and bed raisers

Our guide to sheltered housing covers other options if you want extra support close by.

Step 3: Grants for bigger adaptations

England, Wales and Northern Ireland: Disabled Facilities Grants

GOV.UK says you could get a Disabled Facilities Grant (DFG) from your council if you are disabled and need to change your home. Examples include widening doors, installing ramps or grab rails, a stairlift or level-access shower, improving access to your garden, a downstairs bedroom extension, or adapting heating or lighting controls.

NationMaximum grant (GOV.UK, checked 10 October 2026)
EnglandUp to £30,000
WalesUp to £36,000
Northern IrelandUp to £25,000
ScotlandDFGs are not available; see below

Key points from GOV.UK:

  • How much you get usually depends on household income and savings over £6,000. You may need to pay towards the cost.
  • Some councils may give more.
  • Owners and tenants can apply. You must intend to live in the property during the grant period, usually 5 years.
  • A DFG will not affect any benefits you get.
  • Do not start work before the council approves your application, or you might not get any grant.
  • You can apply again for the same property if your condition changes.
  • Foundations, a government-funded organisation, can help you find support to apply.

Our Disabled Facilities Grant guide walks through the application step by step.

Scotland: mandatory grants and the Scheme of Assistance

The Scottish Government's guide for homeowners says your council must give you a grant for changes it judges essential, called a mandatory grant. Everyone gets 80% of the cost covered, and people who get certain benefits get 100%. Some councils top up the 80% depending on income. Each council publishes a Scheme of Assistance setting out what it considers essential and other help it offers. Start with a care needs assessment from your council's social work team.

If you rent

Council and housing association tenants should contact their landlord first, as many landlords have their own adaptations process. Private tenants usually need their landlord's permission for adaptations. If permission is a problem, get advice; your rights under the Equality Act 2010 may help.

Making adaptations work for arthritis

Arthritis is different from many other conditions because symptoms often change from day to day and can get worse over time. When you discuss adaptations, it helps to think about:

  • Your worst days, not just your average day. Describe what happens during a flare, first thing in the morning and in the evening when you are tired.
  • Your hands as well as your legs. Lever handles, push-button controls, easy-grip window catches and a lightweight front door can matter as much as rails and ramps.
  • Future needs. If your arthritis is progressing, ask whether a level-access shower now could save a second set of works later.
  • Heating. Many people find cold makes stiffness worse. GOV.UK lists heating systems suitable for your needs as something a DFG can cover.
  • Safety. If you have had falls, mention them. Rails, better lighting, removing trip hazards and a personal alarm can all reduce risk.

Template: notes for your assessment

  • My condition: [type of arthritis, joints affected, how long I have had it]
  • A typical good day at home: [what I can do]
  • A bad day or flare: [what I cannot do, how often this happens]
  • Hardest rooms and tasks: [e.g. bathroom – cannot get out of bath; stairs – need two hands on the rail]
  • Falls or near misses in the last year: [when, where, what happened]
  • Who helps me now: [name, how often]
  • What I would like to be able to do again: [e.g. have a shower on my own, get into the garden]
  • Home details: [owner or tenant, landlord's name if renting, number of floors]

Step 4: Save money on housing costs

VAT relief on equipment and adaptations

GOV.UK says that if you are disabled or have a long-term illness, you will not be charged VAT on products designed or adapted for your own personal or domestic use, or on their installation, repairs and spare parts. Examples include stairlifts, adjustable beds and building work like ramps, widening doors or installing a lift or toilet. Your condition must qualify: GOV.UK says this includes a physical impairment that affects your ability to carry out everyday activities, or a condition treated as chronic sickness. You usually sign a declaration for the supplier.

Council Tax: Disabled Band Reduction Scheme

GOV.UK says you may qualify if you live in a larger property than you would need if you or another occupant were not disabled, for example because you need an extra bathroom, kitchen or other room, or extra space to use a wheelchair. If you qualify, your bill is reduced to the next lowest band, or by 17% if you are already in Band A. Apply to your council. Northern Ireland uses domestic rates instead of Council Tax, and has its own Disabled Persons Allowance.

Help with rent

  • Universal Credit can include help with housing costs, covering rent and some service charges. Most new claimants of working age claim this instead of Housing Benefit.
  • Housing Benefit still applies for some people, including many over State Pension age.
  • The bedroom rules: GOV.UK says Housing Benefit can be reduced if you live in social housing and have a spare bedroom (14% for one spare bedroom, 25% for two or more). But some people can have their own bedroom, including a couple who cannot share because of a disability or medical condition, and a non-resident overnight carer who sometimes has to stay overnight.
  • Discretionary Housing Payments from your council may help if your benefit does not cover your rent.

Our financial help directory covers other benefits, including PIP, which is not affected by your housing situation.

Step 5: If your home is no longer suitable

Council and housing association homes

GOV.UK says each council has its own rules and uses a points or banding system based on housing need. You are likely to be offered housing first if, for example, you have a medical condition made worse by your current home. Ask your council about its medical priority form, and include evidence from your GP, OT or rheumatology team about how your home affects your arthritis. Some properties are advertised as suitable for disabled people. In Northern Ireland, apply through the Housing Executive; in Scotland and Wales, ask your council.

Sheltered and extra care housing

Sheltered housing offers your own home with a scheme manager or alarm service, and extra care housing adds on-site care. See our guides to sheltered housing and extra care housing.

Buying or moving privately

If you are planning a move, think about how the home will suit you in 10 or 20 years: level access, a downstairs toilet, space for a walk-in shower, parking close to the door and nearby shops and transport. Our retirement planning guide has more on planning ahead.

A home check for arthritis

Walk through your home and tick anything that is difficult. Take this list to your assessment.

  • ☐ Getting in and out of the front door, including steps and the key
  • ☐ Climbing the stairs, especially at the end of the day
  • ☐ Getting on and off the toilet
  • ☐ Getting in and out of the bath or shower
  • ☐ Turning taps, door handles and window catches
  • ☐ Reaching high or low cupboards
  • ☐ Getting up from chairs or out of bed
  • ☐ Carrying shopping, laundry or bins
  • ☐ Keeping the home warm enough
  • ☐ Getting into the garden

Free, independent help

Citizens Advice, Shelter (England), Shelter Scotland, Shelter Cymru, Housing Advice NI, Turn2us, Scope, Disability Rights UK and Age UK offer free information and advice. Many areas also have a home improvement agency that helps older and disabled people arrange adaptations. We are not connected to any of these organisations.

When to get medical help

Speak to your GP if you are having falls, are struggling to look after yourself, or if pain and stiffness are getting worse. They can review your treatment and refer you for physiotherapy or occupational therapy. Get same-day advice from your GP or NHS 111 if a joint suddenly becomes hot, swollen and very painful, especially with fever. Call 999 if someone has fallen and is badly hurt or cannot get up.

Frequently asked questions

How much is a Disabled Facilities Grant?

On 10 October 2026, GOV.UK said up to £30,000 in England, £36,000 in Wales and £25,000 in Northern Ireland. How much you get usually depends on your income and savings. DFGs are not available in Scotland, which has its own grant system.

Can I get help with adaptations in Scotland?

Yes. Your council must give a mandatory grant for adaptations it judges essential, covering 80% of the cost, or 100% if you get certain benefits. Contact your council's social work team for an assessment.

Will a Disabled Facilities Grant affect my benefits?

No. GOV.UK says a DFG will not affect any benefits you get.

Can I start the work before my grant is approved?

Do not. GOV.UK warns you might not get any grant if you start work before the council approves your application.

Do I pay VAT on a stairlift?

Not if your condition qualifies and the stairlift is for your own personal or domestic use. GOV.UK lists stairlifts as an example.

Can I get a Council Tax reduction because of arthritis?

You may, through the Disabled Band Reduction Scheme, if you need extra space or an extra room because of disability. You may also qualify for income-based Council Tax Reduction from your council.

Can my medical condition help me get a council home?

It can. GOV.UK says councils are likely to offer housing first to people with a medical condition made worse by their current home. Each council has its own rules, so send medical evidence.

article.title: How Arthritis Is Diagnosed: Blood Tests, Scans and Results
article.excerpt: Wondering how doctors work out whether you have arthritis, and which type? A plain-English walk-through of the examination, common blood tests, scans and what your results can and cannot tell you.
article.content:
Quick answer: Arthritis is diagnosed by putting together your symptoms, an examination of your joints and, when needed, blood tests and scans. Osteoarthritis can often be diagnosed without any tests if you are over 45 with typical symptoms. Inflammatory types, such as rheumatoid arthritis, usually need blood tests like CRP, ESR, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP, plus a specialist assessment. No single test confirms most types of arthritis.

The first step: your story

The most useful part of diagnosing arthritis is often the conversation. Your GP, physiotherapist or first contact practitioner will want to know which joints hurt, when the pain started, what makes it better or worse, and how it affects your daily life. Some patterns point strongly towards one type of arthritis rather than another.

  • Stiffness that lasts more than about half an hour in the morning, with swollen, warm joints, suggests inflammation, as in rheumatoid arthritis or psoriatic arthritis.
  • Pain that gets worse with use and eases with rest, with short-lived stiffness, is more typical of osteoarthritis.
  • Sudden, very painful attacks in one joint, often the big toe, suggest gout.
  • Back pain and stiffness that improve with movement and wake you in the second half of the night may point to axial spondyloarthritis.

It helps to bring notes: when symptoms started, which joints are affected, photos of any swelling or rashes, family history of arthritis or psoriasis, and a list of your medicines. Our guide to early signs of rheumatoid arthritis may help you describe what you have noticed.

The examination

The clinician will look at and feel your joints, checking for swelling, warmth, tenderness, creaking, and how far each joint moves. They may look at your skin and nails for signs of psoriasis, check your spine, and ask you to walk, squat or grip. Swollen joints that feel soft or "boggy" are an important sign of inflammation and usually lead to an urgent referral to rheumatology.

Blood tests

Blood tests can support a diagnosis, rule out other causes and give a baseline before treatment. None of them is perfect. Some people with arthritis have normal results, and some people without arthritis have abnormal ones. The most common tests include:

  • CRP (C-reactive protein) and ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate): general markers of inflammation. They rise in inflammatory arthritis but also with infections and many other conditions. They are often normal in osteoarthritis.
  • Rheumatoid factor (RF): an antibody found in many, but not all, people with rheumatoid arthritis. It can also be positive in healthy people, particularly as they get older, and in some other conditions.
  • Anti-CCP antibodies: more specific for rheumatoid arthritis than rheumatoid factor. A positive result makes rheumatoid arthritis more likely.
  • ANA (antinuclear antibodies): used when lupus or a related condition is suspected. A positive ANA is common in healthy people, so it is interpreted alongside symptoms and other tests.
  • Urate (uric acid): helps in assessing gout, although levels can be normal during an attack.
  • HLA-B27: a genetic marker linked to axial spondyloarthritis. Many people with it never develop the condition.
  • Full blood count, kidney and liver function, thyroid tests and vitamin D: to check general health, look for other causes of symptoms, and provide a baseline before medicines are started.

If a test is "negative" it does not always rule arthritis out. For example, some people have seronegative rheumatoid arthritis, where RF and anti-CCP are both negative. That is why examination and specialist opinion matter so much.

Scans and imaging

  • X-rays show bones and the space between them, which narrows when cartilage thins in osteoarthritis. Early inflammatory arthritis may not show on X-ray at all. X-rays are also used as a baseline to track any joint damage over time.
  • Ultrasound can show inflammation in the joint lining and tendons, even when it is hard to feel. Many rheumatology departments use it in clinic.
  • MRI gives detailed pictures of bone, cartilage and soft tissues. It is especially useful for the spine and sacroiliac joints when axial spondyloarthritis is suspected.
  • CT and DEXA scans are used in specific situations, such as looking at complex joints or measuring bone density for osteoporosis.

NICE guidance advises that osteoarthritis can usually be diagnosed clinically, without imaging, in people aged 45 or over with activity-related joint pain and short-lived morning stiffness. Scans are kept for when symptoms are unusual or when the result would change what happens next.

Joint fluid tests

If a joint is swollen, a doctor may draw off some fluid with a needle. Looking at the fluid under a microscope can show crystals, which confirm gout or pseudogout, and testing it can show whether there is infection. A hot, swollen, very painful joint with fever needs same-day assessment, as it could be septic arthritis.

Seeing a rheumatologist

If your GP suspects inflammatory arthritis, NICE recommends urgent referral to a specialist rheumatology service, because early treatment improves long-term outcomes. The GP should not wait for blood test results before referring if you have persistent swollen joints. At the rheumatology clinic you will have a fuller assessment and may have further tests or an ultrasound on the day.

If you are waiting for an appointment and your symptoms get much worse, contact your GP or the rheumatology department. Our newly diagnosed guide covers what to expect next.

Understanding your results

  • You can usually see your blood test results in the NHS App or ask your GP practice for a copy.
  • Reference ranges vary between laboratories. A result just outside the range may not mean anything significant.
  • Results are always interpreted alongside your symptoms and examination. Ask your clinician what each result means for you.
  • If you are told your tests are normal but you still have symptoms, it is reasonable to ask what else could explain them and what the plan is.

Getting a clear diagnosis can take time

Some conditions develop gradually, and the picture becomes clearer over months. You may be told you have "undifferentiated" or "early" inflammatory arthritis at first. This can feel frustrating, but it does not mean nothing can be done. Treatment for symptoms can often start while the diagnosis is confirmed. Keep a symptom diary and keep in touch with your team.

Frequently asked questions

Can a blood test show arthritis?

Blood tests can support a diagnosis of some types of arthritis, such as rheumatoid arthritis, but no single test confirms or rules out most types. Results are combined with your symptoms and an examination.

Do I need an X-ray to diagnose osteoarthritis?

Often not. If you are 45 or over with typical symptoms, osteoarthritis can usually be diagnosed from your history and an examination.

What does a raised CRP mean?

CRP rises with inflammation, which can be caused by inflammatory arthritis, infection or many other conditions. Your clinician will interpret it alongside your symptoms.

Can you have rheumatoid arthritis with a negative rheumatoid factor?

Yes. Some people have seronegative rheumatoid arthritis. Anti-CCP, examination and scans help in diagnosis.

How long does it take to see a rheumatologist?

It varies by area. NICE recommends urgent referral for suspected persistent inflammatory arthritis. If symptoms worsen while you wait, contact your GP or the rheumatology department.

Should I ask for a copy of my test results?

Yes, it can help you understand your condition. Many results are available in the NHS App.

article.title: How NHS Referrals Work for Arthritis: From GP to Specialist
article.excerpt: A step-by-step UK guide to NHS referrals for arthritis: who can refer you, when referrals should be urgent, how booking and triage work, your right to choose in England, and how Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland differ.
article.content:
Quick answer: Your GP or another clinician refers you to the service you need, such as rheumatology, orthopaedics or community MSK physiotherapy. In England most referrals go through the NHS e-Referral Service, you can usually choose your hospital, and your 18-week clock starts when the referral is received. Suspected inflammatory arthritis should be referred urgently, even if blood tests are normal.

Checked on 10 October 2026 against the NHS Choice Framework, the NHS guide to waiting times in England, NHS England information on Advice and Guidance, NHS Digital's e-Referral Service, NHS inform, GOV.WALES, Northern Ireland Department of Health statistics and NICE guidelines.

A referral is how one part of the NHS asks another to see you. For arthritis, that might be your GP referring you to rheumatology, a physiotherapist referring you to orthopaedics, or you referring yourself to community physiotherapy. Understanding how referrals work helps you check yours is on track, make choices, and know what to do if it seems to have stalled.

Who can refer you

  • Your GP, the most common route to hospital specialists such as rheumatology and orthopaedics.
  • Other primary care professionals, such as first contact physiotherapists in GP surgeries, advanced nurse practitioners and pharmacists, depending on local arrangements.
  • Community musculoskeletal (MSK) services, which may refer you on to hospital specialists.
  • Hospital specialists, who may refer you to another specialty or to therapy services.
  • Yourself. The NHS says that in many areas you can refer yourself to NHS community MSK physiotherapy without seeing a GP. Self-referral to NHS Talking Therapies is also available in England.

How a typical referral works in England

  1. Assessment. Your GP or another clinician assesses you and decides whether you need a referral, and how urgently.
  2. Advice before referral (sometimes). NHS England explains that GPs can use Advice and Guidance to ask a specialist for advice before, or instead of, referring you. This might lead to a test, a change in treatment, or advice about which service is most appropriate.
  3. Choice. For a first outpatient appointment with a consultant-led service, you usually have the legal right to choose the provider and the consultant-led team. Tell your clinician your preferences, as they choose the shortlist.
  4. The referral is sent. Most referrals in England go through the NHS e-Referral Service (e-RS), a digital platform used to refer patients and book appointments or send referrals for triage.
  5. Booking or triage. You may book the appointment yourself using the details in your appointment request letter, or the service may triage your referral first and contact you.
  6. The clock starts. The NHS says your waiting time starts when the hospital or service receives your referral letter, or when you book your first appointment through e-RS.
  7. First appointment. You are seen, assessed and may have tests. Your waiting-time clock keeps running while tests are done, until treatment starts or a decision is made that treatment is not needed.

Urgent and routine referrals

Referrals are prioritised by clinical need. For arthritis, the most important urgent route is for suspected inflammatory arthritis:

  • Rheumatoid arthritis and similar conditions. NICE recommends referring any adult with suspected persistent synovitis (joint inflammation) of undetermined cause for a specialist opinion, and referring urgently if the small joints of the hands or feet are affected, more than one joint is affected, or there has been a delay of 3 months or longer since symptoms started. This applies even if blood tests are normal. NICE's quality standard says this referral should happen within 3 working days of seeing a primary care clinician.
  • Suspected new inflammatory arthritis and spondyloarthritis. NICE recommends urgent referral to rheumatology for suspected new-onset inflammatory arthritis, and sets out criteria for referring people with long-term back pain that started before age 45 for a spondyloarthritis assessment.
  • Suspected temporal (giant cell) arteritis, with severe headaches, tenderness at the temples or scalp, jaw pain when eating or vision problems. The NHS says this needs urgent treatment because it can lead to stroke or blindness.
  • Osteoarthritis and most mechanical joint pain are usually routine referrals, often to community MSK services first.

If you think your referral should be urgent, say why: for example, "my finger joints are swollen and I have been stiff for over an hour every morning for six weeks."

Community MSK and triage services

In many areas, referrals for joint, back and muscle problems go first to a community MSK service, sometimes called an interface or triage service. These are often staffed by advanced practice physiotherapists, GPs with a special interest and other specialists. NICE's back pain guideline refers to musculoskeletal interface clinics as a specialist setting.

These services may:

  • assess and treat you directly, for example with physiotherapy, exercise programmes or injections
  • arrange tests such as X-rays, MRI or blood tests
  • refer you on to orthopaedics, rheumatology or a pain service if needed

Being seen in a community service is not a sign that your problem is not being taken seriously. It often means faster access to the right treatment. Ask how and when you would be referred on if needed.

Your right to choose (England)

The NHS Choice Framework explains that when you are referred for a first outpatient appointment with a consultant-led service, you can usually choose:

  • which provider you go to, including many independent hospitals that hold NHS contracts
  • which consultant-led team you see

These choices apply at the point of referral, and normally the same provider goes on to provide the rest of your treatment. They do not apply in some situations, such as if you need urgent or emergency care, are in prison or are a serving member of the armed forces.

If you are likely to wait more than 18 weeks for non-urgent consultant-led treatment, you can ask to change provider. Contact the service treating you or your integrated care board (ICB). If you were not offered a choice, speak to the person who referred you first, then your ICB.

How to check your referral is on track

  • Ask at the time: Which service am I being referred to? Is it urgent or routine? When will it be sent? How will I hear?
  • Look out for a letter, text or email with booking details or confirmation that your referral has been received.
  • If you have an appointment request letter, use the details to book or check your appointment online or by phone.
  • If you hear nothing after a few weeks, contact your GP surgery to confirm the referral was sent, then contact the hospital or service's booking team.
  • Keep a note of the date of referral, the service and any reference numbers.

If your referral is returned or redirected

Sometimes a specialist service returns a referral with advice, or redirects it to a different service, such as community MSK or physiotherapy, because they think that is the most appropriate place to be seen. If this happens:

  • ask your GP what the specialist advised and why
  • check whether you have been referred somewhere else instead
  • if your symptoms are getting worse or have changed, ask your GP to send an updated referral with the new information

What goes in a referral letter

A good referral gives the specialist enough information to prioritise you correctly. It usually includes:

  • your symptoms, how long you have had them and how they are changing
  • examination findings, such as which joints are swollen
  • relevant test results, such as blood tests or X-rays
  • your other health conditions and medicines
  • what has already been tried, and whether it helped
  • how the problem affects your daily life and work
  • the question the referrer wants answered, for example "Is this inflammatory arthritis?" or "Would this patient benefit from joint replacement?"

Specialist teams often triage referrals on paper. If something important is missing, such as swollen joints or a rapidly worsening problem, your referral may be given a lower priority than it needs.

If you move house or change GP while waiting

Tell both your old and new GP surgery, and the hospital, as soon as you know your new address. If you can still travel to the same hospital, ask whether you can stay on its list. If not, ask whether your referral can be transferred to a hospital near your new home and how your waiting time will be treated. If you move between the UK nations, different waiting time rules apply, and you may need a new referral to services in your new area. Keep a record of your original referral date in case you need it.

How referrals differ across the UK

NationKey points
EnglandMost referrals via the NHS e-Referral Service. Legal right to choose provider for first consultant-led outpatient appointment, and right to start treatment within 18 weeks, with exceptions.
ScotlandReferral to your NHS health board's services. Standards of 12 weeks for a new outpatient appointment from receipt of referral and 18 weeks from referral to treatment, plus the legal 12-week Treatment Time Guarantee for planned inpatient and day-case treatment once agreed. No equivalent of England's legal right to choose any provider.
WalesReferral to your local health board. The Welsh Government's referral-to-treatment target is 26 weeks from receipt of referral for 95% of patients, with a maximum of 36 weeks, although these targets are not currently being met.
Northern IrelandReferral to your Health and Social Care (HSC) Trust. Some referrals go first to integrated clinical assessment and treatment services (ICATS). Referrals are prioritised as red flag, urgent or routine, and average waits are published on My Waiting Times NI.

See our waiting list guide for more on each nation's rules, and NHS arthritis pathways simplified for where a referral fits in the bigger picture.

Tips to make your referral as strong as possible

  • Describe the impact. Tell your GP what you cannot do, not just where it hurts. The referral letter should reflect how arthritis affects your work, sleep and daily life.
  • Bring a symptom record. Note which joints swell, how long morning stiffness lasts and what you have tried.
  • Mention related conditions, such as psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease or eye inflammation, which make inflammatory arthritis more likely.
  • Ask for a copy of the referral letter if you would like one, so you can check it is accurate.
  • Prepare for the appointment. See what happens at a rheumatology appointment.

Private referrals

If you choose to pay privately, you may need a referral letter from your GP or another clinician, depending on the provider. If you later want NHS treatment, your private consultant can write to your GP, who can refer you into the NHS. You may then be placed on the NHS waiting list according to clinical need. Read our guide to private treatment costs first.

When to get medical help

Do not wait for a referral to come through if you have:

  • a hot, swollen, very painful joint, especially with fever. Get an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111
  • severe headaches, tenderness at your temples or scalp, jaw pain when eating, or vision problems. The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111, as this could be temporal arteritis
  • back pain with numbness around the bottom or genitals, or new problems controlling your bladder or bowels. Go to A&E or call 999
  • rapidly worsening symptoms, such as more joints swelling week by week. Contact your GP, who can update or upgrade the referral

Frequently asked questions

How long does it take for a GP referral to be received?

It varies. Many referrals are sent electronically. If you have not heard anything within a few weeks, check with your GP surgery that it was sent, then contact the hospital booking team.

When does my 18-week wait start?

In England, from when the hospital or service receives your referral, or when you book your first appointment through the NHS e-Referral Service.

Can I choose which hospital I am referred to?

In England, usually yes, for a first outpatient appointment with a consultant-led service. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland do not have the same legal right to choose.

Can I refer myself to a rheumatologist?

Not usually on the NHS. You can refer yourself to community MSK physiotherapy in many areas, but rheumatology referrals normally come from a GP or another clinician.

What is Advice and Guidance?

It is a way for your GP to ask a specialist for advice before or instead of referring you. It can lead to faster changes in treatment or a referral to the most suitable service.

My referral was sent back. What does that mean?

The specialist may have given advice to your GP, or redirected you to another service such as community MSK. Ask your GP what was advised and what happens next.

article.direct_answer: Your GP or another clinician refers you to the service you need, such as rheumatology, orthopaedics or community MSK physiotherapy. In England most referrals go through the NHS e-Referral Service, you can usually choose your hospital, and your 18-week clock starts when the referral is received. Suspected inflammatory arthritis should be referred urgently, even if blood tests are normal.

faqs.q: How long does it take for a GP referral to be received?
faqs.a: It varies. Many referrals are sent electronically. If you have not heard anything within a few weeks, check with your GP surgery that it was sent, then contact the hospital booking team.

faqs.q: When does my 18-week wait start?
faqs.a: In England, from when the hospital or service receives your referral, or when you book your first appointment through the NHS e-Referral Service.

faqs.q: Can I choose which hospital I am referred to?
faqs.a: In England, usually yes, for a first outpatient appointment with a consultant-led service. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland do not have the same legal right to choose.

faqs.q: Can I refer myself to a rheumatologist?
faqs.a: Not usually on the NHS. You can refer yourself to community MSK physiotherapy in many areas, but rheumatology referrals normally come from a GP or another clinician.

faqs.q: What is Advice and Guidance?
faqs.a: It is a way for your GP to ask a specialist for advice before or instead of referring you. It can lead to faster changes in treatment or a referral to the most suitable service.

faqs.q: My referral was sent back. What does that mean?
faqs.a: The specialist may have given advice to your GP, or redirected you to another service such as community MSK. Ask your GP what was advised and what happens next.

article.title: How to Choose the Right Exercise for Your Arthritis: A Practical Finder (UK)
article.excerpt: A practical exercise finder for people with arthritis that works without any app: answer five simple questions, then use decision tables by joint, ability level and goal to choose safe starting exercises, with links to detailed guides, stop rules and when to get help.
article.content:
Quick answer: The right exercise for arthritis is one you can do safely, enjoy and keep up. Most people need a mix of strengthening for the muscles around painful joints, gentle aerobic activity such as walking, cycling or swimming, and movement or balance work. Choose by your most affected joint, current ability and goal, start small and build up.

"What exercise should I do?" is one of the most common questions people with arthritis ask. There is no single best exercise. The right choice depends on which joints are affected, how active you are now, what you want to be able to do, and what you enjoy. This page works like a simple exercise finder: answer five questions, then use the decision tables to pick a safe starting point. There is no app or login; everything you need is on this page, and you can print it. If you already know which joint and activity you want to work on, you can skip straight to the joint-specific guides linked at the end.

This is general guidance. If you have a physiotherapist, their advice comes first. If you have not exercised for a long time, have heart or lung problems, or have had recent surgery, check with your GP or physiotherapist before starting.

What the guidance recommends

NICE guideline NG226 recommends therapeutic exercise for everyone with osteoarthritis, tailored to the person and including local muscle strengthening and general aerobic fitness. NICE guideline NG100 says adults with rheumatoid arthritis should have access to specialist physiotherapy to improve fitness, encourage regular exercise and learn exercises for joint flexibility and muscle strength.

The UK Chief Medical Officers' guidelines, summarised by the NHS, advise adults to:

  • be active every day, building up to at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week (or 75 minutes of vigorous activity)
  • do strengthening activities on at least 2 days a week
  • for older adults, include activities that improve balance and flexibility on at least 2 days a week
  • reduce long periods of sitting

These are targets to work towards, not a starting point. Any amount of activity is better than none.

Step 1: answer five questions

Write down your answers. They point you to the right rows in the tables below.

  1. Which joint bothers you most? Knee, hip, back, hands and wrists, shoulder, foot and ankle, or several joints.
  2. How much can you do now?
    • Level A: walking is limited to a few minutes, getting up from a chair is hard, or you mainly sit.
    • Level B: you can walk for 10 to 20 minutes and manage stairs, with some pain.
    • Level C: you are fairly active and want to do more, or return to sport or the gym.
  3. What is your main goal? Less pain and stiffness, easier daily tasks, steadier balance, weight loss, more energy, or keeping up a hobby.
  4. Is your arthritis settled or flaring? A flare means joints are hotter, more swollen or more painful than usual for several days.
  5. What do you enjoy, and what is realistic? At home or out, alone or with others, in water or on land, cost and travel.

Step 2: choose by joint

Most affected jointStrength focusGood aerobic choicesGo easy on
KneeThigh (quadriceps), hip and calf: sit-to-stands, straight-leg raises, step-upsWalking, cycling, swimming, water exerciseDeep squats and kneeling, if painful; very hilly walks at first
HipButtock and thigh: bridges, side leg lifts, sit-to-standsWalking, cycling, water exercisePositions advised against after hip replacement; long uphill walks at first
BackCore and buttock: bridges, gentle back extensions, sit-to-standsWalking, swimming, cyclingHeavy lifting with a rounded back, sudden twisting
Hands and wristsGrip and thumb: gentle squeezes, thumb lifts, finger spreadsWalking, cycling (padded grips), water exerciseTight pinching, weight through bent wrists
ShoulderRotator cuff and shoulder blade: band rotations, rows, isometric holdsWalking, cycling, gentle swimmingHeavy overhead lifting, behind-the-neck movements
Foot and ankleCalf and foot: heel raises, towel scrunches, band ankle workCycling, swimming, water exercise, walking in supportive shoesRunning and jumping on hard ground at first
Several jointsWhole-body circuits with light loads, seated if neededWater exercise, walking, tai chi, chair-based classesActivities that load one painful joint repeatedly

Our detailed guides cover each joint: knee, hip, hands, shoulder and foot and ankle, all linked at the end of this page and in the exercise hub.

Step 3: choose by ability level

LevelStart withTypical first weekNext step
A: limitedChair-based exercises, sit-to-stands with hands, seated marching, gentle range-of-movement exercises5–10 minutes, once or twice a dayShort walks indoors, then outdoors; standing exercises holding a worktop
B: moderateHome strength routine for your main joint, plus walking, cycling or swimmingStrength 2–3 days; aerobic 10–20 minutes on other daysMore repetitions, longer walks, a class
C: activeGym or band-based strength training, longer aerobic sessions, balance challengesStrength 2–3 days; aerobic 150 minutes over the weekHeavier resistance, new activities, sport

Step 4: choose by goal

Your goalBest types of exerciseExample
Less pain and stiffnessStrengthening plus daily gentle movementYour joint's home routine 3 times a week and a short daily mobility routine
Easier daily tasksPractise the task itself, built up graduallySit-to-stands for chairs, step-ups for stairs, grip work for jars
Steadier balance, fewer fallsBalance and leg strength, tai chiHeel-to-toe standing, single-leg balance holding on, a tai chi class
Weight lossLow-impact aerobic activity plus strength, alongside diet changesDaily brisk walks or cycling, strength twice a week
More energyRegular gentle aerobic activity, pacedShort walks most days, gradually longer
Confidence and companyGroup classesWater exercise, tai chi, walking groups, chair-based classes

Step 5: settled or flaring?

SituationWhat to do
SettledFollow your chosen plan and build up gradually
Mild flareKeep moving with smaller, gentler versions; reduce strength work on the flaring joint
Bad flare (hot, swollen joints)Gentle range-of-movement only for the affected joints; keep other parts of the body moving; restart gradually
Joint suddenly hot and red with feverDo not exercise it; get urgent medical advice (see below)

Popular activities compared

ActivityJoint loadStrengthFitnessBalanceNotes
WalkingModerateSomeGoodSomeFree, flexible; supportive shoes help
Cycling (incl. static bike)LowSomeGoodLowGood for knees; raise the seat if bending hurts
Swimming and water exerciseVery lowSomeGoodSomeWarm pools are comfortable; see our water exercise guide
Strength trainingAdjustableVery goodSomeSomeBands, body weight or gym machines
Tai chiLowSomeSomeVery goodSlow and gentle; seated versions available
Yoga and PilatesLow to moderateSomeLowGoodChoose beginner or gentle classes; tell the teacher about your arthritis
RunningHighSomeVery goodSomePossible for some people with arthritis; build up slowly

Two worked examples

Imagine someone with knee osteoarthritis who can walk for about 15 minutes (level B), wants to manage the stairs at home more easily, and enjoys being outdoors. Using the tables: the knee row suggests sit-to-stands, straight-leg raises and step-ups for strength, with walking or cycling for fitness. The goal table suggests practising step-ups as the "task" exercise. A realistic first fortnight could be the knee home routine on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, a 15-minute walk on the other days, and step-ups on the bottom stair with a banister, building from 5 to 10 each leg. After two weeks, they would review how the knee settles and add a few minutes to each walk.

Now imagine someone with rheumatoid arthritis affecting the hands, wrists and feet, who tires easily and mostly sits (level A), and whose goal is more energy and confidence. The "several joints" row points to whole-body, low-load options such as water exercise, chair-based classes and tai chi. The ability table suggests starting with 5 to 10 minutes of seated exercises once or twice a day. A realistic start might be a short seated routine each morning, gentle hand exercises after a warm wash, and a weekly warm-water class. On flare days they would keep to gentle range-of-movement only, then build back up. Their rheumatology team could also refer them to specialist physiotherapy.

Fill in your own plan

Use your answers and the tables to fill in this simple plan. Print it or copy it into a notebook.

Part of my planMy choiceHow oftenHow long
Strength exercises (for my main joint) 2–3 days a week 
Aerobic activity Most days 
Movement or balance Daily or 2+ days a week 
My "task" exercise   
What I will do on a flare day   
Date I will review my plan Usually after 2 to 4 weeks

Common barriers and practical fixes

BarrierTry this
"It hurts when I start"Warm up for a few minutes, use warmth beforehand, and start with smaller movements. Many people find pain eases once they get going.
"I am too tired"Do a shorter version at your best time of day. Gentle activity often improves energy over a few weeks.
"I have no time"Split activity into 10-minute chunks, or link exercises to daily routines, such as sit-to-stands during adverts.
"I worry about damaging my joints"Exercise built up gradually is safe for arthritis and is recommended by NICE. Use the pain guide to stay within your limits.
"Classes and gyms cost too much"Walking and home routines are free. Many councils offer reduced-price leisure memberships, and some areas have free or low-cost community classes.
"I lose motivation"Exercise with a friend, join a group, keep a simple tick chart, and set a small goal linked to something you want to do.

Finding support in the UK

In many areas you can refer yourself to NHS physiotherapy for a personalised programme. Ask your GP practice about exercise referral schemes, which offer supervised sessions at local leisure centres, and about group programmes for knee and hip pain such as ESCAPE-pain. Local councils, leisure centres and charities often run walking groups, water exercise, tai chi and chair-based classes for people with long-term conditions.

Five rules that apply to every exercise

  1. Start low, go slow. Begin with less than you think you can do and build up over weeks.
  2. Use a pain guide. Mild discomfort that settles within about 2 hours, or by the next day, is acceptable. If it does not, do less next time.
  3. Mix it up. Combine strength, aerobic and movement or balance work across the week.
  4. Be consistent. Most benefits take 6 to 12 weeks of regular exercise to show.
  5. Make it enjoyable. The best exercise is the one you will keep doing.

When to get medical help

Stop exercising and seek advice if you get sharp pain, a joint that locks or gives way, or new swelling.

  • Call 999 for chest pain, severe breathlessness, or feeling faint or dizzy during exercise that does not settle with rest.
  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with a high temperature or feeling unwell.
  • See your GP or a physiotherapist if you are not sure where to start, have several conditions, keep having flares when you exercise, or are not improving after 6 to 12 weeks. In many areas you can refer yourself to NHS physiotherapy.

What is the best exercise for arthritis?

There is no single best exercise. Most people benefit from a combination of strengthening the muscles around affected joints, low-impact aerobic activity such as walking, cycling or swimming, and gentle movement or balance work. Choose activities that suit your joints and that you enjoy.

Which exercises should I avoid with arthritis?

Avoid anything that causes sharp pain or makes a joint swell, and be cautious with high-impact or heavy activities on a painful joint at first. Very few exercises are off-limits for everyone; it depends on your joints and fitness. After joint replacement, follow your surgical team's advice.

Is walking or swimming better for arthritis?

Both are good. Walking is free, easy to fit into the day and helps bone health. Swimming and water exercise put much less load on the joints, which can help if walking is painful or you have arthritis in several joints. Many people do both.

How much exercise should I do with arthritis?

Work towards the UK guidelines of 150 minutes of moderate activity a week plus strengthening on 2 days, but start with what you can manage, even 5 to 10 minutes, and build up gradually.

Can I exercise with rheumatoid arthritis?

Yes. Regular exercise is recommended for rheumatoid arthritis. When your arthritis is flaring, keep to gentle movement; when it is settled, build up strength and fitness. Ask your rheumatology team about specialist physiotherapy.

Do I need to see a physio before I start?

Not usually for gentle exercise if your arthritis is stable. See a GP or physiotherapist first if you have had recent surgery, a recent fall or injury, heart or lung problems, or you are unsure what is safe.

article.title: How to Sleep Better with Arthritis – A UK Guide
article.excerpt: UK guide to sleeping with arthritis: settle pain before bed, pillows by joint, daytime habits, waking at 3am, and when to see your GP.
article.content:
Quick answer: To sleep better with arthritis, ease pain and stiffness before bed (a warm shower or wheat bag for stiffness, a cool pack earlier if a joint is hot), support painful joints with pillows, keep regular bed and wake times, and keep gentle movement in the day. Ask your GP about medicine timing, and get checked if you snore loudly, gasp at night or your mood is dropping.

Broken nights are one of the most common things people with arthritis tell us about. Pain wakes you, stiffness makes turning over hard, and a bad night makes the next day's pain and tiredness feel louder. The good news is that small, steady changes usually help more than buying one expensive gadget. This UK guide covers what to try tonight and when to ask for help.

Why arthritis can disturb sleep

  • Night pain — joints ache when you are still, and inflammatory arthritis can be worse overnight and early morning
  • Stiffness — turning over or getting up for the toilet can be painful
  • Position — lying on a painful hip, shoulder or knee
  • Medicines — for example steroids taken late in the day can keep some people awake; never change a prescription without advice
  • Worry and low mood — common with long-term pain, and they feed poor sleep (see our arthritis and mental health guide)

Tonight: settle pain before bed

  1. Warmth for stiffness — a warm shower, bath or wheat bag 20–30 minutes before bed. Do not sleep on an electric heat pad.
  2. Cool for a hot, swollen joint — a wrapped cold pack for 10–15 minutes earlier in the evening.
  3. Gentle range-of-motion — a few slow movements for stiff joints from the exercise hub, not a hard workout.
  4. Medicine timing — ask your GP or pharmacist whether the timing of your usual pain relief suits your nights. Our pain relief guide explains the options.

Positions and pillows by joint

  • Knee — a pillow between the knees on your side, or a thin pillow under the knees on your back
  • Hip — lie on the less painful side with a pillow between the knees; a mattress topper can ease pressure
  • Back — on your back with a pillow under the knees, or on your side with knees slightly bent
  • Shoulder — avoid lying on the sore side; hug a pillow to rest the arm
  • Hands — ask your physiotherapist or OT whether a resting splint would help

There is no single "best arthritis mattress". Most people do well with something supportive that does not sag; try a topper before replacing a whole bed.

Daytime habits that change your nights

  • Get up at the same time each day, even after a poor night
  • Keep gentle movement in the day — short walks or seated routines often help sleep more than long naps
  • Pace activity so you are not exhausted and wired at bedtime — see pacing and energy management
  • Cut caffeine after early afternoon and keep alcohol low; it can wake you later in the night
  • Keep the bedroom dark, quiet and comfortably cool

If tiredness hangs on even after better nights, read our arthritis fatigue guide, because fatigue often needs more than sleep alone.

Waking in pain at 3am

Keep a glass of water and anything you need within reach. Change position slowly, do a few ankle and knee bends under the covers, and use a calm breathing routine rather than checking your phone. If you are awake for a long stretch, get up, sit somewhere dim and return when sleepy. If night pain is new, severe, or comes with a hot swollen joint, follow the flare-up guide or our flare action plan.

When to see your GP

  • Poor sleep most nights for more than a few weeks despite these steps — ask about CBT for insomnia (CBT-I), which the NHS recommends ahead of sleeping tablets
  • Loud snoring, gasping or stopping breathing at night (possible sleep apnoea)
  • New or rapidly worsening night pain, night sweats, fever or weight loss
  • Low mood, worry or hopelessness alongside poor sleep
  • You think a medicine is affecting your sleep

Newly diagnosed and still working out a routine? Start with our newly diagnosed guide. If daily living is heavily limited by pain and poor sleep, the Benefits & PIP hub explains what support may be available.

Frequently asked questions

Are sleeping tablets a good idea?

The NHS generally suggests trying sleep habits and CBT-I first. Sleeping tablets are usually short-term only and can raise the risk of falls in older people. Talk to your GP before starting any.

Should I nap?

A short rest of 20–30 minutes in the early afternoon is fine for many people. Long or late naps tend to make nights worse.

Why is my arthritis worse in the morning?

Joints often stiffen when still. Morning stiffness lasting more than about 30 minutes, with swelling, can be a sign of inflammatory arthritis and is worth raising with your GP.

article.title: Hydration, gout and frailty in older adults (UK)
article.excerpt: When gout meets frailty, everyday tasks in a home can shrink faster than the joints alone would suggest. Here we focus on drinks that support joints without f.
article.content:
When gout meets frailty, everyday tasks in a home can shrink faster than the joints alone would suggest. Here we focus on drinks that support joints without flooding the night, for readers in Scotland, with self-management ideas and when to contact a GP, NHS 24 on 111 or 999.

Quick answer: When gout meets frailty, everyday tasks in a home can shrink faster than the joints alone would suggest. Here we focus on drinks that support joints without flooding the night, for readers in Scotland, with self-management ideas and when to contact a GP, NHS 24 on 111 or 999.

A flare in feet can look like sudden frailty. True frailty is a wider loss of reserve: weaker recovery after a quiet week, an infection or a hospital night. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with drinks that support joints without flooding the night, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in Scotland.

Food, fluid and muscle when gout shrinks cooking

Frailty loves skipped meals. Gout makes that easy: sore feet turn a sandwich into a logistics problem. Ready-to-eat protein — yoghurt, cheese, eggs, tinned fish, beans, leftover chicken — is a strategy, not a failure.

A Mediterranean-style pattern (vegetables, fruit, pulses, olive oil, fish when you can) is a familiar UK nutrition message. Keep the spirit, shrink the labour. Frozen vegetables and tinned tomatoes count.

NHS advice is that adults should consider a daily 10 microgram vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter. That is not a cure for gout. Mention it to a pharmacist if you already take other tablets or have kidney problems.

If appetite is falling, drinks can carry nourishment, but night-time fluid can also create toilet rushes on stiff feet. Front-load drinks earlier in the day and keep a well-lit, unhurried route to the loo.

The overlap: painful feet and a frailer body

NICE is clear that exercise is core care for osteoarthritis, not an optional extra after tablets. That still holds if you are becoming frailer, but the dose must respect today's feet and today's energy. Rest has a place in a flare; rest as a lifestyle is how deconditioning joins the diagnosis.

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Painful feet can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual gout.

Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis. Only some also live with frailty. The practical question is not the label. It is whether drinks that support joints without flooding the night is shrinking your home life — and what you can change this week without pretending pain is imaginary.

Things you can try this week in a home

  • Keep a sit-to-stand practice at the height you actually use. A higher chair is not cheating if it lets feet work without a panic haul.
  • After a flare, restart the smallest version of your usual movement within comfort, rather than waiting to feel back to normal. Normal rarely sends an email.
  • Book eye, foot and hearing checks as frailty care, not vanity. Gout already asks a lot of balance.
  • Plan the scariest transfer of the day — often the bathroom — with lighting, a rail conversation and unhurried time. Rushing with stiff feet is how near-misses happen.
  • Ask a pharmacist to look at the whole list if dizziness, constipation or night sedation have arrived with the pain tablets. Do not add a new painkiller just in case.
  • Set an indoor walking loop with places to pause. Painful feet prefer several short bouts to one heroic corridor.

What this can look like in a home

  • Carers doing the last steps of a task to be kind, which removes the last practice the muscles were getting.
  • Transfers that used to be boring — bed, chair, toilet, car — now need a pause, a push-up or a second person, especially when feet are cold.
  • A flare of gout that lasts, then a slower baseline even when the flare eases.
  • A hospital or infection week that ends with clothes feeling looser and stairs feeling taller.
  • Shorter outdoor range, then shorter indoor range, then a home that has quietly rearranged itself around the chair.

When to get help

  • A knock to the head, especially if you take blood thinners — do not sleep it off as a plan.
  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.
  • A hot, very swollen joint with fever, or feeling systemically unwell — seek urgent clinical advice. A joint infection is an emergency.
  • Sudden confusion, new incontinence, or a crash in mobility over hours to days — think infection or delirium, not only arthritis.
  • If you cannot get to the surgery because of gout, ask about a home visit or a proper phone review. Silence is not a care plan.

Help in Scotland if gout and frailty overlap

Should I stop exercising during drinks that support joints without flooding the night?

Complete rest for more than a short flare period usually makes feet and muscle worse. Keep a smaller version: seated strength, indoor loops, or the two sit-to-stands you can still do. If exercise causes pain that spirals or a joint that will not settle, get clinical advice.

Are painkillers the main treatment for frail gout?

No. For osteoarthritis, NICE puts exercise, weight management where relevant, and topical options at the centre. Tablets may help some people some of the time, but in frail adults they need a hard look at stomach, kidneys, heart, constipation and falls. Never share someone else's medicines.

Will I get PIP or Attendance Allowance because I have gout and frailty?

Nobody honest can promise that. These are legal tests about how your difficulties affect daily living or personal care, not about a diagnosis name. Keep a diary of drinks that support joints without flooding the night on typical and bad days. Use GOV.UK and independent advice. Living With Arthritis does not decide claims.

article.title: Hydrotherapy for Arthritis: Benefits, Access and What to Expect (UK)
article.excerpt: Complete UK guide to hydrotherapy for arthritis. Learn about warm-water therapy benefits, finding NHS hydrotherapy pools, what happens in a session.
article.content:
Hydrotherapy — exercise in warm water, typically 33–36°C — is one of the most effective and enjoyable treatments for arthritis. The combination of warmth, buoyancy and water resistance creates an ideal exercise environment where joints can move freely with minimal pain. Recommended by NICE, the NHS and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis), hydrotherapy has a strong evidence base for improving pain, stiffness, strength and function in both osteoarthritis and inflammatory arthritis. This guide explains the benefits, helps you access NHS hydrotherapy services and tells you what to expect.

Quick answer: Hydrotherapy is exercising in warm water, typically 33–36°C, helping arthritis by reducing body weight, allowing easier movement. The warmth relaxes muscles and lessens pain, while water resistance builds strength. NHS sessions, usually 30–45 minutes, are led by a physiotherapist, with courses often lasting 6–12 weeks. Access is usually via GP or rheumatologist referral.

How Hydrotherapy Helps Arthritis

Buoyancy

When immersed to waist depth, your body weight is reduced by approximately 50%. At chest depth, weight-bearing stress is reduced by up to 80%. This allows movements that would be painful on land to be performed with significantly less joint loading. People who struggle to walk comfortably on land often find they can walk, squat and exercise freely in water.

Warmth

Hydrotherapy pools are heated to 33–36°C (compared to standard swimming pools at 26–28°C). This warmth relaxes muscles, increases blood flow to joints, reduces pain perception and improves the elasticity of connective tissues. Many people describe the immediate relief of entering warm water as one of the most pleasant experiences of their arthritis management.

Hydrostatic Pressure

The pressure of water around the body reduces swelling in joints and limbs, provides support during movement, and improves circulation. This is particularly beneficial for people with swollen ankles, knees or hands.

Resistance

Water provides natural resistance to movement — approximately 12 times more resistance than air. This means exercises performed in water provide muscle strengthening without the need for weights or equipment. The resistance is proportional to speed, so you can control the intensity simply by moving faster or slower.

What the Evidence Says

  • A Cochrane review found aquatic exercise significantly improved pain, function and quality of life in knee and hip OA
  • Research published in Physical Therapy found hydrotherapy produced greater improvements in pain and function than land-based exercise for knee OA
  • A systematic review in Rheumatology found that aquatic exercise was beneficial for RA, improving joint tenderness, mood and overall well-being
  • NICE recommends hydrotherapy as part of multimodal management for OA
  • Benefits typically appear within 4–6 weeks of regular sessions

What Happens in a Hydrotherapy Session

A typical NHS hydrotherapy session lasts 30–45 minutes and is led by a physiotherapist or specialist hydrotherapy assistant:

  1. Assessment — Before your first session, a physiotherapist will assess your joints, mobility and goals
  2. Warm-up — Gentle walking and arm movements in the water
  3. Exercises — Tailored exercises targeting your specific joints — may include walking, squats, leg lifts, arm exercises, stretches and balance work
  4. Cool-down — Gentle stretches and relaxation in the warm water

Sessions may be individual (one-to-one with a therapist) or group-based (typically 4–8 people). Group sessions are social and motivating, while individual sessions allow more tailored exercises.

Accessing NHS Hydrotherapy

  • GP referral — Ask your GP to refer you to physiotherapy, specifically requesting hydrotherapy if available locally
  • Direct physiotherapy referral — Many NHS trusts accept self-referrals to physiotherapy
  • Rheumatology team — If you're under a rheumatologist, they can refer directly to hydrotherapy
  • Waiting times — Typically 4–12 weeks, though this varies by area
  • Course length — Usually 6–12 sessions

Finding Hydrotherapy Pools

Dedicated hydrotherapy pools exist at many NHS hospitals, community health centres, some private physiotherapy clinics and charity facilities (Arthritis UK lists some). Not all areas have easy access — if NHS hydrotherapy is unavailable, many public leisure centres offer "warm water" or "gentle aqua" sessions in pools heated to higher temperatures than standard.

Private Hydrotherapy

Private hydrotherapy sessions typically cost £40–£80 per session. Some private health insurance covers hydrotherapy with a GP or consultant referral. Private sessions usually have shorter waiting times and more flexibility in scheduling.

Swimming vs Hydrotherapy

While both involve water, they differ significantly. Hydrotherapy pools are warmer (33–36°C vs 26–28°C), smaller and shallower with easy access (ramps, hoists). Sessions are supervised and exercises tailored to individual needs. Standard swimming is excellent exercise for arthritis but doesn't provide the same therapeutic warmth. Both are beneficial — hydrotherapy is typically more appropriate for those with severe symptoms, while regular swimming maintains fitness once symptoms are better controlled.

Tips for Getting the Most from Hydrotherapy

  • Continue your exercises at home between sessions — your physiotherapist will give you a home programme
  • Arrive early to shower and change at a relaxed pace
  • Bring a water bottle — you can get dehydrated in warm water without realising
  • Rest afterwards if needed — warm-water exercise can be tiring initially
  • After your NHS course ends, continue with public pool sessions to maintain benefits

Hydrotherapy is one of the most effective and enjoyable treatments available for arthritis. If you haven't tried it, ask your GP about access. Our virtual assistant can help you find hydrotherapy pools and warm-water exercise classes near you.

This article is for general information only. Hydrotherapy may not be suitable if you have certain medical conditions (uncontrolled blood pressure, open wounds, certain infections). Your physiotherapist will assess suitability.

Practical next steps for Hydrotherapy for Arthritis: Benefits, Access and What to Expect (UK)

If you came here about Hydrotherapy for Arthritis: Benefits, Access and What to Expect (UK), pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Building a joint-friendly routine

Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

Benefits conversations

Personal Independence Payment (PIP) looks at how your condition affects daily living and mobility, not the diagnosis name alone. Keep a short diary of bad days, help you need with dressing or cooking, and walking limits. Welfare rights advisers at local councils or charities can check forms before you submit them.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

Quick questions about Hydrotherapy Arthritis Benefits Access

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Benefits of Hydrotherapy for Arthritis

  • Pain relief — warm water raises body temperature, increasing blood flow and releasing endorphins
  • Reduced stiffness — heat and gentle movement improve joint mobility
  • Muscle strengthening — water provides natural resistance without joint impact
  • Improved balance — water supports you, making balance exercises safer
  • Psychological benefits — warm water promotes relaxation and stress relief

How to Access Hydrotherapy in the UK

NHS Hydrotherapy

Many NHS trusts offer hydrotherapy through physiotherapy departments:

  1. Ask your GP for a referral to NHS physiotherapy
  2. Request hydrotherapy specifically — not all physiotherapy includes pool sessions
  3. Typical NHS course: 6-8 sessions with a physiotherapist in the pool
  4. Waiting times vary by area — typically 6-12 weeks

Community Hydrotherapy

  • Many leisure centres offer warm water sessions or arthritis-friendly swim times
  • Search "warm water swimming" or "hydrotherapy" on your local council website
  • Some centres offer discounted rates for people with health conditions

What to Expect

  • Water temperature is typically 33-36°C (warmer than a normal pool at 27-29°C)
  • Sessions usually last 30-45 minutes
  • A physiotherapist guides you through exercises in the water
  • You don't need to be a swimmer — exercises are done standing or with floats
  • Wear a comfortable swimsuit; the pool has handrails and steps for easy access

Finding Pools Near You

  • Ask your GP or physiotherapist for local recommendations
  • Check your local council's leisure services website
  • Contact local arthritis support groups — they often know the best facilities
  • Some private physiotherapy clinics have on-site hydrotherapy pools

Hydrotherapy may not be suitable if you have certain heart conditions, skin infections, or open wounds. Discuss with your GP before starting.

article.title: Ice and snow with arthritis: staying steady and what to do if you fall (UK guide)
article.excerpt: Icy pavements with arthritis: when to stay in, grippy shoes and walking aids, how to walk on ice, what to do after a fall and when to call 999.
article.content:
Quick answer: On icy or snowy days, plan around the ice rather than braving it: check the Met Office forecast, put off trips that can wait, wear well-fitting shoes with a good grip, keep your hands free and take small, slow steps. Keep up strength and balance exercises indoors. If you fall, the NHS advises staying calm and checking for injury before getting up slowly. Call 999 if you cannot get up or may have hurt your head, neck, back or hip.

Stiff knees and hips, sore feet, weaker grip and slower reactions make icy pavements harder for people with arthritis, and frailty raises the cost of a fall. This guide is about getting through cold snaps safely: when to stay in, how to set yourself up if you do go out, what to do if you fall, and how to keep your legs strong while the weather keeps you indoors.

Before you go out

  • Check the forecast and any Met Office weather warnings the night before
  • Ask whether the trip can wait until later in the day, when ice has had a chance to thaw, or be done by someone else. Ask your pharmacy whether it delivers prescriptions
  • Keep a few days of food and enough of your regular medicines at home before a cold snap, so you are not forced out
  • Wear warm layers, a hat and gloves. Cold, stiff hands grip a stick or handrail less well
  • Carry a charged mobile phone or wear your personal alarm, and tell someone where you are going
  • Do a five-minute warm-up indoors first — ankle circles, marching on the spot holding a worktop, sit-to-stands — so joints are not cold and stiff on the first step

Shoes and walking aids

  • The NHS advises shoes that fit well, do not slip off and have a good grip. See our walking shoes guide for what to look for with sore feet and joints
  • Slip-on ice grips can help on packed snow and ice. Take them off before walking on shop floors or tiles, where they can be slippery
  • Check the rubber tip (ferrule) on a walking stick or frame. A worn tip slips more easily, and some ferrules are designed for ice
  • Use a walking aid that has been set up for you. A physiotherapist can check the height and type; our walking aids guide explains the options
  • Use a rucksack or cross-body bag so both hands are free for a stick, rail or to break a fall

Walking on ice and snow

  • Take small, slow steps with your feet flat and slightly apart
  • Choose gritted main routes over shortcuts, and use handrails on steps and slopes
  • Watch for ice in shaded spots, on bridges, on drain covers and on smooth paving early in the morning and after dark
  • Hold the car door frame and get both feet on the ground before you stand up from a car
  • Go steady when you come indoors — wet soles on smooth floors cause slips too

Clearing snow and carrying grit are heavy jobs. If you have a heart or lung condition, a flare, or are unsteady, ask a neighbour or family member to do it.

Keeping strong when you are stuck indoors

Days indoors can quietly weaken the muscles that keep you steady. The NHS recommends older adults are active every day and do strength and balance activities at least twice a week.

  • Try short indoor walks every hour and our tai chi for balance routine
  • Our staying active in winter guide has indoor ideas for different joints, and the exercise hub has more
  • Keep the rooms you use warm; see the cold home guide and cold weather and arthritis
  • The NHS advises considering a daily vitamin D supplement from October to early March for bones and muscles — see our winter vitamin D guide

If you fall

The NHS advises staying calm and taking a couple of minutes to check for pain or injury before trying to move. If you feel able to get up:

  • Roll onto your side, then push up onto your hands and knees
  • Crawl to something stable, such as a sturdy chair, wall or railing
  • Put one foot flat on the ground and stand up slowly, holding on
  • Sit and rest before carrying on, and tell someone what happened

If you cannot get up, use your phone or alarm, or shout for help. Keep as warm as you can and keep moving your arms and legs while you wait.

Call 999 if you or someone else has fallen and:

  • cannot get up
  • may have injured their head, neck, back or hip
  • has severe hip pain or cannot put weight on a leg — possible signs of a broken hip
  • has been knocked out, is very drowsy, or has new weakness or problems speaking after a knock to the head

Contact NHS 111 if you have hit your head and take a blood-thinning medicine, feel dizzy or are being sick, or if you are in pain or feel unwell after a fall. A painful, swollen wrist after putting your hand out to break a fall needs checking at an urgent treatment centre or A&E.

If someone else falls, keep them warm and comfortable. Help them up only if they can do most of it themselves — do not try to lift them.

After a fall or a near miss

  • See a GP if you have had a fall or are worried about your balance. In some areas you can refer yourself to a falls service
  • Falls services can check strength, balance, eyesight, bone health and medicines, in line with NICE NG249 on falls assessment and prevention
  • If you broke a bone, ask about a bone health check. Our bone density guide explains why
  • Feeling nervous about going out again is common. Building back with short, planned walks helps — see walking with arthritis
  • Our falls prevention guide covers home safety, medicines and exercise

Frequently asked questions

Is it safer to stay in when it is icy?

For trips that can wait, often yes. But staying in for days on end can weaken muscles and stiffen joints, so keep moving indoors and go out when routes are gritted or thawed.

Does a walking stick help on ice?

A stick at the right height with a good rubber tip can give extra support, but it will not stop a slip on sheet ice. Slow down, use handrails and avoid the worst routes.

Why do my joints feel worse in the cold?

Many people notice more stiffness in cold weather, though research is mixed. Warm up before you go out and keep layers on. Our cold weather guide has more.
