article.title: Inclusive Arthritis and Frailty Support Plan (UK)
article.excerpt: How we are making arthritis and frailty information accessible to everyone, plus your NHS rights to interpreters, accessible information and support.
article.content:
Everyone with arthritis or frailty should be able to understand their condition and get the right help, whatever their language, culture, faith, disability or immigration status. This page sets out how Living With Arthritis plans to make its information more accessible, and the practical rights you have now when using the NHS, such as a free interpreter.

Our aims

Living With Arthritis aims to help people living with arthritis and frailty make informed choices, maintain everyday function and find appropriate professional support. Our education is open to everyone. We want to address barriers experienced by Asian communities, Muslim women, refugees and asylum seekers, and other groups, without assuming everyone has the same needs.

This is a delivery plan, not a claim that every service is already available. Health information on this site is educational and cannot guarantee prevention of joint problems.

First 30 days: listen and make information easier to use

  • invite voluntary feedback about language, disability access, privacy and practical barriers. We will not ask for immigration status or unnecessary medical details.
  • prioritise plain English, readable printouts, captions and accessible page navigation
  • identify trusted community partners and clinical reviewers, and publish only verified qualifications and real review dates

Days 31 to 60: develop culturally appropriate resources

  • plan professionally checked translations based on community demand, starting with Arabic, Urdu and relevant refugee languages
  • co-design resources with Asian communities and Muslim women, covering privacy, modesty, interpreter requests, suitable activity settings and culturally familiar food choices
  • offer information about discussing fasting, medicines and long-term conditions with a clinician, rather than advising people to change treatment themselves
  • provide clear NHS signposting for refugees and asylum seekers, linking to current official guidance rather than promising eligibility for every service

Days 61 to 90: pilot and evaluate

  • pilot accessible education sessions with community partners once staff and safeguarding arrangements are in place
  • focus on individually appropriate strength and balance activity, pacing, falls awareness, nutrition and seeking assessment for persistent symptoms
  • measure accessibility, understanding, usefulness of referrals and participant feedback. We will not claim clinical improvement without suitable evidence.

Your rights when using the NHS now

  • free interpreters: NHS England says patients should be able to have a professional interpreter, including British Sign Language, for GP and hospital appointments. Ask when you book. You should not have to rely on family members, especially children.
  • accessible information: under the Accessible Information Standard, NHS and social care services in England should record and meet your communication needs, such as large print, easy read or a support worker.
  • registering with a GP: you do not need proof of address or immigration status to register with a GP practice in England.
  • a chaperone can be requested for any examination, and you can ask to see a female or male clinician where possible.
  • reasonable adjustments, such as longer appointments, are available for disabled people.

Practical steps for musculoskeletal health

  • speak to a GP or physiotherapist about persistent joint pain, swelling, falls or difficulty with daily tasks
  • ask for activity adapted to your health and ability, particularly if you are frail or at risk of falls. Women-only exercise sessions are available in many areas.
  • discuss medicines, fasting, nutrition and vitamin D with a pharmacist or clinician
  • ask your council for a free needs assessment if you need help at home

These steps support health but cannot prevent every musculoskeletal condition.

Fasting and arthritis medicines

If you fast for religious reasons, talk to your GP, pharmacist or rheumatology team well in advance. Some medicines can be taken at different times, and some people may be advised not to fast for health reasons. Never change or stop medicines without advice.

Get involved

We welcome feedback on how accessible our information is. If you work with a community group and would like to partner with us, please get in touch through our contact page.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.content:
Home life is where arthritis and frailty collide most clearly — transfers, night trips, and the fear of a near-miss. Here we focus on frames, turning circles and sore hands, for readers in England, with self-management ideas and when to contact a GP, NHS 111 or 999.

Quick answer: Home life is where arthritis and frailty collide most clearly — transfers, night trips, and the fear of a near-miss. Here we focus on frames, turning circles and sore hands, for readers in England, with self-management ideas and when to contact a GP, NHS 111 or 999.

Picture the moment in a home when your several joints refuse a simple transfer and you feel your confidence drop faster than the pain score. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with frames, turning circles and sore hands, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in England.

The overlap: pain in several joints and a frailer body

NICE is clear that exercise is core care for osteoarthritis, not an optional extra after tablets. That still holds if you are becoming frailer, but the dose must respect today's several joints and today's energy. Rest has a place in a flare; rest as a lifestyle is how deconditioning joins the diagnosis.

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Pain in several joints can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual arthritis with frailty.

Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis. Only some also live with frailty. The practical question is not the label. It is whether frames, turning circles and sore hands is shrinking your home life — and what you can change this week without pretending pain is imaginary.

What this can look like in a home

In a home, frames, turning circles and sore hands is rarely one dramatic collapse. It is usually a stack of small avoidances. People with arthritis with frailty already know boom-and-bust. Frailty adds a longer payback: a quiet weekend can cost the following Thursday.

  • Night toilet trips, poor lighting and stiff several joints stacking into a falls risk that nobody named.
  • A flare of arthritis with frailty that lasts, then a slower baseline even when the flare eases.
  • Shorter outdoor range, then shorter indoor range, then a home that has quietly rearranged itself around the chair.
  • A hospital or infection week that ends with clothes feeling looser and stairs feeling taller.
  • Skipping meals or drinks because getting to the kitchen with sore several joints feels like a project.

Things you can try this week in a home

None of this is a gym challenge. The aim is to keep several joints moving, keep protein in the day, and keep frames, turning circles and sore hands from becoming the only story in the home. If a physiotherapist, occupational therapist or frailty team has already given you a plan, follow that ahead of a webpage.

  • Set an indoor walking loop with places to pause. Pain in several joints prefer several short bouts to one heroic corridor.
  • If you live in a home, tell one other person the plan for a fall: who to call, where the spare key sits, whether you wear a pendant you can actually press.
  • Use heat for stiffness if your skin is healthy, but protect thin skin. Never fall asleep on a hot water bottle.
  • Ask a pharmacist to look at the whole list if dizziness, constipation or night sedation have arrived with the pain tablets. Do not add a new painkiller just in case.
  • Carers: help the last 20 percent of a task, not the first 80, unless pain or safety says otherwise. Practice is treatment for frailty.
  • Book eye, foot and hearing checks as frailty care, not vanity. Arthritis with frailty already asks a lot of balance.

Home, roles and rhythm with arthritis and frailty

Most frailty lives in ordinary rooms. Rails, lighting, chair height, a kettle that does not demand a full kettle-lift, and a toilet you can get off again are treatment. Occupational therapy exists for this.

Help in England if arthritis and frailty overlap

When to get help

  • Sudden confusion, new incontinence, or a crash in mobility over hours to days — think infection or delirium, not only arthritis.
  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.
  • A hot, very swollen joint with fever, or feeling systemically unwell — seek urgent clinical advice. A joint infection is an emergency.
  • If you cannot get to the surgery because of arthritis with frailty, ask about a home visit or a proper phone review. Silence is not a care plan.
  • A knock to the head, especially if you take blood thinners — do not sleep it off as a plan.

Are painkillers the main treatment for frail arthritis with frailty?

No. For osteoarthritis, NICE puts exercise, weight management where relevant, and topical options at the centre. Tablets may help some people some of the time, but in frail adults they need a hard look at stomach, kidneys, heart, constipation and falls. Never share someone else's medicines.

Will I get PIP or Attendance Allowance because I have arthritis and frailty?

Nobody honest can promise that. These are legal tests about how your difficulties affect daily living or personal care, not about a diagnosis name. Keep a diary of frames, turning circles and sore hands on typical and bad days. Use GOV.UK and independent advice. Living With Arthritis does not decide claims.

Should I stop exercising during frames, turning circles and sore hands?

Complete rest for more than a short flare period usually makes several joints and muscle worse. Keep a smaller version: seated strength, indoor loops, or the two sit-to-stands you can still do. If exercise causes pain that spirals or a joint that will not settle, get clinical advice.

Frailty is a clinical syndrome — not a personality trait — and inflammatory arthritis can make it more visible. This article is about flare care that does not create a deconditioning spiral, written for people and carers in Northern Ireland, especially around a home.

Quick answer: Frailty is a clinical syndrome — not a personality trait — and inflammatory arthritis can make it more visible. This article is about flare care that does not create a deconditioning spiral, written for people and carers in Northern Ireland, especially around a home.

It might be the kettle, the bathroom, the car door or the clinic corridor — a home task that used to be automatic now asks more of several joints than they can give on a stiff morning. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with flare care that does not create a deconditioning spiral, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in Northern Ireland.

Why inflammatory arthritis and frailty so often meet

Arthritis is about joints, tendons and the way pain changes movement. Frailty is about the whole system — muscle, stamina, appetite, mood, medicines and how quickly you bounce back after a setback. Inflammatory arthritis sits in the middle because sore several joints quietly train you to sit more, shorten your stride and skip the movements that keep muscle.

NICE is clear that exercise is core care for osteoarthritis, not an optional extra after tablets. That still holds if you are becoming frailer, but the dose must respect today's several joints and today's energy. Rest has a place in a flare; rest as a lifestyle is how deconditioning joins the diagnosis.

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Pain in several joints can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual inflammatory arthritis.

Small, repeatable steps — not a reinvention

None of this is a gym challenge. The aim is to keep several joints moving, keep protein in the day, and keep flare care that does not create a deconditioning spiral from becoming the only story in the home. If a physiotherapist, occupational therapist or frailty team has already given you a plan, follow that ahead of a webpage.

  • Book eye, foot and hearing checks as frailty care, not vanity. Inflammatory arthritis already asks a lot of balance.
  • Treat a walking aid as joint protection and falls kit, not as a verdict. Wrist-friendly handles matter if several joints include hands.
  • Keep a sit-to-stand practice at the height you actually use. A higher chair is not cheating if it lets several joints work without a panic haul.
  • Carers: help the last 20 percent of a task, not the first 80, unless pain or safety says otherwise. Practice is treatment for frailty.
  • If you live in a home, tell one other person the plan for a fall: who to call, where the spare key sits, whether you wear a pendant you can actually press.
  • Write three daily anchors: a meal, a movement, a conversation. Frailty grows in unstructured days.

Flare, fear and slowing down

In a home, flare care that does not create a deconditioning spiral is rarely one dramatic collapse. It is usually a stack of small avoidances. People with inflammatory arthritis already know boom-and-bust. Frailty adds a longer payback: a quiet weekend can cost the following Thursday.

  • A flare of inflammatory arthritis that lasts, then a slower baseline even when the flare eases.
  • Skipping meals or drinks because getting to the kitchen with sore several joints feels like a project.
  • Carers doing the last steps of a task to be kind, which removes the last practice the muscles were getting.
  • Night toilet trips, poor lighting and stiff several joints stacking into a falls risk that nobody named.

Making a home work harder for you

Walking aids, Blue Badge applications, community transport and downstairs living are all tools. None of them is a moral failure. Used well, they keep you in the world so several joints still get some practice.

When to get help

  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.
  • If you cannot get to the surgery because of inflammatory arthritis, ask about a home visit or a proper phone review. Silence is not a care plan.
  • Unplanned weight loss, repeated falls, or flare care that does not create a deconditioning spiral that is clearly worsening week by week — book the GP and say you are worried about frailty as well as several joints.
  • A hot, very swollen joint with fever, or feeling systemically unwell — seek urgent clinical advice. A joint infection is an emergency.
  • A knock to the head, especially if you take blood thinners — do not sleep it off as a plan.

Who to talk to locally in Northern Ireland

Is a walking aid giving in if I have inflammatory arthritis?

No. An aid that matches your several joints can protect joints, reduce fear and keep you walking far enough to keep muscle. A poorly fitted stick that hurts a wrist is the problem, not the concept. Ask physiotherapy or occupational therapy to look at height and grip.

How do I tell an arthritis flare from a frailty slide?

A flare of inflammatory arthritis is usually more joint pain, stiffness or swelling in a known pattern. A frailty slide is broader: weaker recovery, smaller meals, more time in the chair, maybe confusion or falls. They can happen together. If the whole person is changing, do not only increase pain gel.

Are painkillers the main treatment for frail inflammatory arthritis?

No. For osteoarthritis, NICE puts exercise, weight management where relevant, and topical options at the centre. Tablets may help some people some of the time, but in frail adults they need a hard look at stomach, kidneys, heart, constipation and falls. Never share someone else's medicines.

faqs.a: No. An aid that matches your several joints can protect joints, reduce fear and keep you walking far enough to keep muscle. A poorly fitted stick that hurts a wrist is the problem, not the concept. Ask physiotherapy or occupational therapy to look at height and grip.

faqs.q: How do I tell an arthritis flare from a frailty slide?
faqs.a: A flare of inflammatory arthritis is usually more joint pain, stiffness or swelling in a known pattern. A frailty slide is broader: weaker recovery, smaller meals, more time in the chair, maybe confusion or falls. They can happen together. If the whole person is changing, do not only increase pain gel.

faqs.q: Are painkillers the main treatment for frail inflammatory arthritis?
faqs.a: No. For osteoarthritis, NICE puts exercise, weight management where relevant, and topical options at the centre. Tablets may help some people some of the time, but in frail adults they need a hard look at stomach, kidneys, heart, constipation and falls. Never share someone else's medicines.

article.title: Inflammatory Arthritis: Types, Causes and Treatment (UK Guide)
article.excerpt: Inflammatory arthritis covers conditions like rheumatoid, psoriatic and reactive arthritis, where the immune system — not wear and tear — drives joint damage.
article.content:
Quick answer: Inflammatory arthritis is an umbrella term for immune-driven joint conditions (rheumatoid, psoriatic, reactive arthritis and more), distinct from the mechanical wear of osteoarthritis. It typically causes morning stiffness over 30 minutes, joint swelling and fatigue, and is treated with immune-modulating medication such as DMARDs or biologics alongside exercise and lifestyle measures.

What Is Inflammatory Arthritis?

Inflammatory arthritis is an umbrella term for a group of conditions where the immune system itself causes joint pain, swelling and stiffness — rather than joints simply wearing down over time. This is the key difference from osteoarthritis, the "wear and tear" type most people picture when they hear the word arthritis. In inflammatory arthritis, the immune system mistakenly attacks the lining of the joints (or, in some cases, entheses — the points where tendons attach to bone), triggering ongoing inflammation that can damage cartilage and bone if it isn't treated.

Conditions that fall under this umbrella include rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, and polymyalgia rheumatica. Each has its own pattern and triggers, but they share a common thread: the pain and stiffness come from active inflammation, not mechanical damage, and they generally respond to different treatments than osteoarthritis does.

How It Differs From Osteoarthritis

The distinction matters because it changes what actually helps.

  • Osteoarthritis tends to affect joints that have taken the most physical load over the years — knees, hips, hands — and symptoms typically get worse with activity and better with rest. Treatment focuses on exercise, weight management, and pain relief.
  • Inflammatory arthritis often causes morning stiffness lasting longer than 30 minutes to an hour, can affect smaller joints symmetrically (both hands, both wrists), and may come with fatigue, low-grade fever, or symptoms elsewhere in the body (skin, eyes, gut). Because the root cause is an overactive immune response, treatment usually involves medications that calm the immune system down — not just manage the symptoms.

Getting the right diagnosis early matters a great deal with inflammatory types, because unlike osteoarthritis, untreated inflammation can cause irreversible joint damage within months, not years.

Common Symptoms to Watch For

  • Joint stiffness that is worse first thing in the morning and takes a long time to ease
  • Swelling, warmth or redness over a joint, not just pain
  • Symptoms affecting several joints at once, sometimes symmetrically
  • Fatigue that feels disproportionate to how active you've been
  • In some types: skin changes (psoriasis-like patches), eye redness or irritation, or digestive symptoms
  • Symptoms that don't settle with rest the way mechanical joint pain usually does

No single symptom confirms inflammatory arthritis on its own — a GP will usually combine your symptom pattern with blood tests (such as CRP, ESR, rheumatoid factor or anti-CCP antibodies) and sometimes imaging to work out which type, if any, is involved.

How Inflammatory Arthritis Is Diagnosed

Diagnosis typically starts with a GP, who will ask about your symptom pattern — which joints, how long stiffness lasts, whether it's improved or worsened by movement — and examine the affected joints for swelling or warmth. Blood tests looking for markers of inflammation and specific antibodies help narrow down the type, though a normal blood test doesn't fully rule out inflammatory arthritis, since some people have "seronegative" disease.

If inflammatory arthritis is suspected, the next step is usually a referral to a rheumatologist — a specialist in this exact area — ideally within weeks rather than months, since early treatment with disease-modifying drugs has consistently been shown to give better long-term joint outcomes than delayed treatment.

Treatment Approaches

Because inflammatory arthritis is driven by the immune system, treatment generally centres on calming that immune response, alongside the same lifestyle measures that help any type of arthritis:

  • DMARDs (disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs), such as methotrexate, are often the first line of treatment for conditions like rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis. They work by dampening the underlying immune activity, not just masking pain.
  • Biologic therapies target specific parts of the immune system more precisely and are typically considered when standard DMARDs aren't enough on their own.
  • Short-term steroids (oral or injected) can bring rapid relief during a flare while longer-term treatments take effect.
  • NSAIDs and pain relief help manage symptoms day to day but don't address the underlying inflammation on their own.
  • Physiotherapy and gentle, regular exercise remain important across all types of arthritis — they help maintain joint function and muscle support even while medication addresses the inflammation itself.

Treatment plans are highly individual and depend on which specific condition is involved, how active the disease is, and how you respond to different medications — this is genuinely a case where working closely with a rheumatology team makes a real difference.

Living With Inflammatory Arthritis Day to Day

A diagnosis of inflammatory arthritis is often a lifelong one, but for most people, effective treatment means long periods of low disease activity or remission, not constant flares. Practical things that help day to day include:

  • Pacing activity across the day rather than pushing through until you crash, especially when fatigue is part of your picture
  • Keeping a simple symptom diary so you and your rheumatology team can spot patterns and adjust treatment before a flare gets out of hand
  • Staying as physically active as your joints allow — inactivity tends to make stiffness worse, not better
  • Building a support network, whether that's family, a local support group, or an online community of people managing the same condition
  • Being upfront with your employer where possible about flexibility needs, since fatigue and flare-ups don't always follow a predictable schedule

When to Seek Urgent Advice

Most inflammatory arthritis symptoms build gradually and can be discussed at a routine GP appointment, but a few situations warrant faster attention:

  • A single joint that becomes hot, red, swollen and severely painful very suddenly — this can occasionally indicate a joint infection (septic arthritis), which needs same-day assessment rather than a routine appointment
  • New eye redness or pain alongside joint symptoms, particularly with conditions like ankylosing spondylitis or reactive arthritis, which can involve eye inflammation (uveitis) needing prompt treatment
  • Signs of a significant flare while on immune-suppressing medication, such as a high fever, since these medications can affect the body's ability to fight infection

Knowing these warning signs helps you judge when "wait and see" is reasonable and when it isn't — most day-to-day symptom changes fall into the former category, but it's worth knowing the exceptions.

The Role of a Multidisciplinary Team

Managing inflammatory arthritis well typically involves more than just a rheumatologist. Physiotherapists help maintain joint function and design safe exercise programmes around active disease. Occupational therapists can advise on joint-protection techniques and practical aids for daily tasks during flares. Podiatrists are often involved when arthritis affects the feet, which is common in rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis. Some people also benefit from dietitian input, since maintaining a healthy weight reduces load on affected joints, and specialist nurses often act as the first point of contact between routine rheumatology appointments — genuinely useful for questions that come up between visits rather than waiting months for the next one.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is inflammatory arthritis the same as rheumatoid arthritis? No — rheumatoid arthritis is one specific type of inflammatory arthritis. The umbrella term also covers psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica and others, each with different patterns and triggers.

Can inflammatory arthritis be cured? Most forms can't be cured outright, but modern treatment — particularly when started early — can bring disease activity under control to the point where many people experience long stretches with few or no symptoms.

Does inflammatory arthritis always get worse over time? Not necessarily. Left untreated, it often does progress and can cause lasting joint damage. With appropriate treatment, though, many people's disease activity stabilises or improves rather than steadily worsening.

Is inflammatory arthritis hereditary? Some types have a genetic component that increases risk, but genetics alone don't determine whether someone develops the condition — it's generally considered a combination of genetic susceptibility and environmental triggers.

Key Takeaways

  • Inflammatory arthritis is an umbrella term for immune-driven joint conditions, distinct from the mechanical wear-and-tear of osteoarthritis.
  • Morning stiffness lasting over 30 minutes, joint swelling, and disproportionate fatigue are common red flags worth discussing with a GP.
  • Early diagnosis and treatment matter enormously, since untreated inflammation can cause permanent joint damage.
  • Treatment usually combines immune-modulating medication with the same exercise and lifestyle measures that help any type of arthritis.
  • A diagnosis doesn't mean constant symptoms — effective treatment can bring long periods of stability for most people.

This article provides general information and is not a substitute for personalised medical advice. If you're experiencing symptoms of inflammatory arthritis, speak to your GP about a referral to a rheumatologist.

article.content:
A practical UK guide to knee injections in frail adults: questions worth asking, written for days when energy and joints both feel limited. This guide covers injections as a window for movement, not a cure when knee osteoarthritis affects knees, with a focus on Northern Ireland and a hospital setting.

Quick answer: A practical UK guide to knee injections in frail adults: questions worth asking, written for days when energy and joints both feel limited. This guide covers injections as a window for movement, not a cure when knee osteoarthritis affects knees, with a focus on Northern Ireland and a hospital setting.

Families often notice knee osteoarthritis first as a slower walk across a hospital, then as a person who starts declining invitations. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with injections as a window for movement, not a cure, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in Northern Ireland.

Pain, muscle and recovery: the Northern Ireland picture

Arthritis is about joints, tendons and the way pain changes movement. Frailty is about the whole system — muscle, stamina, appetite, mood, medicines and how quickly you bounce back after a setback. Knee osteoarthritis sits in the middle because sore knees quietly train you to sit more, shorten your stride and skip the movements that keep muscle.

NICE is clear that exercise is core care for osteoarthritis, not an optional extra after tablets. That still holds if you are becoming frailer, but the dose must respect today's knees and today's energy. Rest has a place in a flare; rest as a lifestyle is how deconditioning joins the diagnosis.

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Painful knees can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual knee osteoarthritis.

Tablets, topical options and what not to DIY

Older adults with knee osteoarthritis often collect medicines for pain, sleep, stomach protection, blood pressure and more. Each tablet may have a reason. Together they can add dizziness, constipation, dry mouth or night sedation — all of which make knees less trustworthy.

Do not start, stop or double painkillers because a neighbour swears by them. Some anti-inflammatory tablets are a poor fit with kidney, heart or stomach problems. Some stronger pain medicines increase falls risk. A pharmacist or GP can look at the whole list. This page will not give doses.

A frailty-aware plan for knees

  • Use heat for stiffness if your skin is healthy, but protect thin skin. Never fall asleep on a hot water bottle.
  • Write three daily anchors: a meal, a movement, a conversation. Frailty grows in unstructured days.
  • Put the items you use at dawn — tablets, glasses, walking aid, phone — where you can reach them without a stretch that wrenches knees.
  • Set an indoor walking loop with places to pause. Painful knees prefer several short bouts to one heroic corridor.
  • In Northern Ireland, ask your local Health and Social Care Trust about equipment and care options. Descriptions of grants and benefits here are not predictions of an award.
  • Keep a sit-to-stand practice at the height you actually use. A higher chair is not cheating if it lets knees work without a panic haul.

A Northern Ireland day with knee osteoarthritis and less reserve

  • Shorter outdoor range, then shorter indoor range, then a hospital that has quietly rearranged itself around the chair.
  • Skipping meals or drinks because getting to the kitchen with sore knees feels like a project.
  • A flare of knee osteoarthritis that lasts, then a slower baseline even when the flare eases.
  • Night toilet trips, poor lighting and stiff knees stacking into a falls risk that nobody named.
  • Transfers that used to be boring — bed, chair, toilet, car — now need a pause, a push-up or a second person, especially when knees are cold.

Help in Northern Ireland if knee osteoarthritis and frailty overlap

Red flags — do not wait this out

  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.
  • Chest pain, trouble breathing, or signs of a stroke — 999, not a wait for the knee osteoarthritis nurse.
  • A hot, very swollen joint with fever, or feeling systemically unwell — seek urgent clinical advice. A joint infection is an emergency.
  • If you cannot get to the surgery because of knee osteoarthritis, ask about a home visit or a proper phone review. Silence is not a care plan.
  • Unplanned weight loss, repeated falls, or injections as a window for movement, not a cure that is clearly worsening week by week — book the GP and say you are worried about frailty as well as knees.

Is a walking aid giving in if I have knee osteoarthritis?

No. An aid that matches your knees can protect joints, reduce fear and keep you walking far enough to keep muscle. A poorly fitted stick that hurts a wrist is the problem, not the concept. Ask physiotherapy or occupational therapy to look at height and grip.

Will I get PIP or Attendance Allowance because I have knee osteoarthritis and frailty?

Nobody honest can promise that. These are legal tests about how your difficulties affect daily living or personal care, not about a diagnosis name. Keep a diary of injections as a window for movement, not a cure on typical and bad days. Use GOV.UK and independent advice. Living With Arthritis does not decide claims.

What should a carer do in the hospital without taking over?

Stand nearby for the risky bit, set the environment up (chair height, shoes, light), and leave the bits the person can still do. Taking over every transfer trains both of you into a hoist-by-default life. If moving and handling is already unsafe, stop DIY lifting and ask for a proper care and OT review.

Bring a list of usual arthritis limits — staff cannot guess which transfers were hard before admission. Here we focus on a stepping-stone stay before home, for readers in Scotland, with self-management ideas and when to contact a GP, NHS 24 on 111 or 999.

Quick answer: Bring a list of usual arthritis limits — staff cannot guess which transfers were hard before admission. Here we focus on a stepping-stone stay before home, for readers in Scotland, with self-management ideas and when to contact a GP, NHS 24 on 111 or 999.

It might be the kettle, the bathroom, the car door or the clinic corridor — a hospital task that used to be automatic now asks more of several joints than they can give on a stiff morning. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with a stepping-stone stay before home, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in Scotland.

What to put on the problem list besides several joints

Comprehensive geriatric assessment is a long name for a simple idea: look at movement, memory, mood, medicines, continence, bone, hearing, vision, home and who helps — not only the scan of several joints. Ask for that whole-person look if a stepping-stone stay before home is taking over.

Infection, delirium, constipation, unplanned weight loss and a new inability to get off the floor are frailty red flags. They are not a bad arthritis day. They need timely clinical advice.

Pain, muscle and recovery: the Scotland picture

Small, repeatable steps — not a reinvention

  • In Scotland, ask your local Health and Social Care Partnership, including Self-directed Support conversations about equipment and care options. Descriptions of grants and benefits here are not predictions of an award.
  • After a flare, restart the smallest version of your usual movement within comfort, rather than waiting to feel back to normal. Normal rarely sends an email.
  • If stairs are the bottleneck, get an occupational therapy conversation on the list while you temporarily live downstairs — drifting is how a camp-bed becomes a lifestyle.
  • Book eye, foot and hearing checks as frailty care, not vanity. Arthritis with frailty already asks a lot of balance.
  • If cooking is the barrier, use tinned fish, eggs, yoghurt, beans or leftover protein foods rather than skipping meals. Muscle needs raw material as well as movement.
  • If you live in a hospital, tell one other person the plan for a fall: who to call, where the spare key sits, whether you wear a pendant you can actually press.

How a stepping-stone stay before home shows up in real rooms

  • A flare of arthritis with frailty that lasts, then a slower baseline even when the flare eases.
  • A hospital or infection week that ends with clothes feeling looser and stairs feeling taller.
  • New fear after a near-miss, even if you did not hit the floor. Fear of falling is itself a reason people sit more.

GP, 111 or 999?

This is not personal medical advice. When several joints and frailty overlap, wait until Monday is sometimes right and sometimes dangerous. If you are unsure, NHS 24 on 111 can help you choose. Living With Arthritis cannot triage you.

  • A hot, very swollen joint with fever, or feeling systemically unwell — seek urgent clinical advice. A joint infection is an emergency.
  • Sudden confusion, new incontinence, or a crash in mobility over hours to days — think infection or delirium, not only arthritis.
  • A knock to the head, especially if you take blood thinners — do not sleep it off as a plan.
  • If you cannot get to the surgery because of arthritis with frailty, ask about a home visit or a proper phone review. Silence is not a care plan.
  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.

Scotland services, without inventing a clinic

Start with your GP practice and NHS Scotland services via your GP and Health and Social Care Partnership. For urgent but non-emergency advice use NHS 24 on 111. For chest pain, suspected hip fracture, sudden new weakness, or a fall with a bang to the head on blood thinners, use 999.

In Scotland, NHS Inform is a reliable first read. Rehab, reablement and care at home are organised locally. Island and Highland travel can turn a simple clinic into a two-day event, so ask early about closer blood tests or phone reviews.

Ask about community physiotherapy, occupational therapy, reablement after hospital, podiatry, pharmacy reviews and your local Health and Social Care Partnership, including Self-directed Support conversations. Names of teams change. The functions do not: get you moving, get you equipped, get the medicines tidier, get a human being through the door if you cannot get out.

Age UK and local advice agencies can help with forms. The Charity Commission listing for Living With Arthritis (1218461) is public if you want to check who we are. We are independent of Arthritis UK.

What should a carer do in the hospital without taking over?

Stand nearby for the risky bit, set the environment up (chair height, shoes, light), and leave the bits the person can still do. Taking over every transfer trains both of you into a hoist-by-default life. If moving and handling is already unsafe, stop DIY lifting and ask for a proper care and OT review.

How do I tell an arthritis flare from a frailty slide?

A flare of arthritis with frailty is usually more joint pain, stiffness or swelling in a known pattern. A frailty slide is broader: weaker recovery, smaller meals, more time in the chair, maybe confusion or falls. They can happen together. If the whole person is changing, do not only increase pain gel.

Do I need a geriatrician as well as a rheumatologist?

Not always. Many people are supported by GP, community physio and, where it exists, a frailty team. If medicines are stacking, falls are repeating, or memory and continence are changing alongside arthritis with frailty, ask whether a comprehensive older-person assessment would help.

If the whole person is changing, do not only increase pain gel.

faqs.q: Do I need a geriatrician as well as a rheumatologist?
faqs.a: Not always. Many people are supported by GP, community physio and, where it exists, a frailty team. If medicines are stacking, falls are repeating, or memory and continence are changing alongside arthritis with frailty, ask whether a comprehensive older-person assessment would help.

article.title: JAK Inhibitors: The Next Wave of RA Treatment
article.excerpt: JAK inhibitors reduce rheumatoid arthritis symptoms like pain, swelling, and stiffness by blocking specific immune system pathways that cause inflammation.
article.content:
Quick answer: JAK inhibitors reduce rheumatoid arthritis symptoms like pain, swelling, and stiffness by blocking specific immune system pathways that cause inflammation. They are an option if other treatments haven't worked and can significantly improve quality of life. However, they come with potential side effects, such as infections, and may not be suitable for everyone. Your doctor will assess risks and benefits.

Overview

Tofacitinib, baricitinib and upadacitinib explained for patients.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis editorial team using UK NICE guidance, NHS information and peer-reviewed sources. We aim to update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Randomised trials have shown that JAK inhibitors (Janus kinase inhibitors) can be very effective in reducing the symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis, such as pain, swelling, and stiffness. These medications work by blocking specific pathways in the immune system that contribute to inflammation. For many people, this can lead to significant improvements in their quality of life.

Systematic reviews, which combine the results of multiple studies, confirm these benefits. They also highlight that while these treatments can be powerful, they come with potential side effects that need careful consideration. Clinical guidelines from professional bodies recommend JAK inhibitors for people whose arthritis hasn't responded well to other types of medication, often after trying conventional disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) or biologic therapies.

Overall, the picture from the evidence is that JAK inhibitors are an important addition to the treatment options for rheumatoid arthritis, offering a new pathway to manage the condition for those who need it. The focus is always on balancing the benefits of symptom control with managing any potential risks, tailored to each individual's health.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Stopping medication abruptly: This can lead to your symptoms returning or worsening. Always discuss changes with your doctor first.
  • Ignoring side effects: Even mild side effects should be mentioned to your care team. They can help adjust your treatment or offer solutions.
  • Comparing your progress to others: Everyone's journey with rheumatoid arthritis is unique. Focus on your own improvements and challenges.
  • Not asking questions: If something isn't clear, ask your doctor or nurse. Understanding your treatment helps you manage it better.
  • Neglecting regular exercise: Staying active, even gently, helps maintain joint flexibility and muscle strength. Find what works for you.

When to Speak to a Clinician

While managing rheumatoid arthritis is a long-term journey, there are times when you should seek prompt advice from your doctor, physiotherapist, or rheumatology team. Don't wait for your next routine appointment if you experience any of the following:

  • Sudden, severe pain or swelling in a joint.
  • New or worsening fever, especially if accompanied by chills.
  • Signs of infection, such as redness, warmth, or pus around a joint, or a general feeling of being unwell.
  • Any new, unexplained symptoms that concern you, particularly if they appear shortly after starting a new medication.
  • Rapid loss of function or inability to move a joint that was previously manageable.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are JAK inhibitors and how do they work?

JAK inhibitors are a type of medication that targets specific pathways within your immune system. They block the activity of enzymes called Janus kinases, which play a key role in the inflammatory process linked to rheumatoid arthritis. By doing this, they help to reduce inflammation, pain, and joint damage.

Are JAK inhibitors suitable for everyone with rheumatoid arthritis?

No, they are not suitable for everyone. They are typically considered when other treatments, like conventional DMARDs or biologic therapies, haven't worked well enough for you. Your doctor will assess your overall health, other medical conditions, and potential risks to decide if a JAK inhibitor is a safe and appropriate option for you.

What are the possible side effects of JAK inhibitors?

Like all medications, JAK inhibitors can have side effects. Common ones can include infections (like colds or shingles), headaches, and digestive upset. More serious but less common side effects can include an increased risk of certain serious infections or blood clots. Your doctor will discuss these risks with you before starting treatment and monitor you closely.

Practical next steps for JAK Inhibitors: The Next Wave of RA Treatment

If you came here about JAK Inhibitors: The Next Wave of RA Treatment, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Quick questions about Inhibitors Next Wave Treatment

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

article.title: Joint Fusion vs Replacement: How Surgeons Choose

article.content:
Quick answer: Joint replacement is often preferred for large, weight-bearing joints like the hip and knee, aiming for improved function. Conversely, joint fusion is frequently considered for smaller joints such as those in the wrist or foot, and particularly the ankle, offering pain relief and stability. Both surgeries are typically considered when non-surgical treatments are no longer effective and quality of life is severely impacted.

Overview

The case for fusion in ankles, wrists and small joints.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis editorial team using UK NICE guidance, NHS information and peer-reviewed sources. We aim to update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Current research consistently highlights the importance of a step-wise approach to managing arthritis, starting with non-surgical options. Randomised trials and systematic reviews show that a combination of exercise, physical therapy, and appropriate medications can significantly improve joint function and reduce pain for many people. Surgical interventions, such as joint fusion or replacement, are typically considered when these conservative treatments are no longer effective and a person's quality of life is severely impacted.

Clinical guidelines from leading medical bodies across the UK emphasise shared decision-making, where the person with arthritis and their healthcare team discuss all available options, weighing up the potential benefits and risks of each. The focus is on preserving natural joint function where possible and, when surgery is necessary, choosing the procedure most likely to offer long-term relief and improved mobility, tailored to the individual's specific circumstances and the affected joint.

For smaller joints, like those in the wrist or foot, and particularly for the ankle, fusion (arthrodesis) is often considered a reliable option for pain relief and stability, especially in specific arthritis types. Conversely, for larger, weight-bearing joints like the hip and knee, joint replacement (arthroplasty) often provides superior functional outcomes. The evidence for these preferences is built on decades of patient outcomes and ongoing surgical technique refinements.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Ignoring early symptoms: Hoping pain will simply go away on its own. *Fix: Keep a symptom diary and discuss persistent pain with your family doctor. Overdoing it on good days: Pushing through significant pain, leading to flare-ups. *Fix: Pace yourself and listen to your body, even when feeling well. Stopping medication without advice: Discontinuing prescribed drugs because you feel better. *Fix: Always consult your doctor before making changes to your medication. Avoiding all movement: Fearing that exercise will damage your joints further. *Fix: Engage in gentle, recommended exercises to maintain strength and flexibility. Self-diagnosing online and delaying professional help: Relying solely on internet searches for treatment plans. *Fix: Seek professional medical advice for an accurate diagnosis and personalised care plan.

When to Speak to a Clinician

It's important to reach out to your GP, physiotherapist, or rheumatologist if you notice significant changes in your joint health. Don't wait for your next routine appointment if you experience any of the following:

  • Sudden, severe increase in joint pain.
  • New or rapidly worsening joint swelling or redness.
  • Feeling generally unwell with a fever alongside joint pain.
  • Rapid loss of movement or function in a joint.
  • Joint pain that keeps you awake at night or is present at rest.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happens if I delay treatment for arthritis?

Delaying effective treatment can lead to worsening joint damage and increased pain over time. Early intervention, including medication and lifestyle adjustments, can help slow the progression of the disease and preserve joint function.

How long does recovery take after joint surgery?

Recovery time varies greatly depending on the type of surgery, the joint involved, and your overall health. For some, it might be a few weeks, while for more complex procedures, it could be several months of rehabilitation. Your surgical team will provide a tailored recovery plan.

Can I still be active after joint fusion or replacement?

Absolutely. The goal of these surgeries is often to reduce pain and improve your ability to move. While some activities might need to be modified, many people return to a good level of activity, including walking, swimming, and cycling, following successful recovery.

Gentle cognitive tools

Noticing catastrophic thoughts ("this flare will never end") and reframing them with paced facts can reduce fear without denying real pain. Apps and courses based on cognitive behavioural approaches are available on the NHS in many areas; your surgery can advise what is offered locally.

article.title: Joint Protection Techniques for Arthritis: Easier Ways to Do Everyday Tasks
article.excerpt: Joint protection means doing everyday tasks in ways that put less strain on painful joints. Practical ideas for the kitchen, housework, shopping, work and gardening, plus gadgets that genuinely help. Now with techniques by joint, safe lifting steps, posture, splints and walking aids, and what to change during a flare.
article.content:
Quick answer: Joint protection means doing everyday tasks in ways that put less strain on painful joints. Use larger, stronger joints instead of small ones, spread loads, avoid tight or prolonged grips, change position often, pace activities and use gadgets such as jar openers. It works best alongside regular exercise, and an occupational therapist can tailor advice.

What joint protection is, and what it is not

Joint protection is about working smarter, not doing less. The idea is to reduce unnecessary strain on painful or inflamed joints so you can keep doing the things that matter to you with less pain and fatigue. It is widely taught by occupational therapists (OTs) and is recommended alongside exercise and other treatments for both inflammatory arthritis and osteoarthritis.

It is not about avoiding movement. Joints and muscles need regular activity to stay healthy. The aim is to balance activity and rest, use your body efficiently, and keep strength up so joints are better supported. See our exercise guide for the activity side.

Five core principles

  1. Respect pain. Pain that lasts more than an hour or two after an activity, or is worse the next day, suggests you did too much or did it in a way that strained your joints. Adjust next time rather than pushing through.
  2. Use larger, stronger joints. Carry a bag over your forearm or shoulder instead of gripping handles with your fingers. Push doors open with your shoulder or hip rather than your hand. Close drawers with your hip.
  3. Spread the load. Use both hands to lift a mug or pan. Slide heavy objects along a work surface instead of lifting them. Hold items close to your body, where they feel lighter.
  4. Avoid tight grips and staying in one position. Tight, sustained gripping, such as wringing cloths or holding a pen for a long time, stresses finger joints. Build up handles, change position often and take micro-breaks.
  5. Plan and pace. Spread heavy jobs across the week, alternate hard and easy tasks, and build in rest before you are exhausted. Our guide to energy management and pacing goes into detail.

In the kitchen

  • Use a kettle tipper, or fill the kettle with a jug, so you do not lift a full kettle.
  • Choose lightweight pans with two handles, and use a slotted spoon or a frying basket instead of draining heavy pans.
  • Try a jar opener, electric tin opener and ring-pull opener.
  • Use a perching stool so you can sit to prepare food.
  • Keep everyday items between waist and shoulder height to reduce bending and stretching.
  • Use chunky-handled or angled cutlery and knives, and a spiked chopping board to hold food steady.
  • Buy pre-chopped vegetables or frozen options on bad days. This is sensible planning, not giving up.

Around the house

  • Use long-handled dustpans, mops and grabbers to reduce bending.
  • Choose lever taps and lever door handles, or add tap turners.
  • Carry laundry in smaller loads, or use a trolley. Raise the washing basket onto a chair so you do not bend to the floor.
  • Sit to iron, or choose clothes that need little ironing.
  • Use a lightweight cordless vacuum.
  • Spread cleaning jobs over several days rather than doing everything at once.

Dressing and personal care

  • Sit down to dress, especially for socks, tights and shoes.
  • Try a long-handled shoehorn, sock aid and elastic laces.
  • Choose front-fastening clothes, larger buttons or magnetic fastenings, and zip pulls.
  • Use a toothbrush or hairbrush with a thicker handle, or add foam tubing.
  • Consider an electric toothbrush and pump-action dispensers.

Shopping, work and getting about

  • Use a shopping trolley on wheels, or shop online for heavy items.
  • Ask for bags to be packed lightly.
  • At work, set up your desk so your wrists are straight and your screen is at eye level. Use voice dictation if typing is painful. Our guide to working with arthritis covers reasonable adjustments.
  • In the car, a key turner, cushion and swivel seat can help. See our travel guide.

Gardening and hobbies

  • Use kneelers with handles, long-handled and lightweight tools, and ratchet pruners.
  • Raised beds and containers cut down on bending.
  • Work in short spells and switch between tasks.
  • For crafts, use padded or built-up needles, pens and brushes, and take regular breaks.

Protecting your hands

Hands are often the joints most affected by daily tasks. Along with the principles above, many people find these helpful:

  • Keep hands warm in the mornings. Warm water or a heat pack can ease stiffness.
  • Do regular gentle hand exercises. See our hand exercises guide.
  • Ask about splints. Resting splints worn at night or working splints during the day can support painful wrists and thumbs.
  • Avoid pinching grips, such as carrying plates between thumb and fingers. Use a tray instead.

Getting help and equipment

An occupational therapist can assess how you manage at home and at work and suggest changes, splints and equipment. You can ask your GP, physiotherapist or rheumatology team for a referral, and some areas allow self-referral. Your local council's adult social care team can also arrange a needs assessment for equipment and home adaptations. Many small gadgets are available from pharmacies and online retailers, and some are free on loan through local services. Our guide to occupational therapy for hand pain explains more.

If you are buying equipment, try it first if you can. What helps one person may not suit another.

An example of pacing through the day

Joint protection works best when it is combined with pacing. Here is one way a morning might look for someone with sore hands and knees:

  • Loosen up with a warm shower and gentle hand and knee exercises before tackling anything demanding.
  • Prepare breakfast sitting on a perching stool, using a kettle tipper and a lightweight mug held in both hands.
  • Do 20 minutes of lighter housework, then sit down for a short break with a drink.
  • Split a bigger job, such as changing the bed, into two parts with a rest in between, or share it with someone else.
  • Go for a short walk later in the morning, once stiffness has eased.

Everyone's day is different. The aim is to spread demanding tasks out, switch between different types of activity, and rest before you are exhausted rather than after.

Bathroom and stairs

  • A raised toilet seat, toilet frame or grab rails make sitting and standing easier on knees and hips.
  • A bath board, bath seat or walk-in shower reduces the strain of getting in and out of the bath.
  • Use a long-handled sponge or back brush, and a towelling robe instead of drying with a towel.
  • Fit a second stair rail so you can use both hands, and keep a basket at the top and bottom of the stairs to save extra trips.
  • Your council's adult social care team can assess whether you need equipment or adaptations, and minor adaptations costing under £1,000 are usually provided free in England after an assessment.

Lifting and carrying with less strain

  1. Plan first. Is it too heavy? Can you split the load, use a trolley or ask for help?
  2. Get close. Stand close to the object with your feet hip-width apart.
  3. Bend your knees and hips rather than stooping from the waist, as far as is comfortable for your joints.
  4. Use both hands, palms up, and hold the load close to your body.
  5. Lift smoothly, avoid twisting, and turn by moving your feet.
  6. Carry less, more often. Two lighter bags, one in each hand or a backpack, are easier on joints than one heavy bag.

Techniques by joint

JointTryReduce
Hands and wristsPalms rather than fingers to push and lift; built-up handles; two-handed holds; keep wrists straightTight, sustained or pinching grips; twisting lids and taps with fingers; wringing cloths
KneesHigher chairs and a raised toilet seat; going up stairs with the stronger leg first and down with the more painful leg first; a perching stoolKneeling without a cushion, deep squatting, low seats, carrying heavy loads on stairs
HipsFirm chairs with arms; a long-handled shoehorn and grabber; sitting to dressLow sofas, crossing your legs, very long periods of standing
Back and neckWork at waist height; change position every 20 to 30 minutes; keep screens at eye levelBending and twisting together, long periods looking down, lifting from the floor
ShouldersStore everyday items between waist and shoulder height; use a step stool rather than reaching high; push rather than pullRepeated overhead reaching, carrying heavy bags on one side
Feet and anklesSupportive, cushioned footwear; insoles if advised by a podiatrist; sitting for tasks such as ironing and food preparationStanding for long periods, walking barefoot on hard floors

Posture and positioning

Staying in one position for a long time, even a comfortable one, increases stiffness. Aim to change position at least every 30 minutes. When sitting, choose a chair that lets your feet rest flat on the floor with your hips level with or slightly above your knees. A chair with arms makes standing up easier. At night, a pillow between the knees can be more comfortable for hip or knee pain when lying on your side. Avoid resting with a pillow under the knee for long periods, as this can encourage the knee to stiffen in a bent position.

Splints, supports and walking aids

A physiotherapist, occupational therapist or hand therapist can advise whether a splint or support might help you. Common options include:

  • Thumb splints for thumb-base arthritis, which NICE notes may help people with osteoarthritis of the thumb.
  • Wrist working splints to support the wrist during tasks.
  • Resting splints worn at night for inflamed hands and wrists.
  • Walking sticks, used in the hand opposite the painful hip or knee, to reduce load on the joint. Get the height checked so your elbow is slightly bent.
  • Insoles and supportive footwear for foot and ankle arthritis.

Use supports to make tasks easier, but keep up your exercises so muscles stay strong.

Joint protection during a flare

During a flare, joints are more vulnerable and fatigue is often worse. Extra steps can help:

  • Postpone heavy or non-essential tasks, and ask for help with the rest.
  • Use your gadgets and splints more, and rest the most inflamed joints in a comfortable position.
  • Keep gentle movement going so joints do not stiffen.
  • Use convenience options such as ready-prepared food or online shopping without guilt.
  • Rebuild your normal activities gradually as the flare settles.

Is it working?

After two or three weeks of using these techniques, ask yourself: Do everyday tasks hurt less? Do I have more energy left at the end of the day? Am I doing things I had stopped doing? If not, an occupational therapist can look at what you do and suggest more specific changes. If daily tasks are becoming difficult, you may also be entitled to support such as Personal Independence Payment.

When to get medical help

  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel unwell or have a high temperature.
  • See your GP if you have new joint swelling, morning stiffness that lasts more than 30 minutes, or pain that is steadily getting worse.
  • Ask for an occupational therapy or physiotherapy referral if you are struggling with daily tasks, dropping things, or worried about falls.
  • Contact your rheumatology team if you have inflammatory arthritis and frequent flares are making daily life harder.

Frequently asked questions

Does joint protection mean I should move less?

No. Joint protection is about reducing unnecessary strain, not avoiding activity. Regular exercise remains one of the most important treatments for arthritis.

Does joint protection work for osteoarthritis as well as rheumatoid arthritis?

Yes. The principles help with many types of arthritis, particularly in the hands, knees and hips.

Where can I get arthritis gadgets?

Pharmacies, mobility shops and online retailers sell many items. Occupational therapists and council adult social care teams can advise and may provide some equipment.

How do I know if I am overdoing it?

Pain or fatigue that lasts more than an hour or two after an activity, or is worse the next day, suggests you may need to pace differently.

Can I get an occupational therapy referral on the NHS?

Yes. Ask your GP, physiotherapist or rheumatology team. Some areas also allow self-referral.

Should I wear a splint all the time?

Usually not. Most splints are designed for specific tasks or for night-time. Wearing them all the time can weaken muscles. Follow the advice of the therapist who provided your splint.

Which hand should I use a walking stick in?

Usually the hand on the opposite side to your painful hip or knee. A physiotherapist can check the height and how you are using it.

Are arthritis gadgets available free?

Some equipment may be provided after an occupational therapy or council needs assessment. Many small items are inexpensive to buy, and VAT relief may apply to some equipment for people with a long-term condition.

article.excerpt: If you are navigating joint replacement decisions when frailty is already present, small steady habits usually beat all-or-nothing restarts.
article.content:
If you are navigating joint replacement decisions when frailty is already present, small steady habits usually beat all-or-nothing restarts. This guide covers surgery talks that include stamina, home and recovery when osteoarthritis affects hips or knees, with a focus on England and a GP surgery setting.

Quick answer: If you are navigating joint replacement decisions when frailty is already present, small steady habits usually beat all-or-nothing restarts. This guide covers surgery talks that include stamina, home and recovery when osteoarthritis affects hips or knees, with a focus on England and a GP surgery setting.

A flare in hips or knees can look like sudden frailty. True frailty is a wider loss of reserve: weaker recovery after a quiet week, an infection or a hospital night. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with surgery talks that include stamina, home and recovery, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in England.

Small, repeatable steps — not a reinvention

None of this is a gym challenge. The aim is to keep hips or knees moving, keep protein in the day, and keep surgery talks that include stamina, home and recovery from becoming the only story in the GP surgery. If a physiotherapist, occupational therapist or frailty team has already given you a plan, follow that ahead of a webpage.

  • If stairs are the bottleneck, get an occupational therapy conversation on the list while you temporarily live downstairs — drifting is how a camp-bed becomes a lifestyle.
  • Book eye, foot and hearing checks as frailty care, not vanity. Osteoarthritis already asks a lot of balance.
  • If cooking is the barrier, use tinned fish, eggs, yoghurt, beans or leftover protein foods rather than skipping meals. Muscle needs raw material as well as movement.
  • Treat a walking aid as joint protection and falls kit, not as a verdict. Wrist-friendly handles matter if hips or knees include hands.
  • Use heat for stiffness if your skin is healthy, but protect thin skin. Never fall asleep on a hot water bottle.
  • After a flare, restart the smallest version of your usual movement within comfort, rather than waiting to feel back to normal. Normal rarely sends an email.

Not 'just getting old': surgery talks that include stamina, home and recovery

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Painful hips or knees can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual osteoarthritis.

Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis. Only some also live with frailty. The practical question is not the label. It is whether surgery talks that include stamina, home and recovery is shrinking your GP surgery life — and what you can change this week without pretending pain is imaginary.

Living With Arthritis is an independent UK charity (1218461), not part of Arthritis UK. We write for patients and carers. We do not replace NHS England services via your GP.

Signs the overlap is affecting hips or knees

In a GP surgery, surgery talks that include stamina, home and recovery is rarely one dramatic collapse. It is usually a stack of small avoidances. People with osteoarthritis already know boom-and-bust. Frailty adds a longer payback: a quiet weekend can cost the following Thursday.

  • Carers doing the last steps of a task to be kind, which removes the last practice the muscles were getting.
  • Night toilet trips, poor lighting and stiff hips or knees stacking into a falls risk that nobody named.
  • New fear after a near-miss, even if you did not hit the floor. Fear of falling is itself a reason people sit more.
  • Shorter outdoor range, then shorter indoor range, then a GP surgery that has quietly rearranged itself around the chair.
  • Transfers that used to be boring — bed, chair, toilet, car — now need a pause, a push-up or a second person, especially when hips or knees are cold.

England services, without inventing a clinic

Start with your GP practice and NHS England services via your GP. For urgent but non-emergency advice use NHS 111. For chest pain, suspected hip fracture, sudden new weakness, or a fall with a bang to the head on blood thinners, use 999.

Tablets, topical options and what not to DIY

When to get help

  • Unplanned weight loss, repeated falls, or surgery talks that include stamina, home and recovery that is clearly worsening week by week — book the GP and say you are worried about frailty as well as hips or knees.
  • A knock to the head, especially if you take blood thinners — do not sleep it off as a plan.
  • Sudden confusion, new incontinence, or a crash in mobility over hours to days — think infection or delirium, not only arthritis.
  • If you cannot get to the surgery because of osteoarthritis, ask about a home visit or a proper phone review. Silence is not a care plan.

What should a carer do in the GP surgery without taking over?

Stand nearby for the risky bit, set the environment up (chair height, shoes, light), and leave the bits the person can still do. Taking over every transfer trains both of you into a hoist-by-default life. If moving and handling is already unsafe, stop DIY lifting and ask for a proper care and OT review.

Are painkillers the main treatment for frail osteoarthritis?

No. For osteoarthritis, NICE puts exercise, weight management where relevant, and topical options at the centre. Tablets may help some people some of the time, but in frail adults they need a hard look at stomach, kidneys, heart, constipation and falls. Never share someone else's medicines.

How do I tell an arthritis flare from a frailty slide?

A flare of osteoarthritis is usually more joint pain, stiffness or swelling in a known pattern. A frailty slide is broader: weaker recovery, smaller meals, more time in the chair, maybe confusion or falls. They can happen together. If the whole person is changing, do not only increase pain gel.
