article.title: Knee osteoarthritis: staying steady at home and avoiding falls (UK guide)
article.excerpt: Wobbly on sore knees at home? Safer rooms, strength and balance exercises, walking aids, night tips and what to do if you fall with knee osteoarthritis.
article.content:
If knee osteoarthritis makes you feel wobbly at home, the most useful things are usually stronger thigh muscles, a clutter-free and well-lit route between the rooms you use most, supportive shoes rather than loose slippers, and a walking aid that has been checked for your height. NICE recommends exercise for everyone with osteoarthritis and says walking aids such as a stick are worth considering for knee and hip osteoarthritis. Practise getting up from a chair and simple balance exercises on at least 2 days a week. If your knee keeps giving way, or you have had a fall, see a GP or ask about NHS physiotherapy or a falls service.

This guide is about staying steady indoors when your knees are sore. For the exercises themselves, see our knee exercises for osteoarthritis and sit-to-stand practice. If you have already had a fall, start with rebuilding confidence after a fall.

Why sore knees make you less steady

When a knee hurts, it is natural to move it less and to take shorter, more careful steps. Over time the big thigh muscles (the quadriceps) get weaker, and those are the muscles that stop the knee buckling when you stand, turn or go down a step. Stiffness first thing, a knee that feels like it might give way, and tiredness later in the day can all add up. The good news is that muscle strength and balance can improve at any age with regular practice.

Five changes that help most at home

  • Clear your main route. Walk the path you use most (chair to kitchen, bed to toilet) and move cables, loose rugs and clutter. The NHS also suggests mopping up spills straight away and using non-slip mats in the bathroom
  • Light it. Use bright bulbs on stairs and in hallways and a light you can reach from bed, or a plug-in night light on the way to the toilet
  • Wear proper shoes indoors. Well-fitting shoes or slippers with a back and a grippy sole are steadier than backless or worn-out slippers or socks on a hard floor
  • Put things within reach. Keep everyday items between waist and shoulder height so you are not bending low or stretching on tiptoe with sore knees
  • Have somewhere to hold. A grab rail by the toilet or bath, a second banister, or a sturdy piece of furniture at the turn of a room can make a big difference. An occupational therapist can advise

Strength and balance, a little and often

NICE guidance puts exercise at the centre of osteoarthritis care, and the NHS says adults aged 65 and over should do activities that improve strength, balance and flexibility on at least 2 days a week. For wobbly knees, the most useful are:

  • Sit-to-stand from a firm chair, using your hands at first if you need to — see sit-to-stand practice
  • Seated knee straightening — sit tall, slowly straighten one knee, hold for a moment, then lower
  • Heel raises and sideways leg lifts while holding a kitchen worktop
  • Simple balance practice with a worktop in reach, such as standing with one foot slightly in front of the other

Some discomfort while exercising is common with osteoarthritis and does not mean you are damaging your knee. If pain is clearly worse the next day, do a little less and build up more slowly. Our home exercises for knee pain and balance training guide have more ideas, and the Age UK falls prevention exercises are a good printed routine.

Walking aids and knee supports

NICE says walking aids such as walking sticks are worth considering for osteoarthritis in the hip or knee. A stick is usually held in the hand on the opposite side to the sore knee, and it needs to be the right height. A physiotherapist or occupational therapist can check this for you, and some NHS services lend walking aids. See choosing mobility aids. NICE does not recommend braces, supports or insoles for everyone with osteoarthritis, but they can help some people whose knee is unstable, so ask a physiotherapist before buying one.

Night-time and the toilet

Many wobbles happen at night, when knees are stiff and you are half asleep. Sit on the edge of the bed for a moment before you stand, put a light on, keep your walking aid by the bed, and leave the route to the toilet clear. If you get up several times a night to pass urine, mention it to your GP, as there may be things that help.

If you do fall

The NHS advises staying calm and taking a couple of minutes to check for pain or injury. If you feel able to get up, take your time: roll onto your side, push up onto your hands and knees, crawl to something stable such as a heavy chair, put one foot flat on the floor and stand up slowly, then sit and rest. Kneeling may be painful with knee osteoarthritis, so a cushion or folded towel under your knees can help. If you cannot get up, use a phone or personal alarm, or shout or bang on the floor for help, keep warm with anything you can reach, and keep moving your body. Our falls prevention guide explains personal alarms and planning ahead.

When to get help

  • See a GP after any fall, if your knee keeps giving way, or if you feel unsteady for no clear reason. Ask whether a falls service or NHS physiotherapy could help — in many areas you can refer yourself. See NHS physiotherapy and waiting lists
  • Ask for a medicines review if you feel dizzy or drowsy, as some tablets can affect balance. Do not stop prescribed medicines yourself — see medication reviews
  • Contact NHS 111 if your knee is suddenly hot, red and swollen, especially with a high temperature or feeling unwell
  • Call 999 if someone has fallen and cannot get up, may have hurt their head, neck, back or hip, cannot put weight on their leg, or is very unwell

Frequently asked questions

My knee gives way. Is it the arthritis?

Weak thigh muscles and pain are common reasons a knee with osteoarthritis feels like it is giving way, and strengthening often helps. A knee that locks, gives way after a twist or injury, or keeps buckling should be checked by a GP or physiotherapist.

Should I rest my knee to avoid falling?

Not completely. Resting a lot makes muscles weaker, which can make you less steady. Short rests during a bad day are fine, but keep up gentle movement and build up strength and balance over time.

Is it safe to use the stairs?

For most people, yes, with a rail and good lighting. Going up, lead with your stronger leg; coming down, lead with the sorer leg. If stairs feel unsafe, ask your council for a free care needs assessment, which can look at rails or other equipment.

article.title: Knee Replacement for Arthritis – UK Guide
article.excerpt: Considering a knee replacement for arthritis? UK guide to NHS eligibility, surgery types, waiting times, recovery timeline, and physiotherapy after surgery.
article.content:
Around 100,000 knee replacements are performed each year in the UK, most for osteoarthritis. It's one of the most successful operations in modern medicine, with over 95% of patients reporting significant pain relief. Here's what you need to know about the process in the UK.

Quick answer: Knee replacement is recommended when severe pain affects quality of life, non-surgical treatments fail, and X-rays show significant joint damage. Approximately 100,000 such operations are performed annually in the UK, mostly for osteoarthritis. Recovery typically involves 1-3 days in hospital, followed by physiotherapy. Most people return to light activities in 6-12 weeks, with maximum benefit achieved around 12 months.

When Is Knee Replacement Recommended?

Knee replacement is considered when:

  • Pain is severe and affecting your quality of life
  • Non-surgical treatments (exercise, weight loss, physiotherapy, injections) haven't provided sufficient relief
  • X-rays show significant joint damage
  • You have difficulty with daily activities like walking, climbing stairs, or sleeping

There's no strict age limit — suitability is based on need and overall health.

Types of Knee Replacement

  • Total knee replacement (TKR) — the entire joint surface is replaced. Most common type.
  • Partial (unicompartmental) knee replacement — only the damaged section is replaced. Smaller operation, faster recovery, but not suitable for everyone.
  • Revision surgery — replacing a worn-out previous replacement (less common).

NHS Waiting Times

Current NHS waiting times for knee replacement vary significantly by region:

  • England: average 6-12 months, some areas longer
  • Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland: similar variation
  • You can check hospital waiting times at nhs.uk
  • Remember: you have the right to choose your hospital in England

What to Expect

Before Surgery

  • Pre-assessment clinic — blood tests, ECG, general health check
  • "Prehab" exercises — strengthening exercises before surgery improve recovery
  • Optimise weight and stop smoking if applicable

The Operation

  • Usually under spinal anaesthetic (you're awake but numb from the waist down)
  • Takes approximately 1-2 hours
  • You'll usually stay in hospital for 1-3 days

Recovery Timeline

  • Weeks 1-2 — walking with crutches, starting physiotherapy exercises
  • Weeks 3-6 — increasing mobility, reducing crutch use
  • Weeks 6-12 — most people return to driving and light activities
  • 3-6 months — significant improvement in pain and function
  • 12 months — maximum benefit usually achieved

Physiotherapy After Surgery

Physiotherapy is crucial for a good outcome:

  • NHS physiotherapy is provided post-operatively
  • Exercises focus on regaining range of motion and strength
  • You'll be given a home exercise programme to follow daily
  • Consistency with exercises is the single biggest factor in recovery

Risks and Considerations

  • Infection risk: approximately 1-2%
  • Blood clot risk: reduced with medication and compression stockings
  • Implant lifespan: modern replacements last 20-25+ years
  • Stiffness: some people need manipulation under anaesthetic if the knee doesn't bend well

Knee replacement is a major decision. Discuss all your options with your orthopaedic surgeon, and remember that preparation and post-operative physiotherapy are key to the best outcomes.

Practical next steps for Knee Replacement for Arthritis – UK Guide

If you came here about Knee Replacement for Arthritis – UK Guide, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

Quick questions about Knee Replacement Arthritis Guide

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

Keep expectations kind while you work on knee replacement for arthritis – uk guide. Arthritis symptoms fluctuate; a quieter week does not mean you imagined earlier pain, and a flare does not mean every helpful habit has failed. Adjust one variable at a time so you can see what truly helps.

article.content:
For lasting power of attorney conversations in arthritis and frailty, Motion is lotion still applies: short honest movement, then rest that does not become a lifestyle. This article is about planning while you can still say what you want, written for people and carers in Wales, especially around a home.

Quick answer: For lasting power of attorney conversations in arthritis and frailty, Motion is lotion still applies: short honest movement, then rest that does not become a lifestyle. This article is about planning while you can still say what you want, written for people and carers in Wales, especially around a home.

In Wales, clinicians may talk about frailty as a syndrome. You may simply feel that arthritis with frailty has stolen bounce from ordinary home tasks. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with planning while you can still say what you want, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in Wales.

Pain, muscle and recovery: the Wales picture

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Pain in several joints can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual arthritis with frailty.

Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis. Only some also live with frailty. The practical question is not the label. It is whether planning while you can still say what you want is shrinking your home life — and what you can change this week without pretending pain is imaginary.

Living With Arthritis is an independent UK charity (1218461), not part of Arthritis UK. We write for patients and carers. We do not replace NHS Wales services via your GP and local health board.

A Wales day with arthritis with frailty and less reserve

In a home, planning while you can still say what you want is rarely one dramatic collapse. It is usually a stack of small avoidances. People with arthritis with frailty already know boom-and-bust. Frailty adds a longer payback: a quiet weekend can cost the following Thursday.

  • Transfers that used to be boring — bed, chair, toilet, car — now need a pause, a push-up or a second person, especially when several joints are cold.
  • A hospital or infection week that ends with clothes feeling looser and stairs feeling taller.
  • Carers doing the last steps of a task to be kind, which removes the last practice the muscles were getting.
  • New fear after a near-miss, even if you did not hit the floor. Fear of falling is itself a reason people sit more.
  • Night toilet trips, poor lighting and stiff several joints stacking into a falls risk that nobody named.

Practical self-management for planning while you can still say what you want

None of this is a gym challenge. The aim is to keep several joints moving, keep protein in the day, and keep planning while you can still say what you want from becoming the only story in the home. If a physiotherapist, occupational therapist or frailty team has already given you a plan, follow that ahead of a webpage.

  • Treat a walking aid as joint protection and falls kit, not as a verdict. Wrist-friendly handles matter if several joints include hands.
  • Keep a sit-to-stand practice at the height you actually use. A higher chair is not cheating if it lets several joints work without a panic haul.
  • If cooking is the barrier, use tinned fish, eggs, yoghurt, beans or leftover protein foods rather than skipping meals. Muscle needs raw material as well as movement.
  • If you live in a home, tell one other person the plan for a fall: who to call, where the spare key sits, whether you wear a pendant you can actually press.
  • Use heat for stiffness if your skin is healthy, but protect thin skin. Never fall asleep on a hot water bottle.
  • Plan the scariest transfer of the day — often the bathroom — with lighting, a rail conversation and unhurried time. Rushing with stiff several joints is how near-misses happen.

Making a home work harder for you

Most frailty lives in ordinary rooms. Rails, lighting, chair height, a kettle that does not demand a full kettle-lift, and a toilet you can get off again are treatment. Occupational therapy exists for this.

Who to talk to locally in Wales

When to get help

  • Chest pain, trouble breathing, or signs of a stroke — 999, not a wait for the arthritis with frailty nurse.
  • A hot, very swollen joint with fever, or feeling systemically unwell — seek urgent clinical advice. A joint infection is an emergency.
  • A knock to the head, especially if you take blood thinners — do not sleep it off as a plan.
  • Sudden confusion, new incontinence, or a crash in mobility over hours to days — think infection or delirium, not only arthritis.
  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.

Should I stop exercising during planning while you can still say what you want?

Complete rest for more than a short flare period usually makes several joints and muscle worse. Keep a smaller version: seated strength, indoor loops, or the two sit-to-stands you can still do. If exercise causes pain that spirals or a joint that will not settle, get clinical advice.

Are painkillers the main treatment for frail arthritis with frailty?

No. For osteoarthritis, NICE puts exercise, weight management where relevant, and topical options at the centre. Tablets may help some people some of the time, but in frail adults they need a hard look at stomach, kidneys, heart, constipation and falls. Never share someone else's medicines.

How do I tell an arthritis flare from a frailty slide?

A flare of arthritis with frailty is usually more joint pain, stiffness or swelling in a known pattern. A frailty slide is broader: weaker recovery, smaller meals, more time in the chair, maybe confusion or falls. They can happen together. If the whole person is changing, do not only increase pain gel.

article.title: Diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis later in life: the first months (UK guide)
article.excerpt: Diagnosed with RA later in life? What happens in the first months: tests, starting a DMARD, monthly checks, staying active and when to get help.
article.content:
Rheumatoid arthritis can start at any age, including in your 60s, 70s or later, and it is treated in the same way as at a younger age. In the first months you can expect blood tests and X-rays, a disease-modifying medicine (DMARD) such as methotrexate started as soon as possible, sometimes with a short course of steroids to help while it starts working, and regular checks — NICE recommends monthly checks of inflammation and disease activity until the arthritis is under control. DMARDs can take up to 12 weeks to work, so keep taking them. Keep moving gently every day, ask for a named contact and advice line number, and bring a full list of your other medicines to every appointment.

This guide is for people diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) later in life, and for the family members and carers supporting them, covering roughly the first 3 to 6 months. For a general starting point, see our newly diagnosed guide. For the medicine most people start on, see methotrexate in later life; for long-term check-ups, see RA monitoring in later life.

A diagnosis later in life is common, and treatable

Many people assume aching, stiff joints in later life are simply wear and tear. RA is different: the immune system attacks the lining of the joints, causing pain, swelling and stiffness, often with tiredness and feeling generally unwell. Being older does not mean you will be offered less. NICE recommends the same treat-to-target approach for every adult with RA: get the inflammation down to remission, or to low activity if remission is not possible, as early as you can, because that protects the joints.

It is normal to feel shocked, relieved, angry or low after a diagnosis — sometimes all in the same week. See feelings after an arthritis diagnosis.

What usually happens in the first weeks

  • Tests to set a baseline. NICE recommends a blood test for anti-CCP antibodies (if not already done), X-rays of the hands and feet, and a short questionnaire about everyday tasks, so later improvement can be measured. See how arthritis is diagnosed
  • Starting a DMARD. NICE recommends starting one disease-modifying medicine — methotrexate, leflunomide or sulfasalazine — as soon as possible, ideally within 3 months of persistent symptoms starting. Hydroxychloroquine may be used for milder RA
  • A short steroid "bridge". Your team may suggest a short course of steroid tablets or an injection to ease symptoms while the DMARD starts working
  • Safety checks before methotrexate. Blood tests of your blood count, liver and kidneys, and sometimes a chest X-ray and breathing test

Your first rheumatology appointments can feel rushed. Our guide to what to expect at a rheumatology appointment helps you prepare.

The first three months: checks and patience

NICE recommends that people with active RA have their CRP (a blood marker of inflammation) and a disease activity score such as DAS28 checked monthly by the specialist team until the target is reached. If the first medicine is not enough, the dose is usually increased, then another DMARD added. The NHS notes that some people try 2 or 3 medicines before finding the right one — this is normal, not a failure.

  • DMARDs can take up to 12 weeks to work. Keep taking them, even if you do not feel different yet
  • You will have regular blood tests to check the medicine is safe. If getting to them is hard, see getting to blood tests
  • Ask for a named contact (often a specialist nurse) and the advice line number — NICE says everyone with RA should know how to get rapid help for a flare

Your other medicines matter more now

Many people diagnosed later in life already take tablets for blood pressure, the heart, diabetes or bones. Bring a full, up-to-date list to every appointment, including things you buy yourself. Check with a pharmacist before taking any over-the-counter painkiller or supplement, as some interact with RA medicines — see painkillers in later life. If you are prescribed steroids for more than a short time, ask about protecting your bones; see bone protection on steroids. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.

Staying active from day one

Movement keeps joints mobile and muscles strong, and losing strength in the months around a diagnosis can make it harder to stay independent. The NHS advice for RA is to find a balance: rest inflamed joints when they are hot and swollen, but keep moving, because without movement joints stiffen and muscles weaken.

  • Try low-impact activity such as walking, swimming, cycling or chair-based exercise, and build up gradually. See chair-based exercise for RA and walking while on DMARDs
  • The NHS says older adults should also do activities that improve strength, balance and flexibility on at least 2 days a week. Sit-to-stand practice is a good start
  • If an activity makes your joints warm and swollen or causes severe pain, stop and rest, and try a gentler version next time
  • NICE says people with RA should have access to specialist physiotherapy, occupational therapy for everyday tasks and hand problems, and podiatry for foot problems. Ask your team for a referral

Tiredness, mood and pacing

Fatigue is one of the hardest parts of RA and often improves as the inflammation comes under control. Pacing — spreading tasks through the day and the week — helps. See managing RA fatigue in later life. If you feel low or anxious most days, tell your team or GP: NICE recommends psychological support to help people adjust to living with RA.

For family and carers

  • Come to the first few appointments if you can, and write down what is said
  • Help keep a simple diary of good and bad days, medicines and side effects
  • Help with transport to blood tests and reviews
  • Encourage daily movement rather than doing everything for the person — it protects their strength

Support and money

The NHS signposts two free helplines: the National Rheumatoid Arthritis Society (NRAS) on 0800 298 7650 and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) on 0800 5200 520. If you are over State Pension age and need help with personal care, you may be able to claim Attendance Allowance — see GOV.UK. In England, prescriptions are free from age 60.

When to get help

  • A flare that does not settle: phone your rheumatology advice line — see what to do in a flare
  • Signs of infection while on DMARDs (high temperature, sore throat, new cough): contact your GP, advice line or NHS 111 the same day
  • A single hot, very swollen joint with fever, or feeling very unwell: get urgent same-day help from NHS 111
  • Call 999 for chest pain, difficulty breathing, signs of a serious allergic reaction, or sudden confusion with being very unwell

Frequently asked questions

Is rheumatoid arthritis different when it starts later in life?

The condition and its treatment are the same. What is often different is that you may have other health conditions and medicines to fit around it, so a full medicines list and good communication with your GP matter more.

Am I too old for methotrexate or biologic medicines?

Age alone is not a reason to rule them out. Your team will weigh up your kidneys, liver, lungs, other medicines and preferences with you. Ask them to explain the options in a way that makes sense to you — NICE says they should.

How long until I feel better?

Some people feel steroid relief within days; DMARDs can take up to 12 weeks. Many people find the first few months the hardest, and things improve once the right treatment is found.

article.title: Leflunomide for Arthritis: Blood Tests, Side Effects and Tips
article.excerpt: A practical guide to leflunomide for rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis: how it works, what monitoring involves, common side effects, alcohol, pregnancy planning and when to seek help.
article.content:
Quick answer: Leflunomide is a disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) used for rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis. It usually takes one to three months to work. You will need regular blood tests plus blood pressure and weight checks. Common side effects include diarrhoea, feeling sick and hair thinning. Leflunomide stays in the body for a long time, so plan pregnancy carefully with your team. Never change your dose yourself.

What leflunomide does

Leflunomide is a tablet that slows down the activity of certain immune cells that drive inflammation in inflammatory arthritis. By calming this process it reduces joint pain, swelling and stiffness, and helps protect joints from long-term damage. It is used for rheumatoid arthritis and psoriatic arthritis, often when methotrexate is not suitable or has not worked well enough. It is sometimes combined with other treatments.

Like other DMARDs, it is a long-term treatment rather than a quick painkiller. Read our overview of DMARDs and biologics to see how the options compare.

Taking leflunomide

Leflunomide is taken as a tablet once a day, with or without food. Some teams start with a higher "loading" dose for a few days, but many do not, because it can increase side effects. Your team will decide what suits you. Take it exactly as your rheumatology team advises and never change the dose yourself. If you miss a dose, check your leaflet or ask a pharmacist.

How long until it works?

Most people notice a difference within four to six weeks, and the full effect can take up to three months or a little longer. During this time your team may offer steroids or anti-inflammatory painkillers to help with symptoms.

Monitoring: blood tests, blood pressure and weight

Leflunomide can affect the liver, blood cells and blood pressure, so regular checks are part of treatment. Before you start you will usually have baseline blood tests, a blood pressure reading and your weight recorded. After that, checks are frequent in the first months and then spaced out once things are stable. Your team or GP, under shared-care arrangements, will tell you your schedule. Typical checks are:

  • Full blood count.
  • Liver function tests.
  • Blood pressure, because leflunomide can raise it.
  • Weight, because some people lose weight on it.

Keeping your own record of results and blood pressure readings can help. A home blood pressure monitor is useful if your team suggests it.

Common side effects

Many people take leflunomide without problems. When side effects happen, they are often mild and more common in the early months. They can include:

  • Diarrhoea, feeling sick or tummy pain.
  • Raised blood pressure.
  • Headaches or dizziness.
  • Hair thinning, which usually improves and may reverse after stopping.
  • Rash or itchy skin.
  • Mouth ulcers.
  • Tingling or numbness in the hands or feet, which you should report.
  • Weight loss.

If diarrhoea or other side effects are bothering you, talk to your team rather than just stopping. There are often ways to help, and stopping suddenly can let your arthritis flare.

When to get urgent advice

Contact your GP or rheumatology advice line the same day, or call NHS 111, if you have:

  • A fever, sore throat, chills or other signs of infection.
  • Unexplained bruising, bleeding or looking very pale.
  • Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine or pain in the upper right of your tummy.
  • A new cough or breathlessness.
  • A severe rash, blistering or mouth sores.

Call 999 if you have signs of a severe allergic reaction, such as swelling of the face or throat or difficulty breathing.

Alcohol

Because leflunomide and alcohol can both affect the liver, you will usually be advised to keep alcohol low, and your team may give you a specific limit. Follow their advice. Our guide to arthritis and alcohol explains more.

Pregnancy, fathering a child and the washout

Leflunomide is not safe in pregnancy. It also stays in the body for a long time after the last tablet, sometimes up to two years. That means family planning needs careful thought:

  • Use reliable contraception while taking leflunomide and for as long afterwards as your team advises.
  • If you are thinking about pregnancy, talk to your team well in advance. They can arrange a "washout", where another medicine is taken to clear leflunomide from the body more quickly, followed by blood tests to confirm levels are low enough.
  • Men who are planning to father a child are usually advised to discuss stopping leflunomide and having a washout too.
  • If you become pregnant unexpectedly, contact your team straight away. Do not just stop the tablets without speaking to them.

Our guide to arthritis and pregnancy covers planning in more detail. The long stay in the body also matters if you have serious side effects, as a washout can be used to speed up clearance.

Infections and vaccines

Leflunomide can make you slightly more prone to infections. Wash your hands regularly, keep up to date with the vaccines your team recommends, and seek advice early if you feel unwell with an infection. Live vaccines are generally avoided while you take leflunomide. Read our guide to vaccines on DMARDs and biologics.

Other medicines

Leflunomide can interact with some other medicines, including some that affect the liver or blood. Always tell pharmacists, dentists and doctors that you take it, and check before starting new prescriptions, over-the-counter remedies or supplements. See our guide to medicine and supplement interactions.

If it is not working, or you need to stop

Not every medicine suits every person. If leflunomide has not helped enough after a fair trial, or side effects are a problem, your team may adjust the dose, add another medicine or switch to a different treatment, such as another DMARD or a biologic. Stopping should be planned with your team, because inflammation can return quickly without treatment. Our guide to stopping arthritis medicines safely explains why. If you are worried about taking leflunomide long term, raise it at your next review or call your advice line. Your concerns matter, and there is usually more than one option.

Frequently asked questions

How long does leflunomide take to work?

Most people notice some benefit in four to six weeks, with the full effect taking up to three months or a little longer.

Can I drink alcohol on leflunomide?

You will usually be advised to keep alcohol to a low level because both can affect the liver. Follow the limit your rheumatology team gives you.

Why does leflunomide need a washout?

Leflunomide stays in the body for a long time. A washout uses another medicine to remove it faster, for example before a planned pregnancy or after a serious side effect.

Does leflunomide cause hair loss?

Some people notice hair thinning. It is often mild and usually improves over time or after stopping. Mention it to your team.

Why do I need blood pressure checks on leflunomide?

Families often notice arthritis with frailty first as a slower walk across a community class, then as a person who starts declining invitations. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. None of this is a gym challenge. The aim is to keep several joints moving, keep protein in the day, and keep a seated destination with toilets and benches from becoming the only story in the community class. If a physiotherapist, occupational therapist or frailty team has already given you a plan, follow that ahead of a webpage.

  • Use heat for stiffness if your skin is healthy, but protect thin skin. Never fall asleep on a hot water bottle.
  • Carers: help the last 20 percent of a task, not the first 80, unless pain or safety says otherwise. Practice is treatment for frailty.
  • In England, ask your local council's adult social care team (the Care Act) about equipment and care options. Descriptions of grants and benefits here are not predictions of an award.
  • After a flare, restart the smallest version of your usual movement within comfort, rather than waiting to feel back to normal. Normal rarely sends an email.
  • Set an indoor walking loop with places to pause. Pain in several joints prefer several short bouts to one heroic corridor.
  • Keep a sit-to-stand practice at the height you actually use. A higher chair is not cheating if it lets several joints work without a panic haul.

Pain, muscle and recovery: the England picture

NICE is clear that exercise is core care for osteoarthritis, not an optional extra after tablets. That still holds if you are becoming frailer, but the dose must respect today's several joints and today's energy. Rest has a place in a flare; rest as a lifestyle is how deconditioning joins the diagnosis.

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Pain in several joints can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual arthritis with frailty.

Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis. Only some also live with frailty. The practical question is not the label. In a community class, a seated destination with toilets and benches is rarely one dramatic collapse. It is usually a stack of small avoidances. People with arthritis with frailty already know boom-and-bust. Frailty adds a longer payback: a quiet weekend can cost the following Thursday.

  • Carers doing the last steps of a task to be kind, which removes the last practice the muscles were getting.
  • A flare of arthritis with frailty that lasts, then a slower baseline even when the flare eases.
  • New fear after a near-miss, even if you did not hit the floor. Fear of falling is itself a reason people sit more.
  • Skipping meals or drinks because getting to the kitchen with sore several joints feels like a project.
  • Night toilet trips, poor lighting and stiff several joints stacking into a falls risk that nobody named.

GP, 111 or 999?

This is not personal medical advice. When several joints and frailty overlap, wait until Monday is sometimes right and sometimes dangerous. If you are unsure, NHS 111 can help you choose. Living With Arthritis cannot triage you.

  • Unplanned weight loss, repeated falls, or a seated destination with toilets and benches that is clearly worsening week by week — book the GP and say you are worried about frailty as well as several joints.
  • If you cannot get to the surgery because of arthritis with frailty, ask about a home visit or a proper phone review. Silence is not a care plan.
  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.

Are painkillers the main treatment for frail arthritis with frailty?

No. For osteoarthritis, NICE puts exercise, weight management where relevant, and topical options at the centre. Tablets may help some people some of the time, but in frail adults they need a hard look at stomach, kidneys, heart, constipation and falls. Never share someone else's medicines.

Complete rest for more than a short flare period usually makes several joints and muscle worse. Keep a smaller version: seated strength, indoor loops, or the two sit-to-stands you can still do. If exercise causes pain that spirals or a joint that will not settle, get clinical advice.

Nobody honest can promise that. These are legal tests about how your difficulties affect daily living or personal care, not about a diagnosis name. Quick answer: If walking, rising and recovering all feel harder, arthritis and frailty may be overlapping even without a formal label. This UK guide looks at isolation after walking range shrinks in a home setting, with practical steps, warning signs and Scotland services. It is general information, not personal medical advice.

Picture the moment in a home when your several joints refuse a simple transfer and you feel your confidence drop faster than the pain score. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with isolation after walking range shrinks, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in Scotland.

Pain, muscle and recovery: the Scotland picture

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Pain in several joints can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual arthritis with frailty.

Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis. Only some also live with frailty. The practical question is not the label. It is whether isolation after walking range shrinks is shrinking your home life — and what you can change this week without pretending pain is imaginary.

Living With Arthritis is an independent UK charity (1218461), not part of Arthritis UK. We write for patients and carers. We do not replace NHS Scotland services via your GP and Health and Social Care Partnership.

The mental load of isolation after walking range shrinks

After a fall or a flare of arthritis with frailty, people often need a deliberate confidence plan: one accompanied walk, one visitor, one practised transfer, not a lecture about positive thinking.

NHS talking therapies and social prescribing exist in many parts of Scotland. They are allowed to be for older people with long-term conditions. If low mood, poor sleep or loss of interest last more than a couple of weeks, tell the GP. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, that is urgent — use NHS 24 on 111 or 999.

Carers' mood matters as well. A household cannot run on one exhausted person hauling another off the toilet. A carer's assessment is a practical tool, not a betrayal.

Self-management that respects arthritis with frailty

  • If stairs are the bottleneck, get an occupational therapy conversation on the list while you temporarily live downstairs — drifting is how a camp-bed becomes a lifestyle.
  • Put the items you use at dawn — tablets, glasses, walking aid, phone — where you can reach them without a stretch that wrenches several joints.
  • If cooking is the barrier, use tinned fish, eggs, yoghurt, beans or leftover protein foods rather than skipping meals. Muscle needs raw material as well as movement.
  • Plan the scariest transfer of the day — often the bathroom — with lighting, a rail conversation and unhurried time. Rushing with stiff several joints is how near-misses happen.
  • Use heat for stiffness if your skin is healthy, but protect thin skin. Never fall asleep on a hot water bottle.
  • Book eye, foot and hearing checks as frailty care, not vanity. Arthritis with frailty already asks a lot of balance.

What this can look like in a home

  • A hospital or infection week that ends with clothes feeling looser and stairs feeling taller.
  • A flare of arthritis with frailty that lasts, then a slower baseline even when the flare eases.
  • Shorter outdoor range, then shorter indoor range, then a home that has quietly rearranged itself around the chair.
  • Carers doing the last steps of a task to be kind, which removes the last practice the muscles were getting.
  • Night toilet trips, poor lighting and stiff several joints stacking into a falls risk that nobody named.

Who to talk to locally in Scotland

GP, 111 or 999?

This is not personal medical advice. When several joints and frailty overlap, wait until Monday is sometimes right and sometimes dangerous. If you are unsure, NHS 24 on 111 can help you choose. Living With Arthritis cannot triage you.

  • Sudden confusion, new incontinence, or a crash in mobility over hours to days — think infection or delirium, not only arthritis.
  • If you cannot get to the surgery because of arthritis with frailty, ask about a home visit or a proper phone review. Silence is not a care plan.
  • Unplanned weight loss, repeated falls, or isolation after walking range shrinks that is clearly worsening week by week — book the GP and say you are worried about frailty as well as several joints.
  • A hot, very swollen joint with fever, or feeling systemically unwell — seek urgent clinical advice. A joint infection is an emergency.
  • Chest pain, trouble breathing, or signs of a stroke — 999, not a wait for the arthritis with frailty nurse.

Should I stop exercising during isolation after walking range shrinks?

Complete rest for more than a short flare period usually makes several joints and muscle worse. Keep a smaller version: seated strength, indoor loops, or the two sit-to-stands you can still do. If exercise causes pain that spirals or a joint that will not settle, get clinical advice.

How do I tell an arthritis flare from a frailty slide?

A flare of arthritis with frailty is usually more joint pain, stiffness or swelling in a known pattern. A frailty slide is broader: weaker recovery, smaller meals, more time in the chair, maybe confusion or falls. They can happen together. If the whole person is changing, do not only increase pain gel.

Are painkillers the main treatment for frail arthritis with frailty?

No. For osteoarthritis, NICE puts exercise, weight management where relevant, and topical options at the centre. Tablets may help some people some of the time, but in frail adults they need a hard look at stomach, kidneys, heart, constipation and falls. Never share someone else's medicines.

article.content:
Quick answer: Mediterranean diet, social connection, strength training, sleep and stress management — the evidence stack.

What the evidence says

5 Longevity Habits That Help People With Arthritis Live Longer is one of the most discussed challenges in UK arthritis care. Recent reviews — including NICE guidance and Cochrane summaries — point to a clear pattern: small, consistent changes beat heroic one-off efforts.

Why this matters for prevention & longevity

People living with arthritis report that prevention & longevity is a daily reality, not a "nice to have". When this area is well-managed, pain scores drop, function improves, and flare frequency falls. When it's ignored, the opposite happens — and the costs compound over months.

A simple framework you can use this week

  1. Notice — track one specific factor for three days (e.g. pain after activity, sleep hours, stress level).
  2. Adjust — change one variable at a time so you can see what's actually working.
  3. Review — after a week, compare notes. Keep what helps, drop what doesn't.

What UK clinicians recommend

NHS physiotherapists and rheumatology nurses we work with consistently highlight:

  • Pacing over pushing — short, frequent activity beats long, intense sessions.
  • Heat for stiffness, cold for swelling — applied in 15-minute windows.
  • Social support — patients with strong networks report 25% less pain interference.
  • Professional guidance early — don't wait for things to "settle on their own".

Common myths to ignore

  • "Rest is always best." Not true — appropriate movement is medicine.
  • "It's all in your head." Pain is real; psychology helps because the brain processes pain, not because the pain is imaginary.
  • "Nothing can be done." Modern arthritis care offers dozens of options, from biologics to mindfulness.

Frequently asked questions

Is this approach safe for everyone? Most healthy adults with arthritis can apply these principles, but always check with your GP or rheumatologist if you have other conditions, take immunosuppressants, or have had recent surgery.

How long until I see a difference? Most patients notice small improvements within 2–3 weeks of consistent practice. Larger changes — function, sleep quality, mood — typically appear at 6–8 weeks.

Where can I learn more? Visit our arthritis support hub and exercise library for hundreds of free, UK-focused resources.

It is general information and not a substitute for personalised medical advice.

In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Cross-check major decisions with NHS.uk, your clinical team, and NICE guidance summaries where relevant. Be wary of social posts that promise reversal of arthritis or attack standard medicines without evidence.

Treat articles like this as a starting map, not a personal care plan. Highlight one idea to try for two weeks, then review. If symptoms are new, rapidly worsening, or affecting several joints with fever or unexplained weight loss, contact your GP promptly rather than waiting on self-help alone.

Talking with your clinician

Bring the bottle or a photo to pharmacy or clinic appointments. Pharmacists can flag interactions with methotrexate, anticoagulants and other common arthritis medicines. Document start dates so you and your team can judge benefit honestly after several weeks.

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Quick answer: Lower back stiffness after sitting can stem from various factors, including the condition of joint cartilage, synovial fluid, ligaments, muscles, and nerves. Inflammatory arthritis typically worsens with rest, while degenerative arthritis worsens with prolonged use. Gentle movement and structured exercise, around 150 minutes weekly, often help. Other beneficial approaches include anti-inflammatory eating, weight management, heat applications, and ensuring adequate sleep.

What this guide covers

This piece summarises what the current evidence says about lower back stiffness: why it is worse after sitting, the practical steps that help most, and the red flags that mean you should speak to your GP or physiotherapist.

The underlying mechanism

Arthritis pain rarely has a single cause. Joint cartilage, synovial fluid, ligaments, surrounding muscle and the nervous system all contribute. Understanding which of these is driving your specific symptom is the first step toward targeted relief. For an in-depth condition overview, see our related guide.

Inflammatory and degenerative forms behave differently. Inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid, psoriatic, ankylosing spondylitis) typically worsens with rest and improves with gentle movement. Degenerative arthritis (osteoarthritis) typically worsens with prolonged use. Knowing which pattern matches your day-to-day experience helps you choose the right management approach.

What helps — by strength of evidence

  1. Movement and graded exercise. NICE NG226 (2022) and Cochrane reviews place structured exercise as a first-line treatment. Aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, split into 20–30 minute sessions.
  2. Anti-inflammatory eating. A Mediterranean-style pattern — oily fish twice a week, plenty of vegetables, olive oil, whole grains — is linked to reduced pain scores in OA and RA trials.
  3. Weight management. A 5 percent reduction in body weight reduces knee-OA symptoms measurably; a 10 percent reduction can match the effect of some medications.
  4. Heat and cold. Heat eases stiffness; cold eases acute swelling. Twenty-minute applications, with a towel barrier.
  5. Sleep hygiene. Pain perception rises sharply on fewer than six hours of sleep. Prioritise a consistent bedtime.

A practical seven-day starting plan

Begin with the smallest dose that feels manageable — five minutes of movement, one anti-inflammatory meal a day, a 10 pm screen-off rule. Track only three things weekly: pain on waking (0–10), longest pain-free interval, and one functional win (e.g., climbed stairs without grabbing the rail). Small, consistent inputs outperform big sporadic efforts.

When to seek clinical advice

Book an appointment with your GP or a first-contact physiotherapist if you notice: sudden hot, red, swollen joints; unexplained weight loss alongside joint pain; morning stiffness lasting longer than an hour for more than two weeks; or new numbness or weakness. These can signal inflammatory disease that benefits from early treatment.

Will this approach work alongside my medication? Yes. Exercise, diet and pacing complement prescribed treatments and often improve their effectiveness. Always check with your prescriber before stopping any medication.

How long until I notice a difference? Most people report meaningful improvement at 6–12 weeks of consistent practice. Earlier wins (less morning stiffness, better sleep) often appear within 2–3 weeks.

Is this safe if I have other conditions? The principles above are broadly safe for adults with stable cardiovascular, metabolic and respiratory conditions. If you are unsure, ask your GP for a referral to a first-contact physiotherapist for a tailored plan.

article.title: Acupuncture for Arthritis
article.excerpt: Does acupuncture help arthritis? What NICE says for osteoarthritis, back pain and chronic pain, NHS access, safety, costs and better first steps in the UK.
article.content:
Acupuncture is not recommended by NICE as a treatment for osteoarthritis, and it is not usually offered on the NHS for arthritis. Some people say it eases pain for a short time, and NICE does allow a single course of acupuncture to be considered for chronic primary pain. But exercise, weight management and good pain-relief planning remain the treatments with the strongest backing.

What acupuncture is

Acupuncture involves placing very fine, sterile needles into the skin at chosen points. It comes from traditional Chinese medicine. In the UK it is also practised by some physiotherapists and doctors, who often call it "dry needling" or "Western medical acupuncture". They explain any effect in terms of nerves and pain signals, not energy flow.

A session usually lasts 20 to 40 minutes. Most people feel a brief prick, then a dull ache or tingling around the needle. A course is typically several weekly sessions.

What UK guidance says

NICE's osteoarthritis guideline (NG226) says do not offer acupuncture or dry needling for osteoarthritis. The evidence did not show a meaningful benefit over sham (pretend) acupuncture.

For low back pain and sciatica, NICE (NG59) also advises against acupuncture.

For chronic primary pain, meaning long-term pain with no clear underlying cause such as fibromyalgia, NICE (NG193) says a single course of acupuncture can be considered. It should be delivered by a trained practitioner, within a defined course and in a community setting. This guidance does not cover pain caused by arthritis damage itself, but some people with arthritis also have widespread pain that falls under it.

Why some people still feel it helps

People's experiences vary, and short-term relief is real for some. Possible reasons include:

  • the relaxing setting and one-to-one time
  • distraction and a change in how the nervous system processes pain
  • natural ups and downs in arthritis pain, so improvement may happen anyway
  • expectation, which genuinely affects how much pain we feel

None of this makes acupuncture harmful. It means it is best treated as an optional extra rather than a replacement for proven care.

Is it safe?

In trained hands acupuncture is generally low risk. Common minor effects are small bruises, soreness or feeling light-headed. Talk to your GP or rheumatology team first if you:

  • take blood thinners such as warfarin or a DOAC, or have a bleeding disorder
  • take biologics, methotrexate or steroids, which can raise your infection risk
  • have a pacemaker (some practitioners use electro-acupuncture)
  • are pregnant
  • have lymphoedema or a joint replacement near the treatment area

Practitioners should use single-use needles. Choose someone registered with a professional body, or a physiotherapist registered with the HCPC.

Cost and access in the UK

Acupuncture for arthritis is rarely available on the NHS. Some NHS physiotherapy and pain services offer it for other conditions. Privately, prices vary by area and practitioner. Ask for the full cost of a course before you start, and set yourself a review point. If you notice no real change after three or four sessions, it is reasonable to stop.

What to try first

If you are thinking about acupuncture because your pain is not well controlled, these steps are recommended by NICE and are often more effective:

  • Regular, tailored exercise. Strengthening and general activity is the core treatment for osteoarthritis. A physiotherapist can build a plan around your joints.
  • Weight management. If you are carrying extra weight, losing some reduces load on knees and hips.
  • A pain-relief review. Topical anti-inflammatory gels for knee and hand osteoarthritis are often overlooked. Your pharmacist can advise.
  • Heat, cold and pacing. These are simple ways to calm flare-ups at home.
  • TENS. Some people find it useful for short-term relief at home after a one-off cost.

If you have inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis, the most important treatment is disease-modifying medicine prescribed by your rheumatology team. Acupuncture will not control inflammation or prevent joint damage.

Questions to ask before booking

  • What training and registration do you have?
  • How many sessions do you suggest, and what will it cost in total?
  • How will we judge whether it is working?
  • Do you need to know about my medicines?

Keep a short pain diary before and during the course. It will show you honestly whether it is worth continuing.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Ankylosing Spondylitis: Symptoms and Management
article.excerpt: Ankylosing spondylitis explained: inflammatory back pain signs, how it's diagnosed, NHS treatments from exercise to biologics, and red flags such as uveitis.
article.content:
Ankylosing spondylitis (AS), now often called axial spondyloarthritis, is a long-term inflammatory condition that mainly affects the spine and the joints where the spine meets the pelvis. The classic sign is back pain and stiffness that started before 45, has lasted more than three months, is worse at rest and in the morning, and improves with movement. Daily exercise and medicines can control it well.

Who gets it

AS usually starts in late teens to early 40s. It affects both men and women, although women are often diagnosed later. Many people carry a gene called HLA-B27, but having the gene does not mean you will get AS.

Inflammatory back pain: how it is different

Most back pain is mechanical: it is worse with activity and better with rest. Inflammatory back pain is the opposite:

  • it is worse after rest and in the second half of the night
  • it improves with exercise
  • morning stiffness lasts more than 30 minutes
  • it may wake you in the night
  • there may be pain in the buttocks, sometimes switching sides
  • anti-inflammatory painkillers often help noticeably

Other symptoms

  • pain and swelling in other joints, such as hips, knees or ankles
  • heel pain and pain where tendons attach to bone
  • fatigue
  • uveitis: a painful red eye with blurred vision and light sensitivity. This needs same-day assessment at an eye unit or A&E.
  • links with psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease

Diagnosis

Diagnosis is often delayed because back pain is so common. NICE (NG65) advises GPs to consider referring people with back pain that started before 45 and has lasted over three months to rheumatology if they have features of inflammatory back pain. Tests may include blood tests for inflammation and HLA-B27, and an MRI scan of the pelvis and spine. X-rays may be normal early on.

Treatment

Exercise and physiotherapy. This is central to AS treatment. Daily stretching, posture work, breathing exercises and strengthening help maintain movement. Hydrotherapy can be especially helpful. Many areas run group sessions.

NSAIDs. Anti-inflammatory painkillers are usually the first medicine tried and often work well. Your doctor will check they are safe for you and may add stomach protection.

Biologics and targeted therapies. If NSAIDs do not control symptoms, you may be offered anti-TNF or anti-IL-17 medicines, or a JAK inhibitor, under NICE criteria.

Steroid injections may help a painful joint outside the spine.

Surgery is rarely needed but may include hip replacement if the hip is badly affected.

Living well with AS

  • move every day. Gentle stretches each morning and a longer session several times a week.
  • mind your posture. Sit upright, use a supportive chair and take regular breaks from sitting.
  • stop smoking. It is linked with more severe AS and reduced lung function.
  • sleep on a firm, supportive mattress, with a thin pillow if possible.
  • stay active in sport you enjoy. Swimming is especially good.

Complications to be aware of

Over time, AS can cause the spine to become stiffer and, in some people, bones may fuse. Treatment and exercise reduce this risk. AS also increases the risk of osteoporosis and spinal fractures, which can occur after minor falls. New severe back or neck pain after a fall needs urgent assessment.

Work and support

Many people with AS work full-time. Regular movement breaks, a good chair and desk set-up and flexible hours help. Peer support groups and national charities run exercise sessions and information for people with AS.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • new numbness around your bottom or genitals, problems controlling your bladder or bowels, or new weakness in your legs
  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Arthritis Myths vs Facts
article.excerpt: Common arthritis myths checked against NHS and NICE guidance: exercise, weather, diet, cracking knuckles, age, rest and whether arthritis can be helped.
article.content:
Many common beliefs about arthritis are wrong, and some stop people getting help. Arthritis is not just an old person's condition, exercise does not wear joints out, and there is a lot that can be done to reduce pain. Here we check ten common myths against NHS and NICE guidance.

Myth 1: Arthritis is just part of getting old

Fact: Osteoarthritis does become more common with age, but it is not inevitable, and many older people never develop painful arthritis. Other types, such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis, often start in young or middle-aged adults. Children can get arthritis too. Joint pain at any age deserves proper assessment.

Myth 2: Exercise will wear out my joints

Fact: The opposite is true. NICE (NG226) recommends exercise as a core treatment for osteoarthritis. Moving joints helps keep cartilage healthy, and stronger muscles take load off painful joints. Some aching when you start is normal and does not mean you are causing damage. Start gently and build up.

Myth 3: Rest is the best treatment

Fact: Short rest during a bad flare can help, but long periods of rest make joints stiffer and muscles weaker, which tends to increase pain. Pacing, meaning a steady amount of activity each day, works better than lots of rest followed by bursts of activity.

Myth 4: Cracking your knuckles causes arthritis

Fact: There is no good evidence that knuckle cracking causes arthritis. The sound comes from gas bubbles in the joint fluid. Painless clicking is very common and usually harmless. Clicking with pain, swelling or locking should be checked.

Myth 5: Nothing can be done about arthritis

Fact: There is no cure for most types, but there is a great deal that helps. Exercise, weight management, physiotherapy, pain relief, aids and adaptations and, if needed, joint replacement all help osteoarthritis. For inflammatory arthritis, disease-modifying medicines and biologics can control the condition and prevent damage, and many people reach remission.

Myth 6: Diet can cure arthritis

Fact: No diet cures arthritis. A healthy, balanced diet supports overall health, and losing weight if you are overweight reduces strain on hips and knees. In gout, cutting down on alcohol, sugary drinks and some foods can help reduce attacks. Be wary of products or plans that promise to cure arthritis, and check supplements with your pharmacist, as some interact with medicines.

Myth 7: Arthritis only affects joints

Fact: Inflammatory types can affect the whole body. Rheumatoid arthritis can cause fatigue and affect the lungs, eyes and heart. Lupus can affect skin, kidneys and blood. Even osteoarthritis can affect sleep, mood and work. Good care looks at the whole person.

Myth 8: The weather causes arthritis

Fact: Weather does not cause arthritis. Some people notice their joints feel worse in cold or damp weather, and that experience is real. Keeping warm and active can help. Moving to a sunnier place will not cure arthritis.

Myth 9: If my X-ray looks bad, I must be in a lot of pain

Fact: X-ray changes and pain often do not match. Some people have major changes on X-ray with little pain, and others have severe pain with mild changes. NICE says osteoarthritis can usually be diagnosed without an X-ray. Treatment is guided by your symptoms and how they affect your life, not just a scan.

Myth 10: Joint replacement is the only real answer

Fact: Surgery helps many people with severe hip or knee osteoarthritis, but most people manage well without it. NICE recommends trying exercise, weight management and other non-surgical treatments first. Surgery is considered when symptoms seriously affect quality of life despite these.

Myth 11: Young people do not get arthritis

Fact: Children and young people can develop juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and inflammatory arthritis often starts in people in their twenties and thirties. Sports injuries can also lead to osteoarthritis earlier in life.

Why the myths matter

Believing these myths can lead people to stop moving, delay seeing a doctor or spend money on treatments that do not work. If you are unsure about something you have heard, ask your GP, pharmacist or physiotherapist. Reliable sources include the NHS website and NICE guidance.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Best Exercise for Rheumatoid Arthritis
article.excerpt: The best exercise for rheumatoid arthritis: strength, aerobic, flexibility and hand exercises, how to exercise around flares, and NHS physio support.
article.content:
The best exercise for rheumatoid arthritis is a mix: regular low-impact aerobic activity such as walking, swimming or cycling, strengthening exercises two or more days a week, and daily gentle stretches for stiff joints. Exercise does not make RA worse. It reduces pain, stiffness and fatigue and protects your heart. During a flare, scale it back rather than stopping completely.

Why exercise matters in RA

RA affects much more than joints. It increases the risk of heart disease, can cause muscle loss and often brings heavy fatigue. Regular activity helps with all of these. NICE (NG100) recommends that adults with RA have access to physiotherapy to improve fitness and encourage regular exercise.

Aerobic exercise

This is activity that makes you breathe a little faster and feel warmer.

  • walking — the easiest place to start. Try short walks most days and build up gradually.
  • swimming or water exercise — warm water eases stiffness and supports your weight
  • cycling — a static bike at home or gentle rides outdoors
  • dancing or exercise classes designed for people with joint problems

The UK Chief Medical Officers suggest aiming for 150 minutes of moderate activity a week. You can work towards this in short chunks of 10 minutes or more.

Strengthening

Stronger muscles support and protect your joints. Include strengthening on at least two days a week.

  • sit to stand from a chair
  • wall press-ups
  • step-ups on the bottom stair, holding the banister
  • resistance band exercises for shoulders, arms and legs
  • light hand weights or tins of food

Start with a weight you can lift 10 to 15 times comfortably and add more as you get stronger.

Flexibility and range of movement

Gentle stretches, ideally every day, help keep joints moving. Tai chi, yoga and Pilates can help with flexibility and balance. Tell the instructor about your RA and choose a gentle class.

Hand exercises

Hands are often affected in RA. Simple exercises include making a gentle fist, touching each fingertip to your thumb, and spreading your fingers flat on a table. An occupational therapist or hand therapist can give you a tailored programme and advise on splints.

Exercising around flares

During a flare:

  • rest inflamed joints but keep gently moving them through their range a few times a day to prevent stiffness
  • switch to gentler activity, such as short walks or water exercise
  • avoid strengthening the flaring joint until swelling settles
  • build back up gradually once the flare eases

Use the two-hour pain rule: if pain is noticeably worse two hours after exercise, do a little less next time.

Safety tips

  • warm up for five to ten minutes and cool down afterwards
  • choose supportive footwear
  • if your neck is affected by RA, avoid exercises that put pressure on the neck and tell instructors
  • if you take steroids long-term or have osteoporosis, ask about safe exercise for your bones
  • infection risk is higher on some medicines. Keep water bottles and kit clean.

Getting started

If you are new to exercise or worried about your joints, ask your rheumatology team for a physiotherapy referral, or check whether you can self-refer locally. Many leisure centres run classes for people with long-term conditions. Pick activities you enjoy, as you are more likely to keep them up.

Keeping motivated

Set small goals, such as walking to the end of the road and back each day this week. Exercise with a friend, join a class or use a simple activity tracker. Remember that the benefits of exercise build over weeks, so give it time.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Can Arthritis Be Prevented?
article.excerpt: Can you prevent arthritis? The risk factors you can change, such as weight, injury, smoking and activity, the ones you can't, and how to protect your joints.
article.content:
You cannot always prevent arthritis, because some risk factors such as age, genes and sex cannot be changed. But you can lower your risk of some types, especially osteoarthritis and gout, and reduce how much arthritis affects you if you do develop it. The most useful steps are keeping to a healthy weight, staying active, protecting your joints from injury and not smoking.

Risk factors you cannot change

  • age: osteoarthritis becomes more common over 45
  • sex: osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis are more common in women, gout in men
  • genes and family history: some types run in families
  • past joint problems present from birth or childhood

Knowing these does not mean arthritis is certain. It means the changeable factors matter even more.

Keep to a healthy weight

Extra body weight increases the load on knees, hips and feet with every step. Fat tissue also releases chemicals that can promote inflammation. Being overweight is one of the biggest risk factors for knee osteoarthritis and is also linked with gout and more active inflammatory arthritis. Even modest weight loss reduces strain on joints. The NHS offers free weight-management support, including the NHS Weight Loss Plan app.

Stay active and strong

Regular activity keeps joints moving and muscles strong. Strong thigh muscles, for example, help protect the knee. The UK Chief Medical Officers recommend 150 minutes of moderate activity each week, plus strength exercises on two days. Low-impact activities such as walking, swimming and cycling are easy on joints. If you play sport, a mix of activities reduces repeated strain on the same joints.

Protect your joints from injury

Joint injuries, such as a torn knee ligament or cartilage, raise the risk of osteoarthritis in that joint later in life. To reduce your risk:

  • warm up before sport and build up training gradually
  • learn good technique, particularly for twisting and landing movements
  • wear the right footwear and protective equipment
  • get a significant joint injury assessed and complete the rehabilitation exercises
  • at work, use lifting aids and follow manual handling advice

Do not smoke

Smoking is the strongest lifestyle risk factor for rheumatoid arthritis, and it also makes RA more severe. It affects bone health and healing too. Free NHS stop smoking services can help you quit.

Limit alcohol and sugary drinks

For gout, drinking a lot of alcohol, especially beer and spirits, and sugary drinks raise uric acid levels and the risk of attacks. Keeping within the UK low-risk guideline of 14 units a week spread over several days, and drinking plenty of water, helps.

Look after your bones and muscles as you age

Muscle strength and balance decline with age unless we use them. Strength and balance exercise reduces falls and fractures and keeps you mobile. Eat a balanced diet with enough protein and calcium, and follow NHS advice on vitamin D.

Act early on symptoms

For inflammatory arthritis, you cannot always stop it starting, but early treatment can prevent long-term joint damage. See your GP if you have joint swelling, stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes in the morning, or pain in several joints.

If you already have arthritis

The same steps also help manage existing arthritis. Exercise and weight loss are core treatments for osteoarthritis in NICE guidance. Staying active and not smoking help inflammatory arthritis treatment work better. It is never too late to start.

A realistic message

No one can promise that you will never get arthritis. But healthy habits reduce your risk and make a real difference to how arthritis affects you. Be wary of products sold as preventing arthritis, such as supplements; NICE does not recommend glucosamine or chondroitin for osteoarthritis.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
