article.title: Clicking Joints
article.excerpt: Why joints click, crack or pop, when it's harmless, when it could be arthritis or a cartilage problem, exercises that help and when to see your GP.
article.content:
Clicking, cracking or popping joints are very common and are usually harmless if there is no pain or swelling. The noise often comes from gas bubbles in joint fluid or tendons moving over bone. Grinding or crunching with pain, called crepitus, can be a sign of osteoarthritis. See your GP or physiotherapist if clicking comes with pain, swelling, locking or the joint giving way.

Why joints make noises

  • gas bubbles: joints are surrounded by fluid that contains dissolved gases. Stretching the joint can release a bubble with a pop, as when cracking knuckles. It takes time to build up again, so it usually cannot be repeated straight away.
  • tendons and ligaments can snap over bony areas as you move, especially at the hip, knee and shoulder
  • roughened joint surfaces can create a grinding or crunching feeling, common in osteoarthritis
  • cartilage tears in the knee can cause clicking with catching or locking

Usually nothing to worry about

Clicking is likely to be harmless if:

  • there is no pain
  • there is no swelling
  • the joint moves normally and does not lock or give way
  • it has been happening for a long time without change

Painless clicking does not mean you are developing arthritis. Many people with noisy knees never develop osteoarthritis.

When it might be arthritis

Osteoarthritis can cause:

  • a grating or crunching feeling or sound when moving the joint
  • pain that is worse with activity and eases with rest
  • short-lived stiffness after resting or in the morning
  • swelling, sometimes with knobbly finger joints

It is most common in knees, hips, hands and the spine, mainly after 45.

Other causes to consider

  • kneecap pain (patellofemoral pain): clicking at the front of the knee with pain on stairs, squatting or after sitting
  • meniscus (cartilage) tear: clicking with the knee catching, locking or giving way, often after a twisting injury
  • hypermobility: very flexible joints often click and can be prone to aches and sprains
  • snapping hip: a tendon flicking over the hip bone, usually painless
  • shoulder problems: clicking with pain when lifting the arm

What helps

If clicking is painless, you do not need to do anything. If there is mild pain:

  • strengthen the muscles around the joint. For knees, try sit to stands, step-ups and straight-leg raises.
  • stay active with low-impact activities such as walking, swimming or cycling
  • manage your weight to reduce load on knees and hips
  • use heat or cold for short-term relief
  • check your footwear for good cushioning and support

Many areas let you self-refer to NHS physiotherapy.

When to see a GP or physiotherapist

  • clicking comes with pain that does not improve after a few weeks
  • the joint is swollen, warm or stiff
  • the joint locks, catches or gives way
  • clicking started after an injury
  • you cannot move the joint fully

Your GP or physiotherapist will examine the joint and may suggest exercises, or refer you for imaging if a cartilage or ligament injury is suspected. Osteoarthritis can usually be diagnosed without an X-ray.

Should I stop cracking my knuckles?

There is no good evidence that cracking your knuckles causes arthritis. If it is painless, it is harmless, though you may want to stop if it bothers others. If cracking any joint becomes painful, get it checked.

Clicking and exercise

Many people worry that exercise will make a noisy joint worse. If clicking is painless, it is safe to carry on. If an exercise causes pain as well as clicking, change it, for example by reducing how deep you bend the knee, rather than stopping exercise altogether. Strengthening the surrounding muscles often reduces clicking over time.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Daily Living Tips for Arthritis
article.excerpt: Practical UK tips for living with arthritis day to day: mornings, kitchen, washing, dressing, housework, pacing, gadgets and where to get free help.
article.content:
The biggest wins for daily life with arthritis come from three habits. Spread demanding tasks across the day and week, use your largest and strongest joints rather than small ones, and use simple aids that take the strain. An NHS or council occupational therapist can assess you for free and suggest equipment and changes that suit your home.

Start the day gently

Morning stiffness is common, especially with inflammatory arthritis. Try:

  • a few gentle movements in bed before getting up, such as ankle circles, knee bends and finger stretches
  • a warm shower early in the day to loosen joints
  • laying out clothes the night before
  • timing painkillers, if you take them, so they are working when you get up. Ask your pharmacist how.

Pace yourself

Pacing means doing a steady amount of activity every day rather than overdoing it on good days and paying for it afterwards. Break big jobs into smaller chunks. Alternate heavy and light tasks, and sit down for jobs that do not need you to stand. Plan rest before you need it, not after.

Protect your joints

  • carry bags over your forearm or shoulder, or use a trolley, instead of gripping with fingers
  • push open doors with your shoulder or hip rather than your hand
  • slide heavy pans along the worktop instead of lifting
  • use two hands to lift a mug or kettle
  • avoid staying in one position too long. Get up and move every 30 minutes.

In the kitchen

  • use lightweight pans and a kettle tipper
  • buy pre-chopped vegetables or frozen ingredients on bad days
  • try a perching stool so you can sit while preparing food
  • use jar openers, electric can openers and tap turners
  • cook in batches when you feel well and freeze portions

Washing and dressing

  • a long-handled sponge and a bath board or shower seat reduce reaching and bending
  • grab rails beside the toilet and bath make getting up safer
  • choose clothes with front fastenings, elastic waists and slip-on shoes with good grip
  • a long-handled shoe horn, sock aid and button hook help with stiff hips or hands

Housework and garden

  • spread housework across the week, one room a day
  • use long-handled dusters, lightweight vacuums and a grabber
  • raised beds and kneeling stools make gardening easier
  • keep frequently used items between shoulder and hip height

Getting out and about

Good walking shoes, a walking stick if needed and planned rest stops make outings easier. You may be eligible for a Blue Badge if walking is very difficult. Many supermarkets offer delivery, which can save energy for things you enjoy.

Equipment and adaptations

You can ask your council for a free needs assessment. This can lead to equipment such as rails, raised toilet seats or perching stools, and sometimes home adaptations. Equipment and minor adaptations costing less than £1,000 are usually free in England. Larger changes may be funded by a Disabled Facilities Grant.

Look after your energy and mood

Fatigue and low mood are common and real parts of arthritis. Good sleep habits, regular gentle exercise and staying in touch with friends all help. If you feel low most days, talk to your GP. NHS Talking Therapies accepts self-referrals in England.

Keep moving

Exercise is a core treatment for arthritis according to NICE. Daily movement keeps joints flexible and muscles strong, which makes every other task easier. Even short walks or chair exercises count.

Small changes that add up

You do not need to change everything at once. Pick one area that frustrates you most, such as getting dressed or cooking, and try two or three ideas for a fortnight. Keep what helps and drop what does not. Write down tasks that leave you sore the next day, as these are the ones to break up or adapt.

Ask family and friends for help with specific jobs, such as changing the bed or carrying the shopping in. Accepting help with heavy jobs leaves you more energy for the things that matter to you.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Disability Living Allowance and Arthritis
article.excerpt: DLA and arthritis: DLA is now mainly for children under 16. Adults claim PIP, Adult Disability Payment in Scotland or Attendance Allowance.
article.content:
Disability Living Allowance (DLA) is now mainly for children under 16 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, including children with juvenile arthritis. Most adults cannot make a new claim for DLA. Adults of working age claim Personal Independence Payment (PIP), or Adult Disability Payment in Scotland. People over State Pension age claim Attendance Allowance, or Pension Age Disability Payment in Scotland.

DLA for children with arthritis

Children with arthritis, such as juvenile idiopathic arthritis, may qualify for DLA if they need much more care or supervision than other children of the same age, or have difficulty walking. There are two parts:

  • care component, paid at one of three rates, for help with personal care, supervision or attention day and night
  • mobility component, paid at one of two rates, for difficulty walking or needing supervision outdoors

The child must usually have needed this help for at least three months and be expected to need it for at least six more. Claims are made by a parent or carer.

In Scotland, DLA for children has been replaced by Child Disability Payment, run by Social Security Scotland.

Tips for a child's claim

  • describe a typical day and a bad day, including mornings, school, nights and flares
  • explain help needed with dressing, washing, toileting, eating, getting about, taking medicines and attending appointments
  • include supervision needs, such as managing pain or medicine side effects
  • add evidence from the rheumatology team, school, physiotherapist or occupational therapist
  • keep a diary for a week or two before filling in the form

What happens at 16

When a child on DLA turns 16, they are usually invited to apply for PIP. In Scotland, Child Disability Payment can continue until 18 and then moves to Adult Disability Payment.

Adults already on DLA

Most adults who were on DLA have been moved to PIP. If you were born on or before 8 April 1948, you may still receive DLA as long as you remain eligible. Report any changes in your condition.

PIP for working-age adults

PIP helps with the extra costs of a long-term health condition or disability. It is not means-tested and you can claim whether you work or not. It is based on how your arthritis affects you, not the diagnosis. There are two parts:

  • daily living, for difficulties with tasks such as preparing food, washing, dressing and managing medicines
  • mobility, for difficulties planning journeys or moving around

For arthritis, think about pain, stiffness, fatigue and flares, and whether you can do tasks safely, to an acceptable standard, repeatedly and in a reasonable time.

Adult Disability Payment in Scotland

Adult Disability Payment replaced PIP for people living in Scotland. It has a similar structure but is run by Social Security Scotland, which aims to avoid unnecessary face-to-face assessments.

Attendance Allowance for older people

If you are over State Pension age and need help with personal care or supervision because of arthritis, you may be able to claim Attendance Allowance. There is no mobility part. It is not means-tested. In Scotland, Pension Age Disability Payment is replacing it.

Other help to check

  • Carer's Allowance for someone who cares for you for at least 35 hours a week
  • Blue Badge for parking if walking is very difficult
  • Motability, if you receive the higher mobility rate
  • council tax reduction and help with health costs
  • Universal Credit if you are on a low income or cannot work

Getting help with a claim

Free advice is available from Citizens Advice and local welfare rights services. Some hospitals have benefits advisers. If you disagree with a decision, you can ask for a mandatory reconsideration, and then appeal to a tribunal. Many decisions are changed at appeal, so it is worth challenging a decision you think is wrong.

Keeping up to date

Benefit rules and rates change, often each April. Always check the latest details on GOV.UK or mygov.scot before you apply.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Fibromyalgia: Symptoms, Causes, Diagnosis and Treatment
article.excerpt: Fibromyalgia explained in plain English: widespread pain, fatigue and fibro fog, how it's diagnosed on the NHS, what NICE recommends, and self-help that works.
article.content:
Fibromyalgia is a long-term condition that causes pain all over the body, along with extreme tiredness, poor sleep and problems with memory and concentration, often called "fibro fog". It does not damage joints, and it is not arthritis, though the two can occur together. There is no cure, but exercise, pacing, psychological support and some medicines can help people live well.

Symptoms

  • widespread pain that may feel aching, burning or stabbing
  • increased sensitivity to pain, touch, temperature, noise or bright lights
  • fatigue that is not relieved by rest
  • unrefreshing sleep
  • stiffness
  • fibro fog: problems with memory, concentration and finding words
  • headaches, irritable bowel symptoms and low mood

Symptoms often vary from day to day, with flare-ups triggered by stress, illness, poor sleep or overdoing things.

What causes it

The exact cause is not fully understood. Fibromyalgia is thought to involve changes in how the brain and nerves process pain signals, sometimes called central sensitisation. It often starts after a physical or emotional trigger, such as an injury, infection, surgery or a stressful life event. It is more common in women and can run in families. It is also more common in people with rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and other conditions.

Getting diagnosed

There is no blood test or scan for fibromyalgia. Your GP will ask about your symptoms and may arrange tests to rule out other conditions with similar features, such as an underactive thyroid, vitamin D deficiency, polymyalgia rheumatica or inflammatory arthritis. Diagnosis is based on widespread pain lasting at least three months along with other typical symptoms.

Treatment: what NICE recommends

NICE's chronic pain guideline (NG193) covers fibromyalgia as a type of chronic primary pain. It recommends:

  • exercise programmes tailored to the person, built up gradually
  • psychological therapies such as CBT or acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), to help manage the impact of pain
  • acupuncture, as a single course in some cases
  • an antidepressant may be considered for some people, even if they do not have depression, because some help with pain and sleep

NICE advises against starting many commonly used painkillers for chronic primary pain, including opioids, paracetamol, NSAIDs and gabapentinoids, because the harms are likely to outweigh the benefits. If you already take these, do not stop suddenly. Talk to your GP about a review.

Self-help that makes a difference

  • Start exercise low and slow. Walking, swimming, gentle cycling or tai chi. Increase by small amounts. A short walk most days is better than a long one once a week.
  • Pace yourself. Plan activity and rest so that you do not have big boom-and-bust cycles.
  • Sleep routine. Go to bed and wake at the same time, limit caffeine and screens in the evening.
  • Manage stress. Relaxation, mindfulness or breathing exercises can calm the nervous system.
  • Stay connected. Support groups and talking to friends reduce isolation.

Work and money

You may be entitled to reasonable adjustments at work under the Equality Act 2010. Benefits such as PIP depend on how fibromyalgia affects your daily life rather than the diagnosis itself.

Living well

Fibromyalgia does not shorten life or cause joint damage. Many people find their symptoms improve over time with the right mix of activity, pacing and support. If your symptoms change, such as new swollen joints, weight loss or fevers, see your GP, as these are not typical of fibromyalgia.

Talking to others about fibromyalgia

Because fibromyalgia is invisible, people around you may not understand how it affects you. Explaining that it is a recognised long-term condition, and that energy and pain vary day to day, can help. Some people find it useful to share NHS information with family or their employer. Peer support groups, in person or online, can also offer practical tips and reassurance.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

/blog/lwa-archive-fractures-and-arthriti.answer: Arthritis itself does not make bones break, but several things that come with it can raise your fracture risk. These include falls from pain, stiffness or weak muscles, long-term steroid tablets, inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, and being less active. The good news is that much of that risk can be reduced, and your GP can assess it.

article.title: Fractures and Arthritis: Understanding Bone Injury Risks
article.excerpt: Does arthritis raise your fracture risk? How falls, steroids, rheumatoid arthritis and osteoporosis affect bones, warning signs of a break and UK prevention.
article.content:
Arthritis itself does not make bones break, but several things that come with it can raise your fracture risk. These include falls from pain, stiffness or weak muscles, long-term steroid tablets, inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, and being less active. The good news is that much of that risk can be reduced, and your GP can assess it.

Arthritis and osteoporosis are different

Arthritis affects joints. Osteoporosis is a loss of bone strength that makes bones fragile. The two are often confused, and many people have both. Osteoporosis has no symptoms until a bone breaks, which is why checking your risk matters.

Why fracture risk can be higher with arthritis

Falls. Painful knees or hips, stiff ankles, poor balance and weaker leg muscles all make trips and falls more likely. Most fractures in older adults happen after a fall from standing height.

Steroids. Taking steroid tablets such as prednisolone for three months or more can thin bones. NICE (CG146) lists long-term steroid use as a reason to assess fracture risk.

Rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory conditions. Ongoing inflammation affects bone. RA is one of the factors included in the FRAX fracture risk tool used by GPs.

Being less active. Bones need load to stay strong. When pain stops you moving, bones and muscles both weaken.

Other factors. Age, being female and past menopause, low body weight, smoking, drinking a lot of alcohol, a family history of hip fracture and a previous fracture all add to risk.

Common fractures to know about

  • Wrist — often from putting a hand out when falling
  • Hip — usually after a fall in later life. This is a serious injury that needs emergency care.
  • Spine (vertebral) fractures — can happen with little or no injury. They may show as sudden back pain, loss of height or a more curved upper back.
  • Upper arm and pelvis

Signs a bone may be broken

After a fall or knock, suspect a fracture if there is:

  • pain that is severe or getting worse, especially with movement or weight-bearing
  • swelling or bruising that develops quickly
  • a limb that looks bent, shortened or turned outwards
  • being unable to stand, walk or use the arm
  • sudden, severe back pain, even without a clear injury, if you have osteoporosis or take steroids

People with arthritis sometimes assume new pain is "just the arthritis". If pain is different, sudden or follows a fall, get it checked.

Getting your risk assessed

Ask your GP about a fracture risk assessment if you are over 50 and have arthritis plus any of the risks above, especially long-term steroids or a previous fracture. NICE recommends using a tool such as FRAX or QFracture. A DEXA bone density scan may be offered depending on the result.

If your risk is high, treatment to protect your bones may be offered. Your GP will explain the options and any checks needed.

Reducing your risk

  • Keep moving. Weight-bearing activity such as walking, plus strength and balance exercise, helps bones and lowers fall risk. Tai chi and strength-and-balance classes are good options.
  • Make your home safer. Good lighting, especially at night, grab rails, and removing loose rugs and clutter all help.
  • Review your medicines. Some tablets cause dizziness or drowsiness. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a medicines review, particularly if you take several.
  • Eat for bone health. Include calcium-rich foods and protein. Follow NHS advice on vitamin D, including the autumn and winter supplement advice. Your GP may advise more if you are at high risk.
  • Limit alcohol and stop smoking.
  • Check eyesight and feet. Wear well-fitting shoes with good grip.
  • Ask about steroids. If you need long-term steroids, ask whether bone protection is needed. Never stop steroids suddenly yourself.

After a fracture

A fracture after a minor fall is sometimes called a "fragility fracture" and is a signal to check for osteoporosis. Ask your GP or the fracture team whether this has been done. Many areas have a fracture liaison service. You can also ask for a falls assessment, which NICE (NG249) recommends after a fall.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Frailty and Arthritis: Maintaining Strength, Mobility and Independence
article.excerpt: How arthritis and frailty are linked, early signs of frailty, and practical UK steps to keep your strength, mobility and independence.
article.content:
Frailty is not a normal or inevitable part of ageing. It means your body has less reserve, so a small illness, fall or change in medicines can knock you back more than expected. Arthritis can push people towards frailty by making it harder to stay active. Regular strength and balance exercise, good nutrition, a medicines review and the right support at home can slow or even reverse it.

What frailty means

Doctors use "frailty" to describe a state, not just an age. Two people of 80 can be very different: one walks to the shops every day, the other struggles to get out of a chair. Frailty sits on a scale from mild to severe, and people can move along it in both directions.

How arthritis and frailty are linked

Arthritis pain and stiffness often lead to doing less. Doing less leads to weaker muscles, poorer balance and lower stamina. That makes activity harder still, and the cycle continues. Other links include:

  • sleep problems and fatigue from pain or inflammation
  • side effects of some medicines, such as drowsiness from stronger painkillers
  • low mood and feeling isolated
  • poor appetite or weight loss, which reduces muscle

Early signs to look out for

  • walking more slowly than you used to
  • needing your arms to push up from a chair
  • feeling exhausted much of the time
  • losing weight without trying
  • falls, or nearly falling
  • doing fewer of the things you enjoy, or going out less

If you notice these in yourself or someone you care for, talk to the GP. Many practices identify frailty and can arrange a review.

Building strength

Muscle can be built at any age. The UK Chief Medical Officers advise older adults to do activities that improve strength, balance and flexibility on at least two days a week, and to break up long periods of sitting.

Good starting points:

  • sit to stand from a firm chair, using your arms less over time
  • heel raises while holding the kitchen worktop
  • seated knee straightening to strengthen the front of the thigh
  • wall press-ups for arms and shoulders

Start with a few repetitions and build up slowly. Mild aching that settles within a day is normal. If pain stays worse the next day, do a bit less next time rather than stopping altogether.

Balance and preventing falls

Balance training is one of the best ways to prevent falls. Strength-and-balance programmes, often run by the NHS or local councils, and tai chi are good options. NICE (NG249) recommends that people who have fallen or are at risk are offered a falls assessment and a tailored exercise programme. Ask your GP about local falls prevention services.

Eating to protect muscle

Muscle needs protein and enough overall energy. Include protein at each meal, such as eggs, milk, yoghurt, fish, beans, lentils or meat. If your appetite is poor, smaller meals and nourishing snacks help. Unplanned weight loss should always be mentioned to your GP. Follow NHS advice on vitamin D.

Review your medicines

Taking several medicines increases the risk of dizziness, falls and confusion. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a structured medication review, particularly if you take strong painkillers, sleeping tablets, blood pressure tablets or medicines for mood.

Support to stay independent at home

  • Occupational therapy can suggest equipment and easier ways to do everyday tasks.
  • A council needs assessment is free and can lead to equipment, home adaptations or care support.
  • Personal alarms and good lighting help if you live alone.
  • Benefits such as Attendance Allowance (over State Pension age) are not means-tested.

When to seek help quickly

A sudden drop in your usual abilities, such as new confusion, not being able to get up, or going off your legs over a day or two, can be a sign of infection or another illness. Contact your GP or NHS 111 the same day.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Gout: Causes, Symptoms and Treatment
article.excerpt: Gout explained: sudden painful joints, what causes uric acid build-up, treating attacks, long-term urate-lowering treatment, diet and when to get help.
article.content:
Gout is a type of arthritis caused by a build-up of uric acid in the blood, which forms crystals in joints. It causes sudden attacks of severe pain, swelling and redness, often in the big toe. Attacks are treated with anti-inflammatory medicines. If you have repeated attacks, long-term medicine to lower uric acid, such as allopurinol, can prevent them and protect your joints.

Symptoms

  • sudden severe pain in a joint, often starting at night
  • the joint is hot, red, swollen and very tender, so even a bedsheet can hurt
  • most often the big toe, but also the ankle, foot, knee, wrist, fingers or elbow
  • attacks usually peak within a day and settle over one to two weeks

Over time, without treatment, attacks may become more frequent and affect more joints. Lumps of crystals called tophi can form under the skin.

Causes and risk factors

Uric acid is a waste product made when the body breaks down substances called purines. Gout happens when there is too much in the blood, either because the body makes too much or the kidneys do not remove enough. Risk factors include:

  • being male, or being a woman after menopause
  • family history
  • being overweight
  • high blood pressure, diabetes, heart disease or kidney disease
  • drinking alcohol, especially beer and spirits
  • sugary drinks
  • eating a lot of red meat, offal or seafood
  • some medicines, such as water tablets (diuretics)

Diagnosis

Your GP can often diagnose gout from your symptoms and an examination. A blood test for uric acid (urate) is usually done, ideally a few weeks after an attack, as levels can be misleadingly normal during one. Sometimes fluid is taken from the joint to look for crystals, especially to rule out infection.

Treating an attack

NICE (NG219) recommends:

  • an NSAID, colchicine or a short course of steroids, depending on your health and other medicines
  • resting the joint and raising it
  • a cold pack wrapped in a towel
  • keeping the joint uncovered or using a bed cradle at night

Start treatment as soon as possible. Ask your GP about having medicine at home to start quickly at the first sign of an attack.

Long-term treatment

NICE recommends offering urate-lowering treatment to people who have repeated attacks, tophi, joint damage, kidney disease, or other risk factors. It can be started after a first attack. The usual first choice is allopurinol, with febuxostat as an alternative.

  • treatment usually starts at a low dose and is increased gradually
  • blood tests check uric acid until it reaches a target level
  • you may be given colchicine or an NSAID for the first few months, as attacks can briefly increase when starting treatment
  • treatment is usually lifelong. Do not stop during an attack.

Lifestyle changes

  • lose weight gradually if you are overweight
  • cut down on alcohol, especially beer
  • avoid sugary drinks
  • drink plenty of water
  • eat a balanced diet, limiting red meat, offal and shellfish
  • exercise regularly

Diet alone is rarely enough to control gout but can reduce attacks.

Gout and your heart and kidneys

Gout is linked with heart disease, high blood pressure, diabetes and kidney disease. NICE recommends checking for these. Managing them improves your general health.

When it might not be gout

A hot, swollen joint can also be caused by infection (septic arthritis), which needs urgent treatment. Seek urgent help if you have a fever or feel unwell, or if this is your first attack and you are not sure what it is.

Questions to ask your GP

  • Should I start long-term treatment to lower my uric acid?
  • What is my target uric acid level, and how often will it be checked?
  • What should I take at the first sign of an attack?
  • Could any of my other medicines be making gout more likely?

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Hand Osteoarthritis
article.excerpt: Hand osteoarthritis explained: knobbly finger joints, thumb base pain, exercises, splints, gels, gadgets, NHS treatment and when to see your GP.
article.content:
Hand osteoarthritis commonly affects the joints at the end and middle of the fingers and the base of the thumb. It causes pain, stiffness, knobbly swellings and weaker grip, and is most common in women over 50. It cannot be cured, but hand exercises, anti-inflammatory gels, splints and gadgets help most people. Surgery is occasionally needed for the thumb.

Which joints are affected

  • the joints nearest the fingertips (DIP joints). Bony lumps here are called Heberden's nodes.
  • the middle finger joints (PIP joints). Lumps here are called Bouchard's nodes.
  • the base of the thumb (CMC joint). Causes pain when gripping, pinching, opening jars or turning keys.

The knuckles where the fingers meet the hand are less often affected by osteoarthritis. Swelling there is more typical of rheumatoid arthritis.

Symptoms

  • pain, especially when using your hands
  • stiffness, usually lasting less than 30 minutes in the morning
  • knobbly swellings that may be red and tender while they develop, then settle
  • reduced grip and pinch strength
  • fingers that bend to one side
  • difficulty with fine tasks such as buttons, writing or opening packets

Symptoms are often worst in the first few years and may become less painful over time, even if the lumps remain.

Diagnosis

NICE (NG226) says osteoarthritis can usually be diagnosed from symptoms and examination without an X-ray. See your GP if you have swelling of the knuckles, a lot of morning stiffness, or symptoms in several joints on both hands, as these can suggest inflammatory arthritis.

Exercises

Regular hand exercises help keep fingers moving and maintain strength. Try these each day:

  • make a fist: gently curl your fingers into a loose fist, then stretch them out straight
  • thumb touches: touch the tip of your thumb to each fingertip in turn
  • finger spreads: place your hand flat on a table and spread your fingers apart
  • tabletop: bend your knuckles while keeping your fingers straight, then relax
  • putty or a soft ball: squeeze gently to build grip strength

Warm your hands in warm water first if they are stiff.

Pain relief

NICE recommends topical NSAID gels as a first option for hand osteoarthritis. Rub a small amount into the sore joints. Ask your pharmacist if they are suitable for you. Some people use painkillers for flares. Heat, such as a warm water soak or paraffin wax bath, can ease stiffness.

Splints and support

A thumb splint can ease pain at the base of the thumb by supporting it during activity or at night. An occupational therapist or hand therapist can advise and fit one. Ask your GP for a referral, or check whether you can self-refer.

Gadgets and joint protection

  • jar and bottle openers
  • thick-handled cutlery, pens and kitchen utensils
  • tap turners and key turners
  • lever-style door handles
  • electric can openers and lightweight kettles
  • spreading the load across both hands

Many of these are inexpensive and available from chemists and supermarkets.

Injections and surgery

Steroid injections may be offered for a very painful thumb base joint. Surgery is sometimes offered when thumb base arthritis remains severe despite other treatments. The most common operation removes a small bone at the base of the thumb. Finger joint surgery is less common.

Conditions that can look similar

  • carpal tunnel syndrome, causing tingling and numbness in the thumb and fingers
  • trigger finger, where a finger catches when bending
  • De Quervain's tenosynovitis, causing pain at the thumb side of the wrist
  • rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis

Living with hand osteoarthritis

Pace tasks that use your hands, take breaks and switch between activities. Keeping your hands moving every day helps more than resting them completely. Talk to your employer about adjustments if your work involves a lot of hand use.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Inflammation and Arthritis
article.excerpt: What inflammation means in arthritis, how inflammatory arthritis and osteoarthritis differ, blood tests, treatments and lifestyle steps that help.
article.content:
Inflammation is the body's natural response to injury or infection, causing heat, redness, swelling and pain. In inflammatory arthritis, such as rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis, the immune system wrongly triggers this response in the joints and it keeps going, which can damage them. Osteoarthritis involves much less inflammation. Inflammatory arthritis needs specialist treatment with medicines that calm the immune system.

Inflammation: helpful and harmful

Short-term inflammation is protective. When you sprain an ankle, extra blood flow and immune cells help repair the damage, and the swelling settles. In inflammatory arthritis, inflammation becomes long-term and is directed at healthy tissue. The joint lining (synovium) thickens and produces extra fluid, causing swelling and pain. Over time it can wear away cartilage and bone.

Types of arthritis where inflammation is the main driver

  • rheumatoid arthritis
  • psoriatic arthritis
  • axial spondyloarthritis, including ankylosing spondylitis
  • gout, where crystals trigger sudden intense inflammation
  • lupus and other connective tissue diseases
  • reactive arthritis
  • polymyalgia rheumatica, which mainly affects muscles around the shoulders and hips

What about osteoarthritis?

Osteoarthritis was once seen as simple "wear and tear". We now know it involves the joint working to repair itself, with some low-grade inflammation. Joints may swell at times, particularly during a flare. However, the inflammation is much milder and is not driven by the immune system in the same way, so osteoarthritis is not treated with immune-suppressing medicines.

Signs of inflammatory arthritis

  • swollen, warm joints
  • stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes after waking or resting
  • pain that eases with movement
  • tiredness and feeling generally unwell
  • symptoms in several joints, often on both sides

If you notice these, see your GP. Early treatment protects joints.

How inflammation is measured

Blood tests can show inflammation. The most common are:

  • CRP (C-reactive protein)
  • ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate)

These are not specific to arthritis, as infections and other conditions raise them too. Some people with active inflammatory arthritis have normal results, so doctors also rely on examining your joints. Ultrasound can show inflammation in the joint lining.

Treatments that calm inflammation

  • NSAIDs (anti-inflammatory painkillers) reduce pain and swelling but do not change the disease. They are not suitable for everyone, so check with your pharmacist or GP.
  • Steroids work quickly and are often used for flares or short periods.
  • DMARDs such as methotrexate reduce immune activity and prevent damage. NICE recommends starting them early in RA.
  • Biologics and targeted therapies act on specific inflammatory signals when DMARDs are not enough.

Lifestyle and inflammation

Lifestyle changes cannot replace medicines for inflammatory arthritis, but they support your treatment and general health:

  • stop smoking, which worsens RA and can reduce how well treatment works
  • stay active, as regular exercise has anti-inflammatory effects
  • keep to a healthy weight, because fat tissue produces inflammatory chemicals
  • eat a balanced diet, such as a Mediterranean-style diet rich in vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, oily fish and olive oil
  • sleep well and manage stress

Be wary of products marketed as "anti-inflammatory cures". Supplements can interact with arthritis medicines, so check with your pharmacist first.

Living with inflammatory arthritis

With modern treatment, many people get their inflammation under control. Regular reviews with your rheumatology team, reporting flares promptly and keeping up with blood tests all help keep it that way.

Questions to ask your team

  • Is my arthritis inflammatory, and how active is it?
  • What do my CRP and ESR results mean for me?
  • How will we know if treatment is working?
  • What should I do if I notice new swelling?

Understanding your own results helps you spot changes early and take part in decisions about your care.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Is Arthritis Hereditary?
article.excerpt: Does arthritis run in families? How genes affect risk of osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, AS and gout, and what you can do about it.
article.content:
Arthritis can run in families, but it is rarely passed on directly from parent to child. Genes can raise your risk of several types, including osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis and gout. Having a relative with arthritis does not mean you will get it, and lifestyle factors such as weight, smoking and joint injury also play a big part.

How genes affect risk

Most types of arthritis are caused by a mix of many genes, each having a small effect, plus environmental factors. This is different from conditions caused by a single faulty gene, where the chance of passing it on can be calculated precisely. For arthritis, a family history raises the chance but does not determine the outcome.

Osteoarthritis

Osteoarthritis tends to run in families, particularly in the hands, hips and knees. Knobbly finger joints often appear in several women in the same family. Other factors are also important, such as age, being overweight, previous joint injuries, joint shape and occupation. These can be more influential than genes.

Rheumatoid arthritis

Having a parent or sibling with RA raises your risk, but most people with a family history do not develop it. Several genes are involved, especially those that control the immune system. Smoking is the strongest environmental trigger, particularly in people with certain genes. Not smoking is one of the most useful things relatives of people with RA can do.

Psoriatic arthritis

Psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis often run in families. If a close relative has psoriatic arthritis and you have psoriasis, mention it to your GP, especially if you notice joint pain, swollen fingers or toes or nail changes.

Ankylosing spondylitis

Many people with AS carry a gene called HLA-B27. However, most people with HLA-B27 never develop AS, so testing healthy relatives is not usually helpful. If you have a relative with AS and develop long-lasting back pain that is worse with rest and better with movement, tell your GP.

Gout

Gout can run in families because genes affect how the kidneys clear uric acid. Diet, alcohol, weight, kidney function and some medicines also play a part.

Lupus and juvenile arthritis

Lupus and other autoimmune diseases are more common in families with autoimmune conditions, though the risk to each relative remains low. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis rarely affects more than one child in a family.

Should I have a genetic test?

Genetic tests are not routinely used to predict arthritis risk. Some tests, such as HLA-B27, may help doctors with diagnosis when someone already has symptoms. Home genetic testing kits cannot tell you whether you will develop arthritis, and results can be confusing. Speak to your GP if you are worried.

What you can do if arthritis runs in your family

  • keep to a healthy weight
  • stay active and keep your muscles strong
  • protect your joints from injury and complete rehabilitation after sports injuries
  • do not smoke
  • keep alcohol within recommended limits
  • get symptoms checked early, especially joint swelling, morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes or pain in several joints

Talking to your children

If you have arthritis, it is natural to worry about your children. You can reassure them that most children of people with arthritis do not develop the same condition, and that if they do, it can be treated. Share healthy habits as a family and encourage them to tell a doctor about joint symptoms. If you are planning a pregnancy and take medicines for arthritis, talk to your rheumatology team, as some medicines need to be changed in advance.

Remember that family history is only one piece of the picture. Many people with arthritis have no relatives with the condition, and many with a strong family history stay well.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Joint Pain and Arthritis
article.excerpt: Is your joint pain arthritis? Common causes, signs it may be inflammatory, self-care that helps, when to see a GP and when joint pain is an emergency.
article.content:
Joint pain is not always arthritis. Short-lived pain after overuse or a minor injury usually settles in a few weeks with rest, gentle movement and simple painkillers. Pain that lasts longer, comes with swelling or long morning stiffness, or affects several joints may be arthritis and is worth discussing with your GP. A single hot, red, swollen joint with fever needs urgent help.

Common causes of joint pain

  • Strains, sprains and overuse, for example after gardening, sport or a new activity
  • Osteoarthritis, the most common type of arthritis, usually in knees, hips, hands and the spine, mainly after 45
  • Inflammatory arthritis, such as rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis, where the immune system attacks the joints
  • Gout, causing sudden severe pain, often in the big toe
  • Bursitis and tendinopathy, irritation of the cushioning sacs or tendons around a joint
  • Viral infections, which can cause temporary aches in several joints
  • Joint hypermobility, where joints move further than usual
  • Fibromyalgia, which causes widespread pain that is felt in and around joints

Clues that it might be osteoarthritis

  • you are over 45
  • pain is worse with activity and eases with rest
  • any morning stiffness lasts less than 30 minutes
  • one or a few large joints are affected, or the finger joints nearest the nails

NICE (NG226) says osteoarthritis can usually be diagnosed from symptoms alone, without an X-ray, in people who fit this picture.

Clues that it might be inflammatory arthritis

  • swelling in the joints, particularly the small joints of the hands and feet
  • stiffness for more than 30 minutes in the morning
  • pain that is worse after rest and better with movement
  • several joints affected, often on both sides of the body
  • tiredness, feeling generally unwell or weight loss
  • psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease or a family history of these conditions

NICE (NG100) recommends that people with persistent joint swelling are referred urgently to a rheumatologist, even if blood tests are normal.

Self-care for joint pain

For mild pain that has not lasted long:

  • keep moving gently. Rest the joint for a day or two if very sore, then build activity back up.
  • use an ice pack wrapped in a towel for swelling, or heat for stiffness
  • try simple painkillers or a topical anti-inflammatory gel. Ask your pharmacist what is suitable for you.
  • wear supportive shoes and pace demanding tasks
  • if you are overweight, losing some weight reduces strain on knees and hips

When to see your GP

  • pain has not improved after two weeks of self-care
  • you have swelling, warmth or stiffness that lasts for more than 30 minutes in the morning
  • several joints are painful or swollen
  • pain is stopping you working, sleeping or doing everyday tasks
  • you have other symptoms, such as rashes, mouth ulcers, dry eyes, or a change in bowel habits

Many areas let you self-refer to NHS physiotherapy for joint pain, which can be quicker than waiting for a GP appointment.

What your GP may do

Your GP will ask about your symptoms and examine the joints. Depending on what they find, they may arrange blood tests to check for inflammation and rheumatoid factor, X-rays, or a referral to physiotherapy or rheumatology. Bring a list of which joints hurt, when they are worst and anything that helps.

Keeping a symptom diary

Noting your pain levels, stiffness and any swelling each day for a week or two can help you and your GP spot patterns. Take photos of any swelling, as it may go down before your appointment.

Remember that most joint pain is not serious and many causes improve with time and the right self-care. Getting checked early, though, means that if it is arthritis you can start the right treatment sooner.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Knee Osteoarthritis
article.excerpt: Knee osteoarthritis explained: symptoms, diagnosis, the exercises NICE recommends, weight, pain relief, aids, injections and when knee replacement helps.
article.content:
Knee osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis in the UK. It causes knee pain that is worse with activity, short-lived stiffness, and sometimes swelling and grinding. Exercise to strengthen the leg muscles is the most important treatment, alongside weight loss if needed and simple pain relief. Knee replacement is considered when symptoms seriously affect your life despite these.

Symptoms

  • pain in the knee, often worse with walking, stairs or standing up
  • stiffness after resting or first thing in the morning, usually lasting less than 30 minutes
  • swelling, which can come and go
  • grinding or crunching
  • the knee feeling weak or giving way
  • reduced bending or straightening

Symptoms often go through better and worse periods.

Risk factors

  • being over 45
  • being overweight
  • previous knee injury, such as a torn ligament or cartilage
  • jobs involving lots of kneeling or squatting
  • weak thigh muscles
  • family history
  • being female

Diagnosis

NICE (NG226) says knee osteoarthritis can be diagnosed without X-rays in people over 45 with activity-related joint pain and morning stiffness of no more than 30 minutes. X-ray findings do not always match symptoms. Your GP may arrange tests if the picture is unusual, for example if the knee is hot and swollen or you have symptoms in several joints.

Exercise: the core treatment

NICE recommends therapeutic exercise tailored to each person. For the knee this includes:

  • strengthening: sit to stand, straight-leg raises, step-ups, mini squats holding the worktop
  • aerobic activity: walking, cycling, swimming or water exercise
  • flexibility: gentle stretches for the thigh and calf muscles

Some discomfort during exercise is normal and does not mean you are causing damage. If pain is still increased the next day, reduce the amount a little but keep going. Benefits build over weeks.

Many areas offer NHS group programmes, such as ESCAPE-pain, or self-referral to physiotherapy.

Weight management

If you are overweight, losing weight reduces the load on your knees and can noticeably ease pain. Your GP can refer you to local weight management services.

Pain relief

  • topical NSAID gels are recommended by NICE as a first option for knee osteoarthritis
  • oral NSAIDs may be considered for a short time at the lowest effective dose, with stomach protection if needed
  • paracetamol and weak opioids are not routinely recommended by NICE for osteoarthritis unless used occasionally and short-term

Ask your pharmacist or GP what suits you.

Other things that may help

  • heat or cold packs
  • supportive, cushioned footwear
  • a walking stick, held in the hand opposite the painful knee
  • knee supports or braces for some people
  • TENS machines, which some people find useful

Injections

Steroid injections may give short-term relief during a bad flare and can help you exercise. NICE does not recommend hyaluronic acid injections.

What is not recommended

NICE does not recommend glucosamine or chondroitin, acupuncture, or arthroscopic "washout" surgery for knee osteoarthritis.

Knee replacement

Joint replacement may be considered if pain, stiffness and reduced function substantially affect your quality of life despite non-surgical treatment. Age, weight and smoking should not be barriers to referral on their own, though your surgeon will discuss how they affect risks. Partial knee replacement is an option for some people.

Living with knee osteoarthritis

Keep active, pace demanding tasks, use stair rails and raise low chairs. Many people find their symptoms stay stable or improve with regular exercise and do not need surgery.

Questions to ask your GP or physiotherapist

  • Which exercises are best for my knee, and how many should I do?
  • Is there a group exercise programme near me?
  • Which pain relief is safest for me?
  • At what point should we talk about surgery?

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Long-Term Outlook for Rheumatoid Arthritis
article.excerpt: What is the long-term outlook for rheumatoid arthritis? Remission, work, life expectancy, heart health, and the steps that give you the best future with RA.
article.content:
The outlook for rheumatoid arthritis is much better than it was a generation ago. With early diagnosis and modern treatment, many people reach remission or low disease activity, keep working and live full lives. RA is a long-term condition that usually needs ongoing treatment, and it does raise the risk of heart disease and some other problems, but most of these risks can be reduced.

What has changed

In the past, many people with RA developed serious joint damage and disability. Today, rheumatologists start disease-modifying medicines early and adjust them until the disease is controlled, an approach called "treat to target". Biologic and targeted medicines give further options when standard treatments are not enough.

Remission

Remission means there are few or no signs of active inflammation. Many people reach it, especially when treatment starts within the first few months of symptoms. Some people can later reduce their medicines under specialist supervision, but stopping treatment yourself often leads to a flare.

What affects the outlook

Factors linked with a better outcome include:

  • early diagnosis and treatment
  • good response to the first medicines
  • not smoking
  • staying active
  • keeping to a healthy weight

Factors that may mean more active disease include positive blood tests for rheumatoid factor or anti-CCP antibodies, many swollen joints at diagnosis and early damage on X-rays. These are reasons for close monitoring, not reasons to lose hope.

Living with flares

Even when RA is well controlled, flares can happen. They may be triggered by infections, stress or missed doses. Know who to contact, as many rheumatology teams have an advice line. Steroid injections or short courses can settle a flare while longer-term treatment is reviewed.

Heart health

RA increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes, partly because of inflammation. NICE recommends assessing cardiovascular risk in people with RA. You can lower risk by:

  • getting inflammation under control
  • not smoking
  • regular exercise
  • having blood pressure and cholesterol checked and treated

Other health issues to be aware of

  • osteoporosis, especially with long-term steroids
  • infections, more likely on some treatments. Keep vaccinations up to date.
  • lung problems, which can be linked to RA or rarely to treatment. Report a new cough or breathlessness.
  • eye dryness, sometimes from Sjögren's syndrome
  • anaemia and fatigue
  • low mood, which is common and treatable

Life expectancy

RA has been linked with a shorter life expectancy on average, mainly due to heart disease and infections. With modern treatment and attention to heart health, this gap is narrowing. Your own outlook depends on many things, so ask your team about your personal situation.

Work and everyday life

Many people with RA continue to work. Under the Equality Act 2010, employers must consider reasonable adjustments. Access to Work can help with equipment and travel costs. Occupational therapists can advise on protecting your joints and managing fatigue.

Your part in a good outcome

  • take your medicines as prescribed and attend blood tests
  • tell your team about side effects rather than stopping treatment
  • stay active and keep strong
  • report new swelling or flares early
  • look after your mental health
  • ask questions and be involved in decisions

Planning ahead

If you are thinking about pregnancy, surgery, travel or changing jobs, talk to your team in advance. Many medicines need adjusting in these situations, and planning early makes everything smoother.

Many people find the first year after diagnosis the hardest, as they adjust to the condition and find the right treatment. It often gets easier with time. Support from others with RA, through local groups or national charities, can make a real difference during this period.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

With early diagnosis and modern treatment, many people reach remission or low disease activity, keep working and live full lives. RA is a long-term condition that usually needs ongoing treatment, and it does raise the risk of heart disease and some other problems, but most of these risks can be reduced.

article.title: Lupus and Arthritis: Understanding Joint Symptoms
article.excerpt: How lupus affects the joints, how lupus joint pain differs from rheumatoid arthritis, other symptoms to watch for, NHS diagnosis and treatment, and self-care.
article.content:
Lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus, or SLE) is an autoimmune condition that commonly causes joint pain and stiffness, often in the hands, wrists and knees. Unlike rheumatoid arthritis, lupus joint pain rarely causes lasting joint damage. Lupus can also affect the skin, kidneys, blood and other organs, so it needs specialist care. Treatment can control it well for most people.

Joint symptoms in lupus

Most people with lupus have joint symptoms at some point:

  • pain and stiffness, often in the small joints of hands and wrists, and in knees
  • symptoms on both sides of the body
  • swelling, sometimes mild
  • morning stiffness
  • pain that moves between joints and comes and goes with flares

Joint deformity is uncommon, although some people develop a reversible drift of the fingers called Jaccoud's arthropathy.

How it differs from rheumatoid arthritis

RA and lupus can look similar at first. Differences include:

  • RA is more likely to cause permanent joint damage
  • lupus often comes with other symptoms such as rashes, mouth ulcers and kidney problems
  • blood tests differ: lupus is linked with ANA and anti-dsDNA antibodies, RA with rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP

Some people have overlap features of both.

Other symptoms of lupus

  • extreme tiredness
  • rashes, especially a butterfly-shaped rash across the cheeks and nose, often triggered by sunlight
  • mouth or nose ulcers
  • hair loss
  • fevers
  • fingers that turn white or blue in the cold (Raynaud's)
  • chest pain when breathing in
  • swollen ankles or frothy urine, which can be signs of kidney involvement
  • dry eyes and mouth
  • low mood, anxiety and memory problems

Who gets lupus

Lupus is much more common in women, usually starting between 15 and 45. It is more common in people of African, Caribbean, Asian and Chinese heritage.

Diagnosis

Diagnosis can take time because symptoms vary and come and go. Your GP may arrange blood tests including ANA. A positive ANA alone does not mean you have lupus, as it is found in many healthy people. If lupus is suspected, you will be referred to a rheumatologist. Urine tests check the kidneys.

Treatment

  • hydroxychloroquine is the main long-term treatment for most people. It helps joints, skin and fatigue and reduces flares. Regular eye checks are needed.
  • NSAIDs may ease joint pain if suitable for you.
  • steroids in the lowest effective dose for flares
  • other immune-suppressing medicines, such as methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate, for more active disease
  • biologics, such as belimumab, for some people

Self-care

  • protect your skin from the sun with high-factor sunscreen and covering up
  • pace yourself and plan rest
  • stay active with gentle exercise to help joints and fatigue
  • do not smoke, as it can make lupus worse and reduce how well hydroxychloroquine works
  • look after your heart, as lupus increases cardiovascular risk
  • plan pregnancy with your team, as some medicines need changing and pregnancy needs close monitoring

Living with lupus

Lupus is unpredictable, but many people live full lives with treatment. Keep regular appointments and blood and urine tests, and report new symptoms early.

Questions to ask your rheumatologist

  • Which parts of my body is lupus affecting?
  • How will we monitor my kidneys and blood?
  • How often do I need eye checks on hydroxychloroquine?
  • What should I do in a flare, and who do I contact?
  • Is it safe for me to plan a pregnancy, and when?

Keeping a symptom diary, including photos of rashes or swollen joints, can help your team see patterns between appointments. Support groups for people with lupus can also offer practical tips and reassurance, especially soon after diagnosis.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • chest pain or sudden breathlessness, a seizure, sudden confusion, or severe headache
  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Massage for Arthritis
article.excerpt: Can massage help arthritis? How it may ease pain and stiffness, when to avoid it, safety with medicines and flares, self-massage and UK access.
article.content:
Massage can help some people with arthritis feel less stiff and more relaxed for a short time, but it does not treat the arthritis itself. NICE says manual therapy such as massage should only be used alongside exercise for osteoarthritis, not on its own. Gentle massage is usually safe, but avoid pressing on a joint that is hot, red and swollen.

How massage may help

Arthritis pain is not just about the joint. Muscles around a sore joint often tighten to guard it, and that tension adds its own ache. Massage may help by:

  • easing muscle tightness and spasm around the joint
  • warming tissues so movement feels easier afterwards
  • calming the nervous system and reducing stress, which affects how strongly we feel pain
  • improving sleep for some people

The effects are usually short-lived, from hours to a day or two. That makes massage most useful as a way to get moving: a gentle massage followed by your exercises can make the exercise more comfortable.

What UK guidance says

NICE's osteoarthritis guideline (NG226) says do not offer manual therapy, which includes massage and joint manipulation, unless it is alongside therapeutic exercise. In other words, massage can be a helpful add-on but should not replace strengthening and activity.

For rheumatoid arthritis, NICE (NG100) focuses on disease-modifying medicines and access to physiotherapy and occupational therapy. Massage is not part of standard RA treatment, but many people use it for comfort.

When to avoid or adapt massage

Do not massage directly over a joint that is:

  • hot, red and swollen. This may be an active flare or, more rarely, an infection that needs urgent assessment.
  • recently injured, broken or operated on, unless your surgeon or physiotherapist says it is fine

Take extra care, and tell the therapist, if you:

  • take blood thinners or bruise easily, including from long-term steroids
  • have osteoporosis. Firm pressure over the spine or ribs is not advised.
  • have numbness, poor circulation, varicose veins or a history of blood clots. A hot, swollen calf needs medical advice, not massage.
  • have fragile skin, psoriasis or lymphoedema
  • have fibromyalgia, where firm pressure may feel painful. Lighter pressure is often better.

Massage should not cause sharp pain. A good therapist will adjust the pressure and ask how you feel.

Self-massage you can do at home

You do not need to pay for massage to get some benefit. Try:

  • Hands: rub a little hand cream into each finger, stroking from the tip towards the palm. Gently circle your thumb across the palm.
  • Knees: sitting with your leg supported, stroke the thigh muscles above the knee with flat hands for a few minutes. Avoid pressing hard on the kneecap.
  • Neck and shoulders: use the opposite hand to knead the top of the shoulder gently, or lean against a wall with a soft ball between your back and the wall.
  • Feet: roll your foot slowly over a tennis ball or a cold drinks bottle while seated.

Warming the area first with a warm bath, shower or wheat bag often makes self-massage more comfortable. Keep it gentle and stop if pain increases.

Professional massage in the UK

Massage for arthritis is not usually available on the NHS. Physiotherapists may use soft tissue techniques as part of a wider treatment plan. Privately, look for a therapist with a recognised qualification and insurance, and ask whether they have experience with arthritis. Sports massage is often too firm for inflamed joints, so ask for a gentler approach if needed.

Making massage part of a bigger plan

Massage works best as one tool among several:

  • daily movement and strengthening exercises
  • pacing your activity across the day
  • heat for stiffness and cold for hot, swollen flares
  • the medicines your GP or rheumatology team recommends

If you find you need massage more and more just to keep going, that is a sign to review your treatment with your GP, physiotherapist or rheumatology team.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Neck Arthritis
article.excerpt: Neck arthritis explained: symptoms of cervical spondylosis, exercises and self-care that help, NHS treatment, and warning signs that need urgent care.
article.content:
Neck arthritis, often called cervical spondylosis, is age-related wear in the joints and discs of the neck. It is very common after 40 and often causes no symptoms. When it does, it usually causes neck pain and stiffness that comes and goes. Most people improve with regular movement, good posture and simple pain relief. Rarely it presses on nerves, which needs medical assessment.

Symptoms

  • neck pain and stiffness, often worse after staying in one position
  • pain spreading to the shoulders or base of the skull
  • headaches starting at the back of the head
  • grinding or clicking when turning the head
  • reduced movement, such as difficulty looking over your shoulder when driving

Symptoms usually flare and settle over weeks.

When nerves are involved

Bony changes can sometimes narrow the space for nerves:

  • trapped nerve (radiculopathy): pain, pins and needles, numbness or weakness down one arm into the hand
  • pressure on the spinal cord (myelopathy): less common but more serious. Signs include clumsy hands, difficulty with buttons or writing, unsteady walking and changes in bladder control. This needs prompt assessment.

Other types of arthritis in the neck

Rheumatoid arthritis can affect the top of the neck. If you have RA and develop new neck pain, especially with tingling in the arms, tell your rheumatology team. Ankylosing spondylitis can also cause neck stiffness.

Self-care that helps

  • keep moving. Gentle neck exercises several times a day are better than keeping it still.
  • simple pain relief. Ask your pharmacist about painkillers or anti-inflammatory gels that suit you.
  • heat from a wheat bag or warm shower can ease stiffness
  • check your posture, particularly at a desk or on your phone. Bring screens up to eye level.
  • sleep with a supportive pillow that keeps your neck in line with your spine. Avoid using too many pillows.
  • take regular breaks from driving, screens and close work

Neck collars are not usually recommended, as they can make the neck stiffer.

Gentle neck exercises

Do these slowly, within a comfortable range:

  • chin tucks: sitting tall, gently draw your chin back to make a double chin, hold, then relax
  • side bends: tilt your ear towards your shoulder, hold, then repeat on the other side
  • rotations: turn your head slowly to look over each shoulder
  • shoulder rolls: roll your shoulders backwards in circles

Repeat each a few times, several times a day. Stop if an exercise causes pins and needles or pain into the arm.

NHS treatment

If symptoms do not improve after a few weeks, see your GP or self-refer to physiotherapy if available in your area. A physiotherapist can give you a tailored exercise programme and advice on posture and activities. For persistent nerve symptoms, you may be referred for an MRI scan or to a specialist. Surgery is only considered for a small number of people with significant nerve or spinal cord pressure.

Work and daily life

  • set up your workstation with your screen at eye level and your keyboard close
  • use a headset for long phone calls
  • in the car, adjust the head restraint and mirrors, and turn your body to check blind spots if needed
  • spread jobs such as painting ceilings or hanging washing across the day

Outlook

Most people with neck arthritis keep active and manage well. Pain often comes and goes over the years, and flares usually settle within a few weeks. Staying active and keeping your neck moving is the best long-term approach.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • neck pain with new weakness, clumsiness or numbness in both arms or legs, problems walking, or problems controlling your bladder or bowels
  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
