article.title: New Treatments for Arthritis
article.excerpt: A plain-English guide to newer arthritis treatments in the UK: biologics, biosimilars, JAK inhibitors, research into osteoarthritis, and how to join a trial.
article.content:
The biggest advances have been in inflammatory arthritis, such as rheumatoid, psoriatic and axial spondyloarthritis. Biologic medicines, cheaper biosimilar versions and JAK inhibitor tablets now give many people good control. For osteoarthritis there is still no medicine that reverses joint damage, so exercise and weight management remain the main treatments. Research is active, and you can volunteer for UK trials.

Inflammatory arthritis: more options than ever

Biologics. These target specific parts of the immune system. They include anti-TNF medicines and others that block IL-6, IL-17, IL-23 or B cells. Most are given by injection or infusion. On the NHS, NICE sets the criteria for when they can be offered, usually after standard DMARDs have not worked well enough.

Biosimilars. When a biologic's patent ends, near-identical versions called biosimilars can be made. They work in the same way and have made treatment more affordable for the NHS, so more people can access it. You may be switched to a biosimilar. Ask your team if you have questions.

JAK inhibitors. These are tablets that block signals inside immune cells. They are an option in rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis and axial spondyloarthritis. Safety advice from the MHRA means they may be used with caution in people over 65, smokers and those at higher risk of heart disease, clots or cancer.

Treat to target. Not a drug, but a big shift: teams now measure disease activity regularly and adjust treatment until it is controlled. This approach helps many people reach remission.

Osteoarthritis: what is new and what is not

Osteoarthritis research is looking at medicines that might protect cartilage, injections of various kinds, and better ways to target pain. So far none of these is recommended by NICE as a routine treatment. NICE (NG226) does not recommend hyaluronic acid injections, and it does not recommend glucosamine or other supplements.

What does help, according to NICE, is:

  • regular, tailored exercise, often through structured programmes such as ESCAPE-pain
  • weight loss if needed
  • topical anti-inflammatory gels for knee and hand osteoarthritis
  • joint replacement surgery when other treatments have not helped and symptoms are severe

Newer weight-loss medicines may help some people with osteoarthritis indirectly by reducing weight. They are available on the NHS only under specific criteria.

Be cautious with "breakthrough" claims

Stem cell injections, platelet-rich plasma (PRP) and similar treatments are widely advertised privately. NICE has not recommended them for routine use in arthritis, and they can be expensive. Before paying, ask:

  • What does NICE or my specialist say about it?
  • What are the risks and the full cost?
  • Is this part of a registered research study?

Taking part in research

Clinical trials are how new treatments are proven. In the UK you can search for studies on the NIHR's Be Part of Research website and register your interest. Your rheumatology team may also tell you about trials. Taking part is voluntary, and you can withdraw at any time.

Talk to your team

If your current treatment is not controlling your symptoms, ask your GP or rheumatology team what other options there are. Treatment changes are common, and new options keep arriving.

Questions worth asking at your next review

  • Is my arthritis as well controlled as it could be?
  • Are there other medicines I would be eligible for if this one stops working?
  • Are there any research studies I could take part in?
  • Is a biosimilar version of my medicine available?

Treatment for inflammatory arthritis is personal. What works well for one person may not suit another, so it is normal to try more than one option before finding the right one. Keep a note of your symptoms and side effects between appointments to help your team decide.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Osteoporosis vs Arthritis: What's the Difference?
article.excerpt: Osteoporosis and arthritis are often confused. How they differ in symptoms, causes, tests and treatment, and how to protect bones and joints.
article.content:
Osteoporosis is a condition where bones lose strength and break more easily. Arthritis is a group of conditions that cause pain and inflammation in joints. Osteoporosis has no symptoms until a bone breaks, while arthritis causes pain, stiffness and sometimes swelling. They are different conditions, but many people have both, and some arthritis treatments can affect bone health.

The key differences

What is affected

  • Osteoporosis affects the bones themselves, making them thinner and more fragile.
  • Arthritis affects the joints, where bones meet.

Symptoms

  • Osteoporosis is often called a "silent" condition. You will not feel bones getting weaker. The first sign is often a fracture after a minor fall, or a spinal fracture causing sudden back pain, loss of height or a stooped posture.
  • Arthritis causes joint pain, stiffness, swelling and reduced movement.

Causes

  • Osteoporosis is linked to age, menopause, low body weight, smoking, heavy drinking, family history, long-term steroid use and some medical conditions.
  • Arthritis causes depend on the type, such as joint repair problems in osteoarthritis or the immune system in rheumatoid arthritis.

Tests

  • Osteoporosis is diagnosed with a DEXA bone density scan, usually after a fracture risk assessment by your GP.
  • Arthritis is diagnosed by examination, and sometimes blood tests, X-rays or scans.

Treatment

  • Osteoporosis is treated with medicines that strengthen bones, plus calcium and vitamin D if needed, exercise and fall prevention.
  • Arthritis treatment depends on the type and includes exercise, pain relief, disease-modifying medicines and sometimes surgery.

How they are connected

  • Rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory conditions increase the risk of osteoporosis.
  • Steroid tablets taken for three months or more weaken bones.
  • Reduced activity because of joint pain weakens bones and muscles.
  • Falls are more common in people with painful, stiff joints, and falls are what usually lead to fractures.
  • Both conditions become more common with age, so many older people have both.

Interestingly, people with osteoarthritis do not seem to have lower bone density, but their fall risk can still be higher.

Who should have their bone health checked?

NICE (CG146) recommends fracture risk assessment for:

  • all women aged 65 and over and men aged 75 and over
  • younger people with risk factors such as a previous fragility fracture, long-term steroid use, rheumatoid arthritis, low body weight, smoking or heavy drinking, a family history of hip fracture, or early menopause

If you have arthritis and any of these, ask your GP about an assessment.

Protecting your bones and joints together

  • exercise: weight-bearing activity such as walking, plus strength exercise, helps bones and joints. Balance exercises reduce falls.
  • eat well: include calcium-rich foods such as dairy, fortified plant milks, tinned fish with bones and green leafy vegetables
  • vitamin D: follow NHS advice on vitamin D, especially in autumn and winter
  • stop smoking and limit alcohol
  • prevent falls: keep your home well lit and clutter-free, wear supportive shoes and have your eyesight checked
  • review medicines: ask about bone protection if you take steroids long term

Exercise if you have osteoporosis

Exercise is safe and helpful for most people with osteoporosis. If you have had spinal fractures, avoid sudden, forceful forward bending or twisting, and ask a physiotherapist for guidance. Strength and balance programmes are often available locally.

Common misunderstandings

  • Osteoporosis is not painful in itself. Pain comes from fractures.
  • Arthritis does not turn into osteoporosis, or the other way round.
  • Men can get osteoporosis too.
  • It is never too late to start protecting your bones.

When to see your GP

See your GP if you have joint pain or stiffness that lasts more than a few weeks, if you have broken a bone after a minor fall, or if you have lost height or developed a curved upper back. You can also ask for a fracture risk assessment if you have risk factors.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Pilates for Arthritis
article.excerpt: Is Pilates good for arthritis? How it helps strength, posture and balance, safe adaptations for knees, hips, back and hands, and finding a UK class.
article.content:
Pilates can be a good choice for many people with arthritis. It builds core and muscle strength, improves posture, flexibility and balance, and is low impact. It counts as the kind of therapeutic exercise NICE recommends for osteoarthritis and low back pain. Choose a beginners' or clinical class, tell the instructor about your joints, and adapt moves that cause pain.

What Pilates involves

Pilates is a system of controlled exercises that focus on the deep muscles of the tummy, back and pelvis, along with breathing and posture. Classes are done on a mat or on special equipment called reformers. "Clinical Pilates" is run by physiotherapists and is tailored to people with health conditions.

How it can help arthritis

  • stronger muscles around the hips, knees and spine reduce load on painful joints
  • better posture and core control, which can ease back and neck pain
  • improved balance, lowering the risk of falls
  • gentle flexibility work, helping stiff joints move more freely
  • focus on breathing, which helps some people relax and manage pain

NICE recommends exercise, including muscle strengthening and general fitness, as a core treatment for osteoarthritis (NG226) and low back pain (NG59). It does not recommend one type over another, so choose what you enjoy and can keep doing.

Is it safe?

Pilates is generally safe for arthritis when the level is right. Things to watch:

  • Knees: kneeling can be painful. Use a folded mat or cushion, or swap for standing or lying alternatives.
  • Hips: after a hip replacement, avoid bending the hip past 90 degrees or crossing your legs unless your surgeon allows it.
  • Hands and wrists: weight-bearing on the hands, as in plank, can strain sore wrists. Try forearms or a wall instead.
  • Spine and osteoporosis: avoid deep forward bending and twisting moves such as "roll-ups" if you have osteoporosis or a spinal fracture. A clinical Pilates instructor can advise.
  • Neck: if your neck is affected, for example in RA or ankylosing spondylitis, keep your head supported during exercises that lift the head.

Some muscle tiredness the next day is normal. Sharp pain during an exercise, or pain that lasts more than a day, means you should ease off.

Getting started

  • Ask your physiotherapist whether Pilates suits you and which moves to avoid.
  • Look for a beginners' class, a "Pilates for back care" class or a clinical Pilates class.
  • Check the instructor's qualifications, and tell them about your arthritis and any joint replacements.
  • Start with one class a week and build up.
  • Practise a few moves at home between sessions.

Online videos can be useful once you know the basics, but in-person teaching is safer at first.

Simple moves to try

  • Pelvic tilts: lying on your back with knees bent, gently flatten your back into the mat, then release.
  • Knee rolls: in the same position, let your knees sway slowly to one side and back.
  • Clam: lying on your side with knees bent, lift your top knee while keeping feet together. This strengthens the hips.
  • Bridge: lying on your back, lift your hips slowly, then lower.

Do 5 to 10 of each, slowly and with control.

Cost and access

Pilates is not usually offered as standalone NHS treatment, though some NHS physiotherapy services run classes. Private and leisure centre classes vary in cost. Some gyms include classes in membership.

Pilates as part of a balanced routine

Pilates is a good complement to walking, swimming or cycling. Combining it with some aerobic activity gives you the widest benefits for joints, heart and mood.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Polymyalgia Rheumatica: Symptoms and Treatment
article.excerpt: Polymyalgia rheumatica explained: shoulder and hip stiffness in over-50s, how it's diagnosed, steroid treatment, and the warning signs of giant cell arteritis.
article.content:
Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is an inflammatory condition that causes pain and stiffness in the shoulders, neck and hips, usually in people over 50. Stiffness is worst in the morning and can make it hard to get out of bed or lift your arms. It is treated with steroid tablets, which usually work quickly. Treatment often lasts one to two years before it can be stopped.

Symptoms

  • pain and stiffness in both shoulders, the neck, upper arms, hips and thighs
  • stiffness in the morning lasting more than 45 minutes
  • difficulty getting out of bed, dressing or lifting your arms above your head
  • tiredness, low mood, loss of appetite, weight loss or a mild fever

Symptoms usually come on over days to a couple of weeks.

Link with giant cell arteritis

Some people with PMR develop giant cell arteritis (GCA), where blood vessels in the head become inflamed. GCA can cause sight loss if not treated quickly. Warning signs include a new headache, scalp tenderness, pain in the jaw when chewing, and changes in vision. If you notice these, seek help the same day.

Who gets it

PMR almost always affects people over 50, most often over 70, and is more common in women. The cause is not known.

Diagnosis

There is no single test. Your GP will ask about your symptoms and examine you. Blood tests usually show raised inflammation (CRP or ESR). Other tests check for conditions that can look similar, such as an underactive thyroid, rheumatoid arthritis, muscle problems and some cancers. A quick response to steroids supports the diagnosis. If the picture is not clear, your GP may refer you to a rheumatologist.

Treatment with steroids

Steroid tablets, usually prednisolone, are the main treatment. Most people feel much better within days. If symptoms do not improve within about a week, the diagnosis should be reviewed.

The dose is reduced slowly over many months. This helps prevent symptoms returning and lets your body restart its own steroid production. Most people take steroids for one to two years, and some need them for longer.

  • never stop suddenly. Reduce only as advised.
  • carry a steroid card if you are given one.
  • symptoms may return as the dose is lowered. Tell your GP, as the dose may need a small increase.

Protecting your health on steroids

Long-term steroids can affect bones, blood sugar, blood pressure, weight, mood and skin. Your GP may:

  • assess your fracture risk and offer bone protection
  • check blood pressure and blood sugar regularly
  • check your eyes, as steroids can cause cataracts and glaucoma

If steroids cannot be reduced or are causing problems, a rheumatologist may suggest other medicines alongside, such as methotrexate, or a newer treatment.

Self-help

  • keep moving gently each day, as activity helps stiffness
  • strength exercises help counter muscle weakness from steroids
  • eat a balanced diet to help manage appetite and weight gain from steroids
  • get flu and COVID-19 vaccinations, as infections can be more serious on steroids
  • a hot shower in the morning can ease stiffness

Outlook

Most people with PMR recover fully, though it may take a couple of years. Relapses can happen, so keep in touch with your GP and report symptoms early.

It is normal to feel worried about taking steroids for a long time. Talk to your GP about any concerns, as they can explain how the benefits and risks balance for you and how side effects will be monitored.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a new headache with tenderness of the scalp or temples, pain in the jaw when chewing, or any change in your vision such as blurring, double vision or loss of sight — this may be giant cell arteritis and needs same-day treatment to protect your sight
  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Psoriatic Arthritis: Early Signs and Treatment
article.excerpt: Early signs of psoriatic arthritis, including swollen fingers, heel pain and nail changes, how it is diagnosed on the NHS, and the treatments that help.
article.content:
Psoriatic arthritis causes painful, swollen joints in some people who have psoriasis. Early signs include a whole finger or toe swelling up like a sausage, heel or foot pain, stiffness in the morning, and pitted or lifting nails. It can start before skin psoriasis appears. If you notice these, see your GP, because early treatment can prevent joint damage.

Who gets it

Psoriatic arthritis most often starts between the ages of 30 and 50, but it can happen at any age. Many people with psoriasis never develop it. Having a close relative with psoriasis or psoriatic arthritis increases the chance.

Early signs to look out for

  • dactylitis: a whole finger or toe that becomes swollen, red and painful
  • enthesitis: pain where tendons attach to bone, such as the back of the heel or the sole of the foot
  • joint pain and swelling, often in a patchy pattern and not always on both sides
  • morning stiffness that lasts more than 30 minutes
  • nail changes: pitting, ridges, discolouration or the nail lifting off the nail bed
  • back or buttock pain that is worse with rest and better with movement
  • tiredness
  • eye inflammation (uveitis): a red, painful eye with blurred vision, which needs urgent same-day assessment

Symptoms often come and go in flares.

Getting diagnosed

There is no single test. Your GP will examine you and may arrange blood tests and X-rays. Most people with psoriatic arthritis have a negative test for rheumatoid factor. NICE recommends that people with psoriasis have an annual check for signs of psoriatic arthritis. If inflammatory arthritis is suspected, your GP should refer you to a rheumatologist.

Treatment

The aim is to control inflammation, relieve pain and protect joints.

  • Anti-inflammatory medicines (NSAIDs) can ease pain and stiffness in mild cases.
  • Steroid injections into a swollen joint can settle a flare.
  • DMARDs such as methotrexate, sulfasalazine or leflunomide are used for ongoing inflammation. Methotrexate may also help the skin.
  • Biologics and targeted therapies are used if DMARDs are not enough. These include anti-TNF, anti-IL-17 and anti-IL-23 medicines and JAK inhibitors. NICE sets the criteria for NHS use.

Many treatments help both skin and joints, so your rheumatology and dermatology teams may work together.

Living well with psoriatic arthritis

  • Exercise regularly. It keeps joints flexible and muscles strong. Swimming, cycling and walking are good choices.
  • Manage your weight. Extra weight can increase inflammation and may reduce how well some treatments work.
  • Stop smoking and keep alcohol within limits, especially if you take methotrexate.
  • Look after your heart. Psoriatic disease raises cardiovascular risk, so have blood pressure and cholesterol checked.
  • Foot care. A podiatrist can help with heel pain, insoles and nail problems.
  • Fatigue and mood. These are common. Talk to your team if they are affecting your life.

What the future looks like

With modern treatment, many people with psoriatic arthritis keep working and doing what they enjoy. The key is getting diagnosed early, staying in touch with your team and reporting flares or side effects promptly.

Questions to ask your GP or rheumatologist

  • Could my joint, heel or nail symptoms be psoriatic arthritis?
  • Do I need a referral to rheumatology?
  • What treatment will help both my skin and my joints?
  • What blood tests will I need while on treatment?
  • Who do I contact if I have a flare?

Bring photos of swollen fingers or toes if the swelling has gone down by the time of your appointment. They can help your doctor understand what you are experiencing. A short diary of when symptoms started and how long morning stiffness lasts is also useful.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Reactive Arthritis: Causes, Symptoms and Recovery
article.excerpt: Reactive arthritis explained: the infections that trigger it, symptoms in joints, eyes and urinary tract, NHS treatment, recovery time and when to get help.
article.content:
Reactive arthritis is joint inflammation that develops after an infection elsewhere in the body, usually a sexually transmitted infection such as chlamydia or a bowel infection such as food poisoning. It often affects the knees, ankles or feet, and can also cause sore eyes and pain when weeing. Most people recover fully within a few months to a year.

What causes it

The joint itself is not infected. Instead, the immune system overreacts to an infection somewhere else and starts attacking healthy tissue in the joints. Common triggers include:

  • chlamydia and other sexually transmitted infections
  • bowel infections such as salmonella, campylobacter or shigella, often from food poisoning

Symptoms usually start between one and four weeks after the infection, and sometimes the original infection caused few symptoms. It is most common in young adults. A gene called HLA-B27 makes it more likely.

Symptoms

Joints and tendons

  • pain, swelling and stiffness, often in the knees, ankles or feet
  • usually affects a few joints rather than many, often on one side
  • heel pain or a swollen "sausage" finger or toe
  • lower back or buttock pain

Eyes

  • red, sore or sticky eyes (conjunctivitis)
  • less commonly, uveitis: a painful red eye with blurred vision and light sensitivity. This needs same-day assessment.

Urinary and genital

  • pain or burning when weeing, needing to wee often, or discharge

General

  • tiredness, a mild fever, and sometimes skin rashes or mouth ulcers

Diagnosis

Your GP will ask about recent infections, including stomach upsets and sexual health. There is no single test. You may have blood tests to check for inflammation, urine or swab tests for infections, and sometimes fluid taken from the joint. Testing joint fluid helps rule out septic arthritis, a joint infection that needs emergency treatment.

Treatment

  • Treating the trigger infection. If an STI such as chlamydia is found, antibiotics will be given, and partners should be tested and treated. Sexual health clinics are free and confidential.
  • Anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) are usually the first treatment for joint pain and swelling.
  • Steroid injections into a swollen joint, or steroid tablets, may be used if NSAIDs are not enough.
  • DMARDs such as sulfasalazine or methotrexate may be offered by a rheumatologist if symptoms last longer than six months.
  • Eye drops for eye inflammation, arranged by an eye specialist if needed.

Looking after yourself

  • rest a very painful joint during a flare, then start gentle movement as it settles
  • use cold packs for swollen joints and warmth for stiffness
  • a physiotherapist can help you regain strength and movement
  • pace activity, as fatigue can last for a while

Recovery

Most people get better within a few months to a year. Some have symptoms that come back, and a small number develop long-term arthritis. If symptoms last more than six months, ask about a rheumatology referral.

Reducing the risk of it happening again

Use condoms with new partners, get tested for STIs, and follow good food hygiene. If you have had reactive arthritis before, mention it if you get another infection.

Work, sport and everyday life

During a flare you may need time off work or a break from sport. A fit note from your GP covers longer absences. As the swelling settles, return to activity gradually. Low-impact exercise such as swimming or cycling is often easier on sore knees and ankles than running. Most people are able to return to their usual activities once the inflammation has gone.

If you feel low or anxious while recovering, which is common with any painful condition, talk to your GP. Support is available, and you do not have to wait until you feel at breaking point to ask.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Reduced Mobility
article.excerpt: Struggling to get around with arthritis? Why mobility drops, exercises that help, walking aids, home changes, Blue Badge, benefits and when to get checked.
article.content:
Reduced mobility with arthritis is common, but it is often improvable. Pain, stiffness, weak muscles and fear of falling all play a part, and each can be worked on. A physiotherapist can build an exercise plan. The right walking aid and home changes can make getting around safer. If your mobility drops suddenly, see your GP, as this may need checking.

Why mobility drops

  • Pain in the knees, hips, feet or back makes walking uncomfortable, so you walk less.
  • Stiffness limits how far joints bend, making stairs and getting out of chairs hard.
  • Muscle weakness develops quickly when you are less active and adds to joint strain.
  • Fatigue, common in inflammatory arthritis, saps stamina.
  • Fear of falling can lead people to restrict activity, which weakens balance further.
  • Weight puts extra load on hips and knees.

When to get checked

See your GP if your mobility has dropped noticeably over weeks or months, or if you have new swelling, weakness or numbness. Seek help the same day if it changes over days, for example if you suddenly cannot walk, cannot bear weight after a fall, or have new leg weakness. Treatable causes include a flare of inflammatory arthritis, an infection, a fracture or a nerve problem.

Exercise is the foundation

NICE recommends exercise for everyone with osteoarthritis, tailored to the person. For mobility, focus on:

  • leg strength: sit to stand, step-ups on the bottom stair, seated knee extensions
  • balance: standing on one leg holding the worktop, heel-to-toe walking along a corridor
  • flexibility: gentle daily stretches for hips, knees and ankles
  • walking: short, regular walks, building time gradually

You can often self-refer to NHS physiotherapy. Water-based exercise and tai chi are other good options.

Walking aids

The right aid, correctly fitted, can reduce pain and improve confidence.

  • a walking stick held in the hand opposite the painful leg
  • a rollator with a seat for longer distances
  • a wheelchair or scooter for outings where walking is not practical. Your local wheelchair service assesses for NHS chairs.

A physiotherapist can check the height and show you how to use an aid on stairs and kerbs.

Making home easier

  • stair rails on both sides, grab rails and a second banister
  • raising chairs, beds and toilet seats to reduce bending
  • removing trip hazards and improving lighting
  • moving essentials downstairs if stairs are hard

Ask your council for a free needs assessment. An occupational therapist can advise on equipment and adaptations.

Financial and practical help

  • Blue Badge: for people who find walking very difficult
  • Personal Independence Payment (PIP) if you are of working age, or Attendance Allowance if over State Pension age. In Scotland, Adult Disability Payment has replaced PIP.
  • Motability: if you receive the enhanced mobility rate, you can use it towards a car, scooter or powered wheelchair
  • Concessionary bus passes for disabled people in many areas

Look at the bigger picture

Review your pain relief with your GP or pharmacist so that you can exercise. Ask whether any medicines could be making you dizzy or drowsy. If arthritis in one joint is severe despite treatment, your GP can discuss a referral to consider surgery such as joint replacement.

Keeping some movement every day, even when it is limited, protects the mobility you have and helps rebuild what you have lost.

Setting realistic goals

Think about what you most want to be able to do again, such as walking to the corner shop, managing the stairs or getting in and out of the car. Share this with your physiotherapist so your plan targets it directly. Progress is often slow at first, so measure it over weeks rather than days. A simple record, such as how many times you can stand from a chair in 30 seconds, shows change you might otherwise miss.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis Diagnosis
article.excerpt: How rheumatoid arthritis is diagnosed on the NHS: GP checks, blood tests, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP, scans, referral times and what to expect.
article.content:
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is diagnosed by a rheumatologist, based on your symptoms, an examination of your joints, blood tests and sometimes scans. There is no single test that proves or rules out RA. If your GP finds persistent joint swelling, NICE says you should be referred urgently to rheumatology, even if your blood tests are normal.

Step 1: seeing your GP

Your GP will ask about:

  • which joints are painful or swollen, and whether both sides are affected
  • how long morning stiffness lasts. More than 30 minutes suggests inflammation.
  • how long symptoms have lasted
  • tiredness, weight loss or feeling unwell
  • family history of RA or other autoimmune conditions
  • smoking

They will examine your joints, looking for swelling, warmth and tenderness, especially in the small joints of the hands and feet. A positive "squeeze test", where squeezing across the knuckles or the balls of the feet causes pain, can suggest inflammation.

Step 2: blood tests

Your GP may arrange tests including:

  • CRP and ESR: measure inflammation in the body
  • rheumatoid factor (RF): an antibody found in many people with RA, but also in some healthy people and other conditions
  • anti-CCP antibodies: more specific to RA. A positive result makes RA more likely and may suggest more active disease.
  • full blood count, kidney and liver function: to check general health and help plan treatment

Many people with RA have positive RF or anti-CCP, but not all. A negative result does not rule out RA. This is called "seronegative" RA.

Step 3: referral to rheumatology

NICE (NG100) recommends urgent referral for adults with suspected persistent synovitis of undetermined cause. Refer urgently if:

  • the small joints of the hands or feet are affected
  • more than one joint is affected
  • there has been a delay of three months or longer between symptoms starting and seeking advice

Your GP should not wait for blood test results if they find persistent joint swelling. If you are waiting, ask your GP about pain relief and what to do if things get worse.

Step 4: assessment by a rheumatologist

The rheumatologist will take a detailed history, examine your joints and review tests. They may arrange:

  • X-rays of hands and feet, to look for early damage and to provide a baseline
  • ultrasound, which can show inflammation not obvious on examination
  • MRI occasionally

They will consider other conditions that can look similar, such as psoriatic arthritis, lupus, viral arthritis, gout and polymyalgia rheumatica.

Classification criteria

Rheumatologists may use criteria that score joint involvement, blood tests, inflammation levels and symptom duration. These help with research and consistency, but diagnosis is ultimately based on the rheumatologist's clinical judgement.

After diagnosis

If RA is confirmed, treatment usually begins straight away with a disease-modifying medicine such as methotrexate, sometimes with a short course of steroids. You should be offered:

  • information about RA and your treatment
  • a named contact or advice line
  • access to physiotherapy, occupational therapy and podiatry
  • regular reviews until your disease is controlled

Preparing for appointments

  • write down your symptoms and when they started
  • note how long morning stiffness lasts
  • take photos of swollen joints
  • list your medicines, including over-the-counter products
  • bring questions and someone to support you if you wish

If you are told it is not RA

Sometimes symptoms settle, or another diagnosis is made. If symptoms return or change, go back to your GP. Some people develop RA over time after early, unclear symptoms.

Coping while you wait

Waiting for a diagnosis can be stressful. Keep moving gently, use the pain relief your GP or pharmacist recommends, and note any changes. If new joints become swollen or you feel much worse, contact your GP, as your referral may need to be upgraded.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis Treatment
article.excerpt: How rheumatoid arthritis is treated on the NHS: DMARDs, biologics, steroids, monitoring, physiotherapy and self-care, and why early treatment matters.
article.content:
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is treated with disease-modifying medicines called DMARDs, which calm the immune system and help prevent joint damage. Treatment should start as early as possible, ideally soon after diagnosis by a rheumatologist. The aim is remission or very low disease activity, and many people now reach it. Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and self-care support the medicines.

Why early treatment matters

RA is an autoimmune condition. The immune system attacks the lining of the joints, causing pain, swelling and stiffness. Without treatment this inflammation can damage joints permanently. NICE (NG100) recommends that adults with suspected persistent synovitis are referred urgently to rheumatology and that treatment begins as soon as possible after diagnosis.

The main medicines

Conventional DMARDs. NICE recommends starting with one of these, usually methotrexate. Leflunomide or sulfasalazine are alternatives, and hydroxychloroquine may be used for milder disease. They take several weeks to months to work fully, so it is important to keep taking them even if you do not notice a change straight away.

Short-term steroids. A short course of steroid tablets or an injection may be given to control symptoms quickly while DMARDs start working. NICE advises keeping steroid use as short as possible because of long-term side effects.

Biologic and targeted medicines. If DMARDs do not control the disease well enough, you may be offered a biologic medicine, such as an anti-TNF, or a JAK inhibitor tablet. On the NHS these are offered when disease activity reaches the level set out by NICE.

Pain relief. Painkillers and anti-inflammatory medicines help symptoms but do not change the disease. Your GP or pharmacist will advise on safe use, especially with other medicines.

Treat to target

Your team will measure how active your RA is, often using a score called DAS28. This combines joint counts, blood tests and how you feel. Treatment is adjusted until you reach the target. NICE suggests monthly reviews until the disease is controlled, then an annual review.

Monitoring and safety

DMARDs and biologics need regular blood tests to check blood counts, liver and kidney function. Keep these appointments, as they help catch side effects early. Your team will also advise on:

  • infections: some treatments make infections more likely. Report fever or feeling unwell promptly.
  • vaccines: flu, COVID-19 and pneumonia vaccines are usually recommended. Some live vaccines may not be suitable.
  • pregnancy: some medicines must be stopped well before trying to conceive. Discuss plans early.
  • alcohol: limits apply with methotrexate. Ask your team what is safe for you.

Physiotherapy, OT and podiatry

NICE recommends access to a multidisciplinary team. A physiotherapist can help with exercise to keep joints moving and muscles strong. An occupational therapist can advise on hand function, splints, equipment and work. A podiatrist can help with foot problems, which are common in RA.

What you can do yourself

  • Stay active. Regular exercise reduces stiffness and fatigue and protects your heart.
  • Stop smoking. Smoking makes RA more active and can reduce how well treatment works.
  • Look after your heart. RA raises cardiovascular risk. Have your blood pressure and cholesterol checked.
  • Pace yourself and plan rest around busy days.
  • Learn your flare plan. Ask your team who to contact if your joints become more swollen.

Living with RA day to day

Fatigue is common in RA and can be as hard to live with as pain. It often improves as inflammation is controlled, but pacing, regular gentle exercise and good sleep habits also help. Low mood and anxiety are common too, and talking therapies are available on the NHS through self-referral in England.

If work is getting harder, you may be entitled to reasonable adjustments under the Equality Act 2010, and Access to Work can help with equipment or travel costs. Benefits such as Personal Independence Payment may be available depending on how RA affects your daily life.

If treatment is not working

Tell your team if you still have swollen joints, long morning stiffness or side effects. There are many treatment options, and switching is common. Most people find a combination that works for them.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Shoulder Osteoarthritis
article.excerpt: Shoulder osteoarthritis explained: symptoms, how it differs from frozen shoulder and rotator cuff problems, exercises, injections and when surgery helps.
article.content:
Shoulder osteoarthritis causes a deep, aching pain in the shoulder, stiffness and grinding, and difficulty reaching up or behind your back. It is less common than knee or hip osteoarthritis and is often linked to age, past injury or long-standing rotator cuff problems. Most people are helped by exercise, pain relief and activity changes. Joint replacement is an option if symptoms are severe.

The two shoulder joints

The shoulder has two joints that can be affected:

  • the glenohumeral joint, the main ball-and-socket joint. Arthritis here causes deep pain and stiffness.
  • the acromioclavicular (AC) joint at the top of the shoulder. Arthritis here causes pain at the top of the shoulder, particularly when reaching across your body.

Symptoms

  • aching pain deep in the shoulder, sometimes spreading down the upper arm
  • stiffness and reduced movement, especially turning the arm outwards or reaching up
  • grinding or clicking
  • pain at night, particularly lying on the affected side
  • difficulty with tasks such as hair washing, dressing or reaching high shelves

Conditions that can look similar

  • frozen shoulder: severe stiffness, often with intense pain, usually in people aged 40 to 60 and more common with diabetes
  • rotator cuff problems: pain when lifting the arm out to the side, weakness and pain at night
  • referred pain from the neck: pain that moves down the arm with neck movement
  • polymyalgia rheumatica: stiffness in both shoulders and hips, mainly in over 50s, with severe morning stiffness
  • rheumatoid arthritis, which can affect both shoulders

A GP or physiotherapist can usually tell these apart through examination. An X-ray may be used to confirm shoulder osteoarthritis and plan treatment.

Self-care

  • keep the shoulder moving gently every day to prevent further stiffness
  • pace overhead tasks and keep items you use often at waist to shoulder height
  • heat from a wheat bag can ease stiffness. Cold packs can help after activity.
  • sleep with a pillow supporting the arm, or lie on the other side
  • pain relief: ask your pharmacist about painkillers and anti-inflammatory gels that suit you

Exercises

A physiotherapist can give you a programme. Common exercises include:

  • pendulum swings: lean forward and let the arm hang, then make small circles
  • wall slides: walk your fingers up a wall, in front and to the side
  • assisted movements with a stick, using the good arm to help the sore one
  • strengthening with a resistance band for the rotator cuff and shoulder blade muscles

Some discomfort is normal. If pain is much worse the next day, do a little less.

NHS treatment options

  • physiotherapy: many areas let you self-refer
  • steroid injections: can reduce pain for some weeks to months, helping you do your exercises
  • surgery: for severe pain or loss of function despite other treatments. Options include shoulder replacement, either anatomical or reverse replacement depending on your rotator cuff. For AC joint arthritis, a small operation to remove the end of the collarbone may be offered.

NICE recommends exercise and education for osteoarthritis and referral for joint surgery when symptoms substantially affect quality of life.

Daily life tips

  • use a long-handled brush and sponge for washing
  • choose front-fastening clothes and put the sore arm in first
  • use a step stool rather than reaching up, if your balance is good
  • carry shopping close to your body and split it into lighter bags

Driving and work

If your shoulder limits steering or checking blind spots, you may need to adapt or stop driving until it improves. Tell your employer if work involves reaching or lifting; reasonable adjustments may help.

Outlook

Shoulder osteoarthritis tends to change slowly, and symptoms often go through better and worse spells. Keeping the shoulder moving and the surrounding muscles strong gives you the best chance of staying independent with everyday tasks.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

/blog/lwa-archive-steroid-side-effects-w.question: Steroid Side Effects: What People with Arthritis Should Know
/blog/lwa-archive-steroid-side-effects-w.answer: Steroids such as prednisolone work quickly to calm inflammation, but they can cause side effects. Short courses usually cause mild, temporary effects such as raised appetite, poor sleep or mood changes. Long-term use can thin bones, raise blood sugar and blood pressure, and increase infection risk. Never stop steroid tablets suddenly after more than a few weeks; your doctor will reduce them gradually.

article.title: Steroid Side Effects: What People with Arthritis Should Know
article.excerpt: Steroid tablets and injections for arthritis: short- and long-term side effects, bone protection, steroid cards, never stopping suddenly, and when to get help.
article.content:
Steroids such as prednisolone work quickly to calm inflammation, but they can cause side effects. Short courses usually cause mild, temporary effects such as raised appetite, poor sleep or mood changes. Long-term use can thin bones, raise blood sugar and blood pressure, and increase infection risk. Never stop steroid tablets suddenly after more than a few weeks; your doctor will reduce them gradually.

How steroids are used in arthritis

Steroids, also called corticosteroids, are man-made versions of a hormone your body makes naturally. In arthritis they may be given:

  • as tablets, often prednisolone, for flares or while slower medicines start working
  • as an injection into a joint, to settle one painful, swollen joint
  • as an injection into a muscle, to calm a widespread flare
  • as infusions in hospital, occasionally

For rheumatoid arthritis, NICE (NG100) advises using steroids as short-term bridging treatment and keeping long-term use to a minimum.

Common short-term side effects

  • increased appetite and weight gain
  • difficulty sleeping
  • mood changes, feeling restless, low or irritable
  • indigestion or heartburn. Taking tablets with food in the morning can help.
  • raised blood sugar, especially important if you have diabetes

These usually settle when the dose comes down.

Possible long-term side effects

  • thinner bones (osteoporosis) and higher fracture risk
  • higher blood pressure and blood sugar, sometimes triggering diabetes
  • infections that are more frequent or more serious
  • weight gain around the face and tummy
  • thinning skin and easy bruising
  • muscle weakness, especially in the thighs
  • eye problems such as cataracts or glaucoma

The risk rises with higher doses and longer use. Your doctor will weigh this against the harm uncontrolled inflammation can cause.

Protecting your bones

NICE (CG146) recommends a fracture risk assessment for people taking steroid tablets for three months or more. Your GP may suggest bone-protecting treatment, calcium and vitamin D, or a DEXA scan. Weight-bearing exercise and not smoking also help.

Never stop suddenly

If you take steroid tablets for more than three weeks, your body's own steroid production can switch off. Stopping suddenly can cause a dangerous drop, called adrenal crisis. Your doctor will reduce the dose slowly. You may be given a steroid emergency card. Carry it and show it if you become unwell, need surgery or visit A&E. If you are vomiting and cannot keep tablets down, get medical advice the same day.

Steroid injections into a joint

Joint injections usually cause fewer whole-body effects, but you may notice:

  • a flare of pain for a day or two afterwards
  • flushing of the face
  • a temporary rise in blood sugar if you have diabetes
  • rarely, a small dent or pale patch in the skin at the site

There is a small risk of infection. If the joint becomes hot, red, more swollen and more painful in the days after an injection, especially with fever, seek urgent help. Most people are advised to limit how many injections a joint has each year.

Infections and chickenpox

Steroids can make infections harder to fight. Tell your doctor if you develop a fever or feel unwell. If you have never had chickenpox or shingles and come into contact with someone who has it, contact your GP promptly, as you may need treatment.

Reporting side effects

Tell your GP, pharmacist or rheumatology team about any side effects. You can also report them to the MHRA through the Yellow Card scheme.

Questions to ask your doctor

  • Why do I need steroids, and for how long?
  • How will the dose be reduced?
  • Do I need bone protection or a bone density scan?
  • Should my blood pressure or blood sugar be checked more often?
  • Do I need a steroid emergency card?

Writing your questions down before an appointment makes it easier to get the answers you need.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Sudden Joint Swelling: Causes and When to Seek Help
article.excerpt: What causes sudden joint swelling, from injury and gout to infection and inflammatory arthritis, what to do at home, and when to call 999, NHS 111 or your GP.
article.content:
Sudden joint swelling is most often caused by an injury, gout, pseudogout or a flare of arthritis. A joint that is suddenly hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with fever or feeling unwell, could be an infection called septic arthritis, which is an emergency. Get any unexplained swollen joint checked the same day by NHS 111 or your GP.

Common causes

Injury

A sprain, ligament tear, cartilage tear or fracture can cause swelling within hours. Rapid swelling after a twisting injury may mean bleeding into the joint and should be assessed.

Gout

Crystals of uric acid cause sudden severe pain and swelling, often in the big toe, ankle or knee, frequently starting at night.

Pseudogout (CPPD)

Calcium crystals cause similar attacks, often in the knee or wrist, mainly in older adults.

Septic arthritis

A bacterial infection inside the joint. It usually affects one joint, which is hot, red, swollen and very painful, often with fever. It can damage the joint within days and needs emergency hospital treatment. People with joint replacements, diabetes, weakened immune systems or existing arthritis are at higher risk.

Inflammatory arthritis

Rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and other conditions can cause swelling, often in several joints, with stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes in the morning.

Reactive arthritis

Swelling a few weeks after a bowel or sexually transmitted infection.

Osteoarthritis flare

Knees in particular can swell during a flare, usually after more activity.

Bursitis

Swelling of a fluid-filled sac, such as in front of the knee or behind the elbow. It can become infected.

Other causes

Lyme disease after a tick bite, viral infections and blood disorders are less common causes.

What to do while you wait to be seen

For swelling after a minor injury, if you can still bear weight and there are no warning signs:

  • rest the joint for a day or two
  • use an ice pack wrapped in a towel for up to 20 minutes every few hours
  • raise the joint above heart level when you can
  • use a pharmacist-recommended painkiller or gel
  • avoid heat in the first two days

Gradually start gentle movement as pain allows.

When to see your GP

See your GP if:

  • swelling has not improved after a few days
  • swelling keeps coming back
  • several joints are swollen
  • you have morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes
  • you also have rashes, eye problems, bowel symptoms or psoriasis

NICE recommends urgent referral to a rheumatologist for persistent joint swelling of unknown cause.

Tests you may have

  • blood tests for inflammation, uric acid and infection
  • fluid taken from the joint with a needle to check for infection or crystals
  • X-ray or ultrasound
  • tests for infections that can trigger reactive arthritis

If you already have arthritis

Not every swollen joint is a flare. If one joint is much more swollen and painful than your usual flares, or you feel unwell or feverish, seek urgent advice, especially if you take steroids, DMARDs or biologics, which can hide some signs of infection. Do not stop your medicines without advice, but tell the doctor what you take.

Keeping a record

If swelling comes and goes, take photos and note the date, which joint, any triggers and how long it lasted. This helps your GP or rheumatologist work out the cause.

Most sudden joint swelling turns out to have a treatable cause. Getting checked quickly means you get the right treatment sooner and, for infections, protects the joint from lasting damage.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a swollen joint with a high temperature, shivering or feeling very unwell, especially if you have a joint replacement, diabetes or take immune-suppressing medicines
  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: Types of Arthritis
article.excerpt: The main types of arthritis explained: osteoarthritis, rheumatoid, psoriatic, gout, ankylosing spondylitis, lupus and more, with symptoms and treatment.
article.content:
There are many types of arthritis, but most fall into a few groups. Osteoarthritis is by far the most common and develops gradually. Inflammatory types, such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis, are caused by the immune system. Crystal arthritis, such as gout, causes sudden severe attacks. Each type is treated differently, so getting the right diagnosis matters.

Osteoarthritis

The most common type. The cartilage lining the joint becomes thinner and the joint tries to repair itself, which can cause bony growths and changes in the joint. It most often affects knees, hips, hands and the spine, usually after 45.

Typical symptoms: pain with activity, short-lived stiffness after rest, sometimes swelling and grinding.

Treatment: exercise, weight management, pain relief, aids, and joint replacement for severe cases.

Inflammatory arthritis

The immune system attacks the joints, causing inflammation. Early treatment with disease-modifying medicines prevents damage.

  • Rheumatoid arthritis: usually affects small joints of hands and feet on both sides, with morning stiffness over 30 minutes and fatigue.
  • Psoriatic arthritis: occurs with psoriasis. It can cause swollen "sausage" fingers or toes, heel pain and nail changes.
  • Ankylosing spondylitis (axial spondyloarthritis): mainly affects the spine and pelvis, with back pain that is worse at rest and better with movement, starting before 45.
  • Enteropathic arthritis: linked with Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis.
  • Reactive arthritis: develops after an infection, often a bowel or sexually transmitted infection, and usually settles within months.
  • Juvenile idiopathic arthritis: arthritis that starts before the age of 16.

Crystal arthritis

  • Gout: uric acid crystals form in a joint, causing sudden severe pain, redness and swelling, often in the big toe. Treatment includes medicines for attacks and medicines to lower uric acid long-term.
  • Pseudogout (CPPD): calcium crystals cause similar sudden attacks, often in the knee or wrist, mainly in older people.

Connective tissue diseases

These autoimmune conditions can affect joints and other parts of the body:

  • Lupus (SLE): joint pain, rashes, fatigue and sometimes kidney or blood problems
  • Sjögren's syndrome: dry eyes and mouth with joint pain
  • Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma): skin thickening, cold fingers and joint pain

Conditions that affect muscles and soft tissues

  • Polymyalgia rheumatica: stiffness and pain in shoulders and hips, mainly in over 50s, treated with steroids
  • Fibromyalgia: widespread pain and fatigue. It is not a type of arthritis but often affects people who have arthritis.

Infection in a joint

Septic arthritis is an infection inside a joint. It causes a hot, swollen, very painful joint, often with fever, and is a medical emergency.

How doctors tell them apart

Your GP will ask about which joints hurt, how long stiffness lasts, any swelling and other symptoms such as rashes or bowel problems. Blood tests, X-rays, ultrasound or joint fluid tests may help. Osteoarthritis can usually be diagnosed from symptoms alone. Suspected inflammatory arthritis should be referred to a rheumatologist.

Why the type matters

Treatments differ. Exercise helps all types, but inflammatory arthritis also needs medicines that calm the immune system, while gout needs medicines that lower uric acid. If your arthritis is not improving as expected, ask whether the diagnosis should be reviewed.

Living with arthritis

Whatever the type, staying active, keeping to a healthy weight, pacing and getting support with work, mood and daily tasks all make a difference.

Questions to ask your GP

  • What type of arthritis do you think I have, and why?
  • Do I need blood tests, an X-ray or a referral?
  • What treatment and exercise do you recommend for my type?
  • What should I do if my symptoms change?

It can help to bring a list of the joints affected, how long stiffness lasts and any other symptoms, such as rashes or eye problems. Photos of swollen joints are also useful if the swelling comes and goes.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: What Causes Arthritis?
article.excerpt: What causes arthritis? How age, genes, injury, weight, the immune system, crystals and infection lead to different types, and the risks you can reduce.
article.content:
Arthritis has different causes depending on the type. Osteoarthritis develops when joints cannot fully repair everyday wear and damage, with age, weight, injury and genes all playing a part. Inflammatory arthritis, such as rheumatoid arthritis, happens when the immune system attacks the joints. Gout is caused by crystals, and septic arthritis by infection. Often several factors combine.

Osteoarthritis: repair that cannot keep up

Joints are constantly repairing themselves. In osteoarthritis the balance tips: cartilage thins, the bone underneath thickens and bony growths form. Risk factors include:

  • age: most common after 45
  • being overweight: more load on knees and hips, and inflammatory chemicals from fat tissue
  • joint injury: such as a torn ligament or cartilage, or a fracture into a joint
  • repeated strain: jobs involving heavy lifting, kneeling or squatting
  • genes and family history, especially for hand osteoarthritis
  • being female, especially after menopause
  • joint shape: for example, hip problems from childhood
  • muscle weakness around the joint

Inflammatory arthritis: the immune system

In rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis and lupus, the immune system mistakes healthy tissue for a threat. The exact trigger is often unknown, but contributing factors include:

  • genes, such as HLA-B27 in ankylosing spondylitis
  • smoking, the biggest lifestyle risk for rheumatoid arthritis
  • sex hormones, which may explain why RA and lupus are more common in women
  • having psoriasis or inflammatory bowel disease
  • infections, which can trigger reactive arthritis

Crystal arthritis

Gout happens when uric acid builds up in the blood and forms needle-shaped crystals in joints. Risk factors include genes, kidney problems, being overweight, high blood pressure, drinking a lot of alcohol or sugary drinks, eating large amounts of red meat or seafood, and some medicines such as water tablets.

Pseudogout is caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals and is more common in older people.

Infection

Septic arthritis is caused by bacteria getting into a joint, through the blood, a wound or after surgery. It is more likely in people with joint replacements, diabetes, weakened immune systems or existing arthritis. It needs emergency treatment.

What does not cause arthritis

  • cracking your knuckles: there is no good evidence it causes arthritis
  • cold or damp weather: may make joints feel worse but does not cause arthritis
  • normal exercise: helps keep joints healthy rather than wearing them out

Why understanding causes helps

Knowing what may have contributed to your arthritis can guide treatment. For example, weight loss helps knee osteoarthritis, stopping smoking helps rheumatoid arthritis and medicines that lower uric acid prevent gout attacks.

Risk factors you can change

  • keep to a healthy weight
  • stay active and keep your muscles strong
  • protect your joints at work and in sport
  • do not smoke
  • keep alcohol within recommended limits
  • get symptoms checked early

When to see your GP

See your GP if you have joint pain, swelling or stiffness that lasts more than a few weeks, stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes in the morning, or symptoms in several joints. Early diagnosis helps you get the right treatment.

A combination of factors

For most people, arthritis is not caused by a single thing. A person may inherit genes that raise their risk, injure a knee playing football in their twenties, gain weight in middle age and then develop knee osteoarthritis in their sixties. Similarly, rheumatoid arthritis may develop when someone with a genetic tendency smokes or has another trigger. This is why there is rarely one answer to the question "why me?", and why reducing the risks you can control is worthwhile.

It also means that arthritis is not your fault. Many of the factors involved are outside anyone's control, and what matters most now is getting the right diagnosis and support.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: What Is Arthritis?
article.excerpt: What is arthritis? A plain-English UK guide to what arthritis is, how common it is, the main types and symptoms, how it is diagnosed, treatment and support.
article.content:
Arthritis is a common condition that causes pain and inflammation in joints. It is not one disease but a group of many different conditions. The most common in the UK are osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis. Arthritis can affect people of any age, including children. There is usually no cure, but treatment can reduce pain, keep you moving and, for inflammatory types, prevent damage.

How common is it?

Arthritis and related musculoskeletal conditions affect millions of people in the UK. It is one of the most common reasons for visiting a GP and for time off work. Osteoarthritis is the most common type, followed by rheumatoid arthritis.

How a joint works

A joint is where two bones meet. The ends of the bones are covered with smooth cartilage, and the joint is surrounded by a capsule lined with tissue that produces lubricating fluid. Muscles, tendons and ligaments support and move the joint. Arthritis can affect any part of this system.

Common symptoms

  • joint pain, tenderness and stiffness
  • swelling and warmth
  • restricted movement
  • weakness and muscle wasting
  • tiredness, particularly in inflammatory arthritis

Main types

  • Osteoarthritis: the joint lining wears and the joint struggles to repair. It mainly affects knees, hips, hands and spine.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis: the immune system attacks the joints, often the hands and feet on both sides.
  • Psoriatic arthritis: linked with psoriasis.
  • Ankylosing spondylitis: mainly affects the spine.
  • Gout: crystals form in a joint, causing sudden severe pain.
  • Juvenile idiopathic arthritis: affects children and young people.

How arthritis is diagnosed

Your GP will ask about your symptoms and examine your joints. NICE (NG226) says osteoarthritis can usually be diagnosed without tests in people over 45 with typical symptoms. If inflammatory arthritis is suspected, you may have blood tests and should be referred to a rheumatologist. X-rays, ultrasound or MRI may be used in some cases.

Treatment

Treatment depends on the type of arthritis.

  • Exercise is a core treatment for all types. It reduces pain and stiffness and builds strength.
  • Weight management reduces strain on hips and knees.
  • Pain relief, including topical anti-inflammatory gels and painkillers. Ask your pharmacist what suits you.
  • Physiotherapy and occupational therapy for exercise, aids and joint protection.
  • Disease-modifying medicines (DMARDs) and biologics for inflammatory arthritis.
  • Surgery, such as joint replacement, when other treatments have not helped.

Living with arthritis

  • keep active with a mix of aerobic, strengthening and stretching exercise
  • pace yourself to manage energy
  • use aids and gadgets to make tasks easier
  • look after your mood and sleep
  • know your rights at work under the Equality Act 2010
  • check which benefits you may be entitled to

Support in the UK

Your GP is your first point of contact. Many areas also offer self-referral to physiotherapy. Charities, including Living With Arthritis, provide information and support. Your council can assess your needs at home for equipment and adaptations.

When to see a GP

See your GP if you have joint pain, swelling or stiffness that lasts more than a few weeks, or if pain is stopping you from doing everyday things. Seek help sooner if you have several swollen joints or stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes in the morning.

Outlook

Arthritis affects everyone differently. Many people find their symptoms are manageable with the right mix of treatment, activity and support, and continue to work and enjoy their usual activities.

Questions to ask at your first appointment

  • What type of arthritis do I have?
  • What can I do myself to help?
  • Would physiotherapy or other support help me?
  • What should I do if it gets worse?

Understanding your type of arthritis is the first step towards managing it well.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.title: What Is Rheumatoid Arthritis?
article.excerpt: Rheumatoid arthritis explained in plain English: what it is, early symptoms, causes, how it is diagnosed on the NHS, treatment and living well with RA.
article.content:
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a long-term autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks the lining of the joints, causing pain, swelling and stiffness. It often affects the small joints of the hands and feet on both sides of the body. It can affect people of any adult age. Early treatment with disease-modifying medicines can control it and prevent joint damage.

How RA differs from osteoarthritis

Osteoarthritis develops gradually as joints try to repair everyday wear and damage. RA is caused by the immune system. It produces more inflammation, can affect many joints at once, and can affect other parts of the body such as the lungs, eyes and heart. RA needs specialist treatment from a rheumatology team.

Symptoms

  • pain, swelling and warmth in joints, often the hands, wrists and feet
  • stiffness, especially in the morning or after resting, lasting more than 30 minutes
  • symptoms affecting the same joints on both sides
  • tiredness, sometimes severe
  • feeling generally unwell, a mild fever, or losing weight
  • firm lumps under the skin near joints (rheumatoid nodules) in some people

Symptoms often come and go, with periods of worse symptoms called flares.

Causes and risk factors

The exact cause is not known. A mix of genes and environmental factors seems to be involved. Risk factors include:

  • being female. RA is two to three times more common in women.
  • being middle-aged, though it can start at any adult age
  • a family history of RA
  • smoking, which is the strongest lifestyle risk
  • being overweight

How it is diagnosed

There is no single test. Your GP will examine your joints and may arrange:

  • blood tests for inflammation (CRP and ESR)
  • rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibody tests
  • X-rays or ultrasound

Many people with RA have positive antibody tests, but not all. NICE (NG100) says that adults with persistent joint swelling should be referred urgently to rheumatology even if blood tests are normal. A rheumatologist confirms the diagnosis.

Treatment

  • DMARDs, such as methotrexate, are started as soon as possible to control the immune system.
  • Steroids may be used short-term to calm symptoms quickly.
  • Biologics and targeted medicines are used if DMARDs alone are not enough.
  • Painkillers help symptoms but do not change the disease.
  • Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and podiatry help you stay active and manage daily tasks.

Your team will check your disease activity regularly and adjust treatment until it is under control.

Possible complications

RA increases the risk of heart disease, osteoporosis, carpal tunnel syndrome, and lung and eye problems. Good disease control, not smoking and regular checks reduce these risks.

Living with RA

  • stay active with a mix of aerobic, strength and flexibility exercise
  • stop smoking
  • pace yourself and plan rest
  • get your vaccinations, as some treatments make infections more likely
  • look after your mental health, as low mood is common
  • learn your flare plan and who to contact

Work and support

Many people with RA continue to work. Employers must consider reasonable adjustments, and Access to Work can help with costs. Depending on how RA affects you, benefits such as PIP may be available.

When to see your GP

See your GP if you have joint pain, swelling and stiffness that lasts more than a few weeks, especially in your hands and feet. Early referral makes a real difference to the long-term outlook.

Questions to ask after diagnosis

  • How active is my RA, and what is our treatment target?
  • How long will my medicine take to work?
  • What blood tests do I need, and how often?
  • Who do I contact during a flare?
  • Can I be referred to physiotherapy or occupational therapy?

Writing your questions down before appointments helps you get the most from them.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
