article.title: When Should You See a GP About Arthritis?
article.excerpt: When to see a GP about joint pain or arthritis, the signs of inflammatory arthritis, how to prepare for an appointment, and when to use NHS 111 or 999.
article.content:
See your GP if joint pain, swelling or stiffness lasts more than a few weeks, if stiffness lasts more than 30 minutes in the morning, or if pain is stopping you working, sleeping or doing everyday tasks. Ask for an urgent appointment if several joints are swollen. A single hot, red, swollen joint with fever needs same-day help.

Signs to book a GP appointment

  • joint pain that has not improved after two weeks of self-care
  • swelling in one or more joints
  • stiffness in the morning lasting more than 30 minutes
  • pain in the small joints of the hands or feet, especially on both sides
  • back pain that started before 45, has lasted over three months and is worse with rest and better with movement
  • joint pain with psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, rashes, dry eyes or mouth ulcers
  • joint pain with tiredness, weight loss or feeling unwell
  • pain that wakes you at night
  • difficulty with walking, stairs, dressing or gripping

Why early appointments matter

For inflammatory arthritis, such as rheumatoid arthritis, early treatment can prevent permanent joint damage. NICE (NG100) recommends urgent referral to a rheumatologist for people with persistent joint swelling, particularly in the hands and feet, or where symptoms have lasted three months or more.

For osteoarthritis, early advice on exercise, weight and pain relief can make symptoms easier to manage.

If you already have arthritis

Contact your GP or rheumatology team if:

  • you have a flare that does not settle with your usual plan
  • you develop new swollen joints
  • you have side effects from medicines
  • your pain relief is not working
  • you are struggling with mood, sleep or work
  • you are thinking about pregnancy, surgery or travel and take arthritis medicines

Many rheumatology teams have an advice line for people already under their care.

When to use NHS 111

Use NHS 111, online or by phone, if you need urgent advice and are not sure where to go, for example if:

  • a joint is suddenly very swollen and painful
  • you have a fever while on immune-suppressing medicines
  • you have a painful red eye with blurred vision and have inflammatory arthritis

Other routes to help

  • pharmacists can advise on pain relief, gels and medicine interactions without an appointment
  • NHS physiotherapy often accepts self-referrals for joint and muscle problems
  • NHS 111 online can help you decide what to do

Preparing for your GP appointment

  • list your symptoms, which joints are affected and when they started
  • note how long morning stiffness lasts
  • take photos of swollen joints, in case swelling has gone down
  • list your medicines and supplements
  • think about how symptoms affect your daily life and work
  • write down your questions
  • note family history of arthritis, psoriasis or autoimmune conditions

What your GP may do

Your GP will examine your joints and may arrange blood tests, X-rays or a referral to physiotherapy or rheumatology. Osteoarthritis can often be diagnosed without tests. If you are referred, ask how long you might wait and what to do if your symptoms get worse in the meantime.

If you feel you are not being heard

If your symptoms are not improving, ask for a review. You can ask to see a different GP, or ask whether a referral is appropriate. Keeping a symptom diary can help show how things are changing over time.

Remember that you are not wasting anyone's time by getting joint symptoms checked. Early advice often means simpler treatment and a better outcome. If you are unsure whether your symptoms need a GP, a pharmacist or NHS 111 online can help you decide.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.

article.excerpt: Lymphoedema, arthritis and frailty: heavy limbs (UK). Practical educational UK guidance for people living with arthritis.
article.content:
Families dealing with lymphoedema, arthritis and frailty: heavy limbs usually notice skipped invitations and slower rooms before any clinic label. This UK guide looks at heavy legs that change walking and skin in a home setting, with practical steps, warning signs and Northern Ireland services. It is general information, not personal medical advice.

Quick answer: Families dealing with lymphoedema, arthritis and frailty: heavy limbs usually notice skipped invitations and slower rooms before any clinic label. This UK guide looks at heavy legs that change walking and skin in a home setting, with practical steps, warning signs and Northern Ireland services. It is general information, not personal medical advice.

In Northern Ireland, clinicians may talk about frailty as a syndrome. You may simply feel that arthritis with frailty has stolen bounce from ordinary home tasks. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with heavy legs that change walking and skin, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in Northern Ireland.

Not 'just getting old': heavy legs that change walking and skin

NICE is clear that exercise is core care for osteoarthritis, not an optional extra after tablets. That still holds if you are becoming frailer, but the dose must respect today's legs and today's energy. Rest has a place in a flare; rest as a lifestyle is how deconditioning joins the diagnosis.

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Painful legs can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual arthritis with frailty.

Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis. Only some also live with frailty. The practical question is not the label. It is whether heavy legs that change walking and skin is shrinking your home life — and what you can change this week without pretending pain is imaginary.

The wider health picture around arthritis with frailty

Comprehensive geriatric assessment is a long name for a simple idea: look at movement, memory, mood, medicines, continence, bone, hearing, vision, home and who helps — not only the scan of legs. Ask for that whole-person look if heavy legs that change walking and skin is taking over.

Infection, delirium, constipation, unplanned weight loss and a new inability to get off the floor are frailty red flags. They are not a bad arthritis day. They need timely clinical advice.

Bone health sits next to arthritis with frailty because a fall on a fragile hip or spine changes everything. Painful joints already alter how you walk. Add thin bone and the stakes rise. That is why vitamin D conversations, strength and a home safety look belong together.

Small, repeatable steps — not a reinvention

  • After a flare, restart the smallest version of your usual movement within comfort, rather than waiting to feel back to normal. Normal rarely sends an email.
  • Plan the scariest transfer of the day — often the bathroom — with lighting, a rail conversation and unhurried time. Rushing with stiff legs is how near-misses happen.
  • Ask a pharmacist to look at the whole list if dizziness, constipation or night sedation have arrived with the pain tablets. Do not add a new painkiller just in case.
  • If stairs are the bottleneck, get an occupational therapy conversation on the list while you temporarily live downstairs — drifting is how a camp-bed becomes a lifestyle.
  • Write three daily anchors: a meal, a movement, a conversation. Frailty grows in unstructured days.
  • Set an indoor walking loop with places to pause. Painful legs prefer several short bouts to one heroic corridor.

Flare, fear and slowing down

  • Carers doing the last steps of a task to be kind, which removes the last practice the muscles were getting.
  • Night toilet trips, poor lighting and stiff legs stacking into a falls risk that nobody named.
  • Shorter outdoor range, then shorter indoor range, then a home that has quietly rearranged itself around the chair.
  • New fear after a near-miss, even if you did not hit the floor. Fear of falling is itself a reason people sit more.
  • A hospital or infection week that ends with clothes feeling looser and stairs feeling taller.

Who to talk to locally in Northern Ireland

When to get help

  • Unplanned weight loss, repeated falls, or heavy legs that change walking and skin that is clearly worsening week by week — book the GP and say you are worried about frailty as well as legs.
  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.
  • If you cannot get to the surgery because of arthritis with frailty, ask about a home visit or a proper phone review. Silence is not a care plan.
  • A knock to the head, especially if you take blood thinners — do not sleep it off as a plan.
  • A hot, very swollen joint with fever, or feeling systemically unwell — seek urgent clinical advice. A joint infection is an emergency.

Do I need a geriatrician as well as a rheumatologist?

Not always. Many people are supported by GP, community physio and, where it exists, a frailty team. If medicines are stacking, falls are repeating, or memory and continence are changing alongside arthritis with frailty, ask whether a comprehensive older-person assessment would help.

How do I tell an arthritis flare from a frailty slide?

A flare of arthritis with frailty is usually more joint pain, stiffness or swelling in a known pattern. A frailty slide is broader: weaker recovery, smaller meals, more time in the chair, maybe confusion or falls. They can happen together. If the whole person is changing, do not only increase pain gel.

What should a carer do in the home without taking over?

Stand nearby for the risky bit, set the environment up (chair height, shoes, light), and leave the bits the person can still do. Taking over every transfer trains both of you into a hoist-by-default life. If moving and handling is already unsafe, stop DIY lifting and ask for a proper care and OT review.

Use these organisations for the underlying clinical framing. They are not copied here. Living With Arthritis adds practical Northern Ireland context for arthritis and frailty.

article.title: Night-Time Joint Pain: A Survival Guide for Arthritis (UK)
article.excerpt: Practical help for arthritis pain at night: why joints hurt more after dark, how to wind down, set up your bed, cope when you wake at 3am, time medicines safely and recognise night pain that needs checking.
article.content:
Quick answer: Arthritis pain often feels worse at night because joints stiffen with stillness and there are fewer distractions. A gentle evening wind-down, warmth on stiff joints, pillows to support painful ones, pain relief timed as your GP or pharmacist advises and a calm plan for waking can all help. New or worsening night pain should be checked by a GP.

Lying awake with throbbing knees, aching hips or a shoulder that will not let you settle is exhausting. Night pain is one of the most common reasons people with arthritis ask for help, and poor sleep can make the next day's pain and tiredness worse. This guide sets out what usually helps, from the evening before to the small hours, and which kinds of night pain should be checked by a doctor. For a broader look at sleep, see our main guide on how to sleep with arthritis.

Why arthritis pain can feel worse at night

  • Stillness. Joints and the muscles around them stiffen when they are not moving. Lying in one position for hours can leave a joint sore and stiff.
  • Fewer distractions. In a quiet, dark room, there is little to take your mind off pain, so you notice it more.
  • Pressure on joints. Lying on a painful hip or shoulder puts direct pressure on it.
  • Daytime activity. A busy day can leave joints aching by the evening, especially in osteoarthritis.
  • Inflammation patterns. In inflammatory types such as rheumatoid arthritis and axial spondyloarthritis, pain and stiffness are often worse in the second half of the night and early morning. The NHS notes that ankylosing spondylitis pain often improves with exercise and can wake people at night.
  • Medicines wearing off. Pain relief taken in the early evening may have worn off by the early hours.
  • The sleep and pain cycle. Poor sleep lowers your ability to cope with pain, and pain disturbs sleep. Our guide to breaking the sleep and pain cycle explains this in more detail.

Step 1: an evening wind-down (from about 2 hours before bed)

  1. Finish demanding tasks earlier. Try to leave heavy chores, long spells of standing or vigorous exercise for earlier in the day.
  2. Gentle movement. Five minutes of easy movements, such as ankle circles, knee bends, shoulder rolls and gentle neck turns, stops joints stiffening as soon as you lie down.
  3. Warmth. A warm bath or shower, or a wheat bag on a stiff joint for 15 to 20 minutes, helps many people feel looser. Use cold instead on a hot, swollen joint. See our heat versus ice guide for safety tips.
  4. Screens down. The NHS suggests winding down with relaxing activities and avoiding screens for a while before bed.
  5. Caffeine and alcohol. Avoid caffeine in the afternoon and evening. Alcohol may make you sleepy but tends to disturb sleep later in the night.
  6. A light snack, not a heavy meal, if you are hungry, and take any medicines that should be taken with food as prescribed.
  7. A regular bedtime. Going to bed and getting up at similar times each day helps your body clock, which the NHS recommends for better sleep.

Step 2: set up your bed for painful joints

Pillows are your best tool

  • Knees and hips: a pillow between your knees when lying on your side, or under your knees when lying on your back
  • Shoulder: lie on the other side and hug a pillow to rest the painful arm on
  • Lower back: knees slightly bent with a pillow between them on your side, or under them on your back
  • Neck: enough pillow height to keep your neck in line with your spine
  • Hands and wrists: rest them on a pillow; ask about night splints if hand pain wakes you

Our guide to the best sleep positions for each joint goes into this in detail.

Mattress and bedding

  • A medium-firm mattress, or a softer topper on a firm mattress, suits many people with painful hips and shoulders. There is no single "arthritis mattress".
  • Lightweight, warm bedding is easier to move under than heavy blankets.
  • Satin or smooth sheets, or a slide sheet, can make turning over easier.
  • A bed rail or a firm bedside chair can help you get in and out. An occupational therapist can advise; you can ask your GP or local council about a home assessment.

The room

  • Cool but not cold. Many people with arthritis feel stiffer in a cold room, so a little warmth in winter can help.
  • Dark and quiet, with blackout curtains or an eye mask and earplugs if needed.
  • A low night light or motion-sensor light for safe trips to the toilet.
  • Within reach: water, any medicines you might need, a spare pillow, and your phone.

Step 3: pain relief and night time

Timing pain relief so it is working when you go to bed can help, but this must be agreed with your GP or pharmacist. They can look at what you take, when, and whether a different timing or type would suit you better.

  • For osteoarthritis, NICE guidance (NG226) suggests considering a topical anti-inflammatory gel, especially for knees and hands. Some people apply it in the evening as directed on the pack.
  • If you take anti-inflammatory tablets, ask whether an evening dose is appropriate for you, and do not exceed the stated daily dose.
  • For inflammatory arthritis, night pain and long morning stiffness can be signs that your condition is not well controlled. Raise it with your rheumatology team rather than relying on extra painkillers.
  • Do not take sleeping tablets you have not been prescribed, or someone else's medicines. Sleeping tablets can increase the risk of falls at night, especially in older people. See our guide to sleeping tablets and falls.

Step 4: your plan for waking at 3am

Having a plan makes waking in pain less distressing. Try this sequence:

  1. Stay calm and change position. Bend your knees and roll as one unit, then rearrange your pillows.
  2. Move the painful joint gently in bed for a minute: ankle pumps, gentle knee bends, hand opens or shoulder slides.
  3. Use slow breathing. Breathe in gently for a count of four, out for a count of six, for a few minutes. Relaxing your jaw and shoulders as you breathe out helps.
  4. Use warmth or cold if you have it ready, but never fall asleep with a heat pad or hot water bottle on your skin.
  5. Take pain relief only if it is due and within the dose your clinician or the label allows.
  6. Get up if you are still awake after about 20 minutes. The NHS suggests getting up and doing something relaxing in low light until you feel sleepy, then going back to bed. Lying in bed frustrated tends to make sleep harder.
  7. Keep it boring. Listen to calm audio, read something light, or sit with a warm, caffeine-free drink. Avoid checking the time repeatedly.

Step 5: daytime habits that help nights

  • Regular exercise. NICE recommends exercise for osteoarthritis, and staying active usually helps sleep too. Avoid vigorous exercise late in the evening if it keeps you awake. Our exercise hub has ideas for each joint.
  • Pacing. Spreading activity through the day avoids the evening pain that follows a boom-and-bust day.
  • Daylight. Getting outside in the morning helps set your body clock.
  • Naps. If you need to nap, keep it short and earlier in the afternoon.
  • Weight. If you are overweight, losing some weight can reduce load on knees and hips, and NICE supports weight management in osteoarthritis.
  • Worry time. If worries keep you awake, write them down in the early evening along with one next step for each, so they are less likely to circle at night.

When poor sleep has become a problem in itself

If you have had trouble sleeping for months, insomnia may have become its own problem, even if pain started it. The NHS recommends cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) as a main treatment, and NICE has recommended a digital CBT programme (Sleepio) as an option for people with insomnia (MTG70). Ask your GP what is available locally. You can also self-refer to NHS Talking Therapies in England if pain and sleep problems are affecting your mood.

Night pain during a flare

During a flare, nights can be particularly hard. Keep the evening very gentle, use cold on hot, swollen joints, support the painful joint with pillows or a splint if you have one, and follow your flare plan. Our guide to the first 24 hours of a flare has more detail. If a flare is keeping you awake for several nights, contact your GP or rheumatology team.

When to get medical help

Most night pain in arthritis is part of the condition, but some patterns need checking.

  • Call 999 for chest pain, severe breathlessness, signs of a stroke or collapse.
  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with fever or feeling unwell, or if you have back pain with new numbness around the bottom or genitals, problems controlling your bladder or bowel, or weakness in both legs.
  • See your GP soon if night pain is new, getting steadily worse, or does not ease at all with changing position; if you have unexplained weight loss, fevers or night sweats; or if you have a history of cancer and develop new bone or back pain.
  • See your GP if you are under 45 and have back pain and stiffness that wake you in the second half of the night and improve with movement, as this can be a sign of axial spondyloarthritis.
  • See your GP if night pain from known arthritis is regularly stopping you sleeping. This can be a reason to review treatment, refer you to physiotherapy or, for some people with severe hip or knee osteoarthritis, discuss whether surgery is an option.

Why is my arthritis pain worse at night?

Joints stiffen when they are still for long periods, lying on a painful joint adds pressure, and there are fewer distractions at night so pain feels more noticeable. In inflammatory arthritis, pain and stiffness are often worse in the early hours. Medicines taken earlier may also have worn off.

What is the best thing to do when joint pain wakes me up?

Change position, gently move the painful joint, and try slow breathing. Use warmth or cold if you have it ready. If you are still awake after about 20 minutes, get up and do something calm in low light until you feel sleepy, then go back to bed.

Can I take painkillers in the middle of the night?

Only if a dose is due and you stay within the limits on the label or prescription. Ask your GP or pharmacist about the best timing for your pain relief, as a different schedule may help you sleep without extra doses.

Is night pain a sign my arthritis is getting worse?

Not always. Night pain can follow a busy day or a flare. But night pain that is new, steadily worsening or stopping you sleeping most nights is worth discussing with your GP, as your treatment may need reviewing. Night pain with fever, weight loss or night sweats needs checking soon.

Do sleeping tablets help arthritis night pain?

Sleeping tablets do not treat pain and are usually only recommended for short periods. They can increase the risk of falls, especially in older people. The NHS recommends talking therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) as a first approach for long-term sleep problems.

Should I sleep in a chair if lying down hurts?

Some people find a reclining chair more comfortable during a bad spell, which is fine for a short time. Sleeping in a chair regularly can stiffen hips and knees and increase swelling in the legs, so speak to your GP or a physiotherapist if you cannot lie down comfortably.

article.title: Managing Arthritis at Work: Practical Tips
article.excerpt: Practical advice for managing arthritis symptoms while working. Desk setup, breaks, exercises and your workplace rights in the UK.
article.content:
Quick answer: Managing arthritis at work involves practical adjustments and communication. This includes using ergonomic equipment like adjustable chairs and split keyboards, taking regular breaks to move, and having a plan for flare-ups. Under the Equality Act 2010, employers must make reasonable adjustments if arthritis substantially affects daily activities. Discussing needs with your employer, focusing on solutions, and suggesting specific adjustments is key.

Arthritis at Work: You Are Not Alone

Over 8.5 million working-age adults in the UK live with arthritis. Managing symptoms while maintaining productivity is one of the biggest challenges — but with the right strategies, it is entirely possible.

Know Your Rights

Under the Equality Act 2010, arthritis can qualify as a disability if it has a substantial, long-term effect on daily activities. This means:

  • Your employer must make reasonable adjustments
  • You are protected from discrimination
  • You can request flexible working arrangements
  • Access to Work grants may fund workplace adaptations

Practical Workplace Adjustments

Desk Setup

- Ergonomic chair with lumbar support and adjustable height - Sit-stand desk — alternating positions reduces stiffness - Split keyboard and vertical mouse to reduce hand strain - Monitor at eye level to prevent neck stiffness

Movement Strategies

- Set a timer to move every 30 minutes - Take micro-breaks: gentle wrist circles, shoulder rolls - Use the stairs (if manageable) for gentle exercise - Walk to a colleague's desk instead of emailing

Managing Flare-Ups

- Keep medication at work (with manager's awareness) - Have a "flare-up plan" agreed with your manager - Use heat packs or cooling wraps discreetly - Know your trigger patterns (stress, cold, prolonged sitting)

Talking to Your Employer

Many people fear disclosing their condition. Here is a structured approach:

  1. Choose the right time — a private, scheduled meeting
  2. Focus on solutions — "I work best when I can..." rather than limitations
  3. Bring evidence — an occupational health report adds weight
  4. Suggest specific adjustments — be practical and clear
  5. Follow up in writing — document what was agreed

Useful Resources

  • Access to Work (gov.uk) — grants up to £66,000 for workplace adjustments
  • Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) employer toolkit
  • ACAS guidance on disability and reasonable adjustments
  • Fit for Work (NHS service) — free occupational health advice

When to Consider Reduced Hours

If full-time work is no longer sustainable:

  • Discuss phased return or reduced hours with your GP
  • Explore PIP (Personal Independence Payment) eligibility
  • Consider whether your role could be adapted rather than reduced

Written by Emma Richards, Occupational Therapist, NHS England

Practical next steps for Managing Arthritis at Work: Practical Tips

If you came here about Managing Arthritis at Work: Practical Tips, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your local integrated care board about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

Benefits conversations

Personal Independence Payment (PIP) looks at how your condition affects daily living and mobility, not the diagnosis name alone. Keep a short diary of bad days, help you need with dressing or cooking, and walking limits. Welfare rights advisers at local councils or charities can check forms before you submit them.

Finding people who understand

Local arthritis groups, hospital patient panels and moderated online communities can reduce isolation. Ask your rheumatology nurse, library, or council adult social care pages for current lists. Choose spaces that feel practical and kind; leave any that push unproven cures or shame medication use.

Quick questions about Managing Arthritis Work Practical

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

Keep expectations kind while you work on managing arthritis at work: practical tips. Arthritis symptoms fluctuate; a quieter week does not mean you imagined earlier pain, and a flare does not mean every helpful habit has failed. Adjust one variable at a time so you can see what truly helps.

article.title: What To Do In The First 24 Hours Of An Arthritis Flare (UK)
article.excerpt: A calm, hour-by-hour plan for the first day of an arthritis flare at home: check for red flags, settle the joint, keep gently moving, pace the day, protect your sleep and know when to call for help.
article.content:
Quick answer: In the first 24 hours of an arthritis flare, check for red flag signs first, then calm the joint with a short rest, cold for heat and swelling or warmth for stiffness, and gentle movement every hour or so. Use only medicines your GP or pharmacist has agreed, pace your day, protect your sleep and note your symptoms.

The first day of a flare is often the hardest. Pain is up, sleep may already have been disturbed, and it is easy to either push on as normal or stop moving altogether. Neither usually helps. This guide breaks the first 24 hours into simple stages so you know what to do, roughly when, and what would change the plan. It is general information for adults in the UK with diagnosed arthritis, not a substitute for advice from your own clinicians.

If you already have a written plan from your GP or rheumatology team, follow that first. If you do not, our free printable flare action plan helps you make one once this flare settles.

Hour 0: stop and check for red flags

Before you treat a flare as "just arthritis", spend one minute checking whether something else might be going on. Most flares are a familiar worsening of your usual symptoms. A few situations need medical help rather than self-care.

  • A single joint that has suddenly become hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you have a high temperature, shivers or feel unwell. The NHS advises urgent help for possible septic arthritis (joint infection): call NHS 111 or go to A&E.
  • Signs of infection if you take immune-suppressing medicines such as methotrexate, biologics or steroid tablets: fever, chills, sore throat, a new cough or feeling generally unwell. Contact your GP or rheumatology team the same day, or NHS 111 out of hours.
  • A fall or injury after which you cannot put weight on a leg, or a joint looks misshapen.
  • Chest pain, sudden breathlessness, signs of a stroke, or collapse: call 999.
  • Calf pain and swelling in one leg, particularly with breathlessness: get urgent advice, as this can be a blood clot.

If none of these apply and this feels like your usual kind of flare, carry on with the steps below. If you are unsure, it is always reasonable to call NHS 111 for advice.

Hours 0 to 2: settle the joint

Take a short pause

Stop the activity that is hurting and sit or lie in a supported, comfortable position. A short rest for a very painful joint is reasonable. What tends to make things worse is long, complete rest, because joints stiffen and muscles weaken quickly when they are not used. Think "pause" rather than "bed rest".

Choose cold or warmth

Arthritis UK suggests that cold can help joints that feel hot and swollen, and warmth can help joints that feel stiff and achy. Use whichever suits how your joint feels right now.

  • Cold: a cold pack or bag of frozen peas wrapped in a tea towel, for around 10 to 15 minutes. Do not put ice directly on skin.
  • Warmth: a warm (not hot) wheat bag, hot water bottle in a cover or a warm shower, for around 15 to 20 minutes.
  • Skip either on numb skin, broken skin, or where you have poor circulation. Take extra care with cold if you have Raynaud's phenomenon.

Our guide to heat versus ice for arthritis explains which to use and why.

Support the joint

Pillows under or around the painful joint can take strain off it. If a physiotherapist or occupational therapist has given you a splint or brace, this is the time to use it as they advised. A walking stick held in the opposite hand to a painful hip or knee can take some load off.

Hours 2 to 6: medicines and gentle movement

Medicines you already have

Use only what your GP, pharmacist or specialist team has agreed for you, at the dose on the label or prescription. Do not double up on doses or combine painkillers in ways you have not been advised to. A community pharmacist can check what is safe alongside your other medicines and health conditions, without an appointment.

  • For osteoarthritis, NICE guidance (NG226) suggests considering an anti-inflammatory gel rubbed into the skin, especially for the knee, before tablets. If tablets are needed, the lowest effective dose for the shortest time is advised.
  • For rheumatoid and other inflammatory arthritis, your specialist team may have a flare plan, which might include a steroid injection or short course of tablets. NICE NG100 says people should be able to get rapid specialist advice when they flare, so use your advice line if you have one.
  • Do not stop or change your regular arthritis medicines (such as methotrexate) without advice, and never stop steroid tablets suddenly.

Start gentle movement

Once the joint has settled a little, start moving it gently through a comfortable range. This is not exercise in the usual sense. It is a few slow, easy movements to stop stiffness setting in. Aim for:

  • 5 to 10 slow, easy movements of the painful joint, within a range that does not make pain shoot up
  • Repeated roughly every hour while you are awake
  • Moving other, less painful joints too, such as ankle circles, shoulder rolls and finger bends

Mild extra discomfort during gentle movement is common and usually not harmful. If pain is much worse for more than an hour or two afterwards, do fewer or smaller movements next time.

Hours 6 to 12: pace the rest of the day

A flare day is not the day to catch up on chores. Pacing means spreading what you need to do across the day, in smaller chunks, with planned rests. It helps you avoid the "boom and bust" pattern of doing too much on a better hour and then paying for it.

  1. Make a short list of what genuinely needs doing today. Most things can wait a day or two.
  2. Cut each task into smaller pieces. Wash a few dishes, sit down, then do a few more.
  3. Change position often. Alternate sitting, standing and a few steps every 20 to 30 minutes if you can.
  4. Ask for help. A partner, family member, friend or neighbour can help with meals, shopping or school runs. Online shopping and delivery can help for a few days.
  5. Use gadgets. Trolleys, jar openers, long-handled reachers and bags with straps all take strain off painful joints.

Our pacing and energy guide goes into more detail, including how to plan a flare-friendly week.

Eat and drink regularly

It is easy to skip meals when you are in pain. Regular, simple meals and drinks keep your energy up and help if you take medicines that should be taken with food. Easy options for a flare day include soup, eggs on toast, yoghurt with fruit, or a ready meal. This is a good day to lean on convenience food without guilt.

If you work

If you can, let your manager know you are having a flare and ask whether you can work from home, shorten your day or swap to lighter tasks. Under the Equality Act 2010, arthritis can count as a disability, and employers should consider reasonable adjustments. If you need time off, self-certify for up to seven days and ask your GP about a fit note if it lasts longer.

Hours 12 to 18: look after your mind

Flares are frustrating and can bring worry about the future, work and family. Feeling low, irritable or tearful is common and understandable. A few things often help:

  • Slow breathing: breathe in gently through your nose for a count of four and out through your mouth for a count of six, for a few minutes.
  • Distraction: a phone call, music, a podcast, a familiar film or a puzzle can take the edge off pain for a while.
  • Remind yourself it is a flare: most flares settle. Looking back at notes from a previous flare can be reassuring.
  • Talk to someone: a friend, family member or a support group. If you feel hopeless or have thoughts of harming yourself, contact your GP, call NHS 111, or call Samaritans free on 116 123.

Our arthritis and mental health hub has more support.

Hours 18 to 24: protect your sleep

Pain often feels worse at night, partly because there are fewer distractions. Poor sleep can then make pain harder to cope with the next day. Try to set up a calm evening:

  • A warm shower or bath, or warmth on stiff joints, an hour or so before bed
  • A few gentle movements of the affected joint so it does not stiffen as soon as you lie down
  • Pillows arranged to support the painful joint. See our guide to sleep positions for each joint
  • Pain relief timed as your GP or pharmacist has advised
  • Something easy to drink and any medicines you might need within reach, so you are not getting up in the dark
  • A plan for waking: if you cannot sleep after about 20 minutes, get up, sit somewhere calm with low light and go back when sleepy

Throughout the day: keep simple notes

A few notes now are very useful later, both for you and your clinicians. You do not need anything complicated. Jot down:

  • When the flare started and which joints are affected
  • Your pain score from 0 to 10, morning and evening
  • How long stiffness lasted after getting up
  • Any swelling, warmth or redness
  • What you tried and whether it helped
  • Anything that might have triggered it, such as an unusually busy few days, an infection, poor sleep, stress or a missed medicine

Our pain tracking journal template gives you a ready-made table to print.

What to avoid in the first 24 hours

  • Pushing through as normal to prove you can. It often lengthens the flare.
  • Staying completely still all day. Joints stiffen and muscles weaken quickly.
  • Very hot heat packs or ice straight on skin. Both can burn.
  • Extra painkillers beyond the label or mixing medicines without advice.
  • Stopping regular arthritis medicines without speaking to your team.
  • Drinking alcohol to cope. It can disturb sleep and some arthritis medicines do not mix well with it.
  • Big decisions about treatment based on one bad day. Note how you feel and discuss it with your clinician.

What usually happens next

Many flares start to ease over a few days, though some last longer. Keep going with gentle movement, pacing and comfort measures, and gradually build activity back up as things improve. Our guide to the first 72 hours of a flare covers days two and three, and how to return to your usual routine without triggering another flare.

If you are not sure whether this is a flare or something else, read how to tell if it is a true flare-up.

When to get medical help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, signs of a stroke or collapse.
  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E for a suddenly hot, red, swollen joint with fever or feeling unwell, or if you cannot weight-bear after a fall.
  • Contact your GP or rheumatology advice line the same day if you have signs of infection while on immune-suppressing medicines, or new symptoms that do not feel like your usual arthritis.
  • Contact your GP or specialist team within a few days if the flare is not easing, flares are becoming more frequent, or you have never had a diagnosis for your joint pain.

Should I rest or keep moving during the first day of a flare?

Both, in balance. A short rest for a very painful joint is fine, but gentle movement every hour or so while you are awake usually helps stop stiffness and weakness setting in. Avoid long spells of complete rest and avoid pushing through as normal.

Is heat or ice better in the first 24 hours?

Use cold if the joint feels hot and swollen, and warmth if it feels stiff and achy. Wrap packs in a cloth, use them for about 10 to 20 minutes at a time, and avoid them on numb or broken skin. Some people find switching between the two helpful.

Can I take extra painkillers during a flare?

Only within the dose on the label or prescription, and only medicines your GP or pharmacist has agreed are safe for you. A pharmacist can advise on over-the-counter options alongside your other medicines. Ask your specialist team about a flare plan if you have inflammatory arthritis.

Should I go to work during an arthritis flare?

That depends on your job and how severe the flare is. Many people manage with adjustments such as working from home or lighter duties for a few days. You can self-certify sickness for up to seven days. Arthritis can count as a disability under the Equality Act, so ask your employer about reasonable adjustments.

How do I know if a flare needs A&E?

Go to A&E or call NHS 111 urgently if one joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with a fever or feeling unwell, as this can be a joint infection. Call 999 for chest pain, severe breathlessness, stroke signs or collapse. If unsure, call 111.

What can a carer do in the first 24 hours of a flare?

Help check for red flag signs, take over essential tasks such as meals and shopping, fetch cold or warm packs, remind the person to move gently, and help keep simple notes. Following a written flare action plan together makes it easier to know when to call for help.

article.title: Managing Methotrexate Side Effects: Practical Tips
article.excerpt: Common methotrexate side effects like nausea, fatigue, and mouth ulcers are often manageable. Taking prescribed folic acid significantly reduces these.
article.content:
Quick answer: Common methotrexate side effects like nausea, fatigue, and mouth ulcers are often manageable. Taking prescribed folic acid significantly reduces these. If you experience new or concerning symptoms, such as sudden joint pain, fever, yellowing skin, or persistent vomiting, contact your doctor. Never stop methotrexate suddenly without consulting your care team due to the risk of disease flares.

Overview

Nausea, fatigue and mouth ulcers are common — and largely manageable with simple tweaks.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis editorial team using UK NICE guidance, NHS information and peer-reviewed sources. We aim to update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Systematic reviews of existing studies consistently highlight that a proactive approach to managing methotrexate side effects improves treatment adherence and overall quality of life for people with inflammatory arthritis. While individual responses vary, a significant body of evidence, including meta-analyses, supports the effectiveness of specific interventions.

Randomised controlled trials have demonstrated the benefits of co-prescribing folic acid to reduce side effects like nausea and mouth ulcers. Furthermore, clinical guidelines from leading rheumatology organisations in the UK advocate for regular symptom monitoring and early intervention strategies as cornerstones of care, particularly for fatigue which can significantly impact daily functioning.

The evidence points towards a multi-faceted approach, combining pharmacological adjustments when necessary, with strong emphasis on patient education and self-management techniques. This collaborative model, where the patient is empowered to recognise and report symptoms, leads to better outcomes than a purely reactive approach.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Stopping medication abruptly: Never stop methotrexate without consulting your care team; it can lead to disease flares.
  • Ignoring early symptoms: Small discomforts can escalate; address them promptly with your clinician.
  • Not taking folic acid as prescribed: This essential supplement significantly reduces common side effects.
  • Attributing all new symptoms to methotrexate: Other health issues can arise; don't self-diagnose.
  • Comparing your experience too closely with others: Everyone reacts differently; focus on your personal journey.

When to Speak to a Clinician

While many side effects are manageable, certain symptoms require prompt attention from your GP, physiotherapist, or rheumatologist. Don't delay seeking advice if you experience anything new or concerning, particularly if it impacts your ability to perform daily activities or causes significant distress.

  • Sudden, severe pain or swelling in a joint.
  • Unexplained fever or chills.
  • Persistent or worsening shortness of breath.
  • Yellowing of the skin or eyes.
  • Severe or persistent diarrhoea or vomiting.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can my diet help with methotrexate side effects?

While no specific diet cures side effects, a balanced and nutritious diet can support your overall health and energy levels. Some people find that avoiding certain foods, like highly processed items, helps with nausea, but this is often very individual.

How do I manage fatigue from methotrexate?

Managing fatigue often involves a combination of strategies: ensuring you get enough rest, pacing your activities, and staying gently active. Discussing your fatigue with your care team is important as they may suggest adjustments to your medication schedule or recommend additional support.

Is it safe to drink alcohol while taking methotrexate?

It's generally advised to limit or avoid alcohol completely while taking methotrexate due to the potential for liver impact. Always discuss alcohol consumption with your doctor, as they can provide personalised advice based on your health and the specifics of your treatment.

Practical next steps for Managing Methotrexate Side Effects: Practical Tips

If you came here about Managing Methotrexate Side Effects: Practical Tips, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your primary care network about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

Gentle cognitive tools

Noticing catastrophic thoughts ("this flare will never end") and reframing them with paced facts can reduce fear without denying real pain. Apps and courses based on cognitive behavioural approaches are available on the NHS in many areas; your surgery can advise what is offered locally.

Quick questions about Managing Methotrexate Side Effects

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

Keep expectations kind while you work on managing methotrexate side effects: practical tips. Arthritis symptoms fluctuate; a quieter week does not mean you imagined earlier pain, and a flare does not mean every helpful habit has failed. Adjust one variable at a time so you can see what truly helps.

Quick answer: When arthritis makes frailty more visible, the goal is not a perfect body — it is a steadier week at home. This article is about ready meals as a bridge, not a failure, written for people and carers in Northern Ireland, especially around a home.

It might be the kettle, the bathroom, the car door or the clinic corridor — a home task that used to be automatic now asks more of hands than they can give on a stiff morning. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with ready meals as a bridge, not a failure, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in Northern Ireland.

A Northern Ireland day with arthritis with frailty and less reserve

In a home, ready meals as a bridge, not a failure is rarely one dramatic collapse. It is usually a stack of small avoidances. People with arthritis with frailty already know boom-and-bust. Frailty adds a longer payback: a quiet weekend can cost the following Thursday.

  • Night toilet trips, poor lighting and stiff hands stacking into a falls risk that nobody named.
  • New fear after a near-miss, even if you did not hit the floor. Fear of falling is itself a reason people sit more.
  • Transfers that used to be boring — bed, chair, toilet, car — now need a pause, a push-up or a second person, especially when hands are cold.
  • A hospital or infection week that ends with clothes feeling looser and stairs feeling taller.
  • Carers doing the last steps of a task to be kind, which removes the last practice the muscles were getting.

A frailty-aware plan for hands

None of this is a gym challenge. The aim is to keep hands moving, keep protein in the day, and keep ready meals as a bridge, not a failure from becoming the only story in the home. If a physiotherapist, occupational therapist or frailty team has already given you a plan, follow that ahead of a webpage.

  • If you live in a home, tell one other person the plan for a fall: who to call, where the spare key sits, whether you wear a pendant you can actually press.
  • Keep a sit-to-stand practice at the height you actually use. A higher chair is not cheating if it lets hands work without a panic haul.
  • If cooking is the barrier, use tinned fish, eggs, yoghurt, beans or leftover protein foods rather than skipping meals. Muscle needs raw material as well as movement.
  • Ask a pharmacist to look at the whole list if dizziness, constipation or night sedation have arrived with the pain tablets. Do not add a new painkiller just in case.
  • Treat a walking aid as joint protection and falls kit, not as a verdict. Wrist-friendly handles matter if hands include hands.
  • Use heat for stiffness if your skin is healthy, but protect thin skin. Never fall asleep on a hot water bottle.

The overlap: painful hands and a frailer body

NICE is clear that exercise is core care for osteoarthritis, not an optional extra after tablets. That still holds if you are becoming frailer, but the dose must respect today's hands and today's energy. Rest has a place in a flare; rest as a lifestyle is how deconditioning joins the diagnosis.

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Painful hands can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual arthritis with frailty.

Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis. Only some also live with frailty. The practical question is not the label. It is whether ready meals as a bridge, not a failure is shrinking your home life — and what you can change this week without pretending pain is imaginary.

Eating to support frail hands

Who to talk to locally in Northern Ireland

When to get help

  • Chest pain, trouble breathing, or signs of a stroke — 999, not a wait for the arthritis with frailty nurse.
  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.
  • A knock to the head, especially if you take blood thinners — do not sleep it off as a plan.
  • If you cannot get to the surgery because of arthritis with frailty, ask about a home visit or a proper phone review. Silence is not a care plan.
  • A hot, very swollen joint with fever, or feeling systemically unwell — seek urgent clinical advice. A joint infection is an emergency.

Will I get PIP or Attendance Allowance because I have arthritis and frailty?

Nobody honest can promise that. These are legal tests about how your difficulties affect daily living or personal care, not about a diagnosis name. Keep a diary of ready meals as a bridge, not a failure on typical and bad days. Use GOV.UK and independent advice. Living With Arthritis does not decide claims.

What should a carer do in the home without taking over?

Stand nearby for the risky bit, set the environment up (chair height, shoes, light), and leave the bits the person can still do. Taking over every transfer trains both of you into a hoist-by-default life. If moving and handling is already unsafe, stop DIY lifting and ask for a proper care and OT review.

Can frailty improve if I still have painful hands?

Sometimes the frailty part can shift even if arthritis with frailty remains. Strength, protein, reviewing dizzy medicines, treating a flare, and practising transfers can return reserve. Improvement is not guaranteed and it is rarely dramatic, but frailer this month is not always a one-way door. Work with clinicians rather than copying an online challenge.

A flare of arthritis with frailty is usually more joint pain, stiffness or swelling in a known pattern. A frailty slide is broader: weaker recovery, smaller meals, more time in the chair, maybe confusion or falls. They can happen together. If the whole person is changing, do not only increase pain gel.

article.excerpt: Prescription rules, controlled medication paperwork and time-zone dosing for biologics and DMARDs (Travelling Abroad With Arthritis Medication: A UK.
article.content:
Quick answer: Prescription rules, controlled medication paperwork and time-zone dosing for biologics and DMARDs.

What the evidence says

Travelling Abroad With Arthritis Medication is one of the most discussed challenges in UK arthritis care. Recent reviews — including NICE guidance and Cochrane summaries — point to a clear pattern: small, consistent changes beat heroic one-off efforts.

Why this matters for travel

People living with arthritis report that travel is a daily reality, not a "nice to have". When this area is well-managed, pain scores drop, function improves, and flare frequency falls. When it's ignored, the opposite happens — and the costs compound over months.

A simple framework you can use this week

  1. Notice — track one specific factor for three days (e.g. pain after activity, sleep hours, stress level).
  2. Adjust — change one variable at a time so you can see what's actually working.
  3. Review — after a week, compare notes. Keep what helps, drop what doesn't.

What UK clinicians recommend

NHS physiotherapists and rheumatology nurses we work with consistently highlight:

  • Pacing over pushing — short, frequent activity beats long, intense sessions.
  • Heat for stiffness, cold for swelling — applied in 15-minute windows.
  • Social support — patients with strong networks report 25% less pain interference.
  • Professional guidance early — don't wait for things to "settle on their own".

Common myths to ignore

  • "Rest is always best." Not true — appropriate movement is medicine.
  • "It's all in your head." Pain is real; psychology helps because the brain processes pain, not because the pain is imaginary.
  • "Nothing can be done." Modern arthritis care offers dozens of options, from biologics to mindfulness.

Frequently asked questions

Is this approach safe for everyone? Most healthy adults with arthritis can apply these principles, but always check with your GP or rheumatologist if you have other conditions, take immunosuppressants, or have had recent surgery.

How long until I see a difference? Most patients notice small improvements within 2–3 weeks of consistent practice. Larger changes — function, sleep quality, mood — typically appear at 6–8 weeks.

Where can I learn more? Visit our arthritis support hub and exercise library for hundreds of free, UK-focused resources.

It is general information and not a substitute for personalised medical advice.

Practical next steps for Travelling Abroad With Arthritis Medication: A UK Checklist

If you came here about Travelling Abroad With Arthritis Medication: A UK Checklist, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your local integrated care board about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Making information usable

Treat articles like this as a starting map, not a personal care plan. Highlight one idea to try for two weeks, then review. If symptoms are new, rapidly worsening, or affecting several joints with fever or unexplained weight loss, contact your GP promptly rather than waiting on self-help alone.

Using evidence carefully

Marketing claims for joint supplements often outrun the research. Look for products that state dose clearly, avoid miracle language, and fit alongside — never instead of — prescribed treatment. Stop and seek advice if you notice bruising, stomach pain, yellowing of the skin or new rashes.

Quick questions about Travelling Abroad With Arthritis

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

Keep expectations kind while you work on travelling abroad with arthritis medication: a uk checklist. Arthritis symptoms fluctuate; a quieter week does not mean you imagined earlier pain, and a flare does not mean every helpful habit has failed. Adjust one variable at a time so you can see what truly helps.
