article.title: Septic Arthritis: A Hot, Swollen Joint That Needs A&E
article.excerpt: Septic arthritis is an infection inside a joint that can damage it within days. Learn the warning signs, who is most at risk and what to expect in hospital and afterwards.
article.content:
Get help now

  • Go to A&E or call 999 if a joint suddenly becomes hot, swollen and very painful, you cannot move it or bear weight, and you have a fever, shivers or feel unwell.
  • Go to A&E the same day if you have a joint replacement and it becomes newly painful, red, swollen or starts leaking fluid, or if a joint flares up soon after an injection or operation.
  • If you are not sure, call NHS 111 now and describe your symptoms. If you take medicines that affect your immune system, such as methotrexate, biologics or steroids, say so.
  • Do not wait for it to settle, and do not treat it with leftover antibiotics at home.

Quick answer: Septic arthritis is an infection inside a joint, usually caused by bacteria. It typically causes one hot, swollen, very painful joint that is hard to move, often with a fever. It is a medical emergency because the infection can damage the joint within days and spread to the blood. Go to A&E or call 999 if you think you might have it.

What is septic arthritis?

Septic arthritis happens when germs, most often bacteria, get into the fluid and lining of a joint. The body reacts with intense inflammation. Pus can build up inside the joint, and the infection can quickly start to damage cartilage and bone. It can also spread into the bloodstream and cause sepsis, which is life-threatening.

Germs can reach a joint through the bloodstream from an infection elsewhere, such as the skin, urine or chest. They can also get in directly, through a wound, an animal bite, a joint injection or an operation. The knee is the joint most often affected, followed by the hip, shoulder, ankle and wrist, but any joint can be involved.

Warning signs

Septic arthritis usually comes on over hours to a couple of days. Typical signs are:

  • Severe pain in one joint, often so bad that you cannot bear to move it or have it touched.
  • Swelling, warmth and sometimes redness over the joint.
  • Being unable to walk or put weight on the leg, if a hip, knee or ankle is affected.
  • A high temperature, shivering or feeling generally unwell. Not everyone has a fever, particularly older people and those taking steroids or other medicines that dampen the immune system.

In babies and young children, the signs can be less obvious. A child may refuse to use a limb, cry when a nappy is changed or be very irritable with a temperature. Seek urgent help if you notice this.

Who is most at risk?

Anyone can get septic arthritis, but the risk is higher for people who:

  • Already have joint damage, for example from rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis or gout.
  • Have an artificial joint, such as a hip or knee replacement.
  • Take medicines that lower the immune system, such as steroids, DMARDs or biologics.
  • Have diabetes, kidney disease or liver disease.
  • Are older, particularly over 80.
  • Have recently had a joint injection or joint surgery.
  • Have broken or infected skin, such as leg ulcers or cellulitis.
  • Inject drugs.

Is it septic arthritis or a flare?

This is a very common worry for people who already live with inflammatory arthritis or gout, because a flare can look similar. Clues that point towards infection are one joint that is much worse than your usual flares, pain that is severe and getting worse quickly, a fever or feeling unwell, and symptoms that do not respond to your usual flare plan. A gout attack and an infection can even happen together.

You cannot reliably tell the difference at home, and doctors often cannot tell without testing fluid from the joint. If one joint is suddenly much worse than usual, especially with a fever, get checked the same day. Our guides to what to do in a flare and gout versus pseudogout explain more about typical flares.

What happens in hospital

Doctors will examine you and ask about recent infections, injuries, injections and your medicines. The most important test is to draw off fluid from the joint with a needle, called joint aspiration. This relieves pressure and lets the lab look for bacteria and crystals. You will also usually have:

  • Blood tests, including inflammation markers and blood cultures to check for infection in the bloodstream.
  • An X-ray or ultrasound, and sometimes an MRI, to look at the joint.

Where possible, the joint fluid sample is taken before antibiotics start, but if you are very unwell treatment will not be delayed.

Treatment

Septic arthritis is treated with antibiotics, usually given through a drip at first and then as tablets. The course often lasts several weeks. The exact antibiotic depends on the germ found and local hospital guidance.

Most people also need the infected fluid removed from the joint. This may be done by repeated needle drainage or by an operation to wash out the joint, either through keyhole surgery or an open procedure. If an artificial joint is infected, the orthopaedic team may need to carry out more surgery, sometimes in stages, to clear the infection.

If you take medicines that affect your immune system for arthritis, your team will usually advise pausing some of them while the infection is treated. Only change or stop your arthritis medicines on the advice of your own team.

Recovery and getting moving again

Once the infection is under control, gentle movement and physiotherapy help to stop the joint stiffening and rebuild strength. Recovery can take weeks to months. Some people are left with stiffness or later wear and tear in the joint, which is why early treatment is so important. Ask your team for a clear plan covering:

  • How long to take antibiotics and when to finish them.
  • Which symptoms mean you should come back straight away, such as fever or pain returning.
  • When and how to restart any arthritis medicines that were paused.
  • A graded exercise programme. Our guide to rebuilding after time off your feet may help.

Lowering your risk

  • Look after your skin. Keep cuts clean and covered, and get infected skin or leg ulcers treated promptly.
  • Keep diabetes as well controlled as you can.
  • Stay up to date with vaccines your team recommends. See our guide to vaccines on DMARDs and biologics.
  • If you have a joint replacement, tell dentists and other clinicians, and seek advice promptly for any infection.
  • Know the signs of infection that your rheumatology team has asked you to watch for if you take immune-suppressing medicines.

Frequently asked questions

Is septic arthritis an emergency?

Yes. It can damage a joint within days and spread to the blood. Go to A&E or call 999 if you have a hot, swollen, very painful joint, especially with a fever or feeling unwell.

Can you have septic arthritis without a fever?

Yes. Older people and those taking steroids, DMARDs or biologics may not develop a high temperature. A suddenly very painful, swollen joint still needs urgent checking.

How long does it take to recover from septic arthritis?

Antibiotics usually continue for several weeks, and getting full movement and strength back can take weeks to months with physiotherapy. Some people have lasting stiffness.

Can septic arthritis come back?

It can, particularly in a damaged or artificial joint. Finish the full antibiotic course and return promptly if pain, swelling or fever come back.

Should I stop my methotrexate or biologic if I think I have an infection?

Contact your rheumatology team or the doctor treating you for advice. Many teams recommend pausing some medicines during a serious infection, but do not stop or change doses without advice.

Can a steroid injection cause septic arthritis?

It is a rare complication of any joint injection. Seek urgent advice if a joint becomes increasingly hot, swollen and painful in the days after an injection, especially with a fever.

article.title: Sex and Intimacy With Arthritis: Pain-Free Positions and Techniques
article.excerpt: Maintaining your arthritis sexual function is entirely possible with practical adjustments and open communication. Joint pain, stiffness and fatigue can make physical intimacy challenging, but trying…
article.content:
Maintaining your arthritis sexual function is entirely possible with practical adjustments and open communication. Joint pain, stiffness and fatigue can make physical intimacy challenging, but trying modified positions, using supportive pillows, timing sex around your energy levels and exploring alternative ways to connect can help you maintain a fulfilling, comfortable sex life.

Quick answer: Maintaining your arthritis sexual function is entirely possible with practical adjustments and open communication. Joint pain, stiffness and fatigue can make physical intimacy challenging, but trying modified positions, using supportive pillows, timing sex around your energy levels and exploring alternative ways to connect can help you maintain a fulfilling, comfortable sex life.

Discussing sex and intimacy with arthritis is often avoided, yet it remains a fundamental part of human connection and personal well-being. When you live with a chronic joint condition, the spontaneous nature of physical romance can suddenly feel like a daunting hurdle. You may find yourself worrying about triggering a flare-up, feeling embarrassed about your physical limitations, or simply feeling too exhausted to consider being intimate. These feelings are entirely normal and incredibly common.

Approaching arthritis and intimacy requires a gentle shift in mindset. It involves moving away from expectations of how things used to be, or how they are portrayed in films, and focusing entirely on what works for your body today. You do not have to give up on physical connection because of joint pain. By exploring adapted sex positions arthritis adjustments, and new ways to communicate with your partner, you can rediscover comfort and pleasure. This guide offers practical, everyday advice to help you protect your joints, conserve your energy and enjoy a close, intimate relationship without fear of worsening your symptoms.

Why arthritis affects sexual function

Arthritis impacts physical intimacy through a complex mix of physical, emotional and psychological factors. The most immediate and obvious barrier is joint pain. When your joints are inflamed, swollen and tender, the physical movements required during sex can cause sharp discomfort or aching. This physical pain forces your nervous system into a state of high alert. When your body is fighting pain, it suppresses the parasympathetic nervous system, which is the part of your body responsible for relaxation and sexual arousal. It is incredibly difficult to feel physically aroused when your primary physical sensation is joint pain.

Stiffness is another significant physical barrier. Many forms of arthritis, particularly inflammatory types like rheumatoid arthritis or axial spondyloarthritis, cause severe stiffness after periods of rest. This restricted range of motion means that positions requiring you to bend your knees deeply, open your hips wide, or arch your back may become physically impossible or highly uncomfortable. Muscle spasms often accompany this joint stiffness, as your muscles work overtime to protect your vulnerable joints. Developing a broad understanding of Arthritis Treatment — Your Complete Guide to Managing Joint Pain can help you address these underlying physical symptoms, which in turn provides a better foundation for physical intimacy.

Beyond the physical mechanics, arthritis takes a substantial emotional toll on your sexual function. Living with a chronic condition often changes how you view your own body. You may experience joint deformities, weight changes due to reduced mobility or steroid medications, and skin changes from various treatments. These physical alterations can severely impact your body image and self-esteem. Feeling unattractive or viewing your body merely as a source of pain or a medical problem makes it very difficult to feel desirable to a partner. You might begin to see yourself primarily as a patient rather than a romantic partner, creating an emotional distance in your relationship.

Furthermore, the medications used to manage arthritis can directly affect your sexual function. Certain painkillers, particularly strong analgesics, can dull your physical sensations and significantly lower your libido. Some medications can cause vaginal dryness or erectile dysfunction, adding another layer of difficulty to penetrative sex. Autoimmune conditions like Sjögren’s syndrome, which often occur alongside rheumatoid arthritis, specifically target moisture-producing glands, leading to severe vaginal dryness. Understanding that these barriers are medical and mechanical, rather than a personal failure or a lack of love for your partner, is the first crucial step in reclaiming your intimate life.

Pain-free positions and modifications

Adapting your physical approach to sex is essential for protecting your joints and preventing pain flares. The goal is to minimise stress on your vulnerable areas while maximising comfort and connection. It is helpful to think of physical intimacy as a flexible experience that can be modified to suit your daily symptom levels. Finding the right modifications often requires a bit of trial and error, but focusing on joint protection will make the experience far more enjoyable.

Protecting your hips and knees

Osteoarthritis and inflammatory arthritis frequently target the large weight-bearing joints of the hips and knees. Deep bending (flexion) or opening the legs wide (external rotation) can cause severe pain. Traditional missionary positions, where the person on the bottom must open their hips wide, or positions requiring kneeling, are often the main culprits for hip and knee pain.

Side-lying positions, commonly known as spooning, are excellent alternatives. Both partners lie on their sides facing the same direction. This keeps the spine neutral, removes the need to support body weight on the knees or wrists, and requires minimal hip rotation. If you have hip pain, placing a firm pillow between your knees while spooning will keep your pelvis aligned and prevent your top leg from dragging your hip into a painful downward angle.

If you prefer face-to-face intimacy, modifying the missionary position is possible. The partner with arthritis can lie on their back with a supportive wedge or rolled towels placed under their knees to maintain a slight, comfortable bend without requiring active muscle work to hold the legs up. Alternatively, the partner without arthritis can support the weight of the legs, ensuring they are not pushed back too far.

Supporting the spine and neck

If you have arthritis in your back or neck, such as osteoarthritis of the spine or ankylosing spondylitis, bending, twisting or arching your back will be highly uncomfortable. Maintaining a neutral spine is your primary objective. Avoid any positions that force your chin down towards your chest or arch your lower back severely.

Using a firm memory foam wedge pillow under your lower back and pelvis can provide stability and a comfortable angle without requiring you to actively arch your lumbar spine. When lying on your back, ensure your head is supported by a thin, firm pillow rather than a stack of soft pillows that push your neck forward. If you are the more active partner in a top position, try resting your upper body on your forearms rather than locking your elbows, which takes the strain off your lower back.

Managing hand and wrist pain

The small joints of the hands and wrists are frequently affected by rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis. Supporting your own body weight or your partner’s weight on your hands can cause immediate and lasting pain. It is vital to avoid taking weight through your wrists.

If you are on top, drop down onto your elbows and forearms to distribute your weight more evenly. When gripping or holding your partner, use a flat, open hand rather than curling your fingers tightly. If you enjoy using sex toys, look for ergonomic designs. Many modern devices come with wider handles, textured grips or straps that slide over the back of the hand, meaning you do not need to maintain a tight, painful grip to use them effectively.

Using props, furniture and alternatives

Your bed is not the only place for intimacy, and sometimes standard mattresses do not offer the firm support required for arthritic joints. The edge of the bed is a highly useful tool. The partner with arthritis can lie on their back across the bed with their hips near the edge, feet resting flat on the floor or on a low stool. The other partner can stand or kneel on a soft cushion on the floor. This eliminates the need for the person on the bed to bear weight or stretch their hips awkwardly.

Sturdy, armless chairs can also be helpful. The partner with arthritis can sit comfortably, leaning back slightly, while the other partner straddles them. This position allows the seated person to remain completely supported while still engaging in close, face-to-face intimacy.

Crucially, modifying positions also means broadening your definition of sex. Penetrative intercourse is only one aspect of intimacy. When your joints are severely flaring, shift your focus to mutual masturbation, sensual massage with warm oils, oral sex, or simply spending time naked together skin-to-skin. Taking the pressure off achieving a specific physical act allows you to enjoy intimacy regardless of your current pain levels.

Timing, warm-ups and pain relief

When you live with a chronic condition, relying on spontaneous physical intimacy can sometimes lead to disappointment. Shifting your approach to include a little bit of planning can drastically improve your comfort. Timing your intimacy to align with your body’s natural rhythms is a simple but highly effective strategy.

Take note of when you usually feel your best. If morning stiffness leaves your joints rigid and painful for the first few hours of the day, early morning intimacy might not be practical. Conversely, if you experience severe fatigue by the late evening, waiting until bedtime might mean you lack the energy to enjoy yourself. For many people with arthritis, the middle of the day or early afternoon provides a window where stiffness has eased, but the evening exhaustion has not yet set in. Scheduling time for intimacy might sound unromantic, but it ensures you are setting yourself up for a comfortable, positive experience.

Preparing your joints beforehand is just as important as the act itself. Heat therapy is a wonderful way to relax tense muscles and soothe aching joints before sex. Taking a warm bath or a hot shower together can serve as both effective pain relief and excellent foreplay. The warm water helps to increase blood flow to your joints, reducing stiffness and making movement much easier. If getting in and out of a bath is difficult, using heated blankets or microwavable wheat bags on your most painful joints for twenty minutes beforehand can offer similar benefits.

Gentle movement is another crucial preparation step. Before attempting more active positions, spend a few minutes doing slow, gentle range-of-motion exercises. Slowly rolling your shoulders, gently tilting your pelvis while lying down, or carefully stretching your legs can help lubricate the joints and signal to your body that it is safe to move. Think of it as warming up for a physical activity; your joints require this preparation to perform comfortably.

Do not hesitate to manage your pain proactively. Taking your prescribed analgesics roughly thirty to sixty minutes before you plan to be intimate can take the edge off joint pain, allowing you to focus on pleasure rather than discomfort. Exploring Arthritis Pain Management — A Kind, Practical Guide will give you further ideas on how to incorporate heat, pacing and medication into your routine to ensure pain does not dictate your physical relationship. Keep water-based or silicone-based lubricants on your bedside table to counteract any dryness caused by medications, ensuring that friction does not cause unnecessary discomfort.

Communication with your partner

The emotional mechanics of intimacy are just as important as the physical ones. Arthritis does not just happen to you; it happens to your relationship. Navigating this successfully requires open, honest, and sometimes vulnerable communication with your partner. The silence surrounding chronic pain and sex often causes more damage to a relationship than the physical limitations themselves.

It is very common for partners of people with arthritis to become fearful of causing pain. Your partner might notice you wincing when you get up from a chair and silently decide not to initiate sex because they do not want to hurt you. If this is not communicated, you might interpret their lack of initiation as a loss of attraction or rejection. Meanwhile, they believe they are being protective and caring. This cycle of mutual misunderstanding can quickly lead to resentment and physical distance.

Breaking this silence is essential. Choose a time to talk about intimacy when you are fully clothed, relaxed, and not in the bedroom. Trying to have a complex emotional discussion about pain and modifications while actively trying to have sex is highly stressful. Explain to your partner exactly how your arthritis feels and what movements cause you trouble. If you are in a new relationship, reading up on Dating With Arthritis: When and How to Tell a Partner can provide you with gentle scripts and confidence-building tips for addressing your condition early on.

During intimacy, establishing a clear, simple communication system takes the anxiety out of the experience. A "traffic light" system works incredibly well for many couples. Saying "green" means everything feels good and comfortable. Saying "amber" means a joint is starting to ache, and you need to slow down, change the angle, or adjust a pillow. Saying "red" means the movement is causing sharp pain and you need to stop and change positions immediately. This simple shorthand allows you to communicate your physical boundaries instantly without needing to formulate long explanations while you are trying to be intimate.

Encourage your partner to ask questions and check in with you, but also reassure them that you will speak up if something hurts. When your partner trusts that you will manage your own boundaries and tell them to stop if necessary, they can relax and enjoy the moment without constantly worrying they are doing harm. Celebrate the modifications that work, laugh together when a pile of pillows collapses, and focus on the emotional connection rather than physical perfection.

Managing fatigue and low libido

Fatigue is one of the most debilitating and least understood symptoms of arthritis. This is not ordinary tiredness that can be fixed with a single good night's sleep; it is a profound, whole-body exhaustion caused by your immune system constantly battling inflammation. When you are operating with severely depleted energy levels, sex naturally falls to the very bottom of your priority list. Your body correctly identifies that it needs rest more than it needs physical exertion.

Managing this fatigue requires careful energy conservation throughout your day. Occupational therapists often refer to "pacing" or the "spoon theory," where you have a limited amount of energy to spend each day. If you know you want to be intimate with your partner on a Saturday evening, you may need to plan for a very restful Saturday afternoon, delegating household chores or skipping a tiring social event. Prioritising restorative sleep is also vital for rebuilding your energy reserves, and understanding How Sleep Quality Affects Arthritis Pain: What the Research suggests can help you implement better nighttime routines to combat daily exhaustion.

Low libido is a natural consequence of chronic pain, fatigue, and the mental load of managing a long-term health condition. However, it can also be a direct side effect of the medications you take. Antidepressants, which are frequently prescribed to help manage chronic pain or low mood associated with arthritis, are well-known for reducing sexual desire and making it difficult to reach orgasm. Certain blood pressure medications and strong painkillers can have similar effects.

If you suspect your medication is impacting your sex drive, it is vital that you do not simply stop taking your prescribed treatments. Instead, speak clearly to your GP or rheumatology team about these side effects. They may be able to adjust your dosage, switch you to a different class of medication, or suggest complementary treatments to help improve your libido.

Reclaiming your desire often starts outside the bedroom. Building emotional intimacy through non-sexual touch can help bridge the gap when your libido is low. Holding hands while watching television, sharing a long hug, or giving each other gentle foot rubs keeps you physically connected without the pressure of performance. Engaging in activities that make you feel good about yourself, whether that is wearing clothes that make you feel confident, engaging in gentle hobbies, or treating yourself to a haircut, can slowly rebuild the self-esteem necessary to feel desirable again. Desire often follows action, so starting with gentle, low-pressure closeness can naturally lead to deeper intimacy over time.

When to seek professional help

It is incredibly common to feel embarrassed or awkward about discussing your sex life with healthcare professionals. However, it is vital to remember that doctors, nurses, and therapists deal with the impact of chronic illness on sexual function every single day. It is a standard, recognised part of living with arthritis. According to NICE guidance, your healthcare providers should offer holistic care that addresses how your condition affects all areas of your life, including your relationships and intimacy.

If pain, stiffness or severe dryness is stopping you from enjoying intimacy, book an appointment with your GP or your rheumatology nurse. They can review your current disease control, adjust your pain management plan, or prescribe medical-grade treatments for issues like vaginal dryness or erectile dysfunction. Do not suffer in silence when practical, medical solutions are readily available to improve your quality of life.

You may also benefit greatly from seeing an occupational therapist or a physiotherapist. An occupational therapist can provide expert, practical advice on joint protection, energy conservation, and specific aids or supports that can be used in the bedroom to reduce strain. A physiotherapist can guide you through targeted exercises to strengthen the muscles around your joints, improving your flexibility and stamina over time.

If the emotional strain of living with arthritis is causing conflict in your relationship, or if you and your partner are struggling to communicate about intimacy, seeking help from a relationship counsellor or a sex therapist can be transformative. These professionals provide a safe, neutral space to discuss your fears, process the grief of losing your previous physical abilities, and learn constructive ways to rebuild your physical and emotional connection. Seeking professional help is not a sign of failure; it is a proactive step towards maintaining a healthy, fulfilling partnership despite the challenges of chronic illness.

Key Takeaways

  • Communication is vital; establish a simple system, like red, amber, and green, to safely communicate pain levels during intimacy without breaking the mood.
  • Adapt your physical positions to protect vulnerable joints, using side-lying positions, firm wedge pillows, or the edge of the bed to prevent unnecessary strain.
  • Timing is everything; plan intimacy for the time of day when your joints feel the least stiff and your energy levels are at their highest.
  • Prepare your body beforehand by using warm baths, gentle stretches, and taking your prescribed pain relief thirty to sixty minutes before physical activity.
  • Seek professional support from your GP, rheumatology team, or a therapist if physical limitations, medication side effects, or emotional barriers are impacting your relationship.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can arthritis medications cause vaginal dryness or low libido?

Yes, several medications used to manage arthritis and associated conditions can affect sexual function. Antidepressants, some blood pressure medications, and certain painkillers can lower libido or make climax difficult. Furthermore, autoimmune conditions linked to arthritis, like Sjögren’s syndrome, directly cause severe vaginal dryness. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about managing these specific side effects.

Are there specific sex toys designed for people with hand joint pain?

Absolutely. The adult toy industry has become much more inclusive. Look for ergonomic devices that feature wide, easy-to-hold handles, textured silicone grips, or loops and straps that slide directly over the back of your hand or fingers. These designs allow you to use the device effectively without needing to maintain a tight, painful grip.

How do we maintain intimacy when I am too fatigued for sex?

Intimacy does not solely mean penetrative sex. When your fatigue is severe, focus on low-energy, high-connection activities. Simply cuddling, holding hands, skin-to-skin contact, sharing a bath, or offering a gentle massage can maintain your romantic bond. Removing the pressure to perform physically allows you to stay close without depleting your limited energy reserves.

Is it safe to have sex during an active arthritis flare-up?

It is generally safe, provided you listen to your body and adjust accordingly. During a flare-up, your joints are actively inflamed and highly vulnerable. You should strictly avoid putting weight on flaring joints or stretching them deeply. Focus on gentle, highly supported positions, or explore non-penetrative forms of intimacy until the severe inflammation subsides.

What type of pillows are best for supporting joints during intimacy?

Standard hollow-fibre bed pillows often compress too easily under body weight, offering little joint support. Firm memory foam pillows or specifically designed wedge cushions are far superior. A wedge pillow placed under the lower back or knees provides stable, consistent support that reduces muscle strain and helps maintain comfortable, neutral joint alignment during sex.

How do I bring up the topic of sex with my rheumatology team?

Keep it direct and frame it as a quality-of-life issue. You can say, "My joint pain is making physical intimacy very difficult, and I would like some advice on managing this," or "I am experiencing side effects that are affecting my sex life." Healthcare professionals deal with these entirely normal concerns daily and can offer practical, non-judgemental solutions.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have chest pain, sudden weakness or numbness, severe breathlessness, a suspected broken bone after a fall, or back pain with new loss of bladder or bowel control or numbness around your bottom or genitals.

Contact NHS 111 or your GP urgently if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel unwell or have a fever, or if your symptoms are getting rapidly worse.

In Northern Ireland, clinicians may talk about frailty as a syndrome. You may simply feel that arthritis with frailty has stolen bounce from ordinary sheltered housing tasks. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with alarms, neighbours and joint-bad days, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in Northern Ireland.

Self-management that respects arthritis with frailty

None of this is a gym challenge. The aim is to keep several joints moving, keep protein in the day, and keep alarms, neighbours and joint-bad days from becoming the only story in the sheltered housing. If a physiotherapist, occupational therapist or frailty team has already given you a plan, follow that ahead of a webpage.

  • Use heat for stiffness if your skin is healthy, but protect thin skin. Never fall asleep on a hot water bottle.
  • In Northern Ireland, ask your local Health and Social Care Trust about equipment and care options. Descriptions of grants and benefits here are not predictions of an award.
  • If stairs are the bottleneck, get an occupational therapy conversation on the list while you temporarily live downstairs — drifting is how a camp-bed becomes a lifestyle.
  • Write three daily anchors: a meal, a movement, a conversation. Frailty grows in unstructured days.
  • Ask a pharmacist to look at the whole list if dizziness, constipation or night sedation have arrived with the pain tablets. Do not add a new painkiller just in case.
  • Treat a walking aid as joint protection and falls kit, not as a verdict. Wrist-friendly handles matter if several joints include hands.

What 'frailty' means when you already have arthritis with frailty

NICE is clear that exercise is core care for osteoarthritis, not an optional extra after tablets. That still holds if you are becoming frailer, but the dose must respect today's several joints and today's energy. Rest has a place in a flare; rest as a lifestyle is how deconditioning joins the diagnosis.

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Pain in several joints can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual arthritis with frailty.

Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis. Only some also live with frailty. The practical question is not the label. It is whether alarms, neighbours and joint-bad days is shrinking your sheltered housing life — and what you can change this week without pretending pain is imaginary.

What this can look like in a sheltered housing

In a sheltered housing, alarms, neighbours and joint-bad days is rarely one dramatic collapse. It is usually a stack of small avoidances. People with arthritis with frailty already know boom-and-bust. Frailty adds a longer payback: a quiet weekend can cost the following Thursday.

  • Skipping meals or drinks because getting to the kitchen with sore several joints feels like a project.
  • Carers doing the last steps of a task to be kind, which removes the last practice the muscles were getting.
  • A hospital or infection week that ends with clothes feeling looser and stairs feeling taller.
  • A flare of arthritis with frailty that lasts, then a slower baseline even when the flare eases.
  • Night toilet trips, poor lighting and stiff several joints stacking into a falls risk that nobody named.

Help in Northern Ireland if arthritis and frailty overlap

Home, roles and rhythm with arthritis and frailty

When to get help

  • Unplanned weight loss, repeated falls, or alarms, neighbours and joint-bad days that is clearly worsening week by week — book the GP and say you are worried about frailty as well as several joints.
  • Chest pain, trouble breathing, or signs of a stroke — 999, not a wait for the arthritis with frailty nurse.
  • A hot, very swollen joint with fever, or feeling systemically unwell — seek urgent clinical advice. A joint infection is an emergency.
  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.

How do I tell an arthritis flare from a frailty slide?

A flare of arthritis with frailty is usually more joint pain, stiffness or swelling in a known pattern. A frailty slide is broader: weaker recovery, smaller meals, more time in the chair, maybe confusion or falls. They can happen together. If the whole person is changing, do not only increase pain gel.

Can frailty improve if I still have pain in several joints?

Sometimes the frailty part can shift even if arthritis with frailty remains. Strength, protein, reviewing dizzy medicines, treating a flare, and practising transfers can return reserve. Improvement is not guaranteed and it is rarely dramatic, but frailer this month is not always a one-way door. Work with clinicians rather than copying an online challenge.

Is a walking aid giving in if I have arthritis with frailty?

No. An aid that matches your several joints can protect joints, reduce fear and keep you walking far enough to keep muscle. A poorly fitted stick that hurts a wrist is the problem, not the concept. Ask physiotherapy or occupational therapy to look at height and grip.

article.title: Shingles vaccine and arthritis: who is eligible and is it safe with your medicines? (UK guide)
article.excerpt: NHS shingles vaccine eligibility at 65, 70 to 79 or on strong immune-suppressing medicines, safety with prednisolone, side effects, early shingles signs.
article.content:
On the NHS, the shingles vaccine is offered to everyone turning 65, everyone aged 70 to 79, and adults aged 18 and over with a severely weakened immune system, which can include people on certain medicines that strongly suppress the immune system. It is given as 2 doses. The NHS says the non-live shingles vaccine is safe to have while you take prednisolone. Ask your GP surgery or rheumatology team whether you are eligible, and get vaccinated even if you have had shingles before.

Shingles is more likely, and more likely to cause serious problems, as you get older or if your immune system is weakened. Many arthritis treatments work by calming the immune system, so this is a vaccine worth asking about. This guide covers who is eligible, how arthritis medicines fit in and what to do if you think you have shingles. For the full winter picture, see our vaccines on DMARDs and biologics guide.

Who can get the shingles vaccine on the NHS

The NHS in England offers the shingles vaccine to:

  • people turning 65 on or after 1 September 2023 (if you turned 65 before that date, you become eligible at 70)
  • everyone aged 70 to 79 who has not had it yet
  • adults aged 18 and over with a severely weakened immune system, which the NHS says includes people taking certain medicines that severely weaken the immune system

The age-based offer lasts until your 80th birthday (you can have the second dose until your 81st). Only people with a severely weakened immune system can start the vaccine after 80. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland run similar programmes, so check with your GP surgery about the details where you live.

Do my arthritis medicines make me eligible?

Possibly. Whether your treatment counts as "severely weakened" depends on the medicine, the dose and how long you have taken it, and only your GP or rheumatology team can confirm it. Ask them directly if you take:

  • steroid tablets such as prednisolone, especially at higher doses or for a long time
  • DMARDs such as methotrexate, leflunomide or azathioprine
  • biologics or JAK inhibitors
  • a combination of these

If you are about to start a medicine that suppresses the immune system, ask whether it would be better to have the vaccine first. If you were vaccinated in the past but now have a severely weakened immune system, the NHS says you may need it again.

Is it safe with my medicines?

  • The NHS shingles vaccine is a non-live vaccine. The NHS says non-live vaccines, including the shingles vaccine, are safe to have while you take prednisolone
  • Always tell the nurse or pharmacist which arthritis medicines you take before any vaccine
  • Do not stop or pause your arthritis medicines to have a vaccine unless your own team tells you to
  • You can usually have the shingles vaccine at the same time as the flu, COVID-19 and pneumococcal vaccines. See our flu jab guide

How the vaccine is given

  • 2 doses. For age-based eligibility, they are given 6 to 12 months apart
  • For a severely weakened immune system, they are given 8 weeks to 6 months apart
  • Your GP surgery will usually contact you by letter, text, phone or email. If you think you are eligible and have not heard, contact them
  • If you have a high temperature or feel too unwell for normal activities on the day, wait until you feel better

The NHS says most side effects are mild and settle within 2 or 3 days: a sore, swollen or bruised arm, headache, aching, tiredness, a temperature or shivers. Paracetamol and resting the arm usually help. If your joints ache for a day or two, keep gently moving them as you normally would.

If you think you have shingles

The first signs can be a tingling or painful patch of skin, a headache or feeling generally unwell. A rash of blotches usually appears a few days later, on one side of the body. It turns into itchy blisters that scab.

  • See a pharmacist as soon as possible, ideally within 3 days of the rash appearing. Antiviral medicine works best when started early
  • Ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 if the rash is on your eye or nose, your vision changes, or you have a severely weakened immune system, which can include strong arthritis medicines
  • Tell whoever treats you which arthritis medicines you take, and do not stop them yourself
  • Keep the rash clean, dry and loosely covered, and use a cool compress. While the rash is weeping, avoid pregnant people who have not had chickenpox, people with a weakened immune system and newborn babies

Pain can last for weeks after the rash heals, and sometimes for months (post-herpetic neuralgia). If that happens, ask your GP about nerve pain treatment rather than adding more painkillers yourself. Our painkillers guide explains the options.

Frequently asked questions

I have already had shingles. Do I still need the vaccine?

Yes. The NHS says you can get shingles more than once, so it is important to be vaccinated even if you have had it before.

Will the vaccine cause a flare of my arthritis?

Some people feel achy for a couple of days after any vaccine. That is different from a flare. If joint swelling or stiffness lasts longer than a few days, contact your GP or rheumatology advice line. Our flare-up guide helps you tell the difference.

I am over 80. Can I still have it?

Only if you have a severely weakened immune system. Ask your GP or rheumatology team whether that applies to you.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if someone becomes suddenly confused, struggles to breathe or has signs of sepsis such as blotchy or blue skin or a rash that does not fade when pressed. If you take steroids, our steroids and infection guide lists the signs to act on. For a cough that will not settle, see our chest infection guide.

A flare in several joints can look like sudden frailty. True frailty is a wider loss of reserve: weaker recovery after a quiet week, an infection or a hospital night. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. Food, fluid and muscle when arthritis with frailty shrinks cooking

Frailty loves skipped meals. Arthritis with frailty makes that easy: sore several joints turn a sandwich into a logistics problem. Ready-to-eat protein — yoghurt, cheese, eggs, tinned fish, beans, leftover chicken — is a strategy, not a failure.

A Mediterranean-style pattern (vegetables, fruit, pulses, olive oil, fish when you can) is a familiar UK nutrition message. Keep the spirit, shrink the labour. Frozen vegetables and tinned tomatoes count.

NHS advice is that adults should consider a daily 10 microgram vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter. That is not a cure for arthritis with frailty. Mention it to a pharmacist if you already take other tablets or have kidney problems.

What 'frailty' means when you already have arthritis with frailty

Practical self-management for getting food in without a supermarket marathon

  • If you live in a home, tell one other person the plan for a fall: who to call, where the spare key sits, whether you wear a pendant you can actually press.
  • Put the items you use at dawn — tablets, glasses, walking aid, phone — where you can reach them without a stretch that wrenches several joints.
  • Book eye, foot and hearing checks as frailty care, not vanity. Arthritis with frailty already asks a lot of balance.
  • Plan the scariest transfer of the day — often the bathroom — with lighting, a rail conversation and unhurried time. Rushing with stiff several joints is how near-misses happen.
  • Carers: help the last 20 percent of a task, not the first 80, unless pain or safety says otherwise. Practice is treatment for frailty.
  • Set an indoor walking loop with places to pause. Pain in several joints prefer several short bouts to one heroic corridor.

What this can look like in a home

  • Skipping meals or drinks because getting to the kitchen with sore several joints feels like a project.
  • Transfers that used to be boring — bed, chair, toilet, car — now need a pause, a push-up or a second person, especially when several joints are cold.
  • A flare of arthritis with frailty that lasts, then a slower baseline even when the flare eases.

GP, 111 or 999?

This is not personal medical advice. When several joints and frailty overlap, wait until Monday is sometimes right and sometimes dangerous. If you are unsure, NHS 24 on 111 can help you choose. Living With Arthritis cannot triage you.

  • Chest pain, trouble breathing, or signs of a stroke — 999, not a wait for the arthritis with frailty nurse.
  • A knock to the head, especially if you take blood thinners — do not sleep it off as a plan.
  • A hot, very swollen joint with fever, or feeling systemically unwell — seek urgent clinical advice. A joint infection is an emergency.
  • Sudden confusion, new incontinence, or a crash in mobility over hours to days — think infection or delirium, not only arthritis.
  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.

Who to talk to locally in Scotland

Start with your GP practice and NHS Scotland services via your GP and Health and Social Care Partnership. For urgent but non-emergency advice use NHS 24 on 111. For chest pain, suspected hip fracture, sudden new weakness, or a fall with a bang to the head on blood thinners, use 999.

In Scotland, NHS Inform is a reliable first read. Rehab, reablement and care at home are organised locally. Island and Highland travel can turn a simple clinic into a two-day event, so ask early about closer blood tests or phone reviews.

Ask about community physiotherapy, occupational therapy, reablement after hospital, podiatry, pharmacy reviews and your local Health and Social Care Partnership, including Self-directed Support conversations. Names of teams change. The functions do not: get you moving, get you equipped, get the medicines tidier, get a human being through the door if you cannot get out.

Age UK and local advice agencies can help with forms. The Charity Commission listing for Living With Arthritis (1218461) is public if you want to check who we are. We are independent of Arthritis UK.

Should I stop exercising during getting food in without a supermarket marathon?

Complete rest for more than a short flare period usually makes several joints and muscle worse. Keep a smaller version: seated strength, indoor loops, or the two sit-to-stands you can still do. If exercise causes pain that spirals or a joint that will not settle, get clinical advice.

Can frailty improve if I still have pain in several joints?

Sometimes the frailty part can shift even if arthritis with frailty remains. Strength, protein, reviewing dizzy medicines, treating a flare, and practising transfers can return reserve. Improvement is not guaranteed and it is rarely dramatic, but frailer this month is not always a one-way door. Work with clinicians rather than copying an online challenge.

Will I get PIP or Attendance Allowance because I have arthritis and frailty?

Nobody honest can promise that. These are legal tests about how your difficulties affect daily living or personal care, not about a diagnosis name. The overlap: pain in several joints and a frailer body

Arthritis is about joints, tendons and the way pain changes movement. Frailty is about the whole system — muscle, stamina, appetite, mood, medicines and how quickly you bounce back after a setback. Arthritis with frailty sits in the middle because sore several joints quietly train you to sit more, shorten your stride and skip the movements that keep muscle.

NICE is clear that exercise is core care for osteoarthritis, not an optional extra after tablets. That still holds if you are becoming frailer, but the dose must respect today's several joints and today's energy. Rest has a place in a flare; rest as a lifestyle is how deconditioning joins the diagnosis.

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Pain in several joints can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual arthritis with frailty.

Home, roles and rhythm with arthritis and frailty

Walking aids, Blue Badge applications, community transport and downstairs living are all tools. None of them is a moral failure. Used well, they keep you in the world so several joints still get some practice.

Benefits such as Personal Independence Payment or Attendance Allowance have rules, forms and waiting. Living With Arthritis will not tell you that you will qualify. We will tell you that an honest diary of one night away without pretending you are 40 — the help you need on bad days, not your best Tuesday — is what assessors need if you do apply.

Practical self-management for one night away without pretending you are 40

  • Write three daily anchors: a meal, a movement, a conversation. Frailty grows in unstructured days.
  • Carers: help the last 20 percent of a task, not the first 80, unless pain or safety says otherwise. Practice is treatment for frailty.
  • If stairs are the bottleneck, get an occupational therapy conversation on the list while you temporarily live downstairs — drifting is how a camp-bed becomes a lifestyle.
  • After a flare, restart the smallest version of your usual movement within comfort, rather than waiting to feel back to normal. Normal rarely sends an email.
  • If you live in a home, tell one other person the plan for a fall: who to call, where the spare key sits, whether you wear a pendant you can actually press.
  • Keep a sit-to-stand practice at the height you actually use. A higher chair is not cheating if it lets several joints work without a panic haul.

Signs the overlap is affecting several joints

  • New fear after a near-miss, even if you did not hit the floor. Fear of falling is itself a reason people sit more.
  • A hospital or infection week that ends with clothes feeling looser and stairs feeling taller.
  • Carers doing the last steps of a task to be kind, which removes the last practice the muscles were getting.
  • Transfers that used to be boring — bed, chair, toilet, car — now need a pause, a push-up or a second person, especially when several joints are cold.
  • Shorter outdoor range, then shorter indoor range, then a home that has quietly rearranged itself around the chair.

Help in Northern Ireland if arthritis and frailty overlap

When to get help

  • Unplanned weight loss, repeated falls, or one night away without pretending you are 40 that is clearly worsening week by week — book the GP and say you are worried about frailty as well as several joints.
  • A hot, very swollen joint with fever, or feeling systemically unwell — seek urgent clinical advice. A joint infection is an emergency.
  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.
  • If you cannot get to the surgery because of arthritis with frailty, ask about a home visit or a proper phone review. Silence is not a care plan.
  • A knock to the head, especially if you take blood thinners — do not sleep it off as a plan.

Do I need a geriatrician as well as a rheumatologist?

Not always. Many people are supported by GP, community physio and, where it exists, a frailty team. If medicines are stacking, falls are repeating, or memory and continence are changing alongside arthritis with frailty, ask whether a comprehensive older-person assessment would help.

How do I tell an arthritis flare from a frailty slide?

A flare of arthritis with frailty is usually more joint pain, stiffness or swelling in a known pattern. A frailty slide is broader: weaker recovery, smaller meals, more time in the chair, maybe confusion or falls. They can happen together. If the whole person is changing, do not only increase pain gel.

Is a walking aid giving in if I have arthritis with frailty?

No. An aid that matches your several joints can protect joints, reduce fear and keep you walking far enough to keep muscle. A poorly fitted stick that hurts a wrist is the problem, not the concept. Ask physiotherapy or occupational therapy to look at height and grip.

  • Put the items you use at dawn — tablets, glasses, walking aid, phone — where you can reach them without a stretch that wrenches several joints.

How frames and commodes after a hospital burst shows up in real rooms

  • Skipping meals or drinks because getting to the kitchen with sore several joints feels like a project.
  • A hospital or infection week that ends with clothes feeling looser and stairs feeling taller.
  • Night toilet trips, poor lighting and stiff several joints stacking into a falls risk that nobody named.
  • Shorter outdoor range, then shorter indoor range, then a home that has quietly rearranged itself around the chair.
  • New fear after a near-miss, even if you did not hit the floor. Fear of falling is itself a reason people sit more.

Northern Ireland services, without inventing a clinic

GP, 111 or 999?

This is not personal medical advice. When several joints and frailty overlap, wait until Monday is sometimes right and sometimes dangerous. If you are unsure, your GP out-of-hours service or emergency services as directed on nidirect can help you choose. Living With Arthritis cannot triage you.

  • Unplanned weight loss, repeated falls, or frames and commodes after a hospital burst that is clearly worsening week by week — book the GP and say you are worried about frailty as well as several joints.
  • A knock to the head, especially if you take blood thinners — do not sleep it off as a plan.
  • Chest pain, trouble breathing, or signs of a stroke — 999, not a wait for the arthritis with frailty nurse.
  • A hot, very swollen joint with fever, or feeling systemically unwell — seek urgent clinical advice. A joint infection is an emergency.
  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.

Is a walking aid giving in if I have arthritis with frailty?

No. An aid that matches your several joints can protect joints, reduce fear and keep you walking far enough to keep muscle. A poorly fitted stick that hurts a wrist is the problem, not the concept. Ask physiotherapy or occupational therapy to look at height and grip.

Can frailty improve if I still have pain in several joints?

Sometimes the frailty part can shift even if arthritis with frailty remains. Strength, protein, reviewing dizzy medicines, treating a flare, and practising transfers can return reserve. Improvement is not guaranteed and it is rarely dramatic, but frailer this month is not always a one-way door. Work with clinicians rather than copying an online challenge.

Should I stop exercising during frames and commodes after a hospital burst?

Complete rest for more than a short flare period usually makes several joints and muscle worse. Keep a smaller version: seated strength, indoor loops, or the two sit-to-stands you can still do. If exercise causes pain that spirals or a joint that will not settle, get clinical advice.

Sources and further reading

Use these organisations for the underlying clinical framing. They are not copied here. Living With Arthritis adds practical Northern Ireland context for arthritis and frailty.

  • NHS – Falls (NHS)
  • NICE NG56 – Multimorbidity (NICE)
  • NHS – Osteoarthritis (NHS)
  • NICE NG226 – Osteoarthritis in over 16s (NICE)

article.title: Should You Tell Your Employer About Your Arthritis?
article.excerpt: The article says telling your employer about arthritis can help if done early and met with understanding, because supportive disclosure may improve job…
article.content:
Quick answer: The article says telling your employer about arthritis can help if done early and met with understanding, because supportive disclosure may improve job retention, reduce symptom interference and enable reasonable adjustments. It advises discussing concerns with your GP or rheumatologist, tracking symptoms, preparing clear work-related requests, knowing your rights, and seeking help if symptoms worsen.

Overview

Disclosure has pros and cons — a balanced framework.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis editorial team using UK NICE guidance, NHS information and peer-reviewed sources. We aim to update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Systematic reviews of workplace interventions for chronic conditions consistently highlight the benefits of early, supportive disclosure to employers. These reviews, which synthesise findings from multiple studies, suggest that employees who feel comfortable discussing their health needs with their managers tend to experience better job retention and reduced symptom interference at work. However, the outcomes are most positive when disclosure is met with genuine understanding and practical adjustments, rather than just a formal acknowledgement.

Clinical guidelines from professional bodies in rheumatology and occupational health also emphasise the importance of good communication. They recommend a proactive approach to managing long-term conditions in the workplace, which often starts with an open conversation between employee and employer. This communication ideally leads to reasonable adjustments that support the employee's health without compromising their ability to perform their job effectively.

Furthermore, observational studies looking at patient experiences often reveal that fear of discrimination or negative impact on career progression can be a significant barrier to disclosure. This underscores the need for clear communication strategies and supportive workplace policies to foster an environment where individuals feel safe and empowered to discuss their chronic conditions. The evidence suggests that while disclosure itself is key, the context and response to that disclosure are what ultimately determine its effectiveness.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Waiting until you're struggling badly: Don't delay the conversation until your arthritis is severely impacting your work.
    • Fix: Discuss your condition early, even if symptoms are mild, to allow for proactive planning.
  • Assuming your employer knows your rights: Not all managers are aware of their responsibilities regarding long-term conditions.
    • Fix: Be prepared to educate your employer about reasonable adjustments and your rights under UK law.
  • Focusing only on limitations: Avoid framing the discussion solely around what you can't do.
    • Fix: Emphasise solutions and what you can do with appropriate support.
  • Not having a clear idea of what you need: Going into the conversation without specific requests can lead to vagueness.
    • Fix: Think through potential adjustments (e.g., ergonomic equipment, flexible hours) beforehand.
  • Trying to "power through" without support: Ignoring your symptoms can lead to burnout and worsen your condition in the long run.
    • Fix: Prioritise your health by seeking support and making necessary changes.

When to Speak to a Clinician

It's always a good idea to discuss any concerns about your arthritis with your General Practitioner (GP) or rheumatologist, particularly if your condition is impacting your work. They can provide medical advice, help you understand your rights, and suggest strategies for managing your symptoms effectively in a work setting. Don't hesitate to reach out if you experience any of the following:

  • A significant worsening or change in your usual arthritis symptoms.
  • New pain, swelling, or stiffness that lasts more than a few days.
  • Increased difficulty performing daily tasks or work-related duties.
  • Side effects from medication that are affecting your ability to work.
  • You are considering a significant career change or adjustment due to your arthritis.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will telling my employer about my arthritis affect my career progression?

Legally, your employer cannot discriminate against you because of a long-term condition like arthritis. In fact, declaring your condition can allow your employer to make reasonable adjustments that support your work performance and retention, potentially enhancing your career rather than hindering it.

Do I have to tell my employer everything about my medical condition?

You only need to share information that is relevant to your ability to do your job and any reasonable adjustments you might need. You do not have to disclose every detail of your medical history or treatment if it is not pertinent to your work.

What if my employer doesn't offer the adjustments I need?

If discussions with your employer don't lead to satisfactory reasonable adjustments, you can seek advice from an occupational health specialist, a trade union representative, or an employment advisor. There are resources available to help mediate these conversations and ensure your rights are upheld.

Practical next steps for Should You Tell Your Employer About Your Arthritis?

If you came here about Should You Tell Your Employer About Your Arthritis?, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your primary care network about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Benefits conversations

Personal Independence Payment (PIP) looks at how your condition affects daily living and mobility, not the diagnosis name alone. Keep a short diary of bad days, help you need with dressing or cooking, and walking limits. Welfare rights advisers at local councils or charities can check forms before you submit them.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

Supplements versus meals

Food-first is usually safer than stacking capsules. If you do try a supplement, choose a reputable UK brand, check for interactions with your medicines (especially blood thinners), and give any trial a clear stop date so you can judge whether symptoms truly changed.

Quick questions about Should Tell Your Employer

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

article.title: Shoulder Arthritis Exercises: A Safe UK Home Programme
article.excerpt: A practical UK programme of shoulder arthritis exercises for osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis: ten gentle moves for movement and strength, how to choose your level, a weekly plan, everyday tips, what to avoid, stop rules and when to see a GP or physiotherapist.
article.content:
Quick answer: Safe shoulder arthritis exercises start with gentle movement such as pendulum swings, assisted arm lifts and wall slides, then add strengthening like shoulder blade squeezes, isometric holds and light band rotations. Do movement daily and strength 2 to 3 times a week, within comfort. Sharp pain, sudden weakness or night pain that keeps worsening needs a GP or physio.

Arthritis in the shoulder can make reaching up to a cupboard, doing up a bra, brushing your hair or sleeping on your side painful and difficult. The good news is that regular, well-chosen exercises can help keep the shoulder moving, strengthen the muscles that control it and make everyday tasks easier. This guide gives you a ten-exercise programme in three levels, with clear advice on what to avoid and when to get help. It is general guidance; if a physiotherapist has given you exercises, follow their programme first.

Understanding shoulder arthritis

The shoulder is made up of two main joints. The glenohumeral joint is the ball-and-socket joint where the arm meets the shoulder blade. The acromioclavicular (AC) joint is the small joint at the top of the shoulder where the collarbone meets the shoulder blade. Either can be affected by:

  • Osteoarthritis: more common with age or after an old injury. It typically causes a deep ache, stiffness, a grinding feeling and pain at night.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory arthritis: often affects both shoulders, with swelling, warmth and morning stiffness.
  • Rotator cuff arthropathy: arthritis that develops after a long-standing large rotator cuff tear.

Shoulder arthritis can feel similar to other common shoulder problems, such as frozen shoulder or rotator cuff problems, and these need slightly different approaches. If you have not had a diagnosis, see a GP or physiotherapist. Our page on shoulder arthritis explains symptoms and treatments.

Shoulder arthritis, frozen shoulder or rotator cuff problem?

These conditions can feel similar, and some people have more than one. This table is a rough guide only; a GP or physiotherapist can assess you properly.

ArthritisFrozen shoulderRotator cuff problem
Typical ageUsually over 50, or after an old injuryOften 40 to 60, more common with diabetesAny adult, more common with age
Main featureStiffness, grinding, deep acheGradually increasing stiffness in all directions, often very painful at firstPain lifting the arm out to the side or overhead, sometimes weakness
Can someone else move the arm for you?Limited, with grindingVery limited, even with helpOften moves further with help than on its own
Exercise approachMovement plus strength, within comfortGentle stretching within pain limits; a physio can guide this through the stagesGraded strengthening of the rotator cuff

Why exercise helps

NICE guideline NG226 recommends tailored therapeutic exercise for people with osteoarthritis, and NICE guideline NG100 says adults with rheumatoid arthritis should have access to specialist physiotherapy to learn exercises for joint flexibility and muscle strength. For the shoulder, exercise helps by:

  • keeping the joint moving so stiffness does not build up
  • strengthening the rotator cuff and shoulder blade muscles, which keep the ball centred in the socket
  • improving posture so the shoulder has more room to move
  • making everyday reaching and lifting easier and more confident

Before you start

  • Warm up with gentle shoulder rolls or after a warm shower.
  • Sit or stand tall. A slumped posture limits how far the arm can lift.
  • Move within comfort. Mild stretching or aching is fine. Sharp, catching pain is a sign to ease off.
  • Use the 24-hour check. If your shoulder is more painful the next day, or night pain is worse, do fewer repetitions or a smaller movement next time.
  • After surgery, including shoulder replacement, follow your surgical team's programme rather than this one.

Part 1: movement exercises (daily)

Do 5 to 10 repetitions of each, once or twice a day.

1. Pendulum swings

Lean forward with your good hand on a table and let the painful arm hang down loosely. Gently sway your body so the arm swings forwards and backwards, side to side, and in small circles. Let the arm move with your body rather than lifting it with the shoulder muscles. Do this for 30 to 60 seconds. Our step-by-step guide to pendulum swings and wall slides has more detail.

2. Assisted arm lift (lying down)

Lie on your back with knees bent. Hold the wrist of the painful arm with your other hand and slowly lift both arms up towards the ceiling and back over your head as far as is comfortable. Lower slowly. Lying down supports the shoulder blade and is often easier than standing.

3. Wall slide (forwards)

Stand facing a wall. Place your hands on the wall at chest height and slowly slide them upwards as far as is comfortable, stepping closer to the wall as you go. Hold for a few seconds and slide back down. A towel under the hand helps it glide.

4. Outward rotation with a stick

Sit or stand with your elbows bent at your sides, holding a stick, umbrella or rolled towel in both hands. Use the good arm to gently push the painful arm outwards, keeping the elbow tucked in to your side. Hold for a few seconds and return.

5. Towel behind the back

Hold a towel over one shoulder with the good hand and grasp the lower end behind your back with the painful hand. Gently pull the towel upwards with the top hand to lift the lower hand up your back. Hold for a few seconds. This helps with tasks such as tucking in a shirt.

Part 2: strengthening exercises (2–3 times a week)

Do 8 to 12 repetitions, 1 to 3 sets, on non-consecutive days.

6. Shoulder blade squeeze

Sit or stand tall with your arms by your sides. Gently draw your shoulder blades back and down, as if putting them into your back pockets. Hold for 5 seconds and relax.

7. Isometric holds

Stand with your elbow bent at 90 degrees, close to your side, beside a wall or door frame. Press the back of your hand gently outwards into the wall without moving the arm, hold for 5 seconds, and relax. Repeat pressing the palm inwards and the fist forwards. Use about a third of your effort. These are useful when moving the shoulder against resistance hurts.

8. Band outward rotation

Hold a light resistance band between your hands with elbows bent at 90 degrees and tucked into your sides. Keeping your elbows in, slowly rotate your forearms outwards, stretching the band, then return slowly. A small rolled towel between the elbow and your side can help.

9. Band row

Loop a band around a sturdy door handle at chest height. Holding the ends, pull your elbows back past your sides while squeezing your shoulder blades together. Return slowly.

10. Wall press-up

Stand an arm's length from a wall with your hands on it at shoulder height. Bend your elbows to bring your chest towards the wall, then push back. Keep your body straight. Move your feet further back to make it harder.

Choose your level

LevelWho it suitsWhat to do
GentleVery painful or stiff shoulder, flare-up, severe arthritisExercises 1, 2 and 6, plus isometric holds (7) at low effort. Daily, small range.
StandardCan lift the arm to shoulder heightMovement exercises 1–5 daily; strength exercises 6–10 twice a week.
ProgressingStandard level easy for 2 weeksThicker band, 3 sets, light hand weights for front and side raises up to shoulder height.

A sample week

DayWhat to do
MondayMovement exercises, then strength exercises
TuesdayMovement exercises, a walk
WednesdayMovement exercises
ThursdayMovement exercises, then strength exercises
FridayMovement exercises, a swim or water exercise if you enjoy it
WeekendMovement exercises; a third strength session if you are progressing

Tips for different types of shoulder arthritis

Osteoarthritis

Many people with shoulder OA lose the ability to turn the arm outwards and lift it overhead. Keep working gently on exercises 2, 3 and 4, and build strength in the shoulder blade muscles. Some aching is normal.

Rheumatoid arthritis

During a flare, stick to the gentle level and keep the movements small. When the inflammation is controlled, add strength work. Ask your rheumatology team about specialist physiotherapy, which NICE says should be available to adults with RA.

Severe arthritis or rotator cuff arthropathy

Lying-down exercises, pendulums and isometric holds are often the most comfortable. Strengthening the front of the shoulder (the deltoid) can help with lifting. A physiotherapist can tailor a programme.

Everyday tips

  • Keep frequently used items between waist and shoulder height.
  • Dress the painful arm first and undress it last.
  • Carry bags close to your body, or use a rucksack on both shoulders or a trolley.
  • At night, try lying on your back or the other side with a pillow supporting the painful arm.
  • Use warmth for stiffness and a wrapped cold pack for a hot, painful flare.
  • Break up long spells at a desk or screen with a few shoulder rolls and blade squeezes every 30 to 60 minutes.
  • Use long-handled sponges, hairbrushes and reachers to reduce awkward overhead and behind-the-back movements.

For more practical help, see our wider guide to shoulder pain relief.

Track your progress

Shoulder changes can be slow, so simple checks every week or two help you see progress and stay motivated:

  • How high can you reach up a wall? Mark the spot with a small piece of tape.
  • How far up your back can you reach with the painful hand?
  • Can you do a daily task, such as brushing your hair or reaching a shelf, more easily?
  • How many nights a week does shoulder pain wake you?

Bring these notes to physiotherapy or GP appointments.

Pain relief alongside exercise

Being able to exercise comfortably matters. Talk to a pharmacist or GP about suitable pain relief, such as anti-inflammatory gels or tablets where safe for you. Warmth before exercise and a cold pack afterwards help some people. For persistent pain, a GP or specialist may discuss options such as a steroid injection to make exercise more comfortable, and if pain and loss of function remain severe despite these treatments, a referral to discuss surgery.

What to avoid

  • Forcing the arm into painful positions, especially quickly or with weight.
  • Heavy lifting overhead or behind the head, such as behind-the-neck presses.
  • Hanging from bars or very deep press-ups or dips.
  • Long periods without moving the shoulder at all, which increases stiffness.

When to get medical help

Stop exercising and get advice if you get sharp pain, a sudden loss of strength, or the shoulder feels as if it is slipping out.

  • Call 999 if shoulder or arm pain comes with chest pain, breathlessness, sweating or feeling sick, as this could be a heart attack.
  • Go to A&E after a fall or injury if you cannot move your arm, the shoulder looks out of shape, or you have severe pain.
  • Call NHS 111 or get urgent help if your shoulder is suddenly hot, red and swollen with a high temperature, or you have new pins and needles or weakness down the arm.
  • See your GP or a physiotherapist if pain has not improved after 2 weeks of home treatment, night pain keeps you awake, you cannot lift your arm, or you are not improving after 6 to 12 weeks of exercise. In many areas you can refer yourself to NHS physiotherapy.

What are the best exercises for an arthritic shoulder?

A combination of gentle movement exercises such as pendulum swings, assisted arm lifts and wall slides, and strengthening exercises for the rotator cuff and shoulder blade muscles, such as band rotations, rows and isometric holds. The right mix depends on how stiff and painful your shoulder is.

How often should I do shoulder arthritis exercises?

Movement exercises once or twice a day, and strength exercises 2 or 3 times a week on non-consecutive days. Short, regular sessions work better than occasional long ones.

Can exercise cure shoulder arthritis?

No, but it can reduce pain, improve movement and make daily tasks easier for many people. It is a core part of treatment alongside pain relief, and it can also help prepare you for surgery if that is needed later.

Should shoulder exercises hurt?

Mild aching or stretching is common and acceptable. Sharp or catching pain is not. If your shoulder is more painful the next day or night pain is worse, reduce the range or repetitions.

How long until shoulder exercises help?

Some people notice easier movement within a few weeks. Strength gains and reduced pain usually take 6 to 12 weeks of regular practice. Keep a short note of what you can reach each week to track progress.

Is swimming good for shoulder arthritis?

Many people find water exercise helpful because the water supports the arm. Breaststroke and gentle arm movements in the water are often easier than front crawl. Avoid strokes that cause pain, and start with short sessions.
