article.title: Staying Active with Arthritis in Winter: A UK Guide
article.excerpt: UK winter guide to staying active with arthritis: indoor routines, warm-water sessions, safer outdoor walks, pacing on stiff days and when to see your GP.
article.content:
Quick answer: Keep moving little and often through winter: a short indoor routine most days, strength work two days a week, and walks in daylight on gritted paths with grippy shoes. Warm up indoors first, scale back rather than stop on stiff days, and see your GP or physiotherapist if a joint becomes hot and swollen or you start falling.

Dark evenings, icy pavements and cold, stiff mornings make it easy to move less in winter. Stiff joints then get stiffer, and muscles that protect them weaken. You do not need a gym or a big plan. A few short, regular sessions at home and the odd daylight walk are enough to keep most people ticking over until spring. Motion is Lotion, even in January.

How much activity to aim for

The NHS advises adults to be active every day, build up to about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, and do strengthening activities on at least two days. Older adults are also encouraged to add balance work and break up long spells of sitting. NICE guidance on osteoarthritis puts exercise at the centre of care. If those numbers feel far away, start with what you can do today and add a little each week.

Indoor routines for cold or dark days

  • Ten minutes, twice a day. Pick a few moves from the exercise hub, such as sit-to-stands, heel raises holding the worktop and gentle knee or shoulder movements
  • Chair-based exercise. The NHS sitting exercises and our seated tai chi page suit days when standing is hard
  • Strength twice a week. A resistance band, a bag of tins or your own body weight is enough. Our knee exercises and hip exercises guides show where to start
  • Break up sitting. Stand and walk around the room during TV adverts or every half hour

Warm water and classes

Many leisure centres run warm-water, aqua or gentle swim sessions, and some offer classes for people with joint conditions. Warm water supports your weight and can make movement easier. Our swimming exercises for hip osteoarthritis guide explains how to start. Ask at your local centre what runs near you.

Walking outdoors safely in winter

  • Walk in daylight and on gritted or well-lit routes where you can
  • Wear shoes with a deep, slip-resistant tread. Our walking shoes guide covers what to look for, and slip-on ice grips add traction
  • Take shorter steps, use a stick or walking pole if it helps, and keep a hand free for rails
  • Warm up indoors for a few minutes first, then layer up with gloves, a hat and thermal socks

Our walking with arthritis guide shows how to build up time gradually. If you have fallen or feel unsteady, read the falls prevention guide and tell your GP.

Pacing on cold, stiff days

On a stiff morning, do a smaller version of your routine rather than skipping it. Heat before moving can ease stiffness. If pain is clearly worse a couple of hours after activity, trim the next session instead of stopping altogether. Our pacing guide explains how to plan good and bad days, and the flare-up guide covers what to change during a flare.

Keeping going when motivation drops

  • Book activity into the day like an appointment, ideally around midday when it is lighter
  • Move with someone else, in person or on the phone, so you both show up
  • Keep a simple diary of what you did and how your joints felt; patterns help you and your physio
  • Set a winter goal that fits winter, such as keeping up your sit-to-stands, not matching your summer walks

Short days can also affect mood and sleep. Our mental health guide and sleeping with arthritis guide may help.

Vitamin D and keeping warm

The NHS advises everyone to consider a daily 10 microgram vitamin D supplement from October to March. It supports bones and muscles; it is not a treatment for arthritis pain. Keeping the rooms you use warm also helps. Our cold weather and arthritis guide covers warmth and help with heating costs.

When to get help

  • A joint becomes hot, red and swollen, especially with fever
  • You have had a fall, or feel unsteady more often
  • Pain stops you doing your usual activities for more than a few weeks
  • Chest pain, dizziness or breathlessness during exercise: stop and seek urgent advice

Many areas let you self-refer to NHS physiotherapy; check your GP surgery website or the NHS App. If you are newly diagnosed, start with our newly diagnosed guide, and for everyday pain options see the pain relief guide.

Frequently asked questions

Is it safe to exercise with arthritis in cold weather?

For most people, yes. Warm up indoors, dress in layers, choose safe routes and scale back rather than stop on stiff days.

What exercise is best for arthritis in winter?

A mix of a short daily indoor routine, strength work twice a week and walking or warm-water exercise when you can. The best one is the one you will keep doing.

Should I rest more in winter?

Rest during a flare is fine, but long spells of rest usually make stiffness and weakness worse. Keep a smaller version of your routine going.

article.title: Steroid emergency cards and arthritis: who needs one and when to show it (UK guide)
article.excerpt: On prednisolone or steroid injections? The red NHS Steroid Emergency Card, the blue card, sick-day steps and adrenal crisis 999 signs for carers.
article.content:
If you take steroid medicines such as prednisolone, your own adrenal glands may make less cortisol, the hormone your body needs when it is ill, injured or having surgery. Your doctor or pharmacist will decide whether you need the red NHS Steroid Emergency Card. If you have one, carry it all the time and show it to anyone treating you, so they know you may need extra steroids. Never stop steroid tablets suddenly.

Many people with rheumatoid arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica and other inflammatory conditions take steroids for weeks, months or longer. This guide covers one job: understanding the steroid cards, knowing when to show them, and what to do on a sick day, especially if you are older, living with frailty or caring for someone. For infection warning signs on steroids, see our steroids and infection guide.

Why steroids can make illness more risky

The NHS explains that steroid medicines copy the stress hormones your adrenal glands make. When you take them in doses higher than your body's usual level, your adrenal glands may make less of their own cortisol. This is called adrenal insufficiency. The NHS says it is more likely if you take high doses for a long time, especially tablets and injections, or if you use more than one kind of steroid at the same time, such as a steroid inhaler and a nasal spray.

Most of the time this causes no problems, because your tablets supply what you need. The risk comes when your body needs more cortisol than usual: a bad infection, being sick or having diarrhoea, a fall or injury, or an operation. Without extra steroid, a small number of people can become seriously unwell very quickly. This is called an adrenal crisis, and it is an emergency.

The two steroid cards

  • Red NHS Steroid Emergency Card: your doctor or pharmacist assesses your risk of adrenal insufficiency from the type and dose of steroids you take, and may recommend this card. It tells health professionals that you take steroids that should not be stopped suddenly, and sets out the first steps to take in an emergency. It is the size of a credit card
  • Blue steroid treatment card: the NHS says you will be given this if you take prednisolone for longer than 3 weeks, or at a high dose of more than 40mg a day. It explains how to reduce the risk of side effects and records your doctor, your dose and how long treatment will last

The Society for Endocrinology says the blue card is not replaced by the red one, so keep both if your team has given you both. You can also download a PDF of the red card; some people save it as their phone's lock screen so emergency staff can see it.

Do I need a red card?

Only your own prescriber can say. Ask your GP, pharmacist or rheumatology team if any of these apply and nobody has mentioned a card:

  • you have taken steroid tablets for a long time, or at a high dose
  • you have repeated steroid injections into joints or muscles, as well as other steroids
  • you use several kinds of steroid together, such as tablets plus an inhaler or nasal spray
  • you are coming off steroids slowly after a long course

Bring a full list of your medicines, including inhalers, creams, nasal sprays and recent injections. Our steroid injections versus tablets guide explains the difference.

When to show your card

  • at A&E, to paramedics, and if you are admitted to hospital for any reason
  • before any operation, procedure or scan that involves fasting or sedation, such as a colonoscopy
  • at the dentist, before dental treatment
  • at a new GP, out-of-hours or NHS 111 contact, so they know about your steroids
  • to carers and family, so they can show it for you if you cannot

Sick days: ask for your plan now, not when you are ill

  • Do not stop, skip or lower your steroid dose yourself. The NHS says it can be dangerous to stop prednisolone suddenly, especially after a high dose for a long time
  • When you are unwell, your body may need more steroid, not less. Ask your doctor whether sick day rules apply to you, what dose change (if any) they want, and for how long. Write it on your flare action plan
  • If you are being sick and cannot keep your tablets down, or have severe diarrhoea, get urgent advice from your GP or NHS 111 the same day and tell them you take steroids
  • Do not run out. Order repeat prescriptions early, especially before bank holidays and over Christmas
  • Our winter viruses guide has a sick-day plan for your other arthritis medicines too

When it is an emergency

The NHS lists signs of adrenal crisis that need 999. Call 999 if someone who takes steroids becomes suddenly much worse and has any of these:

  • feeling very dizzy or light-headed, especially when standing up
  • being sick, or severe tummy pain or pain in the side
  • a fast heart rate
  • muscle weakness, pain or spasms, or a headache that will not go away
  • being very drowsy, irritable or confused
  • a seizure (fit) or passing out

Show the red card to the ambulance crew and take the person's medicines, or a list. If you have been given an emergency injection kit and trained to use it, the NHS says call 999 even after you have given the injection. Signs of sepsis, such as fast breathing, blotchy or blue skin and a rash that does not fade, also need 999.

Frailty and steroids: why carers matter

In older people, an adrenal crisis or a serious infection may look like going "off their legs", a fall, new confusion or not eating and drinking. These are reasons to ask for help early, not to wait. If you care for someone on steroids:

  • keep the steroid cards, medicines list and rheumatology advice line number together
  • know where their sick-day plan is written down
  • check repeat prescriptions are ordered in time
  • ask for a carer's assessment if you need more support

Long courses of steroids can also thin bones, so ask about bone protection. Our bone density guide explains the checks.

Frequently asked questions

Do steroid joint injections count?

They can. The Society for Endocrinology says steroids given by any route, including joint injections, inhalers, nasal sprays and creams, can lower your own cortisol, especially when they add up. Ask your team whether your injections change your risk.

I have stopped steroids. Do I still need the card?

Your adrenal glands can take time to recover after a long course. Ask your doctor how long you should keep carrying the card after your last dose.

Where do I get a card?

Your GP, hospital team or pharmacist can give you one. If you think you should have one and do not, ask at your next appointment or speak to your community pharmacist.

article.title: Steroid Injections vs Oral Steroids: When Each Makes Sense
article.excerpt: Steroid injections typically alleviate pain and inflammation in specific joints for several weeks to months, often taking a few days to a week to become effective.
article.content:
Quick answer: Steroid injections typically alleviate pain and inflammation in specific joints for several weeks to months, often taking a few days to a week to become effective. Oral steroids are generally used for widespread inflammation. Neither is a long-term solution, and both carry risks with overuse. They should be part of a broader management strategy including exercise, therapy, and weight management.

Overview

Targeted joint injections and short oral courses each have a role. We unpack the trade-offs.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis editorial team using UK NICE guidance, NHS information and peer-reviewed sources. We aim to update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Systematic reviews of treatment options for arthritis consistently highlight that neither steroid injections nor oral steroids are long-term solutions. While both can be very effective in managing flare-ups and reducing pain, they don't tackle the underlying disease progression. Randomised controlled trials show that steroid injections can provide targeted pain relief for weeks to months, particularly in single inflamed joints or bursae, whereas short courses of oral steroids are generally considered for more widespread inflammation.

Clinical guidelines from professional bodies emphasise that these treatments are part of a broader management strategy. They are most beneficial when used alongside other interventions like regular exercise, physical therapy, weight management where appropriate, and other pain relief methods. The goal is to improve function and quality of life, allowing individuals to engage in activities that support long-term joint health.

The body of evidence also points to potential risks with overuse or high doses of steroids. Repeated steroid injections into the same joint, for instance, can sometimes weaken tissues over time, while prolonged oral steroid use carries a wider range of potential side effects impacting bone density, blood sugar, and susceptibility to infection. Therefore, careful consideration of benefits versus risks is always advised.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Expecting a permanent cure: Neither injections nor oral steroids stop arthritis progression. *Remember they are tools for managing symptoms and flare-ups. Insisting on steroids for every ache: Not every pain is due to inflammation that steroids will help. *Discuss other pain relief options with your clinician. Stopping oral steroids suddenly: This can cause withdrawal symptoms or a flare. *Always follow your clinician's tapering instructions carefully. Ignoring lifestyle changes because of steroid relief: Steroids offer temporary relief, not a pass to neglect movement or diet. *Continue with gentle exercise and healthy eating habits. Having injections too frequently: Frequent injections into the same joint carry risks. *Follow your clinician's advice on injection frequency.

When to Speak to a Clinician

It's really important to know when to seek professional advice, especially when dealing with new or worsening symptoms. While a little discomfort is part of managing arthritis, certain signals suggest it's time to get things checked out by your GP, physiotherapist, or rheumatologist.

  • Sudden, severe joint pain that doesn't ease.
  • New or significantly increased joint swelling and redness.
  • Fever alongside joint symptoms, which could indicate infection.
  • Rapid loss of function or inability to move a joint you could previously move.
  • Symptoms that are getting worse despite following your current treatment plan.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long do steroid injections take to work?

Typically, you might start to feel the effects of a steroid injection within a few days, though for some, it can take up to a week. The full pain relief can then last from several weeks to a few months, depending on the individual and the joint injected.

Can I have multiple steroid injections?

Yes, it's possible to have multiple steroid injections, but your clinician will carefully consider the frequency and number. Too many injections into the same joint can, over time, weaken surrounding tissues, so there are usually limits on how often and how many you can receive.

Are there alternatives to steroids for arthritis flare-ups?

Absolutely. Depending on the type and severity of your arthritis, alternatives might include non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), other pain relief medications, physical therapy, heat or cold packs, and various topical treatments. Your clinician can discuss the best options for your specific situation.

Practical next steps for Steroid Injections vs Oral Steroids: When Each Makes Sense

If you came here about Steroid Injections vs Oral Steroids: When Each Makes Sense, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

Supplements versus meals

Food-first is usually safer than stacking capsules. If you do try a supplement, choose a reputable UK brand, check for interactions with your medicines (especially blood thinners), and give any trial a clear stop date so you can judge whether symptoms truly changed.

Quick questions about Steroid Injections Oral Steroids

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

faqs.q: How long do steroid injections take to work?
faqs.a: Typically, you might start to feel the effects of a steroid injection within a few days, though for some, it can take up to a week. The full pain relief can then last from several weeks to a few months, depending on the individual and the joint injected.

faqs.q: Can I have multiple steroid injections?
faqs.a: Yes, it's possible to have multiple steroid injections, but your clinician will carefully consider the frequency and number. Too many injections into the same joint can, over time, weaken surrounding tissues, so there are usually limits on how often and how many you can receive.

faqs.q: Are there alternatives to steroids for arthritis flare-ups?
faqs.a: Absolutely. Depending on the type and severity of your arthritis, alternatives might include non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), other pain relief medications, physical therapy, heat or cold packs, and various topical treatments. Your clinician can discuss the best options for your specific situation.

article.title: Stopping Arthritis Medication Safely: A Step-By-Step Guide
article.excerpt: Stopping arthritis medication should always be a joint decision with your rheumatologist, even if you feel well. Abruptly stopping or significantly reducing.
article.content:
Quick answer: Stopping arthritis medication should always be a joint decision with your rheumatologist, even if you feel well. Abruptly stopping or significantly reducing effective treatments for inflammatory arthritis can increase flare-up risk and potential joint damage. It is a gradual process, often taking months, with consistent symptom monitoring throughout. If symptoms return, contact your care team promptly.

Overview

Remission feels great — but stopping too quickly risks a flare.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis editorial team using UK NICE guidance, NHS information and peer-reviewed sources. We aim to update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Current scientific understanding strongly supports a careful, measured approach when considering changes to arthritis medication. Randomised trials and systematic reviews consistently show that abruptly stopping or significantly reducing effective treatments for inflammatory arthritis can increase the risk of disease flare-ups and potential joint damage. This is particularly true for conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, where sustained remission is crucial for long-term joint health.

Clinical guidelines from professional bodies universally recommend that any decision to reduce or stop medication should be made in close consultation with a healthcare professional. These recommendations are based on synthesised evidence from countless patient experiences and research studies, highlighting the importance of individualised assessment rather than a 'one-size-fits-all' approach.

The evidence also points to the value of continued monitoring during and after any medication adjustment. Regular assessments help to quickly identify any return of disease activity, allowing for prompt intervention and preventing prolonged periods of increased inflammation, which could lead to irreversible joint changes.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Stopping medication abruptly: Reduces the benefits of treatment and can lead to a quick flare — *Always discuss changes with your specialist first. Deciding based on feeling good for a few days: Symptoms can fluctuate; short-term improvements might not reflect sustained remission — *Monitor symptoms consistently over weeks before considering a review. Failing to track symptoms during reduction: Makes it harder to identify if a medication change is causing problems — *Keep a simple symptom diary throughout the process. Cutting dosage by more than recommended: Can overwhelm your system and trigger a flare — *Follow your clinician's specific dosage reduction plan precisely. Ignoring early warning signs of a flare: Waiting too long to report worsening symptoms can lead to more severe outcomes — *Contact your care team as soon as new or worsening symptoms appear.

When to Speak to a Clinician

It's vital to know when to seek professional advice, especially if you're considering or have started adjusting your arthritis medication. Your healthcare team is there to support you and ensure your condition remains well-managed. Don't hesitate to reach out if you experience any significant changes or concerns.

  • Sudden increase in joint pain or swelling that doesn't improve with rest.
  • New or worsening stiffness, particularly in the mornings.
  • Unexplained fever, fatigue that significantly impacts daily life, or general unwellness.
  • Redness or warmth around multiple joints.
  • Any concerns about medication side effects or if you feel your current treatment isn't working as well.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I stop my medication if I feel completely well?

Even if you feel completely well, stopping medication should always be a joint decision with your rheumatologist. "Feeling well" can sometimes mask underlying disease activity, and stopping too soon can lead to a flare.

How long does it take to safely reduce medication?

The timeframe for safely reducing medication varies greatly depending on your individual condition, the type of medication, and how long you've been in remission. It's often a gradual process that can take months, overseen by your care team.

What should I do if my symptoms return after reducing medication?

If your symptoms return or worsen after reducing medication, contact your rheumatology team or GP promptly. They may advise restarting your previous dose or adjusting your treatment plan to bring your condition back under control.

Practical next steps for Stopping Arthritis Medication Safely: A Step-By-Step Guide

If you came here about Stopping Arthritis Medication Safely: A Step-By-Step Guide, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Peer support etiquette

Share what helps you without prescribing it for others. Conditions, medicines and life circumstances differ. If someone is in crisis, encourage them toward NHS 111, their GP, or emergency services rather than relying on a forum alone.

Quick questions about Stopping Arthritis Medication Safely

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

article.title: Straight Leg Raises: The Foundation Exercise for Knee Osteoarthritis
article.excerpt: Straight leg raises strengthen the quadriceps without bending the knee — the safest entry-point exercise for knee OA. Step-by-step guide with progression.
article.content:
Quick answer: The guide explains that knee osteoarthritis pain can involve cartilage, fluid, ligaments, muscle and the nervous system, and that management depends on symptom patterns. It recommends graded movement, anti-inflammatory eating, weight management, heat or cold, sleep hygiene, and small weekly tracking goals. It advises seeking GP or physiotherapy help for hot swollen joints, weight loss, prolonged stiffness, numbness or weakness.

What this guide covers

This piece summarises what the current evidence says about straight leg raises: the foundation exercise for knee osteoarthritis, the practical steps that help most, and the red flags that mean you should speak to your GP or physiotherapist.

The underlying mechanism

Arthritis pain rarely has a single cause. Joint cartilage, synovial fluid, ligaments, surrounding muscle and the nervous system all contribute. Understanding which of these is driving your specific symptom is the first step toward targeted relief. For an in-depth condition overview, see our related guide.

Inflammatory and degenerative forms behave differently. Inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid, psoriatic, ankylosing spondylitis) typically worsens with rest and improves with gentle movement. Degenerative arthritis (osteoarthritis) typically worsens with prolonged use. Knowing which pattern matches your day-to-day experience helps you choose the right management approach.

What helps — by strength of evidence

  1. Movement and graded exercise. NICE NG226 (2022) and Cochrane reviews place structured exercise as a first-line treatment. Aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, split into 20–30 minute sessions.
  2. Anti-inflammatory eating. A Mediterranean-style pattern — oily fish twice a week, plenty of vegetables, olive oil, whole grains — is linked to reduced pain scores in OA and RA trials.
  3. Weight management. A 5 percent reduction in body weight reduces knee-OA symptoms measurably; a 10 percent reduction can match the effect of some medications.
  4. Heat and cold. Heat eases stiffness; cold eases acute swelling. Twenty-minute applications, with a towel barrier.
  5. Sleep hygiene. Pain perception rises sharply on fewer than six hours of sleep. Prioritise a consistent bedtime.

A practical seven-day starting plan

Begin with the smallest dose that feels manageable — five minutes of movement, one anti-inflammatory meal a day, a 10 pm screen-off rule. Track only three things weekly: pain on waking (0–10), longest pain-free interval, and one functional win (e.g., climbed stairs without grabbing the rail). Small, consistent inputs outperform big sporadic efforts.

When to seek clinical advice

Book an appointment with your GP or a first-contact physiotherapist if you notice: sudden hot, red, swollen joints; unexplained weight loss alongside joint pain; morning stiffness lasting longer than an hour for more than two weeks; or new numbness or weakness. These can signal inflammatory disease that benefits from early treatment.

Frequently asked questions

Will this approach work alongside my medication? Yes. Exercise, diet and pacing complement prescribed treatments and often improve their effectiveness. Always check with your prescriber before stopping any medication.

How long until I notice a difference? Most people report meaningful improvement at 6–12 weeks of consistent practice. Earlier wins (less morning stiffness, better sleep) often appear within 2–3 weeks.

Is this safe if I have other conditions? The principles above are broadly safe for adults with stable cardiovascular, metabolic and respiratory conditions. If you are unsure, ask your GP for a referral to a first-contact physiotherapist for a tailored plan.

This article is general health information, not medical advice. Always consult a qualified healthcare professional for decisions about your individual care.

In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Building a joint-friendly routine

Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery.

Making information usable

Treat articles like this as a starting map, not a personal care plan. Highlight one idea to try for two weeks, then review. If symptoms are new, rapidly worsening, or affecting several joints with fever or unexplained weight loss, contact your GP promptly rather than waiting on self-help alone.

Quick questions about Straight Raises Foundation Exercise

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

article.title: Strength Training With Arthritis: A Safe Beginner's Programme (UK)
article.excerpt: A practical UK beginner's guide to strength training with arthritis: why it helps, how much to do, eight whole-body exercises with easier and harder versions, how to choose weights or bands, a 12-week plan, adapting for flares and medicines, stop rules and when to see a GP or physiotherapist.
article.content:
Quick answer: Strength training is safe and recommended for most people with arthritis. Start with 6 to 8 simple exercises for the legs, hips, back, arms and core, 2 or 3 times a week on non-consecutive days. Do 1 to 3 sets of 8 to 12 slow repetitions, finishing with a few in reserve, and add resistance gradually as it gets easier.

Many people with arthritis worry that lifting weights or doing strength exercises will damage their joints. In fact, the opposite is usually true. Stronger muscles support and protect painful joints, make everyday tasks easier and can reduce pain. This beginner's guide explains why strength training helps, how much to do, eight simple exercises with easier and harder versions, and a 12-week plan to build up safely at home or in a gym.

Why strength training helps arthritis

  • Support for joints. Strong muscles absorb and share load that would otherwise go through the joint.
  • Less pain and better function. NICE guideline NG226 recommends local muscle strengthening as part of therapeutic exercise for everyone with osteoarthritis.
  • Countering muscle loss. People with arthritis often move less, and muscle strength naturally declines with age. Strength training slows and reverses this.
  • Bone health and balance. The NHS says strength exercises help keep bones strong and reduce the risk of falls, especially in older adults.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis. NICE guideline NG100 says adults with RA should have access to physiotherapy to learn exercises for muscle strength and joint flexibility.

How much strength training?

The UK Chief Medical Officers recommend muscle-strengthening activities on at least 2 days a week for all adults, working the major muscle groups: legs, hips, back, abdomen, chest, shoulders and arms. For beginners with arthritis, a good starting point is:

WhatBeginner guide
Sessions2 to 3 a week, with a rest day between
Exercises6 to 8, covering the whole body
Repetitions8 to 12 per set, slow and controlled
SetsStart with 1; build to 2 or 3
EffortModerate: the last few repetitions feel hard, but you could do 2 or 3 more with good form
Rest30 to 90 seconds between sets
Session length15 to 30 minutes

Myths and facts

MythFact
"Lifting weights will wear out my joints."Gradual strength training is recommended for arthritis and helps protect joints by strengthening the muscles around them.
"If it hurts, I am doing damage."Mild discomfort that settles by the next day is common and not harmful. Sharp pain, or pain lasting more than a day, means adjust the exercise.
"I am too old to build muscle."People of all ages, including those in their 80s and 90s, can get stronger with regular training.
"I need a gym."Body weight, bands and household items are enough to start.
"Walking is enough."Walking is excellent, but it does not build strength as much as specific strengthening exercises. UK guidelines recommend both.

A sample beginner session (about 20 minutes)

  1. Warm-up (5 minutes): marching on the spot, arm circles, gentle knee bends and 5 easy sit-to-stands.
  2. Circuit (12 minutes): sit-to-stand, wall press-up, bridge, band row, step-up, shoulder press, heel raise and bird dog or wall plank. Do 1 set of 10 of each, resting 30 to 60 seconds between exercises. In later weeks, go round the circuit twice.
  3. Cool-down (3 minutes): slow walking and gentle stretches for the calves, thighs and chest.

Note how your joints feel that evening and the next morning, and adjust the next session if needed.

Eating to support your muscles

Muscles need fuel to get stronger. Follow a balanced diet in line with the NHS Eatwell Guide, including a source of protein such as fish, eggs, beans, pulses, dairy, tofu or lean meat at each meal. If you have a reduced appetite, are losing weight without trying, or have kidney disease, ask your GP or a dietitian for advice.

Before you start

  • Check with your GP or physiotherapist first if you have heart or lung problems, uncontrolled high blood pressure, recent surgery or a recent fall.
  • Warm up for 5 minutes, for example marching on the spot, arm swings and a few easy repetitions of the first exercise.
  • Breathe out as you lift or push, and in as you lower. Never hold your breath.
  • Move slowly: about 2 seconds to lift and 2 to 3 seconds to lower.
  • Use the 24-hour rule: mild muscle ache or joint discomfort that settles by the next day is fine. If joint pain is worse for longer, or a joint swells, reduce the load or repetitions next time.

Muscle soreness a day or two after a new exercise is normal and different from joint pain. It usually feels like a general ache in the muscle and fades within a few days.

Eight beginner strength exercises

1. Sit-to-stand (legs and hips)

Sit near the front of a firm chair with feet hip-width apart. Lean forward and stand up, then sit down slowly. Easier: use your hands or a higher seat. Harder: arms crossed, a slower lowering, or holding a weight at your chest.

2. Wall press-up (chest, shoulders, arms)

Stand an arm's length from a wall, hands at shoulder height. Bend your elbows to bring your chest towards the wall, then push back. Harder: step your feet further back, or progress to a kitchen worktop.

3. Glute bridge (buttocks, back of thighs)

Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat. Squeeze your buttocks and lift your hips, hold for 2 seconds, and lower slowly. Harder: hold for longer, or march one foot at a time while lifted.

4. Seated or band row (upper back)

Sit tall with a resistance band looped around your feet, or anchored at chest height. Pull your elbows back, squeezing your shoulder blades together, then return slowly. Easier: do it without a band as a shoulder blade squeeze.

5. Step-up (legs)

Using the bottom stair with a banister, step up with one foot, bring the other to join it, and step down slowly. Easier: use a lower step. Harder: a higher step or holding light weights.

6. Shoulder press (shoulders, arms)

Sitting or standing, hold light weights or water bottles at shoulder height and press them up to just below fully straight, then lower slowly. If your shoulders are painful, press only to forehead height or do a front raise to shoulder level instead.

7. Heel raise (calves)

Hold a worktop and rise onto the balls of your feet, pause, and lower slowly. Harder: one leg at a time.

8. Bird dog or wall plank (core)

On hands and knees, slowly stretch one arm forward and the opposite leg back, hold for 3 seconds, and return. If kneeling hurts, stand facing a wall with your forearms on it and lean in, tightening your stomach muscles, for 10 to 20 seconds.

Choosing resistance

TypeGood forTips
Body weightStarting out, at homeSit-to-stands, wall press-ups, bridges, step-ups
Resistance bandsHome, travel, painful hands (use loops or handles)Start with the lightest band; move up when 12 reps feel easy
Hand weights and ankle weightsArms, shoulders, legsStart with 0.5 to 1 kg; water bottles or tins work
Gym machinesControlled movements, easy to adjustAsk staff to set up seats and show you technique

The right weight is one you can lift 8 to 12 times with good form, where the last 2 or 3 repetitions feel hard. If you cannot do 8, it is too heavy. If 12 feels easy, it is time to progress.

A 12-week beginner plan

WeeksSessionsSets and repsFocus
1–22 a week1 set of 8–10, easier versionsLearn the movements, check how joints respond
3–42–3 a week1–2 sets of 10–12Build confidence and consistency
5–82–3 a week2 sets of 10–12Add light resistance or harder versions one exercise at a time
9–122–3 a week2–3 sets of 8–12Increase resistance gradually; review and set new goals

Change only one thing at a time: repetitions, then sets, then resistance. If a joint flares after a change, go back a step for a week.

Adapting for your joints and condition

  • Knees: keep squats and sit-to-stands to a comfortable depth; see our knee exercises.
  • Hips: bridges and side leg lifts are often well tolerated; see our hip exercises. After hip replacement, follow your surgical team's advice.
  • Hands and wrists: use bands with handles or loops, padded grips, or ankle weights on the forearm instead of gripping.
  • Shoulders: keep presses below painful heights; rows and band rotations are usually easier.
  • Back: keep your back in a neutral position, and avoid heavy lifting with a rounded back.
  • Inflammatory arthritis: during a flare, reduce the load on inflamed joints and keep other muscles working. If you take biologics, methotrexate or steroids, strength training is usually safe; our guide to strength training on biologics explains more.
  • Osteoporosis: strength training is helpful for bones, but avoid forceful bending forwards and twisting of the spine. Ask a physiotherapist for advice.

Gym or home?

Both work. Home training is free and convenient. A gym or leisure centre offers machines that make it easier to adjust loads, and staff who can help. Many leisure centres run beginner or over-50s strength classes, and GP exercise referral schemes can offer supervised sessions. If you are frail or find standing exercises hard, seated strength training is a safe place to start; see our seated strength training guide.

Timing and comfort tips

  • Train at the time of day your joints feel best. For many people with inflammatory arthritis, that is later in the morning or afternoon, once stiffness has eased.
  • A warm shower or wheat bag before a session can make movement easier; a wrapped cold pack afterwards can settle a warm, achy joint.
  • If you take pain relief, some people find timing it before exercise helps, but check with your pharmacist or GP what is suitable for you.
  • Wear supportive shoes for standing exercises and use a non-slip mat for floor work.

Common mistakes

  • Starting too heavy or doing too many exercises in the first week.
  • Moving quickly or using momentum instead of slow, controlled lifts.
  • Training the same muscles hard on consecutive days.
  • Stopping when you have a bad day instead of doing a lighter session.
  • Only training the painful joint; whole-body strength matters for function.

Tracking your progress

Write down the exercises, weights or bands, sets and repetitions each session, and how your joints felt the next day. Every 4 weeks, test something practical, such as how many sit-to-stands you can do in 30 seconds or how easily you manage the stairs. Seeing progress on paper helps keep you going.

When to get medical help

Stop the exercise if you get sharp pain, a joint giving way or locking, sudden swelling, or pain that increases with each repetition.

  • Call 999 if you have chest pain, severe breathlessness or feel faint during exercise that does not settle with rest.
  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E if a joint becomes suddenly hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with a high temperature.
  • See your GP or a physiotherapist if joint pain is consistently worse for more than a day after sessions, despite reducing the load, if you are unsure how to adapt exercises, or if you are not improving after 12 weeks. In many areas you can refer yourself to NHS physiotherapy.

Is strength training safe with arthritis?

Yes, for most people. Built up gradually, strength training is safe and is recommended by NICE as part of exercise for osteoarthritis. Start light, move slowly and use the 24-hour rule to judge how your joints respond.

How heavy should weights be with arthritis?

Choose a weight you can lift 8 to 12 times with good form, where the last few repetitions feel hard. Start lighter than you think you need, and increase only when 12 repetitions feel easy for two sessions in a row.

How often should I strength train with arthritis?

Two or three times a week, with at least one rest day in between, covering the major muscle groups. This meets the UK recommendation of strengthening activities on at least 2 days a week.

Should I strength train during a flare?

Reduce or stop loading the flaring joints and keep other muscles working with lighter exercises. Return gradually as the flare settles. If flares are frequent, speak to your GP or rheumatology team.

How long until I get stronger?

Many people notice that exercises feel easier within 4 to 6 weeks, and measurable strength and function gains usually take 8 to 12 weeks of regular training. Keep going to maintain the benefits.

Can older adults with arthritis do strength training?

Yes. Strength training is especially valuable for older adults to maintain independence and reduce falls. Seated and supported exercises are a safe place to start, and many areas offer classes designed for older people.

article.title: Strength Training on Biologics: Is It Safe?
article.excerpt: Strength training is generally safe and recommended for people with arthritis, even those on biologics. Research shows it can improve muscle strength…
article.content:
Quick answer: Strength training is generally safe and recommended for people with arthritis, even those on biologics. It is generally thought that it can improve muscle strength, reduce pain, and boost physical function. It's crucial to start slowly, focus on proper form, and listen to your body, stopping if you experience new or lasting joint pain. Always discuss your exercise plan with your clinician.

Overview

Resistance work is not only safe — it's recommended.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis editorial team using UK NICE guidance, NHS information and peer-reviewed sources. We aim to update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Current research strongly supports the benefits of strength training for people living with arthritis, even those taking biologics. Large-scale reviews of many studies consistently show that carefully planned resistance exercises can improve muscle strength, reduce pain, and boost overall physical function. This evidence comes from a mix of randomised trials and observational studies, which track people over time.

Clinical guidelines from professional bodies across the UK and internationally now routinely recommend strength training as a core part of managing arthritis. These recommendations highlight that, when supervised and adapted to individual needs, the benefits of exercise far outweigh any potential risks. The key is finding the right balance and intensity for each person.

The evidence also suggests that exercise, including strength training, can complement the effects of medications like biologics. While biologics work to reduce inflammation, exercise helps maintain joint mobility and muscle mass, addressing other aspects of living with a long-term condition. This combined approach often leads to better long-term outcomes and a higher quality of life.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Starting too quickly: Gradually increase weights or resistance over several weeks.
  • Ignoring pain: Distinguish between muscle fatigue and joint pain; avoid movements that cause sharp or lasting joint discomfort.
  • Poor form: Focus on correct technique over lifting heavy weights to protect your joints.
  • Inconsistency: Little and often is better than sporadic, intense sessions.
  • Skipping warm-ups/cool-downs: These are crucial for preparing your body and aiding recovery.
  • Not asking for help: A physiotherapist can provide a tailored exercise plan.

When to Speak to a Clinician

While strength training is generally beneficial, there are times when you should seek professional advice before continuing or starting a new routine. If you experience any new or worsening symptoms that concern you, it's always best to get them checked.

Consider speaking to your general practitioner, physiotherapist, or rheumatology specialist if you notice:

  • Sudden, unexplained joint swelling or increased warmth around a joint.
  • New, persistent pain that doesn't subside after activity or rest.
  • Fever, chills, or unusual fatigue alongside your exercise.
  • Significant increase in joint stiffness or loss of movement.
  • Any signs of infection, such as redness or pus, around your joints.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will strength training make my arthritis worse?

No, when done correctly and tailored to your condition, strength training is highly unlikely to worsen your arthritis. In fact, it can protect your joints by strengthening the muscles around them, improving stability and reducing impact during daily activities. Listening to your body and working with a professional are key to a safe and effective programme.

How soon after starting biologics can I begin strength training?

It's generally safe to continue or start strength training once your condition is stable and you're tolerating your biologic medication well. However, always discuss this with your rheumatologist or specialist nurse. They can advise based on your specific health situation and how your body is responding to treatment.

What if I have a flare-up while strength training?

During an arthritis flare-up, it's wise to reduce the intensity and type of exercise. You might switch to gentler activities like walking or stretching, or rest the affected joints. Once the flare-up subsides, you can gradually return to your strength training routine. Always consult your clinician if you're unsure or if the flare-up is severe.

Practical next steps for Strength Training on Biologics: Is It Safe?

If you came here about Strength Training on Biologics: Is It Safe?, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your primary care network about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Gentle cognitive tools

Noticing catastrophic thoughts ("this flare will never end") and reframing them with paced facts can reduce fear without denying real pain. Apps and courses based on cognitive behavioural approaches are available on the NHS in many areas; your surgery can advise what is offered locally.

Quick questions about Strength Training Biologics Safe

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

article.title: Sulfasalazine for Arthritis: What to Expect When Starting
article.excerpt: Starting sulfasalazine for rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis? A plain-English guide to how it works, how long it takes, blood monitoring, common side effects and when to call your team.
article.content:
Quick answer: Sulfasalazine is a disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) used for rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and some other inflammatory conditions. It calms the immune system slowly, so it can take around two to three months to make a real difference. You will need regular blood tests, especially at first. Common side effects include feeling sick, headaches and orange-coloured urine. Always follow your rheumatology team's dosing plan.

What sulfasalazine is and how it works

Sulfasalazine has been used for many decades. It is a combination of a sulfa antibiotic-like part and an aspirin-like part, and it works by damping down the overactive immune response that causes inflammation in the joints. It does not work like a painkiller. Instead it slowly reduces inflammation, which over time eases pain, stiffness and swelling and helps protect joints from damage.

In the UK it is most often used for:

  • Rheumatoid arthritis, on its own or combined with other DMARDs such as methotrexate or hydroxychloroquine.
  • Psoriatic arthritis, particularly when joints in the arms and legs are affected.
  • Some types of spondyloarthritis with peripheral joint involvement, and inflammatory bowel disease.

It is one of several conventional DMARDs. Our guide to DMARDs versus biologics explains where it fits alongside other treatments.

How you take it

Sulfasalazine comes as tablets, usually the enteric-coated (gastro-resistant) type, which are gentler on the stomach. Your team will usually start you on a low dose and increase it step by step over the first few weeks, which helps your body get used to it. The exact plan varies, so follow the schedule your rheumatology team or pharmacist gives you and do not change the dose yourself.

Tips that help many people:

  • Take the tablets with or just after food and a glass of water.
  • Swallow enteric-coated tablets whole. Do not crush or chew them.
  • Set a phone reminder or use a pill organiser.
  • If you miss a dose, check the leaflet or ask your pharmacist. Do not take a double dose to make up.

How long does it take to work?

Sulfasalazine works slowly. Some people notice a change after a few weeks, but it often takes around two to three months to see the full benefit. During that time your team may suggest other ways to control symptoms, such as anti-inflammatory painkillers or a short course of steroids. It is worth sticking with it through this early period unless you have side effects your team is concerned about.

Blood tests and monitoring

Sulfasalazine can occasionally affect blood cells and the liver, so you will have regular blood tests. These are usually more frequent in the first few months, and less often once you have been on a stable dose for a while. Monitoring schedules are set by your team and local shared-care arrangements. The tests usually include:

  • A full blood count, to check white cells, red cells and platelets.
  • Liver function tests.
  • Kidney function tests.

Many people keep a monitoring booklet or use an app to track their results. If you struggle to get to appointments, our guide to getting to blood tests has practical ideas.

Common side effects

Many people take sulfasalazine with few or no problems. Side effects are most likely in the first few months, and some settle as your body adjusts. Common ones include:

  • Feeling sick, loss of appetite, indigestion or tummy pain. Taking tablets with food and building up the dose slowly usually helps.
  • Headaches and dizziness.
  • A rash or itchy skin.
  • Orange or yellow colouring of urine, sweat and tears. This is harmless, but it can stain soft contact lenses, so you may want to switch to glasses or daily lenses.
  • A temporary drop in sperm count in men, which recovers after stopping. Mention this if you are planning a family.

The NHS medicines pages and the patient leaflet in your pack list other, less common side effects.

When to contact your team urgently

Rarely, sulfasalazine can affect the bone marrow, liver or skin in serious ways. Contact your GP or rheumatology advice line the same day, or call NHS 111, if you notice:

  • A sore throat, fever, chills or mouth ulcers.
  • Unexplained bruising or bleeding.
  • Yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes.
  • A widespread rash, blistering or peeling skin, especially with a fever.
  • Unusual breathlessness or a persistent cough.

Call 999 if you have signs of a severe allergic reaction, such as swelling of the lips, tongue or throat or difficulty breathing.

Alcohol, other medicines and vaccines

  • Alcohol: there is no specific interaction, but it is sensible to stay within UK low-risk drinking guidelines. See our guide to arthritis and alcohol.
  • Allergies: tell your team if you are allergic to sulfa antibiotics (sulfonamides) or aspirin, as sulfasalazine may not be suitable.
  • Other medicines: always tell pharmacists and other clinicians you take sulfasalazine, including before buying remedies or supplements. Our guide to medicine and supplement interactions can help.
  • Vaccines: sulfasalazine on its own is not usually strongly immune-suppressing, but check with your team about vaccines, particularly if you take it with other DMARDs. See our vaccines guide.

Pregnancy and breastfeeding

Sulfasalazine is one of the arthritis medicines that can often be continued during pregnancy and breastfeeding, and extra folic acid is usually recommended. Every situation is different, so talk to your rheumatology team before trying for a baby, and let them know as soon as possible if you become pregnant. Our guide to arthritis and pregnancy has more.

If it is not working, or you need to stop

Not every medicine suits every person. If sulfasalazine has not helped enough after a fair trial, or side effects are a problem, your team may adjust the dose, add another medicine or switch to a different treatment, such as another DMARD or a biologic. Stopping should be planned with your team, because inflammation can return quickly without treatment. Our guide to stopping arthritis medicines safely explains why. If you are worried about taking sulfasalazine long term, raise it at your next review or call your advice line. Your concerns matter, and there is usually more than one option.

Frequently asked questions

How long does sulfasalazine take to work?

Many people notice some improvement within a few weeks, but it often takes around two to three months to reach its full effect.

Why has my urine turned orange on sulfasalazine?

Sulfasalazine is a yellow-orange compound and can colour urine, sweat and tears. This is harmless, but it can stain soft contact lenses and some clothing.

Can I drink alcohol while taking sulfasalazine?

There is no specific interaction, but keeping within UK low-risk drinking guidelines is sensible. If you also take methotrexate or leflunomide, follow the alcohol advice for those medicines.

Do I need blood tests on sulfasalazine?

Yes. Regular blood counts and liver and kidney tests are needed, more often at first. Your team or GP will explain your schedule.

Can I take sulfasalazine with methotrexate?

Yes, they are often combined, sometimes with hydroxychloroquine as well. Your team will decide whether a combination suits you.

What should I do if I get a sore throat or fever?

Contact your GP or rheumatology advice line the same day, or call NHS 111. You may need a blood test to check your white cell count.

article.title: How to Support a Friend Newly Diagnosed With Lupus
article.excerpt: To support a friend with new lupus: offer specific practical help, learn the basics of lupus, be flexible with plans (flares are unpredictable).
article.content:
A new lupus diagnosis is frightening and often isolating. Your support as a friend can make an enormous difference — but knowing how to help effectively, without overstepping or inadvertently minimising what your friend is going through, takes thought.

Quick answer: To support a friend with new lupus: offer specific practical help, learn the basics of lupus, be flexible with plans (flares are unpredictable), avoid minimising phrases like "you look well." Lupus UK helpline: 01708 731251.

Friendship and support — openly licensed via Openverse

What Lupus Actually Involves

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks the body's own tissues. It causes joint pain, fatigue, skin rashes (including the characteristic butterfly rash across the cheeks), and can affect internal organs including kidneys, heart and lungs. It is unpredictable — your friend may look fine one week and be unable to function the next. This variability is one of the hardest things for outsiders to understand.

What to Say (and What Not to Say)

Helpful

  • "I'm here for you — what would be most useful right now?"
  • "Would you like me to come with you to an appointment?"
  • "Tell me what a bad day looks like so I can understand better."
  • "I'm bringing dinner on Tuesday — what time works?"

Unhelpful (avoid these)

  • "But you look so well!" — invalidates invisible symptoms
  • "Have you tried [unproven remedy]?" — implies they should be doing more
  • "At least it's not cancer" — minimises a serious chronic condition
  • "You just need to think more positively" — oversimplifies a complex illness

Community and friendship — openly licensed via Openverse

Practical Things You Can Do

  • Offer specific, scheduled help — "I'll pick up your prescription on Thursday" is more useful than "let me know if you need anything."
  • Learn the basics of lupus — understanding what triggers flares and what symptoms to watch for shows you take it seriously.
  • Be flexible with plans — lupus flares are unpredictable. Adopting a "no hard feelings" approach to cancelled plans reduces your friend's anxiety and guilt.
  • Check in regularly without pressure — a simple "how are you today, no need to reply at length" message can mean a lot.

Long-term support — openly licensed via Openverse

Q&A

Question: My friend seems angry and withdrawn since diagnosis — is this normal?
Short answer: Yes. Anger, grief, fear and withdrawal are all normal responses to a significant chronic illness diagnosis. Give your friend space while making clear your support is available whenever they want it.

Question: Where can my friend get specialist support?
Short answer: Lupus UK (01708 731251, lupusuk.org.uk) provides specialist helpline support, local groups and peer contact. Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) also covers lupus.

Practical next steps for How to Support a Friend Newly Diagnosed With Lupus

If you came here about How to Support a Friend Newly Diagnosed With Lupus, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your local integrated care board about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Finding people who understand

Local arthritis groups, hospital patient panels and moderated online communities can reduce isolation. Ask your rheumatology nurse, library, or council adult social care pages for current lists. Choose spaces that feel practical and kind; leave any that push unproven cures or shame medication use.

Peer support etiquette

Share what helps you without prescribing it for others. Conditions, medicines and life circumstances differ. If someone is in crisis, encourage them toward NHS 111, their GP, or emergency services rather than relying on a forum alone.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Quick questions about Support Friend Newly Diagnosed

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

Keep expectations kind while you work on how to support a friend newly diagnosed with lupus. Arthritis symptoms fluctuate; a quieter week does not mean you imagined earlier pain, and a flare does not mean every helpful habit has failed. Adjust one variable at a time so you can see what truly helps.

Quick answer: The post says partners can support someone with arthritis through small daily acts, open communication and practical help with joint-straining tasks. It stresses clinician-led, personalised care combining medication, regular comfortable movement, symptom tracking and lifestyle support. It advises pacing, not stopping prescribed treatment, avoiding quick fixes, and seeking prompt review for swelling, fever, severe pain or rapid loss of function.

Overview

Small daily acts that ease pain and protect relationships.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis editorial team using UK NICE guidance, NHS information and peer-reviewed sources. We aim to update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Systematic reviews consistently highlight the benefit of early and sustained intervention for managing arthritis. These interventions aren't just about medication; they encompass a holistic approach. Clinical guidelines from leading rheumatology bodies across the UK reinforce the importance of patient education, self-management strategies, and tailored physical activity programmes alongside pharmaceutical treatments.

Randomised controlled trials underscore the positive impact of regular, appropriate exercise on pain reduction, joint function, and overall quality of life for people living with various forms of arthritis. The evidence suggests that even seemingly small, daily acts of support from a partner can significantly contribute to adherence to these beneficial lifestyle changes, thereby improving health outcomes and reducing the burden of the condition.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Ignoring early symptoms: Don't wait for severe pain; seek advice as soon as you notice persistent joint issues.
  • Overdoing it on good days: Balance activity with rest to prevent flare-ups; pacing is key.
  • Stopping medication when feeling better: Adhere to your prescribed treatment plan consistently unless advised otherwise by your healthcare provider.
  • Relying solely on quick fixes: Understand that arthritis management is a long-term journey, not a short sprint.
  • Not communicating openly with your partner: Share your good days and bad days to help them understand how best to support you.

When to Speak to a Clinician

While routine monitoring is part of living with arthritis, certain changes warrant prompt attention from your GP, physiotherapist, or rheumatologist. Do not delay seeking medical advice if you experience any of the following:

  • New and unexplained joint swelling that lasts more than a few days.
  • Sudden, severe increase in pain in one or more joints.
  • Signs of infection, such as redness, warmth, or fever around a joint.
  • Rapid loss of movement or function in a joint.
  • New symptoms affecting other parts of your body, like persistent rash or breathing difficulties.

Frequently Asked Questions

How can I explain my arthritis pain to my partner so they truly understand?

Try to use analogies that relate to their experiences, like comparing it to a deep ache after a marathon or constant toothache. Explain how it affects simple daily tasks and how it can fluctuate, even hourly. Being open and honest about your feelings, rather than just the physical pain, can also help them empathise.

What are some simple ways my partner can help me around the house without making me feel helpless?

Your partner can help by taking on tasks that put strain on your joints, such as lifting heavy items, opening stubborn jars, or reaching high shelves. They could also help prepare meals or assist with household chores during a flare. The key is to communicate what you need without feeling like a burden, and to appreciate their efforts.

Is it OK to have sex when I have arthritis pain?

Intimacy is important for relationships, and arthritis doesn't mean you have to stop. Communicate openly with your partner about what feels comfortable and what doesn't. You might find certain positions or times of day are better, perhaps after medication or a warm bath. Experimenting together and focusing on closeness can help maintain intimacy.
