article.title: Weight-Loss Injections and Arthritis: Wegovy and Mounjaro
article.excerpt: Weight-loss injections such as Wegovy and Mounjaro are in the news. This guide explains how they might help arthritis, who can get them on the NHS, side effects, protecting muscle, and what to check if you take arthritis medicines.
article.content:
Quick answer: Weight-loss injections such as Wegovy (semaglutide) and Mounjaro (tirzepatide) are licensed for weight management, not for arthritis. Losing weight can reduce knee and hip pain in osteoarthritis, and a large trial found semaglutide reduced knee pain in people with obesity and knee osteoarthritis. They are available on the NHS only for people who meet set criteria. Side effects are common, and protecting muscle strength matters.

What these medicines are

Wegovy contains semaglutide and Mounjaro contains tirzepatide. Both are weekly injections that copy natural gut hormones involved in appetite and blood sugar control. They make you feel fuller for longer and reduce hunger, which helps people eat less and lose weight. Similar medicines, under different brand names, are used to treat type 2 diabetes.

In the UK they are licensed for weight management in adults who meet certain criteria, alongside a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity. They are not licensed as a treatment for arthritis itself.

How weight loss can help arthritis

Extra body weight increases the load on weight-bearing joints such as the knees and hips. Fat tissue also releases substances that promote inflammation. For people with osteoarthritis who are carrying extra weight, NICE recommends weight loss as part of core treatment, alongside exercise and education, because even modest weight loss can reduce pain and improve function.

There is growing research into weight-loss medicines specifically in people with arthritis. One large trial, published in 2024, found that people with obesity and knee osteoarthritis who took semaglutide lost more weight and reported less knee pain and better physical function than those given a placebo. Research is ongoing, including into whether these medicines have effects on joints beyond weight loss. For people with psoriatic arthritis and other inflammatory conditions, weight loss may help treatment work better, but more research is needed.

Who can get them on the NHS?

NICE has approved both medicines for use on the NHS for some adults living with obesity, usually with at least one weight-related health condition, and with specific body mass index (BMI) thresholds. Access has been phased, with priority given to people with the greatest clinical need, and the arrangements differ between specialist weight management services and GP-led care and across the four UK nations. Eligibility is based on weight and health conditions, not on having arthritis alone.

If you are interested, ask your GP whether you might be eligible and what local weight management support is available. Your GP can also discuss other options, such as NHS weight management programmes and the NHS Digital Weight Management Programme for people with diabetes or high blood pressure.

Buying privately: staying safe

Many people buy these medicines privately through online pharmacies. If you do:

  • Only use a UK-registered pharmacy. You can check registration with the General Pharmaceutical Council.
  • Expect a proper health assessment, including your weight, medical history and current medicines. Be honest about your arthritis and the medicines you take.
  • Never buy from social media, beauty salons or unregulated websites. The MHRA has warned about fake and unsafe weight-loss pens.
  • Tell your GP and rheumatology team that you are taking one, so it is on your record.

Side effects

Side effects are common, especially when starting or increasing the dose, and often improve with time. They include:

  • Feeling sick, vomiting, diarrhoea or constipation.
  • Indigestion, bloating and burping.
  • Tiredness and dizziness.
  • Hair thinning, sometimes linked to rapid weight loss.

Less common but serious side effects include inflammation of the pancreas (severe tummy pain spreading to the back, which needs urgent medical help) and gallbladder problems. Dehydration from vomiting or diarrhoea can affect the kidneys, which matters more if you also take anti-inflammatory painkillers. Read the patient leaflet and seek medical advice if you are worried.

Protecting muscle and bone

When people lose weight quickly, some of the weight lost is muscle. Muscle strength is vital for supporting arthritic joints, balance and staying independent, particularly as you get older. To protect it:

  • Do strength exercises at least twice a week. See our guide to resistance training for arthritis.
  • Eat enough protein at each meal, even when your appetite is low.
  • Keep active every day, for example with walking or swimming.
  • Ask your GP about bone health if you have other risk factors for osteoporosis.

Using them alongside arthritis medicines

  • There are no well-known major interactions with common DMARDs or biologics, but always check with your pharmacist or prescriber.
  • These medicines slow stomach emptying, which may affect how some tablets are absorbed. Your pharmacist can advise.
  • Mounjaro can make oral contraceptive pills less effective, particularly when starting or increasing the dose, so extra contraception may be needed. These medicines should not be used in pregnancy. This matters if you take arthritis medicines that also need careful pregnancy planning, such as methotrexate or leflunomide.
  • If you become unwell with vomiting or diarrhoea, ask your pharmacist or GP whether any medicines, such as NSAIDs, should be paused while you recover. Do not change doses of your arthritis medicines without advice.
  • Tell your surgical team and anaesthetist if you take one before any operation, including joint surgery.

What happens when you stop?

It is generally thought that many people regain weight after stopping these medicines. Building lasting habits around food, activity and sleep while taking them gives you the best chance of keeping benefits. The medicines work best as one part of a wider plan, not on their own.

Weight-loss support without injections

Injections are not suitable or available for everyone. Many people with arthritis lose weight through changes to diet and activity, with support from their GP, a dietitian, a weight management programme or a physiotherapist. See our diet guide and exercise guide.

Frequently asked questions

Can Mounjaro or Wegovy help knee arthritis?

They are not licensed for arthritis, but weight loss can reduce knee pain in osteoarthritis. A large trial found semaglutide reduced knee pain in people with obesity and knee osteoarthritis.

Can I get weight-loss injections on the NHS for arthritis?

Eligibility is based on your BMI and weight-related health conditions, not arthritis alone. Ask your GP whether you might qualify.

Can I take Mounjaro with methotrexate?

There is no well-known major interaction, but check with your pharmacist and tell your rheumatology team. Both need careful pregnancy planning.

Will I lose muscle on weight-loss injections?

Some muscle loss is common with rapid weight loss. Strength exercise and enough protein help protect muscle.

Are weight-loss injections safe to buy online?

Only buy from a UK-registered pharmacy that carries out a proper health assessment. Never buy from social media or unregulated sellers.

Do I need to stop weight-loss injections before joint surgery?

Tell your surgical team and anaesthetist. They will advise what to do, as these medicines slow stomach emptying.

article.title: Weight Management and Arthritis: The Evidence
article.excerpt: Every kilogram of weight loss removes roughly four kilograms of force from each knee step. The evidence on weight, inflammation and joint pain.
article.content:
Quick answer: Weight management is an effective strategy for managing arthritis symptoms. A 5% reduction in body weight can significantly reduce knee osteoarthritis symptoms. A 10% reduction in weight can even produce benefits comparable to some medications. This is achieved through consistent, small changes, tracking outcomes like pain on waking, longest pain-free intervals, and functional improvements.

What this guide covers

This piece summarises what the current evidence says about weight management and arthritis: the evidence, the practical steps that help most, and the red flags that mean you should speak to your GP or physiotherapist.

The underlying mechanism

Arthritis pain rarely has a single cause. Joint cartilage, synovial fluid, ligaments, surrounding muscle and the nervous system all contribute. Understanding which of these is driving your specific symptom is the first step toward targeted relief. For an in-depth condition overview, see our related guide.

Inflammatory and degenerative forms behave differently. Inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid, psoriatic, ankylosing spondylitis) typically worsens with rest and improves with gentle movement. Degenerative arthritis (osteoarthritis) typically worsens with prolonged use. Knowing which pattern matches your day-to-day experience helps you choose the right management approach.

What helps — by strength of evidence

  1. Movement and graded exercise. NICE NG226 (2022) and Cochrane reviews place structured exercise as a first-line treatment. Aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, split into 20–30 minute sessions.
  2. Anti-inflammatory eating. A Mediterranean-style pattern — oily fish twice a week, plenty of vegetables, olive oil, whole grains — is linked to reduced pain scores in OA and RA trials.
  3. Weight management. A 5 percent reduction in body weight reduces knee-OA symptoms measurably; a 10 percent reduction can match the effect of some medications.
  4. Heat and cold. Heat eases stiffness; cold eases acute swelling. Twenty-minute applications, with a towel barrier.
  5. Sleep hygiene. Pain perception rises sharply on fewer than six hours of sleep. Prioritise a consistent bedtime.

A practical seven-day starting plan

Begin with the smallest dose that feels manageable — five minutes of movement, one anti-inflammatory meal a day, a 10 pm screen-off rule. Track only three things weekly: pain on waking (0–10), longest pain-free interval, and one functional win (e.g., climbed stairs without grabbing the rail). Small, consistent inputs outperform big sporadic efforts.

When to seek clinical advice

Book an appointment with your GP or a first-contact physiotherapist if you notice: sudden hot, red, swollen joints; unexplained weight loss alongside joint pain; morning stiffness lasting longer than an hour for more than two weeks; or new numbness or weakness. These can signal inflammatory disease that benefits from early treatment.

Frequently asked questions

Will this approach work alongside my medication? Yes. Exercise, diet and pacing complement prescribed treatments and often improve their effectiveness. Always check with your prescriber before stopping any medication.

How long until I notice a difference? Most people report meaningful improvement at 6–12 weeks of consistent practice. Earlier wins (less morning stiffness, better sleep) often appear within 2–3 weeks.

Is this safe if I have other conditions? The principles above are broadly safe for adults with stable cardiovascular, metabolic and respiratory conditions. If you are unsure, ask your GP for a referral to a first-contact physiotherapist for a tailored plan.

This article is general health information, not medical advice. Always consult a qualified healthcare professional for decisions about your individual care.

Practical next steps for Weight Management and Arthritis: The Evidence

If you came here about Weight Management and Arthritis: The Evidence, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Supplements versus meals

Food-first is usually safer than stacking capsules. If you do try a supplement, choose a reputable UK brand, check for interactions with your medicines (especially blood thinners), and give any trial a clear stop date so you can judge whether symptoms truly changed.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

Quick questions about Weight Management Arthritis Evidence

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep expectations kind while you work on weight management and arthritis: the evidence. Arthritis symptoms fluctuate; a quieter week does not mean you imagined earlier pain, and a flare does not mean every helpful habit has failed. Adjust one variable at a time so you can see what truly helps.

Quick answer: Arthritis steers the joints; frailty steers recovery time. Together they can shrink a week faster than either alone. This UK guide looks at bathroom changes that reduce the scariest transfer of the day in a home setting, with practical steps, warning signs and Scotland services. It is general information, not personal medical advice.

Families often notice arthritis with frailty first as a slower walk across a home, then as a person who starts declining invitations. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with bathroom changes that reduce the scariest transfer of the day, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in Scotland.

Home, roles and rhythm with arthritis and frailty

Walking aids, Blue Badge applications, community transport and downstairs living are all tools. None of them is a moral failure. Used well, they keep you in the world so several joints still get some practice.

Benefits such as Personal Independence Payment or Attendance Allowance have rules, forms and waiting. Living With Arthritis will not tell you that you will qualify. We will tell you that an honest diary of bathroom changes that reduce the scariest transfer of the day — the help you need on bad days, not your best Tuesday — is what assessors need if you do apply.

Keep a social appointment that does not depend on a heroic walk. A library, a faith group with a ramp, a phone befriender or a day centre can be as clinical as a tablet because isolation shrinks appetite, mood and muscle.

Most frailty lives in ordinary rooms. Rails, lighting, chair height, a kettle that does not demand a full kettle-lift, and a toilet you can get off again are treatment. Occupational therapy exists for this.

Not 'just getting old': bathroom changes that reduce the scariest transfer of the day

NICE is clear that exercise is core care for osteoarthritis, not an optional extra after tablets. That still holds if you are becoming frailer, but the dose must respect today's several joints and today's energy. Rest has a place in a flare; rest as a lifestyle is how deconditioning joins the diagnosis.

Practical self-management for bathroom changes that reduce the scariest transfer of the day

  • After a flare, restart the smallest version of your usual movement within comfort, rather than waiting to feel back to normal. Normal rarely sends an email.
  • Use heat for stiffness if your skin is healthy, but protect thin skin. Never fall asleep on a hot water bottle.
  • Book eye, foot and hearing checks as frailty care, not vanity. Arthritis with frailty already asks a lot of balance.
  • Keep a sit-to-stand practice at the height you actually use. A higher chair is not cheating if it lets several joints work without a panic haul.
  • Put the items you use at dawn — tablets, glasses, walking aid, phone — where you can reach them without a stretch that wrenches several joints.
  • Plan the scariest transfer of the day — often the bathroom — with lighting, a rail conversation and unhurried time. Rushing with stiff several joints is how near-misses happen.

Flare, fear and slowing down

  • Carers doing the last steps of a task to be kind, which removes the last practice the muscles were getting.
  • A flare of arthritis with frailty that lasts, then a slower baseline even when the flare eases.
  • Night toilet trips, poor lighting and stiff several joints stacking into a falls risk that nobody named.
  • Skipping meals or drinks because getting to the kitchen with sore several joints feels like a project.
  • A hospital or infection week that ends with clothes feeling looser and stairs feeling taller.

When to get help

  • If you cannot get to the surgery because of arthritis with frailty, ask about a home visit or a proper phone review. Silence is not a care plan.
  • Unplanned weight loss, repeated falls, or bathroom changes that reduce the scariest transfer of the day that is clearly worsening week by week — book the GP and say you are worried about frailty as well as several joints.
  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.
  • Chest pain, trouble breathing, or signs of a stroke — 999, not a wait for the arthritis with frailty nurse.
  • Sudden confusion, new incontinence, or a crash in mobility over hours to days — think infection or delirium, not only arthritis.

Scotland services, without inventing a clinic

Should I stop exercising during bathroom changes that reduce the scariest transfer of the day?

Complete rest for more than a short flare period usually makes several joints and muscle worse. Keep a smaller version: seated strength, indoor loops, or the two sit-to-stands you can still do. If exercise causes pain that spirals or a joint that will not settle, get clinical advice.

How do I tell an arthritis flare from a frailty slide?

A flare of arthritis with frailty is usually more joint pain, stiffness or swelling in a known pattern. A frailty slide is broader: weaker recovery, smaller meals, more time in the chair, maybe confusion or falls. They can happen together. If the whole person is changing, do not only increase pain gel.

Are painkillers the main treatment for frail arthritis with frailty?

No. For osteoarthritis, NICE puts exercise, weight management where relevant, and topical options at the centre. Tablets may help some people some of the time, but in frail adults they need a hard look at stomach, kidneys, heart, constipation and falls. Never share someone else's medicines.

article.content:
Quick answer: Sustained remission in rheumatoid arthritis means stable minimal or no disease activity, not a cure. The article says it is a key treatment goal, often maintained through ongoing medication, monitoring, gentle regular movement and lifestyle support. It advises personalised clinician guidance, symptom tracking, pacing activity, and prompt review for swelling, fever, rapid function loss or medication side effects.

Overview

Remission isn't cure. Understanding the difference changes how you plan.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis editorial team using UK NICE guidance, NHS information and peer-reviewed sources. We aim to update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

The consensus among rheumatology experts and patient advocacy groups is that achieving remission in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a primary treatment goal. Systematic reviews of long-term studies consistently show that individuals who reach and maintain remission experience better quality of life, less joint damage, and improved physical function compared to those with ongoing disease activity. This evidence underpins current clinical guidelines, which strongly advocate for a 'treat-to-target' approach, meaning adjusting treatments until remission or very low disease activity is achieved.

However, clinical guidance also highlights that "remission" can be defined in different ways, from patient-reported outcomes to strict laboratory and physical examination criteria. Randomised trials examining various drug therapies often use these stricter definitions, showing that while remission is increasingly achievable, particularly with early and aggressive treatment, it often requires ongoing medication rather than being a permanent 'cure'.

Therefore, the evidence points to remission as a stable state of minimal or no disease activity, usually maintained through careful management, rather than a total eradication of the disease. This distinction is crucial for managing expectations and planning long-term care.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Stopping medication when feeling well: Your treatment is likely what's keeping you well; stopping without medical advice can cause flare-ups. *Always discuss medication changes with your doctor. Ignoring subtle symptoms: A slight stiffness or an odd ache could be an early warning sign, not just a 'bad day'. *Keep your symptom diary updated and discuss any new or worsening symptoms. Overdoing it on good days: Pushing too hard when you feel good can lead to a setback and increased fatigue. *Pace yourself and listen to your body, even in remission. Neglecting other health aspects: Diet, sleep, and stress management play a huge role in overall well-being with RA. *Focus on a holistic approach to your health, not just medication. Expecting a 'cure' instead of management: While remission is fantastic, it's usually ongoing management rather than a permanent fix. *Understand that sustained remission often means continued vigilance and treatment.

When to Speak to a Clinician

Even in sustained remission, it's important to be aware of signs that might indicate a change in your condition or require medical review. Persistent symptoms should always be checked out.

  • New, persistent joint pain or swelling: Especially if it lasts for more than a few days, or affects joints previously unaffected.
  • Unexplained fever or generally feeling unwell (malaise): These can sometimes indicate a flare or an infection.
  • Significant increase in fatigue: If your energy levels suddenly plummet and rest doesn't help.
  • Rapid loss of function in a joint: If you find you suddenly can't move a joint as you usually could.
  • Side effects from medication: Any new or worsening side effects from your prescribed drugs should always be discussed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I reduce my medication once I'm in sustained remission?

Sometimes, yes, but this must be done very carefully and under the guidance of your rheumatologist. Reducing medication needs to be a shared decision, considering your individual circumstances and risk of flare.

How is 'sustained remission' actually measured?

It's measured using a combination of factors, including your own report of symptoms (like how much pain or stiffness you have), your doctor's examination of your joints, and blood tests to check for inflammation markers. This data is often fed into a specific scoring system.

Does being in remission mean I can stop exercising?

No, regular exercise remains very important. It helps maintain joint flexibility, muscle strength, and overall well-being, even when you're feeling good. Your specialist or a physiotherapist can advise on suitable activities.

Practical next steps for What Sustained Remission Means in RA

If you came here about What Sustained Remission Means in RA, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

article.direct_answer: Sustained remission in rheumatoid arthritis means stable minimal or no disease activity, not a cure. The article says it is a key treatment goal, often maintained through ongoing medication, monitoring, gentle regular movement and lifestyle support. It advises personalised clinician guidance, symptom tracking, pacing activity, and prompt review for swelling, fever, rapid function loss or medication side effects.

faqs.q: Can I reduce my medication once I'm in sustained remission?
faqs.a: Sometimes, yes, but this must be done very carefully and under the guidance of your rheumatologist. Reducing medication needs to be a shared decision, considering your individual circumstances and risk of flare.

faqs.q: How is 'sustained remission' actually measured?
faqs.a: It's measured using a combination of factors, including your own report of symptoms (like how much pain or stiffness you have), your doctor's examination of your joints, and blood tests to check for inflammation markers. This data is often fed into a specific scoring system.

faqs.q: Does being in remission mean I can stop exercising?
faqs.a: No, regular exercise remains very important. It helps maintain joint flexibility, muscle strength, and overall well-being, even when you're feeling good. Your specialist or a physiotherapist can advise on suitable activities.

In Wales, clinicians may talk about frailty as a syndrome. You may simply feel that arthritis with frailty has stolen bounce from ordinary home tasks. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with using wheels so you still get to the park, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in Wales.

The overlap: pain in several joints and a frailer body

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Pain in several joints can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual arthritis with frailty.

Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis. Only some also live with frailty. The practical question is not the label. It is whether using wheels so you still get to the park is shrinking your home life — and what you can change this week without pretending pain is imaginary.

What this can look like in a home

In a home, using wheels so you still get to the park is rarely one dramatic collapse. It is usually a stack of small avoidances. People with arthritis with frailty already know boom-and-bust. Frailty adds a longer payback: a quiet weekend can cost the following Thursday.

  • A hospital or infection week that ends with clothes feeling looser and stairs feeling taller.
  • A flare of arthritis with frailty that lasts, then a slower baseline even when the flare eases.
  • Shorter outdoor range, then shorter indoor range, then a home that has quietly rearranged itself around the chair.
  • Night toilet trips, poor lighting and stiff several joints stacking into a falls risk that nobody named.
  • Transfers that used to be boring — bed, chair, toilet, car — now need a pause, a push-up or a second person, especially when several joints are cold.

Who to talk to locally in Wales

Start with your GP practice and NHS Wales services via your GP and local health board. For urgent but non-emergency advice use NHS 111 Wales. For chest pain, suspected hip fracture, sudden new weakness, or a fall with a bang to the head on blood thinners, use 999.

In Wales, Dewis Cymru can help you browse local support. Rural travel, hills and limited buses matter as much as the joint diagnosis. Ask whether a community hospital, pharmacy service or home visit can cut the journey.

Self-management that respects arthritis with frailty

  • Book eye, foot and hearing checks as frailty care, not vanity. Arthritis with frailty already asks a lot of balance.
  • If stairs are the bottleneck, get an occupational therapy conversation on the list while you temporarily live downstairs — drifting is how a camp-bed becomes a lifestyle.
  • If cooking is the barrier, use tinned fish, eggs, yoghurt, beans or leftover protein foods rather than skipping meals. Muscle needs raw material as well as movement.
  • Ask a pharmacist to look at the whole list if dizziness, constipation or night sedation have arrived with the pain tablets. Do not add a new painkiller just in case.
  • If you live in a home, tell one other person the plan for a fall: who to call, where the spare key sits, whether you wear a pendant you can actually press.
  • Put the items you use at dawn — tablets, glasses, walking aid, phone — where you can reach them without a stretch that wrenches several joints.

Lifestyle changes that are really clinical care

Red flags — do not wait this out

  • Unplanned weight loss, repeated falls, or using wheels so you still get to the park that is clearly worsening week by week — book the GP and say you are worried about frailty as well as several joints.
  • Sudden confusion, new incontinence, or a crash in mobility over hours to days — think infection or delirium, not only arthritis.
  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.
  • A hot, very swollen joint with fever, or feeling systemically unwell — seek urgent clinical advice. A joint infection is an emergency.
  • A knock to the head, especially if you take blood thinners — do not sleep it off as a plan.

Can frailty improve if I still have pain in several joints?

Sometimes the frailty part can shift even if arthritis with frailty remains. Strength, protein, reviewing dizzy medicines, treating a flare, and practising transfers can return reserve. Improvement is not guaranteed and it is rarely dramatic, but frailer this month is not always a one-way door. Work with clinicians rather than copying an online challenge.

Do I need a geriatrician as well as a rheumatologist?

Not always. Many people are supported by GP, community physio and, where it exists, a frailty team. If medicines are stacking, falls are repeating, or memory and continence are changing alongside arthritis with frailty, ask whether a comprehensive older-person assessment would help.

What should a carer do in the home without taking over?

Stand nearby for the risky bit, set the environment up (chair height, shoes, light), and leave the bits the person can still do. Taking over every transfer trains both of you into a hoist-by-default life. If moving and handling is already unsafe, stop DIY lifting and ask for a proper care and OT review.

article.title: Why Exercise Makes Your Arthritis Medication Work Better
article.excerpt: Regular physical activity, including strength training, can make arthritis medication more effective by reducing pain, improving physical function.
article.content:
Quick answer: Regular physical activity, including strength training, can make arthritis medication more effective by reducing pain, improving physical function, and enhancing quality of life. This integrated approach, which combines medication with movement, is recommended in clinical guidelines. Exercise is thought to lower widespread inflammation, maintain healthy weight, strengthen muscles, and improve mood, all of which support treatment response.

Overview

Strength training improves drug efficacy by reducing systemic inflammation.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis editorial team using UK NICE guidance, NHS information and peer-reviewed sources. We aim to update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Systematic reviews looking at several individual studies consistently show that combining regular physical activity, especially strength training, with anti-arthritis medication can lead to better outcomes. These benefits include reduced pain, improved physical function, and a better quality of life compared to medication alone. Clinical guidelines from leading UK health bodies strongly recommend this integrated approach, highlighting that movement is a key component of effective arthritis management.

The exact way exercise helps medication work better isn't fully understood, but it's thought to be partly due to its ability to lower widespread inflammation in the body. Exercise also helps maintain healthy body weight, strengthens muscles around joints, and improves mood, all of which contribute to how well you respond to treatment.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Waiting for full pain relief before moving: Gentle movement can actually help reduce pain over time.
  • Only doing high-impact activities: Focus on low-impact options that protect your joints.
  • Overdoing it on good days: Stick to a consistent level of activity to avoid flare-ups.
  • Ignoring professional guidance: Your healthcare team can tailor advice to your specific condition and needs.
  • Comparing your progress to others: Everyone's journey with arthritis is unique; focus on your own improvements.

When to Speak to a Clinician

While movement is beneficial, there are times when you should always seek advice from your GP, physiotherapist, or rheumatologist. This is especially important if you notice new symptoms or a significant change in your condition.

  • Sudden, severe joint pain or swelling that doesn't settle with rest.
  • Fever, chills, or generally feeling unwell alongside joint symptoms.
  • New numbness, tingling, or weakness in a limb.
  • Rapid loss of movement or function in a joint.
  • Any symptoms that worry you or interfere with your daily life.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does gentle movement count, or do I need to do intense workouts?

Yes, gentle movement absolutely counts! Activities like walking, swimming, or tai chi can be very effective. The key is consistency and finding activities you enjoy that don't aggravate your joints. Intense workouts are generally not recommended for most people with arthritis.

How soon will I notice a difference in how my medication works?

It can take time to notice the full benefits of combining exercise with your medication. Most people find improvements gradually over several weeks or months. Keeping a symptom diary can help you track these changes and discuss them with your healthcare team.

Can exercise replace my arthritis medication entirely?

For most types of arthritis, exercise is a complementary treatment, not a replacement for medication. Your medicines work in specific ways to manage the underlying disease. Exercise helps reduce symptoms, improve function, and support your overall health alongside your prescribed treatment plan.

Practical next steps for Why Exercise Makes Your Arthritis Medication Work Better

If you came here about Why Exercise Makes Your Arthritis Medication Work Better, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your primary care network about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Building a joint-friendly routine

Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery.

Benefits conversations

Personal Independence Payment (PIP) looks at how your condition affects daily living and mobility, not the diagnosis name alone. Keep a short diary of bad days, help you need with dressing or cooking, and walking limits. Welfare rights advisers at local councils or charities can check forms before you submit them.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

Quick questions about Exercise Makes Your Arthritis

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

In a home, meals when the person who cooked is gone is rarely one dramatic collapse. It is usually a stack of small avoidances. People with arthritis with frailty already know boom-and-bust. Frailty adds a longer payback: a quiet weekend can cost the following Thursday.

  • Carers doing the last steps of a task to be kind, which removes the last practice the muscles were getting.

A frailty-aware plan for hands

None of this is a gym challenge. The aim is to keep hands moving, keep protein in the day, and keep meals when the person who cooked is gone from becoming the only story in the home. If a physiotherapist, occupational therapist or frailty team has already given you a plan, follow that ahead of a webpage.

  • Keep a sit-to-stand practice at the height you actually use. A higher chair is not cheating if it lets hands work without a panic haul.
  • Carers: help the last 20 percent of a task, not the first 80, unless pain or safety says otherwise. Practice is treatment for frailty.
  • Ask a pharmacist to look at the whole list if dizziness, constipation or night sedation have arrived with the pain tablets. Do not add a new painkiller just in case.
  • Set an indoor walking loop with places to pause. Painful hands prefer several short bouts to one heroic corridor.
  • In Northern Ireland, ask your local Health and Social Care Trust about equipment and care options. Descriptions of grants and benefits here are not predictions of an award.

No. For osteoarthritis, NICE puts exercise, weight management where relevant, and topical options at the centre. Tablets may help some people some of the time, but in frail adults they need a hard look at stomach, kidneys, heart, constipation and falls. Never share someone else's medicines.

Tablets may help some people some of the time, but in frail adults they need a hard look at stomach, kidneys, heart, constipation and falls. Never share someone else's medicines.

faqs.q: Do I need a geriatrician as well as a rheumatologist?
faqs.a: Not always. Many people are supported by GP, community physio and, where it exists, a frailty team. If medicines are stacking, falls are repeating, or memory and continence are changing alongside arthritis with frailty, ask whether a comprehensive older-person assessment would help.

article.title: Cold home and arthritis: keeping warm and keeping moving (UK)
article.excerpt: Keep warm at home with arthritis without sitting still all day: rooms to heat, a five-minute warm-up, safer moving, and UK heating help to check.
article.content:
Quick answer: A cold home can make stiff joints feel worse and is risky if you are older or living with frailty. Heat the rooms you use, ideally to at least 18°C as the NHS suggests, wear layers, and get up and move for a few minutes every hour rather than staying wrapped up in one chair. Check GOV.UK for heating help and speak to your energy supplier if you are struggling.

When money is tight and joints are sore, it is tempting to heat one room, sit under a blanket and stay put. That keeps you a bit warmer for now, but long spells of sitting stiffen joints and weaken the muscles you need to get up, walk and stay independent. This guide is about staying warm and staying moving at home this winter, and where to get help with heating costs.

Why a cold home matters with arthritis

  • Many people say cold makes their joints stiffer and more painful. Research on why is mixed, but your experience is real
  • The NHS says cold homes raise health risks, especially for older people and people with long-term conditions
  • Cold, stiff muscles make it harder to get out of a chair, which can mean more sitting and a higher risk of falls

Keep warm without sitting still all day

  • Heat the rooms you use most, ideally to at least 18°C if you can. Keep the bedroom warm overnight and close curtains at dusk
  • Layer up: several thin layers, thermal socks, gloves and a hat trap more heat than one thick jumper
  • Move every hour: during TV adverts or every hour, stand up, march on the spot, or walk to the kitchen and back. A few minutes is enough to warm muscles and ease stiffness
  • Warm up stiff joints first: a warm shower, a wheat bag or a hot water bottle wrapped in a cover can ease morning stiffness. Do not sleep on a hot water bottle or electric blanket, and take care if your skin is thin or has poor feeling
  • Eat and drink warm: regular meals and hot drinks help keep your body warm and your energy up

A five-minute warm-up you can do at home

Do this once or twice a day, holding a sturdy chair or worktop for balance:

  1. March on the spot for one minute
  2. Sit to stand from a firm chair, five to ten times, using your hands if you need to
  3. Circle your shoulders and gently open and close your hands
  4. Rise up on your toes and back down, ten times
  5. Slowly bend and straighten each knee while sitting

Stay within comfort and scale back rather than stop on bad days. Our exercise hub and staying active in winter guide have more routines, and the knee and hip exercise guides help if those joints are the problem.

Make moving around the house safer

  • Keep paths clear and rooms well lit, with a night light on the way to the toilet
  • Wear well-fitting slippers with a back and a grippy sole
  • Raise a low chair or bed if getting up is a struggle; an occupational therapist can advise on equipment
  • Our falls prevention guide and joint protection guide have more ideas

Help with heating costs

Check GOV.UK for the Winter Fuel Payment, Cold Weather Payment and Warm Home Discount. Rules differ between England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, so check the version for where you live. If you are struggling to pay, contact your energy supplier early to ask about payment plans and support.

Extra income can make heating affordable. If arthritis affects daily living, see our Benefits and PIP hub, and if you are over State Pension age, our Attendance Allowance guide. Carers may be able to get Carer's Allowance.

When to get help

  • Call 999 if someone is very cold and confused, drowsy, or has slurred speech or slow breathing. These can be signs of hypothermia
  • Get urgent advice if a joint becomes hot, red and swollen, especially with fever
  • See your GP if getting up from a chair or walking indoors is getting harder, or you have fallen. A physiotherapy or frailty review can help

Frequently asked questions

Is it better to rest stiff joints in the cold?

Short rests are fine, but long spells of sitting usually make stiffness worse. Little and often movement is the aim.

Can a carer help without taking over?

Yes. Set up the room, stay nearby for the risky part of a task and leave the parts the person can still do. A carer's assessment can help with support.

See also our cold weather and arthritis guide, vitamin D in winter and pain relief guide.

Everyone's situation is different, so always follow the advice of your own GP, pharmacist or rheumatology team. If you feel very unwell, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent advice, contact NHS 111.

article.title: Working with Arthritis – Your UK Employment Rights
article.excerpt: Know your employment rights when working with arthritis in the UK. Guide to reasonable adjustments, Equality Act protection, Access to Work scheme.
article.content:
Arthritis is recognised as a disability under the Equality Act 2010 if it has a substantial and long-term effect on your ability to carry out normal day-to-day activities. This means you have legal protections at work.

Quick answer: If your arthritis significantly affects daily activities, it's considered a disability under the Equality Act 2010. This protects you from discrimination and harassment at work. Your employer must make reasonable adjustments, such as flexible hours or ergonomic equipment. The Access to Work scheme can also fund equipment and support. You are entitled to Statutory Sick Pay if you need time off.

Your Rights Under the Equality Act 2010

  • Protection from discrimination — your employer cannot treat you less favourably because of arthritis
  • Right to reasonable adjustments — your employer must make changes to remove disadvantages you face
  • Protection from harassment — colleagues cannot bully or mock you because of your condition
  • Protection from victimisation — you cannot be penalised for raising concerns about discrimination

Reasonable Adjustments

Your employer is legally required to make "reasonable adjustments" to help you do your job. Examples include:

  • Flexible working hours — starting later to manage morning stiffness
  • Ergonomic equipment — adjustable desk, ergonomic keyboard, supportive chair
  • Modified duties — avoiding heavy lifting or prolonged standing
  • Working from home — on flare days or regularly
  • Extra breaks — to stretch, move, or manage medication
  • Accessible parking — closer to the workplace entrance
  • Phased return — after illness or surgery

Access to Work Scheme

The government's Access to Work scheme can provide:

  • Funding for specialist equipment or workplace adaptations
  • Support worker costs
  • Help with travel costs if you can't use public transport
  • Mental health support

Apply at gov.uk/access-to-work. The scheme is available to employed and self-employed people.

Talking to Your Employer

  • You don't have to disclose your condition at interview, but it helps to tell your employer once employed so they can make adjustments
  • Ask for an occupational health referral — many employers provide this
  • Put requests for adjustments in writing
  • Keep records of any meetings about your condition

Sick Leave and SSP

If you need time off due to arthritis:

  • You're entitled to Statutory Sick Pay (SSP) — currently £109.40 per week for up to 28 weeks
  • Many employers offer enhanced sick pay beyond SSP
  • If you cannot return to work, you may qualify for Employment and Support Allowance (ESA)

Getting Help

  • ACAS — free workplace advice on 0300 123 1100
  • Citizens Advice — help with employment disputes
  • Disability Rights UK — factsheets on employment and arthritis

Knowing your rights empowers you to have productive conversations with your employer. Most employers want to support you — they just need to understand what you need.

Practical next steps for Working with Arthritis – Your UK Employment Rights

If you came here about Working with Arthritis – Your UK Employment Rights, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Benefits conversations

Personal Independence Payment (PIP) looks at how your condition affects daily living and mobility, not the diagnosis name alone. Keep a short diary of bad days, help you need with dressing or cooking, and walking limits. Welfare rights advisers at local councils or charities can check forms before you submit them.

Benefits conversations

Personal Independence Payment (PIP) looks at how your condition affects daily living and mobility, not the diagnosis name alone. Keep a short diary of bad days, help you need with dressing or cooking, and walking limits. Welfare rights advisers at local councils or charities can check forms before you submit them.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

Quick questions about Working with Arthritis Your

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

Keep expectations kind while you work on working with arthritis – your uk employment rights. Arthritis symptoms fluctuate; a quieter week does not mean you imagined earlier pain, and a flare does not mean every helpful habit has failed. Adjust one variable at a time so you can see what truly helps.

article.title: Workplace Adjustment Letter Templates for Arthritis: Copy-and-Edit Letters and Plans (UK)
article.excerpt: Real, on-page templates you can copy and edit: a reasonable adjustments request, a statutory flexible working request with everything GOV.UK says it must include, a follow-up letter, an occupational health referral request, a request for reasons after a refusal, a phased return plan, a flare plan and an adjustments record.
article.content:
Quick answer: To ask for workplace adjustments for arthritis, write a short letter or email saying you have arthritis, explaining how it affects specific tasks, listing the changes you are asking for and how they would help, and asking for a meeting and a written reply. Keep a copy. For a change to hours, times, days or place of work, you can also make a statutory flexible working request.

Checked on 10 October 2026 against GOV.UK: Reasonable adjustments and GOV.UK: Flexible working. These templates are general information, not legal advice. Edit them to fit your situation.

Asking for help at work can feel awkward, especially if you are worried about how your manager will react. A clear, polite letter takes the pressure off a face-to-face conversation, makes it easier for your employer to act, and gives you a record. This page contains real templates you can copy into an email or document and edit. Replace everything in [square brackets].

Before you write: three things to know

  • Your employer has a legal duty. GOV.UK says employers must make reasonable adjustments so that workers with disabilities or health conditions are not substantially disadvantaged when doing their jobs. In England, Scotland and Wales this comes from the Equality Act 2010; in Northern Ireland, from the Disability Discrimination Act 1995. GOV.UK even gives the example of a special keyboard for someone with arthritis.
  • You may count as disabled if your arthritis has a substantial and long-term effect on your normal daily activities. Long-term usually means 12 months or more. You do not have to use the word "disabled" in your letter, but it can help to say you are asking for reasonable adjustments.
  • Be specific. "My hands are painful" is easy to overlook. "Typing for more than 20 minutes causes severe wrist pain, so I am asking for voice recognition software" is easy to act on.

If you have not yet worked out which tasks are hardest, start with Step 2 of our working with arthritis toolkit.

Template 1: Request for reasonable adjustments

Subject: Request for reasonable adjustments

Dear [manager's name],

I am writing to ask for some reasonable adjustments at work. I have [type of arthritis, for example rheumatoid arthritis / osteoarthritis of the knees], which I have had since [year]. It affects me in the following ways at work:

  • [for example: morning stiffness that lasts about [time], which makes early starts very difficult]
  • [for example: pain in my hands and wrists when typing for long periods]
  • [for example: pain when standing for more than [time]]

I would like to ask for the following adjustments:

  1. [adjustment, for example a start time of 10am on up to [number] days a week] – this would help because [reason].
  2. [adjustment, for example an ergonomic keyboard and vertical mouse] – this would help because [reason].
  3. [adjustment, for example a perching stool at my workstation] – this would help because [reason].

[Optional: My [GP / physiotherapist / occupational therapist / rheumatology team] has suggested [advice]. I am happy to be referred to occupational health if that would help.]

I would welcome a meeting to discuss this. Could you please let me know in writing by [date, for example two weeks from now] whether these adjustments can be made, or suggest alternatives? I would also like to agree a date to review how they are working.

Thank you for your support.

Yours sincerely,
[your name]
[job title, team]
[date]

Template 2: Statutory flexible working request

GOV.UK says all employees can make a flexible working request from their first day in a job, and can make 2 applications in any 12-month period. It says the request must include the date, a statement that it is a statutory request, details of how you want to work flexibly and when you want to start, and whether and when you have made a previous application. This template includes all of those. Your employer may have its own form; Acas also has a free template.

Subject: Statutory request for flexible working

Dear [manager's name],

Date of request: [date]

This is a statutory request for flexible working.

I would like to change my working pattern as follows: [describe the change, for example: to work from home on Mondays and Fridays / to start at 10am and finish at 6pm / to reduce my hours from 37.5 to 30 a week over four days].

I would like this change to start on [date].

[Choose one:] I have not made a previous application for flexible working. / I made a previous application on [date].

[Optional but helpful:] I am asking for this change because I have arthritis, and [explain briefly how the change would help, for example: travelling at peak times when my joints are stiffest causes significant pain]. I would also like this to be considered as a reasonable adjustment. I have thought about how this could work for the team: [for example, how cover, meetings or customer contact would be handled].

I look forward to discussing this with you.

Yours sincerely,
[your name]

GOV.UK says your employer must deal with the request in a reasonable manner, discuss it with you before refusing, and make a decision within 2 months unless you agree to longer. If they refuse, they must give the business reasons.

Template 3: Follow-up if you have not heard back

Subject: Follow-up: request for reasonable adjustments sent on [date]

Dear [name],

On [date] I asked for reasonable adjustments because of my arthritis (copy attached). I have not yet had a response. My symptoms are continuing to affect my work, particularly [example].

Could you please let me know by [date] when we can meet to discuss this, or who else I should contact?

Thank you,
[your name]

Template 4: Request for an occupational health referral

Subject: Request for occupational health referral

Dear [name],

I would like to ask for a referral to occupational health. I have [type of arthritis], and I would find it helpful to have independent advice on adjustments that could help me do my job well, particularly with [tasks].

Please let me know what information you need from me.

Kind regards,
[your name]

Template 5: Asking for reasons after a refusal

Subject: Response to my adjustment request

Dear [name],

Thank you for your reply dated [date] about my request for [adjustment]. I understand that you are not able to agree to this. So that I can understand the decision, please could you explain in writing:

  • the reasons the adjustment is not considered reasonable
  • whether any alternatives have been considered
  • whether Access to Work or occupational health advice has been sought

I would like to suggest the following alternative: [alternative]. I would be grateful for a meeting to discuss this further.

Yours sincerely,
[your name]

If you still think the refusal is unfair, get advice. GOV.UK says that you usually have to make an employment tribunal claim within 6 months of the problem, and you must contact Acas first. Northern Ireland has a different process.

Template 6: Phased return to work plan

A fit note can say you may be fit for work with a phased return. Use this table with your manager to agree the details.

WeekHours and daysDutiesAdjustments in placeCheck-in
1[e.g. 3 half days][e.g. desk-based tasks only][e.g. later start][date]
2
3
4

Agree in advance what happens if a week is too much: for example, staying at the same level for another week rather than stopping.

Template 7: Flare plan

My arthritis flare plan (agreed with [manager] on [date], review on [date])

  • Early signs of a flare for me: [e.g. more swelling in my hands, extreme tiredness]
  • How I will let you know: [e.g. text or phone call to [name] before [time]]
  • What I can usually still do: [e.g. work from home, shorter hours, lighter tasks]
  • Tasks that can be paused or covered: [list]
  • Who covers urgent work: [name]
  • How we will plan my return to full duties: [e.g. a short call after the flare]
  • How flare absence will be recorded: [e.g. as disability-related absence]

Template 8: Adjustments record

Some employers call this a reasonable adjustments passport. It saves you explaining everything again if you get a new manager.

AdjustmentWhy it helpsDate agreedWho arranges itReview date
[e.g. sit-stand desk][e.g. reduces back and hip pain]
[e.g. time off for rheumatology appointments]

Template 9: Time off for medical appointments

Arthritis often means regular appointments: rheumatology reviews, blood tests, physiotherapy or infusions. Agreeing an approach in advance avoids arguments each time.

Subject: Time off for arthritis appointments

Dear [name],

As part of the treatment for my arthritis, I need regular medical appointments. Over the next [period], I expect to need about [number] appointments, for example [blood tests every [number] weeks, a rheumatology review every [number] months]. Most last around [time], including travel.

I would like to agree how this time off will be handled, for example [paid time off / making up the time / using flexible start and finish times], and I am asking for this as a reasonable adjustment. Where I can, I will book appointments at the start or end of the day and give you as much notice as possible.

Kind regards,
[your name]

A short script for the conversation

If you are meeting your manager, it can help to have a few sentences ready:

  1. "I wanted to talk to you about my arthritis and how it affects my work."
  2. "On most days I manage well, but [task] is difficult because [effect], and on bad days [effect]."
  3. "These are the changes I think would make the biggest difference: [one, two, three]."
  4. "I am happy to see occupational health, and Access to Work may be able to help with some costs."
  5. "Could we agree what happens next, and a date to review it?"

Afterwards, send a short email summarising what was agreed.

Tips for getting a good outcome

  • Send it to the right person, usually your line manager, copying HR if that is your workplace's process.
  • Keep copies of everything, and note dates of conversations.
  • Offer solutions. Managers find it easier to say yes when you have thought about how it would work.
  • Mention Access to Work for equipment or support beyond what your employer must provide. See our Access to Work guide.
  • Ask for a review date so adjustments can change if your arthritis does.
  • Use your fit note. If you are off sick, ask the person writing your fit note to suggest changes. See our fit notes guide.

Free, independent advice

Acas gives free advice on workplace rights in England, Scotland and Wales, and the Equality Advisory and Support Service can help with discrimination questions. In Northern Ireland, contact the Labour Relations Agency or the Equality Commission for Northern Ireland. Citizens Advice, Scope, Disability Rights UK and trade unions can also help. We are not connected to these organisations. For more on the law itself, see your disability rights in the UK.

When to get medical help

If work is making your arthritis worse, speak to your GP, physiotherapist or rheumatology team. They can review your treatment and may suggest changes on a fit note. Get same-day advice from your GP or NHS 111 if a joint suddenly becomes hot, swollen and very painful, especially with fever. If stress at work is affecting your mental health, talk to your GP.

Frequently asked questions

Do I have to put my request for adjustments in writing?

No, you can ask in conversation. But writing it down makes it clearer, gives your employer something to act on, and gives you a record.

Do I need a letter from my doctor?

Not usually, but supporting advice from your GP, physiotherapist, occupational therapist or occupational health can help your employer understand what you need.

What is the difference between a flexible working request and a reasonable adjustment?

Any employee can make a statutory flexible working request. A reasonable adjustment is a legal duty that applies when you are disabled and the change would reduce a disadvantage caused by your condition. You can ask for a change in both ways at once.

How many flexible working requests can I make?

GOV.UK says employees can make 2 applications in any 12-month period.

How long does my employer have to reply?

For a statutory flexible working request, GOV.UK says the decision must be made within 2 months unless you agree to longer. There is no fixed deadline for adjustment requests, so ask for a reply by a specific date.

What if my employer refuses?

Ask for the reasons in writing, suggest alternatives, and get free advice from Acas or the Labour Relations Agency in Northern Ireland.

article.direct_answer: To ask for workplace adjustments for arthritis, write a short letter or email saying you have arthritis, explaining how it affects specific tasks, listing the changes you are asking for and how they would help, and asking for a meeting and a written reply. Keep a copy. For a change to hours, times, days or place of work, you can also make a statutory flexible working request.

faqs.q: Do I have to put my request for adjustments in writing?
faqs.a: No, you can ask in conversation. But writing it down makes it clearer, gives your employer something to act on, and gives you a record.

faqs.q: Do I need a letter from my doctor?
faqs.a: Not usually, but supporting advice from your GP, physiotherapist, occupational therapist or occupational health can help your employer understand what you need.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a flexible working request and a reasonable adjustment?
faqs.a: Any employee can make a statutory flexible working request. A reasonable adjustment is a legal duty that applies when you are disabled and the change would reduce a disadvantage caused by your condition. You can ask for a change in both ways at once.

faqs.q: How many flexible working requests can I make?
faqs.a: GOV.UK says employees can make 2 applications in any 12-month period.

faqs.q: How long does my employer have to reply?
faqs.a: For a statutory flexible working request, GOV.UK says the decision must be made within 2 months unless you agree to longer. There is no fixed deadline for adjustment requests, so ask for a reply by a specific date.

faqs.q: What if my employer refuses?
faqs.a: Ask for the reasons in writing, suggest alternatives, and get free advice from Acas or the Labour Relations Agency in Northern Ireland.

Painful shoulders and hands plus slower recovery is a common UK picture in later life. This page explains dressings when shoulders will not allow it if you live with arthritis with frailty, without pretending rest is always safer. Use it alongside your GP, not instead of them.

Quick answer: Painful shoulders and hands plus slower recovery is a common UK picture in later life. This page explains dressings when shoulders will not allow it if you live with arthritis with frailty, without pretending rest is always safer. Use it alongside your GP, not instead of them.

It might be the kettle, the bathroom, the car door or the clinic corridor — a home task that used to be automatic now asks more of shoulders and hands than they can give on a stiff morning. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with dressings when shoulders will not allow it, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in England.

Not 'just getting old': dressings when shoulders will not allow it

Arthritis is about joints, tendons and the way pain changes movement. Frailty is about the whole system — muscle, stamina, appetite, mood, medicines and how quickly you bounce back after a setback. Arthritis with frailty sits in the middle because sore shoulders and hands quietly train you to sit more, shorten your stride and skip the movements that keep muscle.

NICE is clear that exercise is core care for osteoarthritis, not an optional extra after tablets. That still holds if you are becoming frailer, but the dose must respect today's shoulders and hands and today's energy. Rest has a place in a flare; rest as a lifestyle is how deconditioning joins the diagnosis.

Small, repeatable steps — not a reinvention

  • Ask a pharmacist to look at the whole list if dizziness, constipation or night sedation have arrived with the pain tablets. Do not add a new painkiller just in case.
  • Write three daily anchors: a meal, a movement, a conversation. Frailty grows in unstructured days.
  • Book eye, foot and hearing checks as frailty care, not vanity. Arthritis with frailty already asks a lot of balance.
  • If you live in a home, tell one other person the plan for a fall: who to call, where the spare key sits, whether you wear a pendant you can actually press.
  • If stairs are the bottleneck, get an occupational therapy conversation on the list while you temporarily live downstairs — drifting is how a camp-bed becomes a lifestyle.
  • Treat a walking aid as joint protection and falls kit, not as a verdict. Wrist-friendly handles matter if shoulders and hands include hands.

A England day with arthritis with frailty and less reserve

  • A flare of arthritis with frailty that lasts, then a slower baseline even when the flare eases.
  • Shorter outdoor range, then shorter indoor range, then a home that has quietly rearranged itself around the chair.
  • Skipping meals or drinks because getting to the kitchen with sore shoulders and hands feels like a project.

The wider health picture around arthritis with frailty

GP, 111 or 999?

This is not personal medical advice. When shoulders and hands and frailty overlap, wait until Monday is sometimes right and sometimes dangerous. If you are unsure, NHS 111 can help you choose. Living With Arthritis cannot triage you.

  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.
  • Unplanned weight loss, repeated falls, or dressings when shoulders will not allow it that is clearly worsening week by week — book the GP and say you are worried about frailty as well as shoulders and hands.
  • Sudden confusion, new incontinence, or a crash in mobility over hours to days — think infection or delirium, not only arthritis.
  • Chest pain, trouble breathing, or signs of a stroke — 999, not a wait for the arthritis with frailty nurse.
  • A knock to the head, especially if you take blood thinners — do not sleep it off as a plan.

Help in England if arthritis and frailty overlap

Start with your GP practice and NHS England services via your GP. For urgent but non-emergency advice use NHS 111. For chest pain, suspected hip fracture, sudden new weakness, or a fall with a bang to the head on blood thinners, use 999.

In England, some areas have community frailty or neighbourhood teams. Your GP or a social prescriber can explain what exists locally. Pathways differ by integrated care board, so do not assume a named clinic in the next town is available to you.

Ask about community physiotherapy, occupational therapy, reablement after hospital, podiatry, pharmacy reviews and your local council's adult social care team (the Care Act). Names of teams change. The functions do not: get you moving, get you equipped, get the medicines tidier, get a human being through the door if you cannot get out.

Age UK and local advice agencies can help with forms. The Charity Commission listing for Living With Arthritis (1218461) is public if you want to check who we are. We are independent of Arthritis UK.

Should I stop exercising during dressings when shoulders will not allow it?

Complete rest for more than a short flare period usually makes shoulders and hands and muscle worse. Keep a smaller version: seated strength, indoor loops, or the two sit-to-stands you can still do. If exercise causes pain that spirals or a joint that will not settle, get clinical advice.

Is a walking aid giving in if I have arthritis with frailty?

No. An aid that matches your shoulders and hands can protect joints, reduce fear and keep you walking far enough to keep muscle. A poorly fitted stick that hurts a wrist is the problem, not the concept. Ask physiotherapy or occupational therapy to look at height and grip.

How do I tell an arthritis flare from a frailty slide?

A flare of arthritis with frailty is usually more joint pain, stiffness or swelling in a known pattern. A frailty slide is broader: weaker recovery, smaller meals, more time in the chair, maybe confusion or falls. They can happen together. If the whole person is changing, do not only increase pain gel.
